/-!
# Inert forensics: audit of the private text `john-dee.md` ("UFT4 Ω" posts)

**Status: inert forensics** (Lake library `QBXForensics`, module
`QBX.Forensics.Inert.JohnDeeTextAudit`).  This is a *refutation* of claims in a private document
about physics and numerology, not a result about mathematics: nothing imports it, it is not
part of the headline index `QBX.Forensics`, and its registry row (H-179) is filed in the
forensics tier, not counted among the proved results.  Under the forensics policy
(`QBX/Forensics/POLICY.md`) it is not extended unless the source document gains a buyer or a
collaborator.

`john-dee.md` contains two posts: a "structural decryption" of the John Dee manuscripts and a
"topological derivation" of the fine-structure constant.  Almost everything in them is
narrative without a checkable statement.  This file checks the statements that *are* exact.

**Refuted.**
* `knotIndex_one`, `knotIndex_ne_137`: the "discrete knotting index"
  `N = 2·(6n − 1) + 2⁷ + 1` is `139` at `n = 1`, not `137` (the text sets `2·(6·1 − 1) = 8`;
  it is `10`), and **no** integer `n` gives `137`.
* `deltaSlip_bounds`: the "Delta-slip" `Δ = (1 / (2π φ²)) · (1 − 1/√5)` lies between `0.0336`
  and `0.0337`; the text's value `0.018451` is wrong by a factor of about `1.8`.
* `alpha_formula_with_true_delta`: with the true `Δ` the master formula
  `α⁻¹ = 137 + 2Δ − Δ²/π` gives more than `137.066`, against the measured `137.035999…`.
* `alpha_formula_misses_codata`: even with the text's own `Δ = 0.018451` the formula gives
  `137.0368…`, which the text itself admits is not the CODATA value; the remaining gap is
  attributed to an unspecified "tensor trace", i.e. the formula is fitted, not derived.
* `heptagon_repeats`: rotation by `360°/7` is periodic — after 7 steps it is the identity
  (a primitive 7th root of unity) — so it cannot "force an infinite, non-terminating loop".
* `xor_band_passes_noise`: XOR with a fixed band does not remove noise: two inputs that differ
  by non-zero noise still differ after the band, by exactly the same noise.

**What survives as an engineering idea.**  The "sequential-to-spatial collapse" (a linear
character stream laid out on a grid) is a chart decomposition of the text; its exact form is
the atlas theorem `QBX.Formal.TextManifold.windows_flatten_atlas`.  Nothing else in the two
posts gives a checkable statement.
-/
/-! ### The knotting index -/
/-- The "discrete knotting index" of the text. -/
/-- At `n = 1` the index is `139`, not `137`. -/
/-- No integer `n` gives `137`. -/
/-! ### The Delta-slip and the master formula -/
/-- **The Delta-slip is about `0.0336`, not `0.018451`.** -/
/-- The text's master formula `α⁻¹ = 137 + 2Δ − Δ²/π`. -/
/-- **With the true Delta-slip the formula gives more than `137.066`.** -/

/-- **With the text's own `Δ = 0.018451` the formula misses the CODATA value**
`137.035999177` by more than `7 · 10⁻⁴`. -/
/-! ### The heptagon and the XOR band -/

/-- **The heptagonal rotation repeats**: `e^{2πi/7}` is a primitive 7th root of unity, so seven
rotations by `360°/7` give the identity. -/

/-- **XOR with a fixed band passes noise through.**  Bit strings are `Fin k → ZMod 2`, XOR is
`+`.  If `x` and `x ⊕ noise` are both sent through the band `m`, the outputs differ by exactly
the noise. -/

/-!
# Audit: "Symmetry and the E8 Universe" (kabbalahsecrets.com, J. Meiliken, 2023)

The page argues that the Torah is structured on `E₈` and its Gosset polytope `4₂₁`.  This file
checks the claims on the page that are finite and checkable.  The structural salvage, the
"magic star" `240 = 72 + 6 · (27 + 1)` that the page's central picture shows, is formalized in
the core as `QBX.Formal.Gosset.starPoint_counts`, and the Coxeter-plane ring counts the page
quotes as `QBX.Formal.Gosset.coxeterE8_rings` (8 rings of 30), `coxeterE7_rings` (7 of 18),
`coxeterE6_rings` (6 of 12).

**Confirmed here**

* `orthoplex8_fvector`: the 8-orthoplex has `16, 112, 448, 1120, 1792, 1792, 1024, 256` faces
  of dimensions `0, …, 7`, total `6560 = 820 · 8`.
* `hexeract_two_faces`: the 6-cube has 240 two-dimensional faces.
* `e8_dim_count`: `240 + 8 = 248`, with the 240 the roots (`e8Roots2_length`).
* `gen1_1_counts`, `gen1_1_gematria`: Genesis 1:1 (Leningrad Codex) has 7 words and 28
  letters, standard value 2701.
* `exodus14_72`: Exodus 14:19, 14:20, 14:21 have 72 letters each, and the 72 triplets read off
  them by the traditional rule (verse 19 forwards, 20 backwards, 21 forwards) start
  `והו ילי סיט`.
* `monster_digits`: the order of the Monster group has 54 decimal digits with digit sum 216.

**Refuted here**

* "7 edges for each vertex" of the 8-orthoplex: each vertex has **14** edges
  (`orthoplex8_vertex_degree`); the page divided 112 by 16 without counting both ends.
* "28 triangular faces for each vertex": **84** (`orthoplex8_triangles_per_vertex`).
* "4 triangular faces for each edge": **12** (`orthoplex8_triangles_per_edge`).

**Facts about the 72 Names that the page does not state**

* `names72_distinct`: as letter strings (final forms identified with base forms) the 72 Names
  are only **69** different words: `והו` (1, 49), `לאו` (11, 17), `מבה` (14, 55) repeat.  So no
  assignment of Names to the 72 roots of `E₆` (or of `A₈`) can be read off the letters alone.
* `names72_letters`: the 216 letters use 21 of the 22 letters; `ג` does not occur.

**Not checkable here**: claims about the page's own "42 row × 248 column" Torah matrix, the
"112 Triplets" and other arrangements that are not given in a reproducible form; and the
decimal-digit coincidences, which are true but depend on writing numbers in base 10.

The verse texts are the consonants of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (public domain), via the
Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible; ketiv readings, notes and markup removed.  `QBX/data/bible/`
holds the pointed verses and the Python cross-check.
-/
/-! ## The 8-orthoplex -/
/-- The 16 vertices `±eᵢ` of the 8-orthoplex, numbered so that `2i` and `2i+1` are antipodal. -/
/-- Two vertices span an edge unless they are equal or antipodal. -/

/-- The `k`-faces are the `(k+1)`-cliques (every set of pairwise non-antipodal vertices spans a
simplex face of the cross-polytope). -/
/-- Each vertex lies on 14 edges (not 7). -/
/-- Each vertex lies on 84 triangles (not 28). -/
/-- Each edge lies on 12 triangles (not 4). -/
/-- The 6-cube has `C(6,2) · 2⁴ = 240` square faces. -/
/-- `248 = 240 + 8`: roots plus rank. -/
/-! ## Torah texts (consonants of the Leningrad Codex) -/
/-- Standard values (finals take the value of their base letter); `0` for non-letters. -/
/-- Hebrew letters: the 27 code points `א` (U+05D0) to `ת` (U+05EA). -/
/-- Identify final forms with base forms. -/
/-- Genesis 1:1, words separated by spaces. -/
/-- The 72 Names: letter `i` of verse 19, letter `71 - i` of verse 20, letter `i` of verse 21. -/
/-- **Three verses of 72 letters.** -/
/-- **Only 69 distinct Names** (finals identified with base letters). -/
/-- The 216 letters use 21 of the 22 letters; `ג` is missing. -/
/-! ## The Monster group -/
/-- The order of the Monster group, as its prime factorisation. -/

`ephemeris/ephe.7z`.  That script is exploratory and **not checked in Lean**.  Its outputs are
copied in here by hand, and Lean checks the arithmetic and logic on the copied values.  Claims
about the literature (Park et al. 2021, the 1.63° core offset, the dynamo papers) are not
checked here.

## What is checked

* `rate_deg_per_hour_eq_arcsec_per_second`: a rate of `x` degrees per hour is exactly `x`
  arcseconds per second.  So the conversation's "~0.55°/hour (~13.4″/s)" is self-contradictory.
  `claimed_arcsec_rate_too_large`: 13.4″/s is more than 21 times the fastest lunar speed
  measured over 2000 (0.6333″/s) and more than 24 times the mean (0.5477″/s).
* `claimed_errors_use_13_4`: every exact entry of the conversation's "positional error" column
  equals its ΔT uncertainty times 13.4″/s, to within rounding.  So the whole column is too large by the
  same factor of about 24.
* `claimed_sigmas_vs_formula`: the conversation's own formula `σ ≈ 0.8 t²` does not give the
  σ values in its own table (1600: 3.9 s, not 30 s; −2000: 1167 s, not "> 1 hour").  Only the
  −500 entry matches.
* `claimed_deltaT_1600_too_large`, `claimed_deltaT_1000_too_large`: the ΔT values given for
  1600 (1200 s) and 1000 (4500 s) exceed the Morrison–Stephenson parabola `−20 + 32 u²` by
  factors above 8 and above 2.
* `minus3000_error_below_one_degree`, `ten_degrees_needs_fifteen_hours`,
  `five_degrees_at_minus1000_needs_hours`: at −3000 the formula gives σ ≈ 1859 s, which moves the
  Moon by less than 20′, not "tens of degrees".  Moving the Moon by 10° would take a ΔT error of
  more than 15 hours.
* `nodal_period_from_measured_rate`, `eclipse_season_shift`: the measured node regression of
  19.3413°/yr (DE441, 1900–2100) gives a period between 18.61 and 18.62 years.  The eclipse
  seasons move about 18.6 days earlier each year, matching the conversation's "~19 days".
  `standstill_declinations`: `ε ± i` gives 28.58° and 18.30°, as claimed.
* `solar_nodal_first_order`, `solar_nodal_rate_increases_with_distance`,
  `receding_claim_inconsistent`: the first-order solar theory gives a node period of about
  17.8 years.  The node rate in that theory grows with the Moon's distance, as `a^(3/2)`.  The
  sentence "as the Moon receded, Ω_p increased (the orbit precessed faster when closer)"
  contradicts itself.
* `horizons_snippet_span`: the snippet's `range(100)` with a 144-year step reaches the year
  −12231, not "~−3000".  Reaching −3000 takes 36 epochs (`k = 0 … 35`).
* `table144`: the 144-year Moon table built from the archive (46 epochs, AD 2313 back to
  4167 BC).  `table144_years` checks its epochs.  `table144_err_consistent` checks the error
  column against σ × 0.6333″/s.  `table144_err_below_half_degree`: the Moon position
  uncertainty due to ΔT stays below 30′ at every epoch.
* `moon_file_sizes`: the 11 Moon files are 1.30–1.39 MB each, matching "1.3 MB per 600 years".
  Together they are 14 793 105 bytes, so the uncompressed 600-year files for 6600 years exceed
  10 MB.  The 144-year table itself is 3 667 bytes (`table_size_small`).
-/
/-! ### Lunar angular speed -/

/-- Measured over the year 2000 (DE441, longitude in the fixed J2000 ecliptic, sampled every
1.2 h): minimum, mean and maximum lunar speed in degrees per day. -/
/-- Unit conversion: `x` °/h is `x · 3600` arcsec per `3600` s, which is `x` ″/s. -/
/-- The fastest measured lunar speed is 0.6333″/s (to four decimals). -/
/-- 13.4″/s is more than 21 times the fastest and more than 24 times the mean lunar speed. -/
/-! ### The conversation's ΔT table -/

/-- One row of the conversation's ΔT table: era (astronomical year), ΔT (s), σ (s) and the
claimed positional error of the Moon (arcminutes).  For −2000 the table says σ "> 1 hour" and
error "> 5°"; these are entered as the bounds 3600 s and 300′. -/
/-- The rows as stated (2000 has "< 1 s" and "< 14″", omitted). -/

/-- Each of the four rows with exact values (1600 to −500) has error σ · 13.4″/s, converted to
arcminutes, to within 1.5′.  The −2000 row has only bounds ("> 1 hour", "> 5°"); there
3600 s · 13.4″/s = 804′ is above 300′, which is also consistent with 13.4″/s. -/
/-- Centuries from 1820. -/
/-- The conversation's uncertainty formula `σ ≈ 0.8 t²` (seconds). -/
/-- Morrison & Stephenson (2004) long-term parabola for ΔT (seconds). -/

/-- The formula gives 3.872 s, 53.792 s, 139.392 s, 430.592 s and 1167.392 s for the five
eras.  These differ from the table's σ by factors of more than 1.8 except at −500, and at
−2000 the formula gives about 19 minutes, not "> 1 hour". -/

/-- At −3000 the formula gives σ ≈ 1859 s.  Even at the fastest lunar speed, that moves the Moon
by less than 20′. -/

/-- To move the Moon by 10° (36 000″) at no more than 0.6333″/s takes a ΔT error of more
than 15 hours. -/

/-- At −1000, σ from the formula moves the Moon by under 7′.  Moving it by 5° would take more
than 7 hours of ΔT error. -/
/-! ### The 18.6-year nodal cycle -/
/-- Measured regression of the ascending node (DE441, 2684 crossings 1900–2100), °/yr. -/

/-- The eclipse year is 360° divided by the Sun's daily motion relative to the node.  The
eclipse seasons move earlier by (tropical year − eclipse year), which is between 18.5 and
18.7 days per year. -/
/-- Obliquity 23.44° and mean inclination 5.145°: major and minor standstill declinations. -/

/-- First-order solar theory: the node period is `(4/3) · T_sun² / T_moon` (sidereal periods,
inclination factor ignored; it changes this by 0.4%).  It gives between 17.5 and 18 years,
within 5% of the measured 18.61 years. -/

/-- In that theory the node rate is proportional to `n_sun² / n_moon`, and `n_moon ∝ a^(-3/2)`.
So the rate is proportional to `a^(3/2)` and grows as the Moon recedes. -/

/-- "As the Moon receded, Ω_p increased" and "the orbit precessed faster when closer" cannot
both hold for two distances `a₁ < a₂`. -/
/-! ### The Horizons snippet -/

/-- `jds = [2460831.5 - 144*365.25*i for i in range(100)]`: the last epoch is 14 256 Julian
years before 2025, so the year −12231.  The last of the first 36 epochs is −3015. -/
/-! ### The 144-year Moon table from `ephemeris/ephe.7z` -/

/-- Row of `docs/moon_144yr_de441.csv`: index `k`, calendar year of the epoch
`JD 2460831.5 − 52596 k` (0h TT), σ(ΔT) in seconds (rounded) and the Moon position uncertainty
`σ × (lunar speed at that epoch)` in hundredths of an arcminute (rounded). -/
/-- The epochs are 144 years apart: year = 2025 − 144 k, with k running from −2 to 43. -/

/-- Consistency of the error column with the speed bound: allowing ±1 for rounding,
`err ≤ σ · 0.6333 / 60` arcminutes, i.e. `6000 (err − 1) ≤ 6333 (σ + 1)`. -/

/-- Over the whole span of the archive (AD 2313 back to 4167 BC), ΔT uncertainty moves the
Moon by less than 30′ at every 144-year epoch. -/
/-! ### File sizes -/
/-- Sizes in bytes of the 11 Moon files `semom42.se1` … `semo_18.se1`. -/

/-- The 144-year table (`docs/moon_144yr_de441.csv`) is 3 667 bytes, over 2 700 times under
10 MB. -/

/-!
# Audit: the synthetic word `צייוחף` and its "linguistic geometric system"

Source: `new_beginning_word.md` and `new_beginning_word_2.md` (chat transcripts).  The system
has three synthetic words, each given a braid word and a `2 × 2` complex matrix (the
"8-dimensional shadow" is the list of real and imaginary parts of its four entries):

| word | braid word | matrix used in the code |
|---|---|---|
| `צייוחף` (Tsiyuchaf, "isolate") | `[1, 1, 1, 1, 1, -1]` | `diag(-0.809+0.587i, -0.809-0.587i)` |
| `פחיווצ` (Pachivutz, "expand", claimed inverse) | `[-1, -1, -1, -1, -1, 1]` | `diag(0.809-0.587i, 0.809+0.587i)` |
| `טיירמף` (Tayrmaf, "modulate") | `[1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1]` | `[[0, 1], [1, 0]]` |

The entries `±1` are read as `σ₁^{±1}` in the braid group `B₃` (the 2-dimensional Fibonacci
representation the transcript invokes is a representation of `B₃`).

## What holds
* `tsiyuchaf_eval`: the braid word only represents `σ₁⁴`; `pachivutz_eval`: the companion word
  does represent the inverse braid.  `oneGen_eval`: a word in `σ₁` alone is determined by its
  exponent sum, so e.g. `[1, 1, 1, 1]` is the same braid as `[1, 1, 1, 1, 1, -1]`
  (`tsiyuchaf_eq_plain`).
* `zeta_re`: the real part `-0.809` is exactly `cos 144° = -(1 + √5)/4 = -φ/2`, as the
  transcript says.  `idealM_eq_fib_pow`: the exact matrix `diag(e^{4πi/5}, e^{-4πi/5})` is the
  fourth power of `diag(e^{7πi/10}, e^{-7πi/10})`, the determinant-one normalisation of the
  Fibonacci braid generator `diag(e^{4πi/5}, e^{-3πi/5})` (complex-conjugate convention).
* `idealM_det`, `idealM_pow_five`, `idealM_unitary`: determinant 1, unitary, period 5.  The
  "immortal oscillation" is this period; every diagonal matrix of roots of unity has one.

## What fails
* `tayrmaf_eval`, `tayrmaf_image_ne_swap`: the "balanced" braid of `טיירמף` cancels to the
  trivial braid, so every representation sends it to the identity, never to the swap matrix used
  in the code.  `swap_mul_swap`: the swap squares to `1`; it is not a 90° turn.
* `P_eq_neg_T`, `T_mul_P_ne_one`: the companion matrix is the *negative* of the first one, not its
  inverse.  Their product is `diag(-0.309912+0.949766i, …)`, so `test_binary_identity_cancellation`
  fails.  The same holds for the exact matrices (`idealM_mul_neg_ne_one`); the true inverse has
  real parts `-0.809` (`idealM_inv`).
* `cipher_decrypt_re`: in `SovereignMatrixCipher` decryption multiplies by `P T = -T²`; every
  recovered code point is `-0.309912` times the original, hence negative, and Python's `chr`
  raises `ValueError`.  The round trip never works.
* `idealM_mul_entry_norm`: multiplying by a diagonal unitary keeps the modulus of every entry,
  off-diagonal ones included: no "cross-talk" is sheared off.  `idealM_mul_det`: the determinant is
  unchanged; the values `0.16` and `0.31 + 0.18i` reported for the "filtered" matrices are the
  determinants of the input matrices themselves (`ancient8_det`, `ancient10_det`).
* `T_det`: with the rounded constants the determinant is `0.99905`, not `1`.  Hence
  `three_axis_det`: `test_three_axis_loop_conservation` changes the determinant by a factor
  `0.99905²`, a difference of about `5·10⁻⁴`, above its tolerance `10⁻⁵`, so it fails too.
* `sentence_det_norm`: for the exact lexicon every sentence keeps `|det|`, so the "20% safety
  ceiling" of `SentenceValidator` cannot be breached by any sentence.
* `keyring_always_passes`: in `MultiUserKeyRing` every forged key is within `0.09√2 < 0.15` of the
  root, so the handshake accepts every user name.
* `profiler_companion`: the transcript's own `InverseProfiler` forges `ךאבגדה`, not `פחיווצ`;
  `pachivutz_not_reverse`: `פחיווצ` is neither the reverse of `צייוחף` nor an anagram of it.
* `tsiyuchaf_entropy`: the reported "entropy" `2.2516` is the Shannon entropy (bits) of the
  letter frequencies `1,2,1,1,1` of the six letters, i.e. `log₂ 6 - 1/3`; it says nothing about
  geometry.

Not checkable (no definition given): "holographic stability error", "first Chern number" (a
single matrix has none; a Chern number needs a family of states over a closed surface),
"novelty".  The "32-dimensional" Kronecker product of three `2 × 2` matrices is an `8 × 8`
complex matrix, i.e. 128 real numbers.  The noise "threshold" of 20% is a choice of the test, not
a property of the matrix: the deviation from unitarity grows continuously with the noise.
-/
/-! ## Part 1: the braid words -/
/-- The letter `σ₁^{±1}` of `B₃`. -/
/-- Exponent sum of a word. -/
/-- A word using only `σ₁^{±1}` is `σ₁` to the power of its exponent sum. -/
/-- `[1, 1, 1, 1]` is the same braid as `צייוחף`: nothing in the braid is "novel". -/
/-- The swap matrix used in the code for `טיירמף`. -/
/-- No representation of `B₃` sends the braid of `טיירמף` to the swap matrix. -/
/-! ## Part 2: the exact matrix -/
/-- `e^{4πi/5}`, the exact value behind `-0.809 + 0.587i`. -/
/-- The exact matrix `diag(e^{4πi/5}, e^{-4πi/5})`. -/
/-- The determinant-one Fibonacci braid generator (conjugate convention). -/
/-- Even with exact values, "`פחיווצ` = negative of `צייוחף`" does not cancel it. -/
/-- The exact lexicon: `צייוחף`, `טיירמף`, `פחיווצ`. -/
/-- Every sentence over the exact lexicon keeps `|det|`: the 20% check cannot fail. -/
/-! ## Part 3: the rounded constants of the code -/
/-- `TSIYUCHAF` as in the code. -/
/-- `PACHIVUTZ` as in the code. -/
/-- Decryption in `SovereignMatrixCipher`: every recovered value is `-0.309912` times the original. -/
/-- The mock matrix of `test_three_axis_loop_conservation`. -/
/-- `MultiUserKeyRing`: shifts `(h₀ mod 10)/100 + i (h₁ mod 10)/100` always pass the `0.15` test. -/
/-! ## Part 4: letters -/
/-- The `char_pool` of `InverseProfiler`. -/
/-- The seed `int(|Re T⁻¹[0,0]| · 100) % 27` is `26` and the forged companion is `ךאבגדה`. -/
/-- The letter counts of `צייוחף`. -/
/-- The reported entropy is the letter-frequency Shannon entropy `log₂ 6 - 1/3 ≈ 2.2516`. -/

/-!
# The corrected `צייוחף` / `פחיווצ` / `טיירמף` lexicon

Companion to `QBX.Forensics.Inert.NewBeginningWordAudit`.  The corrected Python code
(`QBX/examples/new_beginning_word/`) replaces the companion matrix `פחיווצ = -T` by the complex
conjugate (= inverse) of `צייוחף`, and uses the exact constants `e^{±4πi/5}` instead of
`-0.809 ± 0.587i`.  This file checks that these changes repair what the audit found broken:

* `idealM_mul_idealP`, `idealP_mul_idealM`: the binary pair now cancels to the identity
  (`test_binary_identity_cancellation`).
* `idealP_eq_inv`: the corrected `פחיווצ` matrix is exactly the inverse of `צייוחף`; it is also the
  image of the braid `σ₁⁻⁴` under the Fibonacci generator (`idealP_eq_fib_inv_pow`), matching the
  braid word `[-1, -1, -1, -1, -1, 1]`.
* `fixed_cipher_roundtrip`: encrypting with `צייוחף` and decrypting with `פחיווצ` returns every
  data block unchanged, so the cipher round trip works for every character code.
* `fixed_three_axis_loop`, `fixed_three_axis_det`: the 3-axis loop `פחיווצ · טיירמף · טיירמף ·
  צייוחף` is the identity, so the determinant is conserved exactly
  (`test_three_axis_loop_conservation`).
* `rounded_mul_conj`: why the exact constants are needed.  With the 3-digit constants, even the
  conjugate pair only multiplies to `0.99905 · I`, so a 1e-5 tolerance still fails and the cipher
  would misdecode code points above about 500 (e.g. Hebrew letters, about 1500).
-/
/-- The corrected `פחיווצ` matrix: `diag(e^{-4πi/5}, e^{4πi/5})`, the conjugate of `צייוחף`. -/
/-- The corrected `פחיווצ` is the image of `σ₁⁻⁴` (the braid `[-1,-1,-1,-1,-1,1]`). -/

constants were kept). -/

/-!
# Audit: the "temporal rift" (30 AD vs 33 AD) and the sheaf claims of `Archive.7z`

Two things in the archive go by "rift" or "sheaf obstruction":

1. `puzzlepuzzle.md` §3, "The Chronological Rift (30 AD vs. 33 AD) and the Titulus": the
   crucifixion year is disputed between 30 and 33, and the text reads the discrepancy as a
   "temporal fold" whose nexus is the titulus.  It also says that under the Essene 364-day
   calendar "Nisan 14 always fell on a Wednesday".
2. `functor_homology_report.json`, `cohomology_sheaf_obstructions`, set against the paper's
   Discovery 8, "H¹(X,F)=0 and Betti-0=1: every local semantic section extends globally without
   obstruction".

## Part 1: the chronology as a gluing problem

Read sheaf-theoretically, each source is a local section: a constraint on the crucifixion day.

* **John** (18:28, 19:14, 19:31): a Friday that is the day of preparation, Nisan 14.
* **Synoptics** (Mark 14:12, 15:42): a Friday after the Passover meal, Nisan 15.
* **Luke 3:1 and Pilate's prefecture**: a year in 29–36.  The fifteenth year of Tiberius is
  AD 28/29, and Pilate governed AD 26–36.
* **Astronomy**: the Nisan calendar.  It is reconstructed by `scripts/nisan_calendar.py`
  (exploratory Python, not checked in Lean) for three crescent-visibility thresholds.  Its
  output is transcribed here (`nisan1Evening`).

A global section is a day that satisfies all the constraints at once.  Given the transcribed
table, the following is checked by computation:

* `john_sections`: with John's constraint the global sections are **30 and 33** for the 10.5°
  and 13° thresholds, and only 33 for 8°.  The "rift" between 30 and 33 is a
  non-uniqueness of the global section: two years fit John's data.
* `synoptic_sections`: with the Synoptic constraint there is **no** global section for 10.5°
  and 13°, and only 30 for 8°.
* `john_synoptic_no_gluing`: no day is both Nisan 14 and Nisan 15 of the same calendar.  So the
  John and Synoptic sections never glue, whatever the year.  This is the actual obstruction, and
  it is the long-known Johannine/Synoptic chronology problem.  It disappears only if two
  different calendars were in use.
* `essene_nisan14_tuesday`: the Essene year has 364 = 52 · 7 days, so each date falls on the
  same weekday every year.  In the usual reconstruction the year begins on a Wednesday, which
  makes Nisan 14 a **Tuesday**, not a Wednesday (Nisan 15 is the Wednesday).

The titulus carries no date: the same inscription stands in the 30 and the 33 scenario.  So it
cannot be the point at which the two timelines "match"; it is compatible with both.

## Part 2: the semantic-graph "sheaf obstructions"

The report lists 252 "unassociated orphan nodes", each "shielded" by an
`allocated_homological_parent`.

* `patch_is_a_star`: 251 of the 252 parents are the same node `vox_5f38363fc5`, which is itself
  one of the orphans, attached to `vox_1f193a9b63`.  So the "shielding" adds a star of 252
  edges around one hub.
* `patched_reachable`: in **any** graph, after these edges are added every orphan is connected
  to `vox_1f193a9b63`.  The connectivity is produced by the patch, not found in the data.
* `card_components_ge`: if the orphans had no edges before the patch, as the name
  "unassociated" says, the graph had at least 253 connected components (Betti-0 ≥ 253) before
  the patch.  The reported Betti-0 = 1 is the result of the patch.  (Attaching isolated
  vertices by single edges creates no cycles, so the patch does not change the cycle count H¹
  of the constant sheaf.  The paper's H¹ = 0 cannot be checked, because the graph is not in the
  archive.)

The report's other two blocks show the same pattern.  Its `commutator_norm_optimization` has
`initial_loss` equal to `final_loss` (nothing changed in 5 epochs, yet `"converged": true`).
Its `global_attractor_bridge` sends all 195 invariants to the same attractor (6), so the
"coherence ratio 1.0" is a constant output.  Both are read from the file; neither is formalised
here.
-/

/-!
# Audit: the titulus (John 19:19–20) braided in Hebrew, Greek and Latin

Follow-up to the Genesis 1:1 cross-reference braid audit (registry H-285).  The inscription over the cross was
written "in Hebrew, and Greek, and Latin" (John 19:20; the Textus Receptus order is
εβραιστι ελληνιστι ρωμαιστι).  This file runs the same verified Bible-to-braid model
(`QBX.Formal.Bible.convert 6 true`, 8 strands, encoding `letter-ordinal-v1`, sofit rule on) on
the three versions and on their combination.

**The texts.**

* Greek: John 19:19 as in `TR.json` of `Archive.7z` (`titulusGreek`).
* Latin: Vulgate John 19:19, *Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum* (`titulusLatin`).
* Hebrew: no Hebrew text of the inscription survives; John's Gospel is in Greek.  Two
  reconstructions are checked: Delitzsch's Hebrew New Testament, *ישוע הנצרי מלך היהודים*
  (`titulusHebrew`), and the popular variant with "and", *ישוע הנצרי ומלך היהודים*
  (`titulusHebrewAcrostic`), whose word initials spell יהוה (`acrostic_yhwh`).  Points do not
  change the braid (`QBX.Formal.Bible.convert_mark_invisible`), so unpointed text is used.

**Results (kernel computation).**

* `hebrew_braid`, `greek_braid`, `latin_braid`, `hebrew_acrostic_braid`: words, crossings, writhe,
  closure components and total linking of each language on its own.
* `combine_eq_append`: the braid of the combined titulus is the concatenation of the three braids
  (the model is a monoid homomorphism, `convert_append`); crossings and writhe therefore add up
  and do not depend on the order: 19 + 36 + 26 = 81 crossings, writhe 15 + 30 + 26 = 71
  (`combined_crossings_writhe`).
* `rotate_conj`: a cyclic rotation of the order (H·G·L → G·L·H → L·H·G) conjugates the braid
  group element, so it gives the same closed link (Markov move I, a standard fact not
  re-proved here).  The six orders therefore give at most two links.
* `combined_orders`, `combined_orders_acrostic`: they give exactly two classes, with different
  strand counts per component and different total linking (so, total linking being a link
  invariant, two different links):
  - Hebrew–Greek–Latin (John 19:20, Textus Receptus / KJV order) and its rotations:
    components of 6, 1, 1 strands, total linking 18;
  - Hebrew–Latin–Greek (John 19:20 in the critical text) and its rotations:
    components of 3, 3, 2 strands, total linking 25.
  With the acrostic Hebrew the numbers become 7 + 1 strands / total linking 8, and
  5 + 3 strands / total linking 21.
  So "the" combined titulus has no single braid: its link depends on the order of the
  languages and on which Hebrew reconstruction is used (four different links from two
  reasonable choices).

**Gematria.**

* `hebrew_gematria`: 911 (Delitzsch), 917 (with ו).  `greek_gematria`: 5610, with Ἰησοῦς = 888.
  Latin has no standard letter values; counting only the Roman-numeral letters (chronogram
  convention, U = V) gives 1532 (`latin_numeral_sum`).  Totals 8053 / 8059
  (`trilingual_totals`); neither is triangular (`trilingual_totals_not_triangular`).

**The "Triple-Dalet Titulus" vector of `alphabet_report.md`.**  The report calls the constant
vector `[0.75, …, 0.75]` in 8 dimensions the titulus "fifth language" invariant, says it lies on
the null cone of a split (4, 4) metric, and that it "behaves perfectly as a zero-divisor".

* `split_form_null_of_halves_eq`: the split form `N(first half) − N(second half)` vanishes on
  **every** vector whose two halves agree, in particular on every constant vector.  Being null is
  not special to 0.75 or to the titulus.
* `tripleDalet_normSq`, `tripleDalet_not_zero_divisor`: as an octonion the vector has squared
  norm 9/2 and is **not** a zero divisor (the octonions have none,
  `Refinery.ZeroDiv.octonion_no_zero_divisors`).  Null for an indefinite metric and zero
  divisor are different notions.

The archive's own Probe J output (`probeJ_cross_invariant.json`) reports
`"inv_poly": "x^2 + y^2 - 2"` and `"new_variety?": false`; that is a circle (a curve, not a
surface) and the probe itself does not claim a new variety.  Not formalised here.
-/
/-- Writhe of a short-form braid word: the sum of the crossing signs. -/

/-- Apply one generator to the strand arrangement: swap positions `|g| - 1` and `|g|`
(0-based).  `pos[p]` is the strand (1-based starting position) now at position `p`. -/
/-- Final strand arrangement on `n` strands after the whole word. -/

/-- The orbit of `s` under the closure permutation (at most `fuel` steps).  `pos` is the final
arrangement: the strand starting at `s` ends at position `q` (`pos[q] = s`), and the closure
connects it to the strand starting at `q`. -/
/-- Insert into a sorted list of naturals. -/
/-- Insertion sort on naturals (structural, so it reduces in the kernel). -/

/-- Closure components of a braid word on `n` strands: each component is the sorted list of its
strands (1-based), and components are listed by their smallest strand. -/

/-- Self-writhe of a component: the sum of the signs of the crossings between two strands of
that component. -/
/-- Standard Hebrew letter values (final forms take the value of their base letter). -/
/-- Hebrew gematria (standard values) of a text. -/
/-- Standard Greek (isopsephy) letter values, lower case; final sigma counts as sigma. -/
/-- Greek gematria (isopsephy) of a lower-case unaccented text. -/
/-- Triangular numbers. -/
/-! ### The three texts -/
/-- Hebrew reconstruction of Delitzsch's Hebrew New Testament (John 19:19), unpointed. -/
/-- The popular Hebrew variant with "and" before "king", unpointed. -/
/-- Greek, John 19:19 as in `TR.json` (unaccented). -/
/-- Latin, Vulgate John 19:19. -/

# Verse features: letters, values, double letters, palindromes, number types

The arithmetic definitions used by `scripts/verse_features.py` (experiment E of
`docs/PREREG_KINGS_FEATURES_2026-10-21.md`), fixed here so that the script's numbers can be
checked against a definition rather than trusted.

* Hebrew letters and values: `QBX.Formal.Gematria.Letter` and `standard` (finals 500–900); the
  secondary convention is `hechrachi` (finals count as their base letter).
* Greek letters and values: `greekChars`, `isopsephy` (standard Greek isopsephy, 24 letters,
  final sigma read as sigma).  Accent stripping is done by the script (Unicode NFD) and is not
  modelled here: the test vectors below are the script's normalised strings.
* `doubles`: positions where a letter equals the next one (spaces never count, so only pairs
  inside a word are counted); `palWords`: words of length `≥ 3` equal to their reverse.
* Number types `isMult`, `isSquareB`, `isTriangularB`, `isPrimeB`, `isDecPal`, with
  correctness lemmas `isSquareB_iff`, `isTriangularB_iff`, `isPrimeB_iff`.
* `wordValue_perm`: permuting letters keeps the value, so a null model that shuffles letters
  *inside* a verse can never detect anything about verse values (why the pre-registered null
  shuffles letters across the whole half-corpus).
* Test vectors `gen_1_1` … `john_1_1`: the features printed by the script for five verses
  (`artifacts/verse_features.txt`), checked by `decide +kernel`.  In particular Gen 1:1 has
  value `4631` in the project's standard table and the familiar `2701 = 37 · 73` in mispar
  hechrachi.
-/
/-! ## Letters and values -/
/-- The 27 Hebrew letters in seed order (`א … ת`, then `ך ם ן ף ץ`), as characters. -/
/-- The 24 Greek letters `α … ω` as characters. -/
/-- Standard Greek isopsephy (the obsolete letters for 6, 90, 900 do not occur). -/
/-- The position of a character in a letter list, if it is one of the first `n` entries. -/
/-- The Hebrew letters of a string (anything else, e.g. spaces, is skipped). -/
/-- The Greek letters of a normalised string; final sigma `ς` is read as `σ`. -/
/-- The value of a Greek letter list. -/
/-! ## Words, double letters, palindromes -/
/-- The words of a string: maximal runs of non-space characters. -/
/-- Number of positions where a character equals the next one and is not a space. -/
/-- A palindromic word: at least three letters, equal to its reverse. -/
/-- Number of palindromic words of a string. -/
/-! ## Number types -/
/-- `n` is a multiple of `m`. -/
/-- Perfect square, by the integer square root. -/
/-- Triangular number `k(k+1)/2`, by the integer square root of `2n`. -/
/-- Primality by trial division up to the integer square root. -/
/-- A decimal palindrome with at least two digits. -/
/-! ## Shuffling letters inside a verse keeps its value -/
/-! ## Test vectors (from `artifacts/verse_features.txt`) -/
/-- Words, letters, standard value, hechrachi value, double letters, palindromic words. -/
/-- Words, letters, isopsephy value, double letters, palindromic words. -/

/-- The number types printed for the five verses: Gen 1:1 (4631), Gen 1:2 (6516) and
Deut 34:12 (2598) have none of the six types; Matt 1:1 (6279) is a multiple of 7 only;
John 1:1 (3617) is prime only.  The hechrachi value 2701 of Gen 1:1 is `37 · 73` and the
73rd triangular number. -/

/-!
# Audit of the Meru Foundation primitives (`reference/primary/meru.md`)

**Status: forensics** (Lake library `QBXForensics`, outside the core corpus `QBX.Formal`): an
audit of external source material, kept as a record of which claims survive.

`reference/primary/meru.md` extracts "testable mathematical primitives" from the Meru
Foundation corpus (Stan Tenen) as a JSON block with test specs `T001`–`T013`.  This file
checks the finite, exactly decidable ones.  Letters are `Gematria.Letter = Fin 27` in the seed
order `א … ת ך ם ן ף ץ`, which is exactly the order of the JSON's `decimal` field, so the
JSON's base-3 code of a letter is its ordinal written in base 3 (`digit2 digit1 digit0`).

**Confirmed.**
* `mirror_involutive`, `mirror_fixed_card`, `mirror_moved_card` (T001): digit reversal
  `XYZ ↦ ZYX` is an involution with exactly 9 fixed letters and 18 moved letters (9 pairs), as
  the JSON lists.
* `mirror_eq_coordinate_swap`: on the 27-point cube `{0,1,2}³` digit reversal is the
  reflection swapping the first and last coordinates — an isometry of the cube (one of the
  JSON's integration ideas).
* `jsonCodes_counts` (T002): the JSON's mirror-class counts for Genesis 1:1
  (`Resh/Lamed 3/1`, `Tav/Vav 3/1`, `He/Mem 3/3`, `Bet/Yod 2/3`, `Alef 6`, `Shin 2`,
  `Zadi-final 1`) are right *for the JSON's own code list*.
* `torus_3_10_word_length`, `torus_3_10_is_knot`: `T(3, 10)` is the closure of the 3-strand
  braid `(σ₁σ₂)¹⁰`, a single component, with 20 crossings in that word.  Its tricolourability
  is `QBX.Notes.colourings_tenen` (documentation note `QBX/Notes/TernaryBraids.lean`).
* `loShu_magic`, `seventy_two_decomposition`, `cube_fVector` (T004, T009 and the hypercube
  table): plain arithmetic, all correct.

**Refuted or corrected.**
* `jsonCodes_ne_genesis`: the JSON's `base3_in_order` encodes the two final mems `ם` as `110`
  (`Mem`) but the final tsadi `ץ` as `222` (`Zadi-final`) — the encoding is inconsistent; with
  the JSON's own table (`ם = 212`) the He/Mem class becomes `3/1` (`genesis_counts`).
* `no_perfect_mirror_matching`, `json_no_perfect_mirror_matching` (T003): **no** arrangement
  (spiral or otherwise) pairs all 28 letters of Genesis 1:1 into mirror pairs.  The single
  `ץ = 222` is self-mirror and has no twin; independently Resh/Lamed occur 3 and 1 times.
  T003's expected `all_paired: true, total_pairs: 14` is impossible under either encoding.
* `groupB_not_rotation_orbit`, `groupC_not_rotation_orbit`, `groupD_not_rotation_orbit`,
  `groups_not_subgroups`: the "3-fold" symmetry groups B, C, D are not orbits of the cyclic digit
  rotation `XYZ ↦ YZX` the JSON names as their symmetry, and none of A–D is a subgroup of
  `(ℤ/3)³` (none contains `000`).  `rotation_fixed_card`: the rotation fixes exactly
  `000, 111, 222` (the cube's main diagonal) and has order 3.
* `torus_3_10_genus_formula`: the JSON's `crossing_number = 30` and `genus = 1` for `T(3, 10)`
  contradict the standard torus-knot formulas `c(T(p,q)) = min(p(q−1), q(p−1)) = 20` and
  `g(T(p,q)) = (p−1)(q−1)/2 = 9` (the formulas are classical theorems — Murasugi, Seifert — and
  are cited; only the arithmetic is checked here).
* Tetrahelix: `QBX.Forensics.bcHelix_aperiodic` (in `Tetrahelix.lean`).
* Cocycles C1–C3: `QBX.Forensics.MeruCocycles`.
-/
/-- Base-3 digits of a letter's ordinal: `code = 9·digit2 + 3·digit1 + digit0`. -/
/-- The letter with digits `x y z`. -/
/-- Meru's mirror pairing: digit reversal `XYZ ↦ ZYX`. -/
/-- The cyclic digit rotation `XYZ ↦ YZX`. -/
/-- Nine letters are their own mirror: `000 010 020 101 111 121 202 212 222`. -/
/-- Digit reversal is the coordinate swap `(x, y, z) ↦ (z, y, x)` of the cube `{0,1,2}³`. -/
/-- The rotation `XYZ ↦ YZX` has order 3. -/
/-- Its fixed letters are `000 = א`, `111 = נ`, `222 = ץ` (the cube's main diagonal). -/

/-- Genesis 1:1, `בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ`, with the correct final forms
(`ם` = ordinal 23, `ץ` = 26). -/
/-- The JSON's `base3_in_order`, converted to ordinals. -/

/-- The JSON's code list differs from the verse exactly at the two final mems (positions 13 and
20), which it encodes as plain `Mem` while it encodes the final tsadi as `Zadi-final`. -/
/-- The JSON's mirror-class counts hold for the JSON's code list. -/

/-- With the correct final forms the He/Mem class is `3/1`, and `ם = 212` (self-mirror)
occurs twice. -/

/-- A perfect mirror matching of a 28-letter sequence: a fixed-point-free involution of the
positions pairing every letter with its mirror image.  Arranging the letters on a spiral only
relabels positions, so this covers every spiral arrangement. -/
/-- If a self-mirror letter occurs exactly once, there is no perfect mirror matching. -/

/-- **T003 refuted:** the letters of Genesis 1:1 cannot all be paired by the mirror symmetry,
in any arrangement. -/
/-- The same holds for the JSON's own code list. -/
/-! ### The "symmetry groups" of the alphabet -/
/-- The rotation orbit of a letter. -/
/-- Group B (`Yod 100, Bet 001, Tav 210`) is not a rotation orbit. -/
/-- Group C (`He 011, Mem 110, Samekh 112`) is not a rotation orbit. -/
/-- Group D (`Resh 201, Lamed 102, Zadi 122`) is not a rotation orbit. -/

/-- None of the groups A–D contains `000`, so none is a subgroup of `(ℤ/3)³`; group A
(`Kaf 101, Kaf-final 211`) is not even closed under the mirror map. -/
/-! ### The `(3, 10)` torus knot -/
/-- `T(3, 10)` is a knot (one component). -/
/-- The braid word `(σ₁σ₂)¹⁰` has writhe (= number of crossings, all positive) 20. -/
/-- The standard formulas give crossing number 20 and genus 9 for `T(3, 10)`, not 30 and 1. -/
/-! ### Arithmetic items -/
/-- The Lo Shu square. -/
/-- All rows, columns and both diagonals sum to 15, and the entries are `1 … 9`. -/

/-- `72 = 10 + 50 + 12`: tetractys `1+2+3+4`, the vertices of the five Platonic solids
`4+8+6+12+20`, and the 12 vertices of the cuboctahedron. -/
/-- Number of `k`-faces of the `n`-cube. -/

/-- The JSON's hypercube table (dimensions 0–5) agrees with `C(n,k) 2^{n−k}`, and every row
has Euler characteristic 1. -/

/-!
# The Meru 3-cocycles (`reference/primary/meru.md`, cocycles C1–C3, tests T010–T012)

**Status: forensics** (Lake library `QBXForensics`, outside the core corpus `QBX.Formal`): an
audit of external source material, kept as a record of which claims survive.

The JSON proposes "Base-3 digits as a `ℤ/3` gauge charge" with 3-cocycles

* C1: `α(a,b,c) = ω^{abc}` on `ℤ/3`, presented as *the generator* of `H³(ℤ/3, U(1)) ≅ ℤ/3`;
* C3: `α(a,b,c) = ζ^{abc}` on `ℤ/7`, likewise for `H³(ℤ/7, U(1)) ≅ ℤ/7`;
* C2: three candidates on `(ℤ/3)³` (the 27 letters): `ω^{x₁y₂z₃}`, `ω^{x₁y₁z₁+x₂y₂z₂+x₃y₃z₃}`,
  `ω^{ε_{ijk} xᵢ y_j z_k}`.

Writing cochains additively (exponents, or values in any abelian group `M`), with the
inhomogeneous coboundaries `cobdry2`, `cobdry3`:

* `cobdry3_cobdry2`: `δ ∘ δ = 0` (sanity check of the conventions).
* `cubic_cocycle`, `typeIII_cocycle`, `det_cocycle`: all proposed cochains *are* cocycles
  (T010–T012 pass) — they are trilinear.
* `cyclic_coboundary`: **but for every odd `n` the cocycle `abc` on `ℤ/n` is a coboundary**,
  `abc = δβ` with `β(a,b) = ((n−1)/2)·a²b`.  So C1 and C3 represent the *trivial* class, not the
  generator (`meruC1_trivial`, `meruC3_trivial`), and this persists in `U(1)` coefficients
  (`isCoboundary_map`, `meruC1_trivial_circle`).
* `alt3_cobdry2`: on an abelian group the total antisymmetrisation of any coboundary vanishes.
  For `x₁y₂z₃` it is `1` on the standard basis (`alt3_typeIII`), so **`ω^{x₁y₂z₃}` is a genuinely
  non-trivial 3-cocycle** (the "type III" cocycle), in `ℤ/3` and in `U(1)` coefficients
  (`typeIII_not_coboundary`, `typeIII_not_coboundary_circle`).
* `diag_coboundary`, `det_coboundary`: the other two C2 candidates are coboundaries (explicit
  `β`).  Only one of the three candidates carries a non-trivial "gauge theory".
-/
/-! ### C1 and C3: cyclic groups -/
/-- `abc` is a 3-cocycle on `ℤ/n`. -/
/-- **For odd `n`, `abc` is a coboundary on `ℤ/n`**: `abc = δβ`, `β(a,b) = ((n−1)/2) a² b`. -/
/-- C1 (`ω^{abc}` on `ℤ/3`) is cohomologically trivial. -/
/-- C3 (`ζ^{abc}` on `ℤ/7`) is cohomologically trivial. -/

/-- The same in `U(1)` coefficients: `a, b, c ↦ exp(2πi·abc/3)`, written additively in
`Additive Circle`, is a coboundary. -/
/-! ### C2: the 27 letters as `(ℤ/3)³` -/
/-- The 27 letters as vectors of three base-3 digits. -/
/-- Candidate 1: `x₁ y₂ z₃` (the "type III" cochain). -/
/-- Candidate 2: `x₁y₁z₁ + x₂y₂z₂ + x₃y₃z₃`. -/
/-- Candidate 3: `ε_{ijk} xᵢ y_j z_k = det(x, y, z)`. -/
/-- `alt(x₁y₂z₃)(e₁, e₂, e₃) = 1`. -/

/-- **The type III cocycle is not a coboundary**, with coefficients in any abelian group `M`
into which `ℤ/3` maps with `1 ↦` a non-zero element. -/
/-- In `U(1)` coefficients: `exp(2πi·x₁y₂z₃/3)` is a non-trivial 3-cocycle on `(ℤ/3)³`. -/
/-- The diagonal candidate is a coboundary. -/
/-- The determinant candidate is a coboundary. -/

/-!
# Sefer Yetzirah: the combinatorics, checked

**Status: forensics** (Lake library `QBXForensics`, outside the core corpus `QBX.Formal`): an
audit of external source material, kept as a record of which claims survive.

The finite structures of *Sefer Yetzirah* (SY), with the 22 base letters as ordinals `0 … 21`
of `Gematria.Letter` and `ך ם ן ף ץ` as `22 … 26`.

* `letter_classes`: 3 mothers `א מ ש`, 7 doubles `ב ג ד כ פ ר ת`, 12 simples partition the 22
  letters; `thirty_two_paths`: `32 = 10 + 22`, `10 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4`.
* `gates_card`: the "231 gates" are the `C(22, 2) = 231` unordered pairs of letters (462 ordered).
  In braid terms, 231 is also the number of standard generators `A_{ij}` of the pure braid
  group on 22 strands, one per pair of strands, matching the pairwise linking numbers of
  `QBX.Formal.PureLinkingMatrix` (the count is proved; the presentation of `P₂₂` is cited).
* `stones_houses`: "two stones build two houses … seven build 5040": the number of orderings of
  `n` distinct letters is `n!`.
* **The six seals** (SY 1:13, in the commonly printed ordering): `יהו` above, `יוה` below,
  `היו` east, `הוי` west, `ויה` south, `והי` north.  `seal_bijective`: the six seals are exactly
  the six orderings of three letters, i.e. the six elements of `S₃` — the six possible strand
  permutations of a 3-strand braid (`seal_braid`).  `seal_opposite`: opposite directions
  differ by swapping the last two letters, so the axis is the first letter (`seal_axis`) and
  opposite directions have opposite parity (`seal_opposite_sign`).  `seal_left_action`: `S₃`
  (hence `B₃`) acts on the six seals by relabelling letters, and this action respects
  "opposite", so it acts by symmetries of the cube of directions.
* **The cube of space.**  `ternaryCube_strata`: in the 27-point ternary cube `{0,1,2}³`,
  classifying points by how many coordinates equal the middle value `1` gives
  8 corners, 12 edge midpoints, 6 face centres and 1 centre; `cube_of_space_counts`:
  `12 = #simples` (SY's twelve diagonal edges), `6 + 1 = #doubles` (six directions and the
  holy palace in the middle), `8 = 3 + 5 = #mothers + #finals`.
  `meru_encoding_not_cube_of_space`: Meru's ordinal base-3 encoding does **not** realise this —
  only 6 of the 12 simples land on edge midpoints.
-/
/-! ### The 22 letters -/
/-- The 22 base letters (ordinals `0 … 21`). -/
/-- The three mothers `א מ ש`. -/
/-- The seven doubles `ב ג ד כ פ ר ת`. -/
/-- The twelve simples. -/
/-- The five final forms `ך ם ן ף ץ`. -/
/-- The 231 gates: unordered pairs of distinct letters. -/
/-- Stones and houses: `n` letters can be ordered in `n!` ways. -/
/-! ### The six seals -/
/-- The six directions of SY 1:13. -/
/-- The three letters `י ה ו` as `0, 1, 2`. -/
/-- The seal of a direction, as the ordering `i ↦ (i-th letter of the seal)`. -/
-- יהו
-- יוה
-- היו
-- הוי
-- ויה
-- והי
/-- Each seal uses each of the three letters once: it is a permutation. -/
/-- The seal as an element of `S₃`. -/
/-- **The six seals are exactly the six permutations of `י ה ו`.** -/
/-- The opposite direction. -/
/-- **Opposite directions differ by swapping the last two letters of the seal.** -/

/-- The axis of a direction is the first letter of its seal: `י` for above/below, `ה` for
east/west, `ו` for south/north. -/
/-- Opposite directions have opposite parity. -/

/-- **Relabelling the letters by `π ∈ S₃` respects opposite directions**, so `S₃` acts on the six
seals by symmetries of the octahedron of directions. -/
/-- Every seal is the strand permutation of some 3-strand braid. -/
/-! ### The cube of space and the ternary cube -/
/-- Number of coordinates of a point of `{0,1,2}³` equal to the middle value `1`. -/
/-- **8 corners, 12 edge midpoints, 6 face centres, 1 centre.** -/

/-- The counts match SY's cube of space: 12 simples on the 12 edges, 7 doubles on the
6 faces and the centre, and the 8 corners are as many as the mothers and finals together. -/
/-- Number of base-3 digits of a letter equal to `1`. -/

/-- **Meru's ordinal encoding does not realise the cube of space:** only six simples
(`ו ח י ל ע צ`) sit on edge midpoints. -/

/-!
# The tetrahelix is not periodic

**Status: forensics** (Lake library `QBXForensics`, outside the core corpus `QBX.Formal`): an
audit of external source material, kept as a record of which claims survive.

`reference/primary/meru.md` (primitive `tetrahelix`, test `T005`) gives the dihedral angle of
the regular tetrahedron as `arccos(1/3) ≈ 70.5288°` — correct — and asserts that the column of
face-sharing regular tetrahedra (the Boerdijk–Coxeter helix) closes after "33 tetrahedra per
full turn", with "99 tetrahedra = 3 full turns".

The screw motion carrying one tetrahedron of the Boerdijk–Coxeter helix to the next rotates by
`θ = arccos(−2/3) ≈ 131.81°` about the axis (Coxeter's value, cited here).  By Niven's theorem
(in Mathlib) neither `arccos(1/3)` nor `arccos(−2/3)` is a rational multiple of `π`:

* `tetra_vertices_inner`: the vertices `(±1, ±1, ±1)` with an even number of minus signs form a
  regular tetrahedron whose vertex vectors meet pairwise with cosine `−1/3`; the dihedral angle
  is therefore `π − arccos(−1/3) = arccos(1/3)`.
* `arccos_one_third_not_rat_mul_pi`, `no_edge_tiling`: no whole number of regular tetrahedra
  fits exactly around an edge (the classical gap of five tetrahedra).
* `arccos_neg_two_thirds_not_rat_mul_pi`, `bcHelix_aperiodic`: **no number `k ≥ 1` of
  tetrahedra turns the helix through a whole number of full turns.**  So "33 tetrahedra per
  full turn" (and "99 = 3 turns") can only be approximations; the column never repeats
  exactly.
-/
/-- Vertices of a regular tetrahedron inscribed in the cube `[-1, 1]³`. -/

/-- Distinct vertex vectors have inner product `−1`, each has squared length `3`; so they meet
with cosine `−1/3`, and all six edges have the same length. -/
/-- If `arccos x = r π` for a rational `r` and `x` is rational, Niven's theorem applies. -/
/-- The dihedral angle `arccos(1/3)` is not a rational multiple of `π`. -/
/-- The Boerdijk–Coxeter twist `arccos(−2/3)` is not a rational multiple of `π`. -/
/-- If `k θ = 2π m` with `k ≥ 1`, then `θ` is a rational multiple of `π`. -/
/-- **No whole number of regular tetrahedra closes up around an edge.** -/

/-- **The tetrahelix is aperiodic:** for no `k ≥ 1` do `k` successive Boerdijk–Coxeter twists
add up to a whole number of turns. -/
/-- In particular 33 tetrahedra do not make an exact number of turns, and neither do 99. -/

/-!
# WS9 integration: the full address graph has no blind spots

Couples work stream 1 (the address graph `addrGraph n k M = Q_n □ T^k_M`,
`QBX/Formal/MixedRadixGeometry.lean`) with work streams 2/3 (fork detection,
`QBX/Formal/GaugeFlatness.lean`).  Register item X-07.

Call a coordinate *non-trivial* if moving along it changes the address: every bit, and every cycle
with modulus `M j ≠ 1`.  If there are at least two non-trivial coordinates, every edge of the
address graph lies on a 4-cycle (a commuting square of two moves along different coordinates),
so the address graph has **no bridges** (`addrGraph_not_isBridge`).  Consequently, if consensus
events are exchanged along *every* edge of the address space, every single-event fork of a flat
ledger is detected by the flatness check (`addrGraph_perturb_detected`), so `blind_spots` is empty.

The hypothesis cannot be dropped: `Q_1` alone (`n = 1`, `k = 0`) is a single edge, which is a
bridge (`addrGraph_cube_one_isBridge`).
-/

/-- **Squares kill bridges.** If `x ↦ f x` and `x ↦ g x` are commuting families of edges, then
the edge `a — f a` lies on the 4-cycle `a, g a, f (g a), f a` and is not a bridge, provided the
4-cycle is non-degenerate. -/
/-- An edge `a — b` of the address graph is a single move from `a` in one of three shapes. -/

/-- The number of non-trivial coordinates of `Q_n □ T^k_M`: all bits plus the cycles of
modulus `≠ 1`. -/
/-- Every bit has a partner coordinate. -/
/-- Every cycle has a non-trivial partner coordinate different from it. -/

/-- **No bridges.** If `Q_n □ T^k_M` has at least two non-trivial coordinates, no edge of the
address graph is a bridge. -/

/-!
# L-1: the edge connectivity of the address graph equals its degree

Target L-1 of the WS9 integration register (item X-08). The address graph
`addrGraph n k M = Q_n □ T^k_M` (`MixedRadixGeometry.lean`) is regular of degree

  `addrDegree n k M = n + ∑ⱼ (if M j = 2 then 1 else 2)`

(`addrGraph_ncard_neighborSet`), and its edge connectivity is exactly that degree:

* `addrGraph_isEdgeConnected`: deleting fewer than `addrDegree n k M` edges never disconnects
  the graph (all cycle lengths `M j ≥ 2`);
* `addrGraph_not_isEdgeConnected`: deleting the edges at one address does (`n + k ≥ 1`);
* `addrGraph_edgeConnectivity_eq_degree`: both together, `λ = δ`;
* `addrGraph_fork_detected`: so, with events on every edge of the address space, every fork
  changing a non-empty set of fewer than `addrDegree n k M` events of a flat ledger is detected
  (F6a of `MultiEdgeFork.lean`).

The proof is general graph theory, then an induction over coordinates:

* `boxProd_isEdgeConnected`: `λ(G □ H) ≥ λ(G) + λ(H)` for finite connected graphs with
  `|G| > λ(G)`, `|H| > λ(H)`. If fewer than `a + b` edges are deleted, either the `G`-layers lose
  fewer than `a` edges in total (so every layer stays connected) and at most
  `(a + b − 1)/|G| < b` edges of `H` lose all their copies, or symmetrically.
* `bitIso`, `cycIso`: `Q_{n+1} □ T ≅ K₂ □ (Q_n □ T)` and `Q_n □ T^{k+1} ≅ C_{M 0} □ (Q_n □ T^k)`.
* `cycGraph_isEdgeConnected`: the cycle `C_m` has edge connectivity `2` (`m ≥ 3`), resp. `1`
  (`m = 2`).
-/
/-- Edge connectivity is invariant under graph isomorphism. -/

/-- A graph with two vertices is never `(deg v + 1)`-edge-connected: deleting the edges at `v`
isolates `v`. -/
/-- The deleted edges of `s` lying in the `G`-layer at height `h`. -/
/-- The deleted edges of `s` lying in the `H`-fibre over `g`. -/
/-- The `H`-edges all of whose copies are deleted. -/
/-- The `G`-edges all of whose copies are deleted. -/
/-- **Counting.** Deleted layer edges and deleted fibre edges are different edges of `s`. -/
/-- A `G`-layer with few deleted edges stays connected inside the deleted product. -/

/-- If every `G`-layer stays connected and the `H`-edges with a surviving copy connect `H`, the
deleted product is connected. -/
/-- Deleting fewer than `c` edges (or none) from a preconnected `c`-edge-connected graph. -/

/-- **Edge connectivity of a box product.** `λ(G □ H) ≥ λ(G) + λ(H)` for finite connected
graphs (with `|G| > λ(G)` and `|H| > λ(H)`, automatic for simple graphs of minimum degree
`≥ λ`). -/
/-- Neighbourhoods are transported by isomorphisms. -/
/-- Neighbourhoods in a box product. -/
/-- The single-edge factor `Q_1 = K_2` on `Bool`. -/
/-- The cycle factor `C_m` on `ZMod m`: adjacent iff at cyclic distance one. -/
/-- Degree of the cycle factor: `1` for `m = 2`, `2` for `m ≥ 3`. -/
/-- The cycle `C_m` (`m ≥ 3`) is 2-edge-connected. -/
/-- Edge connectivity of the cycle factor equals its degree. -/
/-- Split off the first bit: `Q_{n+1} □ T = Q_1 □ (Q_n □ T)`. -/
/-- `addrGraph (n+1) k M ≅ K₂ □ addrGraph n k M`. -/
/-- Split off the first cycle: `Q_n □ T^{k+1} = C_{M 0} □ (Q_n □ T^k)`. -/
/-- `addrGraph n (k+1) M ≅ C_{M 0} □ addrGraph n k (M ∘ succ)`. -/

/-- The minimum (= every) degree of `Q_n □ T^k_M`: one per bit, and per cycle `1` if its length is
`2`, else `2`. -/

/-- **L-1, lower bound.** `Q_n □ T^k_M` (all `M j ≥ 2`) is `addrDegree`-edge-connected: deleting
fewer than `n + ∑ⱼ (M j = 2 ? 1 : 2)` edges never disconnects it. -/
/-- Every address has exactly `addrDegree n k M` neighbours. -/

/-- **L-1, upper bound.** With at least one coordinate, deleting the `addrDegree` edges at one
address disconnects it, so the graph is not `(addrDegree + 1)`-edge-connected. -/

/-- **L-1 (X-08): the edge connectivity of the address graph equals its minimum degree.**
`λ(Q_n □ T^k_M) = δ = n + ∑ⱼ (M j = 2 ? 1 : 2)` for all cycle lengths `M j ≥ 2` and `n + k ≥ 1`. -/

/-- **Protocol consequence.** If consensus events are exchanged along every edge of
`Q_n □ T^k_M`, every fork that changes a non-empty set of fewer than `addrDegree n k M` events
of a flat ledger is detected (F6a with `k = λ = δ`). -/

/-!
# F-5 on the address graph (WS9 roadmap step 8, part (b))

`TorusLedgerSectors.lean` (W5, finding F-5) is stated on the toric-code lattice `Edge m`.
Through the edge correspondence of `ToricAddressEdges.lean` (W7) it transfers to the address
graph `T²_m = addrGraph 0 2 (m, m)` itself.

A `ℤ/2` ledger on the address graph assigns a transport `ℓ e ∈ ℤ/2` to every unordered pair of
addresses (only adjacent pairs matter). It is pure gauge (`AddrPureGauge`) if there are address
potentials `p` with `ℓ s(a, b) = p a + p b` for every edge `a — b`.

* `addrPureGauge_iff_toric`: for `m ≠ 1`, `ℓ` is pure gauge on the address graph iff its pull-back
  `ℓ ∘ toricEdge` to the toric-code lattice is pure gauge;
* `addrPureGauge_iff`: **F-5 on addresses** — `ℓ` is pure gauge iff it is flat on every face and
  trivial around both non-contractible cycles;
* `exists_addr_faceFlat_not_pureGauge`: the two cycle bits are independent of the face checks —
  for `m ≥ 3` there is a face-flat ledger on the address graph that is not pure gauge;
* `toricEdge_transEdge`: **F-4 on addresses** — the lattice translation `transEdge s t` of
  `ToricTranslation.lean` (W4: it acts trivially on the logical sectors) is exactly the torus
  shift gate `shiftGate (s, t)` acting on address-graph edges.
-/
/-- A `ℤ/2` ledger on the address graph `T²_m` is pure gauge. -/
/-- The sum of a potential over the two endpoints of an unordered pair. -/
/-- Pure gauge on addresses ⟺ pure gauge on the toric-code lattice (`m ≠ 1`). -/

/-- **F-5 on the address graph.** A `ℤ/2` ledger on `T²_m` (`m ≠ 1`) is pure gauge iff it is flat
on every face and trivial around both non-contractible cycles. -/

/-- For `m ≥ 3` the face checks miss the cycle bits: some face-flat ledger on the address graph is
not pure gauge. -/

/-- **F-4 on the address graph.** Translating a toric-code qubit by `(s, t)` is the torus shift
gate `shiftGate (s, t)` applied to its endpoints in `T²_m`. -/

/-!
# Phase 1: the addressing protocol — the XOR metric of the DHT layer

Migration `013_addressing_protocol.sql` and `qbx.addressing.dht` route an address to the DHT nodes
whose 256-bit identifiers are *closest* to the address key in the XOR metric
`d(x, y) = x XOR y` (Kademlia).  The database computes the distance bytewise on `BYTEA` values
(`addr_xor`), sorts by it with the built-in `BYTEA` order (`ORDER BY addr_xor(node_id, key)`), and
files a node into the routing bucket `addr_bucket = ⌊log₂ d⌋` (255 minus the number of leading zero
bits).

This file proves the facts that make those choices correct:

* `xorDist_self`, `xorDist_comm`, `xorDist_eq_zero_iff`, `xorDist_triangle`: XOR is a metric on
  identifiers (the triangle inequality follows from `xor_le_add`).
* `xorDist_unidirectional`: for a fixed key, distinct nodes are at distinct distances — so ties
  never occur and the closest-node order is total.
* `bucket_ultrametric`: the bucket index is an ultrametric:
  `bucket x z ≤ max (bucket x y) (bucket y z)`.
* `IsKClosest`, `kClosest_unique`, `kClosest_exists`: for every `k ≤ |S|` there is exactly one set
  of `k` nodes of `S` each at most as far from the key as every node outside it, so
  `dht_closest_nodes(key, k)` has a well-defined answer that does not depend on tie-breaking.
* `bytesVal`, `bytesVal_lt_iff_lex`, `bytesVal_zipWith_xor`: for byte strings of equal length the
  lexicographic order (PostgreSQL's `BYTEA` comparison) is the order of the big-endian values, and
  bytewise XOR is XOR of the values; `bytea_xor_order` combines the two: the database's bytewise
  computation sorts nodes by their true XOR distance.
-/
/-! ## The XOR metric -/
/-- The XOR distance between two identifiers. -/
/-- XOR never exceeds the sum. -/
/-- Unidirectionality: from a fixed point, each distance is attained by exactly one identifier. -/
/-- XOR preserves the identifier width: two `n`-bit identifiers are at an `n`-bit distance. -/
/-! ## Routing buckets -/

/-- The routing bucket of `y` as seen from `x`: the position of the highest differing bit
(`addr_bucket`; it is `0` both for `x = y` and for distance `1`, the database returns `NULL`
for `x = y`). -/
/-- The bucket index is an ultrametric. -/
/-! ## The `k` closest nodes -/

/-- `A` is a set of `k` nodes of `S` each at most as far from `t` as every node of `S` outside `A`
(the answer `dht_closest_nodes(t, k)` must return). -/
/-- The `k` closest nodes are unique: no tie-breaking rule can change the answer. -/
/-- For every `k ≤ |S|` some set of `k` closest nodes exists. -/
/-! ## Byte strings: the database's representation -/
/-- The big-endian value of a byte string (digits base 256). -/

/-- For byte strings of equal length the lexicographic order (`BYTEA` comparison) is the order of
their big-endian values. -/
/-- Bytewise XOR of equal-length byte strings is XOR of their big-endian values. -/

/-- The database's closest-node order is the XOR-distance order: for equal-length byte strings
`key`, `u`, `v`, comparing the bytewise XORs `key ⊕ u` and `key ⊕ v` as `BYTEA` values compares
`xorDist key u` and `xorDist key v`. -/

/-!
# Phase 1: soundness and completeness of the adjunction checker

The Phase 1 adjunction engine (`qbx.categorical.adjunction`, migration `005_adjunctions.sql`)
is given functors `F : C ⥤ D`, `G : D ⥤ C` and components

* `η_X : X ⟶ G(F(X))` (the unit) and
* `ε_Y : F(G(Y)) ⟶ Y` (the counit).

It checks the naturality squares of `η` and `ε` (migration 004, possibly only on generating
sets of morphisms, `naturality_of_generators`) and the two triangle identities, object by
object:

* left:  `F(η_X) ≫ ε_{F(X)} = 𝟙 (F X)` for every `X : C`;
* right: `η_{G(Y)} ≫ G(ε_Y) = 𝟙 (G Y)` for every `Y : D`.

This file shows that these checks are exactly right.

* `adjunctionOfChecks` (soundness): data passing every check is an adjunction `F ⊣ G` whose
  unit and counit have the checked components; its hom-set bijection sends `f : F X ⟶ Y` to
  `η_X ≫ G(f)` and `g : X ⟶ G Y` to `F(g) ≫ ε_Y` (`adjunctionOfChecks_homEquiv`,
  `adjunctionOfChecks_homEquiv_symm`) — the transposes computed by the Python engine.
* `exists_adjunction_iff_triangles` (soundness and completeness): natural transformations
  `η`, `ε` are the unit and counit of an adjunction iff both triangle identities hold at every
  object.
* `right_triangle_not_implies_left`, `left_triangle_not_implies_right` (necessity): neither
  triangle identity follows from the other, even for natural `η` and `ε`; so a checker that
  verifies only one of them accepts non-adjunctions.

Composition is written diagrammatically: `f ≫ g` is "first `f`, then `g`", i.e. `g ∘ f`; in
the database this is the row `composition(left_id = g, right_id = f, result_id = g ∘ f)`.
-/

/-- **Soundness of the adjunction engine.**  Components `η_X : X ⟶ G(F(X))` and
`ε_Y : F(G(Y)) ⟶ Y` whose naturality squares commute on generating sets `S` (of `C`) and `T`
(of `D`), and which satisfy both triangle identities at every object, form an adjunction
`F ⊣ G`. -/
/-- The transpose of `f : F X ⟶ Y` under the checked adjunction is `η_X ≫ G(f)`. -/
/-- The inverse transpose of `g : X ⟶ G Y` under the checked adjunction is `F(g) ≫ ε_Y`. -/

/-- **The triangle checks decide adjointness.**  Natural transformations `η : 𝟭 C ⟶ F ⋙ G`
and `ε : G ⋙ F ⟶ 𝟭 D` are the unit and counit of an adjunction `F ⊣ G` if and only if both
triangle identities hold at every object. -/

/-! ### Neither triangle identity implies the other

Both counterexamples use the one-object category `SingleObj ℕ` of the multiplicative monoid
`ℕ` (morphisms are natural numbers, `a ≫ b = b * a`, `𝟙 = 1`) and the terminal category
`Discrete PUnit`.  The component `0` is natural for every functor that sends every morphism to
`1`, because `0` is absorbing; the triangle at the `SingleObj ℕ` side then evaluates to
`0 ≠ 1`, while the triangle at the terminal side holds trivially. -/
/-- In the terminal category every pair of parallel morphisms is equal. -/

/-- **The right triangle identity does not imply the left one**, even for natural `η`, `ε`:
take `F : Discrete PUnit ⥤ SingleObj ℕ` constant, `G` the functor to the terminal category,
and counit component `0`. -/

/-- **The left triangle identity does not imply the right one**, even for natural `η`, `ε`:
the mirror image — `F : SingleObj ℕ ⥤ Discrete PUnit`, `G` constant, unit component `0`. -/

/-!
# Accountability of the merkaba–tower organism

`Organism.lean` (H-283) proves that the organism only marks an obligation done when its
verifier accepted it.  The guarantee is therefore only as strong as the verifier.  This file
proves the three facts behind the strengthened verify phase of `agents/scripts/organism.py`
(decision ORG-002):

1. **Guarded verification** (`guarded_sound`, `guarded_complete`).  Putting an extra guard `g`
   in front of any verifier keeps every guarantee of H-283: a done obligation passed both the
   original check and the guard at the same verify clock, and with an honest check and an
   honest guard the loop still finishes with nothing open.
2. **Unique attribution** (`batch_scope_unique`, `scopeGuard_sound`).  If obligations whose
   write scopes overlap always conflict, then in every wave the organism dispatches, each file
   lies in the write scope of at most one member.  So a change to a file can be charged to a
   single obligation and its role, and the scope guard of the script ("every changed file is
   claimed by the obligation, and that obligation's role may write it") is meaningful.
3. **A tamper-evident journal** (`digest_injective`, `journal_append_only`,
   `journal_unique`).  The script appends every tick to a hash-chained journal: each entry
   stores the digest of all entries before it.  Assuming the link function is injective and
   never returns the root (collision resistance, the usual assumption on SHA-256), a valid
   journal is determined by its head digest, and a journal whose head equals a head published
   earlier extends that earlier journal unchanged.
-/
/-! ### 1. Guarded verification -/
/-- The organism whose verify phase also requires the guard `g`. -/

/-- With a guard, every done obligation passed the original check *and* the guard at the same
odd (verify) clock, and its level is at most `maxLevel`. -/

/-- A guarded organism keeps the other guarantees of H-283: nothing is lost or invented, `done`
is in dependency order, and the loop halts within the same bound. -/
/-- An honest check and an honest guard: the guarded loop still finishes with nothing open. -/
/-! ### 2. Unique attribution of changes -/

/-- Members of a compatible wave whose write scopes share a file are equal, provided
obligations with overlapping scopes always conflict. -/

/-- In every wave the organism dispatches, each file lies in the write scope of at most one
member (when overlapping scopes conflict, as in the script, where `conflict` includes
overlapping paths). -/

/-- The scope guard of `organism.py` at clock `t` for obligation `o`: every file changed since
the wave was dispatched (`changed t`) that lies in `o`'s write scope may be written by `o`'s
role (`permitted o f`), and `o`'s targets still exist (`present t o`, no "fix by deletion"). -/

/-- Everything an organism guarded by `scopeGuard` marks done was accepted by the original
check at some verify clock `t` at which: its targets existed, and every changed file in its
scope was permitted to its role. -/
/-! ### 3. The hash-chained journal -/
/-- The digest of a list of entries: fold the link function from the root. -/

/-- Collision resistance of the link function, as used here: it is injective and never returns
the root. -/
/-- Under collision freedom, the digest determines the list of entries. -/

/-- Check a journal: each entry `(prev, body)` must store the running digest of the entries
before it. -/
/-- A journal is valid when it checks from the root. -/

/-- A valid journal is determined by its bodies: entry `i` stores the digest of the first `i`
bodies. -/
/-- Tamper evidence: two valid journals with the same head digest are equal. -/

/-- Append-only: if a valid journal `j'` has, at position `k`, the head digest published for an
earlier valid journal `j`, then `j` is exactly the first `k` entries of `j'`. -/

/-!
# The task-delegation scheduler of the QBX agent layer

`QBX/agents/scripts/delegate.py` turns a task into role-owned subtasks and runs them in
**waves**: every wave is a set of subtasks that may run at the same time.  This file is the Lean
model of its scheduler (`schedule` in the script, which follows the definitions below line by
line) and proves the properties the orchestration rules
(`agents/docs/orchestration_overview.md`, `multi_agent_topology.md`) ask for.

The model is generic: a subtask is any `α` with an identifier `key`, a list of prerequisite
identifiers `deps`, and a Boolean `conflict` relation (in the script: same role, or overlapping
write sets).  `cap` is `parallelism.max_concurrent_agents` from `agent_manifest.yaml`.

One round (`pick`) scans the remaining subtasks in order and adds a subtask to the wave when all
its prerequisites are done, the wave has fewer than `cap` members and the subtask conflicts with
no member already in the wave.  `rounds` repeats this until a round adds nothing.

* `schedule_waves_bounded` — every wave has at most `cap` subtasks;
* `schedule_waves_compatible` — no two subtasks of a wave conflict (so with the script's
  relation: no two share a role, and their write sets are disjoint);
* `schedule_deps_earlier` — every prerequisite of a scheduled subtask finished in an earlier wave;
* `schedule_perm` — every subtask is either scheduled exactly once or left over;
* `schedule_leftover_blocked` — with `0 < cap`, a left-over subtask is waiting on a prerequisite
  that never finished: the scheduler gives up on no subtask that could still run;
* `schedule_complete` — if the prerequisites are well founded (every prerequisite is a subtask of
  strictly smaller rank), nothing is left over.
-/
/-- A subtask is ready when all its prerequisites are among the finished identifiers. -/
/-- `t` may join the wave `w`: it conflicts with no member, in either direction. -/
/-- One round: scan `ts`, growing the wave `w`; returns the wave and the subtasks not taken. -/
/-- Repeated rounds, with `fuel` as an upper bound on their number. -/

/-- The scheduler: as many rounds as there are subtasks (`schedule_leftover_blocked` shows this
is enough). Returns the waves and the left-over subtasks. -/
/-- No two members of a wave conflict. -/
/-- Every subtask of every wave was ready when its wave started. -/
/-! ### One round -/
/-- If a round starting from the empty wave takes nothing (and `0 < cap`), nothing was ready. -/
/-! ### All rounds -/

/-- After enough rounds, every left-over subtask is not ready, measured against everything that
finished. -/
/-! ### The scheduler -/
/-- Every wave has at most `cap` subtasks. -/

/-!
# The merkaba–tower organism: the orchestration loop of the QBX agent layer

`QBX/agents/scripts/organism.py` is the control loop that sits above the Orchestrator's
scheduler (`delegate.py`, modelled in `Delegation.lean`).  It keeps a list of open
**obligations** (an unproved `sorry`, a registry warning, an ownership error, a to-do from
`project_state.json`, …) and turns them into verified results by alternating two phases:

* **generate** (even clock): take the obligations whose *tower level* is at most the current
  capability level and that are ready, and dispatch one wave of them to role agents with the
  scheduler's round `Delegation.pick` (at most `cap` agents, no two in conflict);
* **verify** (odd clock): an independent check (`verify t o`: the Lean build, the registry
  check, the ownership audit, …) runs on every obligation of the wave; the accepted ones are
  moved to `done`, the others stay open.

If the generate phase finds nothing to dispatch, the capability level is raised by one (the
*tower*: level `k` admits work of level `≤ k`, up to `maxLevel`; levels above `maxLevel` need a
human).  The loop stops when nothing is open or when `window` verify phases in a row accepted
nothing; the plateau counter is the State-of-Thought one-counter automaton
`Sovereign.Organism.feed` of `StoppingCore.lean`.

The two phases are the two tetrahedra of the merkaba: the organism's clock walks the Gray code
of the cube `Q₃`, and the generate phase is exactly the time spent on the even tetrahedron
(`merkaba_phase`).  So every tick crosses from one tetrahedron to the other, and nothing is
accepted in the phase that produced it.

Main results (for any obligations, any verifier and any parameters):

* `run_conserves` — open and done obligations together are always a permutation of the input:
  nothing is lost or invented;
* `run_sound` — every done obligation was accepted by the verifier at an odd (verify) clock,
  and its level is at most `maxLevel`;
* `run_topo` — `done` is in dependency order: every prerequisite of a done obligation is the
  key of an obligation done before it;
* `run_batch` — every dispatched wave has at most `cap` members, no two in conflict, all ready,
  open and within the capability level;
* `run_halts` — the loop halts within `2 (n (window + 1) + window) + 1` ticks, `n` the number
  of obligations;
* `run_complete` — with an honest verifier, levels `≤ maxLevel`, well-founded prerequisites,
  `0 < cap` and `maxLevel - cap₀ < window`, the loop halts with nothing open.
-/
/-- The parameters of the organism. -/
/-- identifier of an obligation (the scheduler's `key`) -/
/-- prerequisite identifiers -/
/-- two obligations may not be dispatched in the same wave -/
/-- at most this many agents per wave -/
/-- tower level of an obligation -/
/-- highest level the organism may raise itself to without a human -/
/-- the independent check at clock `t` -/
/-- stop after this many verify phases in a row without progress -/
/-- The state of the organism. -/
/-- Start: everything open, empty wave, capability level `cap₀`. -/
/-- The loop has stopped: nothing open, or a plateau of `window` verify phases. -/
/-- The open obligations within the capability level. -/
/-- The wave dispatched by the generate phase. -/
/-- Does the verify phase accept `o`? -/
/-- The obligations accepted by the verify phase. -/
/-- Generate phase. -/
/-- Verify phase. -/
/-- One tick. A halted organism rests. -/
/-- `n` ticks. -/
/-- `done` is in dependency order. -/
/-- The invariant of the loop. -/
/-! ### The merkaba clock -/

/-- The organism's position on the cube is the Gray code of its clock; the generate phase is
exactly the time spent on the even tetrahedron of the merkaba. -/
/-- While the organism runs, every tick moves it from one tetrahedron to the other. -/
/-! ### Safety -/
/-! ### Termination -/
/-- Potential: decreases at every tick of a running organism. -/
/-- The organism halts within `2 (n (window + 1) + window) + 1` ticks. -/
/-! ### Completeness -/
/-- The plateau counter is bounded by the escalations still available. -/

/-- With an honest verifier, every level within reach (`≤ maxLevel`), well-founded
prerequisites, at least one agent and a plateau window longer than the number of possible
escalations, the organism halts with nothing open. -/

/-!
# The Stein manifold behind the braid group: configuration space of `n` points in `ℂ`

The braid group `Bₙ` is the fundamental group of the unordered configuration space
`UConfₙ(ℂ) = Confₙ(ℂ) / Sₙ`, and the pure braid group is `π₁ (Confₙ(ℂ))`, where

  `Confₙ(ℂ) = {z ∈ ℂⁿ | zᵢ ≠ zⱼ for i ≠ j}`

(Fox–Neuwirth / Artin; cited, not formalised here).  `Confₙ(ℂ)` is the complement of the zero
set of the Vandermonde polynomial `V(z) = ∏_{i<j} (zⱼ - zᵢ)`, and `z ↦ (z, 1 / V(z))` identifies it
with the *closed* algebraic hypersurface `{(z, t) | t · V(z) = 1} ⊆ ℂⁿ × ℂ`.  A closed complex
submanifold of `ℂᴺ` is a Stein manifold, so this is the standard reason `Confₙ(ℂ)` is Stein.
This file proves the concrete, checkable ingredients of that statement:

* `mem_conf_iff_vandermonde_ne_zero`: `z ∈ Confₙ` iff `V(z) ≠ 0`;
* `isOpen_conf`: `Confₙ` is open in `ℂⁿ`;
* `isClosed_vandermondeHypersurface`: the hypersurface `t · V(z) = 1` is closed;
* `graphMap_isClosedEmbedding`: `z ↦ (z, V(z)⁻¹)` is a closed embedding of `Confₙ` (with the
  subspace topology) onto that hypersurface (`range_graphMap`);
* `differentiable_vandermonde`, `differentiableOn_inv_vandermonde`: `V` is holomorphic on `ℂⁿ`
  and `1 / V` is holomorphic on `Confₙ` — the extra coordinate of the embedding is a holomorphic
  function;
* `vandermonde_perm`, `vandermonde_sq_perm`: permuting the points multiplies `V` by the sign, so
  the discriminant `V²` is `Sₙ`-invariant and descends to `UConfₙ`;
* `perm_free`: `Sₙ` acts freely on `Confₙ`.

"Stein manifold" itself is not defined in Mathlib, and neither is the identification
`π₁ (UConfₙ(ℂ)) ≅ Bₙ`; both remain cited.  See `QBX/docs/design/BRAID_BIOLOGY_STEIN_TWIN.md` §4
for how this enters QBX and why it does not bear on twin primes.
-/
/-- The ordered configuration space of `n` distinct points in `ℂ`. -/
/-- The Vandermonde polynomial `∏_{i<j} (zⱼ - zᵢ)`. -/
/-- `Confₙ` is the non-vanishing locus of the Vandermonde polynomial. -/

/-- The Vandermonde polynomial is a polynomial in the coordinates: it is the evaluation of an
explicit multivariate polynomial with integer coefficients. -/
/-- `V` is holomorphic (complex differentiable) on all of `ℂⁿ`. -/
/-- `Confₙ` is open. -/
/-- `1 / V` is holomorphic on `Confₙ`. -/
/-- The closed hypersurface `{(z, t) | t · V(z) = 1}` in `ℂⁿ × ℂ`. -/
/-- The graph map `z ↦ (z, V(z)⁻¹)` on `Confₙ`. -/

/-- **`Confₙ(ℂ)` is a closed submanifold of `ℂⁿ⁺¹`**: the graph map is a closed embedding onto
the hypersurface `t · V(z) = 1`. -/
/-! ### The symmetric group action -/
/-- Permuting the points multiplies the Vandermonde polynomial by the sign. -/
/-- The discriminant `V²` is invariant under `Sₙ`, so it is a function on `UConfₙ(ℂ)`. -/
/-- `Confₙ` is `Sₙ`-stable. -/
/-- `Sₙ` acts freely on `Confₙ`: a permutation fixing a configuration is the identity. -/
/-! ### The case `n = 2`: `Conf₂(ℂ) ≅ ℂ × ℂ*`, whose fundamental group is `ℤ = B₂`. -/
