/-!
# Stein-lite: holomorphic convexity of `Confₙ(ℂ)`

`BRAID_BIOLOGY_STEIN_TWIN.md` §7 item 5 asks to "define holomorphic convexity for open subsets of
`ℂⁿ` and prove it for `Confₙ`; only then state anything about Stein manifolds in Lean".  This file
does exactly that.

For an open `U ⊆ ℂⁿ` and `K ⊆ U`, the **holomorphically convex hull** is

  `K̂_U = {z ∈ U | |f(z)| ≤ sup_K |f| for every f holomorphic on U}`,

and `U` is **holomorphically convex** if `K̂_U` is compact for every compact `K ⊆ U`.  For open
subsets of `ℂⁿ` this is the defining condition of a Stein manifold (the other two axioms —
separation of points and local coordinates by global holomorphic functions — hold trivially, the
coordinates themselves being global holomorphic functions), and by the Cartan–Thullen theorem it is
equivalent to being a domain of holomorphy.  Those equivalences are cited, not proved.

* `subset_holoHull`: `K ⊆ K̂_U` for compact `K ⊆ U` (so the hull is never smaller than `K`).
* `holoHull_subset_box`: every point of the hull of *any* `K` lies in the compact set
  `{z | ∀ i, |zᵢ| ≤ sup_K |zᵢ|, 1 ≤ (sup_K |1/P|) · |P(z)|}` — obtained from the holomorphic
  functions `zᵢ` and `1/P`.
* `holoConvex_nonvanishing`: **for every entire `P : ℂⁿ → ℂ`, the non-vanishing locus
  `{P ≠ 0}` is holomorphically convex.**
* `holoConvex_conf`: in particular `Confₙ(ℂ) = {V ≠ 0}` (Vandermonde) is holomorphically convex —
  the Stein property of the space whose fundamental group is the pure braid group, now proved in
  the concrete form it takes for domains of `ℂⁿ`.
* `zero_mem_holoHull_sphere`: the hull of the unit sphere contains the origin (maximum modulus), so
  hulls are genuinely larger than `K` and the definition is not vacuous.
* `holoConvex_univ`, `holoConvex_inter`: sanity checks (`ℂⁿ` itself, and intersections of
  non-vanishing loci, e.g. configuration spaces with punctures).
-/
/-- `sup_K ‖f‖` (Lean's `sSup`, which is `0` on the empty set). -/
/-- The holomorphically convex hull of `K` in `U`. -/
/-- `U` is holomorphically convex: hulls of compact subsets are compact. -/
/-- The hull contains `K` (for compact `K ⊆ U`). -/
/-- The compact "box" that traps the hull of any set in `{P ≠ 0}`. -/
/-- **The hull is trapped in the box**, using only the holomorphic functions `zᵢ` and `1/P`. -/

/-- The hull is closed inside any closed set containing it on which all holomorphic functions on
`U` are continuous. -/
/-- **The non-vanishing locus of an entire function on `ℂⁿ` is holomorphically convex.** -/

/-- **`Confₙ(ℂ)` is holomorphically convex** (hence Stein, by the cited equivalence for domains
in `ℂⁿ`). -/
/-- `ℂⁿ` is holomorphically convex. -/
/-- Intersections of non-vanishing loci are non-vanishing loci of the product. -/

/-- **The hull is genuinely larger than `K`** (maximum modulus principle): the hull in `ℂⁿ` of the
unit sphere (sup norm) contains the origin, which is not on the sphere. -/

/-!
# The braid group's own Stein domain: monic polynomials with distinct roots

`HolomorphicConvexity.lean` proves that `Confₙ(ℂ)` (ordered configurations, fundamental group the
*pure* braid group `Pₙ`) is holomorphically convex.  The full braid group `Bₙ` is the fundamental
group of the *unordered* configuration space `UConfₙ(ℂ) = Confₙ(ℂ)/Sₙ` (**cited**: Artin,
Fox–Neuwirth).  This file realises `UConfₙ(ℂ)` concretely as a domain of `ℂⁿ` and proves that it is
holomorphically convex too.

An unordered set of `n` distinct points `{z₁, …, zₙ} ⊂ ℂ` is the same thing as the monic polynomial
`∏ (X − zᵢ)` with distinct roots.  Writing a monic polynomial of degree `n` as
`X^n + aₙ₋₁X^{n−1} + ⋯ + a₀` identifies it with its coefficient vector `a ∈ ℂⁿ` (`monicOf`).

* `uconf n` — the coefficient vectors whose polynomial is separable (has `n` distinct roots).
* `polyDisc` — the resultant `Res(f, f')` of `f = monicOf a` and its derivative, with fixed sizes
  `n, n − 1`.  `mem_uconf_iff_polyDisc_ne_zero`: `a ∈ uconf n ↔ polyDisc a ≠ 0`.
* `differentiable_polyDisc`: `polyDisc` is an entire function of `a` (a determinant whose entries
  are affine in `a`).
* **`holoConvex_uconf`: `UConfₙ(ℂ)` is holomorphically convex** — Stein, by the cited
  equivalence for domains of `ℂⁿ`.  `isOpen_uconf`: it is open.
* The quotient map `rootsMap : Confₙ(ℂ) → UConfₙ(ℂ)`, `z ↦` coefficients of `∏ (X − zᵢ)`:
  * `monicOf_rootsMap`: `monicOf (rootsMap z) = ∏ (X − zᵢ)` (Vieta);
  * `differentiable_rootsMap`: it is holomorphic (the coefficients are the elementary symmetric
    polynomials up to sign);
  * `rootsMap_mem_uconf_iff`: `rootsMap z ∈ UConfₙ ↔ z ∈ Confₙ`;
  * `rootsMap_surjOn`: every point of `UConfₙ` comes from `Confₙ` (fundamental theorem of
    algebra);
  * `polyDisc_rootsMap`: `polyDisc (rootsMap z) = (−1)^{n(n−1)/2} · V(z)²` — the discriminant
    is the signed square of the Vandermonde, so `UConfₙ` and `Confₙ` have matching defining
    functions;
  * `rootsMap_perm`, `rootsMap_eq_iff`: over `UConfₙ` the fibres are exactly the `Sₙ`-orbits
    `z ∘ σ`.  Together with `perm_free` (`Sₙ` acts freely) this is the concrete form of
    `UConfₙ = Confₙ / Sₙ`.

So a QBX braid word on `n` strands is a loop in a holomorphically convex domain of `ℂⁿ`: the space
of monic degree-`n` polynomials with distinct roots, whose fundamental group is `Bₙ`.  The
identification `π₁ ≅ Bₙ` is cited, not proved.
-/
/-- The monic polynomial `X^n + ∑ aᵢ Xⁱ` with coefficient vector `a`. -/
/-- Unordered configurations of `n` distinct points of `ℂ`, as coefficient vectors. -/
/-- The discriminant-type polynomial `Res(f, f')` with fixed sizes `n, n − 1`. -/
/-- The coefficients of `∏ (X − zᵢ)` below degree `n`. -/
/-- Below degree `n`, the coefficients of `monicOf a` are the entries of `a`. -/
/-- `a ∈ UConfₙ` iff the resultant `Res(f, f')` does not vanish. -/
/-- Determinants of holomorphically varying matrices are holomorphic. -/
/-- `polyDisc` is an entire function on `ℂⁿ`. -/
/-- **The unordered configuration space `UConfₙ(ℂ)` is holomorphically convex.** -/
/-- Vieta: the coefficient vector `rootsMap z` gives back `∏ (X − zⱼ)`. -/
/-- The quotient map `Confₙ → UConfₙ` is holomorphic. -/
/-- Every monic polynomial with distinct roots is `∏ (X − zⱼ)` for some `z ∈ Confₙ`. -/

/-- **The fibres of `Confₙ → UConfₙ` are the `Sₙ`-orbits.**  (Only `w` needs distinct entries:
if `rootsMap z = rootsMap w`, then `z` has the same entries as `w`.) -/
/-! ### Discriminant and Vandermonde -/

/-- **The discriminant pulls back to the squared Vandermonde:**
`polyDisc (rootsMap z) = (−1)^{n(n−1)/2} · V(z)²`.  So the defining function of `UConfₙ` pulls
back to the (signed) square of the defining function of `Confₙ`, which is `Sₙ`-invariant
(`vandermonde_sq_perm`). -/

comments.text:
/-!
# Pentagon and hexagon equations for the Fibonacci and Ising anyon models

`qbx_ir.anyon.model` ships two multiplicity-free anyon models, each given by fusion rules,
F-symbols (`f_function`) and R-symbols (`r_symbols`):

* Fibonacci: labels `1, τ`, `τ ⊗ τ = 1 ⊕ τ`, `F^{τττ}_τ = [[φ⁻¹, φ^{-1/2}], [φ^{-1/2}, -φ⁻¹]]`,
  `R^{ττ}_1 = e^{-4πi/5}`, `R^{ττ}_τ = e^{3πi/5}`;
* Ising: labels `1, σ, ψ`, `σ ⊗ σ = 1 ⊕ ψ`, `σ ⊗ ψ = σ`, `ψ ⊗ ψ = 1`,
  `F^{σσσ}_σ = [[1, 1], [1, -1]] / √2`, `F^{ψσψ}_σ = F^{σψσ}_ψ = -1`,
  `R^{σσ}_1 = e^{-πi/8}`, `R^{σσ}_ψ = e^{3πi/8}`, `R^{σψ}_σ = R^{ψσ}_σ = -i`, `R^{ψψ}_1 = -1`;

all other admissible F- and R-symbols are `1`.  This file proves that these exact data are
consistent: they satisfy the **pentagon equation** and **both hexagon equations**
(`fib_pentagon`, `fib_hexagon`, `fib_hexagon_inv`, `ising_pentagon`, `ising_hexagon`,
`ising_hexagon_inv`).

Conventions (as in `qbx_ir.anyon.model`).  `F a b c d e f = [F^{abc}_d]_{e f}` is the change of
basis from `((a ⊗ b) → e) ⊗ c → d` to `a ⊗ ((b ⊗ c) → f) → d`, and `R a b c = R^{ab}_c`.  Both
are extended by `0` when a fusion vertex is not admissible, so the equations below are stated
for **all** labels (the extension by zero is what makes the sums over intermediate labels
meaningful).  Python's `r_symbol` returns `1` whenever one label is the vacuum, without checking
admissibility; it is only ever called on admissible triples, where the two agree.

The proofs are symbolic: the pentagon and hexagon equations are proved for the tables over any
commutative ring containing the relevant algebraic numbers (`fibFK_pentagon`, `fibFK_hexagon`,
`isingFK_pentagon`, `isingFK_hexagon`), and then specialised to the complex numbers used in
Python.
-/
/-! ### The coherence equations -/

/-- The pentagon equation for an F-symbol table `F a b c d e f = [F^{abc}_d]_{ef}`:
`[F^{fcd}_e]_{gl} [F^{abl}_e]_{fk} = ∑_h [F^{abc}_g]_{fh} [F^{ahd}_e]_{gk} [F^{bcd}_k]_{hl}`. -/

/-- The hexagon equation for an F-symbol table `F` and an R-symbol table `R a b c = R^{ab}_c`:
`R^{ca}_e [F^{acb}_d]_{eg} R^{cb}_g = ∑_f [F^{cab}_d]_{ef} R^{cf}_d [F^{abc}_d]_{fg}`.
The second hexagon equation is this one for the reversed braiding
`(a, b, c) ↦ (R^{ba}_c)⁻¹`. -/
/-! ### Fibonacci anyons -/
/-- Fibonacci anyon labels (Python labels `'1'`, `'τ'`). -/
/-- Fusion rules `N^c_{ab} ≠ 0` of the Fibonacci model: `τ ⊗ τ = 1 ⊕ τ`. -/

/-- The Fibonacci F-symbols with `u = φ⁻¹` and `s = φ^{-1/2}` as parameters (zero on
non-admissible vertices). -/

/-- The Fibonacci R-symbols with `R^{ττ}_1 = r1`, `R^{ττ}_τ = rt` (zero on non-admissible
vertices). -/
/-- The Fibonacci pentagon equation holds whenever `u² = 1 - u` and `s² = u`. -/

/-- The Fibonacci hexagon equation with `R^{ττ}_1 = -q`, `R^{ττ}_τ = q³`, for every root `q` of
the tenth cyclotomic polynomial, `u = q² - q³` and `s² = u`.  (For `q = e^{πi/5}`:
`-q = e^{-4πi/5}` and `u = φ⁻¹`.) -/
/-! ### Ising anyons -/
/-- Ising anyon labels (Python labels `'1'`, `'σ'`, `'ψ'`). -/

/-- Fusion rules `N^c_{ab} ≠ 0` of the Ising model: `σ ⊗ σ = 1 ⊕ ψ`, `σ ⊗ ψ = σ`,
`ψ ⊗ ψ = 1`. -/
/-- The Ising F-symbols with `s = 1/√2` as a parameter (zero on non-admissible vertices). -/

/-- The Ising R-symbols `R^{σσ}_1 = r1`, `R^{σσ}_ψ = rpsi`, `R^{σψ}_σ = R^{ψσ}_σ = rsp`,
`R^{ψψ}_1 = rpp` (zero on non-admissible vertices). -/
/-- `√2 · F`, an integer table over `ℤ[√2]`. -/

/-- The (scaled) Ising pentagon equation in `ℤ[√2]`, checked by the kernel on all `3⁹` label
assignments. -/
/-- The Ising pentagon equation holds whenever `s = 1/t` with `t² = 2`. -/

/-- The Ising hexagon equation with `R^{σσ}_1 = -z⁷`, `R^{σσ}_ψ = z³`, `R^{σψ}_σ = -z⁴`,
`R^{ψψ}_1 = -1`, for every `z` with `z⁸ = -1` and `s (z² - z⁶) = 1`.  (For `z = e^{πi/8}`:
`-z⁷ = e^{-πi/8}`, `-z⁴ = -i` and `z² - z⁶ = √2`.) -/

/-!
# The Fibonacci and Ising models of `qbx_ir.anyon` satisfy the pentagon and hexagon equations

The F- and R-symbols of `qbx_ir.anyon.model.fibonacci_model` and `ising_model`, as complex
numbers exactly as written in Python (`PHI = (1 + √5)/2`, `1/PHI`, `1/√PHI`, `1/√2`,
`exp(-4πi/5)`, …), and the proof that they satisfy the pentagon equation and both hexagon
equations (`IsPentagon`, `IsHexagon` in `QBX.Formal.AnyonCoherence`).

The symbolic proofs of `AnyonCoherence.lean` are specialised with `q = e^{πi/5}` (Fibonacci) and
`z = e^{πi/8}` (Ising) for the first hexagon equation, and with their complex conjugates
`e^{-πi/5}`, `e^{-πi/8}` for the second one.
-/
/-! ### Complex-number facts -/
/-- `e^{n x} = (e^x)^n` in the form used below. -/
/-! ### Fibonacci -/
/-- The reversed braiding `(R^{ba}_c)⁻¹` of a Fibonacci R-table. -/
/-- The golden ratio `φ = (1 + √5)/2` (Python `PHI`). -/

/-- The F-symbols of `fibonacci_model()`: `F^{τττ}_τ = [[1/φ, 1/√φ], [1/√φ, -1/φ]]`, all other
admissible F-symbols `1`, zero on non-admissible vertices. -/

/-- The R-symbols of `fibonacci_model()`: `R^{ττ}_1 = e^{-4πi/5}`, `R^{ττ}_τ = e^{3πi/5}`, all
other admissible R-symbols `1`, zero on non-admissible vertices. -/

/-- A non-zero `w` with `w + w⁻¹ = φ` is a root of the tenth cyclotomic polynomial and
`1/φ = w² - w³`. -/
/-- The pentagon equation for the Fibonacci F-symbols of `qbx_ir.anyon`. -/
/-- The (first) hexagon equation for the Fibonacci F- and R-symbols of `qbx_ir.anyon`. -/

/-- The second hexagon equation (reversed braiding `(R^{ba}_c)⁻¹`) for the Fibonacci F- and
R-symbols of `qbx_ir.anyon`. -/
/-- The reversed braiding `(R^{ba}_c)⁻¹` of an Ising R-table. -/

/-- The F-symbols of `ising_model()`: `F^{σσσ}_σ = [[1, 1], [1, -1]]/√2`,
`F^{ψσψ}_σ = F^{σψσ}_ψ = -1`, all other admissible F-symbols `1`, zero on non-admissible
vertices. -/

/-- The R-symbols of `ising_model()`: `R^{σσ}_1 = e^{-πi/8}`, `R^{σσ}_ψ = e^{3πi/8}`,
`R^{σψ}_σ = R^{ψσ}_σ = -i`, `R^{ψψ}_1 = -1`, all other admissible R-symbols `1`, zero on
non-admissible vertices. -/
/-- The pentagon equation for the Ising F-symbols of `qbx_ir.anyon`. -/
/-- The (first) hexagon equation for the Ising F- and R-symbols of `qbx_ir.anyon`. -/

/-!
# When can a braid of two anyons be undone by a phase shift?

Exchanging anyons `a` and `b` twice (a full monodromy) acts on the fusion channel `c` by
`M^{ab}_c = R^{ba}_c R^{ab}_c`.  If this number is the same for every channel `c` that `a ⊗ b`
can fuse to, the double braid is a global phase: a phase shift undoes it and the two anyons
are *separable by a phase shift*.  If it differs between channels, the double braid changes
the relative phase of the channels: it is an entangling operation that no global phase
shift can undo.

For the models of `qbx_ir.anyon` (tables `fibR`, `isingR` of `AnyonModels.lean`):

* `ising_sigma_psi_monodromy` — `σ` around `ψ` (single channel `σ`): the monodromy is `-1`,
  a phase shift by `π`.  Separable by a phase shift.
* `ising_sigma_sigma_monodromy` — `σ` around `σ`: channels `1` and `ψ` get opposite
  monodromies; not separable by a phase shift (this is what makes Ising braiding useful for
  gates such as the Clifford gates).
* `fib_tau_tau_monodromy_ne` — `τ` around `τ`: channels `1` and `τ` get different monodromies;
  not separable by a phase shift (this is what makes Fibonacci braiding universal for quantum
  computation).
-/
/-- The monodromy (double exchange) of `a` and `b` on fusion channel `c`. -/
/-- `σ` around `ψ` is the phase `-1`. -/

/-- `σ` around `σ`: the channel-`ψ` monodromy is minus the channel-`1` monodromy, so the
two differ. -/
/-- `τ` around `τ`: the channels `1` and `τ` get different monodromies. -/

/-!
# Bible text → braid (`qbx_bible`, encoding `letter-ordinal-v1`)

A Lean model of the conversion implemented by `QBX/src/qbx_bible/encode.py`, and proofs of its
properties.

**The model.**  A text is a list of characters.

* `isMark` — the combining marks the Python code drops: Hebrew points and cantillation
  (U+0591–U+05C7 except the punctuation maqqef U+05BE, paseq U+05C0, sof pasuq U+05C3 and
  nun hafukha U+05C6) and the combining diacritics U+0300–U+036F (Greek accents and breathings,
  Latin diacritics, after decomposition).  Unicode decomposition (NFKD) itself is not modelled:
  the model reads text that is already decomposed.  For pointed Hebrew without presentation forms
  (such as the bundled Westminster Leningrad Codex text) NFKD only reorders marks, and they are
  dropped anyway.
* `classify` — the letters: Hebrew `א…ת` (ordinal 1…22; the final forms `ך ם ן ף ץ` take the
  ordinal of their base letter and are flagged final), Greek `α…ω` / `Α…Ω` (1…24, final `ς`
  as `σ`), Latin `a…z` / `A…Z` (1…26).  Every other character separates words.
* `gen m sofit` — on `n = m + 2` strands a letter of ordinal `k` becomes the generator with
  0-based index `(k - 1) % (m + 1)` (Python: `σᵢ`, `i = (k − 1) mod (n − 1) + 1`, 1-based),
  inverted when the letter is final and the sofit rule is on.
* `tokenize` — the words of the text; `convert m sofit s` — the braid word of the whole text.

**Results.**

* `convert_eq_flatMap_tokenize`, `convert_eval_eq_prod_words`: the braid of a verse is the
  product of the braids of its words.
* `convert_append`, `convert_eval_append`: the braid of a passage is the product of the braids of
  its parts (conversion is a monoid homomorphism from texts to `B_n`).
* `convert_mark_invisible`: points, accents and cantillation never change the braid.
* `convert_length`, `convert_writhe`: crossings = letters; writhe = letters − 2·(final letters)
  with the sofit rule on, = letters with it off.
* `sofit_changes_element_iff`: toggling the sofit rule changes the braid group element **iff**
  the text contains a final letter (the discriminating test L2 of the testing plan).
* `decode_convert`: with at least 23 strands and the sofit rule on, a Hebrew text is recovered
  letter for letter (final forms included) from its braid word.
* `genesis_1_1_braid`, `genesis_1_1_braid_23`: on the pointed Westminster Leningrad Codex text of
  Genesis 1:1 the model produces exactly the words the Python implementation outputs.
-/
/-! ### Characters -/
/-- The 22 Hebrew letters in alphabetical order. -/
/-- Final (sofit) forms and their base letters. -/
/-- A combining mark dropped before conversion (see the module docstring). -/
/-- A letter of the text: its 1-based ordinal in its alphabet and whether it is a final form. -/
/-- The letter a character stands for, if any (`qbx_bible.encode.classify`). -/
/-- Hebrew letters, including the final forms. -/
/-- Marks are not letters. -/
/-! ### Words and the encoding -/

/-- Split a text into words: marks are skipped, letters accumulate into the current word, any
other character ends it.  Returns the open (leading) word and the later words. -/
/-- The words of a text, as lists of letters (`qbx_bible.encode.tokenize`). -/
/-- The generator of one letter on `m + 2` strands (`Encoding.generator`). -/
/-- The braid word of one word. -/
/-- The braid word of a text (`encode_text`): all its letters, in reading order. -/
/-- The letters of a text. -/
/-- The number of final letters of a text. -/
/-! ### Verses are products of words, passages are products of verses -/
/-- The words of a text are exactly its letters, split up. -/
/-- Words are never empty. -/
/-- The braid word of a verse is the concatenation of the braid words of its words. -/

/-- **Verse = product of words.**  The braid group element of a verse is the product of the
elements of its words, in reading order. -/

/-- **Passage = product of parts.**  Conversion turns concatenation of texts into
concatenation of braid words. -/
/-- Conversion as a monoid homomorphism from texts to the braid group. -/

/-- **Marks are invisible.**  Inserting a point, accent or cantillation mark anywhere in a text
does not change its braid word. -/
/-! ### Length and writhe -/
/-- One crossing per letter. -/

/-- **Writhe.**  Every letter is a positive crossing except the final letters under the sofit
rule, which are negative. -/

/-- **The sofit test.**  Toggling the sofit rule changes the braid group element of a text if and
only if the text contains a final letter. -/
/-! ### Decoding with at least 23 strands -/

/-- The Hebrew letter of a generator: index `i` is the `i`-th letter, inverted generators give
the final form when the letter has one (`qbx_bible.encode.decode_short`). -/
/-- The 27 Hebrew letters (base and final forms). -/
/-- The decoding check for one character, as a boolean. -/

/-- **Decoding.**  With at least 23 strands and the sofit rule on, the braid word of a Hebrew
text determines its letters exactly: decoding gives back the text with marks and separators
removed (final forms included). -/
/-- The short form (`±i`, 1-based) of a word, as in the Python code. -/

/-- Genesis 1:1, pointed and accented, as in `QBX/data/bible/genesis_1_wlc.tsv`
(Westminster Leningrad Codex). -/
/-- On 8 strands the model gives exactly the word `qbx_bible` outputs for Genesis 1:1. -/
/-- On 23 strands likewise. -/

/-- Genesis 1:1 has 7 words, 28 letters and 3 final letters; its braid has writhe 22, and the
sofit rule changes its braid group element. -/

comments.text:
/-!
# A fast, verified classifier for the Bible-braid conversion

`QBX.Formal.Bible.classify` follows the Python code literally: it searches the alphabets, which
are stored as strings.  Evaluated by the kernel this is slow — every letter is compared with up
to 130 characters, and every mark (points, cantillation: more than half the characters of a
pointed verse) goes through the whole search before being rejected.

`classifyCode` computes the same thing from the code point with a few comparisons of natural
numbers and one lookup in a 27-entry table.  `classifyCode_spec` proves that it agrees with
`classify` on **every** character, so `convertFast` (`convertFast_eq`) can replace `convert` in
any kernel computation without changing what is proved.  The per-verse certificates of
`QBX.Formal.BibleBraidGenesis1` use it.
-/

/-- Hebrew letters by offset from U+05D0 (`א`): ordinal and final flag.  The final forms sit
just before their base letters in Unicode. -/
/-- The letter of a code point, by arithmetic (`classify` on `Char.ofNat n`). -/
-- α … ρ, final ς (as σ), σ … ω
-- Α … Ρ, (U+03A2 is unassigned), Σ … Ω
/-- The code points `classifyCode` looks at. -/
/-- Every character `classify` knows. -/
/-- **The fast classifier is correct**: it agrees with `classify` on every character. -/
/-- The conversion computed with the fast classifier. -/
/-- **`convertFast` is `convert`.** -/

comments.text:
/-!
# Genesis 1: the Lean model agrees with the Python implementation

Generated by `QBX/scripts/gen_lean_bible_table.py` from `QBX/data/bible/genesis_1_wlc.tsv`:
for each of the 31 verses, the pointed text and the braid words that `qbx_bible` outputs on
8 strands (sofit rule on and off) and on 23 strands (sofit rule on).

`genesis_1_model_agrees_with_python` checks that the Lean model `QBX.Formal.Bible.convert`
produces exactly these words for every verse.

**How the check is organised (scaled out).**  Checking the whole table in one kernel
evaluation, as an earlier version of this file did, needed more than 40 GB of memory.  Now
every verse is its own certificate, made of two small kernel evaluations:

* `gen1_k_text`: the verse string is `String.ofList` of an explicit character list.  This
  direction (encoding characters) is several times cheaper for the kernel than decoding the
  string with `String.toList`;
* `gen1_k_fast`: the braid words, computed with the arithmetic classifier `convertFast`, which
  `convertFast_eq` proves equal to `convert`.

`VerseRecord.agrees_of` turns the two into the statement about `convert` and `String.toList`,
and the final theorem collects the 31 verse certificates.  Each certificate is checked
independently (and can be checked in parallel).
-/
/-- One verse with the words the Python implementation outputs. -/
/-- The cross-check of one verse given its characters, as a boolean. -/
/-- The cross-check of one verse, as a boolean. -/

/-!
# Audit of `docs/research/harmonic_bible_braid_bridge.md`

The bridge document mixes claims of several kinds.  This file checks every claim in it that is a
precise mathematical statement about objects QBX already defines, and records the claims that turn
out to be false, with the corrected statement proved instead.

**Lexical encoder (§"Four readings").**
* `lexical_conflates_eq_lt`: `letter-ordinal-v1` gives `a+b=b+a` and `a+b<b+a` the same braid
  word (the symbols are word separators).
* `lexical_not_alpha_invariant`: it gives `a+b=b+a` and `x+y=y+x` different braid group elements
  (on the default 8 strands and on 23 strands).

**Test 1 (22 letters ↦ 22 generators of `B₂₃`).**
* `alphabet_braid_23`: on 23 strands the alphabet `א…ת` is the word `σ₁ σ₂ ⋯ σ₂₂`.
* `alphabet_gen_injective_iff`: the 22 letters get 22 distinct generators iff there are at least
  23 strands.

**A4 / F5 ("gematria factors through the abelianization", "a layer strictly below the braid
layer") — false as stated.**
* `abelian_sigma_eq` (in `BraidSeparability.lean`): every homomorphism from `B_n` to an abelian group takes the
  same value on all generators, so no such homomorphism assigns letters distinct values.
* `gematria_not_abelian_invariant`: in particular gematria (any scheme with two distinct letter
  values, e.g. the seeded table) is not a homomorphism `B₂₃ → ℤ` along the letter encoding.
* `gematria_not_braid_function`: worse, gematria is not a function of the braid at all:
  `אבא` and `באב` encode to the same element of `B₂₃` (braid relation) but have values 4 and 5.
* `wordValue_perm`: what *is* true — gematria is invariant under reordering letters, i.e. it
  factors through the free commutative monoid on the letters (not through `B_n`).

**Name values (§"What checks out exactly", §"The three formal patterns").**
* `names_hechrachi`: with final letters valued as their base letters (mispar hechrachi) every value
  quoted in the document is correct (`אלהים = 86`, `יהוה = 26`, `אדני = 65`, `אל שדי = משה = 345`,
  `אברם = 243 = 3⁵`, `אברהם = 248`, `מה = אדם = 45`, `בליעל = 142`, `תאומיאל = 488`).
* `names_standard`: with the table QBX actually seeds (`Gematria.standard`, finals 500–900) the
  words ending in a final letter get different values (`אלהים = 646`, `אדם = 605`, `אברם = 803`,
  `אברהם = 808`), so `מה ≠ אדם`.  The document's "these are exactly `wordValue` (H-040)" holds for
  the scheme `hechrachi`, not for the seeded table.

**Adam, Lilith, the bride (§"The three, formally").**
* `adam_bride_eq_one`, `adam_lilith_layers`: Adam·bride is the trivial braid; Adam·Lilith has
  Adam's permutation and writhe but is a different braid.

**The commutator (§"The concrete next test") — false as stated.**
* `commutator_not_pure`: `[σ₁, σ₂] = σ₁σ₂σ₁⁻¹σ₂⁻¹` has writhe 0 but its permutation is a 3-cycle,
  not the identity: it is not a pure braid and is not "H-069 in a different guise".

**`7! = 5040` (§"The one strong structural alignment").**
* `perm_layer_seven`: the image of `permHom : B₇ → S₇` has 5040 elements and the kernel (the
  pure braid group `P₇`) is non-trivial.

**The serpent (B5).**
* `braidGroup_two_comm`, `braidGroup_not_comm`: `B₂` is commutative, `B_n` is not for `n ≥ 3`.

**Arithmetic (A3, McClain).**
* `starForms_card`, `starForms_eleven`, `starForms_coprime`: for odd `p ≥ 3` there are `(p-3)/2`
  regular star polygons `{p/k}` up to reflection; 4 for `p = 11`; for prime `p` each is traced in a
  single stroke.
* `pythagorean_comma`, `syntonic_ne_pythagorean`: `3¹²/2¹⁹ = 531441/524288`, and `81/80` (the
  syntonic comma) is a different ratio — the document calls `81:80` "the Pythagorean comma at the
  semitone level", which is a misnomer.
* `septimal_deficiency`, `methuselah`, `sarah_mersenne`, `jacob`: `(7/5)²/2 = 49/50`,
  `969 = 3·17·19`, `127 = 2⁷ − 1` is prime, `147 = 3·7²`.
-/
/-! ### The lexical encoder -/
/-- `letter-ordinal-v1` cannot tell `=` from `<`: both are word separators. -/
/-- Two texts with different reduced Burau entries are different braids. -/

/-- `letter-ordinal-v1` is not invariant under renaming variables, on the default 8 strands and
on 23 strands: `a+b=b+a` and `x+y=y+x` are different braids (their reduced Burau matrices at
`t = -1` differ in the top-left entry, `-1` against `1`). -/
/-! ### Test 1: the alphabet on 23 strands -/
/-- On 23 strands the 22 letters `א…ת` become the 22 generators `σ₁, …, σ₂₂` in order. -/

/-- The 22 Hebrew letters (by ordinal) get pairwise distinct generators on `m + 2` strands iff
`m + 2 ≥ 23`. -/
/-! ### Gematria and the braid layer -/
/-- The gematria letter (index into `Gematria.Letter`, seed order) of a Hebrew character. -/
/-- The gematria value of a Hebrew string under a scheme (non-letters are ignored). -/

/-- No homomorphism `B₂₃ → ℤ` sends the generator of each letter to the letter's gematria value,
for any scheme in which two letters have different values. -/
/-- `אבא` and `באב` are the same braid in `B₂₃` (the braid relation `σ₁σ₂σ₁ = σ₂σ₁σ₂`). -/

/-- **Gematria is not a function of the braid.** No map from `B₂₃` computes the gematria
(seeded table) of a text from the braid of its `letter-ordinal-v1` encoding. -/
/-- Gematria does factor through reordering: it is a function of the multiset of letters. -/
/-! ### Name values -/
/-- Mispar hechrachi with final letters valued as their base letters. -/
/-! ### Adam, Lilith and the bride -/
/-- Adam: `σ₁σ₂` on three strands. -/
/-! ### The commutator `[σ₁, σ₂]` -/
/-! ### The serpent -/
/-! ### Arithmetic -/
/-- The regular star polygons `{p/k}` up to reflection (`k ~ p - k`): `2 ≤ k < p/2`. -/

/-!
# Crossing changes, strand passage and the decatenation bound

`BRAID_BIOLOGY_STEIN_TWIN.md` §7 lists two open items:

* (4) the **crossing change lemma** for general braids: replacing one `σᵢ` by `σᵢ⁻¹` changes one
  linking number by exactly `1`;
* (3) **DNA on `n` strands**: catenanes produced by replication as `n`-component closures, with
  type II topoisomerase acting by crossing changes.

A crossing change is the local move `a · σᵢ · b ⟷ a · σᵢ⁻¹ · b` (`CrossingChange`).  It is exactly
what a type II topoisomerase does to a catenane: cut one double-stranded segment, pass another one
through the gap, reseal.  Results:

* `permHom_crossingChange`, `closureComponents_crossingChange`: the strand permutation, hence the
  set of closure components (the rings of the catenane), is unchanged.
* `crossMatrix_crossingChange`: the crossing matrix changes by `2` in exactly the two symmetric
  entries of the two strands `ccLeft a i`, `ccRight a i` that meet at the changed crossing.
* `linkingNumber_crossingChange`: for any two sets of strands `C, D`, the linking number changes by
  `blockSum (crossE u v) C D`; `blockSum_crossE` evaluates this.
* **Crossing change lemma** (`linkingNumber_crossingChange_of_mem`): if the two strands lie on
  different components `C ∌ v`, `D ∋ v` with `u ∈ C`, the linking number `lk(C, D)` changes by
  exactly `1`; `linkingNumber_crossingChange_self`: a self-crossing of one component leaves its
  linking numbers with every other component unchanged.
* `totalLinking g = Σ_{C ≠ D} |lk(C, D)|` (ordered pairs of components).  `totalLinking_le`: one
  crossing change lowers it by at most `2`.
* **Decatenation bound** (`decatenation_lower_bound`): a sequence of `k` crossing changes (type II
  strand passages) that ends in a link whose components are pairwise homologically unlinked must
  have `totalLinking g ≤ 2k`, i.e. `k ≥ Σ_{unordered pairs} |lk|`.
* **Sharpness for replication catenanes** (`catenane_decatenation`): for the two-ring catenane
  `σ₁^{2m}` (the torus link `T(2, 2m)`, the product of replicating a circular duplex with `m`
  residual intertwinings), the minimum number of strand passages needed to unlink it is
  exactly `|m|`.
* **Sharp decatenation for every braid closure** (section `SharpDecatenation`, below;
  `decatenation_minimum`, `sharp_decatenation`): for every braid on any number of strands, the
  minimum number of strand passages that makes all pairwise linking numbers vanish is exactly
  `Σ_{unordered pairs} |lk|`.  Caveat: "all linking numbers zero" is weaker than "split" — the
  Borromean rings and the Whitehead link have all linking numbers zero but cannot be pulled apart.
-/
/-! ### The local move -/
/-- A crossing change: `a · σᵢ · b ⟷ a · σᵢ⁻¹ · b` (in either direction). -/
/-- The (starting labels of the) two strands that meet at the crossing `σᵢ` placed after `a`. -/
/-- See `ccLeft`. -/

/-- **The crossing matrix under a crossing change**: it changes by `2` exactly in the entries of
the two strands meeting at the changed crossing. -/
/-- The block sum of a single crossing pattern. -/
/-- **Linking numbers under a crossing change** (any sets of strands `C, D`). -/

/-- **Crossing change lemma**: a crossing change between strands on two different components
changes their linking number by exactly `1`. -/

/-- A self-crossing of one component does not change its linking number with any component
disjoint from it. -/
/-! ### Total linking and the decatenation bound -/
/-- Total linking `Σ_{C ≠ D} |lk(C, D)|` over ordered pairs of distinct closure components. -/
/-- The total linking is the sum of the absolute values of the linking spectrum. -/
/-- At most one ordered pair of components `(C, D)` has `u ∈ C` and `v ∈ D`. -/
/-- **One crossing change lowers the total linking by at most `2`.** -/
/-- Along a sequence of `k` crossing changes the total linking drops by at most `2k`. -/

/-- **Decatenation bound.**  If `k` crossing changes (type II strand passages) turn `g` into a link
whose components are pairwise homologically unlinked, then `totalLinking g ≤ 2k`, i.e.
`k ≥ Σ_{unordered pairs of components} |lk|`. -/
/-! ### Replication catenanes `σ₁^{2m}` -/
/-- The two-ring catenane `σ₁^{2m}` has total linking `2|m|`. -/
/-- One strand passage removes one intertwining: `σ₁^{2(m+1)} ⟷ σ₁^{2m}`. -/

/-- **Sharp decatenation of a replication catenane**: `σ₁^{2m}` can be unlinked by `|m|` strand
passages, and no sequence of fewer crossing changes reaches a homologically unlinked pair of
rings. -/

/-!
## Sharp decatenation for every braid closure

The sections above prove the **lower bound**: `k` crossing changes (type II topoisomerase strand
passages) that end in a homologically unlinked link force `totalLinking g ≤ 2k`, and sharpness
for the two-ring catenane `σ₁^{2m}`.  `STRUCTURAL_ENHANCEMENTS.md` §6 item 2 asks for sharpness on
more catenane families.  This section proves it for **every** braid closure, on any number of
strands and with any number of rings (`decatenation_minimum`: matching upper and lower bound):

* `crossMatrix_mul_sigma`, `crossMatrix_mul_sigma_inv`: appending `σᵢ^{±1}` to `g` adds
  `± crossE (ccLeft g i) (ccRight g i)` to the crossing matrix.
* `exists_pos_crossing`, `exists_neg_crossing`: if the block sum of the crossing matrix over
  `C × D` is positive (negative), then some word for `g` has a positive (negative) crossing between
  a strand of `C` and a strand of `D`: `g = a · σᵢ^{±1} · b` with the two strands meeting there split
  between `C` and `D`.
* `totalLinking_step`: if two distinct components have `lk(C, D) ≠ 0`, one crossing change lowers
  the total linking by exactly `2`.
* **Sharp decatenation** (`sharp_decatenation`): every braid closure can be made homologically
  unlinked by exactly `totalLinking g / 2 = Σ_{unordered pairs} |lk|` strand passages, and
  (`decatenation_lower_bound`) no shorter sequence of crossing changes does it.  In particular
  `totalLinking g` is always even (`totalLinking_even`).

So for a chain of `n` replication rings with linking numbers `m₁, …, m_{n−1}` between neighbours
(or any other catenane presented as a braid closure), the minimum number of type II passages
that removes all pairwise linking is `Σ |mⱼ|`.  "Homologically unlinked" (all pairwise linking
numbers zero) is weaker than "split": e.g. the Whitehead link and Borromean rings have all
linking numbers zero, so this count is the minimum for removing *linking numbers*, not for
achieving a split link.
-/
/-- All pairwise linking numbers between distinct closure components vanish. -/
/-! ### Appending one crossing -/
/-! ### Locating a crossing between two components -/
/-- The property proved by induction in `exists_pos_crossing` / `exists_neg_crossing`. -/
/-- If the block sum over `C × D` is positive, some positive crossing joins `C` and `D`. -/
/-- If the block sum over `C × D` is negative, some negative crossing joins `C` and `D`. -/
/-! ### One passage lowers the total linking by exactly two -/

/-- If two distinct components are linked, some crossing change lowers the total linking by
exactly `2`. -/

/-- The bookkeeping behind `totalLinking_step`: if the linking numbers change by `s · e`,
`s = ±1`, where `e` counts the crossing between `u ∈ C` and `v ∈ D`, and `s · lk(C, D) ≥ 1`, then
the total linking drops by exactly `2`. -/

/-- If two distinct components are linked, some crossing change lowers the total linking by
exactly `2`. -/
/-! ### Sharp decatenation -/

/-- **Sharp decatenation.**  Every braid closure can be made homologically unlinked by exactly
`k` strand passages, where `2k = totalLinking g = Σ_{C ≠ D} |lk(C, D)|`.  Together with
`decatenation_lower_bound`, `k = Σ_{unordered pairs} |lk|` is the minimum. -/
/-- The total linking `Σ_{C ≠ D} |lk(C, D)|` is always even. -/

/-- **The minimum number of strand passages.**  There is a sequence of `k` crossing changes
turning `g` into a homologically unlinked closure, and every such sequence has length at least
`k`; here `2k = totalLinking g`, i.e. `k = Σ_{unordered pairs of rings} |lk|`. -/

/-!
# DNA topology as two-strand braid closures: linking number and topoisomerases

A closed circular DNA duplex is, topologically, the closure of a two-strand braid `σ₁ᵏ`: the two
backbones wind around each other `k` half-turns.  QBX's closure invariants (`ClosureLinking.lean`)
give the standard biological bookkeeping exactly:

* `numComponents_sigma_zpow`: the closure of `σ₁ᵏ` has two components (two separate circular
  strands, as in a duplex) iff `k` is even; for odd `k` it is a single circle.
* `linkingSpectrum_duplex`: the duplex `σ₁^{2m}` has linking number `Lk = m` between its strands
  (the spectrum is `{m, m}`, one entry per ordered pair of strands).
* `eq_of_markovEquiv_duplex`: two duplexes are related by Markov moves (so possibly isotopic as closed
  links) only if they have the same `Lk` — so `Lk` is a topological invariant that no
  deformation without strand breakage can change.
* **Topoisomerases.**  A type I topoisomerase passes one strand through a nick, multiplying by
  `σ₁^{±2}` (`Lk ↦ Lk ± 1`, `lk_topoI`); a type II topoisomerase passes a double-stranded segment
  through a double-strand break, which in the two-strand picture multiplies by `σ₁^{±4}`
  (`Lk ↦ Lk ± 2`, `lk_topoII`).  Hence `topoII_reachable_parity`: type II steps alone never change
  the parity of `Lk`, while `topoI_reachable` shows type I steps reach every `Lk`.

The decomposition `Lk = Tw + Wr` (Călugăreanu–White–Fuller) is differential geometry and is not
formalised here; only the integer `Lk`, which is the topological part, is.
See `QBX/docs/design/BRAID_BIOLOGY_STEIN_TWIN.md` §3.
-/
/-- The single crossing of two strands. -/
/-- One full turn of the double helix, `σ₁²` (the Hopf-link braid). -/
/-- A closed duplex with `m` full turns: `σ₁^{2m}`. -/
/-- **Two separate strands iff an even number of crossings.** -/
/-- **The duplex `σ₁^{2m}` has linking number `m`.** -/
/-- The linking number of the two strands of a closed duplex. -/
/-- The duplex as a QBX word (`2|m|` letters of sign `sign m`). -/
/-- **`Lk` is a topological invariant**: duplexes related by Markov moves have equal `Lk`. -/
/-! ### Topoisomerases -/
/-- A type I topoisomerase step (single-strand passage): multiply by `σ₁^{±2}`. -/
/-- A type II topoisomerase step (double-strand passage): multiply by `σ₁^{±4}`. -/
/-- **Type II topoisomerases preserve the parity of `Lk`.** -/
/-- In particular type II steps cannot take an odd-`Lk` duplex to the relaxed state `Lk = 0`. -/
/-- **Type I topoisomerases reach every linking number.** -/

/-!
# Protein folding on a lattice: the parity rule of the HP model

The hydrophobic–polar (HP) model of Lau and Dill places the residues of a protein chain at the
sites of the lattice `ℤᵈ` (`d = 2` square, `d = 3` cubic) along a self-avoiding walk.  Two residues
form a *contact* when they sit at neighbouring sites without being neighbours in the chain; the
energy of a fold is minus the number of contacts between two hydrophobic (`H`) residues.

The lattice `ℤᵈ` is bipartite (colour a site by the parity of its coordinate sum), and every
chain bond changes the colour.  Main results:

* `QBX.Formal.Fold.color_walk`: residue `i` has colour `colour(residue 0) + i`;
* `QBX.Formal.Fold.contact_odd`: a contact `(i, j)` always has `j - i` odd, in every dimension;
* `QBX.Formal.Fold.contact_three_le`: hence `j ≥ i + 3` — no contact skips exactly one residue;
* `QBX.Formal.Fold.energy_eq_zero_of_same_parity`: if all `H` residues sit at positions of the
  same parity, then *every* fold has energy `0` — such sequences cannot be stabilised by
  hydrophobic contacts at all in this model (a design rule, independent of the fold);
* `QBX.Formal.Fold.uTurn_contact`: the four-residue U-turn realises a contact (so the parity
  rule is not vacuous).

These are statements about the lattice model, which is a coarse caricature of real proteins;
see `QBX/docs/design/BRAID_BIOLOGY_STEIN_TWIN.md` §3.
-/
/-- Lattice sites in `ℤᵈ`. -/
/-- Two sites are lattice neighbours (`ℓ¹` distance `1`). -/

/-- A fold of a chain of `n` residues: consecutive residues are lattice neighbours and the walk
is self-avoiding. -/
/-- A (topological) contact: residues at neighbouring sites that are not chain neighbours. -/
/-- The bipartite colour of a site: parity of its coordinate sum. -/
/-- Neighbouring sites have opposite colours. -/
/-- Along a fold, colours alternate. -/
/-- **Parity rule.** In every dimension, a contact joins residues an odd distance apart. -/
/-- Contacts skip at least two residues. -/
/-- An HP sequence: `true` = hydrophobic (`H`), `false` = polar (`P`). -/
/-- The `H–H` contacts of a fold, as a finite set of pairs. -/
/-- HP energy: minus the number of `H–H` contacts. -/

/-- **Design rule.** If all hydrophobic residues occupy positions of one parity, no fold has an
`H–H` contact, so every fold has energy `0`. -/
/-! ### A concrete fold with a contact (square lattice) -/
/-- The U-turn `(0,0) → (1,0) → (1,1) → (0,1)` on the square lattice. -/

comments.text:
/-!
# Rational tangles and site-specific recombination, through `B₃ → SL(2, ℤ)`

In the tangle model of site-specific recombination (Ernst–Sumners), the enzyme-bound DNA is a
pair of strands in a ball — a *2-string tangle* — and the enzymes produce *rational tangles*,
obtained from the zero tangle by twisting the four endpoints.  Conway attached to each rational
tangle a fraction `p/q ∈ ℚ ∪ {∞}` and proved it is a complete invariant (cited, not formalised).
Twisting acts on fractions by Möbius transformations:

* horizontal twist `T ↦ T + 1`, i.e. `(p, q) ↦ (p + q, q)`  — the image of `σ₁`;
* vertical twist `T ↦ T/(T + 1)`, i.e. `(p, q) ↦ (p, p + q)` — the image of `σ₂⁻¹`.

So three-strand braids act on tangle fractions through `b3ToSL2`.  Main results:

* `act_sigma0`, `act_sigma1_inv`: the two twists, as above;
* `primitive_act`: the action preserves `gcd(p, q) = 1` (fractions stay in lowest terms);
* `exists_braid_of_primitive`: every fraction `p/q` in lowest terms is reached from the zero
  tangle `0/1` by some three-strand braid — so (granting Conway's theorem) every rational tangle
  is a braided zero tangle;
* `parity_act`: the *parity class* `(p mod 2, q mod 2)` — which determines how the four endpoints
  are connected inside the tangle, and whether the numerator closure `N(p/q)` is a knot (`p` odd)
  or a two-component link (`p` even) — transforms by the strand permutation of the braid
  (through `S₃ ≅ SL(2, 𝔽₂)`, `PermCongruence.lean`);
* `parity_act_pure`: pure braids never change the parity class.  In particular a pure-braid
  twisting step can never turn a knotted product into a two-component catenane or back.

The knot-theoretic facts quoted (Conway's classification; components of `N(p/q)`) are cited.
See `QBX/docs/design/BRAID_BIOLOGY_STEIN_TWIN.md` §3.
-/
/-- A tangle fraction `p/q` as the vector `(p, q)`. -/
/-- The braid action on tangle fractions. -/
/-- The zero tangle `0/1`. -/
/-- `σ₁` is the horizontal twist `T ↦ T + 1`. -/
/-- `σ₂⁻¹` is the vertical twist `T ↦ T / (T + 1)`. -/
/-- A fraction in lowest terms. -/
/-- **Lowest terms are preserved.** -/
/-- **Every fraction in lowest terms is a braided zero tangle.** -/
/-- The parity class `(p mod 2, q mod 2)`. -/
/-- **The parity class moves by the strand permutation.** -/
/-- Braids with the same strand permutation act identically on parity classes. -/
/-- **Pure braids preserve the parity class.** -/

/-- Example: `σ₁²` (a full horizontal twist, the Hopf-link clasp) sends `0/1` to `2/1`, keeping
the parity class `(0, 1)`. -/

declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem cdMul_linear : ∀ n,
    (∀ (x y z : CD R n), cdMul n x (cdAdd n y z) = cdAdd n (cdMul n x y) (cdMul n x z)) ∧
    (∀ (x y z : CD R n), cdMul n (cdAdd n x y) z = cdAdd n (cdMul n x z) (cdMul n y z)) ∧
    (∀ (c : R) (x y : CD R n), cdMul n x (cdSmul c n y) = cdSmul c n (cdMul n x y)) ∧
    (∀ (c : R) (x y : CD R n), cdMul n (cdSmul c n x) y = cdSmul c n (cdMul n x y))
  | 0 => ⟨fun x y z => mul_add (x : R) y z, fun x y z => add_mul (x : R) y z,
      fun c x y => by show (x : R) * (c * y) = c * (x * y); ring,
      fun c x y => by show (c * x : R) * y = c * (x * y); ring⟩
  | n + 1 => by
    obtain ⟨hr, hl, sr, sl⟩

  | 0, x, y => map_mul f (x : R) y
  | n + 1, x, y => by

      rw [cdMap_add, cdMap_neg, cdMap_mul, cdMap_mul, cdMap_conj]; rfl
    · show cdMap f n (cdAdd n (cdMul n y.2 x.1) (cdMul n x.2 (cdConj n y.1))) = _
      rw [cdMap_add, cdMap_mul, cdMap_mul, cdMap_conj]; rfl

/-!
# Sedenion box kites: the zero-divisor claim of `unified-picture.md`, checked in Lean

The source (`unified-picture.md`, "Leech-Sedenion-Fano Zero-Divisor Stratification") makes claims
about the sedenion vectors `±e_a ± e_(8+b)`.  The sedenions are level 4 of the Cayley–Dickson
tower with the project's product `(a, b)(c, d) = (a c - d̄ b, d a + b c̄)`
(`SpookyPrimes.Sedenion.mul`).  A label `(a, b, s, t)` names `s·e_a + t·e_(8+b)` (`vec`).

Proved here:

* `finrank_annihilator_primitive` — each of the 168 *primitive* vectors (`a ≠ b`, both in
  `1 … 7`; `card_primitive`) has a 4-dimensional real annihilator `{y | u y = 0}`.
* `annihilator_not_primitive` — the other 88 vectors of that shape (`card_not_primitive`) have
  trivial annihilator.
* `ann_symm` — `u w = 0 ↔ w u = 0` on these vectors; `card_ann` — each primitive vector kills
  exactly 8 of them (so the annihilation graph is 8-regular).
* `annGraph_reachable_iff` — the annihilation graph has 7 connected components, indexed by the
  *kite index* `a xor b` (`card_kite`: 24 vectors each); `kite_units`: the component with index
  `k` uses exactly the six imaginary octonion units other than `e_k`, i.e. it misses one point of
  the Fano plane.
* `same_partners_iff`, `not_ann_twin`, `partners_two_classes` — twin classes (same partners) have
  size 4 and are explicit, there is no edge inside a class, and the partners of a vector form
  exactly two classes; so each component collapses to a 6-cycle of classes.

This is de Marrais's box-kite structure.  No Leech lattice, `E₇` or `G₂` enters.

Method.  The linear algebra is reduced to integer-matrix certificates
(`finrank_ker_of_cert`, `injective_of_cert`) whose entries come from the sedenion multiplication
table (`basis_mul_basis`).  Zero products have a closed form (`ann_iff_annF`: the four terms of
`u w` cancel in pairs), every column of a left-multiplication matrix has two non-zero entries
(`mul_fastL_apply`), and the certificates are sparse, so every finite check is evaluated by the
kernel (`decide +kernel`).  No `native_decide` is used: the theorems depend only on `propext`,
`Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound` (registry H-202).
-/
/-- Scalar multiplication on the Cayley–Dickson tower. -/
/-- The Cayley–Dickson product is additive and homogeneous in each argument. -/
/-- Left multiplication by `a`, read in coordinates, is the matrix `Lmat a`. -/
/-- Apply a ring homomorphism to every coordinate. -/

/-- **Kernel certificate.**  Integer matrices `A, B, Q, F` with `A B = 0`, `Bᵀ B = d • 1`,
`d • F = B (Bᵀ F)` and `Q A = e • 1 - F` (`d, e ≠ 0`) force the real kernel of `A` to be the
column span of `B`, of dimension `k`. -/
/-- **Invertibility certificate**: `Q A = e • 1` with `e ≠ 0` makes `A` injective over `ℝ`. -/

/-- A label `(a, b, s, t)` names the sedenion `s·e_a + t·e_(8+b)` with signs `s, t = ±1`
(`true` is `+1`). There are `8 · 8 · 4 = 256` labels. -/
/-- The sign `±1` of a Boolean. -/
/-- The integer coordinates of the sedenion named by a label. -/
/-- The sedenion `s·e_a + t·e_(8+b)` over a commutative ring `R`. -/
/-- **Primitive** labels: `a ≠ b`, both in `1 … 7`. There are `7 · 6 · 4 = 168` of them. -/
/-- The (right) annihilator `{y | u y = 0}` of a real sedenion `u`, as a subspace of `ℝ¹⁶`. -/
/-- Signs of the basis products: `e_i e_j = sigma i j · e_(i xor j)` (row `i`, column `j`). -/
/-- The table as an array. -/

/-- The table packed into one natural number: bit `16 i + j` is set iff `e_i e_j = -e_(i xor j)`
(`sigma_eq_signTable`).  Bit operations on literals are evaluated natively by the kernel, so the
kernel checks below can look up a sign in constant time. -/
/-- `sigma` is the displayed table. -/
/-- Bitwise xor of two indices. -/
/-- **Multiplication table of the sedenion basis** (checked by the kernel). -/
/-- Index of the low basis vector `e_a` of a label. -/
/-- Index of the high basis vector `e_(8+b)` of a label. -/
/-- The left-multiplication matrix of a label's sedenion, read off the multiplication table. -/
/-- Coordinates of the product of two labels' sedenions, from the table. -/

/-- The product of the two named sedenions vanishes (over `ℤ`; equivalently over `ℝ`,
`mul_vec_real_eq_zero_iff`). -/
/-- Over `ℝ` the product of two named sedenions vanishes iff it vanishes over `ℤ`. -/

/-! ### Zero products in closed form

`u w` for `u = s e_a + t e_(8+b)` and `w = s' e_c + t' e_(8+d)` has four terms, at the positions
`a ⊕ c`, `b ⊕ d` (low half) and `8 + (b ⊕ c)`, `8 + (a ⊕ d)` (high half).  It vanishes iff the two
low terms cancel and the two high terms cancel (`ann_iff_annF`). -/
/-- Four signed unit vectors, two in each half, sum to zero iff they cancel in pairs. -/
/-- The closed-form test for a zero product. -/
/-- All 256 labels, as a list. -/
/-- The partner index: a zero product `(a, b, ·, ·)(c, d, ·, ·)` forces `d = a ⊕ b ⊕ c`. -/
/-- The annihilating partners of a label, computed from the closed form (`mem_nbrs`). -/

/-! ### Sparse certificates

Every column of `fastL l` has two non-zero entries (`mul_fastL_apply`), and every label vector has
two non-zero coordinates (`sum_coeffs_mul`).  The certificates below are therefore checked entry by
entry with a constant amount of work per entry, by the kernel (`decide +kernel`). -/
/-- `(G · fastL l) i j`, read off the two non-zero entries of column `j` of `fastL l`. -/
/-- Pairing with a label vector reads two coordinates. -/
/-- `∀ i : Fin 16`, as a Boolean loop. -/
/-- `∀ c : Fin 4`, as a Boolean loop. -/
/-- The conjugate label: `conj(s e_a + t e_(8+b)) = ±s e_a - t e_(8+b)`. -/
/-- The invertibility certificate `L_ū L_u = 2` for a label, entry by entry. -/
/-- The annihilating partners of `l` whose first sign is `+`. -/
/-- The `c`-th entry of a list of (four) partners. -/
/-- The `16 × 4` matrix whose columns are the partners' vectors. -/
/-- Rows of `P Pᵀ` that are non-zero. -/

/-- The certificate matrix `G` with `G · L_u = 2 - P Pᵀ`: row `j` takes row `a ⊕ j` of `L_u`, and
also row `(8 + b) ⊕ j` when `j` is not covered by a partner. -/
/-- `(P Pᵀ) i j`, written out. -/

/-- The certificate checks for a given list of partners: orthogonal of norm `2`, and
`G · L_u = 2 - P Pᵀ`, entry by entry. -/

/-- The kernel certificate for a label: exactly four partners, and the checks of `kerCheckL`.
(The `match` makes the kernel compute the partner list once.) -/
/-- `∀ l : Label`, from a Boolean loop over `allLabels`. -/

/- The largest kernel computation in the file (one sparse `6 × 16` certificate per primitive
label); it needs more than the default heartbeat budget. -/

/-- **Each of the 168 primitive zero divisors `±e_a ± e_(8+b)` (`a ≠ b` in `1 … 7`) has a
4-dimensional real annihilator** `{y ∈ ℝ¹⁶ | u y = 0}`. -/

/-- **The other 88 vectors of the same shape are not zero divisors**: for `a = b` or `a = 0` or
`b = 0`, `u y = 0` forces `y = 0`. -/
/-- The **kite index** `a xor b ∈ {1, …, 7}` of a label (a point of the Fano plane). -/
/-- The twin class of a label: `(a, b, s, t)`, `(a, b, -s, -t)`, `(b, a, s, -t)`, `(b, a, -s, t)`. -/

/-- One pass over all partner lists: a zero product `l m = 0` is between primitive labels, is
symmetric, preserves the kite index, and is shared by the twins of `l`. -/
/-- Zero products among labels only occur between primitive labels. -/
/-- **`u w = 0` is symmetric** on the labels. -/
/-- No label squares to zero. -/

/-- **Every primitive label annihilates exactly 8 labels** (so the annihilation graph on the
168 primitive vectors is 8-regular, with `168 · 8 / 2 = 672` edges). -/
/-- Zero products preserve the kite index. -/
/-- Each kite index `k = 1, …, 7` carries 24 primitive labels. -/

/-- **The kite with index `k` uses exactly the six imaginary octonion units other than `e_k`**:
it misses one Fano point, namely `k`. -/
/-- The annihilation graph on the 168 primitive labels. -/
/-- A root label for each kite index. -/
/-- Every primitive label lies within distance 3 of the root of its kite. -/

/-- **The annihilation graph has exactly 7 connected components, one per Fano point**: two
primitive labels are connected iff they have the same kite index. -/
/-- Twins share partners: every partner of `l` is a partner of each member of its twin class. -/
/-- The twin relation is symmetric. -/

/-- The candidates for a label with the partners of `l`: the partners `m` of the first partner
`p` of `l` that annihilate every partner of `l`, all of which must be twins of `l`.  (The `match`
makes the kernel compute `nbrs l` once.) -/

/-- **Twins.** Two primitive labels have the same annihilating partners iff they lie in the same
twin class (classes of size 4; 42 classes). -/
/-- No zero product inside a twin class. -/
/-- The partners of `l` are exactly the union of the twin classes of two of them. -/

/-- **The quotient by twins is 2-regular**: the 8 partners of a primitive label form exactly two
twin classes.  With 6 classes per kite and the kite connected, each kite's quotient is a 6-cycle. -/

  /-- R02: `σ_i^a σ_j^b → σ_j^b σ_i^a` for `|i - j| ≥ 2`. -/

  /-- R03: `σ_i^e σ_j^e σ_i^e → σ_j^e σ_i^e σ_j^e` for `|i - j| = 1`. -/

/-!
# QBX-IR core: braid words, the braid group, and the rewrite rules R01–R03

This file formalises Phase 10 of the QBX build plan (`QBX/docs/reference/QBX.md` §35–§36):
the core algebraic rewrite system of QBX-IR.

* `BraidGroup n` is the Artin braid group on `n` strands, presented by generators
  `sigma i` (`i : Fin (n - 1)`, crossing the strands at positions `i` and `i + 1`, 0-indexed)
  subject to the braid relation and far commutation.
* `Word n` is the QBX-IR word: a list of letters `σ_i^{±1}`, read bottom to top, as in the
  Python class `qbx_ir.core.braid.Braid` (whose generator indices are 1-indexed).
* `Rule` lists the QBX rewrite rules R01 (inverse cancellation), R02 (far commutation) and
  R03 (Yang–Baxter, in both sign variants); `Step` applies a rule anywhere inside a word.

Main results:

* `QBX.Formal.Step.eval_eq`: every rewrite step preserves the braid group element
  (soundness: "QBX rewrite ⇒ preserves declared semantics", QBX.md §35).
* `QBX.Formal.eval_eq_iff_eqvGen`: two words represent the same braid group element **iff**
  they are connected by rewrite steps used forwards or backwards (completeness of R01–R03).
* `QBX.Formal.wordQuotientEquiv`: the QBX word calculus modulo R01–R03 is isomorphic to `B_n`.
-/
/-- The braid relations of `B_n` as relators in the free group on `Fin (n - 1)`. -/
/-- The Artin braid group on `n` strands. -/
/-- The standard generator `σ_i` of `B_n` (0-indexed: it crosses strands `i` and `i + 1`). -/
/-- The braid (Yang–Baxter / Reidemeister III) relation. -/
/-- Far commutation. -/
/-- A letter of a QBX-IR braid word: `σ_idx` if `pos`, `σ_idx⁻¹` otherwise. -/
/-- A QBX-IR braid word, read bottom to top. -/
/-- The inverse letter. -/
/-- The braid group element of a letter. -/
/-- The braid group element represented by a word. -/
/-- The QBX rewrite rules, as rewrites of short subwords. -/
/-- R02: `σ_i^a σ_j^b → σ_j^b σ_i^a` for `|i - j| ≥ 2`. -/
/-- R03: `σ_i^e σ_j^e σ_i^e → σ_j^e σ_i^e σ_j^e` for `|i - j| = 1`. -/
/-- One rewrite step: apply a rule to a subword. -/
/-- **Soundness.** Every QBX rewrite step preserves the braid group element. -/
/-- Soundness for arbitrary chains of rewrites in either direction. -/
/-! ### The word calculus modulo R01–R03 is a group -/
/-- The inverse word: reverse and invert every letter. -/
/-- The setoid "connected by QBX rewrites". -/
/-- QBX words modulo the rewrite rules R01–R03. -/
/-- The class of a word. -/
/-- The generator `σ_i` as a class of words. -/
/-- The homomorphism `B_n → WordQuot n` sending `σ_i` to the class of the word `[σ_i]`. -/

/-- **Completeness.** Two words represent the same element of `B_n` if and only if they are
connected by a chain of QBX rewrite steps (each used forwards or backwards). -/
/-- Evaluation as a homomorphism out of the word calculus. -/
/-- Every braid group element is represented by some QBX word. -/
/-- The QBX word calculus modulo the rewrite rules R01–R03 is isomorphic to the braid group. -/

/-!
# Reduced Burau / Alexander certificates: the theory

The definitions and theorems of `QBX.Formal.BraidBurauCert` that do not depend on the test
vectors (certificate encodings, uniqueness, Alexander certificates, and the evaluation checks
`checkBurauCert`, `checkAlexCert`, `checkBurauVector`).  Split out so that the test-vector
modules `QBX.Formal.BraidBurauCert.Vectors.*` can be checked in parallel
(`QBX/docs/design/KERNEL_SCALING_PATTERN.md`).  See `QBX.Formal.BraidBurauCert` for the overview.
-/
/-! ### The stored matrix -/
/-- Coefficient `k` of entry `(i, j)` in a flat coefficient list (size `m`, width `w`). -/
/-- Entry `(i, j)` of the matrix encoded by `(lo, w, cs)`. -/
/-- The matrix fields of a `braid_burau` row. -/
/-- The encoding is canonical: the right length, and the window is the smallest one. -/
/-- The matrix a certificate encodes. -/
/-- **The encoding is unique**: a canonical certificate is determined by its matrix. -/
-- a non-zero coefficient at offset `k` of one certificate forces the other window
/-! ### Certificates of words -/
/-- The symbolic reduced Burau matrix over `ℤ[t, t⁻¹]`. -/
/-- `c` is the (matrix part of the) certificate of `w`: canonical, encoding `ρ̄(w)`. -/
/-- **Certificates decide Burau equality exactly.** -/
/-- **Soundness of the transport check.**  Equal braids have equal certificates. -/
/-- **Inequality certificates.**  Different certificates prove different braids. -/
/-! ### Alexander certificates -/
/-- The Laurent polynomial `c₀ + c₁ t + ⋯` of a coefficient list. -/

/-- The normalisation of `qbx_ir.algebra.laurent.Laurent.normalize_unit`: empty (the zero
polynomial), or positive constant coefficient and non-zero last coefficient. -/
/-- The Alexander numerator `det(I - ρ̄(w))` over `ℤ[t, t⁻¹]`. -/

/-- `a` is the Alexander certificate of `w`: normalised, and
`a(t) · (1 + ⋯ + t^{n-1}) = ±t^k · det(I - ρ̄(w))` (Python: `alexander_polynomial`). -/
/-- Two normalised lists whose polynomials differ by a unit `±t^s` are equal. -/
-- the shift is zero
-- the sign is `+`
-- equal lengths
/-- **The Alexander certificate is determined by the Alexander numerator.** -/
/-- Equal braids have equal Alexander certificates. -/
/-- Conjugate braids have equal Alexander certificates. -/

/-- **Non-conjugacy certificates.**  Braids with different Alexander certificates are not
conjugate in `B_n`. -/
/-! ### Deciding certificates by evaluation -/
/-- The entries of `ρ̄(w)` have exponents in `[-length, length]`. -/
/-- The units `1, 2, …, N` of `ℚ`. -/
/-- The window half-width used for a Burau check. -/

/-- The kernel-checkable test: the certificate is canonical, and the matrix it encodes agrees
with `ρ̄(w)` at `t = 1, 2, …, 2B + 1`. -/
/-- **A passed check proves the certificate exactly.** -/
/-- The window half-width used for an Alexander check. -/

/-- The kernel-checkable test of an Alexander certificate with witnesses `k`, `ε`:
`a(t) (1 + ⋯ + t^{n-1}) = ε t^k det(I - ρ̄(w)(t))` at `t = 1, 2, …, 2B + 1`. -/
/-- **A passed check proves the Alexander certificate exactly.** -/
/-! ### Agreement with the Python implementation -/

/-- A test vector `(n, word, exp_min, width, coefficients, alexander, k, ε)`: the certificate
of `qbx_ir.burau_ledger.burau_values` and the witnesses `k`, `ε`
(`scripts/gen_burau_vectors.py`). -/
/-- Both checks for a test vector. -/

/-!
# Reduced Burau / Alexander certificates of the braid ledger (migration 024)

Migration `024_braid_burau.sql` stores, for a registered braid on `n` strands, the symbolic
reduced Burau matrix `ρ̄(B) ∈ GL_{n-1}(ℤ[t, t⁻¹])` (`Word.burau (T 1) (T (-1))`, see
`BurauRep.lean`) and the normalised Alexander polynomial of the closure.  The reference is
`qbx_ir.burau_ledger`.  The matrix is stored as

* `exp_min`, `width`: the smallest common exponent window of the entries;
* `coefficients`: the coefficient of `t^(exp_min + k)` in entry `(i, j)` at index
  `(i · (n-1) + j) · width + k`.

The Alexander polynomial is stored as its coefficient list `c₀, c₁, …` normalised up to
`±t^k` (lowest degree `0`, `c₀ > 0`; empty for `0`).

This file proves, for every strand count:

* `BurauCert.eq_of_mat_eq`: the encoding is unique (a canonical certificate is determined by
  the matrix it encodes), hence
* `burauCert_eq_iff`: two certificates are equal **iff** the Burau matrices are equal;
  `burauCert_eq_of_eval_eq` / `eval_ne_of_burauCert_ne`: equal braids have equal certificates
  (the transport check can never fire on correct data) and different certificates prove
  different braids;
* `alexCert_unique`: the normalised Alexander polynomial is determined by the Alexander
  numerator `det(I - ρ̄(B))`; hence `alexCert_eq_of_eval_eq` and `alexCert_conj`, and
  `not_isConj_of_alexCert_ne`: different Alexander certificates prove that the braids are not
  conjugate in `B_n`;
* `burau_agrees_with_python`: on test vectors the Python certificates are exactly the Lean
  certificates (exact equality of Laurent polynomials, decided by evaluation at enough points,
  `eq_of_evalAt_eq`).

Registry: H-063, H-064.
-/

/-! The test vectors from the Python implementation: 1–4 strands, the trefoil and its mirror,
the figure-eight knot, split closures (Alexander polynomial `0`) and the commutator
`σ₁²σ₂²σ₁⁻²σ₂⁻²`.

Following `QBX/docs/design/KERNEL_SCALING_PATTERN.md`, each vector is a separate definition with
its own kernel check (`burau_check_00` … `burau_check_16`), in the modules
`QBX.Formal.BraidBurauCert.Vectors.*`, which Lake checks in parallel; `burau_checks_pass` combines
them.  The theory lives in `QBX.Formal.BraidBurauCert.Core`. -/
/-- All test vectors, in the order of `scripts/gen_burau_vectors.py`. -/

/-- **Combiner.**  The test vectors pass the kernel-checked evaluation tests: the conjunction of
the seventeen independent checks. -/
/-- A passed vector check proves both certificates exactly. -/

/-- **The Lean model agrees exactly with the Python certificates** on the test vectors: every
stored matrix is exactly `ρ̄(B)` over `ℤ[t, t⁻¹]` and every stored Alexander polynomial is the
normalised Alexander polynomial. -/
/-! ### A non-conjugacy certificate -/
/-- `σ₁σ₂⁻¹σ₁σ₂⁻¹` (closure: the figure-eight knot). -/
/-- `σ₁σ₂⁻¹` (closure: the unknot). -/

/-- **The Alexander certificate detects non-conjugacy.**  `σ₁σ₂⁻¹σ₁σ₂⁻¹` and `σ₁σ₂⁻¹` have the
same writhe (`0`) and both permutations are 3-cycles, but their Alexander certificates
(`1 - 3t + t²` and `1`) differ, so they are not conjugate in `B_3`. -/

/-!
# A free subgroup of the pure braid group and a collision-free hash on group words

`BraidHash.lean` showed that bits read as `σ₁, σ₂⁻¹` give a collision-free hash on bit strings,
i.e. those two letters generate a free *monoid*.  `BRAID_BIOLOGY_STEIN_TWIN.md` §7 item 2 asks
for freeness of a larger letter set via a ping-pong argument.  This file proves the classical
result (Sanov's theorem, lifted to braids):

* `sanov_injective`: the matrices `A² = [[1,2],[0,1]]` and `B² = [[1,0],[2,1]]` generate a
  **free group** of rank 2 in `SL(2, ℤ)`: the homomorphism `F₂ → SL(2, ℤ)` sending the two free
  generators to them is injective.  Proof: Mathlib's ping-pong lemma
  (`FreeGroup.injective_lift_of_ping_pong`) for the action on non-zero integer vectors, with the
  four ping-pong sets given by slopes (`x/y > 1` or `y = 0`; `x/y ≤ −1`; `y/x ≥ 1` or `x = 0`;
  `y/x < −1`), written as quadratic inequalities (`X0`, `Y0`, `X1`, `Y1`).
* `braidSquares_injective`: hence `σ₁²` and `σ₂⁻²` generate a free group of rank 2 inside `B₃`.
  Both are pure braids, so **the pure braid group `P₃` contains a free group of rank 2**
  (`sigma_sq_pure`).
* `freeHash`: a hash on *reduced group words* over the 4-letter alphabet `{σ₁^{±2}, σ₂^{∓2}}`
  (2 bits per letter, backtracking forbidden).  `freeHash_injective`: distinct elements of `F₂`
  (equivalently distinct reduced words) have distinct hashes.  Unlike the monoid hash of
  `BraidHash.lean`, this one also has inverses, so `hash(w⁻¹) = hash(w)⁻¹` (`freeHash_inv`) —
  messages can be "un-hashed" letter by letter on the right.
* **Any number of strands** (section `NStrands`, below): `braidSquaresN_injective`,
  `freeHashN_injective` — the same freeness and collision-freeness in `Bₙ` for every `n ≥ 3`,
  via the reduced Burau representation at `t = −1`.
-/
/-- Non-zero integer vectors `(x, y)`. -/
/-- An integer matrix acting on a vector `(x, y)`. -/
/-- The action of an integer matrix of determinant one on non-zero vectors. -/
/-- `SL(2, ℤ)` acting on non-zero vectors, as a homomorphism to permutations. -/
/-! ### The ping-pong sets -/
/-- Slope `x/y > 1` or `y = 0`. -/
/-- Inverse slope `y/x ≥ 1` or `x = 0`. -/
/-- Inverse slope `y/x < −1`. -/
/-! Disjointness of the four sets. -/
/-! The four ping-pong inclusions. -/
/-- The two generators. -/
/-- **Sanov's theorem**: `A²` and `B²` generate a free group of rank 2 in `SL(2, ℤ)`. -/
/-! ### Braids -/
/-- The free generators in the braid group: `σ₁²` and `σ₂⁻²`. -/
/-- **`σ₁²` and `σ₂⁻²` generate a free group of rank 2 in `B₃`.** -/
/-- Both free generators are pure braids, so the free group lies in `P₃`. -/
/-- The hash of a group word over `{σ₁^{±2}, σ₂^{∓2}}`, as an integer matrix. -/
/-- **No collisions on reduced words**: distinct elements of `F₂` hash differently. -/

/-!
## The free braid hash on any number of strands

The sections above prove that `σ₁²` and `σ₂⁻²` generate a free group of rank 2 in `B₃`, using
the torus map `B₃ → SL(2, ℤ)`, which only exists for three strands.
`STRUCTURAL_ENHANCEMENTS.md` §6 item 1 asks for the statement for `n ≥ 4` strands.  This section
proves it for every `n ≥ 3`, using the reduced Burau representation of `BurauRep.lean` at
`t = −1` (which exists on every `Bₙ`) in place of the torus map:

* `TopBlock`: integer matrices whose rows `2, 3, …` are identity rows.  They are closed under
  products (`TopBlock.mul`), and on them the top-left `2 × 2` block is multiplicative
  (`topLeft_mul`), giving a homomorphism `topLeftHom : topBlockGroup →* GL(2, ℤ)`.
* The Burau matrices of `σ₁^{±1}`, `σ₂^{±1}` are `TopBlock` (they only change rows `0`, `1`) and
  their top-left blocks are `[[1,1],[0,1]]` and `[[1,0],[1,1]]` — the torus matrices.  So the
  Burau images of `σ₁²`, `σ₂⁻²` have top-left blocks `A² = [[1,2],[0,1]]`, `B² = [[1,0],[2,1]]`.
* **`braidSquaresN_injective`**: for every `n ≥ 3`, `σ₁²` and `σ₂⁻²` generate a free group of
  rank 2 in `Bₙ` (by Sanov's theorem `sanov_injective`); both lie in the pure braid group `Pₙ`
  (`sigma_sq_pureN`).
* `freeHashN_injective`: the hash of reduced group words over `{σ₁^{±2}, σ₂^{∓2}}` has no
  collisions in any `Bₙ`, `n ≥ 3`, and is multiplicative.
-/
/-! ### Block-triangular matrices -/
/-- Integer matrices whose rows with index `≥ 2` are rows of the identity matrix. -/
/-- The top-left `2 × 2` block. -/
/-- Invertible `(n − 1) × (n − 1)` integer matrices. -/
/-- Invertible integer matrices `U` with `U` and `U⁻¹` both `TopBlock`. -/
/-- The top-left block as a homomorphism `topBlockGroup n →* GL(2, ℤ)`. -/
/-- The reduced Burau representation of `Bₙ` over `ℤ` at `t = −1`. -/
/-- The free generators `σ₁²`, `σ₂⁻²` in `Bₙ`. -/
/-- The Burau images of the free generators, lifted to `topBlockGroup`. -/
/-- **For every `n ≥ 3`, `σ₁²` and `σ₂⁻²` generate a free group of rank 2 in `Bₙ`.** -/
/-- Both free generators are pure braids, so the free group lies in the pure braid group `Pₙ`. -/
/-- The hash of a group word over `{σ₁^{±2}, σ₂^{∓2}}` in `Bₙ`. -/
/-- **No collisions in any `Bₙ`, `n ≥ 3`**: distinct reduced words give distinct braids. -/

/-!
# Braid hashing: a Cayley hash through `B₃ → SL(2, ℤ)`, its freeness and its collisions

A *Cayley hash* reads a bit string as a word in two group generators and multiplies them out.
QBX already has `b3ToSL2 : B₃ →* SL(2, ℤ)` (`σ₁ ↦ [[1,1],[0,1]]`, `σ₂ ↦ [[1,0],[-1,1]]`).  This
file studies the hash obtained by reading a bit string as a three-strand braid word and applying
`b3ToSL2`.  Which pair of braid letters is used for the two bits decides everything:

* **Bits ↦ `σ₁, σ₂⁻¹` (mixed signs): no collisions over `ℤ`.**  The images are the Stern–Brocot
  matrices `A = [[1,1],[0,1]]`, `B = [[1,0],[1,1]]`, and `braidHash_injective` proves the hash is
  injective on all bit strings.  Corollary `encode_injective`: distinct bit strings give distinct
  braids, i.e. the submonoid of `B₃` generated by `σ₁` and `σ₂⁻¹` is free.
* **Bits ↦ `σ₁, σ₂` (both positive): collisions forced by the braid relation.**
  `posHash_braid_collision` (`010` and `101` collide: that is `σ₁σ₂σ₁ = σ₂σ₁σ₂`) and
  `posHash_twelve_eq_one` (the 12-bit string `(01)⁶` hashes to the identity: `(σ₁σ₂)⁶ = Δ⁴` lies in
  the kernel).  Any hash that factors through the braid group inherits every braid relation as a
  collision (`hash_respects_braid`).
* **Reduction mod `p`: collisions must exist** (`hashMod_not_injective`), since `SL(2, 𝔽_p)` is
  finite.  Freeness over `ℤ` is exactly the Euclidean-algorithm (continued fraction) structure
  of `SL(2, ℕ)`, which is also why such hashes over `𝔽_p` are not considered secure.
* `braidHash_append`: the hash is a monoid homomorphism (hash of a concatenation is the product),
  so it can be computed in parallel and in any bracketing — unlike Merkle–Damgård hashes.

See `QBX/docs/design/BRAID_BIOLOGY_STEIN_TWIN.md` §2.
-/
/-! ### The mixed-sign hash -/
/-- Bit `false ↦ σ₁`, bit `true ↦ σ₂⁻¹`. -/
/-- A bit string as a three-strand braid word. -/
/-- The Stern–Brocot generator matrices. -/
/-- The braid hash of a bit string, as an integer matrix. -/
/-- The hash is a monoid homomorphism from strings under concatenation. -/
/-- **The hash factors through the braid group**: it is `b3ToSL2` of the encoded braid. -/
/-- The two first letters can be read off: `A·N = B·N'` is impossible. -/
/-- **No collisions over `ℤ`.** -/

/-- **The braid monoid generated by `σ₁` and `σ₂⁻¹` is free**: distinct bit strings encode
distinct braids. -/
/-! ### Collisions forced by the braid relation -/

/-- Any hash that factors through `B₃` identifies words equal in `B₃`; in particular every
rewrite R01–R03 is a collision. -/
/-- Bit `false ↦ σ₁`, bit `true ↦ σ₂` (both positive). -/
/-- The positive-letter hash. -/
/-- `010` and `101` collide: the braid relation `σ₁σ₂σ₁ = σ₂σ₁σ₂`. -/
/-- The 12-bit string `(01)⁶` hashes to the identity. -/
/-- The positive hash is not injective. -/
/-! ### Reduction mod `p` -/
/-- The hash reduced modulo `p`. -/
/-- Over a finite ring collisions are unavoidable. -/

/-!
# Invariant certificates of the braid ledger (migration 020)

Migration `020_braid_invariants.sql` stores, for a registered braid, an *invariant
certificate*: the permutation, the writhe, the closure components and the pairwise linking
numbers of the closure, all recomputed by the database from the word.  The reference is
`qbx_ir.invariant_ledger`.  The database also uses the certificates in two ways:

* along every accepted rewrite and derivation the two certificates must agree;
* two braids whose certificates differ are certified *unequal* (`braid_inequality_certified`).

Both uses are sound exactly when every recorded quantity is a function of the braid group
element.  This file proves that, for every strand count `n`:

* `pairSum f p w` is the loop the database runs over the crossings of a word: starting from
  the arrangement `p` of strands, each letter crosses the strands at its two positions and
  adds its sign times a weight `f` of that (unordered) pair of strands;
* `pairSum_eq_of_eval_eq`: for every weight `f`, `pairSum f 1 w` depends only on the braid
  group element of `w`;
* the certificate data are instances: the writhe is the constant weight `1`
  (`pairSum_one_eq_writhe`), the crossing totals per pair of strands are the weight
  `Pi.single e 1` (`Word.crossings`), and the linking totals per pair of closure components
  are an indicator weight (`Word.linkTotal`) whose component labelling is any function of the
  permutation (`linkTotal_eq_of_eval_eq`);
* `InvariantCert` / `Word.cert` collect them; `cert_eq_of_eval_eq` and its contrapositive
  `eval_ne_of_cert_ne` are the soundness of the two uses above;
* `linkTotal_even`: when the labelling is constant along the permutation and `a ≠ b`, the
  linking total is even, so the stored linking number (half of it) is exact;
* `crossings_detect_more`: in `B_3`, `σ₁² σ₂⁻²` has the identity permutation and writhe `0`, but
  its crossing totals certify that it is not the identity — the per-pair data is strictly
  stronger than permutation and writhe.

Registry: H-052, H-053.
-/
/-- The sign of a crossing: `+1` for `σ_i`, `-1` for `σ_i⁻¹`. -/

/-- The unordered pair of strands crossed by the letter `l` when the strands are arranged by
`p` (`p q` is the strand at position `q`). -/

/-- The crossing loop of the database: from the arrangement `p`, each letter adds its sign
times the weight `f` of the pair of strands it crosses, then swaps the two positions. -/
/-- A rule rewrites the crossing loop to itself, from any arrangement. -/

/-- **The crossing loop is an invariant.**  For every weight `f`, the loop run from the initial
arrangement depends only on the braid group element of the word. -/
/-- With the constant weight `1` the crossing loop is the writhe. -/

/-- The crossing totals of a word: for each unordered pair of strands (named by their initial
positions), the sum of the signs of the crossings between them. -/

/-- The linking total of the closure components labelled `a` and `b`, for a labelling `comp`
of the strands: the sum of the signs of the crossings between a strand of one and a strand of
the other.  The stored linking number `lk(C_a, C_b)` is half of it. -/

/-- The linking totals depend only on the braid group element, whenever the components are
labelled by any function `label` of the permutation (as the database does: components are the
cycles of the permutation, numbered by their smallest strand). -/

/-- The data of an invariant certificate: the permutation, the writhe and the crossing totals
per pair of strands.  The stored components and linking numbers are computed from these. -/
/-- The certificate the database computes from a word. -/

/-- **Soundness of the certificates.**  Words representing the same braid have the same
certificate; in particular every accepted rewrite and derivation joins braids with equal
certificates. -/

/-- **Inequality certificates.**  Braids with different certificates are different elements
of `B_n`. -/

/-- Every quantity computed from the certificate (components, linking numbers, …) is a braid
invariant. -/

/-! ### The linking totals are even

The database stores `lk(C_a, C_b)` as half the linking total.  The halving is exact: when the
labelling is constant along the permutation (components are unions of cycles) and `a ≠ b`,
the linking total is even.  The proof counts the pairs of positions `x < y` holding a strand
of `C_a` below a strand of `C_b`: a crossing between `C_a` and `C_b` changes that count by one,
any other crossing leaves it alone, and at the end the strands of each component occupy their
initial positions again. -/

/-- The number of pairs of positions `x < y` holding a strand labelled `a` below a strand
labelled `b`, for the arrangement `p`. -/

/-- **The halving is exact.**  If the labelling `comp` is constant along the permutation of
`w` and `a ≠ b`, the linking total of the components labelled `a` and `b` is even. -/
/-- The word `σ₁ σ₁ σ₂⁻¹ σ₂⁻¹` in `B_3`. -/

/-- **The crossing totals detect more.**  `σ₁² σ₂⁻²` has the identity permutation and writhe
`0`, like the empty word, but its crossing totals differ, so it is not the identity of `B_3`. -/

declarations.signature_heuristic: def hiddenWord : Word 3

declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem hiddenWord_burau : Word.burau (-1 : ℤ) (-1) hiddenWord = !![5, 2; 2, 1]

      ∀ {G : Type} [CommGroup G] (f : BraidGroup 3 →* G), f hiddenWord.eval = 1

/-!
# A braid hidden from the permutation and phase layers, visible to the Burau layer

The braid `σ₁² σ₂⁻²` on three strands (QBX indices `0` and `1`) has trivial permutation and
writhe `0`, so the routing layer and every phase-type invariant
(`abelian_eq_of_writhe_eq`) see it as the identity braid.  Its reduced Burau matrix at
`t = -1` is `[[5, 2], [2, 1]] ≠ 1`, so it is not the identity: the Burau layer sees it.

This is the formal content of "layered disclosure": publishing only a coarse layer of a
braid (its routing permutation, or any phase) reveals nothing about information carried in
the finer layers.
-/
/-- The word `σ₁² σ₂⁻²` on three strands. -/

/-- **Layered disclosure.** `σ₁² σ₂⁻²` is a non-trivial braid with identity permutation and
writhe `0`; hence every abelian (phase-type) invariant takes the same value on it as on the
trivial braid. -/

inductive RuleId
  | r01
  | r02
  | r03
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

/-- The matcher at the head of a word, as in `_match_r01`, `_match_r02`, `_match_r03`:
the rewritten word, or `none` when the rule does not apply there. -/

declarations.name: rewriteHead
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def rewriteHead {n : ℕ} : RuleId → Word n → Option (Word n)
  | .r01, a :: b :: rest => if a.idx = b.idx ∧ a.pos ≠ b.pos then some rest else none
  | .r02, a :: b :: rest =>
      if (a.idx : ℕ) + 2 ≤ b.idx ∨ (b.idx : ℕ) + 2 ≤ a.idx then some (b :: a :: rest) else none
  | .r03, a :: b :: c :: rest =>
      if a.pos = b.pos ∧ b.pos = c.pos ∧ a.idx = c.idx ∧
          ((a.idx : ℕ) + 1 = b.idx ∨ (b.idx : ℕ) + 1 = a.idx) then
        some (b :: a :: b :: rest)
      else none
  | _, _ => none
