/-!
# Phase 1: the fibration checker

The Phase 1 fibration engine (`qbx.categorical.fibration`, migration `010_fibrations.sql`)
records a functor `p : E ⥤ B` together with chosen lifts: for a fibration a morphism
`φ : e' ⟶ e` of `E` registered as the lift of the base morphism `u = p φ` at `e`, for an
opfibration a morphism `φ : e ⟶ e'` registered as the lift of `u = p φ` at `e`.  It checks

* the **cartesian property** of every recorded lift `φ : a ⟶ b` (fibrations): for every
  `h : z ⟶ b` and every base morphism `w : p z ⟶ p a` with `p h = w ≫ p φ` there is exactly one
  `k : z ⟶ a` with `p k = w` and `k ≫ φ = h` — split into *existence* and *uniqueness*;
* dually the **cocartesian property** of every recorded lift of an opfibration;
* **cleavage completeness**: every base morphism `u : b' ⟶ p e` has a recorded lift at `e`.

Results (written in Mathlib's diagrammatic order, `f ≫ g` is `f` then `g`):

* `CartesianCheck`, `isStronglyCartesian_iff_check`: the checker's condition is exactly Mathlib's
  `Functor.IsStronglyCartesian` — the check is sound and complete.
* `CocartesianCheck`, `isStronglyCocartesian_iff_check`: the dual statement for opfibrations.
* `CleavageCheck`, `isFibered_iff_cleavageCheck`: a functor is a (Grothendieck) fibration
  (`Functor.IsFibered`) iff every base morphism into `p e` has a lift at `e` passing the cartesian
  check — so "every recorded lift is cartesian and every `(u, e)` has a recorded lift" is exactly
  the fibration property.
* `cartesianCheck_iff_exists_and_unique`, `cartesian_existence_not_sufficient`,
  `cartesian_uniqueness_not_sufficient`: the check splits into existence and uniqueness of the
  factorization, and neither half implies the other, so the checker needs both.
* `isStronglyCartesian_star_iff_isIso`: over the one-object base (`Functor.star`) a morphism is
  cartesian iff it is an isomorphism.  The test suite uses this as an oracle: a monoid recorded as
  a one-object category over the terminal base has exactly its units as cartesian morphisms.
-/

/-- The cartesian check of migration 010 for a lift `φ : a ⟶ b` over `p φ`: every `h : z ⟶ b`
whose image factors as `w ≫ p φ` factors uniquely as `k ≫ φ` with `p k = w`. -/
/-- The existence half of `CartesianCheck`. -/
/-- The uniqueness half of `CartesianCheck`. -/

/-- The cocartesian check of migration 010 for an opfibration lift `φ : a ⟶ b` over `p φ`: every
`h : a ⟶ z` whose image factors as `p φ ≫ w` factors uniquely as `φ ≫ k` with `p k = w`. -/

/-- Cleavage completeness together with the cartesian check: every base morphism `u : R ⟶ p e`
has a lift `φ : e' ⟶ e` (with `p e' = R` and `p φ = u` up to that identification) that passes
`CartesianCheck`. -/
/-- Over objects that `p` sends to the given ones, "`k` lies over `w`" is just `p k = w`. -/
/-- **Soundness and completeness of the cartesian check.** -/
/-- **Soundness and completeness of the cocartesian check** (opfibrations). -/

/-- **The fibration property is exactly what the checker verifies**: `p` is a fibered category
iff every base morphism into `p e` has a lift at `e` passing the cartesian check. -/
/-- The cartesian check is the conjunction of its existence and uniqueness halves. -/
/-- **Oracle**: over the one-object base, a morphism is cartesian iff it is an isomorphism. -/

/-- Existence of factorizations does not imply the cartesian check: `Bool → Unit` over the
one-object base (every map into `Unit` factors through it, but not uniquely). -/

/-- Uniqueness of factorizations does not imply the cartesian check: `Empty → Unit` over the
one-object base (factorizations are unique, but `𝟙 Unit` has none). -/

/-!
# Foundations: the braid word layer

The braid group itself is canonical in `QBX.Formal.Braid` (`BraidGroup`, `Letter`, `Word`,
`Word.eval`).  This file is the **word layer**: what a QBX braid *word* (a list of letters
`σᵢ^{±1}`, read bottom to top) means, how two words are compared, and which invariants can be
read off a word letter by letter.  Everything in the corpus that consumes words
(`Word.perm`, `Word.writhe`, `Word.crossMatrix`, `Word.burau`, `Word.quantumTrace`,
`leftNormalForm`, …) goes through `Word.eval`, so the layer is:

* `braid_word` — the canonical statement: every braid is the value of a word; two words have the
  same value iff they are related by the rewrite rules R01–R03 iff they have the same Garside left
  normal form; `eval` turns concatenation into multiplication and the formal inverse into the
  group inverse.
* `Word.SameBraid` / `Word.sameBraid` — the **word problem as a decision procedure**: a `Bool`
  test (equality of left normal forms) that is proved to decide equality in `Bₙ`, with a
  `Decidable` instance, so `decide` settles any concrete question "do these words give the same
  braid?".
* `overMatrix` — the **directed crossing matrix** of Burillo–Gutierrez–Krstić–Nitecki (entry
  `(a, b)`: signed number of crossings where the strand starting at `a` passes *over* the strand
  starting at `b`), as a homomorphism `Bₙ →* ℤ^{n×n} ⋊ Sₙ` (`overHom`).

**Insight recorded here (research triage, 2026-10-14).**  The directed matrix looks finer than the
project's symmetric `crossMatrix`, but it is not: its symmetric part is `crossMatrix`
(`overMatrix_add_transpose`) and its antisymmetric part depends only on the permutation — it is
the signed inversion pattern `invSign (permHom n g)` (`overMatrix_sub_transpose`).  Hence
`2 · overMatrix = crossMatrix + invSign ∘ perm` (`two_mul_overMatrix`): the directed matrix carries
exactly the information of the pair `(crossMatrix, permutation)` and no more
(`overMatrix_eq_of_crossMatrix_perm`).  On pure braids it is symmetric and equals the linking
matrix (`overMatrix_pure`), which is the "only if" half of Lemma 1 of the source paper.
-/
/-! ### The word problem as a decision procedure -/
/-- Two words represent the same braid. -/
/-- The executable test: equal Garside left normal forms. -/
/-! ### The canonical statement -/
/-- **The braid word layer, canonical statement.** -/
/-- Induction over braids, one letter at a time (every braid is the value of a word). -/
/-! ### The directed crossing matrix -/
/-- One crossing in which the strand labelled `a` passes over the strand labelled `b`. -/
/-- The image of the generator `σᵢ`: the strand at position `i` passes over the one at `i + 1`. -/
/-- The directed crossing-matrix homomorphism `Bₙ →* ℤ^{n×n} ⋊ Sₙ`. -/

/-- The directed crossing matrix: entry `(a, b)` is the signed number of crossings in which the
strand starting at `a` passes over the strand starting at `b`. -/
/-- Reading one more letter: the cocycle rule of the directed crossing matrix. -/
/-- Reading one more letter: the cocycle rule of the crossing matrix. -/

/-- The signed inversion pattern of a permutation: `+1` at `(a, b)` if `a < b` and the strands
starting at `a`, `b` end in the opposite order, `-1` at `(b, a)` in that case, `0` otherwise. -/
/-- The symmetric part of the directed crossing matrix is the crossing matrix. -/
/-- The antisymmetric part of the directed crossing matrix depends only on the permutation. -/

/-- The directed crossing matrix carries no information beyond the crossing matrix and the
permutation. -/
/-- On a pure braid the directed crossing matrix is symmetric and equals the linking matrix. -/
/-- The directed matrix of one generator: a single over-crossing, not symmetric. -/
/-! ### Worked checks -/
/-- The braid relation, settled by the decision procedure. -/
/-- The Borromean braid word `(σ₁σ₂⁻¹)³`. -/

/-- The Borromean braid is pure and its directed crossing matrix is zero (so its crossing and
linking matrices vanish too), yet it is not the trivial braid — the decision procedure says so
directly.  This is Example 5 of the cabled-braids paper: the crossing matrix does not detect
pure braids. -/

/-!
# Foundations: the Cayley–Dickson tower `ℝ → ℂ → ℍ → 𝕆 → 𝕊 → …`

**Canonical definition:** `SpookyPrimes.Sedenion.CD R n` (`refinery/SpookyPrimes/Sedenion/Basic.lean`),
level `n` of dimension `2ⁿ`, with `cdMul`, `cdConj`, `cdNormSq`.  Every QBX statement about the
tower should use it.

Other representations, and why they exist:

* `QBX.Formal.Certificates.CayleyDickson` — the same doubling product on `List Int`, generated by
  `qbx_micro/cert.py` in core Lean only, so that the law-failure witnesses can be re-checked in
  other proof assistants.  It is a *certificate format*, not a second theory.
* `Sovereign`'s Cayley–Dickson development (`sovereign/`) — independent, not importable from QBX.

`cayleyDickson_tower` packages the defining fact of the tower — **the norm composes exactly at the
levels `n ≤ 3` (Hurwitz: dimensions 1, 2, 4, 8)** — with its geometric form, the Hopf map being
sphere-to-sphere exactly at the same levels (`Foundations/Hopf.lean`).  Both are proved
elsewhere (`Refinery.CD.cdNormSq_mul_iff_le_three`, `hopfCD_sphere_iff_le_three`); this module
only states them together.

/-!
# Geometric containers: carrier, metric, declared curvature

This is the Lean side of the container format (`QBX/containers/README.md`, decision CNT-001).
A *container* is a carrier with an `ℕ`-valued distance seen from a base point, finite balls, and a
*declared* curvature class.  The declaration is checkable: `Container.IsCurvatureCorrect` says
that the ball-volume profile `r ↦ #{x | d(o, x) ≤ r}` really has the declared growth.

Curvature is read off volume growth, the sense the design document uses
("finite volume / polynomial volume / exponential volume"):

* `positive` (closed) — the volume profile is bounded;
* `flat` — unbounded, but at most polynomial;
* `negative` — at least exponential (`2 ^ r ≤ V (k * r)` for some `k ≥ 1`).

This is a coarse, large-scale notion (the one Gromov's growth classification sees); it is not
sectional or Ollivier–Ricci curvature.  A finite torus `ℤ/m × ℤ/n` is declared flat through its
development, the lattice `ℤ²`, which covers it (`torusCover_surjective`).

Main results:

* `CurvatureClass.Holds.unique` — the three classes are mutually exclusive, so a declaration is
  either right or wrong (`poly_not_dominates_exp` is the analytic input);
* `hypercube_correct`, `lattice_correct`, `tree_correct` — the hypercube `{0,1}ⁿ` (Hamming
  distance) is positive, the lattice `ℤᵏ` (`ℓ¹` distance, `k ≥ 1`) is flat, the infinite binary
  tree (tree distance) is negative;
* `Container.prod`, `Container.prod_correct` — the product container (sum metric) is correct
  when declared with the composition table `CurvatureClass.prod`: negative absorbs everything,
  flat absorbs positive, positive × positive is positive.
-/
/-! ### Curvature classes of volume profiles -/
/-- The declared large-scale curvature of a container. -/
/-- No polynomial bound `C (k r + 1)ᵈ` dominates `2 ʳ` for all `r`. -/
/-- Bounded volume profile. -/
/-- At most polynomial volume profile. -/
/-- At least exponential volume profile. -/
/-- What it means for a volume profile to have a given curvature class. -/
/-- Composition table for products: negative absorbs everything, then flat, then positive. -/
/-- The three curvature classes are mutually exclusive: a declaration is right or wrong. -/

/-- The product rule on profiles: if `V` is squeezed between each factor and their product, its
class is `prod a b`. -/
/-! ### Containers -/
/-- A container: carrier, base point, `ℕ`-valued distance, finite balls, declared curvature. -/
/-- The set of states. -/
/-- Distance (the only thing consumers see). -/
/-- The base point the container is observed from. -/
/-- The ball of radius `r` about `origin`, as a finite set. -/
/-- The declared curvature. -/
/-- The volume profile `r ↦ #(ball r)`. -/
/-- The declared curvature is the true one. -/
/-- A container's true curvature is unique, so at most one declaration is correct. -/
/-- Product of containers: pairs, sum metric, product base point. -/

/-- **Composition rule.** The product of correctly declared containers, declared with the
composition table, is correctly declared. -/
/-! ### Positive: the hypercube `{0,1}ⁿ` -/
/-- Hamming distance on `{0,1}ⁿ`. -/
/-- The hypercube container (Hamming distance, base point `0…0`), declared positive. -/
/-! ### Flat: the lattice `ℤᵏ` -/
/-- `ℓ¹` distance on `ℤᵏ`. -/
/-- The lattice container `ℤᵏ` (`ℓ¹` distance, base point `0`), declared flat. -/
/-- The lattice covers the torus `ℤ/m × ℤ/n`: the torus is the quotient of `ℤ²` by its periods. -/
/-! ### Negative: the infinite binary tree -/
/-- Length of the longest common prefix of two lists. -/

/-- Tree distance between two vertices of the binary tree (vertices = finite paths from the
root): go up to the last common ancestor, then down. -/
/-- All paths of length at most `r`. -/
/-- The binary-tree container (tree distance, base point the root), declared negative. -/
/-! ### Worked composites -/
/-- A tree of hypercubes (e.g. a cache tree whose nodes are codewords) is negative. -/
/-- A lattice of hypercubes (the torus–hypercube design, developed) is flat. -/
/-- Declaring a lattice positive is detected as wrong. -/

/-!
# Reading frames and the direction group: closing the 4-versus-8 gap

`ScriptDirection.lean` proves that the direction changes of a braid diagram form the group
`Dir ≅ (ℤ/2)³` (flip the strand numbering, reverse the reading order, mirror the crossings).
`LanguageMatrix.lean` records, for each of 70 languages, a *line direction* (4 values: LTR, RTL,
TTB, BTT) and a *progression* (the direction in which successive lines advance, 4 values).
The two results were parallel; this file composes them.

* A **reading frame** is a line direction together with a progression perpendicular to it.  There
  are exactly 8 (`card_frame`), and every one of the 70 register entries is a frame
  (`register_frames_valid`).
* A frame has an **axis** (horizontal or vertical lines) and two senses (line forward/backward,
  progression forward/backward).  The reference frames are Latin `(LTR, TTB)` and, turned through
  90°, Literary Chinese `(TTB, RTL)`.
* `Frame.toDir` sends a frame to the *rigid* direction change that converts its reference frame
  into it: line reversed ↦ `rev`, progression reversed ↦ `flip`; no mirror.
  `frameEquiv : Frame ≃ Axis × RigidDir` — the 8 frames are exactly the 2 axes times the 4 rigid
  elements of `Dir`.  The 4 reading directions are the 2 axes times `{1, turnOver}`
  (`lineDirEquiv`).  The other 4 elements of `Dir` (the reflections, which differ by `chiral`)
  are not reading frames: they change crossing signs, which no writing convention does.
* Consequence (`frame_change_invariants`): changing between frames of the same axis preserves the
  closure data of a braid — writhe, number of components and linking spectrum.

**Sequential bidirectional passes.**  Reading a braid forward and then backward,
`bipass g = g · rev g`, always gives a *pure* braid (`bipass_pure`), so its closure always has
`n` components and a full `n × n` linking matrix (`numComponents_bipass`), even when `g` itself
closes to a knot.  Its writhe is twice that of `g`.  It is trivial exactly when the word is
mirror-symmetric (`bipass_eq_one_iff`: `g = mirror g`), so the double pass measures the
chirality of the reading.  Forward-then-backward and backward-then-forward are conjugate, so
they close to the same link data (`numComponents_bipass_rev`).  Finally the labelled linking matrix
of the double pass is exactly the crossing matrix of the single pass (`linkMatrix_bipass`): the
double pass converts crossing data, which is not a link invariant of `g`'s own closure, into a
genuine linking matrix.

/-!
# Foundations: the Hopf fibration `S¹ → S³ → S²` (one statement, referenced everywhere)

The Hopf fibration appears in the direction group, the torus braids, the Gosset/E₈ work, the
toric code, the Hebrew work and the language work.  QBX defines exactly **three** Hopf maps, and
this module is where they meet:

| map | file | coordinates |
|---|---|---|
| `Connections.hopf q = q i q̄` | `Connections/QuaternionHopf.lean` | `ℍ` — **canonical** |
| `Connections.hopfC z w = (2 z w̄, ‖z‖² − ‖w‖²)` | `Connections/HopfStrands.lean` | `ℂ²` |
| `Connections.hopfCD n x y = (2 x ȳ, |x|² − |y|²)` | `Connections/CayleyDicksonHopf.lean` | level `n` of the Cayley–Dickson tower |

* `hopf_fibration` — the canonical statement: `hopf` maps `S³` onto `S²`, every fibre is exactly a
  circle (right multiplication by unit complex numbers), and `hopf` is `SU(2)`-equivariant
  (`hopf (u q) = u · hopf q · ū`).  It packages results proved in `QuaternionHopf.lean`; it does not
  re-prove them.
* `hopf_eq_hopfC` — the quaternionic and complex maps are the same map: under
  `q = a + b i + c j + d k ↦ (z, w) = (a + b i, c − d i)` the `i`, `j`, `k` components of `hopf q`
  are the real part, the imaginary part and minus the real part of `hopfC z w` (up to that
  coordinate rotation of the base `S²`).
* `hopfCD_one_eq_hopfC` — the Cayley–Dickson map at level 1 (`CD ℝ 1 = ℂ`) is `hopfC`.
  So all three are one fibration, and `hopfCD_sphere_iff_le_three` (Hurwitz `1, 2, 4, 8`) says
  where the family stops.

Every other mention of the Hopf fibration in the project uses one of these three maps (or the
Hopf *link* `σ₁²`, a different object: two linked fibres) and should cite this module.
Sovereign's `SpinFoamCoherent` (`w i w⋆`) and `Algebra.HopfLift` (Chern number 1) restate the
quaternionic map inside `sovereign/`, which QBX may not import; they are listed in
`QBX/docs/design/FOUNDATIONS.md`.
-/
/-- **The Hopf fibration, canonical statement.** -/
-- `S³ → S²`
-- onto
-- every fibre contains the circle through any of its points …
-- … and is exactly that circle
-- `SU(2)`-equivariance
/-- **The quaternionic and complex Hopf maps agree** under `q ↦ (q.re + q.imI i, q.imJ − q.imK i)`. -/
/-- **The Cayley–Dickson Hopf map at level 1 is the complex Hopf map** (`CD ℝ 1 = ℝ × ℝ = ℂ`). -/

/-!
# Foundations: the linking matrix

**Canonical definitions:** `QBX.Formal.crossMatrix` (`LinkingMatrix.lean`; for any braid, the
signed crossing count between strands, a crossed homomorphism `Bₙ → ℤ^{n×n}`) and
`QBX.Formal.linkMatrix = crossMatrix / 2` (`PureLinkingMatrix.lean`; the labelled linking matrix
of the closure of a pure braid).

`linking_matrix` packages its defining properties: symmetric with zero diagonal; additive on pure
braids (a homomorphism `Pₙ → Sym₀(n, ℤ)`); invariant under conjugation by pure braids; onto all
symmetric integer matrices with zero diagonal; and realised from *any* braid by the forward–backward
reading pass (`linkMatrix_bipass`, `Foundations/DirectionGroup.lean`).

Where it is used: closure invariants (`ClosureLinking.lean`), direction invariance
(`ScriptDirection.lean`, `Dir.linkingSpectrum_act`), the 70-language matrix
(`seventy_language_matrix`, which is `linkMatrix_range` at `n = 70`), and — as the same
"cocycle on edges, invariant on cycles" pattern — the gauge / consensus layer (`GaugeFlatness.lean`,
holonomy as a homomorphism from based loops, i.e. from `π₁`, *not* from `H₁`; correction F2) and the
toric code (`ToricCode.lean`, logical sectors as `H₁(T², ℤ/2)`).  Those are analogies of shape, not
theorems about `linkMatrix`; no formal map between them is claimed here.
-/
/-- **The linking matrix, canonical statement.** -/

# QBX foundations

The recurring structures of the project, each stated once (decision FND-001,
`QBX/docs/design/FOUNDATIONS.md`):

* `Foundations.Container` — geometric containers: carrier, metric, declared curvature, the product
  rule (the coordination layer of `QBX/containers/`).
* `Foundations.DirectionGroup` — the direction group `(ℤ/2)³`, the 8 reading frames, and the
  forward–backward pass.
* `Foundations.Hopf` — the Hopf fibration `S¹ → S³ → S²`; the three QBX Hopf maps agree.
* `Foundations.CayleyDickson` — the tower and the Hurwitz cut-off `n ≤ 3`.
* `Foundations.Linking` — the linking matrix.
* `Foundations.BraidWord` — the braid word layer: words, their value, the word problem as a
  decision procedure (`Word.SameBraid` is `Decidable`), letter-by-letter induction, and the
  directed crossing matrix (`overMatrix`), which is shown to carry exactly the information of the
  crossing matrix plus the permutation.

Braid groups themselves are canonical in `QBX.Formal.Braid` (`BraidGroup`, `Word`,
`eval_eq_iff_eqvGen`, `wordQuotientEquiv`) and `QBX.Formal.Streams.FullTwist` (Coxeter element,

/-!
# Self-linking with an explicit framing convention

`QBX/docs/design/JLN_REVIEW.md` §4 leaves open the self-linking / framing part of the
"total Hopf invariant" of `plan_2.md`: the writhe of a braid word is **not** an invariant of its
closure, so a self-linking number is only meaningful once a framing convention is fixed and one
says exactly which Markov moves preserve it.  This file does that.

**Convention.** The closure of a braid word `w` on `n` strands is given the *blackboard framing*
(the framing pushed off in the projection plane).  Its total framing number is `writhe w`.  The
**self-linking number** is `sl(w) = writhe w − n` (the braid form of Bennequin's self-linking
number); its mirror companion is `sl⁻(w) = writhe w + n`.

Results (`Σ n, Word n` is a braid word together with its strand count):

* `selfLink_braid`, `selfLink_conj` — `sl` is unchanged by braid relations and conjugation;
* `selfLink_stab_pos` — unchanged by **positive** stabilisation `B ↦ σ₁ · shift B`;
* `selfLink_stab_neg` — lowered by exactly `2` by **negative** stabilisation `B ↦ σ₁⁻¹ · shift B`;
* `selfLink_posMarkov` — hence `sl` is an invariant of *positive Markov equivalence* (braid
  relations, conjugation and positive stabilisation only);
* `selfLinkNeg_negMarkov` — dually `sl⁻ = writhe + n` is an invariant of negative Markov
  equivalence;
* `selfLink_not_markov_invariant` — neither is an invariant of full Markov equivalence: the
  one-strand empty word and `σ₁⁻¹` on two strands both close to the unknot but have
  `sl = −1` and `sl = −3`;
* `selfLink_markov_mod_two` — what survives every Markov move is the parity of `sl`.
-/
/-- The blackboard self-linking number `writhe − strand count`. -/
/-- The mirror self-linking number `writhe + strand count`. -/
/-- Positive stabilisation preserves the self-linking number. -/
/-- Negative stabilisation lowers the self-linking number by exactly `2`. -/
/-- Negative stabilisation preserves the mirror self-linking number. -/
/-- A Markov move whose stabilisations (if any) all have sign `b`. -/
/-- Equivalence generated by Markov moves with stabilisations of a single sign `b`. -/
/-- Signed Markov equivalence implies Markov equivalence. -/
/-- **The self-linking number is an invariant of positive Markov equivalence.** -/
/-- **The mirror self-linking number is an invariant of negative Markov equivalence.** -/
/-- **The parity of the self-linking number survives every Markov move.** -/
/-- The empty word on one strand (closure: the unknot). -/
/-- `σ₁⁻¹` on two strands: a negative stabilisation of `unknot1` (closure: the unknot). -/

/-- **`sl` is not an invariant of the closed link**: two Markov-equivalent words (both closing to
the unknot) have different self-linking numbers.  A framing convention must therefore say which
stabilisations it allows; with blackboard framing, only positive ones. -/
/-- Likewise the writhe (total blackboard framing) is not a Markov invariant. -/

/-!
# Garside's uniqueness theorem for the left normal form (registry H-057)

`BraidNormalForm.lean` proves that the left normal form computed by migration 021 is *sound*
(equal normal forms give equal braids).  This file proves the converse for every strand count:
**equal braids have equal left normal forms** (`leftNormalFormComplete`), so
`LeftNormalFormComplete n` holds for all `n` and the answer "different" of
`braid_normal_form_equal` is proved.

The proof uses the lattice of simple braids (`WeakOrder.lean`) and no positive braid monoid:

* `nfHead x y`, `nfTail x y`: the left-weighted factorisation of the product of two simple
  braids (`x · (∂x ∧ y)`, `(∂x ∧ y)⁻¹ · y`).
* `lmul x L`: the left multiplication of a list of simple factors by a simple braid, one
  factor at a time.  It respects products of simple braids (`lmul_germ`) and keeps lists
  left-weighted (`lmul_normal`, the "domino rule").
* `NormalState n`: the normal forms `(k, [A₁, …, A_m])` (factors `≠ 1`, `≠ Δ`, consecutive
  factors left-weighted).  `nfAction : B_n →* Perm (NormalState n)` is a group action in which
  every normal form `ν` is the image of the empty normal form under its own braid
  (`nfAction_nfValue`).
* The algorithm of `leftNormalForm` always produces a normal form (`leftNormalForm_normal`).

Hence two words with the same braid have the same normal form.
-/
/-! ### Left-weighted factorisation of a pair of simple braids -/

/-- A pair of simple braids is left-weighted when no generator can be moved from the front of
the second to the back of the first. -/
/-- The part of `y` that is moved to the back of `x`: `∂x ∧ y`. -/
/-- The first factor of the left-weighted factorisation of `x · y`. -/
/-- The second factor of the left-weighted factorisation of `x · y`. -/
/-- The key identity behind the germ property: `∂s ∧ (t · (∂t ∧ A)) = t · (∂(st) ∧ A)`. -/

/-- **Germ property** of the factorisation: multiplying by `s` then by `t` (with `s · t`
simple) on the left of `y` is the same as multiplying by the simple braid `s · t`. -/
/-- **Domino rule**: left multiplication keeps consecutive factors left-weighted. -/

/-!
# The gate group of `ws5_braid_ops` (WS5)

A Python `Gate` (`QBX/foundation/ws5_braid_ops/gate_action.py`) stores an explicit permutation
of bit positions and an explicit torus shift, and acts by `a ↦ shift(perm(a))`.  This file
models it as `Gate n k M` and proves:

* `Gate.act_compose`, `Gate.act_identity`, `Gate.act_inverse` and the `Group` / `MulAction`
  instances: `compose` (Python `compose`) is an associative action, `identity` acts trivially,
  and `inverse` is a two-sided inverse (PROPERTIES P5.2);
* `Gate.act_bijective` (P5.3);
* `Gate.eq_of_act_eq` / `Gate.ext_iff_act`: the action is faithful, so equality of the stored
  data (Python dataclass equality) is the same as equality of the functions on addresses;
* `Gate.addrDist_act` (P5.1) and `cycDist_natCast` (the Lean cyclic distance is the Python
  formula `min(d % m, m − d % m)` with `d = |x − y|`);
* `braidToGate`: the braid gate is the gate of the braid's shadow, a group homomorphism
  `B_n →* Gate`; `braidGate_sigma_inv` (σᵢ⁻¹ has the same gate as σᵢ) and
  `braidGate_not_faithful` (σᵢ² ≠ 1 in `B_n` acts trivially: the shadow forgets braiding, as
  `BRAID_FULL_TWIST_NOTE` states).
-/
/-- A Python `Gate`: an explicit permutation of bit positions and an explicit torus shift. -/
/-- The bit permutation (`Gate.perm`): bit `i` moves to position `perm i`. -/
/-- The torus shift (`Gate.shift`). -/
/-- `Gate.__call__`: permute the bits, then shift the cycles. -/
/-- Python `compose(g, h)`: apply `h`, then `g`. -/
/-- Python `identity_gate`. -/
/-- Python `Gate.inverse`. -/
/-- The gates form a group under `compose` (the product `S_n × ∏ⱼ ℤ/Mⱼ`). -/
/-- The gates act on the addresses. -/
/-- **P5.3.** Every gate is a bijection of the address space. -/
/-- The action is faithful: a gate is determined by what it does to addresses. -/
/-- Dataclass equality of gates is extensional equality of their actions. -/
/-- **P5.1.** Every gate is an isometry of the address metric. -/

/-- The Lean cyclic distance agrees with the Python formula of `MixedRadixSpace.distance`:
for residues `x, y < m`, `d = |x − y| % m` and the distance is `min(d, m − d)`. -/
/-- The gate of a braid: its permutation shadow with no torus shift. -/
/-- The inverse generator has the same gate as the generator. -/
/-- `σᵢ²` acts trivially on every address. -/
/-- **The shadow forgets braiding.**  `σᵢ² ≠ 1` in `B_n`, yet its gate is the identity. -/

/-!
# Gate locality, the XOR mask and the Toffoli gate (WS9 step 12, amendment FA-050)

Register items X-04, H-05 (gate locality) and H-02, X-03 (the gate set is not universal; the
XOR mask of sketch A-1 / amendment FA-050 and the Toffoli gate of decision D-3).

* `addrDist_braidGate_sigma`: the gate of `σ_i` moves an address by `0` (its bits `i`, `i+1`
  agree) or `2` (they differ); `addrDist_braidGate_sigma_mem`: always `∈ {0, 2}`. A braid
  generator is therefore never a single address-graph edge: it is a "diagonal" of a square.
* `addrDist_shiftGate_self`: a torus shift moves every address by the same amount
  `∑ⱼ cycDist 0 (t j)`.
* `MaskedGate` models the Python `Gate` with its `mask` (`a ↦ shift(perm(a) ⊕ mask)`):
  `MaskedGate.act_compose` (Python `compose`), `MaskedGate.act_ofGate` (mask `0` is the old
  gate), `MaskedGate.addrDist_act` (still an isometry) and `maskedGate_transitive` (any address
  is mapped to any other: the weight obstruction of `GateReachability.lean` disappears);
  `addrDist_mask_self`: a mask moves every address by its Hamming weight.
* `toffoli`: flip bit `t` iff bits `c₁`, `c₂` are set; `toffoli_involutive`,
  `addrDist_toffoli_le` (local: distance `≤ 1`) and `toffoli_not_isometry`, hence
  `toffoli_ne_maskedGate`: no masked gate equals a Toffoli gate (it is not affine), which is why
  D-3's classical stage needs it in addition to masks.
-/
/-! ### Locality of braid and shift gates -/
/-- **Gate locality (step 12).** `σ_i` moves an address by `0` or `2`. -/
/-- A torus shift moves every address by the same amount. -/
/-! ### The masked gate (FA-050) -/
/-- The Python `Gate` with its XOR mask: `a ↦ shift(perm(a) ⊕ mask)`. -/
/-- `Gate.__call__` with a mask. -/
/-- Python `compose(g, h)`: apply `h`, then `g`; the mask of `h` is moved by `g`'s permutation. -/
/-- A gate without mask. -/
/-- Masked gates are isometries of the address metric. -/

/-- **Transitivity.** With the XOR mask every address can be mapped to every other one (compare
`exists_gate_act_eq_iff`, `GateReachability.lean`: without the mask, only addresses of equal
bit weight). -/
/-- A pure mask moves every address by the Hamming weight of the mask. -/
/-! ### The Toffoli gate -/
/-- Toffoli: flip bit `t` iff bits `c₁` and `c₂` are both set. -/
/-- Toffoli is local: it moves an address by at most one edge. -/
/-- Toffoli is not an isometry (three distinct positions). -/
/-- No masked gate (in particular no permutation / shift / mask gate) is a Toffoli gate. -/

/-!
# WS9 integration: what the braid/torus gate set can and cannot reach

The gate set of `ws5_braid_ops` (`Gate n k M`, `QBX/Formal/GateGroup.lean`) acts on the address
space `Q_n □ T^k_M` by a bit permutation followed by a torus shift; braids act through their
permutation shadow (`braidToGate`).  This file settles the *expressiveness* question for that gate
set (WS9 register item X-03):

* `weight_act`: every gate preserves the Hamming weight of the hypercube coordinates
  (a conservation law; braid gates are "conservative logic").
* `exists_gate_act_eq_iff`: two addresses lie in the same gate orbit **iff** their bit parts have the
  same Hamming weight.  So the gate group has exactly `n + 1` orbits on the bits, one per weight,
  and is transitive on the torus factor.
* `exists_braid_shift_eq_iff`: the same holds with the bit permutation restricted to permutation
  shadows of braids (every permutation is one: `permHom_surjective`).
* `not_exists_gate_eq_flipBit`: no gate realises a single bit flip, although a bit flip is an edge
  of the address graph.  The gate set therefore cannot by itself implement general (even classical,
  reversible) computation on the hypercube; a weight-changing primitive must be added.
* `shift_conj`: under any homomorphism into the gate group, conjugate elements get the same torus
  shift; so per-strand windings of the torus-braid shadow cannot be represented by `Gate` (X-05).
-/
/-- Hamming weight of the hypercube coordinates of an address. -/
/-- **Conservation law.** Every gate preserves the Hamming weight of the bits. -/
/-- Braid gates preserve the Hamming weight. -/
/-- Two bit strings of equal weight differ by a permutation of positions. -/

/-- **Orbits of the gate group.** An address can be moved to another by a gate iff their bit
parts have the same Hamming weight. -/

/-- The same orbits arise from braids: an address can be moved to another by a braid gate
followed by a torus translation iff the bit parts have the same Hamming weight. -/
/-- The address with all bits `false` and all cycles `0`. -/

/-- **No gate is a bit flip.** A single bit flip — an edge of the address graph — is not
realised by any gate of the braid/torus gate set. -/
/-! ### Shifts only see abelian data (guidance for the torus braid group, register item X-05) -/
/-- The torus-shift component of a gate, as a homomorphism to the (abelian) shift group. -/

/-- **Conjugate elements have the same torus shift.**  For any group `G` and any homomorphism
`φ : G →* Gate n k M`, conjugate elements of `G` are sent to gates with the same torus shift.
In the torus-braid shadow `S_n ⋉ (ℤ²)ⁿ` (the D3 target) the unit windings of two different
strands are conjugate by a transposition, so no homomorphism from the shadow into the gate group
can tell the windings of individual strands apart: through `Gate`, only abelian (total-winding)
data of the strands is visible. -/

/-!
# Gauge connections on graphs: flatness, pure gauge, and fork detection

Formal targets F1–F4 of `QBX/foundation/ws6_certificates/SPEC.md`, plus the fork-detection
theorem behind the foundation's success metric ("a fork is detected by geometry alone").

A *connection* on a simple graph `G` with values in a group `K` assigns a transport
`transport u v : K` to every directed edge, with `transport v u = (transport u v)⁻¹`.  The
holonomy of a walk is the ordered product of the transports along it (the convention of
`ws2_gauge.holonomy`: `T(v) = T(parent) · g(parent, v)`).

* `holonomy_append`, `holonomy_reverse` — holonomy turns concatenation of walks into
  multiplication and reversal into inversion (**F2**, corrected: holonomy is a homomorphism from
  based loops, i.e. from the fundamental group; it factors through `H₁` only when `K` is
  abelian — see `holonomy_not_homological` for a counterexample).
* `isFlat_iff_isPureGauge` — every closed walk has trivial holonomy iff there are node
  potentials `p` with `transport u v = (p u)⁻¹ * p v` (**F1**).  No connectedness is needed.
* `isFlat_iff_fundamental` — for *any* choice of a root `r v` in each component and *any* walk
  `w v` from `r v` to `v` (e.g. the tree paths of any spanning forest), the connection is flat
  iff the fundamental holonomy `hol (w u) * transport u v * (hol (w v))⁻¹` is trivial on every
  edge (**F4**).  Consequently the verdict does not depend on the roots or the spanning forest
  (`fundamental_verdict_independent`, **F3**).
* `isFlat_perturb_of_isBridge` / `perturb_trivial_of_not_isBridge` — a single-edge fork is
  detected by the flatness check **iff the edge is not a bridge**: changing the transport on a
  bridge of a flat connection leaves it flat, and on an edge that lies on a cycle any non-trivial
  change breaks flatness.
-/
/-- A `K`-valued connection on the simple graph `G`. -/
/-- Transport along the directed edge `u → v`. -/
/-- Traversing an edge backwards applies the inverse transport. -/
/-- Holonomy (parallel transport) along a walk: the ordered product of edge transports. -/
/-- A connection is flat when every closed walk has trivial holonomy. -/
/-- A connection is pure gauge when it is induced by node potentials. -/

/-- Holonomy is the ordered product of the transports over the darts (directed edges) of the
walk: it factors through the free monoid on darts. -/

/-- **F2 (concatenation).** Holonomy is multiplicative under concatenation of walks.  This is
the factorisation principle `Sovereign.HomDecomp.prod_map_of_eq_append` applied to
`holonomy_eq_prod_darts` and `Walk.darts_append`: the dart list turns concatenation of walks
into concatenation of lists. -/
/-- **F2 (reversal).** Reversing a walk inverts its holonomy. -/
/-- The holonomy of a pure-gauge connection telescopes. -/
/-- A flat connection has trivial holonomy on every walk whose endpoints coincide. -/

/-- **F4.** Fix any root `r v` for every node, constant along edges (one root per connected
component), and any walk `w v` from `r v` to `v` (for instance the paths of a spanning forest).
Then the connection is flat iff every fundamental holonomy is trivial. -/

/-- **F3.** The verdict of the fundamental-cycle check does not depend on the roots or on the
spanning forest used to reach each node. -/
/-- A chosen root in the connected component of `v`. -/

/-- **F1.** A connection is flat iff it is pure gauge.  No connectedness assumption is needed:
potentials are chosen independently on each connected component. -/
/-! ### Single-edge forks -/

/-- Change the transport on the edge `a → b` by right multiplication with `k` (and on `b → a`
accordingly).  This is the operation `build_forked_events` performs on one event. -/
/-- Holonomy along a walk that avoids the edge `s(a, b)` is unchanged by the perturbation. -/

/-- **Undetectable fork.** Perturbing the transport on a bridge of a flat connection leaves it
flat: the change is a gauge transformation of one side of the bridge.  So no flatness check —
and, since flat connections are exactly the pure-gauge ones, no holonomy-based check at all —
can see a fork on a bridge. -/

/-- **Detected fork.** If the edge `s(a, b)` is not a bridge (it lies on a cycle), a perturbation
that keeps the connection flat must be trivial.  Equivalently: every non-trivial single-edge fork
on a non-bridge edge of a flat connection is caught by the flatness check. -/

/-- **Fork detection, both directions.** For a flat connection and a non-trivial change `k ≠ 1`
of one edge's transport, the perturbed connection is non-flat iff the edge is not a bridge. -/
/-! ### F2 correction: holonomy does not factor through `H₁` for non-abelian groups -/
/-- Two triangles `0-1-2` and `0-3-4` sharing the vertex `0` (a "bow tie"). -/
/-- The bow-tie graph. -/
/-- Transports of `bowtieConn`. -/
/-- An `S₃`-valued connection on the bow tie: `swap 0 1` on edge `0-1`, `swap 1 2` on `0-3`. -/
/-- The triangle `0 → 1 → 2 → 0`. -/
/-- The triangle `0 → 3 → 4 → 0`. -/
/-- The commutator loop `A · B · A⁻¹ · B⁻¹` of the two triangles. -/

/-- **F2 as originally stated is false.** There is a graph, an `S₃`-valued connection and a
closed walk that traverses every edge equally often in both directions (so its class in the cycle
space `H₁` is zero) whose holonomy is not the identity.  Holonomy is a homomorphism from based
loops (`holonomy_append`), i.e. from `π₁`, not from `H₁`. -/

    c.holonomy (p.concat h) = c.holonomy p * c.transport v w

    (hpar : c.holonomy (w v) = c.holonomy (w u) * c.transport u v) :
    c.holonomy (w u) * c.transport u v * (c.holonomy (w v))⁻¹ = 1 ∧
    c.holonomy (w v) * c.transport v u * (c.holonomy (w u))⁻¹ = 1

declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem isFlat_iff_nonForest (r : V → V) (hr : ∀ u v, G.Adj u v → r u = r v)
    (w : ∀ v, G.Walk (r v) v) (par : V → V → Prop)
    (hpar : ∀ u v, G.Adj u v → par u v →
      c.holonomy (w v) = c.holonomy (w u) * c.transport u v) :
    c.IsFlat ↔ ∀ u v, G.Adj u v → ¬ par u v → ¬ par v u →
      c.holonomy (w u) * c.transport u v * (c.holonomy (w v))⁻¹ = 1

declarations.name: forest_recursion
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem forest_recursion (r : V → V) (w : ∀ v, G.Walk (r v) v) (par : V → V → Prop)

/-!
# The fundamental-cycle algorithm checks only non-tree edges

`isFlat_iff_fundamental` (F4) checks the fundamental holonomy
`hol (w u) * transport u v * (hol (w v))⁻¹` on *every* edge.  The implementation
`ws2_gauge.holonomy.fundamental_holonomies` computes it only for the edges that are not
spanning-forest edges, in either orientation: on a forest edge it is trivial by construction,
because the forest path to the child is the path to the parent followed by that edge
(`T(v) = T(parent) · g(parent, v)`).  This file proves that skipping the forest edges is sound.

* `isFlat_iff_nonForest` — given a parent relation `par` whose edges satisfy the transport
  recursion `hol (w v) = hol (w u) * transport u v`, the connection is flat iff the fundamental
  holonomy is trivial on every edge `{u, v}` with neither `par u v` nor `par v u`.
* `holonomy_concat` — the recursion holds whenever `w v` is `w u` extended by the edge `u → v`,
  i.e. for the paths of a BFS / DFS spanning forest.
-/
/-- Extending a walk by one edge multiplies its holonomy by that edge's transport. -/
/-- On a forest edge the fundamental holonomy is trivial, in either orientation. -/

/-- **The algorithm of `fundamental_holonomies` is sound and complete.**  Fix roots `r`
(constant along edges), walks `w v` from `r v` to `v`, and a parent relation `par` such that
along every parent edge the walks satisfy the transport recursion.  Then the connection is flat
iff the fundamental holonomy is trivial on every edge that is not a parent edge in either
direction. -/

/-- The parent recursion holds for the paths of a spanning forest built by extending the
parent's path by one edge (BFS / DFS). -/

/-!
# Phase 1: Hebrew primacy — the gematria functor and Torah sheaves

Migration `014_hebrew_primacy.sql` and `qbx.hebrew` treat gematria as a *functor* (skill
`hebrew_primacy_rules.md`, rules R1–R3, R7): words over the 27 Hebrew letters (22 letters and the
five final forms) form the free monoid on the letters, numbers form the monoid `(ℕ, +)`, and a
gematria scheme sends a word to the sum of its letters' values.  The **naturality obligation**
(R2) recorded in `gematria_obligation` is the square

```
Letters* --concat--> Letters*
   |                    |
  gem                  gem
   v                    v
   ℕ ------ sum ------> ℕ
```

i.e. `gem (u ++ w) = gem u + gem w`.  Torah sections are sections of a sheaf (R5): the passage
presheaf built by `build_torah_presheaf` has, over a set `U` of verses, the single section
`{v ↦ text v | v ∈ U}` when every verse of `U` has a recorded text, and no section otherwise.

Results:

* `wordValue`, `wordValue_append`, `wordValue_nil`: the value of a word under a scheme; it
  makes the naturality square commute for *every* scheme (`mapping_rules`).
* `gemHom`, `gemHom_toAdd`: the same map as a monoid homomorphism `FreeMonoid Letter →* ℕ`
  (in multiplicative notation) — gematria is a functor between one-object categories.
* `additive_eq_wordValue`: an additive map on words is determined by its values on the 27
  letters, so `check_gematria_functor` only has to check the letter table of a scheme.
* `obligation_square_of_values`, `obligation_value_mismatch_of_square`: if the three values
  of a recorded obligation are the scheme's values, the square commutes; hence a
  `naturality_square` report always comes with a `naturality_value` report.
* `standard`, `standard_strictMono`, `standard_injective`, `final_ne_base`: the seeded table
  (1–400 for the 22 letters, finals 500–900; not strict mispar hechrachi, which gives a final
  its base value — see `Engine/GematriaConvention.lean`) gives the 27 letters 27 distinct values; in particular
  every final form differs from its base form (R7).
* `wordValue_not_injective`: gematria is not injective on words (`אב` and `ג` are both 3), so it
  is a mixing input, never an address.
* `textSheaf`, `textSheaf_locality_and_gluing`, `textSheaf_subsingleton`,
  `textSheaf_nonempty_iff`: the passage presheaf passes both halves of the sheaf check on every
  space, has at most one section over each open set, and has one exactly when every point of the
  open set has a text.
-/
/-! ## Words and schemes -/
/-- The 27 Hebrew letters in seed order: `א … ת` (ordinals 1–22), then `ך ם ן ף ץ` (23–27). -/
/-- The value of a word under a gematria scheme `v`: the sum of its letters' values. -/
/-- The naturality square of rule R2 commutes for every scheme. -/
/-- Gematria as a monoid homomorphism from the free monoid on the letters to `(ℕ, +)`. -/
/-- An additive map on words that agrees with `v` on single letters is `wordValue v`. -/
/-- A recorded obligation whose three values are the scheme's values commutes. -/
/-- Contrapositive: a failed square means some recorded value is not the scheme's value. -/
/-! ## The seeded table -/
/-- The seeded values (`hebrew_letter`, `qbx.hebrew.gematria.GEMATRIA`). -/
/-- In seed order the values strictly increase. -/
/-- The base form of each final letter: `כ מ נ פ צ` (ordinals 11, 13, 14, 17, 18). -/
/-- The final forms `ך ם ן ף ץ` (ordinals 23–27). -/
/-- Rule R7: each final form has a value different from its base form. -/
/-- `א ב` and `ג` have the same value, so gematria does not identify words. -/
/-! ## The passage presheaf of a Torah site -/
/-- The passage presheaf: over `U`, the assignments of each verse of `U` to its recorded text. -/
/-- The passage presheaf is a sheaf: both halves of the check pass on every cover. -/
/-- At most one section over each open set (the database records a single label). -/
/-- A section over `U` exists exactly when every verse of `U` has a text. -/

/-!
# Gematria does not factor through the braid group

A design note (`alphabet_theory`, "Weave A") proposed that gematria is the composite
`A* → Bₙ → ℤ`: encode a text as a braid (`Bible.convertHom`), then apply a homomorphism to `ℤ`.
This is false for every strand count and every gematria in which two letters have different
values.  The reason is the braid relation: in a commutative target `σᵢσᵢ₊₁σᵢ = σᵢ₊₁σᵢσᵢ₊₁`
forces `φ(σᵢ) = φ(σᵢ₊₁)`, so a homomorphism `Bₙ → ℤ` cannot tell the generators apart.

Results:

* `hom_sigma_eq`: a homomorphism from `Bₙ` to a commutative group takes the same value on every
  generator.
* `hom_eq_zpow_writhe`: every homomorphism `Bₙ → ℤ` is `k · writhe` (`n ≥ 2`).
* `braid_reading_eq`: hence every `ℤ`-valued braid reading of a text is
  `k · (#letters − 2 · #finals)` (with the sofit rule) or `k · #letters` (without).
* `gematria_not_through_braid`: no homomorphism `φ : B_{m+2} → ℤ` has `φ ∘ convert = gem` for an
  additive `gem` that gives `א` and `ב` different values; in particular not for the standard
  values `1, 2, …` (`hechrachi_not_through_braid`).

What does hold is the free-monoid statement already in `QBX.Formal.Gematria` (`gemHom`:
gematria is a monoid homomorphism out of the free monoid on letters).

The centroid of the weighted Hebrew alphabet (`alphabet_theory/README.md`):

* `sum_base_values`: the 22 base letters have values summing to `1495`, so the centroid is
  `1495 / 22 = 67.95…`, within `1/2` of `68` (`centroid_near_68`).
* `chaim_value_base`: `חיים` has value `68` when the final mem counts as `40`; with the seeded
  table of this project (finals `500 … 900`, `QBX.Formal.Gematria.standard`) its value is `628`
  (`chaim_value_seeded`).
-/
/-! ## Homomorphisms out of the braid group -/
-- a * b * a = b * a * b in a commutative group gives a = b
/-- **A homomorphism to a commutative group is constant on the generators.** -/
/-- **Every homomorphism `Bₙ → ℤ` is a multiple of the writhe** (`n ≥ 2`). -/
/-! ## Braid readings of texts -/

/-- **Every `ℤ`-valued braid reading of a text is a multiple of its writhe**, i.e. of
`#letters − 2·#finals` under the sofit rule. -/

/-- **Gematria does not factor through the braid group.**  If an additive `gem` on texts gives
`א` and `ב` different values, no homomorphism `φ : B_{m+2} → ℤ` satisfies
`φ (braid of s) = gem s` for all texts `s`. -/

/-- Mispar hechrachi on characters: `א … ת ↦ 1 … 400`, final forms at their base value, every
other character `0`. -/
/-- The gematria of a text: the sum of its characters' values. -/
/-! ## The centroid of the Hebrew alphabet -/
/-- The 22 base letters sum to `1495`. -/
/-- The centroid `1495 / 22` is within `1/2` of `68`. -/
/-- `חיים` with the final mem valued as mem (`40`): `8 + 10 + 10 + 40 = 68`. -/
/-- With the seeded table (final mem `ם = 600`) `חיים` is `8 + 10 + 10 + 600 = 628`. -/

  | _, [], _ + 1 => []

/-!
# Coxeter elements: `240 = 8 · 30`, `126 = 7 · 18`, `72 = 6 · 12`

For a simple system `α₁, …, α_n` the Coxeter element is `c = s₁ s₂ ⋯ s_n`, the product of the
simple reflections.  Its order is the Coxeter number `h`, and it acts on the roots with every
orbit of size exactly `h`.  In the Coxeter-plane (Petrie) projection each orbit is a regular
`h`-gon, i.e. one ring of the familiar pictures.

Proved here by kernel computation, in doubled coordinates where the reflection in a root `a` is
`v ↦ v - (⟨v, a⟩ / 4) a`:

* `simpleE8_cartan`, `simpleE7_cartan`, `simpleE6_cartan`: the chosen simple systems have the
  Cartan matrices of `E₈`, `E₇`, `E₆`.  They are nested: the `E₇` system is the `E₈` one
  minus its first root, and lies in `perp 1`; the `E₆` system drops one more and lies in
  `perp 2` (the chain of `QBX.Formal.Gosset.Ladder`).
* `refl_mem`: simple reflections permute the 240 roots.
* `coxeterE8_minimalPeriod`: every root has minimal period exactly 30 under `c`, so
  `h(E₈) = 30`; `coxeterE8_rings`: the roots fall into **8 rings of 30** (`ringsE8`, each ring
  listed in orbit order).
* `coxeterE7_minimalPeriod`, `coxeterE7_rings`: **7 rings of 18** on the 126 roots of `E₇`.
* `coxeterE6_minimalPeriod`, `coxeterE6_rings`: **6 rings of 12** on the 72 roots of `E₆`.

The rings are given as explicit data and checked: `c` sends each entry to the next one
(cyclically), the entries of a ring are distinct, and the rings together are a permutation of the
roots.  `minimalPeriod_of_cycle` turns this into the statement about minimal periods.
-/
/-- Reflection in the root `a` (doubled coordinates, `⟨a, a⟩ = 8`). -/
/-- The Coxeter element `s₁ s₂ ⋯ s_n` of a list of simple roots. -/
/-! ## Cycles and minimal periods -/
/-- `f` steps through `L` cyclically. -/
/-- **Cycles have minimal period equal to their length.** -/
/-- A Boolean form of `IsCycleOf`, for kernel evaluation. -/
/-- Rings that cover a root set: each ring a cycle of `f` without repeats, of length `n`. -/
/-- Cartan matrix `(⟨αᵢ, αⱼ⟩ / 4)`. -/
/-- Simple reflections permute the roots. -/
/-! ## The rings -/
/-- The 8 Coxeter orbits of `E8`, each listed in orbit order `r, c r, c² r, …`. -/
/-- The 7 Coxeter orbits of `E7`, each listed in orbit order `r, c r, c² r, …`. -/
/-- The 6 Coxeter orbits of `E6`, each listed in orbit order `r, c r, c² r, …`. -/
/-- **8 rings of 30**: the rings are a permutation of the 240 roots. -/
/-- **`h(E₈) = 30`**: every root has minimal period 30 under the Coxeter element. -/
/-- **7 rings of 18** on the 126 roots of `E₇`. -/
/-- **6 rings of 12** on the 72 roots of `E₆`. -/

/-!
# The Gosset ladder: an exact address structure on the 240 vertices of `4₂₁`

The 240 roots of `E₈` (doubled coordinates, `QBX.Formal.Connections.e8Roots2`) are the
vertices of the Gosset polytope `4₂₁`.  Two vertices are joined by an edge when their inner
product is `1` (doubled: `4`), i.e. the angle between them is `60°`.

This file fixes one **flag**: eight roots `f₁, …, f₈` that are pairwise at `60°`
(`flag_clique`).  The flag gives the vertex set two nested filtrations.

* **Layers** (`layer k`): roots at `60°` to each of `f₁, …, f_k`.  Their sizes are
  `240, 56, 27, 16, 10, 6, 3, 1, 0` (`layer_length`).  The first six are the vertex counts of the
  Gosset family `4₂₁, 3₂₁, 2₂₁, 1₂₁, 0₂₁, -1₂₁`: each layer is the vertex figure of the
  previous one (`layer_succ`).
* **Orthogonal complements** (`perp k`): roots orthogonal to each of `f₁, …, f_k`.  Their sizes
  are `240, 126, 72, 40, 20, 8, 2, 0, 0` (`perp_length`), the root counts of
  `E₈ ⊃ E₇ ⊃ E₆ ⊃ D₅ ⊃ A₄ ⊃ A₂×A₁ ⊃ A₁`.

Further results:

* `shell_counts`: seen from any vertex, the vertices sit in five shells by inner
  product `2, 1, 0, -1, -2` with sizes `1, 56, 126, 56, 1`.
* `edge_count`: `4₂₁` has `6720` edges.
* `flagCoord_nodup`: the eight inner products with the flag are a complete address: different
  roots have different flag coordinates.  Each coordinate lies in `{-2, …, 2}`
  (`flagCoord_range`).

Everything is a finite computation checked by the kernel (`decide +kernel`); no
`native_decide`.
-/
/-- A fixed flag of eight pairwise-adjacent roots (doubled coordinates). -/
/-- The flag consists of roots. -/
/-- The flag roots are pairwise adjacent (angle `60°`). -/
/-- The flag cannot be extended: no root is adjacent to all eight flag roots. -/
/-- Layer `k`: roots adjacent to each of the first `k` flag roots. -/
/-- Roots orthogonal to each of the first `k` flag roots. -/
/-- **The exceptional chain** `E₈ ⊃ E₇ ⊃ E₆ ⊃ D₅ ⊃ A₄ ⊃ A₂×A₁ ⊃ A₁` by root count. -/

/-- Each layer is the vertex figure of the previous one: layer `k+1` is the set of members of
layer `k` adjacent to the flag root `f_{k+1}`. -/

/-- **Shells**: from every vertex the inner products `2, 1, 0, -1, -2` (doubled
`8, 4, 0, -4, -8`) occur `1, 56, 126, 56, 1` times. -/
/-- **`4₂₁` has 6720 edges** (the degree sum is `240 · 56 = 13440`). -/

/-- Flag coordinates: the inner products with the eight flag roots, divided by `4` so that a
root gets integer coordinates in `{-2, …, 2}`. -/
/-- The division by `4` in `flagCoord` is exact. -/
/-- **Flag coordinates are a complete address**: distinct roots get distinct coordinates. -/

/-!
# The magic star: `240 = 72 + 6 + 6 · 27` under `E₈ ⊃ A₂ × E₆`

The first two flag roots `f₁, f₂` (`QBX.Formal.Gosset.flag`) are at `60°`, so `±f₁, ±f₂,
±(f₁ - f₂)` form an `A₂` root system.  Projecting each root `r` of `E₈` to the pair
`(⟨r, f₁⟩, ⟨r, f₂⟩)` (in units of the root inner product) sorts the 240 roots into 13 points of
the `A₂` weight lattice (`starPoint_counts`):

* the origin carries the **72** roots of `E₆` (the roots orthogonal to `f₁` and `f₂`);
* the six roots of `A₂` itself each sit alone at the six outer points;
* the six points `±(1,1), ±(1,0), ±(0,1)`, the vertices of a **hexagram** (two opposed
  triangles: the weights of the `3` and `3̄` of `A₂`), each carry **27** roots.

So `240 = 72 + 6 · (27 + 1)`.  This picture is known in the literature as the "E8 magic star";
it is the projection described, in other language, by the page the user pointed to (a central
Magen David of six points, each with 27 roots attached, around 72 central roots).

* `starPoint_counts`: the 13 fibre sizes.
* `star_fibre_is_2_21`: each of the six 27-root fibres is internally a copy of the `2₂₁`
  graph: every member is at `60°` to exactly 16 others of its fibre and orthogonal to 10.
* `star_fibre_one_one`: the fibre over `(1, 1)` is exactly layer 2 of the Gosset ladder (the
  27 lines of `QBX.Formal.Gosset.lines27`).
* `dim_e8_branching`: the dimension count `248 = 8 + 78 + 27·3 + 27·3` behind it, as
  arithmetic (the Lie-algebra statement itself is not formalized).

/-- The centre is the `E₆` root system (`perp 2`). -/
/-- The six hexagram points. -/

/-- **Each hexagram fibre is a copy of the `2₂₁` graph** (16 neighbours at `60°`, 10
orthogonal, within its own fibre). -/
/-- The `(1, 1)` fibre is layer 2 of the Gosset ladder. -/

/-!
# The 27 vertices of `2₂₁`, the 27 lines, and the 72 roots of `E₆`

Layer 2 of the Gosset ladder (`QBX.Formal.Gosset.layer 2`) is a set of 27 roots: the vertices of
the Gosset polytope `2₂₁`.  Classically these are the 27 lines on a smooth cubic surface: two
lines are **skew** when the corresponding vertices are joined by an edge of `2₂₁` (inner
product `1`, doubled `4`) and **meet** when the vertices are orthogonal.

Proved here by kernel computation:

* `skew_meet_degrees`: every line is skew to 16 others and meets 10 (`27 = 1 + 16 + 10`).
* `skew_edges`, `meet_edges`: `216` skew pairs (the edges of `2₂₁`) and `135` meeting pairs.
* `tritangent_count`: `45` triples of mutually meeting lines (the tritangent planes).
* `sixes_count`, `no_skew_seven`: there are exactly `72` sets of six mutually skew lines
  ("sixes") and no seven mutually skew lines.
* `six_of_root`, `six_injective`, `sixes_from_roots`: the `72` roots of `E₆`
  (`perp 2`, the roots orthogonal to `f₁, f₂`) correspond one-to-one with the 72 sixes, by
  `α ↦ {lines at 60° to α}`.
* `double_six`: the sixes of `α` and `-α` are disjoint, and each line of one meets exactly five
  lines of the other: they form a double-six.  So the `36` pairs `±α` give the `36` double-sixes.

Counts of cliques use `cliques`, whose meaning is fixed by `cliques_eq`.
-/
/-- The 27 lines: vertices of `2₂₁`. -/
/-- The 72 roots of `E₆`. -/
/-- Skew lines: adjacent in `2₂₁`. -/
/-- Meeting lines: orthogonal. -/
/-- Inner products among the 27 take only the values `2` (self), `1` (skew), `0` (meet). -/
/-- **`27 = 1 + 16 + 10`**: each line is skew to 16 lines and meets 10. -/
/-- **`2₂₁` has 216 edges** (skew pairs). -/
/-- **135 meeting pairs.** -/
/-- **45 tritangent planes**: triples of mutually meeting lines. -/
/-- **72 sixes**: sets of six mutually skew lines. -/
/-- No seven lines are mutually skew. -/
/-- The six attached to an `E₆` root: the lines at `60°` to it. -/
/-- The six of `α`, as a sublist of the 27. -/
/-- Each `E₆` root gives six mutually skew lines. -/
/-- Different roots give different sixes. -/
/-- Every six arises from a root. -/
/-- `-α` is again an `E₆` root. -/

/-- **Double-sixes**: the sixes of `α` and `-α` are disjoint and each line of the first meets
exactly five lines of the second. -/

/-- In the language of the specification: the number of 6-element sets of mutually skew lines
is 72. -/

/-!
# The Gosset structure layer

Exact layers on the 240 vertices of the Gosset polytope `4₂₁` (= roots of `E₈`, doubled
coordinates): five shells, the flag and the Gosset ladder `240 → 56 → 27 → 16 → 10 → 6 → 3 → 1`,
the chain `E₈ ⊃ E₇ ⊃ E₆ ⊃ D₅ ⊃ A₄ ⊃ A₂×A₁ ⊃ A₁`, the 27 lines and 72 sixes, the magic star
`240 = 72 + 6 · (27 + 1)`, and the Coxeter rings `8 × 30`, `7 × 18`, `6 × 12`.
Design notes: `QBX/docs/design/GOSSET_STRUCTURE.md`.
-/

/-!
# `H³(ℤ/n, U(1)) ≅ ℤ/n`, generated by the carry cocycle

This file is self-contained: it defines the explicit cochain complex it works with, constructs
the standard generator of `H³(ℤ/n, U(1))`, and computes `H³(ℤ/n, U(1))` itself from Mathlib's
group cohomology.  Nothing in it is cited.

The audit `QBX.Forensics.MeruCocycles` showed that the Meru cocycles C1 (`ω^{abc}` on `ℤ/3`) and
C3 (`ζ^{abc}` on `ℤ/7`) are coboundaries, i.e. *not* generators of `H³(ℤ/n, U(1))` as the source
claims.  The replacement (`HEBREW_HOPF_TERNARY.md` §4 item 2) is the standard generator

  `ω(a, b, c) = exp(2πi · a · (b + c − [b + c]ₙ) / n²) = exp(2πi · a · carry(b, c) / n)`,

where `a, b, c ∈ {0, …, n − 1}` and `carry(b, c) ∈ {0, 1}` is the carry digit of `b + c` in base
`n`.  Cochains are written additively, with values in `AddCircle 1 = ℝ/ℤ` (the additive form of
`U(1)`).

**Explicit cochains** (any abelian group `G`, coefficients in any abelian group `M`):
`cobdry2`, `cobdry3` (inhomogeneous coboundaries), `IsCocycle3`, `IsCoboundary3`,
`cobdry3_cobdry2` (`δ ∘ δ = 0`), `isCoboundary_map` (change of coefficients), and the
antisymmetrisation test `alt3_cobdry2`, `not_coboundary_of_alt3`.

**The carry cocycle.**
* `carry_cobdry2`: the carry is an integer 2-cocycle on `ℤ/n` (the "adding with carry" identity).
* `cobdry3_carryCochain`: the integer 3-cochain `a · carry(b, c)` has coboundary
  `n · carry(a, b) · carry(c, d)` — divisible by `n`, so it vanishes after dividing by `n`.
* `genCocycle_isCocycle`: `ω` is a 3-cocycle with `U(1)` coefficients.
* `nsmul_genCocycle`: `n · ω = 0`, so the class of `ω` has order dividing `n`.
* `sum_cobdry2_telescope`: for any 2-cochain `β` on `ℤ/n` and any `g`,
  `Σₖ (δβ)(g, k, g) = 0`.  This is the invariant that detects non-trivial classes.
* `sum_genCocycle`: `Σₖ ω(1, k, 1) = 1/n` (only `k = n − 1` produces a carry).
* `zsmul_genCocycle_not_coboundary`, `genCocycle_order`: for `n ≥ 2`, `m · ω` is a coboundary
  iff `n ∣ m`; the class of `ω` has order exactly `n`.
* `ternaryGenerator`, `heptadGenerator`: the cases `n = 3` and `n = 7` that replace Meru's
  C1 and C3.

**The computation of `H³`** (section `H3Computation`, below): `card_h3` (`H³(ℤ/n, U(1))` has
exactly `n` elements, via Mathlib's periodic resolution for finite cyclic groups),
`cls_eq_zero_iff` (the explicit `IsCoboundary3` agrees with Mathlib's `H³`), and
`cohomologous_to_genCocycle` (every 3-cocycle is cohomologous to some `m · ω`).  Together with
`genCocycle_order`: **`ω` generates `H³(ℤ/n, U(1)) ≅ ℤ/n`.**

For `n = 3` the classes `ω, ω²` are the associators of the two non-trivial pointed fusion
categories `Vec_{ℤ/3}^ω` (the "ℤ/3 anyons with a twisted associator"); the cohomology computation
here is what distinguishes them from the untwisted `Vec_{ℤ/3}` that C1 secretly describes.
-/
/-! ### Inhomogeneous cochains on an abelian group -/
/-- Coboundary of a 2-cochain: `(δβ)(a,b,c) = β(b,c) − β(a+b,c) + β(a,b+c) − β(a,b)`. -/
/-- Coboundary of a 3-cochain. -/
/-- A 3-cocycle. -/
/-- A 3-coboundary (cohomologically trivial 3-cocycle). -/
/-- Pushing a coboundary forward along a homomorphism of coefficients gives a coboundary. -/
/-- Total antisymmetrisation of a 3-cochain. -/
/-- **The antisymmetrisation of a coboundary vanishes** (the group being abelian). -/
/-! ### The carry digit -/
/-- The carry digit of `b + c` in base `n` (with `b, c` represented in `{0, …, n − 1}`). -/
/-- **The carry is a 2-cocycle**: `carry(c,d) − carry(b+c,d) + carry(b,c+d) − carry(b,c) = 0`. -/
/-! ### The integer cochain `a · carry(b, c)` -/
/-- The integer 3-cochain `a · carry(b, c)`. -/
/-- `δ(a · carry(b, c)) = n · carry(a, b) · carry(c, d)`. -/
/-! ### The `U(1)`-valued generator -/

/-- **The generator** `ω(a, b, c) = a · carry(b, c) / n ∈ ℝ/ℤ`, i.e.
`exp(2πi · a(b + c − [b + c]ₙ)/n²)` written additively. -/
/-- `ω` is a 3-cocycle with `U(1)` coefficients. -/
/-- Every integer multiple of `ω` is a 3-cocycle. -/
/-- `n · ω = 0` pointwise. -/
/-! ### Detecting non-trivial classes -/
/-- **Telescoping**: for every 2-cochain `β` on `ℤ/n` and every `g`, `Σₖ (δβ)(g, k, g) = 0`. -/
/-- `Σₖ carry(1·k·1) = 1`: exactly one `k`, namely `n − 1`, produces a carry. -/
/-- **`m · ω` is not a coboundary unless `n ∣ m`.** -/
/-- **The class of `ω` has order exactly `n`**: `m · ω` is a coboundary iff `n ∣ m`. -/
/-- In particular `ω` itself is not a coboundary. -/

/-- The replacement for Meru C1: `exp(2πi · a · carry₃(b, c)/3)` on `ℤ/3` is a non-trivial
3-cocycle whose class has order `3`. -/
/-- The replacement for Meru C3: the carry cocycle on `ℤ/7`, of order `7`. -/

/-!
## Computing `H³(ℤ/n, U(1))` with Mathlib

This section proves that `H³(ℤ/n, U(1))` is cyclic of order `n`, which is what makes the
order-`n` class of `ω` a generator.  It uses
Mathlib's group cohomology (`groupCohomology`, defined by inhomogeneous cochains) and its
computation of the cohomology of a finite cyclic group from the periodic resolution
(`Rep.FiniteCyclicGroup.groupCohomologyIsoOdd`).

Here `U1Rep n` is `ℝ/ℤ = AddCircle 1` (the additive form of `U(1)`) as a trivial representation
of `ℤ/n` (written multiplicatively, `CycG n`).

* `h3Map_bijective`, `h3Equiv`, `card_h3`: `H³(ℤ/n, U(1))` is in bijection with `ZMod n`; in
  particular it has exactly `n` elements.  (Periodic resolution: `H³ ≅ ker(N)/im(g − 1)`; for the
  trivial action `g − 1 = 0` and `N = n·`, whose kernel in `ℝ/ℤ` is `(1/n)ℤ/ℤ`.)
* **Bridge to the explicit cochains** above: `toM3`, `toM2` turn functions
  `ℤ/n × ℤ/n × ℤ/n → ℝ/ℤ` into Mathlib's inhomogeneous cochains, and the Mathlib differentials
  become `cobdry3`, `cobdry2` (`d_toM3`, `d_toM2`).  `cls f` is the Mathlib class of an explicit
  3-cocycle, and `cls_eq_zero_iff`: **`cls f = 0` iff `f` is a coboundary in the sense of
  `IsCoboundary3`.**  So the explicit notions compute the same `H³` as Mathlib's.
* **Generator** (`cohomologous_to_genCocycle`): for `n ≥ 2`, every 3-cocycle
  `f : ℤ/n × ℤ/n × ℤ/n → ℝ/ℤ` is cohomologous to `m · ω` for some integer `m`, and `m` is unique
  mod `n` (`genCocycle_order`).  So `ω` generates `H³(ℤ/n, U(1)) ≅ ℤ/n`, and
  `ternaryGenerator`/`heptadGenerator` are generators for `n = 3, 7`
  (`ternary_classification`, `heptad_classification`).
-/
/-- In a short complex of modules, a cycle whose homology class vanishes is a boundary. -/
/-- A cocycle with zero class in `H^{m+1}(G, A)` is the differential of an `m`-cochain. -/
/-- The differential of an `m`-cochain has zero class in `H^{m+1}(G, A)`. -/
/-- `ℤ/n`, written multiplicatively (Mathlib's group cohomology uses multiplicative groups). -/
/-- `U(1) = ℝ/ℤ` as a trivial `ℤ/n`-representation over `ℤ`. -/
/-! ### `H³(ℤ/n, U(1))` has `n` elements -/
/-- `j ↦ j/n`, as an element of `ker(N : ℝ/ℤ → ℝ/ℤ)`. -/
/-- `j ↦ [j/n] ∈ H³(ℤ/n, U(1))`, via the periodic resolution. -/
/-- **`H³(ℤ/n, U(1)) ≃ ℤ/n`** (as sets; `h3Map` is the bijection `j ↦ [j/n]`). -/
/-- **`H³(ℤ/n, U(1))` has exactly `n` elements.** -/
/-! ### Bridge to the explicit cochains -/
/-- A project 3-cochain as a Mathlib inhomogeneous 3-cochain. -/
/-- A project 2-cochain as a Mathlib inhomogeneous 2-cochain. -/
/-- Mathlib's differential on 3-cochains is `cobdry3`. -/
/-- Mathlib's differential on 2-cochains is `cobdry2`. -/
/-- The Mathlib cohomology class of a project 3-cocycle. -/

/-- **The explicit and the Mathlib notions of triviality agree**: the class of a project
3-cocycle vanishes in Mathlib's `H³(ℤ/n, U(1))` iff it is a coboundary in the sense of
`IsCoboundary3`. -/
/-! ### Linearity of `cls` -/
/-! ### The carry cocycle generates `H³` -/

/-- **Every 3-cocycle `ℤ/n × ℤ/n × ℤ/n → ℝ/ℤ` is cohomologous to an integer multiple of the carry
cocycle `ω`.**  With `genCocycle_order` (the multiple is unique mod `n`), this says that `ω`
generates `H³(ℤ/n, U(1)) ≅ ℤ/n`. -/

/-- The carry cocycle on `ℤ/3` generates `H³(ℤ/3, U(1))`: every 3-cocycle is cohomologous to
`m · ω₃`, and `m · ω₃` is trivial iff `3 ∣ m`. -/
/-- The carry cocycle on `ℤ/7` generates `H³(ℤ/7, U(1))`. -/

/-!
# Gate action of the braid group on the address space `Q_n □ T^k`

Formal targets B1 and B2 of `QBX/foundation/ws6_certificates/SPEC.md`, and the isometry
property of the gate set of `QBX/foundation/ws5_braid_ops`.

An address is a pair `(bits, cycles)` with `bits : Fin n → Bool` (the hypercube factor) and
`cycles j : ZMod (M j)` (the torus factor with moduli `M`).  A braid acts through its
permutation shadow `permHom : B_n →* S_n` by permuting bit positions (`bitGate σ` sends the bit
at position `i` to position `σ i`, as `permutation_gate` does in Python), and a torus translation
`shiftGate t` adds `t` to the cycles.

* `perm_shadow_satisfies_braid_relations`, `perm_shadow_far_commute` (**B1**, **B2**): the
  transpositions `σ_i ↦ (i i+1)` satisfy the braid relations in `S_n` (a corollary of the
  homomorphism `permHom` of `QBX.Formal.Invariants`).
* `braidGate_mul`, `braidGate_one`: `b ↦ braidGate b` is an action of `B_n` on addresses.
* `braidGate_braid`, `braidGate_far_commute`: the gates satisfy the braid relations.
* `addrDist_bitGate`, `addrDist_shiftGate`: every bit-permutation gate and every torus
  translation is an isometry of the address metric (Hamming distance on bits plus cyclic
  distance on each cycle), so every composite gate is one too (`addrDist_gate`).
* `bitGate_shiftGate_comm`: the two kinds of gates commute.
-/
/-- An address of `Q_n □ T^k_M`. -/
/-- Hypercube coordinates. -/
/-- Torus coordinates. -/
/-- Permute bit positions: the bit at position `i` moves to position `σ i`. -/
/-- Translate the torus coordinates by `t`. -/
/-- The gate of a braid: the bit permutation of its permutation shadow. -/
/-- **B1.** The permutation shadow satisfies the braid relation. -/
/-- **B2.** The permutation shadow satisfies far commutation. -/
/-- The gates of `σ_i` satisfy the braid relation. -/
/-- The gates of distant `σ_i` commute. -/
/-- Cyclic distance on `ZMod m`: the shorter way around. -/

/-- The address metric: Hamming distance on bits plus cyclic distance on every cycle
(`MixedRadixSpace.distance`). -/
/-- Every composite gate (bit permutation followed by a torus translation) is an isometry. -/
/-- Braid gates are isometries. -/

/-!
# Declared invariants of the QBX rewrite rules

Every QBX rewrite rule declares that it preserves `braid_group_element`, `strand_count`,
`permutation` and `writhe` (`qbx_ir.algebra.rewriting`, QBX.md §22).  This file proves those
declarations for every strand count `n`:

* `permHom : B_n →* Perm (Fin n)` and `writheHom : B_n →* Multiplicative ℤ` are group
  homomorphisms, so they factor through the braid group;
* `Word.perm` and `Word.writhe` are the word-level computations performed by the Python
  functions `permutation` and `writhe`, and they agree with the homomorphisms
  (`permHom_eval`, `writheHom_eval`);
* `Step.preserves`: a rewrite step preserves the group element, the permutation and the writhe.

As consequences, each `σ_i` has infinite order (`orderOf_sigma`) and `B_n` is non-abelian for
`n ≥ 3` (`sigma_mul_sigma_ne`).
-/
/-- The left strand position crossed by `σ_i`. -/
/-- The right strand position crossed by `σ_i`. -/
/-- The transposition of positions `i` and `i + 1`: the permutation induced by `σ_i`. -/
/-- The two strand positions crossed by `σ_i` are different. -/
/-- A transposition is an involution. -/
/-- Conjugating a transposition by a transposition. -/
/-- The permutation homomorphism `B_n → S_n`. -/

/-- The permutation of a word, computed letter by letter.  `w.perm p` is the (initial position
of the) strand that ends at position `p`, as in the Python function `permutation`. -/
/-- The writhe (exponent-sum) homomorphism `B_n → ℤ`, written multiplicatively. -/
/-- The writhe of a word: the sum of its crossing signs. -/
/-- Writhe is additive under concatenation of words. -/

/-- **Declared semantics.** A QBX rewrite step preserves the braid group element, the induced
permutation and the writhe (the strand count is fixed by the type `Word n`). -/
/-- The declared invariants are preserved along any chain of rewrites in either direction. -/
/-- Each generator `σ_i` has infinite order. -/
/-- Adjacent generators do not commute; in particular `B_n` is non-abelian for `n ≥ 3`. -/

/-!
# Audit of the Connes-rigidity papers of J. L. Nielsen: direct versus semidirect products

Sources (in `QBX/docs/design/`): *On the Invalidity of the Claimed Disproof of Connes’ Rigidity
Conjecture* (Sections 3–7, Appendices A–B) and *Connes’ Rigidity Conjecture: Disproof of the
Counterexamples and Proof of the Theorem* (Appendix §A).

The critique argues that the "zero-cocycle group" of the published formalisation is a direct
product `Z^{2n} × Sp(2n, Z)` and therefore (1) has the lattice in its centre, so it is not ICC,
and (2) surjects onto the lattice, so it cannot have property (T).  Both steps are correct **for
a direct product**; they are proved here in Mathlib form (`prod_not_isICC`,
`prod_center_infinite`, `fstHom_surjective`).

The critique's own correspondence table, however, identifies the groups of the published code as
`Λ = D ⋊ K` and `Γ = E(n) ⋊ K`: **semidirect** products for a non-trivial action of `K`.
"Zero cocycle" refers to the abelian extension `0 → V → D → B → 0` being split (`D = V × B`), not
to the action of `K` being trivial.  For a semidirect product both steps fail in general:

* `SemidirectProduct.inl_mem_center_iff'`: a lattice element is central iff it is central in the
  lattice and fixed by the whole acting group;
* `SemidirectProduct.left_mul_hom_iff`: the projection `(n, g) ↦ n` is multiplicative iff the
  action is trivial.

The smallest test case is the affine group `ℤ² ⋊ SL(2, ℤ)` with the standard action
(`SL(2, ℤ) = Sp(2, ℤ)`):

* `affSL_left_not_hom` — the projection to the lattice is not a homomorphism, so the property-(T)
  obstruction (Theorem 1 of the critique) does not apply to it;
* `affSL_center_eq_bot` — the centre is trivial (no lattice element is central);
* `affSL_conjugatesOf_inl_infinite` — every non-zero lattice element has infinitely many
  conjugates, so the ICC obstruction does not apply either.

The later paper (Appendix §A, "Scope of Part A") restricts the obstructions to the
"trivial-action reading", which is the correct scope; these theorems make that scope precise.

## The function-valued Kazhdan axiom

Appendix A of the critique (`NielsenCritique.lean`) postulates `kazhdan_finite_abelianisation`:
a group with property (T) admits no surjective **function** onto an infinite abelian group.  The
classical statement (Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette, Cor. 1.3.5) is about surjective
**homomorphisms**.  `kazhdanFunctionSchema_kills` shows the function version denies property (T)
to every group with an element of infinite order, and `kazhdanFunctionSchema_kills_SL3` applies
it to `SL(3, ℤ)`, which has property (T) by Kazhdan's theorem.  So no predicate satisfying that
axiom can be property (T).  The later paper drops the axiom; `fstHom_surjective` is the
homomorphism statement it keeps.
-/
/-! ### ICC and the centre -/

/-- A group is *ICC* (infinite conjugacy classes) when every non-identity element has infinitely
many conjugates.  This is the hypothesis of Connes' rigidity conjecture. -/
/-- A central element is its own only conjugate. -/
/-- A non-trivial centre rules out ICC. -/
/-! ### Direct products (the critique's argument, correct as stated) -/
/-- In `A × G` with `A` abelian, every `(a, 1)` is central. -/

/-- **Critique, Section 6 (direct-product case).**  `A × G` with `A` abelian and non-trivial is
not ICC. -/
/-- If moreover `A` is infinite, the centre of `A × G` is infinite. -/

/-- **Critique, Theorem 1, Step 2 (direct-product case).**  The projection `A × G → A` is a
surjective homomorphism onto the abelian factor. -/
/-! ### Semidirect products: where both steps break -/

/-- A lattice element `inl n` of `N ⋊[φ] G` is central iff `n` is central in `N` and fixed by
every `φ g`. -/
/-- The projection `(n, g) ↦ n` of `N ⋊[φ] G` is multiplicative iff the action is trivial. -/
/-! ### The affine group `ℤ² ⋊ SL(2, ℤ)` -/
/-- The lattice `ℤ²`, written multiplicatively. -/
/-- The standard action of `SL(2, ℤ)` on `ℤ²`. -/

/-- The affine group `ℤ² ⋊ SL(2, ℤ)`: the `n = 1` case of the lattice-by-symplectic semidirect
products discussed in the papers. -/
/-- The transvection `[[1, k], [0, 1]]`. -/
/-- The transvection `[[1, 0], [k, 1]]`. -/
/-- The only lattice vector fixed by all of `SL(2, ℤ)` is `0`. -/

/-- **Correction to the critique, Theorem 1.**  In `ℤ² ⋊ SL(2, ℤ)` the projection onto the
lattice is not a homomorphism. -/
/-- A matrix of `SL(2, ℤ)` fixing every vector is the identity. -/
/-- **Correction to the critique, Section 6.**  The centre of `ℤ² ⋊ SL(2, ℤ)` is trivial. -/
/-- No non-zero lattice element of `ℤ² ⋊ SL(2, ℤ)` is central. -/
/-- Conjugating a lattice element by `g` applies the action. -/

/-- **Correction to the critique, Section 6.**  Every non-zero lattice element of
`ℤ² ⋊ SL(2, ℤ)` has infinitely many conjugates. -/
/-! ### The function-valued Kazhdan axiom -/

/-- The shape of the axiom `kazhdan_finite_abelianisation` of `NielsenCritique.lean`: a group
satisfying `P` admits no surjective *function* onto an infinite abelian group. -/
/-- Any type receiving an injection from `ℤ` surjects (as a set) onto `ℤ`. -/

/-- Any predicate satisfying the function-valued schema fails on every group that has an element
of infinite order. -/
/-- `SL(3, ℤ)`, the classical example of a group with property (T). -/
/-- The elementary matrix `1 + E₀₁` of `SL(3, ℤ)`. -/

/-- **The function-valued axiom contradicts Kazhdan's theorem.**  Any predicate satisfying the
schema of `NielsenCritique.lean` is false on `SL(3, ℤ)`, which has property (T). -/

inductive Classification (G H : Type u) [Group G] [Group H] : Type u
  /-- The image intertwines into a group-algebra leg. -/
  | degenerateI
  /-- The Cartan subalgebra intertwines into the group algebra. -/
  | degenerateII
  /-- The rigid case, returning group morphisms `δ₁ : G → G` and `δ₂ : G → H`. -/

/-- The objects Connes' conjecture is about, left uninterpreted as in the appendix. -/

declarations.name: SkeletonBase
declarations.signature_heuristic:
structure SkeletonBase where
  /-- von Neumann algebras. -/
  VNAlg : Type v
  /-- The group von Neumann algebra `L(G)`. -/
  L : ∀ (G : Type u) [Group G], VNAlg
  /-- The Bernoulli crossed product `L^∞(X) ⋊ G`. -/
  Crossed : ∀ (G : Type u) [Group G], VNAlg
  /-- Tensor product of algebras. -/
  Tensor : VNAlg → VNAlg → VNAlg
  /-- `*`-isomorphisms. -/
  VNIso : VNAlg → VNAlg → Type v
  /-- ICC. -/
  IsICC : ∀ (G : Type u) [Group G], Prop
  /-- Kazhdan's property (T). -/
  HasPropertyT : ∀ (G : Type u) [Group G], Prop

/-- Connes' rigidity conjecture, relative to an interpretation `B`. -/

declarations.name: ConnesConjecture
declarations.signature_heuristic: def ConnesConjecture (B : SkeletonBase.{u, v}) : Prop

declarations.name: SkeletonAxioms
declarations.signature_heuristic:
structure SkeletonAxioms (B : SkeletonBase.{u, v}) where
  /-- `*`-homomorphisms. -/
  VNHom : B.VNAlg → B.VNAlg → Type w
  /-- The twisted comultiplication `Θ`. -/
  twistedComult : ∀ {G H : Type u} [Group G] [Group H],
    B.VNIso (B.L G) (B.L H) → VNHom (B.Crossed G) (B.Tensor (B.Crossed G) (B.Crossed H))
  /-- Ioana's classification. -/
  classify : ∀ {G H : Type u} [Group G] [Group H],
    VNHom (B.Crossed G) (B.Tensor (B.Crossed G) (B.Crossed H)) → Classification G H
  /-- Case (I) is excluded. -/
  not_degenerateI : ∀ {G H : Type u} [Group G] [Group H], B.IsICC G → B.IsICC H →
    B.HasPropertyT G → B.HasPropertyT H → ∀ Φ : B.VNIso (B.L G) (B.L H),
      classify (twistedComult Φ) ≠ Classification.degenerateI
  /-- Case (II) is excluded. -/
  not_degenerateII : ∀ {G H : Type u} [Group G] [Group H], B.IsICC G → B.IsICC H →
    B.HasPropertyT G → B.HasPropertyT H → ∀ Φ : B.VNIso (B.L G) (B.L H),
      classify (twistedComult Φ) ≠ Classification.degenerateII
  /-- The returned `δ₂` is injective. -/
  rigid_d2_injective : ∀ {G H : Type u} [Group G] [Group H], B.IsICC G → B.IsICC H →
    B.HasPropertyT G → B.HasPropertyT H → ∀ (Φ : B.VNIso (B.L G) (B.L H)) (d1 : G →* G)
      (d2 : G →* H), classify (twistedComult Φ) = Classification.rigid d1 d2 →
        Function.Injective d2
  /-- The returned `δ₂` is surjective. -/
  rigid_d2_surjective : ∀ {G H : Type u} [Group G] [Group H], B.IsICC G → B.IsICC H →
    B.HasPropertyT G → B.HasPropertyT H → ∀ (Φ : B.VNIso (B.L G) (B.L H)) (d1 : G →* G)
      (d2 : G →* H), classify (twistedComult Φ) = Classification.rigid d1 d2 →
        Function.Surjective d2
