/-!
# The axiom package of the claimed proof of Connes' rigidity is equivalent to the conjecture

Source: *Connes’ Rigidity Conjecture: Disproof of the Counterexamples and Proof of the Theorem*
(J. L. Nielsen, `QBX/docs/design/`), Appendix §B, `ConnesAppendix.lean`.

That appendix declares opaque objects (`VNAlg`, `L`, `Crossed`, `Tensor`, `VNIso`, `VNHom`,
`IsICC`, `HasPropertyT`), two opaque operations (`twistedComult`, `classify`) and four
propositional axioms (`not_degenerateI`, `not_degenerateII`, `rigid_d2_injective`,
`rigid_d2_surjective`), and derives `connes_rigidity` from them.  The appendix itself says the
part is "a proof skeleton" in which "no operator algebra is verified".

This file makes the status of the skeleton exact.  The objects the conjecture is *about* —
`L`, `VNIso`, `IsICC`, `HasPropertyT` (together with `Crossed`, `Tensor`) — form a
`SkeletonBase`.  The remaining declarations form `SkeletonAxioms B`.  Then:

* `connes_of_skeletonAxioms` — the axioms imply the conjecture for `B` (this is the appendix's
  `connes_rigidity`, with Mathlib's `Group` and `MonoidHom` in place of the hand-rolled ones);
* `skeletonAxioms_of_connes` — conversely, **whenever the conjecture holds for `B`, all the
  remaining axioms can be satisfied** (with `VNHom` a one-point type and `classify` returning a
  bijection supplied by the conjecture);
* `skeletonAxioms_iff_connes` — so the axiom package is satisfiable over `B` exactly when the
  conjecture holds over `B`.

In other words the ten axioms carry precisely the content of the conjecture, no more and no
less: the formal file certifies the case analysis, and the mathematical burden sits entirely in
`rigid_d2_surjective` together with `not_degenerateI/II`.  This does not say the paper's argument
is wrong; it says the Lean appendix is not evidence for it beyond the cited theorems.  (The
universes of the groups and of the algebra objects are kept arbitrary.)
-/
/-- Ioana's trichotomy as the appendix encodes it. -/
/-- The image intertwines into a group-algebra leg. -/
/-- The Cartan subalgebra intertwines into the group algebra. -/
/-- The rigid case, returning group morphisms `δ₁ : G → G` and `δ₂ : G → H`. -/
/-- The objects Connes' conjecture is about, left uninterpreted as in the appendix. -/
/-- von Neumann algebras. -/
/-- The group von Neumann algebra `L(G)`. -/
/-- The Bernoulli crossed product `L^∞(X) ⋊ G`. -/
/-- Tensor product of algebras. -/
/-- `*`-isomorphisms. -/
/-- Kazhdan's property (T). -/
/-- Connes' rigidity conjecture, relative to an interpretation `B`. -/

/-- The remaining declarations of the appendix (`VNHom`, `twistedComult`, `classify` and the four
propositional axioms), over a fixed base `B`. -/
/-- `*`-homomorphisms. -/
/-- The twisted comultiplication `Θ`. -/
/-- Ioana's classification. -/
/-- Case (I) is excluded. -/
/-- Case (II) is excluded. -/
/-- The returned `δ₂` is injective. -/
/-- The returned `δ₂` is surjective. -/
/-- The appendix's `connes_rigidity`: the axioms imply the conjecture. -/

/-- The classification used to model the axioms from the conjecture: return a bijection when
one exists. -/

/-- **Converse.**  If the conjecture holds for `B`, every remaining axiom of the appendix can be
satisfied over `B`. -/

/-- **The axiom package is equivalent to the conjecture.**  Over any interpretation of the
objects the conjecture is about, the appendix's remaining axioms are satisfiable iff Connes'
rigidity conjecture holds for that interpretation. -/

declarations.name: HoCat
declarations.signature_heuristic:
structure HoCat where
  /-- Objects. -/
  Obj : Type
  /-- Homotopy classes of maps. -/
  Hom : Obj → Obj → Type
  /-- Identities. -/
  id : (X : Obj) → Hom X X
  /-- Composition. -/
  comp : {X Y Z : Obj} → Hom X Y → Hom Y Z → Hom X Z

/-- Bundle sets with contravariant pullback. -/

declarations.name: BundleFunctor
declarations.signature_heuristic:
structure BundleFunctor (C : HoCat) where
  /-- Isomorphism classes of bundles over `X`. -/
  Bun : C.Obj → Type
  /-- Pullback. -/
  pull : {X Y : C.Obj} → C.Hom X Y → Bun Y → Bun X
  pull_id : ∀ {X} (E : Bun X), pull (C.id X) E = E
  pull_comp : ∀ {X Y Z} (f : C.Hom X Y) (g : C.Hom Y Z) (E : Bun Z),
    pull (C.comp f g) E = pull f (pull g E)

/-- `B` classifies the bundles: `f ↦ f^*E` is a bijection `[X, B] ≃ Bun X`. -/

declarations.name: Classifies
declarations.signature_heuristic:
structure Classifies (C : HoCat) (F : BundleFunctor C) (B : C.Obj) where
  /-- The universal bundle. -/
  E : F.Bun B
  /-- The classifying map of a bundle. -/
  classify : {X : C.Obj} → F.Bun X → C.Hom X B
  pull_classify : ∀ {X} (b : F.Bun X), F.pull (classify b) E = b
  classify_pull : ∀ {X} (f : C.Hom X B), classify (F.pull f E) = f

/-- Homotopy equivalence. -/

declarations.name: HEquiv
declarations.signature_heuristic:
structure HEquiv (C : HoCat) (P Q : C.Obj) where
  /-- Forward map. -/
  toFun : C.Hom P Q
  /-- Backward map. -/
  invFun : C.Hom Q P
  left : C.comp toFun invFun = C.id P
  right : C.comp invFun toFun = C.id Q

/-- Kernel 3 (Yoneda): two classifying objects are equivalent. -/

declarations.name: classifying_unique
every_field_configuration_is_in_the_bundle
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem every_field_configuration_is_in_the_bundle (C : HoCat) (F : BundleFunctor C) {B : C.Obj}
    (h : Classifies C F B) (X : C.Obj) (b : F.Bun X) : ∃ f : C.Hom X B, F.pull f h.E = b

/-!
# Audit of the TUFT "Lean Forcing Core" (`TUFT_Forcing_Core.lean`)

Source: *Canonical Field, Beltrami Action, Spectral Geometry, and Particle Mass Derivations*
(J. L. Nielsen, `QBX/docs/design/`), Appendix B.  The appendix lists five kernels.  Kernels 1, 3,
4 and 5 are correct as stated; Kernel 2 is correct as algebra but does not support the
conclusion drawn from it.

## Kernel 2: "a domain admits no nontrivial product decomposition"

The appendix proves that a ring product `R × S` (both non-trivial) has zero divisors, and
concludes that since `H*(CP^∞; ℤ) ≅ ℤ[c₁]` is a domain there is "no ring splitting, no bundle
factorization".  The algebra is right (`prod_not_isDomain`, `idempotent_trivial`).  The
inference is not, because the ring that a *product of bundles* produces is not a ring product:

* a principal `G₁ × G₂`-bundle that factors as a fibre product is classified by a map into
  `BG₁ × BG₂`, a **Cartesian product of spaces**;
* by the Künneth theorem (cited, not formalised here) the cohomology of a product of spaces with
  torsion-free cohomology of finite type is the **tensor product** `H*(X) ⊗ H*(Y)`; a ring
  product `H*(X) × H*(Y)` is the cohomology of the **disjoint union** `X ⊔ Y`;
* the tensor product of two domains of this kind is again a domain:
  `tensor_polynomial_isDomain` shows `ℤ[x] ⊗_ℤ ℤ[y]` is a domain (it is `ℤ[x, y]`,
  `mvPolynomial_two_isDomain`).

So `CP^∞ × CP^∞ = B(U(1) × U(1))`, which classifies the decomposable `U(1) × U(1)`-bundles, has
a domain as cohomology ring.  "The cohomology ring is a domain" therefore does not rule out a
product decomposition of the bundle, and Kernel 2 does not certify Corollary 4 of the paper.

## Kernels 3 and 4: what is and is not checked

`classifying_unique` (ported below) is the Yoneda argument: two objects representing the same
functor are equivalent.  It is correct.  The physical content sits in the hypothesis
`hComplete : Classifies C F B` ("the unified base classifies every bundle over every admissible
space"); `every_field_configuration_is_in_the_bundle` is that hypothesis's field
`pull_classify`, restated (`every_field_configuration_eq_field`).  Note also that the finite
shells `S^{2n+1} → CP^n` used in the rest of the paper do **not** satisfy `Classifies` (they
classify line bundles only over complexes of dimension at most `2n`); only the limit `CP^∞` does.
-/
/-! ### Kernel 2: the algebra is right -/

/-- In a domain the only idempotents are `0` and `1` (the appendix's
`domain_idempotents_trivial`). -/

/-- A product of two non-trivial rings is not a domain (the appendix's
`product_has_zero_divisors`). -/
/-! ### …but the relevant algebra is the tensor product -/

/-- `ℤ[x] ⊗_ℤ ℤ[y] ≅ (ℤ[x])[y]`: the algebraic side of the Künneth isomorphism
`H*(CP^∞ × CP^∞) ≅ H*(CP^∞) ⊗ H*(CP^∞)`. -/

/-- **Correction to Kernel 2.**  The tensor product of two polynomial rings — the cohomology ring
of `CP^∞ × CP^∞ = B(U(1) × U(1))` — is a domain, although that space classifies decomposable
`U(1) × U(1)`-bundles. -/
/-- `ℤ[x, y]` is a domain. -/
/-! ### Kernels 3 and 4, ported -/
/-- The appendix's abstract homotopy category (no laws needed). -/
/-- Objects. -/
/-- Homotopy classes of maps. -/
/-- Identities. -/
/-- Composition. -/
/-- Bundle sets with contravariant pullback. -/
/-- Isomorphism classes of bundles over `X`. -/
/-- Pullback. -/
/-- `B` classifies the bundles: `f ↦ f^*E` is a bijection `[X, B] ≃ Bun X`. -/
/-- The universal bundle. -/
/-- The classifying map of a bundle. -/
/-- Homotopy equivalence. -/
/-- Forward map. -/
/-- Backward map. -/
/-- Kernel 3 (Yoneda): two classifying objects are equivalent. -/
/-- Kernel 4 as stated in the appendix. -/

/-- Kernel 4 is the hypothesis `Classifies` read off: its witness is the field `classify` and its
proof is the field `pull_classify`. -/

/-!
# Audit of *A Critique of N. Furey's "Standard Model Symmetries and the Nested Embeddings of
`ℝ ⊂ ℂ ⊂ ℍ ⊂ 𝕆`"* (J. L. Nielsen, July 2026)

Source: `QBX/docs/design/JLN_Critique of Furey.pdf`.

## Confirmed (Sections 1–5 of the critique)

* `nested_chain_sup` / `nested_vs_direct_finrank` — for a chain `U₁ ≤ U₂ ≤ U₃ ≤ U₄` of subspaces
  of dimensions `1, 2, 4, 8` the sum is `U₄` (dimension 8) while the external direct sum has
  dimension `15`; the gap `7 = 1 + 2 + 4` is exactly the overlap counted again.
* `finrank_direct_sum_HCR` — concretely `dim_ℝ (ℍ ⊕ ℂ ⊕ ℝ) = 7`, while all three sit inside
  `ℍ` (dimension 4).
* `no_injective_ringHom_prod` / `no_algebra_embedding_HCR` — the critique's core point in its
  strongest form: a direct sum `R ⊕ S` with componentwise multiplication (both factors
  non-trivial) has the non-trivial idempotent `(1, 0)`, so it admits **no injective ring
  homomorphism into any domain**.  In particular `ℍ ⊕ ℂ ⊕ ℝ` does not embed as an algebra into
  `ℍ`, nor into any division algebra — the nested tower cannot be recovered from the direct sum
  without quotienting the overlap.

## Corrected (Section 6)

The critique says that equal traces `Tr(c_O P_O) = Tr(c_H P_H) = Tr(c_C P_C)` "applied to blocks
of dimension 8, 4 and 2" force the coefficients `1/3 : 1/2 : 1`.  `equal_trace_ratios_842`
shows that blocks of ranks `8, 4, 2` force `c_H = 2 c_O` and `c_C = 4 c_O`, i.e. `1/4 : 1/2 : 1`,
and `equal_trace_ranks_of_third_half_one` shows that the coefficients `1/3 : 1/2 : 1` require
ranks in the proportion `3 : 2 : 1`.  The substantive point of the critique (the constraint is
imposed, and its output is the charge ratio) survives, but the block ranks behind `1/3 : 1/2 : 1`
are not `8, 4, 2`; they are those of the projectors `P_{O2}, P_H, P_C` actually used by Furey.

## Corrected (Section 12)

The critique states that "the unit quaternions are a subset of `CP¹`".  The Hopf map
`S³ → S² = CP¹` is not injective — `hopf_not_injective_on_sphere` exhibits two distinct unit
quaternions with the same image (every fibre is a whole circle,
`QBX.Formal.Connections.hopf_fiber_eq_circle`) — so `S³` fibres *over* `CP¹`; it is not a
subset of it.  The same applies to `S⁷ → CP³`: it uses only the complex structure of `ℂ⁴` and
does not see the octonion product (the octonionic Hopf fibration is `S⁷ → S¹⁵ → S⁸`, see
`QBX.Formal.Connections.CayleyDicksonHopf`).
-/
/-! ### Nested chains versus direct sums -/
/-- The sum of a chain of subspaces is its top member. -/

/-- **Critique, Section 1.**  A chain of subspaces of dimensions `1 ⊂ 2 ⊂ 4 ⊂ 8` spans 8
dimensions, while the external direct sum of the same four spaces has 15. -/

/-- With an 8-dimensional first slot (the octonions as a real vector space), the direct sum has
dimension 15. -/
/-! ### No algebra embedding of a direct sum into a domain -/

/-- **"You cannot multiply nested objects without quotienting overlap."**  A direct sum of two
non-trivial rings with componentwise multiplication has no injective ring homomorphism into a
domain. -/

/-- `ℍ ⊕ ℂ ⊕ ℝ` (componentwise product) does not embed as a ring into `ℍ`, although `ℝ ⊂ ℂ ⊂ ℍ`
as subalgebras. -/
/-! ### The equal-trace constraint -/

/-- **Correction to Section 6.**  Equal traces on blocks of ranks `8, 4, 2` force
`c_H = 2 c_O` and `c_C = 4 c_O` (ratios `1/4 : 1/2 : 1`), not `1/3 : 1/2 : 1`. -/

/-- The coefficients `1/3, 1/2, 1` satisfy the equal-trace condition exactly when the block ranks
are in the proportion `3 : 2 : 1`. -/
/-! ### The Hopf map is not injective -/

/-- **Correction to Section 12.**  Two distinct unit quaternions (`1` and `i`) have the same
image under the Hopf map `S³ → S² = CP¹`: the unit quaternions fibre over `CP¹`, they are not a
subset of it. -/

/-!
# Spectral claims on the Hopf shell `S³`: what is exact, and two corrections

Sources (in `QBX/docs/design/`): *The Complex Hopf Fibration as the Canonical Space for
Gauge–Gravity Unification* (Theorems 17, 23, 24, 29, Proposition 5), the summary of the spectral
zeta function in `plan.md` (§ "The Nested Shell Hierarchy"), and *The Double Hopf Framework with
Complex Time* (Section 5, "Proof of Closure").

## The Beltrami zeta function on `S³` (exact)

`plan.md` records Nielsen's spectral zeta function of `B = ⋆d` on the `S³` shell as
`ζ_B(s) = Σ_{ℓ ≥ 1} ℓ(ℓ+2) / (ℓ+1)^s` (eigenvalue `ℓ + 1`, multiplicity `ℓ(ℓ+2)`; this is one sign
of the curl spectrum `±(ℓ+1)` on coexact 1-forms of the unit sphere).  Writing `m = ℓ + 1` the
multiplicity is `m² − 1`, so

* `zetaB_eq_tsum` — for `Re s > 3`, `Σ ℓ(ℓ+2)/(ℓ+1)^s = ζ(s − 2) − ζ(s)` (Riemann zeta);
* `zetaB` is therefore the meromorphic continuation, and `zetaB_zero` — `ζ_B(0) = 1/2`.

Consequently `ζ_B'(0) = ζ'(−2) − ζ'(0) = −ζ(3)/(4π²) + ½ log 2π` (the derivative values are
classical; only the value at `0` is formalised here).  This is the exact input to every
"zeta-regularised determinant" of the `S³` shell: it is a fixed number, so it cannot by itself
produce a sector-dependent mass hierarchy without further, separately justified, choices.

## Correction 1: two incompatible readings of the eigenvalues

Theorem 23 says the eigenvalues `λ_k` of `B` *are* the masses; Theorem 24 (iii) says `λ_k` is the
mass *squared* (`(□ + λ_k) φ = 0`); Proposition 5 uses `Λ_k = k(k + 2n − 2)` — on `S³`
(`n = 2`) this is `k(k+2)`, the spectrum of the **scalar Laplacian**, not of the first-order
operator `⋆d` (whose eigenvalues on `S³` are `±(k+1)`).  `scalar_eigenvalue_not_square` shows
that `k(k+2)` is never the square of an integer for `k ≥ 1`
(`(k+1)² = k(k+2) + 1`, `scalar_eigenvalue_succ_sq`), so `Λ_k` cannot be `λ_k²` either.  The three
statements give three different mass ratios (e.g. `m₂/m₁ = 3/2`, `√(3/2)`, or `8/3`).

## Correction 2: Clebsch–Gordan selection does not stop the cascade

The Double Hopf paper (Section 5.2) argues that because `V_{k₁} ⊗ V_{k₂}` only contains
`V_k` with `|k₁ − k₂| ≤ k ≤ k₁ + k₂`, "only finitely many `k` interact, preventing uncontrolled
cascades".  Each single coupling is finite, but repeated coupling is not: with `CGReach k₀`
the set of (doubled) spins reachable from `k₀` by iterated Clebsch–Gordan coupling,

* `cgReach_unbounded` — from any seed `k₀ ≥ 1` arbitrarily large `k` are reachable;
* `cgReach_all_of_one` — from `k₀ = 1` (spin ½) **every** `k` is reachable.

So the selection rule bounds the growth per step (`k ≤ k₁ + k₂`) but places no bound on the
cascade; closure needs an additional estimate.
-/
/-! ### The Beltrami zeta function of the `S³` shell -/
/-- The continuation of `Σ_{ℓ ≥ 1} ℓ(ℓ+2)/(ℓ+1)^s`: `ζ(s − 2) − ζ(s)`. -/

/-- For `Re s > 3` the Dirichlet series of the `S³` Beltrami spectrum is `ζ(s − 2) − ζ(s)`.
(The `ℓ = 0` term vanishes, so the sum may start at `ℓ = 0`.) -/
/-! ### Scalar-Laplacian eigenvalues are not squares of curl eigenvalues -/
/-- For `k ≥ 1` the scalar eigenvalue `k(k+2)` of `S³` is not a perfect square. -/
/-! ### Iterated Clebsch–Gordan coupling -/

/-- Doubled spins `k = 2j` reachable from `k₀` by repeated `SU(2)` Clebsch–Gordan coupling:
`V_a ⊗ V_b ⊇ V_c` iff `|a − b| ≤ c ≤ a + b` and `a + b + c` is even. -/

/-- **Correction to the Double Hopf closure argument.**  Starting from spin ½ every spin is
reached. -/
/-- Coupling a reachable spin with itself doubles it. -/

/-- **Correction to the Double Hopf closure argument.**  From any non-trivial seed, arbitrarily
large spins are reached. -/

/-!
# Audit of the Lambda Irreducibility Theorem (Riemann Hypothesis paper, Thm. 1.6.1)

Source: J. L. Nielsen's Riemann Hypothesis paper, Definitions 1.4.3, 1.5.3, 1.5.4 and Theorem
1.6.1 (see `todo.md`).  Two paradigms `L` (linear) and `C` (curved) each come with a class of
models; a *translation pair* `(T_{L→C}, T_{C→L})` gives round-trip operators
`R_L = T_{C→L} ∘ T_{L→C}` and `R_C = T_{L→C} ∘ T_{C→L}`.  The paper defines

* the **Λ-obstruction** `Λ_P(S) := S_P △ R_P(S)_P`, the models of paradigm `P` on which `S` and
  its round trip disagree (Def. 1.5.3);
* `S` is **Λ-irreducible** if `Λ_L(S) ≠ ∅` and `Λ_C(T_{L→C}(S)) ≠ ∅` (Def. 1.5.4);

and claims (Thm. 1.6.1): *if `S` is Λ-irreducible then `ZFC ⊬ S` and `ZFC ⊬ ¬S`.*

Everything is stated for an arbitrary *satisfaction system* — a type of sentences, a type of
models and a satisfaction relation `sat` — and then instantiated with Mathlib's first-order logic
(`FO.*`).  Provability over a theory is modelled semantically, as truth in all its models; for
first-order theories this is equivalent to derivability by Gödel's completeness theorem (cited,
not formalised here).

## Results

* `obstruction_eq_symmDiff`: `obstruction` is Def. 1.5.3 verbatim (`S_P △ R_P(S)_P`).
* **What the argument actually proves** (`obstruction_eq_empty_of_provable`,
  `independent_of_irreducible`): *if the round trip `R_L` sends sentences valid on the
  `L`-paradigm to valid ones, and refuted ones to refuted ones*, then Λ-irreducibility gives
  independence.  This is a hypothesis about the **translation pair**, not about ZFC.
* **Vacuity for sound pairs** (`not_irreducible_of_sound`): if the pair is semantically
  round-trip sound on the `L`-paradigm (the condition the paper derives for any translation that a
  ZFC proof would "induce"), then *no* sentence is Λ-irreducible.  So on the paper's own reading
  the hypothesis of Thm. 1.6.1 can be satisfied only by pairs the proof does not talk about.
* **The theorem is false as stated** (`irreducible_idNeg`, `lambdaIrreducibility_false`): for the
  pair `(id, ¬)` *every* sentence is Λ-irreducible as soon as both paradigms have a model, provable
  sentences included.  `FO.lambdaIrreducibility_false` instantiates this for every first-order
  theory with a model (in particular for ZFC, if ZFC is consistent).
* **Irreducibility is a property of the pair, not of the sentence**
  (`irreducibility_depends_on_pair`): the same provable sentence is Λ-irreducible for one pair
  and not for another (the identity pair), while provability does not mention any pair.
* **ZFC needs no translation** (`provable_of_equiv`, `FO.provable_and_irreducible`): if the
  theory proves `S_C` and proves `S_L ↔ S_C`, it proves `S_L` directly — and this is compatible
  with `S_L` being Λ-irreducible for some pair.  This is the critique's main point: RH_L and RH_C
  are both sentences of the one theory, and their equivalence is a theorem of that theory.
* **Condition (3) of Def. 1.4.3 is empty for syntactic translations**
  (`FO.roundTrip_elementary_invariant`): truth of *any* sentence, in particular of `R(S)` for any
  map `R` on sentences, is preserved by elementary embeddings.
-/
/-- The models of `S` in the paradigm `P`, `S_P`. -/

/-- **Definition 1.5.3.**  The Λ-obstruction: models of `P` on which exactly one of `S`, `R S`
holds. -/
/-- A translation pair `(T_{L→C}, T_{C→L})`. -/
/-- The identity pair. -/
/-- **Definition 1.5.4.**  `S` is Λ-irreducible for the pair `τ`. -/
/-- `S` is provable over the theory whose models are `Th` (semantically). -/
/-- `S` is refutable over the theory whose models are `Th` (semantically). -/

/-- **Theorem 1.6.1, as stated**: every Λ-irreducible sentence (for every translation pair) is
neither provable nor refutable. -/

/-- Semantic round-trip soundness of a pair on the `L`-paradigm: `R_L` preserves truth in every
model of `PL`. -/
/-! #### What the argument proves: a theorem about the pair -/

/-- If `R` sends `P`-valid sentences to `P`-valid ones and `P` consists of models of the theory,
a provable sentence has empty obstruction. -/

/-- If `R` sends `P`-refuted sentences to `P`-refuted ones, a refutable sentence has empty
obstruction. -/

/-- **The correct, relative form of Theorem 1.6.1.**  If the round trip `R_L` preserves validity
and refutation on the `L`-paradigm (which consists of models of the theory), then a sentence with
nonempty `L`-obstruction — in particular a Λ-irreducible one — is independent.  The hypotheses
`hval`, `href` are properties of the chosen translation pair; nothing about provability in the
theory forces them. -/
/-- **Vacuity for sound pairs**: a round-trip-sound pair admits no Λ-irreducible sentence. -/
/-! #### The statement as given is false -/
/-- The pair `(id, ¬)`, for a negation `neg` on sentences. -/
/-- For the pair `(id, ¬)` **every** sentence is Λ-irreducible once both paradigms have a model. -/

/-- **Theorem 1.6.1 is false as stated**: in any satisfaction system with a negation, if the
theory proves some sentence and both paradigms have a model, the statement fails. -/

/-- **Irreducibility depends on the pair**: every sentence is Λ-irreducible for `(id, ¬)` and
not Λ-irreducible for the identity pair. -/

/-- **No translation is needed**: if the theory proves `S_C` and proves `S_L ↔ S_C`, it proves
`S_L`. -/
/-! ### Instantiation: first-order logic -/
/-- Satisfaction of a sentence in a model of `T`. -/
/-- The tautology `⊤ → ⊤`, true in every structure. -/

/-- **Theorem 1.6.1 fails for every consistent first-order theory** (taking both paradigms to be
all models): the tautology `⊤ → ⊤` is provable and Λ-irreducible for the pair `(id, ¬)`. -/

/-- A theory may prove `S_L` directly, through `S_L ↔ S_C` and `S_C`, while `S_L` is
Λ-irreducible for some translation pair. -/

/-- **Condition (3) of Def. 1.4.3 is automatic**: for *any* map `R` on sentences, the truth of
`R S` is invariant under elementary embeddings. -/

/-!
# Audit of the `Λ⁺⁺` invariant (Yang–Mills paper, Def. 4.19)

Source: J. L. Nielsen's Yang–Mills paper, Definition 4.19, Theorem 6.11 and the "Path 1" chain
(see `todo.md`).  For a family of admissible encodings `E`, a generating set of loops `Γ`, loop
holonomies `H_{γ,E} ∈ G`, a conjugation-invariant defect functional `Δ` and a local defect scale
`τ(a) > 0` (with `τ(a) ∼ a⁴`), the paper defines

  `Λ⁺⁺(a) := inf_E sup_γ Δ(H_{γ,E}) / τ(a)`

and claims `Λ⁺⁺(a) ≥ ε(G) > 0` uniformly for small `a`.

## What is checked here

* `lambdaPP` is Definition 4.19, verbatim, for an arbitrary group `G`.
* **The correct part** (`worstDefect_conj`, `lambdaPP_gauge_orbit`): since `Δ` is
  conjugation-invariant, a re-encoding that acts on the loop holonomies by conjugation (a gauge
  transformation) cannot change the worst-case normalised defect.  On a single gauge orbit the
  infimum over encodings is attained by every encoding.  So "no admissible encoding can flatten the
  holonomy" holds for gauge re-encodings, and it holds trivially.
* **The gap** — uniformity in `a` is the whole content, and it is a statement about the coupling.
  In the one-plaquette `SU(2)` model (`modelLambda`), the plaquette holonomy at lattice scale `a`
  and effective coupling `κ` is the torus element `diag(e^{i a²κ}, e^{-i a²κ})`, the defect is the
  paper's `Δ(U) = 1 - ½ Re tr U` (`su2Defect`, conjugation-invariant by `su2Defect_conj`), the
  encodings are all `SU(2)` gauge transformations, and `τ(a) = a⁴`.  Then
  (`modelLambda_eq`) `Λ⁺⁺(a) = (1 - cos(a²κ)) / a⁴`, and
  - `modelLambda_le`: `Λ⁺⁺(a) ≤ κ² / 2`;
  - `modelLambda_ge`: `Λ⁺⁺(a) ≥ (2/π²) κ²` as long as `a²|κ| ≤ π`.

  So `Λ⁺⁺(a)` is pinned between two constant multiples of `κ(a)²`:
  - `uniform_bound_iff`: **a uniform bound `Λ⁺⁺(a) ≥ ε > 0` for `a ∈ (0, a₀)` holds iff the
    effective coupling is bounded away from zero on `(0, a₀)`**;
  - `modelLambda_tendsto_zero`, `no_uniform_bound_of_tendsto_zero`: if the coupling runs to zero
    as `a → 0⁺` (asymptotic freedom), then `Λ⁺⁺(a) → 0` and **no `ε(G) > 0` exists**;
  - `runningCoupling`, `no_uniform_bound_running`: the one-loop running form
    `κ(a)² = 1 / log(1/a)` is such a coupling.

  Every ingredient of Definition 4.19 is present in this model (non-Abelian `G = SU(2)`, a
  conjugation-invariant defect built from a faithful representation, `τ(a) = a⁴`, an infimum over a
  nontrivial class of encodings).  Positivity of `Λ⁺⁺` uniformly in `a` is therefore **not** a
  structural consequence of the definition: it is equivalent to the coupling not running to zero,
  which is exactly the input the paper assumes ("fixed `μ_a`") rather than derives.

  `modelLambda_const_pos` records the other side: at *fixed* coupling `κ ≠ 0` the bound does hold,
  `Λ⁺⁺(a) ≥ 2κ²/π²` for all small `a`, which is the regime the paper's argument actually treats.
-/
/-! ### Definition 4.19 for an arbitrary group -/
/-- A defect functional on `G` is conjugation-invariant. -/
/-- **Definition 4.19.**  `Λ⁺⁺ := inf_E sup_γ Δ(H_{γ,E}) / τ`, for holonomies `hol E γ`. -/

/-- The worst-case normalised defect of one encoding is unchanged when every loop holonomy is
conjugated (by a loop-dependent element): a gauge re-encoding cannot flatten the holonomy. -/

/-- **On a gauge orbit the infimum over encodings is trivial**: if every encoding's holonomies are
loopwise conjugate to those of a reference encoding `hol₀`, then `Λ⁺⁺` is the worst normalised
defect of `hol₀`. -/
/-! ### The paper's defect functional on `SU(2)` -/
/-- The group `SU(2)`. -/
/-- The defect functional `Δ(U) = 1 - ½ Re tr U` of the fundamental (faithful) representation. -/
/-- `Δ` is conjugation-invariant. -/
/-- The torus element `diag(e^{iθ}, e^{-iθ})`. -/
/-- The torus element as an element of `SU(2)`. -/
/-! ### The one-plaquette weak-coupling model -/

/-- The one-plaquette model at lattice scale `a` and effective coupling `κ`: the encodings are all
`SU(2)` gauge transformations `e`, there is one loop (the plaquette), its holonomy is
`e · diag(e^{i a²κ}, e^{-i a²κ}) · e⁻¹`, and `τ(a) = a⁴`. -/
/-- Upper bound: `Λ⁺⁺(a) ≤ κ² / 2`. -/
/-- Lower bound: `Λ⁺⁺(a) ≥ (2/π²) κ²` while `a²|κ| ≤ π`. -/

/-- At *fixed* coupling `κ ≠ 0` the uniform bound holds: `Λ⁺⁺(a) ≥ 2κ²/π²` for `0 < a ≤ 1`
once `|κ| ≤ π`.  (This is the regime the paper's argument treats.) -/

/-- **A uniform positive lower bound on `Λ⁺⁺` is equivalent to the coupling being bounded away
from zero** (on a range of scales where `a²|κ(a)| ≤ π`, i.e. the plaquette angle has not wrapped). -/

/-- **Asymptotic freedom kills the bound**: if the coupling runs to zero as `a → 0⁺`, then
`Λ⁺⁺(a) → 0`. -/

/-- Consequently **no `ε(G) > 0` bounds `Λ⁺⁺(a)` from below for small `a`** when the coupling runs
to zero. -/
/-- The one-loop running coupling, `κ(a)² = 1 / log(1/a)`. -/
/-- With the one-loop running coupling, `Λ⁺⁺(a) → 0`: there is no uniform `ε(G) > 0`. -/

/-!
# Audit of *Topological Quantum Error Correction on the Microtubule Bundle* (Nielsen–Semita)

Source: `QBX/docs/design/JLN_Topological Quantum Error Correction on the Microtubule Bundle via
the Hopf Fibration, Beltrami Flow Potential, and Lambda Residue.pdf`.

The QBX gauge layer (`QBX.Formal.GaugeFlatness`: connections on graphs, holonomy, flatness,
single-edge perturbations) is the discrete version of the paper's "connection on the bundle over
the neuronal base `M`", so several claims can be checked directly.

## Theorem 1 ("Holonomy protection") is false as stated

The paper's Theorem 1 says a perturbation `δA` supported in a contractible set `U` leaves the
holonomy of every non-contractible cycle unchanged, because "a representative of `[γ]` can be
chosen that avoids `U`".  That fails whenever every representative must cross `U` (e.g. `M` a
circle and `U` an arc).  `triangle_local_change_detected`: on the 3-cycle, changing the
transport on a single edge of the trivial (flat) connection changes the holonomy of the cycle.
(This is the general fact `Connection.perturb_detected_iff_not_isBridge` of the QBX library:
a single-edge change is visible exactly on edges that lie on a cycle.)

What *is* invariant is the holonomy under a **gauge transformation** (`holonomy_gaugeTransform`:
conjugation by the value at the base point, `holonomy_gaugeTransform_closed_comm`: no change for
an abelian structure group), i.e. `δA = dχ`, not under an arbitrary local `δA`.  A holonomy code
therefore needs syndrome measurement and correction, as in the toric code; locality of the
error alone does not protect the logical information.

## A tree-shaped base stores nothing

For a dendrite the base is an interval or a branching tree (paper, §2.1 and Remark 1).
`acyclic_perturb_flat`: on an acyclic graph every single-edge change of a flat connection stays
flat (starting, e.g., from the flat `trivConn`) — holonomy
around cycles, the paper's logical operators, carries no information on such a base.  The
paper's suggestion that the circumferential direction of each microtubule provides "the second
noncontractible direction" moves the code from the base to the fibre, which is a different code
(the paper's own Section 1 distinguishes the two).

## Arithmetic in Sections 2.2 and 7

* `intersections_all_pairings` — with `m + n` intersections per period for an `m`-start left
  and an `n`-start right helix, the 16 left/right pairings of `{3, 5, 8, 13}` give `232`
  intersections, not `145`.  `intersections_unordered_pairs` shows `145` is the sum over the 10
  *unordered* pairs `m ≤ n`, which merges the distinct pairings (left 3, right 5) and
  (left 5, right 3).
* `distance_twelve_not_six_correcting`, `unique_decoding` — a code of distance `d` corrects
  `t` errors iff `2t + 1 ≤ d`, so `t = ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋`, not `⌊d/2⌋`.  The paper's values for
  `d = 13` (`t = 6`) and `d = 11` (`t = 5`) are right, but for 12 protofilaments `t = 5`, not 6.
* `binomial_values` — the coefficients behind the logical-error table (`C(13,7) = 1716`,
  `C(11,6) = 462`) are right; the 12-protofilament estimate should use `C(12,6) p⁶ = 924 p⁶`.
-/
/-! ### Helical intersections -/
/-- The helix start numbers used in the paper. -/
/-- Over all 16 (left, right) pairings, `Σ (m + n) = 232`. -/
/-- `145` is the sum over unordered pairs `m ≤ n` only. -/
/-- The torus intersection number of the classes `(1, m)` and `(1, -n)` is `m + n`. -/
/-! ### Code distance and correctable errors -/

/-- If distinct codewords are at distance at least `2t + 1`, a word within distance `t` of two
codewords determines them: errors of weight `≤ t` are uniquely decodable. -/

/-- **Correction to §7.6.**  Two codewords at distance 12 and a word at distance 6 from both:
a distance-12 code cannot correct all weight-6 errors. -/
/-- The binomial coefficients behind the logical-error estimates. -/
/-! ### Holonomy under local perturbations and gauge transformations -/
/-- The trivial connection. -/

/-- **Theorem 1 of the paper fails.**  On the 3-cycle, changing the trivial connection on the
single edge `0 — 1` gives a connection that is no longer flat: the holonomy of the cycle
`0 → 1 → 2 → 0` changes. -/
/-- The gauge transformation of a connection by vertex values `p`. -/
/-- Holonomy transforms by the gauge values at the end points. -/

/-- **The correct protection statement.**  For an abelian structure group, gauge transformations
(of any support) do not change the holonomy of a closed walk. -/
/-! ### Acyclic bases -/
/-- On an acyclic graph, changing a flat connection on any one edge leaves it flat. -/

/-!
# Audit of the Navier–Stokes paper, part 2: flux, bias and blowup (§6, §7)

Source: J. L. Nielsen and L. Semita, *The Solution to the Navier–Stokes Problem* (revised May
2026).  The blowup chain (Theorem 7.10) is: flux coercivity (Thm 6.2) + phase non-cancellation
(Thm 6.4) + a positive helical bias `H_{<j₀}` (Def. 6.1, Prop. 7.2) + bias persistence
(Lemmas 6.11–6.12) + the frontier bootstrap (Thm 7.5, Lemma 7.6) + Navier–Stokes scaling
(Remark 6.10, Cor. 7.7).  Each link is checked below; the PDE objects enter only through the
algebraic properties the paper itself uses.

## What is checked here

* **Theorem 6.2 (flux coercivity) is false as stated** — `flux_coercivity_forces_nonpos`.  The
  transfer `T_{≥j₀}[u,u,u]` is cubic in `u`, `E_{≥j₀}` quadratic, `‖∇u_{<j₀}‖_∞` of degree one, and
  `H_{<j₀}` of degree zero (the paper: "the bias is scale-invariant").  Replacing `u` by `s u` with
  `s → 0⁺` turns the claimed inequality into `c₁ 2^{2j₀} H E ≤ 0`.  So it can hold for every `u`
  only if `H_{<j₀}(u) E_{≥j₀}(u) ≤ 0` for every `u`, contradicting the paper's own datum with
  `H > 0` and `E_{≥j₀} > 0`.  (The paper's proof stops mid-way with "— wait: this would make `c₁`
  data-dependent", which is this degree mismatch.)
* **Theorem 6.4 (phase non-cancellation) is false as stated** — `phase_noncancellation_false`.  At
  `T = 1/Φ` the time average of `e^{iΦt}` is `(e^{i} − 1)/i`, of modulus `2 sin ½ ≈ 0.96`, for every
  `Φ > 0` (`phaseAverage_at_inv`).  So `sup_T |…| ≤ C_δ |Φ|^{−δ}` fails for every `δ > 0`, `C_δ`.
* **The "helical bias" of Definition 6.1 does not measure helicity** — `biasNumerator_eq`,
  `biasNumerator_mirror`, `helicity_mirror`, `bias_ge_one`, `bias_lt_two`.  Since curl acts by `+|k|`
  on `P₊u` and `−|k|` on `P₋u`, the numerator `⟨P₊u, curl P₊u⟩ − ⟨P₋u, curl P₋u⟩` equals
  `Σ |k| (|û₊|² + |û₋|²)`: it is unchanged by exchanging the two helicities (mirror image), whereas
  the helicity `⟨u, curl u⟩` changes sign.  With sharp dyadic shells, `1 ≤ H_{<j₀} < 2` for every
  nonzero field.  So "homochiral bias `a₀ > 0`" holds for every field, mirror-symmetric ones
  included, and the value `H ≈ 0.001` of Proposition 7.2 is impossible.
* **The explicit datum has no chirality at all** — `helical_balance_real_direction`,
  `datum_helically_balanced`.  Definition 7.1 sets `u₀ = curl(0, 0, f)` (both for `ϵ = 0` and
  `ϵ ≠ 0`), so `û₀(k) = i f̂(k) (k₂, −k₁, 0)`: a complex scalar times a real vector.  For such a
  vector the two helical projections `P_± = ½(I ∓ i k̂ ×)` have equal norm at every `k`, so the
  helicity spectrum of `u₀` vanishes identically.  The homochirality required by Theorem 7.3 and
  Lemma 7.4 fails for the paper's own datum.
* **Corollary 7.7's rescaling is wrong** — `sup_norm_dilate`, `hypothesis3_rescaled_fails_large`,
  `hypothesis3_never_of_viscous`.  For `v₀(x) = λ u₀(λx)`, `∇v₀(x) = λ² (∇u₀)(λx)`, and a sup-norm
  does not see dilations: `‖∇v₀‖_∞ = λ² ‖∇u₀‖_∞`, not `λ⁻¹ ‖∇u₀‖_∞`.  The paper itself says the
  rescaled solution has "the same viscosity `ν`".  Hypothesis 3 for `v₀` therefore reads
  `c₁ a₀/2 > 2ν + C λ² G`, which fails for all large `λ`, and for no `λ` at all once
  `ν ≥ c₁ a₀ / 4`.  The "any `ν > 0`" claim is unsupported.
* **The spectral frontier of Theorem 7.5 is constant** — `frontier_is_zero`.  It is defined as
  `min {j : E_{≥j} ≥ θ E_tot}`; the lowest shell always qualifies, so `j*(t)` is the lowest index for
  every field and every time, and cannot be "nondecreasing and unbounded" (Lemma 7.6).
* **Lemma 7.6 Step 4 does not follow from Step 2** — `frontier_upper_bounds_do_not_diverge`.  Step 2
  gives only upper bounds `Δt_j ≤ log(1/θ)/(δ 4^j)`; these are compatible with
  `Σ 4^j Δt_j < ∞`, so the divergence of `∫ 2^{2j*}` claimed in Step 4 needs a lower bound.
* **Lemma 6.11 Step 4 and Lemma 6.12** — `persistence_step_gap`, `restart_bound_degrades`: the
  bounds `D(t) ≤ U`, `D(0) ≤ U` do not give `N/(2D(t)) ≥ N/(2D(0))`; restarting a "half of the
  initial value" bound loses a factor 2 each time, so the bound tends to 0.
* **Correct**: the comparison ODE of Lemma 7.4 (`comparison_ode_solution`):
  `y(t) = y₀/(1 − (c√y₀/4) t)²` solves `y' = (c/2) y^{3/2}`, blowing up at `T* = 4/(c√y₀)`.
-/
/-! ### Theorem 6.2: a degree-3 quantity cannot dominate a degree-2 one -/
/-- If `A ≤ s B` for every `s > 0` then `A ≤ 0`. -/

/-- **Theorem 6.2 forces `H E ≤ 0` for every field.**  `T` (the transfer `T_{≥j₀}`) is cubic, `H`
(the bias `H_{<j₀}`) scale-invariant, `E` (the energy `E_{≥j₀}`) quadratic and `G`
(`‖∇u_{<j₀}‖_∞`) 1-homogeneous under `u ↦ s u`, `s > 0`; `K = 2^{2j₀}`, `K' = 2^{j₀}`.  If
`T u ≥ c₁ H u K E u − c₂ K' G u E u` for all `u`, then `H u E u ≤ 0` for all `u`. -/

/-- Consequently, under the same hypotheses, **no field has both positive bias and positive
high-frequency energy** — the situation of Proposition 7.2 and Corollary 7.7. -/
/-! ### Theorem 6.4: the time average does not decay in `Φ` -/
/-- The time average `(1/T) ∫₀ᵀ e^{iΦt} dt`. -/
/-- At `T = 1/Φ` the average is `(e^{i} − 1)/i`, independent of `Φ`. -/

/-- **Theorem 6.4 is false**: for every `δ > 0` and every constant `C`, some integer frequency
`Φ > 0` and some `T > 0` give `|(1/T)∫₀ᵀ e^{iΦt} dt| > C Φ^{−δ}`. -/
/-! ### Definition 6.1: the bias functional is blind to chirality -/

/-- Numerator of Definition 6.1, `⟨P₊u, curl P₊u⟩ − ⟨P₋u, curl P₋u⟩`, for a field with finitely
many modes `i`, wavenumber `κ i = |k|`, helical amplitudes `a i = P₊û`, `b i = P₋û`; curl acts by
`+κ` on `P₊u` and by `−κ` on `P₋u`. -/
/-- The helicity `⟨u, curl u⟩ = ⟨P₊u, curl P₊u⟩ + ⟨P₋u, curl P₋u⟩`. -/

/-- Denominator of Definition 6.1, `Σ_j 2^j ‖P_j u‖²`, with sharp shells: mode `i` lies in shell
`s i`. -/
/-- The numerator is `Σ |k| (|û₊|² + |û₋|²)`: a sum of positive terms, not a helicity. -/
/-- **The bias is mirror-invariant**: exchanging the helicities does not change it. -/
/-- Whereas the helicity changes sign under the mirror exchange. -/
/-- **`H_{<j₀} ≥ 1` for every nonzero field** (sharp shells `2^{s i} ≤ |k| < 2^{s i + 1}`). -/
/-- **`H_{<j₀} < 2` for every nonzero field.** -/
/-! ### Definition 7.1: the explicit datum is helically balanced -/
/-- The cross product `n × w` of a real vector with a complex vector. -/

/-- The helical projector of §6.2, `P_σ w = ½ (w − σ i n × w)` (`σ = 1` for `P₊`, `σ = −1` for
`P₋`, `n = k̂`). -/

/-- **A complex multiple of a real vector has equal `P₊` and `P₋` parts**, for every direction
`n`. -/

/-- **The datum of Definition 7.1 is helically balanced at every wavenumber.**  For
`u₀ = curl (0, 0, f)` one has `û₀(k) = c · (k₂, −k₁, 0)` with `c = i f̂(k)`; its `P₊` and `P₋`
parts have equal norm, so its helicity spectrum vanishes. -/
/-! ### Corollary 7.7: rescaling makes Hypothesis 3 harder, not easier -/

/-- **A sup-norm does not see dilations**: `sup_x ‖λ² g(λx)‖ = λ² sup_y ‖g y‖`.  With
`g = ∇(u₀)_{<j₀}` this is `‖∇(v₀)_{<j₀'}‖_∞ = λ² ‖∇(u₀)_{<j₀}‖_∞` for `v₀(x) = λ u₀(λx)`. -/

/-- **Hypothesis 3 for the rescaled datum fails for all large `λ`**: with the correct gradient
scaling, it reads `c₁ a₀ / 2 > 2ν + C λ² G`. -/
/-- **For `ν ≥ c₁ a₀ / 4` no rescaling satisfies Hypothesis 3**, so "any `ν > 0`" fails. -/
/-! ### Theorem 7.5 / Lemma 7.6: the frontier -/
/-- `E_{≥j}` for a field with shells `0, …, N−1`. -/

/-- **The frontier `j* = min {j : E_{≥j} ≥ θ E_tot}` is always the lowest shell**, for every
energy distribution (hence at every time) and every `θ ≤ 1`. -/

/-- **Lemma 7.6, Step 4 does not follow from Step 2**: step times obeying Step 2's upper bound
`Δt_j ≤ L / (δ 4^j)` can have `Σ 4^j Δt_j < ∞`. -/
/-! ### Lemmas 6.11–6.12: persistence -/

/-- **Lemma 6.11, Step 4**: from `D(t) ≤ U` and `D(0) ≤ U` one cannot conclude
`N/(2 D(t)) ≥ N/(2 D(0))`. -/

/-- **Lemma 6.12**: restarting a "at least half the initial value" bound loses a factor `2` each
time: the sequence `a₀ / 2^n` satisfies every restart condition and tends to `0`. -/
/-! ### Lemma 7.4: the comparison ODE (correct) -/

/-- **Correct**: `y(t) = y₀ / (1 − (c√y₀/4) t)²` solves `y' = (c/2) y^{3/2}` (written `y √y`)
while `(c√y₀/4) t < 1`; it blows up at `T* = 4/(c√y₀)`. -/

/-!
# Audit of the Navier–Stokes paper, part 1: spectral arithmetic (§2, §4)

Source: J. L. Nielsen and L. Semita, *The Solution to the Navier–Stokes Problem* (revised May
2026), root of this project.  The paper labels Hopf–Beltrami modes on `S³` by a fiber index
`m ∈ ℤ` and a base degree `k ∈ ℕ`, with combined eigenvalue `Λ(m, k) = m² + k(k+1)` and curl
eigenvalue `±√Λ(m, k)` (§2.2), and builds the "spectral irreducibility" principle on the claim that
the two ladders `{m²}` and `{k(k+1)}` are "arithmetically incommensurate" with "irrational ratios"
(§1.1, §4.3, §10.2(3)).

## What is checked here

* `resonance_identity` — **correct**: with `m = m₁ + m₂`, the resonance mismatch of §4.3 is
  `2 m₁ m₂ + k(k+1) − k₁(k₁+1) − k₂(k₂+1)`.
* `eigenvalue_ratio_rational` — **the ratios are rational**: both ladders are integers, so every
  ratio `m² / (k(k+1))` is a rational number.  The "irrational ratios" of §4.3/§9/§10 do not exist.
* `curl_eigenvalue_irrational` — **the stated curl spectrum is not the curl spectrum of `S³`**: for
  every `k ≥ 1`, `√Λ(0, k) = √(k(k+1))` is irrational (`pronic_not_square`).  The curl operator on
  co-exact 1-forms of the round unit `S³` has integer eigenvalues (classical; the project's
  `HopfSpectralAudit` uses the same integer spectrum), so the labelling `curl Φ = ±√Λ Φ` cannot be
  right for the whole column `m = 0`.
* `beltrami_level_set` — the three labels `(2,1), (−2,1), (0,2)` have the same eigenvalue `Λ = 6`,
  three distinct fiber indices and two distinct base degrees.  In the paper's own model (§2.3: a
  field in one curl eigenspace is Beltrami and an exact solution, the nonlinearity being a gradient)
  such a set is dynamically invariant and finite, while Theorem 4.1 as stated (no Beltrami exclusion)
  asserts that every such set generates an infinite cascade.  The abstract's qualifier "outside the
  Beltrami subspace" is missing from the theorem.
* `noncoprime_density_pos` — Remark 4.2 gives the coprime density as `6/π²` and then calls the
  non-coprime data "a null set"; their density is `1 − 6/π² > 0`.
* `dyadicShell_card` — the dyadic annulus `A_j = {(m,k) ∈ ℤ × ℕ : 2^j ≤ |m| + k < 2^{j+1}}` of
  Lemma 4.5 contains **exactly `3 · 4^j`** lattice points.  Lemma 4.5 uses "lattice area
  `∼ π(2^j)²/2`" and Theorem 6.3 uses "`∼ 3π 2^{2j}`" for the same set; neither is right, and
  `π/2 · 4^j / 8 ≈ 0.2 · 4^j` (the Lemma 4.5 proof's own numbers) does not give `18 · 4^j`.
* `wigner3jSq` — the squared Wigner 3j symbol for integer spins, via Racah's closed formula, checked
  against standard values (`wigner3jSq_sanity`).  Lemma 4.4 lists five "nonzero" symbols:
  - `(1 2 3; 1 2 −3) = √7/7` — **correct** (`lemma44_first_correct`);
  - `(3 2 5; −3 2 −5)`, `(5 2 7; −5 2 −7)`, `(7 2 9; −7 2 −9)`, `(9 2 11; −9 2 −11)` — the
    bottom rows do not sum to zero, so all four symbols **vanish** (`lemma44_symbols_vanish`);
  - with the signs repaired, the values are `1/√(2J+1) = 1/√11, 1/√15, 1/√19, 1/√23`, so only
    `√11/11` matches; the stated `√39/39`, `√55/55`, `√75/75` are wrong (`lemma44_repaired_values`).
-/
/-! ### The two spectral ladders -/
/-- The paper's combined eigenvalue `Λ(m, k) = m² + k(k+1)` (§1.2, §2.2). -/
/-- **Correct (§4.3).**  The resonance mismatch for `m = m₁ + m₂`. -/
/-- **The fiber/base ratios are rational** (against "irrational ratios", §4.3, §9, §10). -/
/-- `k(k+1)` is never a perfect square for `k ≥ 1` (it lies strictly between `k²` and `(k+1)²`). -/

/-- **The stated curl eigenvalue `√Λ(0, k)` is irrational for every `k ≥ 1`**, whereas the curl
spectrum of the round `S³` consists of integers. -/

/-- **A finite Beltrami level set meeting the hypotheses of Theorem 4.1**: three fiber indices
`2, −2, 0`, two base degrees `1, 2`, one eigenvalue `Λ = 6`. -/

/-- **Remark 4.2**: with coprime density `6/π²`, the non-coprime data have positive density
`1 − 6/π²`; they are not a null set. -/
/-! ### Lattice points in the dyadic annulus (Lemma 4.5, Theorem 6.3) -/
/-- Labels `(m, k)` with `|m| + k = n`. -/
/-- There are `2n + 1` labels with `|m| + k = n`. -/
/-- The dyadic annulus `A_j = {(m, k) : 2^j ≤ |m| + k < 2^{j+1}}` of Lemma 4.5. -/

/-- **The annulus `A_j` has exactly `3 · 4^j` lattice points** (not `π 4^j / 2`, Lemma 4.5, nor
`3π 4^j`, Theorem 6.3). -/
/-! ### Wigner 3j symbols (Lemma 4.4) -/

/-- Factorial of an integer argument (`0` for negative arguments; these never occur in a nonzero
term below). -/
/-- The alternating sum in Racah's formula for the 3j symbol `(j₁ j₂ j₃; m₁ m₂ m₃)`. -/

/-- **The square of the Wigner 3j symbol** `(j₁ j₂ j₃; m₁ m₂ m₃)` for integer spins, by Racah's
formula: it vanishes unless `m₁ + m₂ + m₃ = 0`, `|mᵢ| ≤ jᵢ` and the triangle condition holds, and
otherwise equals `Δ(j₁ j₂ j₃) · ∏ (jᵢ + mᵢ)! (jᵢ − mᵢ)! · (Σ_t …)²`. -/
/-- Sanity checks of `wigner3jSq` against standard tabulated values and an orthogonality sum. -/
/-- The selection rule: a 3j symbol vanishes unless the bottom row sums to zero. -/
/-- **Lemma 4.4, first symbol — correct**: `(1 2 3; 1 2 −3)² = 1/7`, i.e. the symbol is `√7/7`. -/

/-- **Lemma 4.4, the other four "nonzero" symbols vanish**: `(j 2 (j+2); −j 2 −(j+2))` has bottom
row summing to `−2j ≠ 0`, for `j = 3, 5, 7, 9` (indeed for every `j ≥ 1`). -/

/-- **Lemma 4.4 with the signs repaired**: the stretched symbols have squares `1/11, 1/15, 1/19,
1/23`; the stated `√39/39, √55/55, √75/75` (squares `1/39, 1/55, 1/75`) are wrong. -/

/-!
# Audit of *Paradox Lost: Quantum Gravity, the Total Verlinde Formula, and the Resolution of the
Black Hole Information Paradox* (J. L. Nielsen, August 2026)

Source: `QBX/docs/design/JLN_Paradox Lost…pdf`, Section 5.2 (Theorem 7) and equations (19)–(25).
The QBX anyon layer (`QBX.Formal.AnyonModels`: Fibonacci and Ising fusion, F- and R-symbols)
works with exactly this kind of modular data, so the finite claims can be checked.

## The bipartition does not exist

The proof splits the `V(k) = k + 1`-dimensional Hilbert space into a black-hole factor of
dimension `k − m + 1` and a radiation factor of dimension `m + 1`, and takes the entropy of a
maximally entangled state on their tensor product.  A tensor factorisation of a
`(k+1)`-dimensional space needs the dimensions to multiply to `k + 1`:

* `bipartition_dim_iff` — `(k − m + 1)(m + 1) = k + 1` iff `m = 0` or `m = k`; so for every
  intermediate step `0 < m < k` the claimed factorisation is impossible;
* `direct_sum_dim` — the dimensions do not add up to `k + 1` either (`k + 2`).

The Page-curve formula `S = log min(k − m + 1, m + 1)` is therefore not derived from a state on
the stated Hilbert space.

## `Z(S³)` is not a dimension

The paper sets `Z(M) = dim H(M)` for the closed 3-manifold `S³` and equates it with `k + 1`.
In Chern–Simons theory `Z(Σ × S¹) = dim H(Σ)`; `k + 1` is `dim H(T²)`, while
`Z(S³) = S₀₀ = √(2/(k+2)) sin(π/(k+2))`.  `S00_pos_lt_one`: for `k ≥ 1` this lies strictly
between 0 and 1, so it is not the dimension of any Hilbert space.

## The truncated Clebsch–Gordan rule needs a parity condition

Equation (21)ff. states `N_{j₁ j₂}^{j₃} = 1` iff `|j₁ − j₂| ≤ j₃ ≤ min(j₁ + j₂, k − j₁ − j₂)`.
`nielsenRule_two_one_one_one` shows this predicts `N_{½ ½}^{½} = 1` at level `k = 2`, while the
Verlinde formula with the paper's own S-matrix (19) gives `0`
(`verlinde_k2_half_half_half`).  The missing condition is `j₁ + j₂ + j₃ ∈ ℤ` (in the QBX Ising
model, `σ × σ = 1 + ψ` has no `σ` channel).
-/
/-! ### Dimensions -/

/-- **The claimed bipartition exists only at the endpoints.**  For `m ≤ k`,
`(k − m + 1)(m + 1) = k + 1` iff `m = 0` or `m = k`. -/
/-- The two dimensions add up to `k + 2`, not `k + 1`. -/
/-! ### The modular S-matrix of `SU(2)_k` -/
/-- `S_{ab} = √(2/(k+2)) sin(π (a+1)(b+1)/(k+2))` in doubled labels `a = 2j`, equation (19). -/
/-- `Z(S³) = S₀₀` lies strictly between 0 and 1 for `k ≥ 1`. -/
/-- `S₀₀` is not a natural number for `k ≥ 1`. -/

/-- **Verlinde formula at level 2:** `N_{½ ½}^{½} = Σ_ℓ S_{½ℓ}³ / S_{0ℓ} = 0` (the S-matrix is
real and symmetric, so `S* = S`). -/

/-- The truncated Clebsch–Gordan rule as stated in the paper, in doubled labels:
`|a − b| ≤ c ≤ min(a + b, 2k − a − b)` (no parity condition). -/
/-- The paper's rule predicts `N_{½ ½}^{½} = 1` at level 2 … -/
/-- … but `a + b + c` is odd, which is exactly the case the Verlinde formula excludes. -/

/-!
# Audit of the Yang–Mills paper, Theorem 12.1(3): `Λ⁺⁺` for an Abelian group

Source: J. L. Nielsen and L. Semita, *The Proof of the Yang–Mills Mass Gap*, root of this project.
Theorem 12.1 ("Abelian No-Go") states for `G = U(1)^k`: "(3) The `Λ⁺⁺` invariant is identically
zero: no cocycle routing produces non-trivial defects", and Theorem 12.2 uses this for the
direction "mandatory mass gap ⇒ `G` non-Abelian".

Definition 4.19 (`lambdaPP` in `LambdaPlusPlusAudit.lean`) makes sense for any group.  Here it is
evaluated for `G = U(1)` (Mathlib's `Circle`) with the defect `Δ(z) = 1 − Re z` (the `U(1)` analogue
of the paper's `1 − ½ Re tr`), one plaquette with holonomy `e^{i a²κ}`, all `U(1)` gauge
transformations as encodings and `τ(a) = a⁴`:

* `u1Defect_conj` — the defect is conjugation-invariant (trivially, `U(1)` is commutative);
* `abelianModelLambda_eq` — `Λ⁺⁺(a) = (1 − cos(a²κ))/a⁴`;
* `abelianModelLambda_eq_su2` — **this is exactly the value of the non-Abelian `SU(2)` model**
  (`modelLambda`) at the same coupling: `Λ⁺⁺` does not distinguish `U(1)` from `SU(2)`;
* `abelianModelLambda_pos` — at fixed coupling `κ ≠ 0`, `Λ⁺⁺(a) ≥ 2κ²/π² > 0` for all
  `0 < a ≤ 1`.  So **Theorem 12.1(3) is false**: `Λ⁺⁺` is not identically zero for an Abelian group,
  and a positive `Λ⁺⁺` cannot be what separates the non-Abelian case.

What does vanish for an Abelian group is a *commutator*, not the holonomy defect; Definition 4.19
contains no commutator.
-/
/-- The `U(1)` defect `Δ(z) = 1 − Re z`. -/

/-- The one-plaquette Abelian model: encodings are `U(1)` gauge transformations `e`, the plaquette
holonomy is `e · e^{i a²κ} · e⁻¹`, `τ(a) = a⁴`. -/

/-- **`Λ⁺⁺` cannot tell `U(1)` from `SU(2)`**: the Abelian model has exactly the value of the
`SU(2)` model at the same coupling and scale. -/

/-- **Theorem 12.1(3) is false**: for `G = U(1)` at fixed coupling `κ ≠ 0` (`|κ| ≤ π`), `Λ⁺⁺` is
bounded below by a positive constant uniformly in `0 < a ≤ 1`. -/

/-!
# Audit of the Riemann Hypothesis paper, Proofs IIa and III (Thm. 2.8.4, Def. 3.3.1)

Source: J. L. Nielsen, *Riemann Hypothesis: ZFC Lambda Irreducibility Obstruction*, root of this
project.  (Theorem 1.6.1 of the same paper is audited in `LambdaIrreducibilityAudit.lean`.)

## Theorem 2.8.4 (Zero Rigidity ⇒ RH)

Given an off-line zero `s₀` of an admissible zero realization `Z`, the proof forms
`Z' = (Z \ {s₀, s̄₀}) ∪ {1 − s₀, 1 − s̄₀}` and asserts (condition 1) that `Z'` is again invariant
under `s ↦ 1 − s`, "since the replacement exchanges `{s₀, s̄₀}` with their functional-equation
images".

`swapRealization_not_symmetric`: **for every multiset `Z` invariant under `s ↦ 1 − s` and every
`s₀ ∈ Z` with `Re s₀ ≠ ½`, the multiset `Z'` is not invariant under `s ↦ 1 − s`.**  The point
`1 − s₀` gains multiplicity while its mirror image `s₀` loses it.  So `Z'` is never an admissible
realization, and the argument gives no contradiction with Zero Rigidity.  The argument uses nothing
about `ζ`; if it were valid it would prove that every symmetric multiset lies on the line.

## Definition 3.3.1 (Phase Rigidity Principle)

PRA forbids "localized holonomy defects in the interior of `U`" for the connection
`ω = (1/2πi) ξ'/ξ ds`.  Near a simple zero `s₀`, `ξ'/ξ = 1/(s − s₀) + (holomorphic)`, and the
holonomy of a small loop around `s₀` is `1` *whatever* `Re s₀` is
(`holonomy_defect_location_blind`, for the principal part).  Zeros on the critical line are
detected exactly like zeros off it; so PRA as stated excludes all nontrivial zeros, including the
known zeros on the critical line, and it cannot single out `Re s = ½`.
-/

/-- The modified realization of the proof of Theorem 2.8.4:
`Z' = (Z \ {s₀, s̄₀}) + {1 − s₀, 1 − s̄₀}` (as multisets). -/

/-- **Condition 1 fails for `Z'`**: if `Z` is invariant under `s ↦ 1 − s` and contains `s₀` with
`Re s₀ ≠ ½`, then `Z'` is not invariant under `s ↦ 1 − s`. -/

/-- **The holonomy of the principal part `1/(s − s₀)` around `s₀` is `1` for every `s₀`**: the
"holonomy defect" of PRA does not depend on `Re s₀`. -/

declarations.signature_heuristic:
inductive MarkovMove : (Σ n, Word n) → (Σ n, Word n) → Prop
  /-- Words that are equal in `B_n`. -/
  | braid {n : ℕ} {w w' : Word n} (h : w.eval = w'.eval) : MarkovMove ⟨n, w⟩ ⟨n, w'⟩
  /-- Conjugation `a b a⁻¹ ↦ b`. -/
  | conj {n : ℕ} (a b : Word n) : MarkovMove ⟨n, a ++ b ++ a.inv⟩ ⟨n, b⟩
  /-- Stabilisation `σ₁^{±1} · shift(B) ↦ B`. -/
  | stab {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (b : Bool) (w : Word n) :
      MarkovMove ⟨n + 1, firstLetter hn b :: w.shift⟩ ⟨n, w⟩

/-- Markov equivalence: the equivalence relation generated by the Markov moves.  By Markov's
theorem two braids are Markov equivalent exactly when their closures are isotopic links. -/

/-!
# Markov invariance of the quantum-trace Jones polynomial

`qbx_ir.quantum.representation.jones_from_quantum_trace` evaluates the Jones polynomial of the
closure of a braid through the `U_q(sl₂)` representation:

  `V(t)|_{t^{1/2} = −q⁻¹} = q^{−2w} · Tr(μ^{⊗n} ρ(B)) / (q + q⁻¹)`,   `μ = diag(q⁻¹, q)`,

where `w` is the writhe and `ρ(B) = ρ(g_k) ⋯ ρ(g_1)` (`quantum_trace`).  This file proves, for
every field `K`, every non-zero `q` and every strand count, that this number is an invariant of
the closed braid (Markov's moves):

* `jonesQT_eq_of_eval_eq`: words equal in `B_n` have the same value;
* `jonesQT_conj`: conjugation `a b a⁻¹ ↦ b` does not change it;
* `jonesQT_stab`: (left) stabilisation `B ↦ σ₁^{±1} · shift(B)` from `n` to `n + 1` strands
  does not change it;
* `jonesQT_markov`: hence it is constant on Markov equivalence classes (`MarkovEquiv`), i.e. it
  depends only on the closure.

The proof uses: `μ ⊗ μ` commutes with `Ř^{±1}` (the R-matrix preserves the weight), the cyclicity
of the trace, and the partial quantum trace `∑ₓ μₓ Ř(x a, x b) = q^{±2} δ_{ab}`.
-/
/-! ### The enhanced trace -/
/-- The enhancement `μ = diag(q⁻¹, q)` on one tensor factor. -/
/-- The diagonal of `μ^{⊗ n}`. -/
/-- The enhanced (Markov) trace `Tr(μ^{⊗ n} M)`. -/
/-- Python `quantum_trace`: `Tr(μ^{⊗ n} ρ(g_k) ⋯ ρ(g_1))` for the word `g_1 ⋯ g_k`. -/
/-- Python `jones_from_quantum_trace`: `q^{−2w} · Tr(μ^{⊗ n} ρ(B)) / (q + q⁻¹)`. -/
/-! ### Words: shift and inverse -/
/-- `shift(B)`: the braid `B` on strands `2, …, n + 1` of `n + 1` strands. -/
/-- `shift(B)` for words. -/
/-- The letter `σ₁^{±1}` on `n + 1 ≥ 2` strands. -/
/-! ### Markov equivalence -/
/-- One Markov move between braid words with any number of strands. -/
/-- Words that are equal in `B_n`. -/
/-- Conjugation `a b a⁻¹ ↦ b`. -/
/-- Stabilisation `σ₁^{±1} · shift(B) ↦ B`. -/

/-- Markov equivalence: the equivalence relation generated by the Markov moves.  By Markov's
theorem two braids are Markov equivalent exactly when their closures are isotopic links. -/
/-! ### Entries of the local matrices -/
/-- Two states agree away from the sites `i` and `j`. -/
/-! ### Reversal: Python's operator order -/
/-- An R-matrix that is symmetric as a matrix on `V ⊗ V`. -/
/-- Python's operator order does not matter for the trace. -/
/-! ### Weight conservation: `μ^{⊗ n}` commutes with the representation -/
/-- `R` preserves the weight: `μ ⊗ μ` commutes with it. -/
/-! ### Stabilisation: the partial quantum trace -/
/-- `I ⊗ M`: the matrix `M` acting on the last `n` of `n + 1` tensor factors. -/
/-- The partial quantum trace of `R` over the first tensor factor is `c · I`. -/
/-! ### Main results -/
/-! ### Normalisation -/

/-- The trivial braid on `n + 1` strands closes to the `(n + 1)`-component unlink:
`V = (q + q⁻¹)^n`; in particular the unknot has `V = 1`. -/
/-! ### Agreement with the Python implementation -/

/-- A test vector `(n, word, q_num, q_den, V_num, V_den)`: the value `V` of
`jones_from_quantum_trace` at `q = q_num / q_den`, computed exactly from the Kauffman-bracket
Jones polynomial `jones_polynomial` at `t^{1/2} = −q⁻¹` (the two Python functions agree on every
vector to floating-point precision). -/

/-- Test vectors from the Python implementation, 1–3 strands, `q ∈ {2, 3, −1/2}`: unknot and
two-component unlink, `σ₁^{±1}`, the Hopf link `σ₁²`, both trefoils `σ₁^{±3}`, the figure-eight
knot `σ₁σ₂⁻¹σ₁σ₂⁻¹`, `σ₁σ₂` (unknot), and two further braids on three strands. -/

/-- The Lean model gives exactly the Python values on the test vectors (checked by the
kernel). -/
/-! ### Consequences: the trefoil is knotted and chiral -/
/-- The (right-handed) trefoil `σ₁³` on two strands. -/
/-- Its mirror image `σ₁⁻³`. -/

/-- **The trefoil is knotted**: the closure of `σ₁³` is not Markov equivalent to the closure of
the trivial one-strand braid (the unknot). -/
/-- **The trefoil is chiral**: `σ₁³` and its mirror `σ₁⁻³` are not Markov equivalent. -/

declarations.name: bracketAux
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def bracketAux (A Ai d : R) (n : ℕ) : Match → ℕ → Word n → R
  | m, L, [] => d ^ (L + closeLoops n m - 1)
  | m, L, l :: w =>
    if l.pos then
      A * bracketAux A Ai d n m L w + Ai * bracketAux A Ai d n (upd (2 * n - 2 - l.idx) m)
        (L + updLoop (2 * n - 2 - l.idx) m) w
    else
      Ai * bracketAux A Ai d n m L w + A * bracketAux A Ai d n (upd (2 * n - 2 - l.idx) m)
        (L + updLoop (2 * n - 2 - l.idx) m) w

declarations.name: map_bracketAux
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem map_bracketAux {S : Type*} [CommRing S] (f : R →+* S) (A Ai d : R) (n : ℕ) :
    ∀ (m : Match) (L : ℕ) (w : Word n),
      f (bracketAux A Ai d n m L w) = bracketAux (f A) (f Ai) (f d) n m L w
  | m, L, [] => by simp [bracketAux]
  | m, L, l :: w => by
    simp only [bracketAux]
    split_ifs <;> simp [map_bracketAux f A Ai d n]

end Recursion

/-! ### The bracket recursion -/

/-- The Temperley–Lieb expansion of the Kauffman bracket (Python `kauffman_bracket`), state by
state: `bracketAux A Ai d n m L w` is the bracket contribution of the diagram `m` carrying `L`
closed loops, still to be multiplied by the letters of `w`.  A letter `σ_i^{±1}` splits it into
`A^{±1} · m` and `A^{∓1} · m e_i`; at the end the closure is taken, and every loop beyond the
first counts `d`. -/
/-! ### Expansion of the representation in the Temperley–Lieb algebra -/
/-- The Temperley–Lieb generator `E` acting at the crossing of a letter. -/

/-- The Kauffman skein of a letter: `A · 1 + A⁻¹ · E` for `σ_i`, `A⁻¹ · 1 + A · E` for
`σ_i⁻¹` (with `q = -A²`). -/
/-- The Kauffman skein of a word, multiplied out in word order. -/

/-- **The R-matrix is the Kauffman skein up to a scalar**: with `q = -A²`,
`ρ(σ_i^{±1}) = (-A)^{±1} (A^{±1} · 1 + A^{∓1} · E_i)`. -/

/-- **State-sum expansion.**  Multiplying the diagram `m` (carrying `L` loops) by the Kauffman
skeins of the letters of `w` and taking the quantum trace gives the bracket recursion. -/

/-- **The quantum trace is the Kauffman bracket.**  For `q = -A²` and `d = q + q⁻¹ = -A² - A⁻²`,
`Tr(μ^{⊗ n} ρ(B)) = (-A)^{w(B)} · d · ⟨B̂⟩`, where `⟨B̂⟩` is the Temperley–Lieb state sum of
Python `kauffman_bracket` (normalised by `⟨O⟩ = 1`). -/

/-!
# Kauffman bracket and Jones certificates (migration 023)

A certificate row `(exp_min, width, coefficients)` encodes `∑ₖ cₖ A^{exp_min + k}` (`certPoly`, the
one-entry case of the Burau encoding of migration 024).

* `bracketPoly_eq_of_eval_eq`, `bracketPoly_conj`: the bracket is a braid and conjugacy invariant;
* `certPoly_inj`: a canonical certificate is determined by its polynomial; `bracketCert_eq_iff`,
  `bracketCert_eq_of_eval_eq`;
* `not_markovEquiv_of_jonesCert_ne`, `jonesCert_eq_of_markovEquiv`: Jones certificates and
  isotopy of closures;
* `checkBracketCert`, `checkJonesCert` and `isBracketCert_of_check`, `isJonesCert_of_check`:
  kernel-checkable evaluation tests (at `A = 1, …, 2B + 1`) that prove certificates exactly.
-/
/-! ### Braid invariance of the bracket -/
/-- The bracket is recovered from the Jones polynomial and the writhe. -/
/-- **Equal braids have equal brackets.** -/
/-- **The bracket is a conjugacy invariant.** -/
/-! ### Certificates -/

/-- The Laurent polynomial `∑ₖ cₖ A^{lo + k}` stored in a certificate row `(lo, width, coeffs)`
(the one-entry case of the Burau encoding). -/
/-- **The encoding is unique**: a canonical certificate is determined by its polynomial. -/
/-- `c` is the (canonical) bracket certificate of `w`. -/
/-- `c` is the (canonical) Jones certificate of `w` (variable `A`). -/
/-- **Exact decision of bracket equality.** -/
/-- Equal braids have equal bracket certificates. -/
/-- **Different Jones certificates prove non-isotopic closures.** -/
/-- Markov-equivalent braids have equal Jones certificates. -/
/-! ### Kernel-checkable tests -/
/-- `∑ₖ cₖ x^{lo + k}`: the value of a certificate polynomial at a rational point. -/
/-- The bracket state sum at `A = x`. -/
/-- The Jones polynomial at `A = x`. -/
/-- The half-width of the window for a check. -/

/-- A canonical certificate whose values at `1, …, 2B + 1` agree with those of a polynomial in
the window `[-B, B]` encodes that polynomial. -/
/-- The bracket check: canonical, and the values at `A = 1, …, 2B + 1` agree. -/
/-- **A passed bracket check proves the certificate exactly.** -/
/-- The Jones check. -/
/-- **A passed Jones check proves the certificate exactly.** -/

/-- A test vector: strand count, word (short form), bracket certificate
`(exp_min, width, coefficients)` and Jones certificate `(exp_min, width, coefficients)`. -/
/-- Both checks for a test vector. -/
/-- A passed vector check proves both certificates exactly. -/

/-- The bracket polynomial `d = -A² - A⁻²`. -/
/-- The window of a partial bracket: `len + 2 (L + len + n)` on both sides. -/
/-! ### The bracket polynomial -/

/-- **The Kauffman bracket** `⟨B̂⟩ ∈ ℤ[A, A⁻¹]` of the closure of `w` (Python
`kauffman_bracket`), normalised by `⟨O⟩ = 1`. -/
/-! ### The Jones polynomial -/

/-- **Jones polynomial from the quantum trace.**  With `q = -A²` (and `d = -A² - A⁻² ≠ 0`), the
`U_q(sl₂)` value of `JonesMarkov.lean` is `(-A³)^{-w} ⟨B̂⟩`, Python's `jones_polynomial` formula. -/

/-- **The Jones polynomial** of the closure, in the variable `A = t^{-1/4}`:
`V = (-A³)^{-w} ⟨B̂⟩ = (-1)^w A^{-3w} ⟨B̂⟩` (Python `jones_polynomial`, before the change of
variable `A^k ↦ t^{-k/4}`). -/
/-- Evaluating the Jones polynomial at `A = u` gives the quantum-trace value at `q = -u²`. -/
/-! ### Markov invariance -/
/-- Every Laurent polynomial lies in some window. -/
/-- Two Laurent polynomials with the same values at every non-zero rational are equal. -/

/-- The Jones polynomial of a braid word with any number of strands, as a function of the pair
`(n, w)` (strand count `0` gives the empty diagram). -/

/-- **The Jones polynomial is an invariant of the closed braid**: Markov-equivalent braids (on at
least one strand) have the same Jones polynomial. -/
/-- Braids whose Jones polynomials differ have non-isotopic closures. -/

/-!
# Temperley–Lieb states as non-crossing matchings

`qbx_ir.algebra.polynomial_invariants.kauffman_bracket` multiplies a braid word out in the
Temperley–Lieb algebra.  Its states are planar matchings of the `2n` boundary points of a
diagram on `n` strands (Python: a tuple `match` of length `2n`).  This file models them.

**Coordinates.**  We number the boundary points *around the boundary*: the top points
`0, …, n-1` from left to right, then the bottom points from right to left, so the bottom point of
strand `k` is `2n - 1 - k`.  (Python numbers the bottom point of strand `k` as `n + k`; the two
numberings differ by this fixed relabelling.)  In these coordinates

* a planar matching is an involution `m` of `{0, …, 2n-1}` whose pairs do not interleave
  (`Valid.noncross`), and every pair encloses an even number of points (`Valid.parity`);
* the identity diagram pairs `p` with `2n - 1 - p` (`idMatch`);
* multiplying by `e_i` on the right (Python's update) caps the adjacent points
  `c = 2n - 2 - i` and `c + 1` and joins their former partners (`upd`); a closed loop appears
  exactly when `c` and `c + 1` were already paired (`updLoop`);
* closing the first strand (top point `0` to bottom point `2n + 1` of a diagram on `n + 1`
  strands) removes the two end points and joins their partners (`close`); a closed loop appears
  exactly when they were paired (`closeLoop`).  `closeLoops` closes all strands one by one; it
  counts the loops of the closure of the diagram.

Main facts: `valid_id`, `Valid.upd`, `Valid.close` (the three operations keep a matching valid),
and `one_le_closeLoops` (the closure of a diagram on at least one strand has a loop).
-/

/-- A Temperley–Lieb state: a matching of the boundary points `0, …, 2n-1` (values beyond `2n`
are irrelevant). -/
/-- The pairs `{p, p'}` and `{r, r'}` interleave (their chords cross). -/
/-- A pair of adjacent points is crossed by nothing. -/
/-- A pair `{p, p}` is crossed by nothing. -/

/-- Capping the adjacent points `c`, `c + 1` cannot create a crossing: a pair crossing the new
pair `{x, y}` crossed `{c, x}` or `{c + 1, y}`. -/
/-- Joining the partners of the two end points `0` and `2n + 1` cannot create a crossing. -/
/-- `m` is a planar matching of the `2n` boundary points. -/

/-- The identity diagram: top point `j` is joined to the bottom point `2n - 1 - j` of the same
strand. -/
/-! ### Right multiplication by `e_i` -/

/-- Cap the adjacent boundary points `c`, `c + 1` and join their former partners (Python:
`match · e_i` with `c = 2n - 2 - i`).  If `c` and `c + 1` were already paired, the matching does
not change and a closed loop is produced. -/
/-- `1` if capping `c`, `c + 1` closes a loop, else `0`. -/
/-- The values of `upd c m` in the non-loop case. -/

/-- The pair of `p` after capping `c`, `c + 1`: the new cap, the joined partners, or an old pair
avoiding all four points. -/
-- the old pair through a point avoiding the four special points does not cross `{x, y}`
/-! ### Closing the first strand -/

/-- Close the first strand of a diagram on `n + 1` strands: remove the end points `0` (top of
strand `0`) and `2n + 1` (bottom of strand `0`), join their partners, and renumber. -/
/-- `1` if closing the first strand closes a loop (its two end points are paired), else `0`. -/
/-- The number of loops of the closure: close the strands one by one. -/
/-- The values of `close n m`. -/

    (hyc1 : y ≠ c + 1) (hxy : x ≠ y) (nc : ¬ Interleave c x (c + 1) y) :
    (x < n ∧ y < x) ∨ (x < n ∧ c + 1 < y) ∨ (n ≤ x ∧ x < c ∧ y < n) ∨

declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem core_mul {q : K} (hq : q ≠ 0) {n c x y : ℕ} (hc0 : n ≤ c) (hxc : x ≠ c) (hxc1 : x ≠ c + 1)
    (hyc : y ≠ c) (hyc1 : y ≠ c + 1) (hxy : x ≠ y) (pc : (c + x) % 2 = 1)
    (pc1 : (c + 1 + y) % 2 = 1) (nc : ¬ Interleave c x (c + 1) y) (la lb ui uj : Fin 2) :
    ∑ α, ∑ β, pw q n c x β la * pw q n (c + 1) y α lb * (capW q α β * cupW q ui uj) =
      pw q n c (c + 1) uj ui * pw q n x y la lb

declarations.name: core_mul_loop
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem core_mul_loop {q : K} (hq : q ≠ 0) {n c : ℕ} (hc0 : n ≤ c) (ui uj : Fin 2) :
    ∑ α, ∑ β, pw q n c (c + 1) β α * (capW q α β * cupW q ui uj) =
      (q + q⁻¹) * pw q n c (c + 1) uj ui

declarations.name: core_close
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem core_close {q : K} (hq : q ≠ 0) {n x y : ℕ} (hx : 0 < x) (hxy : x < y)
    (hy : y < 2 * n + 1) (px : x % 2 = 1) (py : (2 * n + 1 + y) % 2 = 1) (la lb : Fin 2) :
    ∑ t, muEntry q t * (pairW q (n + 1) 0 x t la * pairW q (n + 1) y (2 * n + 1) lb t) =
      pairW q n (x - 1) (y - 1) la lb

declarations.name: core_close_loop

theorem core_close_loop (q : K) (n : ℕ) :
    ∑ t, muEntry q t * pairW q (n + 1) 0 (2 * n + 1) t t = q + q⁻¹

/-!
# Temperley–Lieb diagrams as matrices in the `U_q(sl₂)` representation

The R-matrix of `qbx_ir.quantum.representation` splits as `Ř = q·I - E` (`sl2R_eq_sub`), where
`E = tlE q` is a rank-one matrix on `V ⊗ V`: a *cap* `capW` (top) times a *cup* `cupW` (bottom).
This file assigns to every planar matching `m` of the boundary points of a diagram on `n` strands
(`TLMatch.lean`) a matrix `phi q n m` on `V^{⊗ n}`: a product over the pairs of `m`, with `capW`
for a pair on the top, `cupW` for a pair on the bottom, a Kronecker delta for a through strand,
and a sign `(-1)^{g/2}`, `g` the number of points the pair encloses.

* `phi_id`: the identity diagram gives the identity matrix;
* `phi_mul_E` (**Temperley–Lieb action**): multiplying `phi m` on the right by `E` on strands
  `i, i + 1` gives `phi (upd c m)` — Python's update — times `q + q⁻¹` if a loop closes;
* `ptrace_phi` (**closing a strand**): the partial quantum trace over the first strand,
  `∑ₓ μₓ (phi m)(x a, x b)`, is `phi (close m)` times `q + q⁻¹` if a loop closes;
* `qTrace_phi`: hence `Tr(μ^{⊗ n} phi m) = (q + q⁻¹)^{closeLoops n m}` — every loop of the
  closure counts `q + q⁻¹`.

The proofs reduce to identities between the weights of at most four pairs (`core_mul`,
`core_close`), where the non-crossing and parity conditions of `Valid` decide which pairs can
occur.
-/
/-! ### Weights -/
/-- The cup (bottom) weight: `B(0,1) = q`, `B(1,0) = -1`. -/
/-- The Temperley–Lieb generator on `V ⊗ V`: `E(ab, ce) = T(a, b) B(c, e)`. -/

/-- The label of boundary point `p` in the matrix entry `(s, u)`: top point `j` reads `s j`,
bottom point `2n - 1 - k` reads `u k`. -/
/-- The weight of the pair `{a, b}`, `a < b`, with labels `la`, `lb`. -/
/-- The weight of the pair `{a, b}` in either order. -/
/-! ### The two core identities -/
/-! ### Right multiplication: the core identity -/

/-- The possible positions of the partners `x` of `c` and `y` of `c + 1` (bottom points `c`,
`c + 1`) in a planar matching. -/

/-- **Core identity of the Temperley–Lieb action** (no loop): the weights of the pairs `{c, x}`,
`{c + 1, y}` contracted with `E` give the weights of the cup `{c, c + 1}` and the pair `{x, y}`. -/
/-- **Core identity of the Temperley–Lieb action** (loop): capping a cup gives `q + q⁻¹`. -/
/-! ### Closing the first strand: the core identity -/

/-- **Core identity of the closure** (no loop): the partners `x < y` of the end points `0` and
`2n + 1` of the first strand become a pair of the closed diagram. -/
/-- **Core identity of the closure** (loop): a closed strand counts `q + q⁻¹`. -/

declarations.signature_heuristic:

    {p : ℕ} (hp : p < 2 * n) (h0 : m (p + 1) ≠ 0) (hN : m (p + 1) ≠ 2 * n + 1) :

declarations.name: ptrace_phi
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem ptrace_phi {q : K} (hq : q ≠ 0) {m : Match} (hv : Valid (n + 1) m) (a b : Fin n → Fin 2) :
    ∑ t, muEntry q t * phi q (n + 1) m (Fin.cons t a) (Fin.cons t b) =
      (q + q⁻¹) ^ closeLoop n m * phi q n (close n m) a b

declarations.name: qTrace_phi
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem qTrace_phi {q : K} (hq : q ≠ 0) :
    ∀ {n : ℕ} {m : Match}, Valid n m → qTrace q (phi q n m) = (q + q⁻¹) ^ closeLoops n m
  | 0, m, _ => by
    simp [qTrace, phi, closeLoops, muDiag]
  | n + 1, m, hv => by
    rw [qTrace, sum_fun_succ]
    simp only [muDiag_cons]
    rw [Finset.sum_comm]
    have : ∀ s : Fin n → Fin 2, ∑ x, muEntry q x * muDiag q s *
        phi q (n + 1) m (Fin.cons x s) (Fin.cons x s) =
        muDiag q s * ((q + q⁻¹) ^ closeLoop n m * phi q n (close n m) s s)

/-!
# Kauffman bracket and Jones certificates of the braid ledger (migration 023)

`qbx_ir.algebra.polynomial_invariants.kauffman_bracket` computes the Kauffman bracket `⟨B̂⟩` of
the closure of a braid by multiplying the word out in the Temperley–Lieb algebra
(`⟨σ_i⟩ = A·1 + A⁻¹·e_i`, `⟨σ_i⁻¹⟩ = A⁻¹·1 + A·e_i`, every closed loop beyond the first
counting `d = −A² − A⁻²`), and `jones_polynomial` returns `V = (−A³)^{−w} ⟨B̂⟩`.  The
certificates of Phase 3 item 2 store both polynomials (reference: `qbx_ir.jones_ledger`; the SQL
layer, migration `023_braid_jones.sql`, is reserved and not written yet).

The Lean model (`TL.bracketAux`, `TL.bracketPoly`, `TL.jonesPoly`) follows the Python state
recursion: planar matchings (`TLMatch.lean`), the update `match · e_i` (`TL.upd`) and the
closure loop count (`TL.closeLoops`).

**Bridge to the quantum trace (H-062).**  The matrix of a planar matching on `V^{⊗ n}`
(`TL.phi`, `TLMatrix.lean`, `TLPhi.lean`) satisfies `phi m · E_i = d^{loop} · phi (m e_i)`
(`TL.phi_mul_E`) and `Tr(μ^{⊗ n} phi m) = d^{closeLoops}` (`TL.qTrace_phi`); with `q = −A²` the
R-matrix is the Kauffman skein, `Ř = −A (A·1 + A⁻¹·E)` (`TL.localMat_sl2R`, `TL.repMat_eq_kaufW`).
Hence, for every field and every `A ≠ 0`:

* `TL.quantumTrace_eq_bracket`: `Tr(μ^{⊗ n} ρ(B)) = (−A)^w · d · ⟨B̂⟩`;
* `TL.jonesQT_eq_bracket`: the quantum-trace Jones value of `JonesMarkov.lean` is
  `(−A³)^{−w} ⟨B̂⟩`, i.e. the Python Jones polynomial.

**Consequences.**

* `TL.jonesPoly_markov`: the Jones polynomial (in `ℤ[A, A⁻¹]`) is invariant under Markov's
  moves — it depends only on the closed link; `TL.not_markovEquiv_of_jonesPoly_ne`;
* `TL.bracketPoly_eq_of_eval_eq`, `TL.bracketPoly_conj`: the bracket is an invariant of the braid
  group element and of conjugacy;
* `TL.certPoly_inj`, `TL.bracketCert_eq_iff`: the stored encoding is unique, so two bracket
  certificates are equal iff the brackets are equal;
* `TL.not_markovEquiv_of_jonesCert_ne`: different Jones certificates prove non-isotopic closures;
* `TL.isBracketCert_of_check`, `TL.isJonesCert_of_check`: a kernel-checkable evaluation test
  proves a certificate exactly; `TL.jones_agrees_with_python`: the Python certificates are exactly
  the Lean ones on the test vectors;
* `TL.hopf_not_unlink`, `TL.trefoil_not_mirror`, `TL.figureEight_not_trefoil`,
  `TL.figureEight_not_unknot`: concrete non-isotopy certificates.

Registry: H-278, H-279, H-280, H-281.
-/

/-- **The Lean model agrees exactly with the Python certificates** on the test vectors: every
stored bracket is exactly `⟨B̂⟩` and every stored Jones polynomial is exactly `V` in
`ℤ[A, A⁻¹]`. -/
/-! ### Non-isotopy certificates -/

/-- **The Hopf link is linked**: the closure of `σ₁²` is not isotopic to the two-component
unlink (closure of the trivial braid on two strands). -/
/-- **The trefoil is chiral**: the closures of `σ₁³` and `σ₁⁻³` are not isotopic. -/
/-- The figure-eight knot (closure of `σ₁σ₂⁻¹σ₁σ₂⁻¹`) is not the trefoil. -/

/-- **The figure-eight knot is knotted**: it is not isotopic to the unknot (closure of the
trivial one-strand braid). -/

/-!
# Writing direction inside a logic: the Lambek calculus

Most theorem provers (Lean, Rocq, Agda, Isabelle, HOL Light, Mizar, Metamath, …) work in logics
whose contexts admit **exchange**: hypotheses can be reordered freely, so the order in which they
were written carries no information.  A braid remembers far more than an order (`ProverExchange`
shows what a symmetric logic forgets).  At the other extreme is the **Lambek calculus**, the logic
of word order used in categorial grammar: it has no exchange at all, and it has two implications,
`A / B` ("an `A` once a `B` follows on the right") and `B \ A` ("an `A` once a `B` precedes on the
left").  This is where writing direction lives at the level of logic.

This file formalises the (associative, product) Lambek calculus `L` and proves:

* `Deriv.mirror`, `deriv_mirror_iff` — **direction symmetry**: reversing the direction of writing
  (reverse the antecedent, swap `/` with `\`, swap the factors of `•`) maps derivations to
  derivations.  A grammar for a left-to-right language turns into a grammar for the same language
  written right-to-left, with no loss.
* `Deriv.sound` — soundness for language (free monoid) models, with Mathlib's `Language`.
* `exchange_not_admissible` — exchange is not admissible: `p, q ⊢ p • q` is derivable but
  `q, p ⊢ p • q` is not.
* `transitive_sentence`, `transitive_sentence_mirror` — the English transitive-verb type
  `(np\s)/np` and its mirror image `np\(s/np)` both derive a sentence from `np, verb, np`.
-/
/-- Lambek types over a set of atoms. -/
/-- `rdiv A B` is `A / B`: an `A` once a `B` follows on the right. -/
/-- `ldiv B A` is `B \ A`: an `A` once a `B` precedes on the left. -/
/-- `prod A B` is `A • B`: an `A` followed by a `B`. -/

/-- Sequent derivability in the Lambek calculus `L` (antecedents of the right rules for the
implications are non-empty, as in Lambek's original system). -/
/-! ### Direction symmetry -/
/-- Writing in the opposite direction: swap the two implications and the factors of products. -/
/-- An antecedent written in the opposite direction. -/

/-- **Direction symmetry.** Writing a derivable sequent in the opposite direction gives a
derivable sequent. -/
/-! ### Language models -/
/-- Interpretation of types as languages (sets of strings), given languages for the atoms. -/
/-- Interpretation of an antecedent: the concatenation of its languages. -/
/-- **Soundness** for language models. -/
/-! ### Exchange is not admissible -/
/-- The model sending the atom `b` to the one-letter language `{[b]}`. -/
/-- **Exchange is not admissible** in the Lambek calculus: word order matters. -/
/-! ### A transitive sentence and its mirror image -/
/-- Atoms of a toy grammar: noun phrases and sentences. -/
/-- The English transitive verb type `(np\s)/np`. -/
/-- `np, (np\s)/np, np ⊢ s` ("John loves Mary"). -/
/-- The same sentence written in the opposite direction: the verb type becomes `np\(s/np)`. -/
