/-!
# Link-coupling channel: superposition and its blind spot

Channel 2 of the five-channel machine (`QBX/docs/design/MULTIPROVER.md`).  The closure
`L(β)` of a braid has a linking spectrum (one integer per ordered pair of closure components),
a Markov invariant (`ClosureLinking.lean`).  For pure braids every strand is its own component
and the linking numbers form a symmetric integer matrix (`PureLinkingMatrix.lean`).

* `link_superposition`: on pure braids the coupling is linear — the linking matrix of a product
  is the sum of the linking matrices.  Two pure braids stacked on the same strands couple with
  no interaction term: as an "oscillator network" the linking channel is a *linear* network.
* `linkMatrix_commutator`: consequently the channel is blind to commutators of pure braids.
* `blindBraid` (`= σ₁²σ₂⁻²σ₁⁻²σ₂²`): a non-trivial pure 3-braid (`blindBraid_ne_one`, from the
  free group generated by `σ₁²`, `σ₂⁻²`) whose closure has the same number of components and
  the same linking spectrum as the trivial braid (`blindBraid_link_agrees`).  Detecting it needs
  a non-abelian channel (Burau, Garside fold) — or Milnor's higher linking invariants, which
  this channel does not compute.
-/
/-- **Superposition** of the link coupling on pure braids. -/
/-- The linking matrix vanishes on commutators of pure braids. -/
/-- The blind braid `σ₁² σ₂⁻² σ₁⁻² σ₂²`, the commutator of the two free generators. -/

/-- **The link-coupling channel cannot tell the blind braid from the identity**: same closure
components (three unknotted strands) and the same linking spectrum (all zero). -/

/-!
# The five-channel resonance machine

A braid word `β` is read simultaneously by five channels (`QBX/docs/design/MULTIPROVER.md`):

| channel      | reading                                                        | file                   |
|--------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------|
| `fold`       | Garside fold (path of permutohedron vertices) + walk endpoint  | `BraidPolytope.lean`   |
| `link`       | number of closure components + linking spectrum                | `LinkCoupling.lean`    |
| `anchor`     | generic Burau matrix over `ℤ[t, t⁻¹]` (monodromy)               | `TorusAnchor.lean`     |
| `harmonic`   | resonance set `{θ | some eigenvalue of ρ̄(β)(e^{iθ}) has |λ| = 1}` | `HarmonicSweep.lean`   |
| `oscillator` | Jones invariant at every root of unity `e^{iπ/r}`              | `OscillatorChannel.lean` |

Main results:

* `Channel.agree_of_eval_eq` — every channel is *sound*: equal braids give equal readings.
* `resonance_iff` — **a braid identity holds iff all five channels resonate**:
  `(∀ c, c.Agree w w') ↔ w.eval = w'.eval`.  The "if" direction is carried by the fold channel,
  which is complete (Garside uniqueness).
* `verdict` — the decision procedure (`proved` / `refuted` with a witness channel):
  `verdict_eq_proved_iff` (sound and complete), `verdict_proved_iff_defect` (equivalently,
  the defect `β₁ β₂⁻¹` folds to the identity), and `verdict_ne_proved_of_disagree` (a
  disagreement in *any* channel is a valid refutation — the channels never contradict the
  decider).
* `heal`, `defect_eq_one_iff` — healing: the defect word repairs a refuted identity.
* Partial resonances (channels disagree, the interesting case):
  - `sq_sq_partial`: `σ₁²` vs `σ₂²` — link, harmonic and oscillator agree; fold and anchor
    refute (conjugate but distinct braids);
  - `blind_partial`: `σ₁²σ₂⁻²σ₁⁻²σ₂²` vs the identity — the link channel agrees, fold refutes;
  - `sigma_pow_harmonic_silent`: `σ₁^k` vs the identity — the harmonic channel agrees for
    every `k` (the trefoil `σ₁³` is harmonically silent), fold refutes for `k > 0`;
  - `hidden_harmonic_refutes`: `σ₁²σ₂⁻²` vs the identity — the harmonic channel refutes at
    `θ = π`.
-/
/-! ### The five readings -/
/-- The five channels. -/
/-- The torus-anchor reading: the generic reduced Burau matrix over `ℤ[t, t⁻¹]`. -/

/-- The harmonic reading: the set of sweep angles at which `ρ̄(β)(e^{iθ})` has an eigenvalue
on the unit circle. -/
/-- Agreement of two words in one channel. -/
/-- **Soundness of every channel**: equal braids have equal readings. -/
/-- **The resonance theorem**: a braid identity `w = w'` holds iff all five channels agree. -/
/-! ### The verdict -/
/-- The verdict of the machine. -/
/-- The decision procedure: run the (complete) fold channel. -/
/-- **The verdict is sound and complete.** -/
/-- A refutation names a channel that really disagrees, and the braids really differ. -/

/-- **No channel ever contradicts the decider**: a disagreement in any one channel is a valid
refutation. -/

/-- The verdict can be computed on the single braid `β₁ β₂⁻¹`: the identity holds iff this
defect folds to the empty normal form. -/
/-! ### Healing -/
/-- The defect of a claimed identity `w = w'`. -/

/-!
# Milnor triple linking: closing the blind spot of the link channel

The link-coupling channel (`LinkCoupling.lean`) reads only pairwise linking numbers, so it is
blind to commutators of pure braids: the blind braid `σ₁²σ₂⁻²σ₁⁻²σ₂²` has the same closure
components and the same (all-zero) linking spectrum as the trivial braid
(`blindBraid_link_agrees`).  The classical cure is Milnor's *triple* linking number `μ̄(123)`,
read off from the Magnus expansion of the longitudes of the Artin action.

* `artin` : the **Artin representation** `B₃ →* Aut(F₃)`,
  `σᵢ : xᵢ ↦ xᵢ xᵢ₊₁ xᵢ⁻¹, xᵢ₊₁ ↦ xᵢ` (the braid relation is checked on generators).
* `magnusCoeff w m` : the coefficient of the monomial `X_{m₁} ⋯ X_{m_k}` in the Magnus
  expansion `xᵢ ↦ 1 + Xᵢ`, `xᵢ⁻¹ ↦ 1 - Xᵢ + Xᵢ² - ⋯` of a word `w` of the free group.
* `milnor123 β` : the coefficient of `X₁X₂X₃` in the Magnus expansion of `β(x₃)`.  For a pure
  braid `β(x₃) = w x₃ w⁻¹`, and this is the coefficient of `X₁X₂` in the longitude `w`
  (independent of the choice of `w`), i.e. Milnor's invariant `μ(1,2;3)`.  As a function of the
  braid group element it is automatically a braid-isotopy invariant.
* `milnor123_blind` / `milnor123_one` : `μ(1,2;3) = -1` on the blind braid and `0` on the
  identity, so **the Milnor channel refutes `blind = 1`** although the link channel agrees
  (`milnor_closes_blind_spot`).
* `milnor123_borromean` : the Borromean braid `(σ₁σ₂⁻¹)³` has `μ(1,2;3) = 1`.
* `milnor123_sigma_sq` : the channel vanishes on `σ₁²` (whose closure is a Hopf link plus an
  unknot: pairwise linking only).

That `μ(1,2;3)` (read this way) agrees with Milnor's `μ̄(123)` of the closed link, up to the
usual indeterminacy, is classical and **cited**, not proved here; what is proved is that the
quantity is a well-defined function on `B₃` that separates the blind braid from `1`.
-/
/-! ### The Artin representation of `B₃` on `F₃` -/
/-- Image of the free generator `x_j` under `σ_i` (`pos = true`) or `σ_i⁻¹` (`pos = false`). -/
/-- The endomorphism of `F₃` induced by a letter. -/
/-- The automorphism of `F₃` induced by `σ_i`. -/
/-- **The Artin representation** `B₃ →* Aut(F₃)`. -/
/-- The Artin action of a word, letter by letter (`artin(ab) = artin(a) ∘ artin(b)`). -/
/-! ### The truncated Magnus expansion -/
/-- Coefficient of `Xᵢᵏ` in the Magnus series of `xᵢ` (`1 + Xᵢ`) or `xᵢ⁻¹` (`Σ (-Xᵢ)ᵏ`). -/

/-- The coefficient of the monomial `m` in the Magnus expansion of the word `w`
(the product of the letter series, in order). -/

/-- **Milnor's triple linking reading** `μ(1,2;3)`: the coefficient of `X₁X₂X₃` in the Magnus
expansion of the image of `x₃` under the braid. -/
/-- The Borromean braid `(σ₁σ₂⁻¹)³`. -/

/-- **The Milnor channel closes the blind spot of the link channel.**  The blind braid and the
identity have the same closure components and linking spectrum, but different triple linking
readings. -/

/-!
# The QBX node network: lookup, distributed scheduling, equivocation

Lean side of node steps 5–7 of `alphabet_theory/next_steps_distilled.md` §4 (the Python side is
`QBX/src/qbx_live/{dht,distributed,consensus}.py`, spec in `QBX/docs/design/NODE_NETWORK.md`).

**Step 5 — lookup on `Q_n □ T^k_M`.** Every node has an address; a summary is stored at the
address its key hashes to (and replicated on the neighbours of that address).
* `greedy_arrives` — *any* greedy lookup (each hop is one move that lowers the distance to the
  target by one; Python `greedy_next` makes one particular choice) reaches the target after
  exactly `addrDist a b` hops.  `greedyRoute` is one such lookup (`greedyRoute_arrives`).
* `addrDist_le_addrDiam`, `exists_addrDist_eq_addrDiam` — the hop count is at most
  `addrDiam n k M = n + ∑ⱼ ⌊M j / 2⌋`, and this bound is attained.
* `lookup_survives_link_failures` — after fewer than `addrDegree n k M` links fail, every node can
  still reach every address (edge connectivity, `addrGraph_isEdgeConnected`).
* `ncard_replicaSet`, `replica_survives` — the replica set of an address (the address and its
  neighbours) has `addrDegree + 1` members, so it survives any `addrDegree` node failures;
  `replicas_can_all_fail` shows `addrDegree + 1` failures can remove it.

**Step 6 — distributed scheduling.**
* `flatten_blocks`, `distributed_correct` — cutting a word into consecutive blocks (one per node),
  summarising each block on its node and combining the results *in block order* by any reduction
  schedule gives the summary of the whole word.
* `sum_balancedSizes`, `balancedSizes_bounds` — the balanced cut gives `N` blocks whose sizes add
  up to the word length and differ by at most one.
* `roundRobin_wrong` — the order matters: dealing chunks round-robin and multiplying each node's
  chunks locally gives the wrong permutation already for three chunks on two nodes.

**Step 7 — equivocation.** A node `v` reports a state `claim v w` to each neighbour `w`; the edge
transport is `(claim v w)⁻¹ * claim w v` (`claimConn`).
* `claimConn_isFlat_of_consistent` — if every node reports the same state to all its neighbours
  the ledger is flat.
* `single_liar_isFlat_iff` — if only `u` may deviate, and any two neighbours of `u` are joined by
  a walk avoiding `u`, then the ledger is flat **iff `u` reports one state to all its
  neighbours**.  So flatness detects *equivocation* (telling neighbours different things), not a
  consistent lie (which is a gauge change).
* `addrGraph_neighbors_linked` — the address graph (all `M j ≥ 2`) satisfies that hypothesis, so
  `addrGraph_single_liar_isFlat_iff`: on the address graph, a single node's equivocation is always
  detected.
-/
/-! ## Step 5: lookup on the address graph -/

/-- **Greedy lookups arrive.** Let `r t` be the node holding the query after `t` hops, starting
at `a`.  If every hop from a node other than `b` is a move lowering the distance to `b` by one,
and the query stays put once at `b`, then it is at `b` after exactly `addrDist a b` hops. -/
/-- One greedy hop towards `b` (stay at `b`). -/
/-- The greedy lookup from `a` to `b`: the node holding the query after `t` hops. -/
/-- **Every address is reached** by the greedy lookup, after `addrDist a b` hops. -/
/-- The diameter of `Q_n □ T^k_M`: `n + ∑ⱼ ⌊M j / 2⌋`. -/
/-- **Hop bound.** Every lookup needs at most `addrDiam n k M` hops. -/
/-- The hop bound is attained. -/

/-- **Lookups survive link failures.** If fewer than `addrDegree n k M` links fail, every node can
still reach every address. -/
/-- The replica set of an address: the address and its neighbours. -/

/-- **Replicas survive node failures.** If at most `addrDegree n k M` nodes fail, some replica of
every address survives. -/

/-- The bound in `replica_survives` is sharp: `addrDegree + 1` failures can take out every
replica. -/
/-! ## Step 6: distributed scheduling -/
/-- Cut a list into consecutive blocks of the given sizes; the last block takes the rest. -/
/-- The balanced block sizes for `m` chunks on `N` nodes: the first `m % N` nodes get one extra. -/

/-- **The order matters.** Deal the chunks `σ₁, σ₂, σ₁` (as permutations) round-robin to two nodes,
let each node multiply its own chunks, and multiply the two results: the answer differs from the
product of the chunks in order. -/
/-! ## Step 7: equivocation -/

/-- The ledger built from the nodes' reports: `claim v w` is the state node `v` reports to its
neighbour `w`, and the edge `v → w` carries `(claim v w)⁻¹ * claim w v`. -/
/-- **Consistent reports give a flat ledger.** -/
/-- Along a walk that avoids the only possibly dishonest node, the holonomy telescopes. -/

/-- **A single equivocating node is detected.** Suppose every node other than `u` reports its
true state `p v` to all neighbours, and any two neighbours of `u` are joined by a walk avoiding
`u`.  Then the ledger is flat iff `u` reports one and the same state to all its neighbours. -/
/-- A walk between distinct vertices visits a neighbour of its start. -/

/-- **Neighbours are linked around a vertex** in a `d`-edge-connected graph, at every vertex of
degree at most `d`: delete all edges at `u` except the one to `w₁`; fewer than `d` edges are gone,
so a path from `w₂` to `w₁` survives, and it cannot pass through `u`, which now has only one
neighbour. -/

/-- In the address graph (all `M j ≥ 2`) any two neighbours of a node are joined by a walk
avoiding it. -/

/-- **On the address graph, a single node's equivocation is always detected**: if only `u` may
deviate, the ledger is flat iff `u` reports one state to all its neighbours. -/

/-!
# Bridge: the Sovereign organism controls the resonance machine

The Sovereign organism (`Sovereign.Organism.*`) supplies three control mechanisms with proved
guarantees.  This file connects them to the five-channel machine.

* **Kelly allocation (`Organism.Kelly`).**  A harmonic probe at an angle `θ` on the universal arc
  `|θ| < 2π/n` can never refute anything: every braid resonates there
  (`arc_mem_resonanceSet`, from `resonance_universal_n`).  Hence its empirical refutation rate is
  `0` on *every* list of test pairs (`refutationRate_arc`), its Kelly fraction is `0`, and the
  beam never keeps it (`arc_probe_pruned`).  The organism automatically spends no compute on the
  silent arc.
* **Cycle guard (`Organism.Derivation`, re-exported by `Organism.Cycles`).**  The
  channel-dependency graph of the machine and of the healing pipeline are certified acyclic
  (`machine_wellFounded`, `healing_wellFounded`), and the feedback edge that would make healing
  circular is rejected (`circular_healing_rejected`).
* **Stopping (`Organism.StoppingCore`, re-exported by `Organism.Stopping`).**  If a healing
  run keeps its energy, velocity and consistency streams good up to step `t`, the online
  stopping test fires (`stop_of_good`) — the stopping rule of the organism terminates the
  healing loop.

Only the Mathlib-only cores `Organism.Derivation` and `Organism.StoppingCore` are imported, not
`Organism.Cycles` / `Organism.Stopping`, whose state-of-thought dependencies cost about 8
minutes of cold build on the critical path (`docs/BUILD_DEPENDENCIES.md`).

`Organism.Guard` and `Organism.CurvatureBound` speak about Cayley–Dickson thought states
(zero-divisor traps, relative curvature); they have no braid-channel counterpart and are not used.
-/
/-! ### The silent arc and Kelly pruning -/
/-- On the universal arc every braid has a unimodular Burau eigenvalue. -/
/-- A harmonic probe at `θ` refutes the pair `(w, w')` if exactly one of them resonates at `θ`. -/
/-- Empirical refutation rate of the probe at `θ` on a list of test pairs. -/
/-- **The silent arc never refutes.** -/
/-- Kelly branches for a list of probes `(θ, payoff)`. -/

/-- **The organism prunes the silent arc**: a probe on the universal arc gets Kelly fraction
`0` and is never a survivor of the beam, whatever the test pairs. -/
/-! ### Acyclicity of the channel and healing graphs -/

/-- Channel dependencies: `0` fold, `1` link (reads the permutation of the fold),
`2` anchor, `3` harmonic (specialises the anchor), `4` oscillator, `5` verdict. -/

/-- Healing pipeline: `0` input, `1` spectral energy, `2` Fano span, `3` heat flow (uses the
energy), `4` gap filling (energy, Fano, flow), `5` anchors, `6` output. -/
/-- Letting the input depend on the output makes the pipeline circular; the guard rejects it. -/
/-! ### The stopping rule terminates a healing run -/
/-- **A healing run whose streams stay good is stopped by the organism.** -/

/-!
# Oscillator channel: the Jones invariant at roots of unity and quantum dimensions

Channel 5 of the five-channel machine (`QBX/docs/design/MULTIPROVER.md`).  At
`q = e^{iπ/r}` the Temperley–Lieb / Jones–Wenzl theory truncates: the Jones–Wenzl projector
`p_k` has Markov trace the quantum integer `[k+1]_q`, and these are the quantum dimensions of
the `SU(2)` level `r - 2` modular category.  This file proves the finite facts behind that
picture and wires the channel to the existing Jones invariant.

* `qInt_root_of_unity`: `(q^k - q^{-k}) / (q - q^{-1}) = sin(kπ/r) / sin(π/r)` at
  `q = e^{iπ/r}`, so the quantum integers are the real numbers `quantumDim r k`.
* `quantumDim_rec`: the Chebyshev / Jones–Wenzl trace recursion
  `[k+1] = [2]·[k] - [k-1]`, with loop value `[2] = 2 cos(π/r)` (`quantumDim_two`).
* `quantumDim_pos`, `quantumDim_self`: `[k] > 0` for `0 < k < r` and `[r] = 0` — the
  truncation: exactly `r - 1` simple objects survive.
* `quantumDim_symm`: `[r - k] = [k]` (charge conjugation symmetry of the spectrum).
* `quantumDim_fib`, `fib_fusion`: at `r = 5` the loop value is the golden ratio `φ` and
  `φ² = 1 + φ` (Fibonacci fusion `τ ⊗ τ = 1 ⊕ τ`); `quantumDim_ising`: at `r = 4` it is `√2`.
* `oscillator_eq_of_eval_eq`, `oscillator_markov`: the Jones invariant evaluated at
  `e^{iπ/r}` is a braid invariant and a Markov (closed-link) invariant, for every `r ≥ 1`.
-/
/-- The quantum integer `[k]` at `q = e^{iπ/r}`: `sin(kπ/r) / sin(π/r)`. -/
/-- The root of unity `q = e^{iπ/r}`. -/

/-- **Quantum integers at roots of unity.**  At `q = e^{iπ/r}` (`r ≥ 2`),
`(q^k - q^{-k}) / (q - q^{-1}) = sin(kπ/r) / sin(π/r)`. -/
/-- The loop value `[2] = 2 cos(π/r)`. -/
/-- **Jones–Wenzl trace recursion** `[k+2] = [2]·[k+1] - [k]`. -/
/-- **Truncation**: `[r] = 0` at `q = e^{iπ/r}`. -/

/-- **Positivity**: `[k] > 0` for `0 < k < r`, so exactly the `r - 1` labels `1, …, r - 1`
carry non-zero quantum dimension. -/
/-- **Charge-conjugation symmetry** of the spectrum: `[r - k] = [k]`. -/
/-- **Fibonacci** (`r = 5`): the loop value is the golden ratio. -/
/-- Fibonacci fusion `τ ⊗ τ = 1 ⊕ τ` at the level of quantum dimensions: `φ² = 1 + φ`. -/
/-- **Ising** (`r = 4`): the loop value is `√2`. -/
/-! ### The oscillator channel reading -/
/-- The oscillator channel: the Jones invariant of the closure, evaluated at `e^{iπ/r}`. -/
/-- The oscillator reading is a braid invariant. -/
/-- The oscillator reading is a conjugacy invariant. -/
/-- The oscillator reading only depends on the closed link (Markov invariance). -/
/-- The loop value of the oscillator channel: `q + q⁻¹ = [2] = 2 cos(π/r)`. -/
/-- For `r ≥ 3` the unknot is normalised (`V = 1`) in the oscillator channel. -/

/-!
# Partial resonances: where the channels disagree

Concrete braids of `B₃` on which some channels of the machine agree with the comparison braid
and others refute it.  These are the cases where a single invariant would give the wrong
answer, and where `resonance_iff` needs *all* channels (in fact, the complete fold channel).
-/
/-- `σ₁`, `σ₂` and their inverses in `B₃`. -/
/-! ### `σ₁²` versus `σ₂²`: conjugate but different -/

/-- **Partial resonance of `σ₁²` and `σ₂²`**: link, harmonic and oscillator channels agree,
fold and torus anchor refute. -/
/-! ### The blind braid: invisible to the link channel -/

/-- **Partial resonance of the blind braid and the identity**: the link channel agrees, the
fold channel refutes. -/
/-! ### `σ₁^k`: harmonically silent -/
/-- If the second row of the Burau matrix is `(0, 1)` then `1` is an eigenvalue: resonance. -/

/-- **`σ₁^k` is harmonically silent**: for every `k` (the trefoil is `k = 3`) its resonance set
is the whole circle, exactly as for the trivial braid; only the fold channel tells them apart
(for `k > 0`). -/
/-! ### `σ₁²σ₂⁻²`: refuted by the harmonic channel at `θ = π` -/

/-- **The harmonic channel refutes `σ₁²σ₂⁻² = 1`**: at `θ = π` the trivial braid resonates
but `σ₁²σ₂⁻²` does not (its trace is `6 > 2`, eigenvalues `3 ± 2√2`). -/

/-!
# The certified chunk scheduler of the multi-prover

The five-channel machine (`QBX.Formal.MultiProver.Machine`) was first stated for whole braid
words.  This file makes its scheduler a client of `QBX.Formal.TextManifold`: a braid word is cut
into chunks, every chunk is summarised independently, and the summaries are combined by **any**
reduction schedule (sequential, balanced tree, any number of workers).  The combined summary is
*proved* equal to the summary of the whole word, so the scheduler is certified rather than
heuristic.

The chunk summary carries the homomorphic readings of the machine:

| component | reading                                    | combine                  |
|-----------|--------------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| `braid`   | the braid group element `w.eval`            | group multiplication     |
| `perm`    | the permutation of the strands             | composition              |
| `writhe`  | the exponent sum                           | addition                 |
| `anchor`  | the reduced Burau matrix over `ℤ[t, t⁻¹]`  | matrix multiplication    |

The readings that are *not* homomorphisms (Garside normal form, linking spectrum, resonance set,
Jones values) are functions of the braid group element, so they are computed once, from the
combined `braid` component, and are still exact (`channels_agree_of_summary`).

## Main results

* `summaryHom` — the chunk summary as a monoid homomorphism out of the free monoid on letters;
  `summaryHom_ofList` identifies it with the direct readings.
* `schedule_correct` — **certified scheduling**: for any chunking of `w` and any reduction
  schedule whose leaves are the chunk summaries, the schedule evaluates to the summary of `w`
  (via `TextManifold.mapReduce` and `TextManifold.ReduceTree.eval_eq_prod`).
* `balanced_schedule_correct`, `balanced_schedule_depth` — the balanced schedule is correct and
  needs `⌈log₂ (number of chunks)⌉` rounds.
* `verdict_scheduled` — the machine's verdict on `w = w'` can be computed from the scheduled
  summaries: it is `proved` iff the two combined braid components agree.
* `channels_agree_of_summary` — equal combined braid components imply agreement in all five
  channels.
* `braid_segment` — random access: the braid element of any segment `[i, j)` of a word is
  `P i⁻¹ * P j` for the running prefix products (`TextManifold.segment_eq_prefix`).
-/

/-- The chunk summary: braid element, permutation, writhe (multiplicatively), and the reduced
Burau matrix over `ℤ[t, t⁻¹]`. -/
/-- The summary of a word, read directly. -/
/-- The summary as a monoid homomorphism out of the free monoid on letters. -/
/-- The homomorphism computes the direct summary on every word. -/

/-- **Chunking the summary** (map–reduce): the summary of a word cut into chunks is the product
of the chunk summaries. -/

/-- **Certified scheduling.**  For any chunking of `w` and any reduction schedule whose leaves are
the chunk summaries (in order), running the schedule gives the summary of `w`. -/
/-- **The balanced schedule is correct.** -/
/-- **The balanced schedule needs `⌈log₂ (number of chunks)⌉` rounds.** -/

/-- **The verdict from scheduled summaries.**  For any schedules `t`, `t'` for the words `w`,
`w'`, the machine proves `w = w'` iff the braid components of the scheduled results agree. -/

/-- **Every channel from the combined summary.**  If the combined braid components of two
words agree, the words agree in all five channels (including the non-homomorphic ones, which
are functions of the braid element). -/

/-- **Random access.**  The braid element of the segment `[i, j)` of a word is `P i⁻¹ * P j`,
where `P k` is the braid element of the first `k` letters. -/

declarations.name: TLFamily
declarations.signature_heuristic:
structure TLFamily (K A : Type*) [Field K] [Ring A] [Algebra K A] (m : ℕ) where
  δ : K
  e : ℕ → A
  sq : ∀ i, i < m → e i * e i = δ • e i
  up : ∀ i, i + 1 < m → e i * e (i + 1) * e i = e i
  down : ∀ i, i + 1 < m → e (i + 1) * e i * e (i + 1) = e (i + 1)
  far : ∀ i j, i + 2 ≤ j → j < m → Commute (e i) (e j)

namespace TLFamily

variable {A : Type*} [Ring A] [Algebra K A] {m : ℕ} (T : TLFamily K A m)

/-- The Jones–Wenzl elements: `jw (n+1)` is the projector on `n+1` strands, built from

comments.text:
/-!
# Temperley–Lieb algebras and Jones–Wenzl projectors as operators

Item 3 of `QBX/docs/design/MULTIPROVER.md` §7.  The oscillator channel
(`OscillatorChannel.lean`) uses the quantum integers `[k]` as the traces of the Jones–Wenzl
projectors; this file constructs the projectors themselves, as elements of an arbitrary
algebra in which Temperley–Lieb generators act, and proves Wenzl's theorem.

A *Temperley–Lieb family* with `m` generators and loop value `δ` in a `K`-algebra `A` is a
sequence `e 0, e 1, …` satisfying, for indices below `m`,

* `eᵢ² = δ eᵢ`,  `eᵢ eᵢ₊₁ eᵢ = eᵢ`,  `eᵢ₊₁ eᵢ eᵢ₊₁ = eᵢ₊₁`,  `eᵢ eⱼ = eⱼ eᵢ` for `|i - j| ≥ 2`.

(`A` can be a matrix algebra, so the results are statements about operators.)

* `qInt δ k`: the quantum integers `[0] = 0`, `[1] = 1`, `[k+2] = δ[k+1] - [k]`.
* `TLFamily.jw`: the Jones–Wenzl recursion `p₁ = 1`,
  `p_{n+2} = p_{n+1} - ([n+1]/[n+2]) p_{n+1} eₙ p_{n+1}`.
* `TLFamily.jw_spec` (**Wenzl's theorem**): if `[1], …, [n+1]` are non-zero, then `p_{n+1}` is
  an idempotent annihilated on both sides by `e₀, …, e_{n-1}`.
* `TLFamily.wenzl_trace_step`: `eₙ p_{n+1} eₙ = ([n+2]/[n+1]) pₙ eₙ` — the partial-trace
  identity behind "the trace of `p_k` is `[k+1]`".
* `TLFamily.kauffman_braid`, `TLFamily.kauffman_inv`: with `δ = -A² - A⁻²`, the elements
  `gᵢ = A + A⁻¹ eᵢ` are invertible and satisfy the braid relations (the Kauffman bracket
  representation of the braid group).
* `TLFamily.kauffman_absorb`: a crossing on strands of a Jones–Wenzl projector is absorbed as
  the scalar `A`: `gᵢ p_{n+1} = A p_{n+1}` for `i < n`.
* `TLFamily.jw_unique`: the Jones–Wenzl projector is the unique element of the form
  `1 + (non-unital algebra generated by e₀, …, e_{n-1})` killed on the right by them.
* `TLFamily.markov_trace_jw`: for a normalised Markov trace `τ`, `τ(p_{n+1}) = [n+2]/δ^{n+1}`
  (a model satisfying the hypotheses is in `TemperleyLiebQTrace.lean`).
-/

/-- The quantum integers `[k]` as polynomials in the loop value `δ = [2]`
(Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind). -/
/-- A Temperley–Lieb family: `m` generators `e 0, …, e (m-1)` with loop value `δ`. -/

/-- The Jones–Wenzl elements: `jw (n+1)` is the projector on `n+1` strands, built from
`e 0, …, e (n-1)`; `jw 0 = 1` by convention. -/
/-- `jw k` only involves `e 0, …, e (k-2)`, so it commutes with `e j` for `j ≥ k`. -/

/-- The partial-trace step: `eₙ p_{n+1} eₙ = ([n+2]/[n+1]) pₙ eₙ`, given that `pₙ` is
idempotent. -/

/-- **Wenzl's theorem.** If `[1], …, [n+1] ≠ 0` and `n ≤ m`, then `p_{n+1}` is idempotent,
absorbs `pₙ` on both sides, and is killed on both sides by `e 0, …, e (n-1)`. -/

/-- The partial-trace identity `eₙ p_{n+1} eₙ = ([n+2]/[n+1]) pₙ eₙ`, under the hypotheses of
Wenzl's theorem. -/
/-! ### Uniqueness -/
/-- The generators `e 0, …, e (n-1)`. -/

/-- The non-unital subalgebra generated by `e 0, …, e (n-1)`: linear combinations of non-empty
words in these generators. -/

/-- **Uniqueness of the Jones–Wenzl projector.**  An element `x ∈ 1 + ⟨e 0, …, e (n-1)⟩`
annihilated on the right by `e 0, …, e (n-1)` is `p_{n+1}` (annihilation on one side already
forces it; by symmetry the same holds for the left side). -/
/-! ### Markov traces -/

/-- **Markov trace of the Jones–Wenzl projectors.**  If `τ` is a normalised linear functional,
tracial on the algebra generated by the `eᵢ`, with the Markov property `τ(x eₙ) = δ⁻¹ τ(x)` for `x` in the algebra generated by `e 0, …, e (n-1)`,
then `τ(p_{n+1}) = [n+2] / δ^{n+1}` (the unnormalised trace `δ^{n+1} τ` gives `[n+2]`). -/
/-! ### The Kauffman bracket representation of the braid group -/
/-- The Kauffman crossing `gᵢ = a + a⁻¹ eᵢ`. -/
/-- With `δ = -a² - a⁻²` the Kauffman crossing is invertible, with inverse `a⁻¹ + a eᵢ`. -/
/-- **Braid relation** for the Kauffman crossings (with `δ = -a² - a⁻²`). -/
/-- Distant Kauffman crossings commute. -/

/-- **Crossings are absorbed by Jones–Wenzl projectors**: a crossing between two strands of
`p_{n+1}` acts as the scalar `a`. -/

/-!
# The spin-chain model of `TL₃`: Jones–Wenzl projectors as 8 × 8 matrices

A concrete operator realisation of the abstract theory in `TemperleyLieb.lean`, showing that
the hypotheses are satisfiable and the projectors are non-trivial.

For `q ≠ 0` in a field `K`, the `U_q(sl₂)` Temperley–Lieb generator acts on `K² ⊗ K²` by

    E = [[0, 0, 0, 0], [0, q, -1, 0], [0, -1, q⁻¹, 0], [0, 0, 0, 0]],

a rank-one operator with `E² = (q + q⁻¹) E`.  On three spins `(K²)^{⊗3}` put
`e₀ = E ⊗ 1` and `e₁ = 1 ⊗ E`.

* `spinTL`: these form a Temperley–Lieb family with loop value `δ = q + q⁻¹`.
* `spinTL_trace_jw2`, `spinTL_trace_jw3`: for generic `q` (`[2], [3] ≠ 0`) the Jones–Wenzl
  projectors `p₂ ⊗ 1` and `p₃` have trace `6` and `4` — `p₃` projects onto the
  4-dimensional spin-`3/2` subspace, the top irreducible summand of `(K²)^{⊗3}`.
* `spinTL_two_jw3_ne_zero`: at `q = 2` over `ℚ` the hypotheses hold and `p₃ ≠ 0`, so Wenzl's
  theorem is not vacuous.
-/
/-- Three spins. -/
/-- The two-site Temperley–Lieb operator `E` as a function of in/out spins. -/
/-- The generators, indexed by `ℕ` (zero beyond the two generators of `TL₃`). -/
/-- The spin-chain Temperley–Lieb family of `TL₃` (two generators), `δ = q + q⁻¹`. -/
/-- The trace of `p₂ ⊗ 1` on three spins is `6`. -/

/-- **The Jones–Wenzl projector `p₃` on three spins has trace `4`**: it is the projector onto
the spin-`3/2` subspace (for generic `q`, i.e. `[2], [3] ≠ 0`). -/
/-- At `q = 2` over `ℚ`, `p₃` is a non-zero idempotent killed by `e₀` and `e₁`. -/

/-!
# Jones–Wenzl projectors at roots of unity: wiring into the oscillator channel

The oscillator channel (`OscillatorChannel.lean`) evaluates at `q = e^{iπ/r}`, where the
loop value is `δ = [2] = 2 cos(π/r)` and the quantum integers are
`quantumDim r k = sin(kπ/r)/sin(π/r)`.

* `qInt_quantumDim`: the abstract quantum integers `qInt δ k` of `TemperleyLieb.lean` at
  `δ = 2 cos(π/r)` are exactly `quantumDim r k`.
* `jw_spec_root_of_unity`: in any Temperley–Lieb family with loop value `2 cos(π/r)`, the
  Jones–Wenzl projectors `p₁, …, p_{r-1}` exist and satisfy Wenzl's theorem.
* `qInt_root_of_unity_self`: the recursion breaks down at the next step, because `[r] = 0`.
  This is the truncation behind "exactly `r - 1` simple objects" of the oscillator channel.
-/
/-- At `δ = 2 cos(π/r)` the Chebyshev quantum integers are `sin(kπ/r)/sin(π/r)`. -/

/-- **Wenzl's theorem at roots of unity.**  If the loop value is `2 cos(π/r)`, the projector
`p_{n+1}` exists (idempotent, killed by `e 0, …, e (n-1)`) for every `n + 1 < r`. -/

/-- **Truncation**: at loop value `2 cos(π/r)` the quantum integer `[r]` vanishes, so the
Jones–Wenzl recursion cannot produce `p_r`. -/

/-!
# The quantum (Markov) trace on the spin-chain model of `TL₃`

For the spin-chain operators of `TemperleyLiebModel.lean`, the quantum trace
`τ(x) = tr(K^{⊗3} x) / (q + q⁻¹)³`, `K = diag(q, q⁻¹)`, is a normalised Markov trace on the
algebra generated by `e₀, e₁`:

* `adjoin_comm_qK`: that algebra commutes with `K^{⊗3}`, so `τ` is tracial on it
  (`qtr_cyclic`);
* `qtr_markov`: `τ(x eₙ) = δ⁻¹ τ(x)` for `x` generated by `e₀, …, e_{n-1}`;
* `spinTL_qtrace_jw3`: hence, by the general `markov_trace_jw`, the quantum trace of the
  Jones–Wenzl projector `p₃` is the quantum dimension `[4] = δ³ - 2δ` of spin `3/2`.

This shows the hypotheses of `markov_trace_jw` are satisfiable.
-/
/-! ### The quantum (Markov) trace -/
/-- One-site weights `diag(q, q⁻¹)` (the action of the quantum group's `K`). -/
/-- Three-site weights. -/
/-- The diagonal operator `K ⊗ K ⊗ K`. -/
/-- The normalised quantum trace `τ(x) = tr(K^{⊗3} x) / (q + q⁻¹)³`. -/
/-- Everything generated by `e₀, e₁` commutes with `K^{⊗3}`. -/
/-- The algebra generated by `e₀` alone is spanned by `1` and `e₀`. -/
/-- **The quantum trace is a Markov trace on the spin-chain `TL₃`.** -/
-- `x` is a scalar
/-- The quantum trace is tracial on the algebra generated by `e₀, e₁`. -/

/-- **Quantum dimension of spin `3/2`.**  The quantum trace of the Jones–Wenzl projector
`p₃` on three spins is `[4] = δ³ - 2δ` (unnormalised), as predicted by `markov_trace_jw`. -/

comments.text:
/-!
# The three-fold way for the five channels

Dyson's three-fold way sorts complex representations by their antiunitary symmetries.  An
*antilinear structure* on `ℂ^m` is a map `J v = A · v̄` (with `A` a complex matrix); it commutes
with a matrix `M` iff `A · M̄ = M · A`, and `J² = A · Ā`.  A family of matrices `S` is

* of **real** type if some such `J` commutes with all of `S` and `J² = +1`
  (indicator `+1`, division algebra `ℝ`);
* of **quaternionic** type if some such `J` commutes with all of `S` and `J² = −1`
  (indicator `−1`, division algebra `ℍ`);
* of **complex** type if neither exists (indicator `0`, division algebra `ℂ`).

(`HasJ`, `IsType`.)  For irreducible families real and quaternionic exclude each other (Schur);
that general fact is not proved here, but it is proved for the one family where it matters
(`su2_not_real`).

This file replaces a draft that classified the channels by a lookup table.  Every entry of the
table below is now a theorem about the actual matrices the channel computes, and two entries of
the draft turned out to be wrong:

| channel      | family of matrices                                    | type            | theorem                    |
|--------------|-------------------------------------------------------|-----------------|----------------------------|
| `fold`       | permutation matrices of `Word.perm`                   | real            | `fold_isReal`              |
| `link`       | abelian character `t ^ writhe`, `t ∉ ℝ`               | complex         | `writheChar_isComplex`     |
| `anchor`     | reduced Burau matrices at `t ∉ ℝ`, `n ≥ 2`            | complex         | `anchor_isComplex`         |
| `harmonic`   | `burauAt θ`, `sin θ ≠ 0`                              | complex         | `harmonic_isComplex`       |
| `harmonic`   | `burauAt π` (`t = −1`)                                 | real            | `harmonic_pi_isReal`       |
| `oscillator` | its classical limit `SU(2)` on the fundamental strand | quaternionic, not real | `su2_isQuaternionic`, `su2_not_real` |

Corrections to the draft:
* the draft called `harmonic` *real on the universal arc*.  It is unitary there (Squier's form),
  but unitary is not real: away from `t = ±1` the trace of `σ₁` is `n − 2 − t ∉ ℝ`, and any
  invertible commuting antilinear `J` forces every trace to be real (`trace_conj_eq_of_hasJ`).
* the draft typed the oscillator by `r mod 4` (Fibonacci `r = 5` complex, Ising `r = 4`
  quaternionic).  All simple objects of `SU(2)_k` are self-dual, so none is of complex type; the
  standard Frobenius–Schur indicator of the spin-`j` object is `(−1)^{2j}` (cited, not proved).
  What is proved is the classical statement for the fundamental strand: `SU(2)` acting on `ℂ²`
  has a commuting `J` with `J² = −1` and none with `J² = +1`.  The level-indexed replacement of
  the old table is `spinType`.

Further results:
* `SymmetryType.indicator` is a bijection onto `{1, 0, −1}` (`indicator_injective`,
  `range_indicator`).
* `dotProduct_perm`: the permutation representation preserves the symmetric form `Σ vᵢwᵢ`.
* `burauAt_neg`, `neg_mem_resonanceSet`, `two_pi_sub_mem_resonanceSet`: conjugation exchanges
  the harmonic readings at `θ` and `−θ`, so the resonance set is symmetric and half of the sweep
  is redundant (used by the runtime router, `qbx_live/routing.py`).
* `clifford_one_equiv`, `clifford_two_equiv`: the first entries of the Clifford period-8 table
  (`cliffordType`) are derived from Mathlib — `Cl₀,₁ ≅ ℂ`, `Cl₀,₂ ≅ ℍ`; `cliffordType_period`.
* `card_azClasses`, `card_azComplex`, `card_azReal`, `card_azDyson`: the Altland–Zirnbauer
  classes `(T², C², S)` number `10 = 2 + 8`, and the three with no charge conjugation and no
  chiral symmetry are Dyson's three.

Not formalized: Schur exclusivity in general; the Frobenius–Schur indicators of `SU(2)_k`; the
remaining Clifford algebras `Cl₀,ₙ`, `n ≥ 3`; any link between Bott periodicity and the
Cayley–Dickson property-loss ladder.
-/
/-! ## 1. The three types and the indicator -/
/-- Dyson's three symmetry types. -/
/-- The Frobenius–Schur indicator. -/
/-! ## 2. Antilinear structures -/
/-- An antilinear `J v = A · v̄` commuting with every matrix of `S`, with `J² = ε`. -/
/-- The three-fold-way type of a family of matrices. -/

/-- **Traces are real under an invertible antilinear symmetry.**  If `J² = ε ≠ 0` and `J`
commutes with `M`, then `tr M` is real. -/
/-- A family containing a matrix with non-real trace is of complex type. -/
/-- A family of real matrices is of real type (`J` = complex conjugation). -/
/-! ## 3. The fold channel: permutation matrices -/
/-- The permutation representation preserves the symmetric bilinear form `Σ vᵢ wᵢ`. -/
/-- The fold channel's linear representation: `β ↦` the permutation matrix of `perm β`. -/
/-- **The fold channel is of real type.** -/
/-! ## 4. The link channel: abelian characters -/
/-- The one-dimensional character `β ↦ t ^ f(β)` of an integer reading `f`. -/
/-- A character taking a non-real value somewhere is of complex type. -/
/-- A character with real base is of real type. -/
/-- **The writhe character of the link channel is of complex type at non-real `t`.** -/
/-! ## 5. The anchor and harmonic channels: Burau matrices -/
/-- The anchor channel specialised at `t`: the reduced Burau matrices `ρ̄(β)(t)`. -/
/-- The trace of `ρ̄(σ₁)(t)` is `n − 2 − t`. -/
/-- **The anchor channel is of complex type at every non-real `t`** (`n ≥ 2`). -/
/-- The harmonic channel at angle `θ`: the matrices `burauAt θ β`. -/

/-- **The harmonic channel is of complex type off `t = ±1`**, in particular on the whole
universal arc except `θ = 0`. -/
/-- **At `θ = π` (`t = −1`) the harmonic channel is of real type**: the matrices are integral. -/

/-! ### Consequence for scheduling: half of the sweep is redundant

Complex type does not mean the harmonic channel has no antilinear symmetry at all: complex
conjugation does not commute with `burauAt θ`, but it *exchanges* `θ` and `−θ`.  So the
resonance set is symmetric and a sweep over `[0, π]` determines the whole reading. -/
/-- Complex conjugation exchanges the harmonic readings at `θ` and `−θ`. -/
/-- **The resonance set is symmetric under `θ ↦ −θ`.** -/

/-- **Sweep folding.**  On the grid `θ_k = 2πk/N` the samples `k` and `N − k` agree, so only
`k ≤ N/2` has to be computed. -/
/-! ## 6. The oscillator's fundamental strand: `SU(2)` is quaternionic -/
/-- `ε = [[0, −1], [1, 0]]`, the matrix of the quaternionic structure on `ℂ²`. -/
/-- The fundamental representation of `SU(2)`. -/

/-- **`SU(2)` has a quaternionic structure**: `J v = ε v̄` commutes with every `U ∈ SU(2)` and
`J² = −1`. -/

/-- **`SU(2)` has no real structure**: no antilinear `J` commuting with `SU(2)` has `J² = +1`.
So the fundamental strand is quaternionic and not real. -/

/-- The level-indexed replacement of the draft's `r mod 4` table: the spin-`j` object
(`twoJ = 2j`) of `SU(2)_k` is real for integer `j` and quaternionic for half-integer `j`.  This is
a table recording the standard Frobenius–Schur indicator `(−1)^{2j}`; the case `twoJ = 1` is
`su2_isQuaternionic` + `su2_not_real` in the classical limit. -/
/-! ## 7. The channel classification -/
/-- **The five channels exhibit all three types.** -/
/-! ## 8. Clifford algebras: the period-8 table and its first entries -/

/-- The type of the real Clifford algebra `Cl₀,ₙ` (generators squaring to `−1`):
`ℝ, ℂ, ℍ, ℍ⊕ℍ, M₂(ℍ), M₄(ℂ), M₈(ℝ), M₈(ℝ)⊕M₈(ℝ)`, then period 8.  A table; entries `1` and `2`
are derived below. -/
/-- `Cl₀,₁ ≅ ℂ`: one generator with `e² = −1`. -/
/-- `Cl₀,₂ ≅ ℍ`: two anticommuting generators with `e₁² = e₂² = −1`. -/
/-! ## 9. The tenfold way: `10 = 2 + 8` -/

/-- Admissible Altland–Zirnbauer data `(T², C², S)`: `T², C² ∈ {0, ±1}`, chiral `S ∈ {0, 1}`;
`S` is forced (`S = 1` iff both `T` and `C` are present) unless `T = C = 0`. -/
/-- **There are ten Altland–Zirnbauer classes.** -/
/-- The two complex classes (`T = C = 0`, Bott period 2). -/
/-- The eight real classes (Bott period 8). -/
/-- Dyson's three classes are those without charge conjugation or chiral symmetry. -/

/-!
# Torus anchor: the determinant and trace of the Burau monodromy

Channel 3 of the five-channel machine (`QBX/docs/design/MULTIPROVER.md`).  The reduced Burau
matrix `ρ̄(β)(t)` is the monodromy of the braid acting on the punctured disk (homology of the
infinite cyclic cover).  Its two basic characters are its determinant and its trace.

* `det_burauGen`, `det_burau`: for every strand count, `det ρ̄(σᵢ) = -t`,
  `det ρ̄(σᵢ⁻¹) = -t⁻¹`, so `det ρ̄(β) = (-1)^{length} · t^{writhe}` (`det_burau_field`).
  The determinant only sees length parity and writhe: it is the *trivial anchor*.
* `det_burau_circle`: on the unit circle `t = e^{iθ}`,
  `det ρ̄(β)(e^{iθ}) = (-1)^{length} e^{i·writhe·θ}`: the determinant loop has modulus 1 and
  winds `writhe` times around the origin.
* `trace_burau_conj`, `det_burau_conj`: trace and determinant are conjugacy invariants.
-/
/-- The generator matrix is a rank-one perturbation of the identity. -/
/-- `det ρ̄(σᵢ^{±1}) = -t^{±1}`, for every strand count. -/
/-- The determinant of the Burau matrix of a word is the product of the letter determinants. -/
/-- Over a field, `det ρ̄(β)(t) = (-1)^{length} · t^{writhe}`. -/

/-- On the unit circle the determinant loop is `θ ↦ (-1)^{length} e^{i·writhe·θ}`: it has
modulus one and winding number `writhe`. -/
/-- The determinant loop has modulus one on the unit circle. -/
/-- The trace of the Burau matrix is a conjugacy invariant. -/
/-- The determinant of the Burau matrix is a conjugacy invariant. -/

/-!
# The five-channel resonance machine (index)

See `QBX/docs/design/MULTIPROVER.md` for the design and `QBX.Formal.MultiProver.Machine` for
the aggregate theorems; `QBX.Formal.MultiProver.Scheduler` is the certified chunk scheduler
(map–reduce over any reduction schedule, proved equal to whole-word evaluation),
`QBX.Formal.MultiProver.KellyScheduler` allocates tick budgets to the channels by their Kelly
fractions (graduated prover: Kelly-allocated refuters, then the complete fold channel), and
`QBX.Formal.MultiProver.ThreeFoldWay` proves the three-fold-way type (real / complex /
quaternionic) of each channel's matrices.  `QBX.Formal.MultiProver.NodeNetwork` covers the node
network: greedy lookup on the address graph, distributed scheduling, and detection of a single
equivocating node; `QBX.Formal.MultiProver.ChannelGeometry` answers the Fano-line and ten-point
questions (Steiner triple systems, the Desargues configuration, identity lines among the channels);
`QBX.Formal.MultiProver.IdentityLines` shows `{link, harmonic, oscillator}` is not an identity line,
classifies the identity lines on three strands and computes their dual hypergraph.
`QBX.Formal.MultiProver.CliffordChannel` proves the Clifford braiding theorem and builds the

machine as a sixth channel and relates it to the fold, anchor and oscillator channels.
-/

/-!
# Phase 1: soundness of the naturality-square checker

The Phase 1 natural-transformation checker (`qbx.categorical.natural_transformation`,
migration `004_natural_transformations.sql`) verifies the naturality square

```
F(X) --F(f)--> F(Y)
 |              |
η_X            η_Y
 v              v
G(X) --G(f)--> G(Y)
```

i.e. `F(f) ≫ η_Y = η_X ≫ G(f)`, for a *finite* list of morphisms `f`.  This file justifies the
two shortcuts the checker takes and documents a defect of the original database trigger.

## Checking generators suffices

* `naturalitySquare F G η` — the morphisms whose square commutes — is closed under identities
  and composition (`naturalitySquare.isMultiplicative`).
* `naturality_of_generators`: if every morphism is a composite of morphisms in `S` (that is,
  `S.multiplicativeClosure = ⊤`) and the square commutes for each morphism in `S`, then it
  commutes for every morphism; `natTransOfGenerators` packages this as a natural
  transformation.
* `naturality_of_edges`: for a free category `Paths V` on a quiver, checking one square per
  edge of the quiver suffices.

## Incremental checking while components are registered

Components `η_X` are registered one object at a time, in the order of a list `l`.
`checkedAt prev x f` says that registering `η_x` after the objects `prev` evaluates the square of
`f`: one endpoint of `f` is `x` and the other one is `x` or already registered.

* `checkedBy_of_mem` (completeness): once every endpoint of `f` has been registered, the square
  of `f` has been evaluated at some step.  Hence if every evaluated square commuted, `η` is
  natural (`naturality_of_incremental`).
* `triggerCheckedBy_iff`: the trigger of the original migration 004 only walked morphisms
  *out of* the new object and skipped *every* endomorphism.  For a registration order without
  repetitions, it evaluates the square of `f` exactly when `f` is not an endomorphism and the
  target of `f` was registered strictly before its source.  In particular it never evaluates
  the square of `f : X ⟶ Y` when `η_X` is registered first (`trigger_misses_forward`).
-/
/-- The morphisms `f : X ⟶ Y` whose naturality square `F(f) ≫ η_Y = η_X ≫ G(f)` commutes. -/
/-- Commuting naturality squares are closed under identities and composition. -/

/-- **Generator sufficiency.**  If every morphism of `C` is a composite of morphisms in `S`, it
suffices to check the naturality square on the morphisms in `S`. -/

/-- The natural transformation obtained from a family of components whose squares commute on a
generating set of morphisms. -/

/-- **Free categories.**  For functors out of the path category of a quiver, checking the
naturality square on each edge suffices. -/

/-- Registering the component at `x`, after the objects `prev`, evaluates the square of `f`:
one endpoint of `f` is `x` and the other endpoint is `x` or was registered earlier. -/
/-- The square of `f` is evaluated at some step of the registration order `l`. -/

/-- **Completeness of the incremental checker.**  Once both endpoints of `f` are registered,
the square of `f` has been evaluated. -/
-- the target is registered last (or both at once)
-- the source is registered last

/-- **Soundness of incremental enforcement.**  If every square evaluated during registration
commuted, then every square between registered objects commutes. -/

/-- The original migration-004 trigger: registering `η_x` walks the morphisms *out of* `x`,
skips every endomorphism, and evaluates the square when `η` of the target already exists. -/
/-- The square of `f` is evaluated by the original trigger at some step of `l`. -/

/-- **What the original trigger checks.**  For a registration order without repetitions, the
trigger evaluates the square of `f` exactly when `f` is not an endomorphism and its target was
registered strictly before its source. -/

/-- **The original trigger is incomplete.**  If `η_X` is registered before `η_Y`, the square of
a morphism `f : X ⟶ Y` is never evaluated by the trigger, although both components exist. -/
/-- **The original trigger skips non-identity endomorphisms.** -/

/-!
# Candidate obstacle C3 · Scaling (homogeneity) mismatch

**Pattern.** An inequality `B(u) ≤ A(u)` is claimed "for every `u`" between quantities of different
homogeneity under the natural scaling of the problem (amplitude `u ↦ s u`, or dilation
`u ↦ λ u(λ ·)`).  Checked at one scale, it looks plausible; but the two sides scale differently,
so the inequality fails at another scale, or it holds only when the smaller-degree side is `≤ 0`.
Related slip: a norm is assigned the wrong scaling (a sup-norm picks up no Jacobian).

**Definition.** `HomogeneousOfDegree d f`: `f (s • u) = s ^ d * f u` for all `s > 0`.

**Counterexample.** `A(u) = u³`, `B(u) = u²/2` on `ℚ`: `B ≤ A` at `u = 1` but not at `u = 1/4`
(`not_scale_free`).

**Repaired statement.** If `A` has degree `a`, `B` degree `b < a`, and `B ≤ A` everywhere, then
`B ≤ 0` everywhere (`le_zero_of_dominated_by_higher_degree`): a positive lower-degree quantity can
never be dominated by a higher-degree one at all scales.

**Worked examples in this repository** (Navier–Stokes paper, `JLN/NavierStokesFluxAudit.lean`):
* Theorem 6.2 bounds a cubic transfer below by a quadratic energy times a scale-invariant bias;
  this forces `H E ≤ 0` for every field (`flux_coercivity_forces_nonpos`).
* Corollary 7.7 scales `‖∇v₀‖_∞` by `λ⁻¹`; the sup-norm of `λ² g(λ ·)` is `λ² ‖g‖_∞`
  (`sup_norm_dilate`).
-/

/-- **Counterexample**: `u²/2 ≤ u³` holds at `u = 1` and fails at `u = 1/4`. -/

/-- **Repaired statement**: if `B` (degree `b`) is dominated by `A` (degree `a > b`) at every
point, then `B ≤ 0` at every point. -/

/-- **Worked example** (Navier–Stokes Cor. 7.7). -/

/-!
# Obstacle O1 · The construction used is not the one the conclusion needs

**Pattern.** A property is established for one construction and then used for another that "looks
the same" (a ring product for a tensor product, `⊕` for `⊗`, a braid for its closure, `G × H` for
`G ⋊ H`).  The inference is sound exactly when the property only depends on an invariant that
the two constructions share.

**Definition.** `Transfers inv x y`: the substitution of `y` for `x` is safe for every conclusion
that is a function of the invariant `inv`.

**Counterexample.** Dimension does not transfer from `V × W` to `V ⊗ W`: for `V = W = ℚ³` the
dimensions are `6` and `9` (`not_transfers_prod_tensor`).

**Repaired statement.** For finite-dimensional `V, W` of dimensions `a, b`, the two dimensions
agree iff `(a, b) = (0, 0)` or `(2, 2)` (`finrank_prod_eq_finrank_tensor_iff`); so "`⊕` can stand
in for `⊗`" is true only in those two cases.

**Worked example in this repository.** The strand crossing matrix is an invariant of the braid,
not of its closure (`braid_not_closure`, from `StrandMatrixMarkov.lean`).
-/

/-- **The obstacle, as a definition.** Replacing `x` by `y` is safe for conclusions read off the
invariant `inv` iff `inv x = inv y`. -/
/-- A conclusion that depends only on the invariant does transfer. -/
/-- `finrank (V × W) = finrank V + finrank W` and `finrank (V ⊗ W) = finrank V * finrank W`. -/
/-- **Counterexample**: for `V = W = ℚ³`, `dim (V × W) = 6 ≠ 9 = dim (V ⊗ W)`. -/
/-- The arithmetic behind the repair: `a + b = a b` iff `a = b = 0` or `a = b = 2`. -/

/-- **Repaired statement**: `V × W` and `V ⊗ W` have the same dimension iff
`(dim V, dim W)` is `(0, 0)` or `(2, 2)`. -/

/-- **Worked example**: one Markov conjugation move changes the strand crossing matrix, so it is a
braid invariant that does not transfer to the closed link. -/

comments.text:
/-!
# Obstacle O2 · The Lean file certifies a restatement of the hypothesis

**Pattern.** A theorem `H → C` is presented as a proof of `C`, but either `H` *is* `C` in other
words (a restatement), or `H` can never hold (vacuity).  In both cases the formal proof is correct
and certifies nothing about `C`.

**Definitions.** `IsRestatement H C` (`H ↔ C`) and `Vacuous H` (`∀ x, ¬ H x`).

**Counterexample.** A vacuous hypothesis proves every conclusion, including false ones
(`vacuous_proves_false`); a restated hypothesis leaves `C` exactly as open as before
(`restatement_not_evidence`: there are `H ↔ C` with `C` false).

**Repaired statements.** State the equivalence as the theorem (`restatement_is_the_theorem`), and
add the witness that makes a conditional result non-vacuous (`nonvacuous_conclusion`).

**Worked examples in this repository.**
* `Λ⁺⁺ ≥ ε > 0`: a uniform lower bound holds **iff** the coupling is bounded away from zero
  (`lambdaPlusPlus_restatement`), and it fails for the running coupling
  (`lambdaPlusPlus_fails_running`).
* Λ-irreducibility is vacuous for round-trip-sound translation pairs (`lambda_vacuous`).
-/
/-- **The obstacle (restatement).** The hypothesis is the conclusion in other words. -/
/-- **The obstacle (vacuity).** No instance satisfies the hypothesis. -/
/-- A vacuous hypothesis proves any conclusion. -/

/-- **Counterexample (vacuity)**: a correct proof of `∀ x, H x → False` exists for the vacuous
`H = fun _ => False`, so such a theorem is no evidence for its conclusion. -/

/-- **Counterexample (restatement)**: `H → C` is provable whenever `H ↔ C`, also when `C` is
false; so the implication carries no information about `C`. -/

/-- **Repaired statement (restatement)**: the honest theorem is the equivalence itself; then `C`
follows exactly when `H` is established independently. -/

/-- **Repaired statement (vacuity)**: a conditional result together with one witness of its
hypothesis gives an instance of the conclusion. -/

/-- **Worked example**: a uniform positive lower bound on `Λ⁺⁺` (one-plaquette model) is a
restatement of "the coupling is bounded away from zero". -/
/-- **Worked example**: with the one-loop running coupling there is no uniform bound. -/

/-- **Worked example**: for a round-trip-sound translation pair no sentence is Λ-irreducible,
so a theorem with Λ-irreducibility as hypothesis is vacuous there. -/

/-!
# Obstacle O3 · An axiom that says more than the cited theorem

**Pattern.** A published theorem about *structure-preserving maps* (homomorphisms, continuous
maps, natural transformations) is encoded as an axiom quantifying over *all functions*.  The axiom
is then strictly stronger than the theorem, and typically false.

**Definitions.** `HomSchema G`: every homomorphism `G →* ℤ` (written multiplicatively) is trivial
— the shape of "finite abelianisation".  `FunctionSchema G`: every *function* `G → ℤ` is
constant.

**Counterexample.** For the two-element group the hom schema holds and the function schema fails
(`homSchema_not_functionSchema`); the function schema fails for every non-trivial group
(`not_functionSchema`).

**Repaired statement.** The hom schema holds for every finite group (`homSchema_of_finite`), and
the function schema implies it (`homSchema_of_functionSchema`) but not conversely.

**Worked example in this repository.** The function-valued "Kazhdan" axiom schema denies property
(T) to `SL(3, ℤ)` (`kazhdan_function_schema_overstates`, from `JLN/ConnesAudit.lean`).
-/
/-- **The cited theorem's shape**: every homomorphism to `ℤ` is trivial. -/
/-- **The axiom's shape**: every function to `ℤ` is constant. -/
/-- The function schema is stronger. -/
/-- **Counterexample**: the function schema fails in every non-trivial group. -/
/-- **Repaired statement**: the hom schema holds for every finite group. -/
/-- **Counterexample, concretely**: in `ℤ/2` the hom schema holds and the function schema fails. -/

/-- **Worked example**: the function-valued Kazhdan axiom schema is false on `SL(3, ℤ)`, which has
property (T). -/

comments.text:
/-!
# Obstacle O4 · "Local ⇒ detected" without a gauge condition

**Pattern.** A claim that every local change of a connection is detected (by a syndrome, a
holonomy, an energy), made without quotienting by gauge transformations.  Gauge transformations
are local changes that no gauge-invariant observable can see.

**Setting.** A `ℤ`-valued connection on the cycle with `n` vertices: `A i` sits on the edge
`i → i + 1`.  The observable is the holonomy `hol A = ∑ i, A i`; a gauge transformation `g` changes
`A i` to `A i + g (i + 1) - g i`.

**Definition.** `DetectsAllChanges n`: any two different connections have different holonomy.

**Counterexample.** On the cycle with `n ≥ 2` vertices a gauge transformation at a single vertex
changes the connection and not the holonomy (`not_detectsAllChanges`).

**Repaired statement.** Holonomy is gauge invariant (`hol_gauge`), and a change `δ` is invisible to
the holonomy iff it is a gauge transformation (`hol_add_eq_iff_coboundary`): exactly the gauge
orbit is undetected.

**Worked example in this repository.** The microtubule QEC "Theorem 1" (`JLN/MicrotubuleAudit.lean`):
holonomy around closed loops is gauge invariant (`microtubule_gauge_invariance`).
-/
/-- A `ℤ`-valued connection on the `n`-cycle: `A i` sits on the edge `i → i + 1`. -/
/-- The holonomy around the cycle. -/
/-- The gauge transformation by vertex potentials `g`. -/
/-- **The claim as made**: every change of the connection changes the holonomy. -/
/-- **Repaired statement, part 1**: the holonomy is gauge invariant. -/

/-- **Counterexample**: on the cycle with at least two vertices, the gauge transformation at the
vertex `1` is a local change that the holonomy does not see. -/
/-- A change `δ` is a gauge transformation of `A` iff `A + δ = gauge g A` for some `g`. -/

/-- **Repaired statement, part 2**: a change `δ` leaves the holonomy unchanged iff it is a gauge
transformation. -/
-- the potential: partial sums of `δ`

/-- **Worked example**: in the microtubule audit, holonomy around a closed walk commutes with
gauge transformations. -/

/-!
# Obstacle O5 · Finite (or positive) per step ≠ finite (or positive) overall

**Pattern.** A bound that holds at every step (every scale, every coupling round) is used as if it
held uniformly over all steps.  Infinitely many steps can drive a pointwise-positive quantity to
`0`, or a pointwise-bounded increment to infinity.

**Definitions.** `PositiveAtEachStep f` (`∀ n, 0 < f n`) and `UniformlyPositive f`
(`∃ ε > 0, ∀ n, ε ≤ f n`); `StepBounded a c` (`∀ n, a (n + 1) ≤ a n + c`) and `Bounded a`.

**Counterexamples.** `f n = 1 / (n + 1)` is positive at each step and not uniformly positive
(`not_uniform_inv_succ`); `a n = n` grows by `1` per step and is unbounded (`not_bounded_id`).

**Repaired statements.** Over finitely many steps, positive at each step is uniform
(`uniformlyPositive_of_finite`); a positive sequence with a positive limit is uniformly positive
(`uniformlyPositive_of_tendsto`); a step bound gives the linear bound `a n ≤ a 0 + c n`
(`le_of_stepBounded`), not a uniform one.

**Worked examples in this repository.** `Λ⁺⁺(a) > 0` at every lattice spacing but `→ 0` with the
running coupling (`lambdaPlusPlus_pointwise_not_uniform`); Clebsch–Gordan selection rules bound
each coupling step, yet the cascade reaches arbitrarily large spin (`cg_cascade_unbounded`).
-/
/-- Positive at every step. -/
/-- **What the conclusion needs**: a single positive lower bound for all steps. -/
/-- **Counterexample**: `1 / (n + 1)` is positive at every step but not uniformly positive. -/

/-- **Repaired statement (finitely many steps)**: positive at each of finitely many steps is
uniformly positive. -/

/-- **Repaired statement (positive limit)**: positive at every step and convergent to a positive
limit implies uniformly positive. -/
/-- Increments bounded by `c` at each step. -/
/-- **What the conclusion needs**: one bound for all steps. -/
/-- **Counterexample**: `a n = n` grows by `1` per step and is unbounded. -/
/-- **Repaired statement**: a step bound gives only the linear bound `a n ≤ a 0 + c n`. -/

/-- **Worked example**: with the one-loop running coupling, `Λ⁺⁺` has no uniform positive lower
bound, although it is positive at each lattice spacing. -/
/-- **Worked example**: iterated Clebsch–Gordan coupling reaches arbitrarily large spins. -/

/-!
# Obstacle O6 · Operator / spectrum mismatches

**Pattern.** The eigenvalues of one operator are used for another: those of `D` where `D²` is
meant (mass for mass²), of `⋆d` for the scalar Laplacian, of an operator on one space for its
restriction to another.  The spectra are related but not equal.

**Definition.** `IsEigenvalue A μ`: some non-zero `v` has `A v = μ v`.

**Counterexample.** For `A = diag(1, 2)`, `2` is an eigenvalue of `A` but not of `A²`
(`eigenvalue_not_of_sq`).

**Repaired statement.** Eigenvalues map by the polynomial: `μ` eigenvalue of `A` gives `μ ^ k`
eigenvalue of `A ^ k` (`isEigenvalue_pow`); for `D²` the right numbers are the squares.

**Worked example in this repository.** On `S³`, `k (k + 2)` (a scalar Laplacian eigenvalue) is
never a perfect square, so it is not the square of a `⋆d` eigenvalue
(`laplacian_eigenvalue_not_square`, from `JLN/HopfSpectralAudit.lean`).
-/
/-- `μ` is an eigenvalue of the square matrix `A`. -/

/-- **Repaired statement**: an eigenvector of `A` for `μ` is an eigenvector of `A ^ k` for
`μ ^ k`. -/
/-- The example operator `diag(1, 2)`. -/
/-- **Counterexample**: `2` is an eigenvalue of `diag(1, 2)` but not of its square. -/
/-- **Worked example**: `k (k + 2)` is never a perfect square (`k ≥ 1`). -/

/-!
# Obstacle O7 · Small arithmetic slips that propagate into tables

**Pattern.** A count is computed once by hand, slightly wrong, and then reused (in a table, a
ratio, a "coincidence").  The cure is to derive the count from a formula proved for every
parameter, and to check the table entries against it.

**Setting.** The `n`-orthoplex (cross-polytope): vertices `±eᵢ`, labelled `(i, s)`; two vertices
are adjacent iff they are not equal and not antipodal, i.e. iff `i ≠ j`.

**Definition.** `degree n v`: the number of neighbours of `v`.

**Counterexample.** A table entry "7 edges per vertex of the 8-orthoplex" is wrong: the degree
is `14` (`orthoplex_eight_degree`); the triangle count per vertex is `84`, not `28`
(`orthoplex_eight_triangles`).

**Repaired statement.** The degree of every vertex of the `n`-orthoplex is `2 (n - 1)`
(`degree_eq`), for every `n`.

**Worked example in this repository.** The forensics audit of the 8-orthoplex counts
(`QBX.Forensics.Inert.KabbalahSecretsE8Audit.orthoplex8_vertex_degree`,
`orthoplex8_triangles_per_vertex`; inert forensics, not imported here).  The Furey trace ratios
(`QBX.Formal.JLN.Furey.equal_trace_ratios_842`) are another instance.
-/
/-- Vertices of the `n`-orthoplex: `(i, s)` is `±eᵢ`. -/
/-- Adjacency in the `n`-orthoplex: different axes. -/
/-- The degree of a vertex. -/
/-- **Repaired statement**: every vertex of the `n`-orthoplex has degree `2 (n - 1)`. -/
/-- **Counterexample**: the 8-orthoplex has degree `14`, not `7`. -/
/-- Triangles through a vertex: unordered pairs of adjacent neighbours. -/
/-- **Counterexample**: `84` triangles through each vertex of the 8-orthoplex, not `28`. -/

/-!
# The obstacle library O1–O7

The recurring failure modes of the audited corpus (`QBX/docs/design/JLN_REVIEW.md` §1,
`QBX/docs/design/OBSTACLE_LIBRARY.md`), one file per obstacle.  Each file has the same three
parts:

1. **a definition** of the pattern (the property the faulty argument uses, next to the one the
   conclusion needs);
2. **a counterexample**, checked in Lean, showing that the faulty inference fails;
3. **a repaired statement**: the correct version, proved in general,

followed by aliases of the worked examples elsewhere in the repository (mostly the JLN audits),
so that each link is checked by the compiler.

| File | Obstacle | Definition | Counterexample | Repaired statement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `O1WrongConstruction` | the construction used is not the one needed | `Transfers` | `not_transfers_prod_tensor` (`dim (ℚ³ × ℚ³) = 6 ≠ 9`) | `finrank_prod_eq_finrank_tensor_iff` |
| `O2RestatedHypothesis` | the file certifies its own hypothesis | `IsRestatement`, `Vacuous` | `restatement_not_evidence`, `vacuous_proves_false` | `restatement_is_the_theorem`, `nonvacuous_conclusion` |
| `O3Overstatement` | an axiom says more than the cited theorem | `HomSchema`, `FunctionSchema` | `homSchema_not_functionSchema` | `homSchema_of_finite` |
| `O4LocalGauge` | "local ⇒ detected" without gauge | `DetectsAllChanges` | `not_detectsAllChanges` | `hol_gauge`, `hol_add_eq_iff_coboundary` |
| `O5PerStepOverall` | per step ≠ overall | `UniformlyPositive`, `Bounded` | `not_uniform_inv_succ`, `not_bounded_id` | `uniformlyPositive_of_finite`, `uniformlyPositive_of_tendsto`, `le_of_stepBounded` |
| `O6SpectrumMismatch` | eigenvalues of the wrong operator | `IsEigenvalue` | `eigenvalue_not_of_sq` | `isEigenvalue_pow` |
| `O7ArithmeticSlip` | a hand count propagates into tables | `degree` | `orthoplex_eight_degree`, `orthoplex_eight_triangles` | `degree_eq` |
| `C3ScalingMismatch` (candidate) | sides of an inequality scale differently | `HomogeneousOfDegree` | `not_scale_free` | `le_zero_of_dominated_by_higher_degree` |
-/

/-!
# Perspectives, witnesses, lost pasts and forced patterns

First Lean layer of the cross-domain plan (`docs/CROSS_DOMAIN_INVARIANTS_PLAN_2026-10-14.md`).
Each section turns one of the plan's questions into a statement that can actually be proved, and
says exactly how far that statement reaches.

**A. Recovering a text from its witnesses** (textual criticism as error correction).
* `majority_unique`: if at a position fewer than half of the `k` witnesses are corrupted, the
  original reading is the *only* reading held by a strict majority.
* `majority_reconstruct`: so the per-position strict-majority reading returns the original text
  exactly, with no choices involved.
* `ambiguous_of_half`: the threshold is sharp.  Once half of the witnesses may be corrupted, two
  different originals fit the same witnesses, so no procedure can tell them apart.

**B. "Different perspectives of the same thing"**.
* `common_source_exists`: every family of accounts is consistent with one common source.  So
  "these are all perspectives of one thing" can never be refuted by the accounts alone.
* `card_le_of_explains_all`: the claim has content only when the source is small: a source space
  that explains every possible combination of accounts has at least as many states as there are
  combinations.

**C. Pasts that can and cannot be recovered**.
* `past_recoverable_iff_injective`: an evolution can be undone by some reconstruction exactly when
  it never sends two pasts to the same present.
* `loss_is_permanent`: once two pasts have merged, no later process separates them again.
* `group_past_recoverable`: when evolution acts by a group (e.g. braid words), the past is always
  `w⁻¹ • present`.

**D. Patterns forced by arithmetic** (shared shapes are not evidence of contact).
* `schlafli_spherical_iff`: the regular polyhedra `{p, q}` are exactly the five Platonic ones.
* `schlafli_flat_iff`: the regular plane tilings are exactly `{3,6}`, `{4,4}`, `{6,3}`.
* `platonic_euler`: each of the five satisfies `V − E + F = 2`.
* `crystallographic_restriction`: a rotational symmetry of order `n` of a plane lattice pattern
  (equivalently, a primitive `n`-th root of unity satisfying a monic integer quadratic) needs
  `n ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}`.

**E. What an observer on the base of a fibration can know**.
* `observable_blind_to_fibre`: anything computed from the image `hopf q ∈ S²` is the same at every
  point of the fibre circle over it.
* `observable_determines_fibre`: and that is the only loss: two points of `S³` with the same image
  lie on the same fibre circle.

Nothing here is a statement about real texts, peoples or history.  The theorems say what any
reconstruction method can and cannot do once the data is encoded; the encoding itself is the
plan's empirical part.
-/
/-! ## A. Recovering a text from its witnesses -/
/-- Number of the `k` witnesses that read `a`. -/
/-- Number of witnesses that do **not** read `a` (the corrupted ones, if `a` is the original). -/
/-- `a` is held by a strict majority of the witnesses. -/

/-- **Unique majority.** If fewer than half of the witnesses are corrupted relative to `a`, then
`a` is the only reading held by a strict majority. -/

/-- **Exact reconstruction.** Witnesses `w j : Fin n → α` of a text `x : Fin n → α`.  If at every
position fewer than half of the witnesses are corrupted, then any rule that picks, at each
position, a reading held by a strict majority returns `x` exactly. -/
/-- … and such a rule exists: the original itself is a strict majority at every position. -/

/-- **The threshold is sharp.** If up to `t` of `k` witnesses may be corrupted with `k ≤ 2 t`,
then for any two different readings `a ≠ b` there are witnesses consistent with both `a` and `b`
as the original.  No method, however clever, can then decide between them. -/
-- corrupted relative to `a`: the witnesses with index `≥ k / 2` that read `b ≠ a`
/-! ## B. "Different perspectives of the same thing" -/

/-- **A common source always exists.** Whatever the accounts `x i ∈ X i` are, one source (the
tuple of all of them) projects onto every one.  So agreement with a common source is no evidence
by itself. -/

/-- **When a common-source claim has content.** If a source space `S`, read through the
perspectives `π i : S → X i`, can explain every combination of accounts, then `S` has at least as
many states as there are combinations.  A small source that explains many independent accounts is
impossible; a common-source hypothesis is testable only through such size limits. -/
/-! ## C. Pasts that can and cannot be recovered -/

/-- **Recoverable past.** An evolution `f : P → Q` (with `P` inhabited) can be undone by some
reconstruction `g` exactly when `f` never merges two pasts. -/

/-- **Loss is permanent.** If `f` has merged two pasts, then so has every later process `g ∘ f`:
no subsequent evolution separates them again. -/

/-- **Group evolution loses nothing.** When the step from past to present is the action of a group
element `w` (a braid word acting on strand positions, a rotation, a cipher key), the past is
`w⁻¹ • present`. -/
/-! ## D. Patterns forced by arithmetic -/

/-- `{p, q}`: `q` regular `p`-gons around each vertex close up into a sphere exactly when
`1/p + 1/q > 1/2`, i.e. `(p - 2)(q - 2) < 4`. -/
/-- … and tile the flat plane exactly when `(p - 2)(q - 2) = 4`. -/

/-- **Only five regular polyhedra.** For `p, q ≥ 3`, `{p, q}` closes into a sphere exactly for
the tetrahedron `{3,3}`, octahedron `{3,4}`, cube `{4,3}`, icosahedron `{3,5}` and dodecahedron
`{5,3}`. -/

/-- **Only three regular tilings of the plane**: triangles `{3,6}`, squares `{4,4}`,
hexagons `{6,3}`. -/

/-- Vertex, edge and face counts `(V, E, F)` of the regular polyhedron `{p, q}`:
`E = 2pq / (4 − (p−2)(q−2))`, `V = 2E / q`, `F = 2E / p`. -/

/-- **Euler's formula for the five.** Each Platonic solid has `V − E + F = 2`, with `p F = 2 E =
q V`; the counts are tetrahedron `(4, 6, 4)`, octahedron `(6, 12, 8)`, cube `(8, 12, 6)`,
icosahedron `(12, 30, 20)`, dodecahedron `(20, 30, 12)`. -/

/-- Arithmetic core of the crystallographic restriction: `φ(n) ≤ 2` exactly for
`n ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}` (for `n ≥ 1`). -/
-- a unit `x` of `ℤ/n` other than `1` and `n - 1`

/-- **Crystallographic restriction.** If a primitive `n`-th root of unity `ζ ∈ ℂ` is a root of a
monic integer polynomial of degree at most `2` — which is what it means for a rotation of order `n`
to map a plane lattice to itself (its matrix has integer characteristic polynomial
`X² − tX + 1`) — then `n ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}`.  So 5-, 7-, 8-, … fold symmetry cannot occur in any
periodic tiling, mosaic or crystal, in any culture. -/
/-! ## E. What an observer on the base of a fibration can know -/

/-- **Blind to the fibre.** Any observable `O` computed from the base point `hopf q ∈ S²` takes the
same value at every point `q · (a + b i)` (`a² + b² = 1`) of the fibre circle through `q`. -/

/-- **… and blind to nothing else.** Two points of the same norm with the same base point differ
by a fibre phase: the base sees exactly the fibre circles. -/

/-!
# Theorem provers and the braid: what the exchange rule sees

Every sequent-style logic has to say what may be done with the order of hypotheses.  There are
three classical answers, and they correspond to three groups acting on `n` hypotheses:

* **no exchange** (ordered logics, the Lambek calculus of `LambekDirection.lean`): only the
  trivial rearrangement; order is meaning;
* **braided exchange** (braided monoidal categories, the logic of anyons): the braid group `Bₙ`;
  swapping two hypotheses has a handedness, and swapping twice is not the identity;
* **symmetric exchange** (intuitionistic, classical and linear logic, and the type theories of all
  mainstream proof assistants): the symmetric group `Sₙ`.

This file makes the comparison precise for QBX's braid group.

* `exchange` — hypotheses rearranged by a braid, through its permutation; this is a left action
  of `Bₙ` on contexts (`exchange_mul`, `exchange_one`).
* `exchange_eq_iff` — two braids act identically on contexts iff they have the same permutation:
  a logic with symmetric exchange sees exactly `permHom` and nothing more.
* `exchange_sigma_sq`, `sigma_sq_ne_one` — a double swap `σᵢ²` is invisible to symmetric exchange
  but is not the trivial braid: braided exchange is strictly finer.
* `permHom_fibre_infinite` — for `n ≥ 2` every permutation is the image of infinitely many braids,
  so every symmetric exchange step hides infinitely many braided ones; `fibre_linkMatrix` shows the
  hidden information includes the whole labelled linking matrix.
* `provers` — a register of 16 provers and their logics; `provers_symmetric_count` and
  `only_grail_ordered`: 15 of them have symmetric exchange, the categorial-grammar prover Grail has
  none.  **Consequence for QBX:** in Lean, Rocq, Agda, Isabelle, HOL, Mizar, Metamath, … a braid
  can only be represented as *data* (an element of a group defined inside the logic, as this
  development does), never through the structural rules of the logic itself; and a translation
  between two such provers only has to preserve that data.

The register entries (foundations, classical or not) are standard descriptions entered by hand;
Lean checks the statements made about the table.
-/
/-! ### Exchange through the permutation -/

/-- Rearranging a context of `n` hypotheses by a braid, as a logic with symmetric exchange does:
the hypothesis in position `p` afterwards is the one in position `(perm g)⁻¹ p` before. -/
/-- `σᵢ` swaps the hypotheses in positions `i` and `i + 1`. -/
/-- A double swap is invisible to symmetric exchange. -/
/-- …but it is not the trivial braid (its writhe is `2`). -/
/-- Symmetric exchange sees exactly the permutation of a braid. -/

/-- Every permutation is the image of infinitely many braids (`n ≥ 2`): each symmetric exchange
step hides infinitely many braided ones. -/

/-- The information hidden by symmetric exchange includes the whole labelled linking matrix: for
every symmetric zero-diagonal integer matrix there is a braid that acts on contexts exactly like
the identity but has that linking matrix. -/
/-! ### A register of provers -/
/-- The logical foundation of a prover. -/
/-- Calculus of inductive constructions. -/
/-- Martin-Löf type theory. -/
/-- Quantitative type theory. -/
/-- Higher-order logic (simple type theory). -/
/-- ZFC set theory in first-order logic. -/
/-- Tarski–Grothendieck set theory in first-order logic. -/
/-- First-order logic (with equality / theories). -/
/-- Quantifier-free first-order logic with induction. -/
/-- The Edinburgh logical framework LF. -/
/-- Multimodal Lambek calculus (categorial grammar). -/
/-- The exchange discipline of the prover's contexts. -/
/-- One entry of the register. -/
/-- Sixteen provers. -/

/-- The only prover in the register whose logic has no exchange is the categorial-grammar
prover Grail. -/

/-- No prover in the register has braided exchange: a braid can enter these systems only as
data. -/

/-!
# The labelled `n × n` linking matrix of a pure braid (the "70 × 70 language matrix")

`plan_2.md` asks for a 70 × 70 symmetric matrix of integer linking numbers, one row and column
per language strand.  `ClosureLinking.lean` showed that the linking numbers which are invariants
of the closed link are those *between closure components*, and the components are the cycles of
the braid's permutation.  So a matrix with one row per strand exists exactly when every strand
closes up on itself, i.e. for **pure braids** (`permHom n g = 1`).  This file builds that matrix
and determines precisely which matrices occur.

* `linkMatrix g a b = crossMatrix g a b / 2`; for pure braids the halving is exact
  (`two_mul_linkMatrix`), the matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and its off-diagonal entries
  are the linking spectrum of the closure (`linkingSpectrum_eq_linkMatrix`).
* `linkMatrix_mul` — on pure braids it is additive: `linkMatrix (g * h) = linkMatrix g +
  linkMatrix h`, so it is a group homomorphism from the pure braid group to the additive group
  of integer matrices (`linkHom`).
* `linkMatrix_conj` — conjugating by any braid `h` relabels the rows and columns by the
  permutation of `h`; conjugating by a pure braid leaves the labelled matrix unchanged.
* `permHom_surjective` — every permutation of strands is realised by a braid.
* `linkMatrix_realizable` — **every** symmetric integer matrix with zero diagonal is the linking
  matrix of a pure braid.  So the only constraints on a "cross-language linking matrix" are
  symmetry, zero diagonal and integrality; there are `n(n-1)/2` independent integer entries.
* `seventy_language_matrix` — the case `n = 70`: every symmetric zero-diagonal `70 × 70` integer
  matrix arises, and `card_pairs_seventy` counts its `2415` free entries.
-/
/-! ### Every permutation is realised -/
/-! ### The linking matrix -/
/-- The labelled linking matrix: half the strand-crossing matrix. -/
/-- On pure braids the linking matrix is additive. -/
/-- Conjugation by any braid relabels rows and columns by its permutation. -/
/-- Conjugation by a pure braid leaves the labelled matrix unchanged. -/

/-- For a pure braid the off-diagonal entries of the linking matrix are exactly the linking
spectrum of the closure. -/
/-! ### The pure braid group and the homomorphism -/
/-- The pure braid group: braids whose strands all return to their starting positions. -/
/-- The linking matrix as a homomorphism from the pure braid group. -/
/-! ### Realisability -/
/-- The matrices that occur as linking matrices of pure braids. -/

/-- The elementary matrix with `1` in positions `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` is realisable: it is the
linking matrix of a conjugate of `σ₁²` (two strands that wind once around each other). -/
-- a braid moving the crossing positions to the strands `a`, `b`

/-- A symmetric matrix with zero diagonal is the sum of its upper-triangular entries times the
elementary symmetric matrices. -/

/-- **Realisability.** Every symmetric integer matrix with zero diagonal is the linking matrix of
a pure braid. -/

/-- The linking matrices of pure braids are exactly the symmetric integer matrices with zero
diagonal. -/
/-! ### Seventy languages -/

/-- **The 70 × 70 language matrix.**  For 70 language strands, the labelled linking matrices of
pure braids are exactly the symmetric `70 × 70` integer matrices with zero diagonal. -/
/-- The 70 × 70 matrix has `70 · 69 / 2 = 2415` independent entries. -/
