/-!
# One- and two-loop gauge β-functions of the Noncommutative Standard Model

This file extends `RequestProject.NCG.Running` (one-loop coefficients and asymptotic freedom)
with the following.

1. **One-loop coefficients from the Seeley–DeWitt coefficient `a₄`.** In the background field
   method, the logarithmic divergence of the one-loop effective action of a field whose
   fluctuation operator is of Laplace type `-∇² - E` is `(ln Λ²)/(16π²)` times its `a₄`
   coefficient. The only part of `a₄` that involves the background gauge field is
   `(1/360)(180 tr E² + 30 tr Ω²)` (`SovereignEngine.SeeleyDeWitt.SeeleyDeWittInvariants.a4`,
   the coefficient of `RequestProject.SeeleyDeWitt`). For each type of fluctuating field we
   record the Lorentz trace of `Ω² = F² ⊗ 1` and of `E²`, and the statistical weight with which
   `log det` enters the effective action. This gives the familiar weights
   `-11/3` (gauge boson plus ghosts), `2/3` (Weyl fermion) and `1/3` (complex scalar) of the
   one-loop coefficient `b = -11/3 C₂(G) + 2/3 Σ_Weyl T + 1/3 Σ_scalar T`
   (`heatKernel_oneLoopB`).
2. **The field content of the NCG Standard Model.** The fermions are the 16 Weyl fermions per
   generation of `H_F` (hypercharges `NCG.Anomaly.smY`). The bosons are the inner fluctuations
   of `D_F`: the `U(1) × SU(2) × SU(3)` gauge fields and one complex Higgs doublet.
3. **One-loop coefficients.** For three generations, in GUT normalisation,
   `(b₁, b₂, b₃) = (41/10, -19/6, -7)` (`oneLoop_SM`). These agree with `NCG.b1`, `NCG.b2`,
   `NCG.b3` of `RequestProject.NCG.Running` (`oneLoop_eq_NCGRunning`).
4. **Two-loop coefficients.** From the general two-loop formula for a product gauge group:
   `b_ij = [[199/50, 27/10, 44/5], [9/10, 35/6, 12], [11/10, 9/2, -26]]` (`twoLoop_SM`).
5. **The RG system.** `dα_i⁻¹/dt = -b_i/(2π) - Σ_j b_ij α_j/(8π²) + c_i y_t²/(32π³)` with
   `t = ln(μ/μ₀)`. It has an exact linear one-loop solution (`oneLoop_alphaInv_solution`), which
   agrees with the solution of `RequestProject.NCG.Running` (`alphaInv_of_IsRGESolution`).
   In the pure-gauge two-loop system, `α₁⁻¹` and `α₂⁻¹` always lie on or below their one-loop
   lines, because their rows of `b_ij` are non-negative (`twoLoop_alphaInv_le_oneLoop`).
-/
/-! ## One-loop weights from the Seeley–DeWitt coefficient `a₄` -/

/-- The four types of fluctuating field in the background-field computation of the one-loop
effective action: gauge bosons (real vectors), Faddeev–Popov ghosts (complex anticommuting
scalars), complex scalars and Weyl fermions. -/

/-- Dimension of the Lorentz representation of the field (4 for vectors, 1 for scalars and
ghosts, 2 for Weyl spinors). This is the Lorentz trace of `Ω_{μν}Ω^{μν} = F_{μν}F^{μν} ⊗ 1`,
in units of `Σ_{μν} tr_R F_{μν}F^{μν}`. -/

/-- Lorentz trace of `E²` in units of `Σ_{μν} tr_R F_{μν}F^{μν}`. For vectors `E_{ab} = 2F_{ab}`,
which gives `Σ_{ab} E_{ab}E_{ba} = -4 ΣF²`. For spinors `E = ½ σ^{μν}F_{μν}`, which gives
`tr E² = -2ΣF²` on a Dirac spinor and hence `-1` on a Weyl spinor. Scalars and ghosts have
no gauge-dependent `E`. -/

/-- Weight of `log det` of the fluctuation operator in the one-loop effective action:
`+½` for a real boson, `-1` for complex ghosts, `+1` for a complex scalar, and `-½` for a
Weyl fermion (`log det` of a first-order Weyl operator is `½ log det` of its square, with
fermionic sign). -/

/-- The gauge-field part of the Seeley–DeWitt coefficient `a₄` of the fluctuation operator:
`(1/360)(180 tr E² + 30 tr Ω²)`, the `E²` and `F²` terms of `a₄` in `RequestProject.SeeleyDeWitt`. -/

/-- The Seeley–DeWitt invariants of a field with only a background gauge field switched on (flat
space, unit `∫ Σ tr_R F²`): only `∫E²` and `∫F²` are non-zero. -/

/-- `a4Gauge` is the Seeley–DeWitt coefficient `a₄` of `RequestProject.SeeleyDeWitt`, evaluated
on the flat-space gauge background. -/

/-- Contribution of one field of this type to the one-loop β coefficient `b`, normalised by
the Dynkin index of its internal representation: `4 × (statistical weight) × a₄`. -/

/-- **Gauge boson plus ghosts: `-11/3`.** A vector gives `4·½·(-5/3) = -10/3` and the ghosts give
`4·(-1)·(1/12) = -1/3`. -/
/-- **Weyl fermion: `2/3`.** -/
/-- **Complex scalar: `1/3`.** -/

/-- **The one-loop coefficient from the heat kernel.** Summing the `a₄`-weights over the gauge
multiplet (Dynkin index `C₂(G)`), the Weyl fermions (total index `T_F`) and the complex
scalars (total index `T_S`) gives the coefficient `NCG.oneLoopB` used in
`RequestProject.NCG.Running`. -/
/-! ## Field content of the NCG Standard Model -/

/-- A multiplet of `SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1)_Y`: dimension of the colour representation (`1` or `3`,
with `3̄` treated like `3`), dimension of the isospin representation (`1` or `2`) and
hypercharge `Y` (convention `Q = T₃ + Y`). -/
/-- Dynkin index of the singlet or fundamental representation of `SU(n)`: `0` or `½`. -/
/-- Quadratic Casimir of the singlet or fundamental of `SU(d)`: `0` or `(d² - 1)/(2d)`. -/

/-- Dynkin index of a multiplet with respect to the gauge factor `i` (`0 = U(1)_Y` in GUT
normalisation `g₁² = (5/3) g'²`, `1 = SU(2)_L`, `2 = SU(3)_C`), multiplied by the dimension
of the representation of the other factors. -/
/-- Quadratic Casimir of a multiplet with respect to the gauge factor `i`. -/
/-- Adjoint Casimirs `C₂(G) = (0, 2, 3)` of `U(1)_Y`, `SU(2)_L` and `SU(3)_C`. -/

/-- **One generation of `H_F` as left-handed Weyl multiplets**, with the hypercharges
`NCG.Anomaly.smY`: `Q_L = (3,2)_{yQ}`, `u^c = (3̄,1)_{-yu}`, `d^c = (3̄,1)_{-yd}`,
`L = (1,2)_{yL}`, `e^c = (1,1)_{-ye}`, `ν^c = (1,1)_{-yν}`. -/
/-- **The scalar inner fluctuation of `D_F`: one complex Higgs doublet `(1,2)_{1/2}`.** -/

/-- One generation of `smWeyl` has sixteen Weyl components, the per-generation dimension of the
particle half of `H_F` (`NCG.card_HF`: `dim H_F = 32 N`). -/
/-! ## One- and two-loop coefficients -/

/-- **One-loop coefficient** for gauge factor `i` with `N` generations, assembled from the
heat-kernel weights: `b_i = -11/3 C₂(G_i) + 2/3 N Σ_Weyl S_i + 1/3 Σ_scalar S_i`. -/

/-- **Two-loop coefficient** `b_ij` for `N` generations (general formula for a product gauge
group, gauge and matter contributions):
`b_ij = -34/3 C₂(G_i)² δ_ij + N Σ_Weyl S_i (2 C_j + 10/3 C₂(G_i) δ_ij)
        + Σ_scalar S_i (4 C_j + 2/3 C₂(G_i) δ_ij)`. -/

/-- **The one-loop coefficients of the three-generation NCG Standard Model**:
`(b₁, b₂, b₃) = (41/10, -19/6, -7)`. -/
/-- The heat-kernel coefficients agree with those of `RequestProject.NCG.Running`. -/

/-- **The two-loop coefficients of the three-generation NCG Standard Model**:
`b_ij = [[199/50, 27/10, 44/5], [9/10, 35/6, 12], [11/10, 9/2, -26]]`. -/

/-- **Top-Yukawa contribution to the two-loop gauge β-functions**: `-c_i y_t²/(16π²)²` with
`c = (17/10, 3/2, 2)`. -/
/-! ## The renormalization group system -/
/-- One-loop coefficients of the three-generation model, as real numbers. -/
/-- Two-loop coefficients of the three-generation model, as real numbers. -/

/-- **The two-loop RG system for the inverse fine-structure constants** `α_i⁻¹ = 4π/g_i²`, with
`t = ln(μ/μ₀)` and top Yukawa coupling `y_t(t)`:
`dα_i⁻¹/dt = -b_i/(2π) - Σ_j b_ij α_j/(8π²) + c_i y_t²/(32π³)`.
This is `dg_i/dt = g_i³/(16π²) [b_i + (Σ_j b_ij g_j² - c_i y_t²)/(16π²)]` rewritten for
`α_i⁻¹`. -/
/-- The one-loop truncation of the RG system: `dα_i⁻¹/dt = -b_i/(2π)`. -/
/-- **Exact one-loop running**: `α_i⁻¹(t) = α_i⁻¹(0) - b_i t/(2π)`. -/

/-- **Compatibility with `RequestProject.NCG.Running`.** For a positive solution `g` of the
one-loop equation `dg/dt = b g³/(16π²)`, `α⁻¹ = 4π/g²` runs linearly:
`α⁻¹(t) = 4π/g₀² - b t/(2π)`. -/
/-- The rows of `b_ij` for `U(1)_Y` and `SU(2)_L` are non-negative. -/

/-- **Two-loop effects make `α₁⁻¹` and `α₂⁻¹` run faster.** In the pure-gauge two-loop system
(`y_t = 0`), with all couplings positive, the inverse couplings of `U(1)_Y` and `SU(2)_L` lie
on or below their one-loop lines: `α_i⁻¹(t) ≤ α_i⁻¹(0) - b_i t/(2π)`. -/

/-!
# Gravitational waves on the almost-commutative geometry `M × F`

## 1. Linearized gravity of a plane gravitational wave

We work in Fourier space with the Minkowski metric `η = diag(−1, 1, 1, 1)`. A plane wave
`h_{μν}(x) = h_{μν} e^{i k·x}` is described by its polarization tensor `h` and its wave
covector `k`; derivatives become `∂_μ ↦ i k_μ`.

* The linearized Riemann tensor (`linRiemann`) is invariant under linearized diffeomorphisms
  `h_{μν} ↦ h_{μν} + k_μ ξ_ν + k_ν ξ_μ` (`linRiemann_gauge_invariant`): the curvature carried by
  a gravitational wave is a diffeomorphism-invariant observable.
* In transverse–traceless gauge the linearized Ricci tensor is `R_{νσ} = −½ k² h_{νσ}`
  (`linRicci_of_TT`), so a non-zero TT wave solves the vacuum Einstein equations iff `k` is
  null, `k² = 0` (`gw_vacuum_iff_null`): gravitational waves travel at the speed of light.
* For a wave travelling along `z`, the TT conditions in temporal gauge leave exactly the two
  polarizations `h₊` and `h×` (`tt_polarizations`).

## 2. Coupling of the spectral action of `M × F` to the wave

The Dirac operator of `M × F` is `D = D_M ⊗ 1 + γ_M ⊗ D_F` (`productDirac`). A metric
perturbation changes `D_M ↦ D_M + ε V` with `V` odd (`V γ_M = −γ_M V`), and so
`D ↦ D + ε (V ⊗ 1)` (`productDirac_perturb`).
* `D² = D_M² ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ D_F²` (`productDirac_sq`), so the perturbed spectral action moments are
  `Tr D⁴ = N_F Tr D_M(ε)⁴ + 2 Tr D_M(ε)² Tr D_F² + N_M Tr D_F⁴`
  (`productDirac_trace_pow_four`): the wave couples to the finite geometry only through the
  Yukawa/Higgs invariant `Tr D_F²` multiplying the gravitational term `Tr D_M(ε)²`.
* The wave perturbation commutes with the finite algebra `1 ⊗ A_F`, so the internal (Higgs)
  fluctuations are unchanged (`gw_internal_fluctuations_unchanged`).
* A torsion term `T_M ⊗ 1` commuting with the functions on `M` commutes with the whole algebra
  `C(M) ⊗ A_F`, so all inner fluctuations and their gauge transformations are unchanged
  (`torsion_product_oneForm`, see `RequestProject.NCGTorsionGravity`).
-/
/-! ### 1. Linearized gravity -/

/-- The diagonal entries of the Minkowski metric `η = diag(−1, 1, 1, 1)` (equal to those of
`η⁻¹`). -/
/-- Minkowski product of covectors `k² = η^{μν} k_μ k_ν`. -/

/-- The **linearized Riemann tensor** of a plane wave with polarization `h` and wave covector
`k` (Fourier transform of `½(∂_ν∂_ρ h_{μσ} + ∂_μ∂_σ h_{νρ} − ∂_μ∂_ρ h_{νσ} − ∂_ν∂_σ h_{μρ})`,
up to the overall factor `i² = −1`). -/

/-- A **linearized diffeomorphism** generated by the vector field `ξ e^{ik·x}`:
`h_{μν} ↦ h_{μν} + k_μ ξ_ν + k_ν ξ_μ`. -/
/-- **Diffeomorphism invariance of the gravitational-wave curvature.** -/
/-- The **linearized Ricci tensor** `R_{νσ} = η^{μρ} R_{μνρσ}`. -/

/-- The **transverse–traceless (TT) gauge** conditions: `h` symmetric, traceless
(`η^{μν} h_{μν} = 0`) and transverse (`η^{μρ} k_μ h_{ρν} = 0`). -/

/-- General form of the linearized Ricci tensor:
`R_{νσ} = ½(k_ν (k·h)_σ + k_σ (k·h)_ν − k² h_{νσ} − k_ν k_σ tr h)`. -/
/-- In TT gauge, `R_{νσ} = −½ k² h_{νσ}`. -/

/-- **Gravitational waves propagate on the light cone.** A non-zero TT plane wave solves the
linearized vacuum Einstein equations `R_{μν} = 0` iff its wave covector is null. -/
/-- The wave covector `k_μ = ω(−1, 0, 0, 1)` of a wave of frequency `ω` travelling along `z`. -/
/-- `k_z` is null. -/
/-- The **plus polarization** `e₊ = e_x ⊗ e_x − e_y ⊗ e_y`. -/
/-- The **cross polarization** `e× = e_x ⊗ e_y + e_y ⊗ e_x`. -/

/-- **The two polarizations of a gravitational wave.** For a wave along `z` (`ω ≠ 0`), a
polarization tensor satisfies the TT conditions in temporal gauge (`h_{0ν} = 0`) iff it is a
combination `h₊ e₊ + h× e×` of the plus and cross polarizations. -/
/-! ### 2. The spectral action of `M × F` coupled to the wave -/

/-- The **Dirac operator of the almost-commutative geometry `M × F`**:
`D = D_M ⊗ 1 + γ_M ⊗ D_F`. -/

/-- **The gravitational-wave perturbation of `M × F`**: replacing `D_M` by `D_M + ε V`
changes the product Dirac operator by `ε (V ⊗ 1)`. -/
/-- `D² = D_M² ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ D_F²` when `γ_M² = 1` and `D_M γ_M = −γ_M D_M`. -/

/-- **Coupling of the spectral action of `M × F` to the geometry of `M`.** For an odd
`D_M` (in particular the perturbed `D_M + ε V` of a gravitational wave),
`Tr D⁴ = N_F Tr D_M⁴ + 2 Tr D_M² Tr D_F² + N_M Tr D_F⁴`. -/

/-- The gravitational-wave perturbation of `D_M` is odd if `V` is: the hypothesis of
`productDirac_trace_pow_four` is preserved by the perturbation. -/
/-- `X ⊗ 1` commutes with `g ⊗ a` whenever `X` commutes with `g`. -/
/-- The **finite algebra** `1 ⊗ A_F` acting on `L²(M, S) ⊗ H_F`. -/

/-- **The wave does not change the internal (Higgs) fluctuations.** The inner fluctuations
`Σ aᵢ [D, bᵢ]` with `bᵢ ∈ 1 ⊗ A_F` of the perturbed Dirac operator `D + ε (V ⊗ 1)` coincide
with those of `D`. -/

/-- The **algebra `C(M) ⊗ A_F`** of the almost-commutative geometry, where `CM` is a set of
(multiplication operators by) functions on `M`. -/

/-- **Torsion on `M × F` preserves the gauge sector.** A torsion term `T_M` on `M` commuting
with the functions gives `T = T_M ⊗ 1` commuting with `C(M) ⊗ A_F`; hence all inner
fluctuations of `D + T` coincide with those of `D`, and the gauge transformation law is the one
of `D` (`NCG.Torsion.gauge_covariance_add_torsion`). -/

/-!
# The hypercharges of `H_F` from the unimodularity condition

The gauge group of the Noncommutative Standard Model is the unitary group of
`A_F = ℂ ⊕ ℍ ⊕ M₃(ℂ)` acting on `H_F` through the adjoint action `ξ ↦ u J_F u J_F⁻¹ ξ`,
restricted by the unimodularity condition `det π(u) = 1`. Infinitesimally, for `x` in the Lie
algebra `𝔲(A_F)` of anti-Hermitian elements, the generator is `π(x) + J_F π(x) J_F⁻¹` and the
unimodularity condition is `Tr π(x) = 0`.

We prove that unimodularity forces the `𝔲(1)` part of `M₃(ℂ)` to be `-λ/3`, and that the
resulting generator acting on the particle sector of `H_F` is exactly the Standard Model gauge
generator `gaugeGen N smY (2λ) q M`: **the Standard Model hypercharges `smY` are derived from the
spectral data `(A_F, H_F, J_F)`**, not put in by hand.
-/
/-- `x = (λ, q, m) ∈ A_F` lies in the Lie algebra `𝔲(A_F)` of anti-Hermitian elements. -/

/-- The infinitesimal adjoint action `π(x) + J_F π(x) J_F⁻¹` restricted to the particle sector
of `H_F` (`J_F π(x) J_F⁻¹` acts on particles as the complex conjugate of the antiparticle block
of `π(x)`). -/
/-- The trace of the representation `π(x)` of `A_F` on `H_F`. -/

/-- **The unimodularity condition.** For `x ∈ 𝔲(A_F)` and `N ≥ 1` generations, `Tr π(x) = 0`
on `H_F` if and only if `Tr m = -λ`. -/
/-- The `𝔰𝔲(3)` generator `M = m̄ - (λ/3)` extracted from `x = (λ, q, m)`. -/

/-- **The Standard Model hypercharges from unimodularity.** For a unimodular `x ∈ 𝔲(A_F)`, the
adjoint action on the particle sector of `H_F` is the Standard Model gauge generator with
hypercharges `smY`, `U(1)_Y` parameter `2λ`, `SU(2)_L` generator `π_ℍ(q)` and `SU(3)_C`
generator `m̄ - λ/3`; these generators are traceless, so the adjoint action lies in the gauge
algebra `gaugeAlgebra N smY`. -/

/-- The infinitesimal adjoint action `ad(x) = π(x) + J_F π(x) J_F⁻¹` of `x ∈ A_F` on all of
`H_F`, with `J_F = U_F ∘ (complex conjugation)`. -/
/-- A unimodular element of `𝔲(A_F)`: anti-Hermitian with `Tr π(x) = 0` on `H_F`. -/

/-- **Gauge anomaly freedom of the Noncommutative Standard Model, from the spectral data.**
For `N ≥ 1` generations and any three unimodular generators `x, y, z ∈ 𝔲(A_F)`, acting on the
full finite Hilbert space `H_F` by the adjoint action `ad = π + J_F π J_F⁻¹`, every triangle
anomaly `Σ_σ Tr(γ_F ad(x) ad(y) ad(z))` and the mixed gravitational anomaly `Tr(γ_F ad(x))`
vanish. No counterterm is needed: the cancellation is exact. -/
/-! ### The gauge algebra is a Lie algebra -/
/-- **Closure under commutators**: `[X(b,Q,M), X(b',Q',M')] = X(0, [Q,Q'], [M,M'])`. -/

/-- The gauge algebra `𝔲(1)_Y ⊕ 𝔰𝔲(2)_L ⊕ 𝔰𝔲(3)_C` on `H_F` is a Lie subalgebra of
`𝔤𝔩(V_N)`: the anomaly form is defined on a genuine gauge Lie algebra. -/

/-- **Finite real even spectral triple of KO-dimension 6.**
The data `(A, H = ℂⁿ, D, J = U ∘ K, γ)` together with all axioms of a real even spectral

declarations.name: KO6Triple
declarations.signature_heuristic:
structure KO6Triple (A : Type*) [Ring A] [StarRing A] [Algebra ℝ A]
    (n : Type*) [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] where
  /-- The `*`-representation of `A` on `H = ℂⁿ`. -/
  rep : A →⋆ₐ[ℝ] Matrix n n ℂ
  /-- The finite Dirac operator. -/
  D : Matrix n n ℂ
  D_hermitian : D.IsHermitian
  /-- The grading (chirality) operator. -/
  γ : Matrix n n ℂ
  γ_hermitian : γ.IsHermitian
  γ_sq : γ * γ = 1
  γ_rep : ∀ a, Commute γ (rep a)
  γ_D : γ * D = -(D * γ)
  /-- The unitary part of the real structure `J = U ∘ K`. -/
  U : Matrix n n ℂ
  U_unitary : U ∈ Matrix.unitaryGroup n ℂ
  /-- `J² = 1` (`ε = 1`). -/
  J_sq : U * conjM U = 1
  /-- `J D = D J` (`ε' = 1`). -/
  J_D : U * conjM D = D * U
  /-- `J γ = - γ J` (`ε'' = -1`). -/
  J_γ : U * conjM γ = -(γ * U)
  /-- Order-zero condition: `[a, J b J⁻¹] = 0`. -/
  order_zero : ∀ a b, Commute (rep a) (U * conjM (rep b) * Uᴴ)
  /-- First-order condition: `[[D, a], J b J⁻¹] = 0`. -/
  first_order : ∀ a b, Commute (D * rep a - rep a * D) (U * conjM (rep b) * Uᴴ)

namespace KO6Triple

variable {A : Type*} [Ring A] [StarRing A] [Algebra ℝ A] (T : KO6Triple A n)

omit [DecidableEq n] in

comments.text:
/-!
# Finite real spectral triples of KO-dimension 6

This file sets up the abstract notion used in the Noncommutative Standard Model: a *finite*
real even spectral triple `(A, H, D, J, γ)` of KO-dimension `6 (mod 8)`.

* `H = n → ℂ` is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, and operators are matrices `Matrix n n ℂ`.
* `A` is a real `*`-algebra acting on `H` through a `*`-representation `rep`.
* `D` is a self-adjoint (Dirac) operator.
* `γ` is a grading: self-adjoint, `γ² = 1`, commuting with `A` and anticommuting with `D`.
* `J` is an antiunitary *real structure*.  Every antiunitary operator on `ℂⁿ` is of the form
  `J = U ∘ K` with `U` unitary and `K` complex conjugation, so we record `J` by `U`
  (`realStructure U v = U (conj v)`).
* KO-dimension `6` fixes the signs `J² = ε`, `J D = ε' D J`, `J γ = ε'' γ J` to be
  `(ε, ε', ε'') = (1, 1, -1)`.
* The order-zero condition `[a, J b* J⁻¹] = 0` and the first-order condition
  `[[D, a], J b* J⁻¹] = 0`.  (Since `rep` is a `*`-map, `J b* J⁻¹` ranges over the same set as
  `J b J⁻¹` when `b` varies, so we state both conditions with `J b J⁻¹`.)

In matrix form, `J X J⁻¹ = U X̄ U⁻¹` where `X̄` is the entrywise conjugate (`conjM X`).
The conditions of the structure are stated in this matrix form, and the lemmas at the end
of the file translate them back to statements about the antilinear operator `J` itself.
-/
/-- Entrywise complex conjugation `X ↦ X̄` of a matrix. -/

/-- The antilinear *real structure* `J = U ∘ K` determined by a matrix `U`:
`J v = U (v̄)`. -/

/-- The KO-dimension sign table `(ε, ε', ε'')` for the real structure `J`
(`J² = ε`, `J D = ε' D J`, `J γ = ε'' γ J`) in the even KO-dimensions `0, 2, 4, 6`. -/

/-- **Finite real even spectral triple of KO-dimension 6.**
The data `(A, H = ℂⁿ, D, J = U ∘ K, γ)` together with all axioms of a real even spectral
triple of KO-dimension `6`, with signs `(ε, ε', ε'') = koSigns 6 = (1, 1, -1)`. -/
/-- The `*`-representation of `A` on `H = ℂⁿ`. -/
/-- The finite Dirac operator. -/
/-- The grading (chirality) operator. -/
/-- The unitary part of the real structure `J = U ∘ K`. -/
/-- Order-zero condition: `[a, J b J⁻¹] = 0`. -/
/-- First-order condition: `[[D, a], J b J⁻¹] = 0`. -/
/-- `J² = 1` as a statement about the antilinear operator `J`. -/
/-- `J D = D J` as a statement about operators. -/
/-- `J γ = -γ J` as a statement about operators. -/

/-- `J` intertwines `b` with the operator `U b̄ U⁻¹` appearing in the order-zero and
first-order conditions: `J (b v) = (U b̄ U*) (J v)`. -/
/-- `J` is antiunitary: `⟨J v, J w⟩ = conj ⟨v, w⟩` (with `⟨v, w⟩ = Σ v̄ᵢ wᵢ`). -/

/-!
# The CP-violating Jarlskog invariant of the PMNS matrix

We parametrize the (Dirac) PMNS matrix in the standard (PDG) form

  `U = R₂₃(θ₂₃) · U₁₃(θ₁₃, δ) · R₁₂(θ₁₂)`
    `= [[c₁₂c₁₃, s₁₂c₁₃, s₁₃e^{-iδ}],`
       `[-s₁₂c₂₃ - c₁₂s₂₃s₁₃e^{iδ}, c₁₂c₂₃ - s₁₂s₂₃s₁₃e^{iδ}, s₂₃c₁₃],`
       `[s₁₂s₂₃ - c₁₂c₂₃s₁₃e^{iδ}, -c₁₂s₂₃ - s₁₂c₂₃s₁₃e^{iδ}, c₂₃c₁₃]]`

and compute its Jarlskog invariant `J_CP = Im(U_{e2} U_{μ3} U*_{e3} U*_{μ2})`
(`NCG.jarlskog` of `RequestProject.NCG.CKM`):

* `pdgMatrix_unitary` : the parametrized matrix is unitary;
* `pdg_is_pmns` : every such matrix is the PMNS mismatch `U_e† U_ν` of some lepton mass
  matrices, with arbitrary prescribed masses;
* `jarlskog_pdg` : **`J_CP = c₁₂ s₁₂ c₂₃ s₂₃ c₁₃² s₁₃ sin δ`**;
* `jarlskog_pdg_sq_le` : `J_CP² ≤ 1/108`, i.e. `|J_CP| ≤ 1/(6√3)`;
* `jarlskog_pdg_ne_zero` : `J_CP ≠ 0` for mixing angles in `(0, π/2)` and `sin δ ≠ 0`;
* `jarlskog_pdg_eq_max_mul_sin` : for angles in `[0, π/2]`,
  `J_CP = J_max sin δ` with `J_max = √(s₁₂²c₁₂²) √(s₂₃²c₂₃²) √(s₁₃²) c₁₃²`
  expressed through `sin²θᵢⱼ`;
* `jarlskogMax_numerical` : for the input values `sin²θ₁₂ = 0.303`, `sin²θ₂₃ = 0.572`,
  `sin²θ₁₃ = 0.02203`, `0.0329 < J_max < 0.0331`, so `J_CP ≈ 0.033 sin δ`.
-/
/-- The CP phase `e^{iδ} = cos δ + i sin δ`. -/
/-- The rotation `R₂₃(θ)` in the `(2,3)` plane. -/
/-- The complex rotation `U₁₃(θ, δ)` in the `(1,3)` plane carrying the CP phase. -/
/-- The rotation `R₁₂(θ)` in the `(1,2)` plane. -/

/-- The **standard parametrization of the PMNS matrix**
`U(θ₁₂, θ₂₃, θ₁₃, δ) = R₂₃(θ₂₃) U₁₃(θ₁₃, δ) R₁₂(θ₁₂)`. -/

/-- **The Jarlskog invariant of the PMNS matrix**:
`J_CP = c₁₂ s₁₂ c₂₃ s₂₃ c₁₃² s₁₃ sin δ`. -/
/-- The standard parametrization is unitary. -/

/-- **Every standard-parametrized matrix is a PMNS mismatch.**  For any prescribed squared
charged-lepton masses `m²_e` and neutrino masses `m²_ν`, taking `He = diag(m²_e)` and
`Hν = U diag(m²_ν) U†` with `U = U(θ₁₂, θ₂₃, θ₁₃, δ)` gives lepton mixing data whose PMNS
matrix `U_e† U_ν` is `U`. -/
/-- **Maximal CP violation bound**: `J_CP² ≤ 1/108`, i.e. `|J_CP| ≤ 1/(6√3) ≈ 0.096`. -/
-- `(c s)² ≤ 1/4` and `s₁₃² c₁₃⁴ ≤ 4/27`

/-- **CP violation is generic**: for mixing angles in `(0, π/2)` and a CP phase with
`sin δ ≠ 0`, the Jarlskog invariant of the PMNS matrix is nonzero. -/

/-- The **maximal Jarlskog invariant** `J_max = √(s₁₂²c₁₂²) √(s₂₃²c₂₃²) √(s₁₃²) c₁₃²`
expressed through `sᵢⱼ² = sin²θᵢⱼ` (so that `J_CP = J_max sin δ`). -/
/-- **`J_CP = J_max sin δ`** for mixing angles in the physical range `[0, π/2]`. -/

/-- **Numerical value of `J_max`** for the input values `sin²θ₁₂ = 0.303`, `sin²θ₂₃ = 0.572`,
`sin²θ₁₃ = 0.02203`: `0.0329 < J_max < 0.0331`.  Hence `J_CP ≈ 0.033 sin δ`. -/

/-!
# The leptonic sector of the finite spectral triple

We extend the finite spectral triple of `RequestProject.NCGKO6` / `RequestProject.NCG.SMTriple`
to the lepton sector.

* **Lepton states of `H_F`.**  `nuL i`, `nuR i`, `eL i`, `eR i` and `nuRbar i` are the basis
  vectors of `H_F` carrying the left/right-handed neutrino, the left/right-handed charged
  lepton and the antiparticle of the right-handed neutrino of generation `i`.
* **Dirac and Majorana masses on `H_F`.**  `DSM_nuL_nuR`, `DSM_eL_eR`, `DSM_nuR_nuRbar`
  read off the Dirac neutrino mass matrix `Yν`, the charged-lepton mass matrix `Ye` and the
  Majorana mass matrix `YR` from the finite Dirac operator `D_F`; `DSM_nuL_nuLbar` shows that
  there is no left-handed Majorana mass term.
* **Three generations.**  `LeptonData` packages a 3-generation Dirac neutrino mass matrix,
  a charged lepton mass matrix and a symmetric Majorana matrix; `LeptonData.toYukawa` puts
  them into `D_F` and `LeptonData.triple` is the resulting KO-dimension 6 real spectral
  triple on `H_F` (`dim H_F = 96`).
* **Seesaw.**  `neutralMass` is the symmetric `2N × 2N` neutral-lepton mass matrix
  `𝓜 = [[0, m_D], [m_Dᵀ, M_R]]` in the Majorana basis `(ν_L, ν_R^c)`; `seesaw_block_diag`
  is the *exact* seesaw theorem: for invertible `M_R`,
  `Lᵀ 𝓜 L = diag(-m_D M_R⁻¹ m_Dᵀ, M_R)` with `L = [[1, 0], [-M_R⁻¹ m_Dᵀ, 1]]` invertible.
  The light Majorana mass matrix `m_ν = -m_D M_R⁻¹ m_Dᵀ` is symmetric.
-/
/-! ### Lepton basis states of `H_F` -/

/-- The right-handed neutrino `ν_R` of generation `i` in `H_F`
(particle, right-handed, isospin up, lepton colour). -/

/-- The left-handed neutrino `ν_L` of generation `i` in `H_F`
(particle, left-handed, isospin up, lepton colour). -/
/-- The right-handed charged lepton `e_R` of generation `i` in `H_F`. -/
/-- The left-handed charged lepton `e_L` of generation `i` in `H_F`. -/
/-- The antiparticle `ν̄_R` of the right-handed neutrino of generation `i` in `H_F`. -/
/-- The antiparticle `ν̄_L` of the left-handed neutrino of generation `i` in `H_F`. -/
/-! ### Reading off the lepton mass matrices from `D_F` -/

/-- **Dirac neutrino mass matrix on `H_F`.**  The matrix element of `D_F` between `ν_L`
and `ν_R` of generations `i, j` is `(Yν)ᵢⱼ`. -/
/-- The Dirac mass term is Hermitian: `⟨ν_R j, D_F ν_L i⟩ = conj (Yν)ᵢⱼ`. -/

/-- **Charged lepton mass matrix on `H_F`.**  The matrix element of `D_F` between `e_L` and
`e_R` is `(Ye)ᵢⱼ`. -/

/-- **Majorana (seesaw) term on `H_F`.**  The matrix element of `D_F` between `ν_R` and
`ν̄_R` is `(YR)ᵢⱼ`. -/
/-- There is no left-handed Majorana mass term in `D_F`: `⟨ν_L, D_F ν̄_L⟩ = 0`. -/
/-- There is no `ν_L`–`ν̄_R` term in `D_F` (the Majorana term only couples `ν_R` and `ν̄_R`). -/
/-- Neutrinos do not mix with charged leptons in `D_F`: `⟨ν_L, D_F e_R⟩ = 0`. -/
/-! ### Three-generation lepton data -/

/-- **Three-generation lepton data**: the Dirac neutrino mass matrix `mD`, the charged
lepton mass matrix `me` and the symmetric Majorana mass matrix `MR` of the right-handed
neutrinos (all `3 × 3` complex matrices). -/
/-- Dirac neutrino mass matrix `m_D` (couples `ν_L` to `ν_R`). -/
/-- Charged lepton mass matrix `m_e` (couples `e_L` to `e_R`). -/
/-- Majorana mass matrix `M_R` of the right-handed neutrinos. -/
/-- The Majorana mass matrix is symmetric. -/

/-- The Yukawa data of `D_F` determined by the lepton data (quark Yukawas set to zero;
they play no role in the leptonic sector). -/

/-- **The leptonic finite spectral triple**: for any three-generation lepton data the finite
Dirac operator `D_F`, with Dirac neutrino masses and Majorana seesaw terms, is part of a real
spectral triple of KO-dimension 6 on `H_F` (of dimension `96`). -/
/-- `dim H_F = 96` for three generations. -/

/-- In the leptonic triple, `D_F` contains the Dirac neutrino mass matrix `m_D`,
the charged-lepton mass matrix `m_e` and the Majorana mass matrix `M_R`. -/
/-! ### The seesaw mechanism -/

/-- The **neutral-lepton mass matrix** in the Majorana basis `(ν_L, ν_R^c)`:
`𝓜 = [[0, m_D], [m_Dᵀ, M_R]]`. -/
/-- The neutral-lepton mass matrix is symmetric when `M_R` is. -/
/-- The **light (seesaw) neutrino Majorana mass matrix** `m_ν = -m_D M_R⁻¹ m_Dᵀ`. -/
/-- The seesaw mass matrix is symmetric (a Majorana mass matrix) when `M_R` is. -/
/-- The block-triangular change of basis `L = [[1, 0], [-M_R⁻¹ m_Dᵀ, 1]]` of the seesaw. -/
/-- The seesaw change of basis is invertible (it has determinant `1`). -/

/-- **Exact seesaw theorem.**  For an invertible symmetric Majorana matrix `M_R`, the
neutral-lepton mass matrix is congruent (as a Majorana mass matrix, `𝓜 ↦ Lᵀ 𝓜 L`) to the
block-diagonal matrix `diag(m_ν, M_R)`, with light neutrino mass matrix
`m_ν = -m_D M_R⁻¹ m_Dᵀ`.  No approximation `m_D ≪ M_R` is needed. -/
/-- The seesaw mass of the three-generation lepton data. -/

/-!
# Majorana CP phases and leptogenesis in the Noncommutative Standard Model

The finite Dirac operator `D_F` of the Noncommutative Standard Model contains a Majorana mass
term `M_R` for the right-handed neutrinos (`NCG.LeptonData`, `NCG.DSM_nuR_nuRbar`), and the
light neutrinos get the symmetric seesaw Majorana mass matrix `m_ν = −m_D M_R⁻¹ m_Dᵀ`
(`NCG.seesawMass`).

## 1. Majorana CP phases

* The leptonic mixing matrix of Majorana neutrinos is `U = U_PDG(θ₁₂, θ₂₃, θ₁₃, δ) · P`,
  `P = diag(1, e^{iα/2}, e^{iβ/2})` (`majoranaPMNS`); it is unitary, and the Majorana phases do
  not enter the Jarlskog invariant (`jarlskog_majoranaPMNS`).
* Majorana phases cannot be removed: a rephasing `ν ↦ e ν` of a Majorana field keeps its mass
  real and positive iff `e = ±1` (`majorana_rephase_real_iff`). The Majorana-type invariant
  `Im((U_{e1} Ū_{e2})²)` is invariant under all remaining rephasings (`majoranaInv_rephase`)
  and equals `−c₁₂² s₁₂² c₁₃⁴ sin α` (`majoranaInv_pmns`); it is non-zero iff `sin α ≠ 0` for
  non-degenerate mixing angles (`majoranaInv_pmns_ne_zero_iff`).
* **Invariant of the mass matrix itself.** `I(m) = Im(m_{ee} m_{μμ} m̄_{eμ}²)` is invariant under
  charged-lepton rephasing (`massInv_rephase`) and vanishes for real (CP-conserving) mass
  matrices (`massInv_of_real`); so `I(m) ≠ 0` means that the Majorana phases cannot be rotated
  away (`massInv_ne_zero_not_real`). For a two-flavour Majorana mass matrix
  `m = R(θ) diag(m₁, m₂ e^{iα}) R(θ)ᵀ`:
  `I(m) = c² s² m₁ m₂ (m₁² − m₂²) sin α` (`massInv_twoFlavour_phase`).
* **The spectral seesaw generates a non-zero Majorana CP phase**: for explicit lepton data of the
  spectral triple, the seesaw mass matrix has `I(m_ν) = 24 ≠ 0` (`spectral_seesaw_majorana_cp`).

## 2. Leptogenesis

* **Origin of the asymmetry.** For a decay amplitude `c₀ + c₁ L` (tree coupling `c₀`, one-loop
  coupling `c₁`, loop function `L`) the CP-conjugate amplitude is `c̄₀ + c̄₁ L`, and
  `|A|² − |Ā|² = 4 Im(c₀ c̄₁) Im(L)` (`cp_asymmetry_interference`): an asymmetry needs both a
  CP-violating phase of the couplings and an absorptive part of the loop.
* The exact one-loop CP asymmetry in the decay of the lightest heavy neutrino `N₁` is
  `ε_L = (1/8π) Σ_{j=2,3} Im[((Y†Y)_{1j})²]/(Y†Y)_{11} · f(M_j²/M₁²)` with
  `f(x) = √x (1 + 1/(1 − x) − (1 + x) ln((1 + x)/x))` (`epsilonL`, `loopF`).
* `f(x) < 0` for `x > 1` (`loopF_neg`); `ε_L = 0` if the Yukawa couplings are real
  (`epsilonL_of_real`); `ε_L > 0` whenever the CP phases have the right sign
  (`epsilonL_pos`); `ε_L(tY) = t² ε_L(Y)` (`epsilonL_smul`).
* **The three Sakharov conditions** hold simultaneously for explicit lepton data of the spectral
  triple (`spectral_leptogenesis_sakharov`): the Majorana term of `D_F` violates lepton number
  (and `B − L`) by two units (`majorana_violates_lepton_number`); the exact asymmetry is
  `ε_L = −t² f(M₂²/M₁²)/(4π) > 0`; and `N₁` decays out of equilibrium, `Γ_{N₁} < H(T = M₁)`.
-/
/-! ### Majorana PMNS matrix -/
/-- The Majorana phase matrix `P = diag(1, e^{iα/2}, e^{iβ/2})`. -/

/-- The **leptonic mixing matrix of Majorana neutrinos**
`U = U_PDG(θ₁₂, θ₂₃, θ₁₃, δ) · diag(1, e^{iα/2}, e^{iβ/2})`. -/
/-- The Majorana PMNS matrix is unitary. -/

/-- **The Majorana phases do not enter the Jarlskog invariant**: `J_CP(U_PDG · P) = J_CP(U_PDG)`.
They are CP phases of a different (Majorana) type. -/

/-- **Majorana phases are not removable.** A rephasing `ν ↦ e ν` (`|e| = 1`) of a Majorana
field multiplies its mass `m > 0` by `e²`; the mass stays real and positive iff `e = ±1`. -/
/-- The **Majorana-type rephasing invariant** `Im((U_{e i} Ū_{e j})²)`. -/

/-- `majoranaInv` is invariant under all rephasings allowed for Majorana neutrinos: arbitrary
phases `d` of the charged leptons and signs `e = ±1` of the neutrino mass eigenstates. -/

/-- **The Majorana invariant of the Majorana PMNS matrix**:
`Im((U_{e1} Ū_{e2})²) = −c₁₂² s₁₂² c₁₃⁴ sin α`. -/

/-- **Non-zero Majorana CP phase.** For non-degenerate mixing angles the Majorana invariant is
non-zero iff `sin α ≠ 0`. -/
/-! ### Rephasing invariant of the Majorana mass matrix -/
/-- The **Majorana CP invariant of a mass matrix** `I(m) = Im(m_{ii} m_{jj} m̄_{ij}²)`. -/

/-- `I(m)` is invariant under charged-lepton rephasing `m ↦ P m P`, `P = diag(p)`, `|pᵢ| = 1`
(the transformation of a Majorana mass matrix `ν̄ᶜ m ν` under `ν ↦ P ν`). -/
/-- `I(m) = 0` for a real (CP-conserving) mass matrix. -/

/-- **Majorana CP violation cannot be rotated away**: if `I(m) ≠ 0`, no charged-lepton
rephasing makes the Majorana mass matrix real. -/
/-- The real rotation `R(θ)` in two flavours. -/

/-- The **two-flavour Majorana mass matrix** `m = R(θ) diag(m₁, b) R(θ)ᵀ` with a real mass `m₁`
and a complex mass `b` (for `b = m₂ e^{iα}`, `α` is the Majorana phase). -/
/-- `I(m) = c² s² m₁ (m₁² − |b|²) Im b` for the two-flavour Majorana mass matrix. -/

/-- **The Majorana phase of a two-flavour mass matrix**: for `m = R(θ) diag(m₁, m₂ e^{iα}) R(θ)ᵀ`,
`I(m) = c² s² m₁ m₂ (m₁² − m₂²) sin α`. -/

/-- **A Majorana mass matrix generates a non-zero Majorana CP phase** exactly when there is
mixing (`sin 2θ ≠ 0`), the masses are non-zero and non-degenerate, and `sin α ≠ 0`. -/
/-! ### The seesaw of the spectral triple -/

/-- Explicit **three-generation lepton data** of the spectral triple: Dirac neutrino mass
matrix `m_D` with a complex phase, no charged-lepton masses, `M_R = 1` (units of the Majorana
scale). -/

/-- **The spectral seesaw generates a non-zero Majorana CP phase**: for the lepton data
`exampleLeptonData` of the finite spectral triple, the light Majorana mass matrix
`m_ν = −m_D M_R⁻¹ m_Dᵀ` has Majorana invariant `I(m_ν) = 24 ≠ 0`, so it cannot be made real by
any rephasing. -/
/-! ### Leptogenesis -/

/-- **CP asymmetry from interference.** For a decay amplitude `A = c₀ + c₁ L` and its
CP conjugate `Ā = c̄₀ + c̄₁ L`, `|A|² − |Ā|² = 4 Im(c₀ c̄₁) Im(L)`. -/

/-- The **loop function** of the CP asymmetry of heavy-neutrino decays (vertex plus self-energy):
`f(x) = √x (1 + 1/(1 − x) − (1 + x) ln((1 + x)/x))`. -/
/-- **Sign of the loop function**: `f(x) < 0` for `x > 1`. -/
/-- The hermitian matrix `Y† Y` of the neutrino Yukawa couplings. -/

/-- The **exact one-loop CP asymmetry** of the decays of the lightest heavy neutrino `N₁`:
`ε_L = (1/8π) Σ_{j=2,3} Im[((Y†Y)_{1j})²]/(Y†Y)_{11} · f(M_j²/M₁²)`. -/
/-- **CP conservation forbids an asymmetry**: `ε_L = 0` for real Yukawa couplings. -/
/-- `ε_L(t Y) = t² ε_L(Y)` for real `t ≠ 0`. -/

/-- **Positivity of the asymmetry.** If `(Y†Y)_{11} > 0`, `0 < M₁ < M₂, M₃`, and the CP phases
satisfy `Im[((Y†Y)_{1j})²] ≤ 0` with strict inequality for `j = 2`, then `ε_L > 0`. -/
/-- The basic CP-violating Yukawa texture `Y₀ = [[1, 1 − i, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]`. -/

/-- **Exact value of the asymmetry** for the Yukawa couplings `t Y₀`:
`ε_L = −t² f(M₂²/M₁²)/(4π)`. -/
/-- **`ε_L > 0`** for the Yukawa couplings `t Y₀` and any heavy spectrum `0 < M₁ < M₂`. -/
/-! ### Lepton number violation by the Majorana term of `D_F` -/

/-- The **lepton number** of a basis state of `H_F`: `+1` for leptons, `−1` for antileptons,
`0` for quarks and antiquarks. -/
/-- Lepton number on the colour index: `1` on leptons, `0` on quarks. -/

/-- **The Majorana mass term of `D_F` violates lepton number by two units** (and `B − L`, since
these states carry no baryon number): if `(M_R)_{ij} ≠ 0`, `D_F` has a non-zero matrix element
between `ν_R` (`L = 1`) and `ν̄_R` (`L = −1`). -/
/-- The Dirac neutrino Yukawa coupling conserves lepton number. -/
/-! ### Out-of-equilibrium decay and the three Sakharov conditions -/
/-- Tree-level total decay width of `N₁`: `Γ = (Y†Y)_{11} M₁/(8π)`. -/

/-- The Hubble rate in the radiation era at temperature `T`:
`H(T) = 1.66 √g* T²/M_Pl`, with `g* = 106.75` and `M_Pl = 1.22 × 10¹⁹ GeV`. -/
/-- The heavy Majorana spectrum `M = (10¹⁰, 10¹¹, 10¹²) GeV`. -/

/-- **Leptogenesis lepton data of the spectral triple**: Dirac Yukawa couplings `10⁻⁴ Y₀`
and the diagonal Majorana mass matrix `M_R = diag(10¹⁰, 10¹¹, 10¹²) GeV`. -/

comments.text:
/-!
# Spectral free energy of the neutrino sector: normal versus inverted hierarchy

We attach to a Hermitian (mass-squared) operator `H` the heat-kernel partition function and
free energy of the spectral action with cutoff `f(x) = e^{-β x}`,

  `Z_β(H) = Tr e^{-β H}`,      `F_β(H) = -(1/β) log Z_β(H)`     (`β > 0`),

as in the heat-trace expansion `Tr e^{-t D²}` of `RequestProject.SeeleyDeWitt`, applied to the
neutrino block `H = D_ν D_ν† = m_ν m_ν†` of the finite Dirac operator.

* `partitionFn_conj`, `LeptonMixing.freeEnergy_neutrino` : `F_β` only depends on the
  neutrino masses, not on the mixing (the PMNS matrix): `F_β(Hν) = -(1/β) log Σᵢ e^{-β m²ᵢ}`.
* `normalSpectrum`, `invertedSpectrum` : the two neutrino mass orderings compatible with the
  measured splittings `δ = Δm²₂₁ > 0` (solar) and `Δ = |Δm²₃₁|` (atmospheric), with lightest
  squared mass `m₀ ≥ 0`: normal `m₁ < m₂ < m₃` and inverted `m₃ < m₁ < m₂`.
* `spectralFreeEnergy_normal_lt_inverted` : for equal lightest mass, the normal hierarchy has
  strictly smaller free energy than the inverted one (for every `β > 0`);
  `freeEnergy_normal_lt_inverted` is the same statement for the matrices `Hν`, for arbitrary
  PMNS mixing in either case.
* `normal_hierarchy_isLeast` / `normal_hierarchy_unique_minimizer` : among all spectra
  compatible with the splittings (both orderings, all lightest masses `m₀ ≥ 0`), the free
  energy is minimized exactly at the normal hierarchy with massless lightest neutrino.
* `cutoffAction_normal_gt_inverted` : a caveat.  The bosonic spectral action
  `Tr f(D²)` with a positive *decreasing* cutoff `f` itself is **larger** for the normal
  hierarchy; it is the free energy `-(1/β) log Tr e^{-βD²}` (a decreasing function of
  the spectral action) that is minimized.
-/
/-! ### Heat-kernel partition function and free energy -/

/-- The **heat-kernel partition function** `Z_β(H) = Re Tr e^{-β H}` (the spectral action
with cutoff function `e^{-β x}`). -/
/-- The **spectral free energy** `F_β(H) = -(1/β) log Z_β(H)`. -/
/-- The partition function of a mass spectrum `m²`: `Σᵢ e^{-β m²ᵢ}`. -/
/-- The free energy of a mass spectrum `m²`: `-(1/β) log Σᵢ e^{-β m²ᵢ}`. -/
/-- `Tr e^{U D U†} = Σᵢ e^{dᵢ}` for unitary `U` and diagonal `D = diag(d)`. -/

/-- **The partition function only sees the spectrum**: for any unitary `U` (e.g. a mixing
matrix), `Z_β(U diag(m²) U†) = Σᵢ e^{-β m²ᵢ}`. -/
/-- **The free energy only sees the spectrum.** -/

/-- **The neutrino free energy is independent of lepton mixing**: for any lepton mixing data,
`F_β(Hν) = -(1/β) log Σᵢ e^{-β m²_{ν,i}}`, whatever the PMNS matrix is. -/
/-- Shifting all squared masses by `c` shifts the free energy by `c`. -/
/-! ### Normal versus inverted hierarchy -/

/-- Squared neutrino masses `(m₁², m₂², m₃²)` of the **normal hierarchy** with lightest squared
mass `m₀`, solar splitting `δ = m₂² - m₁²` and atmospheric splitting `Δ = m₃² - m₁²`. -/

/-- Squared neutrino masses `(m₁², m₂², m₃²)` of the **inverted hierarchy** with lightest
squared mass `m₀ = m₃²`, solar splitting `δ = m₂² - m₁²` and atmospheric splitting
`Δ = m₁² - m₃²`. -/
/-- The normal hierarchy is ordered as `m₁² < m₂² < m₃²` when `0 < δ < Δ`. -/
/-- The inverted hierarchy is ordered as `m₃² < m₁² < m₂²` when `0 < δ` and `0 < Δ`. -/
/-- The inverted hierarchy has a strictly smaller partition function. -/

/-- **Normal hierarchy has lower free energy.**  For every inverse temperature `β > 0`,
lightest squared mass `m₀` and atmospheric splitting `Δ > 0`, the spectral free energy of
the normal hierarchy is strictly smaller than that of the inverted hierarchy. -/

/-- **Normal hierarchy has lower free energy, at the level of the neutrino mass matrices.**
If `Hν` has the normal and `Hν'` the inverted spectrum (with the same lightest mass and
splittings), then `F_β(Hν) < F_β(Hν')`, for arbitrary lepton mixing in both cases. -/

/-- The set of neutrino spectra compatible with the splittings `δ`, `Δ`: normal or inverted
ordering with any lightest squared mass `m₀ ≥ 0`. -/

/-- **The normal hierarchy minimizes the spectral free energy**: among all spectra
compatible with the splittings, the minimum of `F_β` is attained at the normal hierarchy with
massless lightest neutrino. -/

/-- **Uniqueness of the minimizer**: the normal hierarchy with massless lightest neutrino is
the only admissible spectrum attaining the minimal free energy. -/
/-! ### Caveat: the spectral action itself -/
/-- The (neutrino part of the) spectral action `Tr f(D²) = Σᵢ f(m²ᵢ)` with cutoff `f`. -/

/-- **Caveat.**  For a strictly decreasing cutoff function `f` (as in the spectral action
principle), the spectral action `Tr f(D²)` itself is *larger* for the normal hierarchy than
for the inverted one.  It is the free energy `-(1/β) log Tr e^{-β D²}`, a decreasing function
of the spectral action with `f = e^{-β x}`, which is minimized by the normal hierarchy. -/

/-!
# The PMNS matrix as the unitary mismatch of lepton mass eigenstates

The charged-current (W-boson) interaction of the leptons is diagonal in the flavour basis:
it couples `e_{L,α}` to `ν_{L,α}` via `Σ_α ē_{L,α} ν_{L,α} = ⟨e, ν⟩`.  The mass matrices of
`D_F`, however, are arbitrary.  Going to mass eigenstates, `e_L = U_e e'_L` and
`ν_L = U_ν ν'_L`, where `U_e, U_ν` are unitaries diagonalizing the (left-handed)
mass-squared matrices, the charged current becomes `⟨e', U_PMNS ν'⟩` with

  `U_PMNS = U_e† U_ν`.

* `LeptonMixing He Hν` : unitary diagonalizations of the charged-lepton and the neutrino
  mass-squared matrices `He`, `Hν`;
* `LeptonMixing.pmns` : the PMNS matrix `U_e† U_ν`;
* `pmns_unitary` : it is unitary;
* `chargedCurrent_mass_basis` : the flavour-diagonal charged current becomes the PMNS matrix
  in the mass basis;
* `pmns_neutrino_mass` : in the charged-lepton mass basis the neutrino mass-squared matrix is
  `U_PMNS diag(m²_ν) U_PMNS†`;
* `pmns_eq_one_iff` : there is no mixing iff both sectors are diagonalized by the same unitary;
* `exists_leptonMixing` : such diagonalizations (hence a PMNS matrix) always exist, by the
  spectral theorem, for Hermitian `He`, `Hν` — e.g. `He = m_e m_e†`, `Hν = m_D m_D†`
  (Dirac neutrinos, `diracMassSq_isHermitian`) or `Hν = m_ν† m_ν` (Majorana neutrinos);
* `takagi_diagonalizes` : a Takagi factorization `U_νᵀ m_ν U_ν = diag(m)` of a Majorana mass
  matrix diagonalizes `m_ν† m_ν`, so the seesaw mass matrix of `NCGLeptonSector` fits into the
  same framework;
* `pmns_rephase`, `jarlskog_pmns_rephase` : re-choosing the phases of the mass eigenstates
  rephases the PMNS matrix and leaves its Jarlskog invariant unchanged, so `J_CP` is a
  well-defined observable of the mismatch.
-/

/-- The **left-handed mass-squared matrix** `M M†` of a Dirac mass matrix `M`
(coupling left-handed to right-handed fields). -/
/-- `M M†` is Hermitian. -/

/-- The **left-handed mass-squared matrix** `m† m` of a Majorana mass matrix `m`
(mass term `ν_Lᵀ m ν_L`). -/
/-- `m† m` is Hermitian. -/

/-- **Lepton mixing data**: unitaries `U_e`, `U_ν` diagonalizing the Hermitian
mass-squared matrices `He` of the charged leptons and `Hν` of the neutrinos,
`U_e† He U_e = diag(m²_e)`, `U_ν† Hν U_ν = diag(m²_ν)`.  The columns of `U_e`, `U_ν` are the
mass eigenstates expressed in the flavour basis. -/
/-- Charged-lepton mass eigenstates. -/
/-- Neutrino mass eigenstates. -/
/-- Squared charged-lepton masses. -/
/-- Squared neutrino masses. -/

/-- The **Pontecorvo–Maki–Nakagawa–Sakata matrix** `U_PMNS = U_e† U_ν`: the unitary
mismatch between charged-lepton and neutrino mass eigenstates. -/
/-- **The PMNS matrix is unitary.** -/

/-- **The charged current in the mass basis.**  The W-boson coupling is flavour diagonal,
`Σ_α ē_{L,α} ν_{L,α} = ⟨e, ν⟩`.  Writing the fields in terms of mass eigenstates,
`e = U_e e'`, `ν = U_ν ν'`, it becomes `⟨e', U_PMNS ν'⟩`: the lepton mixing matrix is exactly
the mismatch `U_e† U_ν`. -/

/-- In the charged-lepton mass basis the neutrino mass-squared matrix is
`U_PMNS diag(m²_ν) U_PMNS†`. -/

/-- The charged-lepton mass-squared matrix is diagonal in its own mass basis, while the
neutrino one is obtained from the PMNS matrix: the two relations together say that the
PMNS matrix is the change of basis between the two sets of mass eigenstates,
`U_ν = U_e U_PMNS`. -/

/-- **No mixing iff aligned mass bases**: `U_PMNS = 1` iff the neutrino and
charged-lepton mass eigenstates coincide. -/

/-- **Existence of the PMNS matrix.**  For Hermitian mass-squared matrices (such as
`m_e m_e†` and `m_D m_D†` or `m_ν† m_ν`) unitary diagonalizations always exist
(spectral theorem), so a PMNS matrix `U_e† U_ν` is always defined. -/

/-- **Takagi factorization diagonalizes `m† m`.**  If a unitary `U` brings a Majorana mass
matrix to real diagonal form, `Uᵀ m U = diag(d)`, then `U† (m† m) U = diag(d²)`.  So the
neutrino mass eigenstates of a Majorana mass matrix (e.g. the seesaw mass `seesawMass`)
are the columns of `U`, with squared masses `d²`. -/
-- `conj U * Uᵀ = 1`
/-! ### Rephasing invariance -/

/-- Re-choosing the phases of the mass eigenstates, `U_e ↦ U_e diag(d)`, `U_ν ↦ U_ν diag(e)`,
rephases the PMNS matrix: `U_PMNS ↦ diag(d̄) U_PMNS diag(e)`. -/

/-- **The Jarlskog invariant is a physical observable of the mismatch**: it does not depend
on the choice of phases of the lepton mass eigenstates. -/

/-- **PMNS matrix of the leptonic spectral triple, Dirac neutrinos.**  For every
three-generation lepton data the charged-lepton mass matrix `m_e` and the Dirac neutrino
mass matrix `m_D` of `D_F` admit unitary diagonalizations of `m_e m_e†` and `m_D m_D†`,
hence a unitary PMNS matrix. -/

/-- **PMNS matrix of the leptonic spectral triple, seesaw (Majorana) neutrinos.**  The light
neutrino mass matrix `m_ν = -m_D M_R⁻¹ m_Dᵀ` produced by the Majorana term of `D_F` defines,
together with `m_e`, a unitary PMNS matrix. -/

/-!
# Breaking Pati–Salam to the Standard Model through the finite Dirac operator

This file continues `RequestProject.NCGPatiSalamTriple`. The Majorana entry `M = majo Y_R` of
the finite Dirac operator couples `ν_R` to `ν̄_R`. It breaks the Pati–Salam algebra
`A_PS = ℍ_R ⊕ ℍ_L ⊕ M₄(ℂ)` to the Standard Model algebra `A_SM = ℂ ⊕ ℍ ⊕ M₃(ℂ)`:

* `ps_majorana_commute_iff_mem_SM`: `a ∈ A_PS` commutes with the Majorana part of `D_F`
  exactly when `a ∈ A_SM`, provided `Y_R ≠ 0`.
* `mem_SM_of_firstOrder`: if `a` satisfies the first-order condition against every
  `b ∈ A_PS`, then `a ∈ A_SM`.
* `ps_firstOrder_iff_mem_SM`: under the Pati–Salam Yukawa relations `Y_ν = Y_u`, `Y_e = Y_d`,
  the converse also holds.
* `psFiniteTriple_not_firstOrder`: the Pati–Salam triple violates the first-order condition.
* `innerFluct_SM_majorana`: inner fluctuations by `A_SM` leave the Majorana block fixed.
* `innerFluct_PS_majorana`: a self-adjoint Pati–Salam fluctuation rescales it to
  `(1 + 2t) M`. So the Majorana entry is a dynamical scalar field `σ` only in the
  Pati–Salam model, and its vacuum value `Y_R ≠ 0` breaks `A_PS` to `A_SM`.
-/
/-! ## Products of the Majorana block with the Pati–Salam representation -/

/-- An element of `A_PS` whose right-handed quaternion has no `j, k` part, whose `4 × 4`
matrix is block-diagonal, and whose lepton–lepton entry matches, lies in `A_SM`. -/
/-- A nonzero matrix has a nonzero entry. -/
/-! ## The Majorana term breaks `A_PS` to `A_SM` -/

/-- **The Majorana mass term selects the Standard Model algebra.** Suppose the Majorana
matrix is nonzero, `Y_R ≠ 0`. An element `a ∈ A_PS` commutes with the Majorana part
`[[0, M], [M*, 0]]` of `D_F`, i.e. `M π_anti(a) = π_part(a) M` and
`M* π_part(a) = π_anti(a) M*`, exactly when `a ∈ A_SM = ℂ ⊕ ℍ ⊕ M₃(ℂ)`. -/

/-- The commutator `[D_F, π_PS(a)]` in block form. The off-diagonal blocks are the
commutators of `π_PS(a)` with the Majorana part. -/
/-- The element `e = (0, 0, 1) ∈ A_PS`. Its image is the projection onto antiparticles. -/

/-- **The first-order condition forces `a ∈ A_SM`.** If `Y_R ≠ 0` and `a ∈ A_PS` satisfies
`[[D_F, π(a)], J_F π(b) J_F⁻¹] = 0` for every `b ∈ A_PS`, then `a` lies in the Standard Model
subalgebra. The pair `(a, e)` with `e = (0, 0, 1)` already suffices. -/
/-- `Pℓ + P_q = 1` on the colour index. -/
/-- With equal lepton and quark Yukawa matrices, `yuk A A = 1 ⊗ A` is colour-blind. -/

/-- Under the Pati–Salam Yukawa relations `Y_ν = Y_u`, `Y_e = Y_d`, the Yukawa part of `D_F`
commutes with the `M₄(ℂ)` colour action. -/

/-- **The first-order condition breaks `A_PS` to `A_SM`.** Suppose the Majorana matrix is
nonzero (`Y_R ≠ 0`) and the Yukawa couplings obey the Pati–Salam relations `Y_ν = Y_u`,
`Y_e = Y_d`. Then `a ∈ A_PS` satisfies the first-order condition
`[[D_F, π(a)], J_F π(b) J_F⁻¹] = 0` against every `b ∈ A_PS` exactly when `a` lies in the
Standard Model subalgebra `ℂ ⊕ ℍ ⊕ M₃(ℂ)`. -/

/-- **The Pati–Salam triple violates the first-order condition** whenever `Y_R ≠ 0`. The
element `(j, 0, 0) ∈ A_PS`, whose right-handed quaternion is not complex, fails it. -/
/-! ## Inner fluctuations -/

/-- **Standard Model fluctuations do not fluctuate the Majorana entry.** For every inner
fluctuation `D_A = D + A + J A J⁻¹` with `A = Σ π(aᵢ)[D, π(bᵢ)]` and `aᵢ, bᵢ ∈ A_SM`, the
Majorana block of `D_A` (particle–antiparticle) is still `M = majo Y_R`. -/

/-- The self-adjoint Pati–Salam fluctuation with parameter `t`:
`A = t (1 - e)[D, e] + t e [D, 1 - e]`, where `e = (0, 0, 1)`. -/
/-- The second entries `bᵢ` of the Pati–Salam fluctuation: `(e, 1 - e)`. -/

/-- **Pati–Salam fluctuations make the Majorana entry dynamical.** The self-adjoint inner
fluctuation `A = t(1 - e)[D, e] + t e[D, 1 - e]`, with `e = (0, 0, 1) ∈ A_PS` and `t ∈ ℝ`,
rescales the Majorana block of `D_A = D + A + J A J⁻¹` to `(1 + 2t) M`. So the Majorana
entry becomes a scalar field `σ` (the singlet component of the Pati–Salam field `Σ`), and the
vacuum `σ = Y_R ≠ 0` breaks `A_PS` to `A_SM` (`ps_firstOrder_iff_mem_SM`). -/

/-!
# Pati–Salam vector leptoquarks, their mass from the Majorana vev, and `K_L → μ e`

This file extends `RequestProject.NCGPatiSalamWRBound`. It adds the `SU(4)` vector leptoquarks
`X^α_μ` of the Pati–Salam model, their gauge interactions, and their mass matrix from the
Majorana expectation value. It then proves lower bounds on `M_LQ` from the lepton-flavour
violating kaon decays `K_L → μ e` and `K⁺ → π⁺ μ e`.

**Mass matrix from the Majorana vev.**
* The Majorana block of the finite Dirac operator is `vevDir ⊗ Y_R`, where `vevDir = e_{ν_R}` on
  right-handed isospin ⊗ colour (`majo_eq_vevDir_mul`). The Pati–Salam scalar obtained by
  fluctuating this block has its vev `⟨Δ⟩ = v_R · vevDir` in the lepton-colour direction.
* `gaugeMassSq` is the gauge boson mass matrix `M²(h,h') = 2 Re tr(S(h)ᴴ S(h'))`, where
  `S(h) = G(h)⟨Δ⟩ + ⟨Δ⟩G(h)ᵀ` and `G(h) = g_R h_R ⊗ 1 + g_4 1 ⊗ h_c`. It is computed in closed
  form (`gaugeMassSq_eq`), is positive semidefinite, and vanishes on `h` exactly when
  `G(h) ν_R = 0` (`gaugeMassSq_self_eq_zero_iff`).
* Breaking pattern. The `SU(3)_c` generators stay massless (`colorGen_massless`), and so does the
  hypercharge `Y = T_{3R} + (B-L)/2` (`hyperGen_massless`). `T_{3R}`, `B - L`
  (`gaugeMassSq_BL`) and `W_R^±` (`gaugeMassSq_T1R`) get masses. So
  `SU(4) → SU(3)_c × U(1)_{B-L}`, and then `SU(2)_R × U(1)_{B-L} → U(1)_Y`, both driven by the
  same Majorana vev.
* **The leptoquark block** (`gaugeMassSq_lqGen`). On the six leptoquark generators `T^α_k` of
  `SU(4)` the mass matrix is `M_LQ² · 1₆`, with `M_LQ² = g_4² v_R²`. The leptoquarks do not mix
  with `T_{3R}` or `B - L`.

**Gauge interactions.** `lqCoupling g4 X = (g_4/√2)(X^α E_{ℓα} + h.c.)` is the `SU(4)` gauge field
of the complex leptoquarks (`lqCoupling_eq_sum_gen`). It changes quarks into leptons and has no
quark–quark or lepton–lepton part. It acts with the same matrix on both chiralities
(`lqField_antiOp`), so the coupling is vector-like. At low energies, exchange gives the
four-fermion coefficient `C = g_4²/(2M_LQ²) = 1/(2v_R²)` (`lqFourFermion_lqMass`).

**Kaon decays.**
* `klMuERate`: `Γ(K_L → μ^± e^∓)` from the chirally enhanced pseudoscalar operator.
* `MLQ_gt_1200TeV`: with the inputs `KLInputs`, `BR(K_L → μe) < 4.7 × 10⁻¹²` implies
  `M_LQ > 1.2 PeV`. `ps_lqMass_gt_1200TeV` gives the same bound for the mass eigenvalue
  `M_LQ = g_4 v_R`, together with `v_R > 1.2 PeV/g_4`.
* `MLQ_gt_50TeV_Kplus`: the vector channel of `K⁺ → π⁺ μ⁺ e⁻` with
  `BR < 1.3 × 10⁻¹¹` implies `M_LQ > 50 TeV`.
* `klMuE_constraint_satisfiable` shows the hypotheses can be met (a `2 PeV` leptoquark is
  allowed). `MLQ_bound_needs_g4` shows the numerical bound depends on the input `g_4 ≥ 0.75`.

**What is modelled, not derived.** Several steps are encoded in the rate formulas and the input
ranges rather than proved in Lean:
* the Fierz rearrangement of the vector–vector operator into the pseudoscalar operator;
* the PCAC matrix element and the two-body phase space;
* the value of `g_4` at `M_LQ`, which is an input and not obtained by running;
* QCD running of the pseudoscalar operator from `M_LQ` down to the kaon scale. This running
  enhances the operator, so leaving it out weakens the bound;
* quark–lepton flavour alignment (`d ↔ e`, `s ↔ μ` in the same `SU(4)` multiplet).
The numerical inputs (`f_K`, `m_s + m_d`, `τ_{K_L}`, `g_4`) are external.
-/
/-- The lepton colour, the fourth colour of `SU(4)` (`Sum.inl 0` in `Col = Fin 1 ⊕ Fin 3`). -/

/-- Right-handed isospin ⊗ colour, the index set of the `SU(2)_R × SU(4)` fundamental on which
the Majorana field acts (one generation). -/
/-- The right-handed neutrino direction: up-type isospin and lepton colour. -/

/-- **Direction of the Majorana vacuum expectation value.** The Majorana block `majo Y_R` of the
finite Dirac operator is `e_{ν_R} ⊗ Pℓ ⊗ Y_R` (`majo_eq_vevDir_mul`). Its isospin ⊗ colour
factor `e_{00} ⊗ Pℓ` is the direction of the expectation value of the Pati–Salam scalar that
comes from fluctuating the Majorana term. Here `Pℓ` projects on the lepton colour. -/
/-- The vev direction is the matrix unit at `ν_R`. -/

/-- **The covariant derivative on the Majorana field.** For a Lie algebra element `h = (h_R,
h_L, h_c)` the Majorana field sees `g_R h_R ⊗ 1 + g_4 1 ⊗ h_c` on isospin ⊗ colour. It carries
no `SU(2)_L` charge. -/

/-- **The gauge variation of the Majorana vev.** The Majorana field `Δ` is symmetric in isospin
⊗ colour (it pairs `ν_R` with `ν_R`), so it transforms as `Δ ↦ UΔUᵀ`. The linearised action of
`h` on `⟨Δ⟩ = v_R · vevDir` is `S(h) = G(h)⟨Δ⟩ + ⟨Δ⟩G(h)ᵀ`, where `G(h) = covGen`. -/

/-- The column `c(h)_x = G(h)_{x, ν_R}` of the covariant generator at `ν_R`. The gauge boson
mass matrix depends on `h` only through `c(h)` (`trace_vevShift`). -/
/-- Entries of `S(h)`: `S(h)_{xy} = v_R (δ_{y,ν_R} c(h)_x + δ_{x,ν_R} c(h)_y)`. -/

/-- **The gauge boson mass matrix generated by the Majorana vev.** The kinetic term `tr|D_μΔ|²`
evaluated at `⟨Δ⟩` gives `½ M²(h,h') A^h A^{h'}` with `M²(h,h') = 2 Re tr(S(h)ᴴ S(h'))`. This is
the mass matrix of the `SU(2)_R × SU(4)` gauge fields in the basis of Hermitian generators `h`.
We normalise so that `M_W = g v/2` for the Standard Model doublet with vev `(0, v/√2)`. -/

/-- The mass matrix in terms of the column `c(h)`: `M²(h,h') = 4 v_R² Re(Σ_x c̄(h)_x c(h')_x +
c̄(h)_{ν_R} c(h')_{ν_R})`. -/
/-- Diagonal entries: `M²(h,h) = 4 v_R² (Σ_x |c(h)_x|² + |c(h)_{ν_R}|²)`. -/
/-- The mass matrix is positive semidefinite. -/

/-- **The unbroken generators.** For `v_R ≠ 0`, a generator is massless (`M²(h,h) = 0`) exactly
when `c(h) = 0`, i.e. when `G(h)` annihilates `ν_R`. These generators form the stabiliser of the
Majorana vev. -/
/-- A generator with `c(h) = 0` has no mass mixing with any generator. -/
/-- A generator with `c(h) = 0` has no mass mixing with any generator (right argument). -/
/-- The mass matrix is symmetric. -/
/-! ### The unbroken generators -/
/-- An `SU(3)_c ⊂ SU(4)` generator `diag(0, m)`, acting only on the three quark colours. -/
/-- `SU(3)_c` generators annihilate `ν_R`. -/

/-- **`SU(4) → SU(3)_c`: the gluons stay massless.** Every `SU(3)_c` generator is massless and
does not mix with any other gauge field. -/

/-- The combination `(g_4 T_{3R}, 0, g_R (B-L)/2)`. Its covariant generator is `g_R g_4 (T_{3R}
+ (B-L)/2) = g_R g_4 Y` (`covGen_hyperGen`). -/

/-- The covariant generator of `hyperGen` is proportional to the hypercharge `Y = T_{3R} ⊗ 1 + 1
⊗ (B-L)/2`. -/
/-- The hypercharge annihilates `ν_R`: `Y(ν_R) = 1/2 - 1/2 = 0`. -/
/-- **`SU(2)_R × U(1)_{B-L} → U(1)_Y`: the hypercharge boson stays massless.** -/
/-! ### The broken generators -/
/-- `T_{3R}` alone is broken: `M²(T_{3R}, T_{3R}) = 2 g_R² v_R²`. -/

/-- **`U(1)_{B-L}` is broken by the Majorana vev**: `M²((B-L)/2, (B-L)/2) = 2 g_4² v_R²`. Only
the combination `Y` survives (`hyperGen_massless`). -/
/-- The `SU(2)_R` generator `σ₁/2`. -/
/-- The charged `W_R` mass from the Majorana vev: `M²(σ₁/2, σ₁/2) = g_R² v_R²`. -/
/-! ### Leptoquarks -/
/-- The weights `(1/2, i/2)` of the two real leptoquark generators. -/

/-- **The leptoquark generators of `SU(4)`.** For a quark colour `α` and `k ∈ {0,1}`: `T^α_0 =
(E_{αℓ} + E_{ℓα})/2` and `T^α_1 = i(E_{αℓ} - E_{ℓα})/2`. These six generators connect the lepton
colour `ℓ` with the quark colours. They are the generators of `SU(4)` outside `SU(3)_c ×
U(1)_{B-L}`. -/
/-- The leptoquark generators as Pati–Salam Lie algebra elements `(0, 0, T^α_k)`. -/
/-- The leptoquark generators are Hermitian. -/
/-- The leptoquark generators are traceless, so they lie in `su(4)`. -/
/-- The leptoquark generators are normalised: `tr((T^α_k)²) = 1/2`. -/
/-- `c(T^α_k)` is supported at `(u, α)`, with value `g_4 w_k`. -/
/-- **The Pati–Salam leptoquark mass squared** `M_LQ² = g_4² v_R²`. -/

/-- **The leptoquark block of the mass matrix.** On the six leptoquark generators the mass
matrix is `M_LQ² · 1₆` with `M_LQ² = g_4² v_R²`. So the Majorana vev gives all six real
leptoquark fields, i.e. the three complex vector leptoquarks `X^α_μ`, the common mass `M_LQ =
g_4 v_R`. -/
/-- The leptoquarks do not mix with `T_{3R}`. -/
/-- The leptoquarks do not mix with `B - L`. -/
/-! ### The Majorana vev -/

/-- **The Majorana block is `vevDir ⊗ Y_R`.** Entry by entry, the right-handed block of `majo
Y_R` is the vev direction on isospin ⊗ colour times `Y_R` on generations. So the colour
structure of the Majorana mass term is the lepton-colour direction that breaks `SU(4)` to
`SU(3)_c`. -/
/-! ### The leptoquark gauge field -/

/-- **The leptoquark gauge field.** For complex vector leptoquark fields `X^α_μ` (`α` a quark
colour) the `SU(4)` gauge field is `(g_4/√2)(X^α E_{ℓα} + X̄^α E_{αℓ})`. Acting on the colour
index, it turns a quark of colour `α` into a lepton with coupling `g_4/√2`, and a lepton into a
quark. -/
/-- The leptoquark gauge field as a Pati–Salam Lie algebra element `(0, 0, lqCoupling)`. -/

/-- **Normalisation of the leptoquark vertex.** For real fields `A^α_0, A^α_1`, `g_4 Σ_α (A^α_0
T^α_0 + A^α_1 T^α_1)` equals the leptoquark gauge field with `X^α = (A^α_0 - i A^α_1)/√2`. So
the complex leptoquark couples with strength `g_4/√2`, and its mass term is `M_LQ² |X|²`. -/
/-- The leptoquark gauge field is Hermitian. -/
/-- The leptoquark gauge field is traceless. -/
/-- The leptoquark field has no lepton–lepton component: `Pℓ X Pℓ = 0`. -/
/-- The leptoquark field has no quark–quark component: `P_q X P_q = 0`. -/
/-- The leptoquark field does not act on the isospin index of particles. -/

/-- **The leptoquark coupling is vector-like.** On `H_F` the leptoquark field acts through the
colour index with the same matrix on the right-handed and the left-handed block. Its couplings
to `q̄_L γ^μ ℓ_L` and `q̄_R γ^μ ℓ_R` are equal (`g_4/√2`). In `K_L → μ e` this gives the
chirally enhanced pseudoscalar operator. -/
/-! ### The four-fermion interaction -/

/-- **The four-fermion coefficient from leptoquark exchange**, `C = g_4²/(2 M_LQ²)`. At momenta
`≪ M_LQ`, exchanging `X` between the vertices `(s, μ)` and `(d, e)` gives `C (s̄ γ^μ μ)(ē γ_μ
d)` plus Hermitian conjugate. -/
/-- `C = (g_4/√2)²/M_LQ²`: two vertices `g_4/√2` and the propagator `1/M_LQ²`. -/

/-- **The Pati–Salam vector leptoquark mass** `M_LQ = √(g_4² v_R²)`, the eigenvalue of the
leptoquark block of the mass matrix. -/
/-- `M_LQ² = g_4² v_R²`. -/

/-- The four-fermion coefficient depends only on the Majorana vev: `C = g_4²/(2 M_LQ²) = 1/(2
v_R²)`. -/

/-- **The kaon pseudoscalar matrix element** `|⟨0|s̄ γ₅ d|K⁰⟩| = f_K m_K²/(m_s + m_d)` (from the
PCAC relation). The argument `msd` is `m_s + m_d`. -/

/-- **The rate `Γ(K_L → μ^± e^∓)` (both charge states).** Fierzing the vector–vector operator `C
(s̄ γ^μ μ)(ē γ_μ d)` gives, from its `LR` and `RL` parts, a pseudoscalar operator with
coefficient `C_P = C`, as `(s̄ γ₅ d)(ē γ₅ μ)`. With `K_L ≈ (K⁰ ± K̄⁰)/√2`, `m_e = 0` and both
charge states summed, `Γ = C_P² |⟨0|s̄γ₅d|K⟩|² (m_K² - m_μ²)²/(8π m_K³)`. The
helicity-suppressed axial-vector part is dropped. -/
/-- The branching ratio `BR = Γ τ/ħ`. -/
/-- `Γ(K_L → μe) = C_P² f_K² m_K (m_K² - m_μ²)²/(8π (m_s + m_d)²)`. -/

/-- **Inputs for `K_L → μ e`** (GeV, seconds). The ranges are modelling assumptions, not derived
in Lean.
* `fK ≥ 0.155` (kaon decay constant `f_K ≈ 155.7 MeV`).
* `0.4976 ≤ mK ≤ 0.4977` (`m_{K⁰}`), `0.1056 ≤ mmu ≤ 0.1057` (`m_μ`).
* `0 < msd ≤ 0.1`: `m_s + m_d` (MS-bar at 2 GeV, `≈ 0.098`).
* `tauL ≥ 5.1 × 10⁻⁸ s` (`τ_{K_L} = 5.116 × 10⁻⁸ s`).
* `0 < hbar ≤ 6.583 × 10⁻²⁵ GeV s`.
* `g4 ≥ 0.75`: the `SU(4)` coupling at `M_LQ`, i.e. `g_3` there (`α_s(1 PeV) ≈ 0.05` gives `g_3
  ≈ 0.8`). -/

/-- **`M_LQ > 1.2 PeV` from `BR(K_L → μe) < 4.7 × 10⁻¹²`.** With the inputs of `KLInputs`,
suppose the leptoquark-mediated branching ratio is below the experimental limit `4.7 × 10⁻¹²`.
Then `M_LQ > 1.2 × 10⁶ GeV = 1.2 PeV`. -/

/-- **`M_LQ > 1.2 PeV` for the leptoquark mass generated by the Majorana vev.** Here `M_LQ = g_4
v_R` is the leptoquark eigenvalue of the mass matrix (`gaugeMassSq_lqGen`). Under the `K_L → μe`
limit, `M_LQ > 1.2 PeV` and `v_R > 1.2 PeV / g_4`. -/
/-- Upper bound on the `K_L → μe` branching ratio at the central inputs, using `π > 3.14`. -/

/-- The hypotheses of `MLQ_gt_1200TeV` can be met: with the central inputs (`f_K = 0.1557`, `m_s
+ m_d = 0.098`, `τ = 5.116 × 10⁻⁸ s`, `ħ = 6.582 × 10⁻²⁵ GeV s`, `g_4 = 0.8`), a `2 PeV`
leptoquark satisfies `BR(K_L → μe) < 4.7 × 10⁻¹²`. -/

/-- **The numerical bound depends on `g_4`.** With `g_4 = 0.5` and the other central inputs, a
`1 PeV` leptoquark satisfies the `K_L → μe` limit. So `M_LQ > 1.2 PeV` rests on the input `g_4 ≥
0.75`. -/

/-- **The rate `Γ(K⁺ → π⁺ μ⁺ e⁻)`, vector channel.** The `LL + RR` part of the Fierzed operator
contains `(C/2)(s̄ γ^μ d)(ē γ_μ μ)`. With `⟨π⁺|s̄ γ^μ d|K⁺⟩ = f₊ (p_K + p_π)^μ`, `Γ = (C/2)² f₊²
m_K⁵ I/(768π³)`, where `I` is the phase-space integral (`I ≈ 0.6` for massless leptons, less
with `m_μ`). For massless leptons the scalar channel `(s̄d)(ēμ)` does not interfere with the
vector channel, so this is a lower bound on the rate in that limit. -/

/-- **Inputs for `K⁺ → π⁺ μ⁺ e⁻`** (modelling assumptions): `f₊ ≥ 0.96`, `m_{K⁺} ≥ 0.4936 GeV`,
phase-space factor `I ≥ 0.4`, `τ_{K⁺} ≥ 1.23 × 10⁻⁸ s`, `ħ ≤ 6.583 × 10⁻²⁵ GeV s`, `g_4 ≥ 0.75`. -/

/-- **`M_LQ > 50 TeV` from `BR(K⁺ → π⁺ μ⁺ e⁻) < 1.3 × 10⁻¹¹`** (vector channel only). This is
much weaker than the `K_L → μe` bound, because the vector channel has no chiral enhancement. -/

/-!
# QCD running of the `K_L → μ e` operator

`RequestProject.NCGPatiSalamLeptoquarkRunning` proves `M_LQ > 1.2 PeV`
(`NCG.PatiSalam.MLQ_gt_1200TeV_running`), but evaluates the tree-level coefficient
`C_P = g₄²/(2 M_LQ²)`, fixed at `μ = M_LQ`, against the hadronic matrix element
`f_K m_K²/(m_s + m_d)` taken at the low scale (`m_s + m_d ≤ 0.1 GeV`, MS-bar at `2 GeV`).
This file adds the QCD running of the pseudoscalar operator `(s̄ γ₅ d)(ē γ₅ μ)` between the two
scales, and shows that leaving it out was conservative.

With `t = ln μ`, the quark mass `m(t)` runs as `dm/dt = -γ_m(t) m` with `γ_m ≥ 0` (at one loop
`γ_m = 6 C_F α_s/(4π) > 0`). The combination `m · s̄γ₅d` is renormalisation-group invariant, so the
Wilson coefficient of `s̄γ₅d` runs like the mass: `dC/dt = -γ_m(t) C`.

* `OperatorRunning.ratio_eq` : `C(t)/m(t)` does not depend on `t`, so the amplitude
  `C(μ) f_K m_K²/m(μ)` is the same at every scale.
* `OperatorRunning.m_antitoneOn` : the mass decreases as the scale increases.
* `OperatorRunning.C_low_ge` : running down from `M_LQ` enhances the coefficient,
  `C(μ₀) ≥ C(M_LQ)` for `μ₀ ≤ M_LQ` when `C(M_LQ) ≥ 0`.
* `MLQ_gt_1200TeV_opRunning` : with the coefficient run down to the scale `μ₀` at which
  `m_s + m_d` is quoted, `BR(K_L → μ e) < 4.7 × 10⁻¹²` still implies `M_LQ > 1.2 PeV`.
* `constOperatorRunning`, `klMuE_opRunning_satisfiable` : the hypotheses can be met, by explicit
  solutions with constant `γ_m = 0.05`; a `10 PeV` leptoquark then passes the `K_L → μ e` limit.
-/

/-- **Running of the quark mass and the pseudoscalar Wilson coefficient.** As functions of
`t = ln μ`, the mass `m = m_s + m_d` and the coefficient `C` of `(s̄ γ₅ d)(ē γ₅ μ)` both solve
`dX/dt = -γ_m(t) X`, where the mass anomalous dimension satisfies `γ_m(t) ≥ 0`. The mass is
positive. -/

/-- **The amplitude is scale independent.** `C(t)/m(t) = C(s)/m(s)` for all `t, s`, so
`C(μ) ⟨0|s̄γ₅d|K⟩(μ) = C(μ) f_K m_K²/m(μ)` is the same at every scale. -/

/-- **The mass decreases with the scale.** Since `dm/dt = -γ_m m ≤ 0`, `m(t) ≤ m(s)` whenever
`s ≤ t`. -/

/-- **Running down enhances the coefficient.** If `s ≤ t` and `C(t) ≥ 0`, then
`C(s) = C(t) m(s)/m(t) ≥ C(t)`. -/

/-- **`M_LQ > 1.2 PeV` with the operator run down to the hadronic scale.** Take the inputs of
`MLQ_gt_1200TeV_running`, and an `OperatorRunning` whose coefficient equals the tree-level value
`g₃(M_LQ)²/(2 M_LQ²)` at `μ = M_LQ`, and let `μ₀ ≤ M_LQ` be the scale at which the matrix
element (with the input `m_s + m_d`) is evaluated. Suppose the branching ratio computed with the
run-down coefficient `C(μ₀)` is below `4.7 × 10⁻¹²`. Then `M_LQ > 1.2 × 10⁶ GeV`. -/

/-- Explicit solutions with constant anomalous dimension `γ_m = 0.05`: `m(t) = 0.098 e^{-0.05 t}`
and `C(t) = C₀ e^{-0.05 (t - t₀)}`, so that `C(t₀) = C₀`. -/

/-- **The operator-running bound is not vacuous.** With the central hadronic inputs (quark mass
quoted at `μ₀ = 1 GeV`, so `m(0) = 0.098`), the six-flavour running from `α_s(M_Z) = 0.118`, and
the explicit operator running with `γ_m = 0.05` matched to the tree-level coefficient at
`M_LQ = 10 PeV`, the branching ratio is below `4.7 × 10⁻¹²`. -/

/-!
# The leptoquark bound with `g₄(M_LQ)` obtained from the running strong coupling

`RequestProject.NCGPatiSalamLeptoquark` proves `M_LQ > 1.2 PeV` from
`BR(K_L → μ e) < 4.7 × 10⁻¹²` (`NCG.PatiSalam.MLQ_gt_1200TeV`), but takes `g₄ ≥ 0.75` at the
leptoquark mass as an external input. This file removes that input.

At the breaking scale the `SU(4)` coupling matches the colour coupling, `g₄ = g₃`
(`NCG.PatiSalam.ps_to_sm_matching`). Below `M_LQ` the colour coupling runs with the one-loop
renormalisation group equation `dg/dt = β(t) g³/(16π²)`, `t = ln(μ/M_Z)`, of
`RequestProject.NCGRunning`. The coefficient `β(t)` may vary with `t` (quark thresholds), and is
only required to satisfy `β(t) ≥ -23/3`, the five-flavour value; the six-flavour value
`b₃ = -7` (`NCG.b3_SM`) satisfies it. Starting from `α_s(M_Z) ≥ 0.117`:

* `inv_sq_le_of_rge_bounded` : `1/g(t)² ≤ 1/g(0)² + c t/(8π²)` whenever `β ≥ -c`.
* `StrongRunning.coupling_ge` : `g₃(μ) ≥ 0.75` for every `M_Z ≤ μ ≤ 1.2 PeV`.
* `MLQ_gt_1200TeV_running` : with `g₄ = g₃(M_LQ)` and the hadronic inputs of
  `KLHadronicInputs`, `BR(K_L → μ e) < 4.7 × 10⁻¹²` implies `M_LQ > 1.2 PeV`. The argument is
  self-consistent: if `M_LQ ≤ 1.2 PeV`, then `g₄(M_LQ) ≥ 0.75`, and the fixed-coupling bound
  gives `M_LQ > 1.2 PeV`.
* `strongRunning_nonempty`, `klMuE_running_satisfiable` : the hypotheses can be met, by the
  explicit six-flavour solution `rgeSol (-7)` with `α_s(M_Z) = 0.118`, and a `3 PeV` leptoquark
  then passes the `K_L → μ e` limit.
-/

/-- **Running with a bounded one-loop coefficient.** Suppose `g > 0` solves
`dg/dt = β(t) g³/(16π²)` for `t ≥ 0`, with `β(t) ≥ -c`. Then `1/g(t)² ≤ 1/g(0)² + c t/(8π²)`
for all `t ≥ 0`. This generalises `NCG.inv_sq_eq_of_rge` (constant `β = b`) to a coefficient
that changes at quark thresholds. -/

/-- **The running strong coupling below the leptoquark scale.** `MZ` is the `Z` mass (in GeV)
and `alphaS = α_s(M_Z)`. The function `g` is the colour coupling as a function of
`t = ln(μ/M_Z)`: it starts at `g(0) = √(4π α_s(M_Z))` and solves the one-loop equation
`dg/dt = β(t) g³/(16π²)` with `β(t) ≥ -23/3` (the five-flavour value; the six-flavour value is
`b₃ = -7`) for all `t ≥ 0`. -/
/-- The colour coupling `g₃(μ) = g(ln(μ/M_Z))` at the scale `μ` (in GeV). -/

/-- **`g₃(μ) ≥ 0.75` up to `1.2 PeV`.** For `M_Z ≤ μ ≤ 1.2 × 10⁶ GeV`, the running colour
coupling is at least `0.75`: the input `g₄ ≥ 0.75` of `KLInputs` is a consequence of
`α_s(M_Z) ≥ 0.117` and one-loop running. -/

/-- **The hadronic and lifetime inputs of the `K_L → μ e` bound.** These are the fields of
`KLInputs` without the coupling `g₄`, which is now computed from the running. -/

/-- Completing the hadronic inputs by a coupling `g₄ ≥ 0.75` gives the inputs of
`MLQ_gt_1200TeV`. -/

/-- **`M_LQ > 1.2 PeV` with the running coupling.** Take the hadronic inputs of
`KLHadronicInputs`, the running colour coupling of `StrongRunning`, and the matching
`g₄ = g₃(M_LQ)` at the leptoquark mass (`ps_to_sm_matching`). Suppose the leptoquark is heavier
than the `Z` and `BR(K_L → μ e) < 4.7 × 10⁻¹²`. Then `M_LQ > 1.2 × 10⁶ GeV`. No lower bound on
`g₄` is assumed. -/

/-- The explicit six-flavour solution `rgeSol (-7)` from `α_s(M_Z) = 0.118` at
`M_Z = 91.1876 GeV` satisfies the hypotheses of `StrongRunning`. -/
/-- The hypotheses of `StrongRunning` can be met. -/

/-- **The running bound is not vacuous.** With the central hadronic inputs and the six-flavour
running from `α_s(M_Z) = 0.118`, a `3 PeV` leptoquark satisfies
`BR(K_L → μ e) < 4.7 × 10⁻¹²`. -/

  su2L : ∀ h, IsSU2LGen h →

    f0 / (24 * Real.pi ^ 2) * (gR ^ 2 * (trace (h.gaugeOp N * h.gaugeOp N)).re) = 1 / 4

    f0 / (24 * Real.pi ^ 2) * (g4 ^ 2 * (trace (h.gaugeOp N * h.gaugeOp N)).re) = 1 / 4

structure PSSpectralAction (N : ℕ) where
  /-- The index set of the spectrum. -/
  ι : Type
  [countable : Countable ι]
  /-- The spectrum of the fluctuated Dirac operator `D_A`. -/
  D : @DiscreteSpectrum ι countable
  /-- The cutoff function `f`. -/
  c : LaplaceCutoff
  /-- The Seeley–DeWitt coefficients `a₀, a₂, a₄, …` (indexed `0, 1, 2, …`). -/
  a : ℕ → ℝ
  heat : HeatTraceExpansion 4 a (@DiscreteSpectrum.heatTrace ι countable D)
  /-- The couplings `g_L, g_R, g₄`. -/
  g : Fin 3 → ℝ
  /-- The Yang–Mills integrals `∫ Fᵢ²`. -/
  YM : Fin 3 → ℝ
  /-- All other contributions to `a₄`. -/
  aRest : ℝ
  a4_split : a 2 = aRest + 2 / 3 * ∑ i, g i ^ 2 *
    (trace ((![genL, genR, gen4] i).gaugeOp N * (![genL, genR, gen4] i).gaugeOp N)).re * YM i

comments.text:
/-!
# The Pati–Salam spectral action and gauge coupling unification

This file continues `RequestProject.NCGPatiSalamTriple` and `RequestProject.NCGPatiSalamBreaking`,
and connects them to `RequestProject.NCGUnification` and `RequestProject.SpectralActionExpansion`.

* **Gauge generators on `H_F`.** A Lie algebra element `h = (h_R, h_L, h_c)` of
  `su(2)_R ⊕ su(2)_L ⊕ su(4)` acts on `H_F` through the complexified Pati–Salam
  representation `P(h)` (`PSGen.op`, which extends `repPS`: `repPS_eq_op`). In the fluctuated
  Dirac operator the gauge field appears through `A + J A J⁻¹`, so the generator acting on
  `H_F` is `G(h) = P(h) - J P(h) J⁻¹` (`PSGen.gaugeOp`).
* **The trace form** (`trace_gaugeOp_mul`). For traceless `h_R, h_L`:
  `Tr_{H_F}(G(h) G(h')) = 4N (s + s̄)` with `s = tr(h_R h_R') + tr(h_L h_L') + tr(h_c h_c')`.
  So each normalised generator (`tr h² = 1/2`) of each of `SU(2)_L`, `SU(2)_R`, `SU(4)` has
  `Tr_{H_F}(G²) = 4N` (`trace_gaugeOp_sq_of_normalised`), and generators of different factors
  are orthogonal.
* **The Seeley–DeWitt expansion.** `PSSpectralAction` records the spectrum of the fluctuated
  Dirac operator `D_A` on `M × F`, its heat-trace expansion, and the Yang–Mills part of the
  Seeley–DeWitt coefficient `a₄`. `ps_spectralAction_expansion` proves
  `Tr f(D_A/Λ) = (4π)⁻² (f₄ a₀ Λ⁴ + f₂ a₂ Λ²) + (4π)⁻² f₀ a₄^rest
  + Σᵢ f₀/(24π²) gᵢ² Tr(Gᵢ²) ∫ Fᵢ² + O(Λ⁻²)`.
* **Unification at `Λ_GUT`.** Canonical normalisation `f₀ gᵢ² Tr(Gᵢ²)/(24π²) = 1/4` of the
  three Yang–Mills terms (`PSCanonicalGauge`) forces `g_L = g_R = g₄`
  (`ps_gauge_unification`). The Standard Model couplings obtained from the same spectral
  action satisfy `g₂ = g_L`, `g₃ = g₄` and `1/g'² = 1/g_R² + (2/3)/g₄²`
  (`ps_to_sm_matching`). They obey the Standard Model spectral boundary condition, so
  `sin²θ_W = 3/8` at `Λ_GUT` (`ps_sin2W_three_eighths`). The hypercharge
  `Y = T_{3R} + (B - L)/2` has `Tr_{H_F}(G_Y²) = 20N/3 = 2N · 10/3`
  (`trace_gaugeOp_hypercharge`), the Standard Model value in `CanonicalGauge`.
-/
/-! ## Gauge generators on `H_F` -/

/-- A (complexified) element `h = (h_R, h_L, h_c)` of the Lie algebra of
`U(2)_R × U(2)_L × U(4)`, acting on right-handed isospin, left-handed isospin and the four
colours. -/
/-- The `su(2)_R` component. -/
/-- The `su(2)_L` component. -/
/-- The `su(4)` component. -/
/-- `h` acting on particles: `h_R ⊗ 1` on right-handed and `h_L ⊗ 1` on left-handed isospin. -/
/-- `h` acting on antiparticles: `1 ⊗ h_c ⊗ 1` on the colour index. -/
/-- The complexified Pati–Salam representation `P(h)` on `H_F`. -/

/-- **The gauge generator on `H_F`**, `G(h) = P(h) - J P(h) J⁻¹`. The gauge field enters the
fluctuated Dirac operator through `A + J A J⁻¹` with `A = i P(h)`. -/
/-- The invariant bilinear form `s(h, h') = tr(h_R h_R') + tr(h_L h_L') + tr(h_c h_c')`. -/

/-- `P(h)` extends the Pati–Salam representation: `π_PS(q_R, q_L, m) = P(q_R, q_L, m)`, where
the quaternions are read as `2 × 2` complex matrices. -/

/-- **The trace form of the gauge generators on `H_F`.** For `h, h'` whose isospin components
are traceless:
`Tr_{H_F}(G(h) G(h')) = 4N (s + s̄)`, `s = tr(h_R h_R') + tr(h_L h_L') + tr(h_c h_c')`. -/
/-! ## Normalised generators of the three factors -/

/-- A normalised hermitian generator of `SU(2)_L`: `h_R = 0`, `h_c = 0`, `h_L = h_L*`,
`tr h_L = 0`, `tr h_L² = 1/2`. -/
/-- A normalised hermitian generator of `SU(2)_R`. -/
/-- A normalised hermitian generator of `SU(4)`. -/
/-- Any generator with `s(h, h) = 1/2` and traceless isospin parts has `Tr_{H_F}(G²) = 4N`. -/

/-- **All normalised generators of `SU(2)_L`, `SU(2)_R` and `SU(4)` have the same trace**
`Tr_{H_F}(G²) = 4N` on `H_F`. This is the group-theoretic origin of `g_L = g_R = g₄`. -/

/-- Generators of different factors are orthogonal: `Tr_{H_F}(G(h) G(h')) = 0` when
`s(h, h') = 0` (for instance `h ∈ su(2)_L`, `h' ∈ su(4)`). -/
/-- The isospin generator `T₃ = diag(1/2, -1/2)`. -/
/-- The `SU(3) ⊂ SU(4)` generator `λ₃/2` acting on the first two quark colours. -/
/-- `(B - L)/2 = diag(-1/2, 1/6, 1/6, 1/6)` on the four colours (leptons first). -/
/-- The standard generator `T_{3L}`. -/
/-- The standard generator `T_{3R}`. -/
/-- The standard `SU(4)` generator `λ₃/2`, which lies in `SU(3)_c ⊂ SU(4)`. -/
/-- **The hypercharge** `Y = T_{3R} + (B - L)/2` as a Pati–Salam generator. -/

/-- **The hypercharge trace.** `Tr_{H_F}(G_Y²) = 20N/3 = 2N · 10/3` for
`Y = T_{3R} + (B - L)/2`. This is the trace behind the `U(1)_Y` normalisation of the
Standard Model spectral action (`NCG.SpectralAction.CanonicalGauge.u1`). It splits as
`4N + (2/3)·4N`, the `T_{3R}` part plus the `(B - L)/2 = √(2/3) T₁₅` part. -/
/-! ## Canonical normalisation and unification -/

/-- **Canonical normalisation of the Pati–Salam Yang–Mills terms at the cutoff `Λ_GUT`.** For
each factor `SU(2)_L`, `SU(2)_R`, `SU(4)` and each normalised generator `T` of it, the
coefficient `f₀/(24π²) g² Tr_{H_F}(G(T)²)` of `∫ F^a_{μν} F^{aμν}` in the spectral action
equals `1/4`. This is the convention of `NCG.SpectralAction.CanonicalGauge`. -/
/-- `PSCanonicalGauge` in closed form: `f₀/(24π²) · 4N g_i² = 1/4` for each factor. -/

/-- **Gauge coupling unification at `Λ_GUT` in the Pati–Salam spectral action.** Canonical
normalisation of the Yang–Mills terms forces `g_L² = g_R² = g₄²` and
`f₀ g² = 3π²/(2N)`, the same value as in the Standard Model (`gauge_unification`). For
positive couplings, `g_L = g_R` and `g₄ = g_R`. -/
/-- For positive couplings, `PSCanonicalGauge` gives `g_L = g_R` and `g₄ = g_R` exactly. -/
/-- `PSCanonicalGauge` is satisfiable: take `g_L = g_R = g₄ = √(3π²/(2N f₀))`. -/

/-- **Tree-level matching of Pati–Salam and Standard Model couplings at `Λ_GUT`, derived from
the spectral action.** Suppose the Pati–Salam Yang–Mills terms are canonically normalised
(`PSCanonicalGauge`), and so are the Standard Model Yang–Mills terms obtained from the same
spectral action (`CanonicalGauge`, with `N` generations). If all couplings are positive, then
`g₂ = g_L`, `g₃ = g₄` and `1/g'² = 1/g_R² + (2/3)/g₄²`. The hypercharge relation follows
from `Y = T_{3R} + (B - L)/2` (`trace_gaugeOp_hypercharge`). Together with
`ps_gauge_unification` this gives `g₄ = g₃ = g_L = g₂ = g_R` at `Λ_GUT`. -/

/-- **Conversely, the Pati–Salam normalisation implies the Standard Model spectral boundary
condition.** If the Pati–Salam Yang–Mills terms are canonically normalised and the Standard
Model couplings are defined by tree-level matching (`g₂ = g_L`, `g₃ = g₄`,
`1/g'² = 1/g_R² + (2/3)/g₄²`), then the Standard Model Yang–Mills terms are canonically
normalised (`CanonicalGauge`). -/

/-- **`sin²θ_W = 3/8` at `Λ_GUT` from Pati–Salam unification.** Under the hypotheses of
`ps_canonical_implies_sm`, the Standard Model couplings at `Λ_GUT` satisfy
`α₁ = α₂ = α₃` (GUT normalisation) and `sin²θ_W = 3/8`
(`NCG.GaugeRunning.spectral_sin2W_three_eighths`). -/
/-! ## The Seeley–DeWitt expansion of `Tr f(D_A/Λ)` -/

/-- **Spectral data of the fluctuated Pati–Salam Dirac operator `D_A` on `M × F`.**
* `D` is the spectrum of `D_A` (eigenvalues with multiplicity, with trace-class heat kernel).
* `c` is the cutoff `f`.
* `heat` is the Seeley–DeWitt heat-trace expansion `Tr e^{-tD_A²} ∼ (4πt)⁻² Σ aₖ tᵏ`.
* `a4_split` decomposes `a₄ = a 2`. Its Yang–Mills part is
  `(2/3) Σᵢ gᵢ² Tr_{H_F}(G(Tᵢ)²) YMᵢ` for the three factors
  `i = SU(2)_L, SU(2)_R, SU(4)`, with `YMᵢ = ∫ F^a_{iμν} F^{aμν}_i` and `Tᵢ` the standard
  generators `genL, genR, gen4`. This is `(1/360) · 30 · 8 ∫ Tr_{H_F}(F²)`, the `F²` term of
  the Seeley–DeWitt `a₄` (`SeeleyDeWittInvariants.a4`), normalised as in
  `NCG.SpectralAction.CanonicalGauge`. All remaining contributions (gravity, Higgs, `Σ`) are
  in `aRest`. -/
/-- The index set of the spectrum. -/
/-- The spectrum of the fluctuated Dirac operator `D_A`. -/
/-- The cutoff function `f`. -/
/-- The Seeley–DeWitt coefficients `a₀, a₂, a₄, …` (indexed `0, 1, 2, …`). -/
/-- The couplings `g_L, g_R, g₄`. -/
/-- The Yang–Mills integrals `∫ Fᵢ²`. -/
/-- All other contributions to `a₄`. -/
/-- The spectral action `Tr f(D_A/Λ)`. -/

/-- **The Seeley–DeWitt expansion of the Pati–Salam spectral action.** As `Λ → ∞`,
`Tr f(D_A/Λ) = (4π)⁻² (f₄ a₀ Λ⁴ + f₂ a₂ Λ² + f₀ a₄^rest)
  + Σ_{i ∈ {L, R, 4}} f₀/(24π²) · gᵢ² · 4N · ∫ Fᵢ² + O(Λ⁻²)`,
with `f₀ = m₀`, `f₂ = m₋₁`, `f₄ = m₋₂` the moments of the cutoff. The coefficient
`f₀/(24π²) gᵢ² Tr_{H_F}(Gᵢ²) = f₀/(24π²) gᵢ² · 4N` of each Yang–Mills term is the same for
all three factors up to the coupling. This is why canonical normalisation forces
`g_L = g_R = g₄` (`ps_gauge_unification`). -/

/-- The Yang–Mills coefficient of factor `i` in the expansion, `f₀/(24π²) gᵢ² · 4N`. The
Pati–Salam couplings are canonically normalised exactly when all three equal `1/4`. -/

/-- `PSSpectralAction` is inhabited: a single zero mode with the heat-kernel cutoff
`f(x) = e^{-x²}`, all of `a₄` in `aRest`, and vanishing Yang–Mills integrals. -/

    (n : Type*) [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] where
