/-!
# Finite commutative spectral triples, the spectral action and expander mixing

A finite commutative spectral triple `(A, H, D)` has `A = C(V) = (V → ℂ)` acting on
`H = ℓ²(V)` by diagonal multiplication operators (`rep`) and a self-adjoint Dirac operator `D`.

* `FiniteCommSpectralTriple.spectralAction_exp_eq_mgf` — the spectral action `Tr exp(D/Λ)`
  equals `|V|` times the moment generating function (Mathlib's `ProbabilityTheory.mgf`) of the
  spectral measure of `D`, evaluated at `1/Λ`.
* `ncg_expander_mixing` — the Expander Mixing Lemma in spectral-triple form:
  `|Tr(P D Q J) - (d/|V|) Tr P Tr Q| ≤ λ₂(D) ‖P‖₂ ‖Q‖₂`, with `J = |V| P₀`.
* `literal_trace_mixing_fails` — the version with the literal trace `Tr(P D Q)` is false.
* `abs_le_nontrivialSpectralRadius_of_disconnected` — a disconnected geometry has no gap.
* `twinSpectralTriple` — the spectral triple of the twin quotient of a graph, with Dirac
  operator `D = 4 B_χ`, together with the specialised statements.
-/
/-! ## The algebra, the Hilbert space and the representation -/

/-- The representation `π : A → B(H)` of the commutative C*-algebra `A = C(V) = (V → ℂ)` on
`H = ℓ²(V) = EuclideanSpace ℂ V` by multiplication operators, i.e. diagonal matrices. -/

/-- A **finite commutative spectral triple** `(A, H, D)` with `A = C(V)` acting on
`H = ℓ²(V)` by multiplication operators and a self-adjoint Dirac operator `D`. (In finite
dimension every commutator `[D, π(a)]` is automatically bounded.) -/
/-- The Dirac operator. -/
/-- The Dirac operator is self-adjoint. -/
/-! ## The spectral action and the moment generating function -/

/-- The eigenvalues of the Dirac operator (with multiplicity), i.e. the spectrum of the
geometry. -/
/-- **The spectral action** `Tr f(D/Λ)`, defined through the continuous functional calculus. -/
/-- The spectral action is the sum of `f(λᵢ/Λ)` over the spectrum of `D`. -/

/-- **The spectral measure** of the geometry: the uniform probability measure on the spectrum
of `D` (eigenvalues counted with multiplicity), `μ_D = |V|⁻¹ ∑ᵢ δ_{λᵢ}`. -/

/-- The integral of any function against the spectral measure is the average over the
spectrum. -/

/-- The moment generating function of the spectral measure is
`M(t) = |V|⁻¹ ∑ᵢ exp(t λᵢ)`. -/

/-- **The spectral action computes the moment generating function of the spectrum:**
`Tr exp(D/Λ) = |V| · M_D(1/Λ)`, where `M_D` is the moment generating function of the spectral
measure of `D`. -/

/-- The spectral action with `f(x) = xᵏ` (and `Λ = 1`) is the `k`-th moment:
`Tr Dᵏ = |V| ∫ xᵏ dμ_D`. -/
/-! ## Expander mixing in spectral-triple form -/

/-- The all-ones matrix `J = |V| · P₀`, where `P₀` is the projection onto the constant
functions. The functional `X ↦ Tr(X J) = ⟨𝟙, X 𝟙⟩` is the vector state of the constant
function (unnormalised). -/
/-- `D` has constant row sums `d` (i.e. `D 𝟙 = d 𝟙`): the regularity of the geometry. -/

/-- **The nontrivial spectral radius** `λ₂(D)`: the largest absolute value `|μ|` of an
eigenvalue `μ` of `D` having an eigenvector orthogonal to the constant functions. For a
`d`-regular graph this is the usual expander parameter `max(|λ₂|, |λₙ|)`. -/
/-- The Hilbert–Schmidt norm `‖X‖₂ = √(Tr X* X)`. -/
/-- An orthogonal projection in `A = C(V)`: `p* = p = p²`. -/
/-- An eigenvalue of `D` (with a nonzero eigenvector) lies in the real spectrum of `D`. -/
/-- Every nontrivial eigenvalue is bounded by the nontrivial spectral radius. -/

/-- A Hermitian matrix whose eigenvalues are bounded by `c` in absolute value satisfies
`|⟨x, M y⟩| ≤ c ‖x‖ ‖y‖`. -/
/-- For a self-adjoint `D` with constant row sums `d`, the column sums are also `d`. -/
/-- The centred Dirac operator `D - (d/|V|) J` is self-adjoint. -/

/-- Every eigenvalue of the centred operator `D - (d/|V|) J` is bounded in absolute value by
`λ₂(D)`: eigenvectors orthogonal to `𝟙` are nontrivial eigenvectors of `D`, and an eigenvector
not orthogonal to `𝟙` must have eigenvalue `0` because `D - (d/|V|) J` kills `𝟙`. -/

/-- **Expander geometry requires connectedness.** If `D` has constant row sums `d` and the
geometry splits into two nonempty pieces `S`, `Sᶜ` that `D` does not connect, then
`|d| ≤ λ₂(D)`. The vector `|Sᶜ| 𝟙_S - |S| 𝟙_{Sᶜ}` is then a nontrivial eigenvector with
eigenvalue `d`, so the expander mixing bound is no better than the trivial one. -/
/-- For self-adjoint `a, b ∈ A`, `Tr(π(a) D π(b) J) = ⟨a, D b⟩`. -/

/-- For indicator projections `P = 1_S`, `Q = 1_T`, the Perron-weighted trace `Tr(P D Q J)` is
the total `D`-weight of the edges from `S` to `T`. -/

/-- **The noncommutative-geometric Expander Mixing Lemma.** Let `(A, H, D)` be a finite
commutative spectral triple whose Dirac operator is `d`-regular. For every self-adjoint
`P ∈ A` (in particular every orthogonal projection `P`, see `IsProjection`) and every `Q ∈ A`
(in particular every orthogonal projection `Q`),
`|Tr(P D Q J) - (d/|V|) Tr(P) Tr(Q)| ≤ λ₂(D) ‖P‖₂ ‖Q‖₂`,
where `J = |V| P₀` is the (unnormalised) projection onto the constants, so that
`Tr(P D Q J) = ⟨𝟙, P D Q 𝟙⟩` counts the `D`-weighted edges between the supports of `P` and
`Q` (`trace_rep_indicator`). Only `P* = P` is needed; no hypothesis on `Q` is required. -/

/-- For an orthogonal projection `P ∈ A`, `‖P‖₂ = √(Tr P)` (the square root of the number of
points in its support). -/
/-- The trace of an orthogonal projection `P ∈ A` is nonnegative. -/

/-- **Expander mixing for two orthogonal projections, in counting form:** for orthogonal
projections `P, Q ∈ A`,
`|Tr(P D Q J) - (d/|V|) Tr(P) Tr(Q)| ≤ λ₂(D) √(Tr P · Tr Q)`. -/

/-- **The literal trace `Tr(P D Q)` cannot replace `Tr(P D Q J)`.** If `D` has zero diagonal
(no loops) and `λ₂(D) < d` (a spectral gap, when `d` is the degree), then the inequality
`|Tr(P D Q) - (d/|V|) Tr(P) Tr(Q)| ≤ λ₂ ‖P‖₂ ‖Q‖₂` fails for `P = Q = 1`. -/
/-! ## The spectral triple of the twin quotient of a graph -/

/-- **The Dirac operator of the twin quotient**: `D = 4 B_χ`, four times the `0/1` adjacency
matrix `B_χ` of the twin quotient graph, acting on `H = ℓ²(V/twin)`. When every twin class has
four elements (as for the sedenion annihilation graph) this is exactly the equitable quotient
matrix of the adjacency operator, see `twinDirac_eq_equitableQuotientMatrix`. -/
/-- `D = 4 B_χ` is the complexification of `4 •` the real quotient adjacency matrix `B_χ`. -/

/-- If every twin class has four elements, `D = 4 B_χ` is the (complexified) equitable quotient
matrix of the adjacency operator of the graph. -/

/-- **The spectral triple `(A, H, D)` of the twin quotient**: `A = C(V/twin)` acting on
`H = ℓ²(V/twin)` by multiplication, with Dirac operator `D = 4 B_χ`. -/
/-- `D = 4 B_χ` has zero diagonal: twins are never adjacent, so the quotient has no loops. -/
/-- If the twin quotient graph is `k`-regular, then `D = 4 B_χ` has constant row sums `4k`. -/

/-- **Spectral action of the twin quotient = moment generating function of its spectrum:**
`Tr exp(D/Λ) = |V/twin| · M(1/Λ)` for `D = 4 B_χ`, where `M` is the moment generating function
of the (uniform) spectral measure of `D`. -/

/-- **Expander Mixing Lemma on the twin quotient, in spectral-triple form.** If the twin quotient
graph is `k`-regular, then for every self-adjoint `P ∈ A = C(V/twin)` (in particular every
orthogonal projection) and every `Q ∈ A`,
`|Tr(P D Q J) - (d/|V/twin|) Tr(P) Tr(Q)| ≤ λ₂(D) ‖P‖₂ ‖Q‖₂` with `D = 4 B_χ`, `d = 4k`. -/

/-- **Expander Mixing Lemma on the twin quotient for two orthogonal projections**, counting
form: `|Tr(P D Q J) - (d/|V/twin|) Tr(P) Tr(Q)| ≤ λ₂(D) √(Tr P · Tr Q)`. -/

declarations.name: ip_aroot
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem ip_aroot (v : Fin n → ℤ) (i j : Fin n) : ip v (aroot i j) = v i - v j

declarations.name: refl_aroot
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem refl_aroot (i j : Fin n) (h : i ≠ j) (v : Fin n → ℤ) :
    refl (aroot i j) v = v ∘ swap i j

declarations.name: aroot_comp_swap
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem aroot_comp_swap (i j k l : Fin n) :
    aroot k l ∘ swap i j = aroot (swap i j k) (swap i j l)

declarations.name: aroot_apply
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem aroot_apply (i j m : Fin n) :
    aroot i j m = (if m = i then 1 else 0) - (if m = j then 1 else 0)

declarations.name: aroot_inj
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem aroot_inj {i j k l : Fin n} (hij : i ≠ j) (h : aroot i j = aroot k l) :
    i = k ∧ j = l

declarations.name: neg_aroot
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem neg_aroot (i j : Fin n) : -aroot i j = aroot j i

declarations.name: card_roots
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem card_roots (n : ℕ) : (roots n).card = n * n - n

declarations.name: card_posRoots_eq
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem card_posRoots_eq (n : ℕ) :
    (posRoots n).card = ((Finset.univ.offDiag).filter (fun p : Fin n × Fin n => p.1 < p.2)).card

declarations.name: card_posRoots_seven

declarations.name: negRoots

declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem roots_eq_pos_union_neg (n : ℕ) :
    roots n = posRoots n ∪ negRoots n ∧ Disjoint (posRoots n) (negRoots n)

declarations.name: card_negRoots

declarations.name: card_roots_eq_two_mul
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem card_roots_eq_two_mul (n : ℕ) : (roots n).card = 2 * (posRoots n).card

declarations.name: neg_mem_roots
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem neg_mem_roots {a : Fin n → ℤ} (ha : a ∈ roots n) : -a ∈ roots n

declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem refl_mem_roots {a b : Fin n → ℤ} (ha : a ∈ roots n) (hb : b ∈ roots n) :
    refl a b ∈ roots n

declarations.name: ip_self_roots
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem ip_self_roots {a : Fin n → ℤ} (ha : a ∈ roots n) : ip a a = 2

declarations.name: ip_roots_bound
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem ip_roots_bound {a b : Fin n → ℤ} (ha : a ∈ roots n) (hb : b ∈ roots n) :
    -2 ≤ ip b a ∧ ip b a ≤ 2

declarations.name: neg_not_perm
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem neg_not_perm (hn : 0 < n) : ¬ ∃ σ : Perm (Fin n), ∀ v : Fin n → ℤ, v ∘ σ = -v

declarations.name: fanoLine
declarations.signature_heuristic: def fanoLine : Fin 7 → Finset (Fin 7)

declarations.name: fanoLine_card
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem fanoLine_card : ∀ t, (fanoLine t).card = 3

declarations.name: fano_unique_line
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem fano_unique_line (i j : Fin 7) (hij : i ≠ j) :
    ∃! t, i ∈ fanoLine t ∧ j ∈ fanoLine t

declarations.name: subRoots
declarations.signature_heuristic: def subRoots (S : Finset (Fin n)) : Finset (Fin n → ℤ)

declarations.name: mem_subRoots
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem mem_subRoots {S : Finset (Fin n)} {a : Fin n → ℤ} :
    a ∈ subRoots S ↔ ∃ i j, i ∈ S ∧ j ∈ S ∧ i ≠ j ∧ aroot i j = a

declarations.name: refl_mem_subRoots
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem refl_mem_subRoots {S : Finset (Fin n)} {a b : Fin n → ℤ} (ha : a ∈ subRoots S)
    (hb : b ∈ subRoots S) : refl a b ∈ subRoots S

declarations.name: card_subRoots_line
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem card_subRoots_line (t : Fin 7) : (subRoots (fanoLine t)).card = 6

declarations.name: fano_partition_roots
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem fano_partition_roots :
    ∀ a ∈ roots 7, ∃! t, a ∈ subRoots (fanoLine t)

declarations.name: roots_seven_eq_biUnion
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem roots_seven_eq_biUnion : roots 7 = Finset.univ.biUnion (fun t => subRoots (fanoLine t))

declarations.name: IsE8Root
declarations.signature_heuristic: def IsE8Root (y : Fin 8 → ℤ) : Prop

declarations.name: a6_sub_e8
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem a6_sub_e8 (i j : Fin 7) (hij : i ≠ j) :
    IsE8Root (2 • aroot (Fin.castSucc i) (Fin.castSucc j))

/-!
# The 21 vectors and their 42-element "dual": the root system `A₆`

Follow-up to `QBX.Notes.PolytopeBraidLattice`, which showed that no reflection-closed set (and
no Weyl orbit in `ℝ⁸`) has 21 elements. The natural repair is to double: 21 vectors together
with their negatives give 42, and the 21 vectors are then the **positive roots** of a root system
with 42 roots. This file checks that this works, and for which root system.

* `card_roots_seven`, `card_posRoots_seven`, `roots_eq_pos_union_neg`, `card_roots_eq_two_mul`:
  the vectors `e_i - e_j` (`i ≠ j`) in `ℤ⁷` are 42 roots of `A₆`; the 21 with `i < j` are the
  positive roots and the other 21 are exactly their negatives.
* `refl_mem_roots`, `neg_mem_roots`, `ip_self_roots`, `ip_roots_bound`: it is a crystallographic
  root system. The reflection in `e_i - e_j` is the transposition `i ↔ j` of coordinates
  (`refl_aroot`), so the 21 positive-root reflections are the 21 transpositions of `S₇`, the
  Weyl group. All roots have length² 2, so the coroots are the roots: `A₆` is self-dual.
* `neg_not_perm`: unlike `E₈`, negation is not in the Weyl group, so the 21 ↔ 21 pairing is a
  symmetry of the root system that is not a product of its reflections.
* `irreducible_count_42`: among the irreducible root systems (`Aᵣ, Bᵣ, Cᵣ, Dᵣ, E₆₋₈, F₄, G₂`),
  only `A₆` has 42 roots. (The classification itself is not formalized; this checks the count
  formulas.) `A₆` is simply laced, i.e. of type ADE.
* `fano_partition_roots`, `roots_seven_eq_biUnion`, `refl_mem_subRoots`, `card_subRoots_line`:
  the seven Fano lines split the 42 roots into seven `A₂` subsystems of 6 roots each (21 positive
  roots = 7 lines × 3 pairs), because every pair of points lies on exactly one line.
* `a6_sub_e8`: placed on the first seven coordinates of `ℝ⁸`, the 42 roots are `E₈` roots.
-/
/-- Integer dot product on `ℤⁿ`. -/
/-- The root `e_i - e_j` of type `A`. -/
/-- The reflection `v ↦ v - ⟨v, α⟩ α`. -/
/-! ## The root system `A_{n-1}` -/
/-- All roots `e_i - e_j`, `i ≠ j`. -/
/-- The positive roots `e_i - e_j`, `i < j`. -/
/-- **`A₆` has 42 roots.** -/
/-- **`A₆` has 21 positive roots.** -/
/-- The negatives of the positive roots. -/

/-- **The 42 = 21 + 21 split.** Every root is positive or the negative of a positive root, and
not both. -/
/-- `|Φ| = 2 |Φ⁺|`: the negatives are the "dual half". -/
/-- Closed under negation. -/

/-- **Closed under its own reflections** (a root system). The reflection in `e_i - e_j` is the
transposition of coordinates `i ↔ j`. -/

/-- Every root has squared length 2, so the coroot `2α/⟨α,α⟩` equals `α`: the system is
**self-dual** (`A₆^∨ = A₆`). -/
/-- **Crystallographic**: all Cartan integers `⟨β, α⟩` lie in `[-2, 2]`. -/

/-- Negation is **not** in the Weyl group `Sₙ` of `A_{n-1}` (`n ≥ 1`): no coordinate permutation
sends every vector to its negative. (Contrast with `E₈`, where `-1` is a product of eight
reflections, `PolytopeBraidLattice.negChain_eq`.) The 21 ↔ 21 pairing of `A₆` is therefore an
outer symmetry, not a Weyl element. -/
/-! ## Which irreducible root systems have 42 roots? -/

/-- Root counts of the irreducible root systems: `A_r: r(r+1)`, `B_r, C_r: 2r²`,
`D_r: 2r(r-1)`, `E₆: 72`, `E₇: 126`, `E₈: 240`, `F₄: 48`, `G₂: 12`. -/
/-! ## The Fano plane decomposes `A₆` into seven `A₂`'s -/

/-- The seven lines of the Fano plane on the points `0, …, 6` (the octonion units `e₁ … e₇`
shifted down by one; the lines `{i, j, i xor j}`). -/
/-- Two distinct points lie on exactly one line. -/
/-- The roots supported on a subset `S` of coordinates. -/

/-- Roots on a subset form a sub-root-system (closed under its own reflections); on a 3-element
set this is `A₂`, with 6 roots. -/

/-- **The 42 roots of `A₆` split into seven `A₂` subsystems, one per Fano line** (`7 · 6 = 42`;
on positive roots, `7 · 3 = 21`). Every root lies in exactly one of them. -/

/-- The Gosset lattice `E₈` in doubled coordinates (`y = 2x`), as in
`Sovereign.Steering.GossetE8`: all `yᵢ` even or all odd, and `4 ∣ ∑ yᵢ`. A root is a lattice
vector with `⟨x, x⟩ = 2`, i.e. `y ⬝ y = 8`. -/
/-- The `A₆` roots, placed on the first seven coordinates of `ℝ⁸`, are `E₈` roots. -/

/-!
# Gram-matrix audit of the 21 positive roots of `A₆`, and other checkable claims

Follow-up to `QBX.Notes.A6Doubling`. A pasted analysis proposed comparing the probe's 21 vectors
with the positive roots of `A₆` through their `21 × 21` Gram matrix, and it gave reference
values for that matrix. This file computes the reference values exactly. Several of the pasted
values are wrong; the correct ones are below. Report: `docs/A6_GRAM_AUDIT_2026-10-20.md`.

**The Gram matrix `G` of the 21 positive roots `e_i - e_j` (`i < j`) of `A₆`:**

* `gram_entries`, `gram_diag`, `gram_eq_two_iff`: the entries are `-1, 0, 1, 2`, with `2` exactly
  on the diagonal (no two positive roots are antipodal).
* `gram_counts`: off the diagonal there are **140** entries `+1`, **210** entries `0` and **70**
  entries `-1` (not 105 / 210 / 105 as claimed).
* `row_06`: rows are **not** uniform: the row of `e₀ - e₆` (the highest root) has ten `+1` and
  no `-1` (not "5 / 10 / 5 per row").
* `gram_sum`: all entries add up to `112 = |2ρ|²`, where `2ρ = (6, 4, 2, 0, -2, -4, -6)`.
* `gram_sq`: **`G² = 7 G`**, so `G / 7` is a projection. Hence (`eigen_zero_or_seven`) every
  eigenvalue is `0` or `7`; `gramQ_trace`, `gramQ_rank`, `gramQ_nullity`: trace `42`, rank `6`,
  nullity `15`. The spectrum is **`7` (six times) and `0` (fifteen times)**, not
  `{7, 3.5 ×5, 0 ×15}` (that list has trace `24.5 ≠ 42`).

**Mean angles are not a root-system test.**
* `gram_counts` gives the mean off-diagonal angle of the 21 positive roots as
  `(140·60° + 210·90° + 70·120°)/420 = 85°`, which lies outside the 60/90/120° values although
  the vectors are an honest `A₆` half-system.
* `allRoots_counts`, `allRoots_gram_sum`: for all 42 roots the inner products are symmetric
  (`420` at `±1`, `42` at `-2`), so the mean cosine is `0`; the mean angle, counting the 21
  antipodal pairs, is `92.2°`. Neither number says anything about being a root system.

**General facts used to judge the other claims.**
* `crystallographic_angle`: if `2⟨a,b⟩/⟨a,a⟩` and `2⟨a,b⟩/⟨b,b⟩` are integers `m, n`, then
  `m n = 4 cos² θ ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}`. Any two roots of a crystallographic root system meet at
  `90°, 60°, 120°, 45°, 135°, 30°, 150°` (or `0°, 180°`). A set with other angles is not a
  crystallographic root system. Testing this needs all pairwise angles, not their mean.
* `reflection_norm`: a reflection `v ↦ v - 2⟨v,a⟩/⟨a,a⟩ a` preserves the norm *exactly*, in
  every real inner-product space (no Monte-Carlo pass rate is needed).
* `reflections_generate_S7`: the 21 transpositions (the positive-root reflections, by
  `A6Doubling.refl_aroot`) generate `S₇`.
* `det_one_isUnit`: a matrix with determinant `1` is invertible, so "det = 1 (singular)" is a
  contradiction in terms.
* `golay23_perfect`, `golay24_not_perfect`, `no_perfect_length24`: the sphere-packing equality
  `2¹² · Σ_{k≤3} C(n,k) = 2ⁿ` holds for the binary Golay code of length **23**, not for the extended
  `[24, 12, 8]` code. Indeed **no** binary code of length 24 is perfect for any radius `1 … 23`.
-/
/-- Index set of the 21 positive roots `e_i - e_j`, `i < j`, of `A₆`. -/
/-- There are 21 positive roots. -/
/-- Closed form of the inner product of two `A`-type roots. -/
/-- The closed form agrees with the inner product. -/
/-- The `21 × 21` Gram matrix of the positive roots. -/
/-- `gram` is the Gram matrix of the positive roots. -/
/-- Gram entries lie in `{-1, 0, 1, 2}`. -/
/-- Diagonal entries are `2` (roots have length² 2). -/
/-- `2` occurs only on the diagonal; `-2` never occurs (no antipodal pairs). -/
/-- Number of entries of `G` equal to `c`. -/
/-- **Entry counts of `G`:** 21 twos, 140 ones, 210 zeros, 70 minus-ones, no `-2`. -/
/-- The mean off-diagonal angle of the positive roots, from `gram_counts`, is `85°`. -/
/-- Number of entries equal to `c` in row `p`. -/
/-- Rows are not uniform: the row of the highest root `e₀ - e₆` has ten `+1`s and no `-1`. -/
/-- The entries add up to `112 = |2ρ|²`. -/
/-- The Gram matrix over `ℚ`. -/
/-- `G² = 7 G` over `ℚ`. -/
/-- **Every eigenvalue of `G` is `0` or `7`.** -/
/-- **`rank G = 6`** (`G/7` is a projection, whose rank is its trace `42/7`). -/

/-- **The kernel of `G` has dimension 15.** With `rank G = 6`, `G² = 7G`: eigenvalue `7`
has multiplicity 6 and eigenvalue `0` has multiplicity 15. -/
/-- Every vector in the range of `G` is an eigenvector with eigenvalue `7`. -/
/-- All `A₆` roots, ordered pairs `(i, j)`, `i ≠ j`. -/
/-- Over all 42 roots the inner products sum to `0` (mean cosine `0`). -/
/-- Number of ordered pairs of roots of `A₆` with inner product `c`. -/
/-- Inner-product counts over all ordered pairs of the 42 roots: symmetric in sign. -/
/-- **The 21 positive-root reflections (transpositions `i ↔ j`, `i < j`) generate `S₇`.** -/
/-- **Reflections preserve the norm exactly.** -/

/-- **Crystallographic angle restriction.** If both Cartan numbers of `a, b` are integers
`m, n`, then `m n = 4 cos² ∠(a, b)` and `0 ≤ m n ≤ 4`. -/
/-- A matrix with determinant `1` is invertible (not singular). -/
/-- **Perfect:** the binary Golay code of length 23 (`2¹²` words, radius 3) fills `𝔽₂²³`. -/
/-- A Hamming ball of radius 3 in `𝔽₂²⁴` has 2325 points. -/

/-- **The extended Golay code is not perfect:** no number of radius-3 balls in length 24
fills `2²⁴` points exactly (`2325` is odd). -/

/-- No binary code of length 24 is perfect, for any radius `1 … 23`: the ball size never
divides `2²⁴`. -/

/-!
# Sedenion box kites as `A₆` roots: box kites are Fano *points*, `A₂` blocks are Fano *lines*

A pasted analysis claimed that "the 168 box-kite structures are indexed by `PSL(2,7)`" and that
"each of the seven `A₂` blocks of `A₆` represents a box kite". This file tests the second claim
against the box-kite structure proved in `QBX.Formal.BoxKites`.

* `QBX.Formal.BoxKites` already shows: 168 primitive zero divisors `±e_a ± e_(8+b)`, falling into
  **7** box kites (connected components, `annGraph_reachable_iff`), with 24 vectors each, and
  42 twin classes of 4. So 168 counts vectors, and there are 7 box kites, not 168.
* `rootOf`, `rootOf_eq_iff`, `image_rootOf`: sending the label `(a, b, s, t)` to the root
  `s t (e_a - e_b)` of `A₆` (indices shifted to `0 … 6`) is constant exactly on twin classes, and
  its image is all of the 42 roots. So **the 42 twin classes correspond one-to-one to the 42
  roots of `A₆`.**
* `kite_eq_xor`: the box kite of a label is the xor `(i+1) xor (j+1)` of its root's indices.
* `same_kite_orth`: two roots in the same box kite are orthogonal or opposite. So each box kite
  is a `3 A₁` (three mutually orthogonal pairs `±r`), **not** an `A₂` (`line_has_sixty`: an `A₂`
  block always contains roots at 60°). `ann_orth`: zero products `u w = 0` only join labels whose
  roots are orthogonal.
* `third_on_line`: the box kite of `e_i - e_j` is the third point of the Fano line through
  `i, j`. So box kites correspond to the 7 **points** of the Fano plane, while the `A₂` blocks of
  `A6Doubling.fano_partition_roots` correspond to the 7 **lines**. Both are partitions of the
  same 42 roots into 7 groups of 6, and they are exchanged by point–line duality.
-/
/-- Shift a nonzero index `1 … 7` of `Fin 8` down to `0 … 6`. -/

/-- The ordered pair of the root attached to a label `(a, b, s, t)`: the root is
`s t (e_a - e_b)`, i.e. `e_a - e_b` if `s = t` and `e_b - e_a` otherwise. -/
/-- The `A₆` root attached to a label. -/
/-- **Zero products join only orthogonal roots.** -/
/-- The root of a primitive label is a genuine root (`i ≠ j`). -/
/-- Every ordered pair `i ≠ j` occurs. -/
/-- Two primitive labels give the same root pair iff they are twins. -/
/-- **Two primitive labels give the same `A₆` root iff they are twins** (same partners). -/
/-- **The roots of the 168 primitive labels are exactly the 42 roots of `A₆`.** -/
/-- The box kite of a label is the xor of its root's (1-based) indices. -/
/-- **Roots in one box kite are orthogonal or opposite** (a `3 A₁`, never an `A₂`). -/
/-- The third point `(i+1) xor (j+1)`, shifted back to `0 … 6`. -/
/-- **The box kite of `e_i - e_j` is the third point of the Fano line through `i, j`.** -/
/-- An `A₂` block contains roots at 60° (`⟨e_i - e_j, e_i - e_k⟩ = 1`). -/

/-!
# Braid "compression" and Chern-number "integrity guards": what can and cannot hold

A pasted note made three engineering claims. This file checks the mathematical content of each.
Report: `docs/CD_ZERO_DIVISOR_BRAID_CHERN_AUDIT_2026-10-20.md`.

## 1. "Any text can be compressed into a braid polynomial"

* `no_lossless_shortening`: an injective (= lossless) encoder of all `n`-bit strings must output
  at least one string of length `≥ n`. This holds for *every* encoding, braid-based or not
  (pigeonhole: there are `2ⁿ` inputs but only `2ⁿ - 1` shorter bit strings).
* Jones and Alexander polynomials are invariants of the *closed* braid, so they take equal
  values on conjugate braids. In Lean: `B3` is Artin's braid group on three strands (presented
  group, one braid relation), `s1_ne_s2` and `s1s2_ne_s2s1` show its generators and the words
  `σ₁σ₂`, `σ₂σ₁` are distinct, and `classFunction_not_injective` shows that **no** function `f`
  with `f (g h) = f (h g)` is injective on `B3`. So such a polynomial cannot be decoded back to
  the braid word, let alone the text.

## 2. "A Chern number jumps to a fraction when memory is corrupted"

We use the standard lattice (Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki) Chern number on an `L × L` periodic grid:
the link angles `ax`, `ay` are arbitrary real numbers, the plaquette flux is the curl wrapped into
`(-π, π]`, and the Chern number is the total flux divided by `2π`.

* `latticeChern_isInt`: for **every** choice of link data, including corrupted data, the
  result is an integer. So a check of the form "the Chern number is no longer an integer"
  can never fire.
* `latticeChern_singleLink_lt` and `latticeChern_singleLink_pi`: changing one link angle from
  `t` (with `|t| < π`) to `π` changes the Chern number from `0` to `1`. So the integer is not
  immune to a single local change, and an arbitrarily small change can flip it.
-/
/-! ### 1a. Pigeonhole: no lossless encoder shortens every input -/
/-- Lists of booleans of length `< n`, as a finset. -/

/-- **No lossless shortening.** An injective encoder of `n`-bit strings into bit strings has
an input whose code is at least `n` bits long. This applies to any scheme, including encoding
text as braid words or as polynomials written out in bits. -/
/-! ### 1b. Conjugation-invariant braid invariants forget the word -/
/-- The single braid relation `σ₁ σ₂ σ₁ = σ₂ σ₁ σ₂`, written as a relator. -/
/-- Artin's braid group on three strands, `⟨σ₁, σ₂ | σ₁ σ₂ σ₁ = σ₂ σ₁ σ₂⟩`. -/
/-- The generator `σ₁`. -/
/-- The generator `σ₂`. -/
/-- The permutation of the strand endpoints: `σ₁ ↦ (0 1)`, `σ₂ ↦ (1 2)`. -/
/-- `σ₁ ≠ σ₂` in `B₃`. -/
/-- The braid words `σ₁ σ₂` and `σ₂ σ₁` are different braids. -/
/-- `σ₂` is a conjugate of `σ₁`: `σ₂ = (σ₁ σ₂) σ₁ (σ₁ σ₂)⁻¹`. -/

/-- A **class function** (`f (g h) = f (h g)`, as for the Jones or Alexander polynomial of the
closure, or the trace of any representation) takes the same value on `σ₁` and `σ₂`. -/
/-- A class function cannot tell `σ₁ σ₂` from `σ₂ σ₁`. -/

/-- **No class function on `B₃` is injective.** So no conjugation-invariant braid invariant
(Jones polynomial, Alexander polynomial, character of a representation) can be decoded back
into the braid word. -/
/-! ### 2. The lattice Chern number is an integer for every input -/
/-- Sites of the `L × L` periodic lattice (a discrete torus). -/
/-- Lattice curl of the link angles around the plaquette with lower-left corner `p`. -/
/-- The plaquette flux: the curl wrapped into `(-π, π]`. -/
/-- The lattice Chern number: total plaquette flux divided by `2π`. -/
/-- The curl sums to zero over the torus (every link occurs once with each sign). -/

/-- **Integrality for every input.** Whatever real numbers the link angles are (correct,
noisy, or corrupted), the lattice Chern number is an integer. -/
/-- The link configuration that is zero except for the `x`-link at the origin, which is `t`. -/
/-- Any single-link value `t` with `|t| < π` gives Chern number `0`. -/

/-- Setting the same link to `π` gives Chern number `1`. Together with
`latticeChern_singleLink_lt`, an arbitrarily small change of a single link can change the
Chern number. -/

/-!
# The Cayley–Dickson ladder and sedenion zero divisors: what the pasted note gets right

Report: `docs/CD_ZERO_DIVISOR_BRAID_CHERN_AUDIT_2026-10-20.md`.

## The property-loss table (correct)

`cd_ladder` collects, in one statement, the facts proved earlier in `Refinery.CDPropertyLoss`,
`Refinery.CDLossPersistence` and `Refinery.ZeroDivisorNorm`. `complex_no_compatible_order` adds the
precise form of "ℂ loses ordering": no linear order on `ℂ` makes it an ordered ring.

`cd_ladder_kept` records what the table leaves out: **every** Cayley–Dickson level, including
the sedenions, is still flexible (`(x y) x = x (y x)`) and satisfies `(x x) x = x (x x)`. So the
descent is not a loss of all structure.

## The zero divisors (partly right, partly wrong)

Here a (left) zero divisor is a nonzero real sedenion `a` with `a b = 0` for some nonzero `b`.

* `isZeroDivisor_smul`: nonzero real multiples of zero divisors are zero divisors, so the zero
  divisors (with `0`) form a **cone**. This part of the note is right.
* `zeroDivisors_not_closed_add`: `e₁ + e₁₀` and `e₁ - e₁₀` are zero divisors, but their sum `2 e₁`
  is not. So the zero divisors do not form a linear subspace.
* `zeroDivisor_mul_not_injective`: multiplying by the zero divisor `e₁ + e₁₀` sends the two
  different inputs `0` and `e₅ + e₁₄` to the same output. A zero divisor therefore **destroys**
  information; it cannot act as a lossless compression map.
-/
/-! ### The ladder -/

/-- **ℂ cannot be ordered.** There is no linear order on `ℂ` compatible with its ring operations
(squares would be `≥ 0`, but `i² = -1`). -/

/-- **The property-loss column of the table is correct.** Over the reals:
level 1 (ℂ) is commutative, level 2 (ℍ) is not but is associative, level 3 (𝕆) is not
associative but is alternative and has no zero divisors, level 4 (𝕊) is not alternative and
has zero divisors; and each loss persists at every higher level. -/

/-- **What is not lost.** At every level `n` of the tower (sedenions `n = 4` included) the
algebra is flexible and third-power associative. -/
/-! ### Zero divisors -/
/-- A (left) zero divisor of the real sedenions: `a ≠ 0` and `a b = 0` for some `b ≠ 0`. -/
/-- The zero divisors form a cone: nonzero real multiples of zero divisors are zero divisors. -/

/-- `2 e₁` (the sum of the two zero divisors above) lies in the octonion half, where left
multiplication scales norms, so it is not a zero divisor. -/

/-- **The zero divisors are not a linear subspace**: `e₁ + e₁₀` and `e₁ - e₁₀` are zero divisors,
their sum is nonzero, and it is not a zero divisor. -/

/-- **Multiplication by a zero divisor loses information**: left multiplication by `e₁ + e₁₀`
sends the different inputs `0` and `e₅ + e₁₄` to the same output `0`. -/

/-!
# Cosmohedra and associahedra: tree-level face counts

Source: N. Arkani-Hamed, C. Figueiredo, F. Vazão, *Cosmohedra* (`Cosmohedra.tar.gz`, `main.tex`).

Polygon vertices are `0, 1, …, n-1` in cyclic order; a chord `(i, j)` with `i < j` is a pair of
non-adjacent vertices.

* **Associahedron `Assoc_n`** (dimension `n-3`): faces are sets of pairwise non-crossing chords
  (*partial triangulations*); vertices are complete triangulations, facets single chords.
* **Cosmohedron `Cosmo_n`** (dimension `n-3`): faces are "russian dolls", collections of nested
  sub-polygons in which every sub-polygon that contains another one is completely covered by
  the sub-polygons inside it.  Equivalently, a face is a recursive dissection: the full polygon
  is either left alone or cut by a non-empty set of non-crossing chords, and each piece is again
  either left alone or cut, and so on.  The codimension of a face is the number of polygons that
  are cut.  So facets are the non-empty partial triangulations, and vertices are the dolls in
  which every non-triangle is cut by exactly one chord.

This file

1. counts chords and partial triangulations explicitly (`diagonals`, `partialTriangulations`);
2. computes the face numbers of `Cosmo_n` from the recursive description (`cosmoFaces`);
3. checks the paper's claims against these computations and checks that the face numbers of
   both polytopes satisfy the Euler–Poincaré relation, a necessary condition for a face lattice
   of a polytope;
4. checks that the paper's recursion for the number of wavefunction terms `Ψ_n` gives the
   vertex count of `Cosmo_n`.
-/
/-! ## 1. Chords and partial triangulations -/
/-- `(i, j)` is a chord (diagonal) of the convex `n`-gon with vertices `0, …, n-1`. -/
/-- The chords of the convex `n`-gon. -/
/-- Two chords cross in their interiors (their endpoints interleave). -/

/-- Partial triangulations of the `n`-gon: sets of pairwise non-crossing chords.  These label the
faces of `Assoc_n` (and, when non-empty, the facets of `Cosmo_n`). -/

/-- Number of partial triangulations of the `n`-gon with exactly `k` chords
(= number of faces of `Assoc_n` of codimension `k`). -/
/-- Face numbers of `Assoc_n` listed by codimension `0, 1, …, n-3`. -/
/-- The `n`-gon has `n(n-3)/2` chords: the facet count of `Assoc_n` (checked for `3 ≤ n ≤ 12`). -/

/-- Face numbers of the associahedra `Assoc_4, …, Assoc_7` (codimension `0, 1, 2, …`).  The last
entry is the number of vertices = complete triangulations. -/
/-! ## 2. Face numbers of the cosmohedron from the recursive description -/
/-- Coefficient-list addition (polynomials in one variable `t`, lowest degree first). -/
/-- Coefficient-list multiplication. -/
/-- Drop trailing zero coefficients. -/

/-- Entry `k` of a table holds, for the `k`-gon, the pair `(F k, G k)` where
* `F k` = face polynomial of `Cosmo_k`: coefficient of `t^c` = number of russian dolls of the
  `k`-gon in which exactly `c` polygons are cut (= faces of codimension `c`);
* `G k` = sum over **all** dissections of the `k`-gon (including the trivial one) of the product
  of `F` over the pieces. -/

/-- Weight of a gap of `g` polygon edges between two consecutive vertices of the piece containing
the edge `(0, k-1)`: a single edge (`g = 1`) contributes `1`; otherwise the `(g+1)`-gon beyond the
gap is dissected arbitrarily (`G (g+1)`). -/
/-- Sum over compositions of `j` into `r` positive gaps of the product of the gap weights. -/

/-- Sum over **non-trivial** dissections of the `k`-gon of the product of `F` over the pieces,
organised by the piece containing the edge `(0, k-1)` (which has `m + 1` vertices, `2 ≤ m ≤ k-2`). -/
/-- A `k`-gon is either left alone (`1`) or cut (`t ×` non-trivial dissections). -/
/-- The table for polygons with `0, 1, …, n` vertices (entries below `3` are placeholders). -/

/-- Face numbers of `Cosmo_n` by codimension `0, 1, …, n-3`: entry `0` is the polytope itself,
entry `1` the facets, the last entry the vertices. -/

/-- Face numbers of the cosmohedra `Cosmo_4, …, Cosmo_12`, by codimension.  `Cosmo_5` is a
decagon (10 edges, 10 vertices); `Cosmo_6` has 44 facets, 114 edges and 72 vertices. -/
/-! ## 3. The paper's claims, and the Euler–Poincaré relation -/
/-- Alternating sum `a₀ - a₁ + a₂ - …` of a list of face numbers. -/

/-- **Euler–Poincaré for cosmohedra.**  For a `d`-polytope, counting faces by codimension
(including the polytope itself), `∑ (-1)^c f^c = (-1)^d`.  The face numbers of `Cosmo_n`
obtained from the russian-doll description satisfy this for every `n` from `3` to `12`. -/

/-- **Euler–Poincaré for associahedra** (`n = 3, …, 7`), from the explicit partial
triangulations. -/

/-- **Facets of `Cosmo_n` are the non-empty partial triangulations** (the paper: "the total
number of facets of the cosmohedron is equal to the total number of all (not just complete)
triangulations of the `n`-gon").  Checked for `n = 4, …, 7` against the explicit enumeration. -/

/-- **Vertices of `Assoc_n` are counted by Catalan numbers**: `C_{n-2}` complete triangulations
(`n = 3, …, 7`). -/

/-- The paper's recursion for the number of terms of the tree-level wavefunction,
`Ψ₃ = 1`, `Ψ_n = ∑_{k=3}^{n-1} (k-1) Ψ_k Ψ_{n+2-k}`, as a table `[Ψ₀, …, Ψ_n]`
(entries below `3` are placeholders `0`). -/
/-- `Ψ_n`, the number of terms in the `n`-point tree-level wavefunction. -/

/-- **Vertices of `Cosmo_n` = wavefunction terms `Ψ_n`**: the last face number (codimension
`n-3`, i.e. the vertices, i.e. the maximal russian dolls) equals the paper's `Ψ_n` for
`n = 3, …, 12`. -/
/-- The values `Ψ_3, …, Ψ_12`. -/

/-! ## 4. The pentagon: `Assoc_5` and the flip graph

The two-dimensional associahedron `Assoc_5` is a pentagon.  Its vertices are the five
triangulations of a pentagon and its edges are *flips* (replace one chord by the other diagonal
of the quadrilateral it sits in).  This is the pentagon of the pentagon equation for F-moves in
`QBX.Formal.AnyonCoherence` (`IsPentagon`): an F-move is a flip of the dual trivalent tree, and
the equation compares the two flip paths (of lengths 2 and 3) between opposite vertices. -/
/-- Two triangulations of the `n`-gon differ by a flip: they share all chords but one. -/
/-- Complete triangulations of the `n`-gon. -/
/-- The five triangulations of the pentagon, in cyclic flip order. -/

/-- **The flip graph of the pentagon is a 5-cycle**: the five listed sets are exactly the
triangulations, consecutive ones (cyclically) differ by a flip, and every triangulation has
exactly two flip neighbours. -/

/-!
# Two checks on the pipeline descriptions

Report: `docs/ZERO_DIVISOR_USAGE_AUDIT_2026-10-20.md`.

## `voxel_nesting.py`: every word vector is the zero vector

`VerseVoxel.build_word_vectors` sets `base = [gematria] * dim` and then
`vector = (base - base.mean()) / (base.std() + 1e-8)`. A constant vector minus its mean is `0`, so
in exact arithmetic **every word vector is `0`**, whatever the word (`standardize_const`). Hence
every verse vector (a mean of word vectors) and every shell vector is `0` too, and the gematria never
reaches the vectors (`standardize_const_indep`). There is also no `E₈` or Leech-lattice step
anywhere in the script.

## `TopQuarkFixedPoint.lean`: the Pendleton–Ross ratio does not give 173 GeV

The module defines `R* = y_t² / g₃² = 2/9` and, separately, puts in `y_t* = 0.993` by hand.
Then it checks `0.993 · 246.22 / √2 ∈ (171, 175)`. If one actually uses `R* = 2/9`, then
`y_t = g₃ √(2/9)` and `m_t = y_t v / √2 = g₃ v / 3` (`mt_of_ratio`). For any strong coupling
`g₃ < 1.23` (the measured value at `m_Z` is about `1.22`), this is **below 101 GeV**
(`mt_of_ratio_lt`), far from the measured `≈ 172.5 GeV`. The `[171, 175]` window therefore comes
from the hand-chosen `0.993`, not from the fixed point.

/-- The standardisation step of `build_word_vectors`. -/
/-- **Standardising a constant vector gives the zero vector.** -/
/-- So the word vector does not depend on the gematria value at all. -/
/-- Top mass from the ratio `R = y_t² / g₃²`: `m_t = √R · g₃ · v / √2`. -/
/-- With the Pendleton–Ross value `R* = 2/9`, `m_t = g₃ v / 3`. -/
/-- **For `g₃ < 1.23` and `v = 246.22 GeV`, the fixed-point mass is below 101 GeV.** -/

/-!
# Checks of the concrete claims in `stuff.md` (2026-10-19)

`stuff.md` mixes standard mathematics, testable numerical claims and statements that are not
mathematics. This file checks the testable ones that the corpus did not already cover. Report:
`docs/STUFF_TRIAGE_2026-10-19.md`.

1. **Root systems have even size** (`even_card_of_neg_closed`, `even_card_of_reflection_closed`,
   `reflection_closed_card_ne_21`). Every finite set of non-zero vectors that is closed under
   the reflections in its own members is closed under `v ↦ -v`, so it has an even number of
   elements. The claimed "closed 21-vector orbit" from the letters טסאצ cannot be such a set.
2. **Weyl-group orbits in `ℝ⁸` have even size** (`negChain_eq`, `weyl_closed_even`,
   `weyl_closed_card_ne_21`). Eight reflections in mutually orthogonal roots `e_i ± e_j` of
   `D₈ ⊂ E₈` compose to `v ↦ -v`. Hence every finite set of non-zero vectors closed under the
   reflections of `D₈` (in particular every orbit of the Weyl group of `E₈`) has even size. No
   Weyl orbit of a non-zero vector has 21 elements.
3. **Permutahedron and braids** (`orderOf_swap_mul_swap_adjacent`,
   `orderOf_swap_mul_swap_disjoint`, `permFaces_values`, `perm_euler`,
   `perm_twoFaces_hex_square`). The vertices of the permutahedron `Perm_n` are the permutations
   of `n` letters and its edges are the adjacent transpositions `sᵢ`. A 2-face is a coset of a
   subgroup `⟨sᵢ, sⱼ⟩`, a polygon with `2 · orderOf (sᵢ sⱼ)` sides: a **hexagon** when `j = i+1`
   (order 3, the braid relation `sᵢ sᵢ₊₁ sᵢ = sᵢ₊₁ sᵢ sᵢ₊₁`) and a **square** otherwise
   (order 2, the commutation relation). Faces of `Perm_n` of dimension `k` are ordered set
   partitions of `{1, …, n}` into `n - k` blocks (`permFaces`); the face numbers are checked for
   `n ≤ 5`, and the number of 2-faces equals `(n-2) · n!/6` hexagons plus
   `C(n-2, 2) · n!/4` squares.
4. **The `j`-function coefficient `196884`** (`j_coeffs_from_E4`). From
   `E₄ = 1 + 240 q + 2160 q² + …` (the theta series of `E₈`: 240 roots, 2160 vectors of norm 4)
   and `Δ = q ∏ (1 - qᵐ)²⁴`, the identity `E₄³ = Δ · (q⁻¹ + 744 + 196884 q + …)` holds through
   order `q²`. The number `196884 = 1 + 196883` therefore comes from the `E₈` lattice alone; no
   text corpus enters. The character of the `E₈` lattice vertex algebra itself is
   `E₄/η⁸ = q^{-1/3}(1 + 248 q + 4124 q² + …)` (`e8_vertexAlgebra_character`): its first
   non-trivial coefficient is `248 = dim E₈`, not `196884`.
5. **One-loop cosmohedron numbers** (`oneLoopCosmo_edges_forced`, `oneLoopCosmo_not_simple`).
   For a 3-dimensional polytope with 108 vertices and 62 facets, Euler's relation forces exactly
   168 edges, and `2 · 168 > 3 · 108`, so the polytope is not simple. The edge count 168 carries
   no information beyond the vertex and facet counts.

/-! ## 1. Root systems have even size -/

/-- In an additive group without 2-torsion, a finite set closed under negation that does not
contain `0` has even size. -/
/-- The orthogonal reflection of `v` in the hyperplane perpendicular to `α`. -/
/-- A reflection sends its own root to its negative. -/

/-- **Root systems have even size.** A finite set of non-zero vectors that is closed under the
reflections in its own members has an even number of elements. -/
/-- In particular, no root system (in the sense above) has 21 elements. -/
/-! ## 2. Weyl-group orbits in `ℝ⁸` have even size -/
/-- The reflection `v ↦ v - ⟨v, α⟩ α` in a root `α` with `⟨α, α⟩ = 2`. -/
/-- The `D₈` root `e_i + s e_j` (an `E₈` root when `i ≠ j` and `s = ±1`). -/
/-- The roots `e_i ± e_j` (`i ≠ j`) have squared length 2. -/
/-- Reflecting in `e_i - e_j` and then in `e_i + e_j` negates coordinates `i` and `j`. -/
/-- Eight reflections in the mutually orthogonal roots `e₀ ± e₁, e₂ ± e₃, e₄ ± e₅, e₆ ± e₇`. -/

/-- **`-1` lies in the Weyl group of `D₈` (hence of `E₈`):** the eight reflections compose to
`v ↦ -v`. -/

/-- **Weyl-invariant sets in `ℝ⁸` have even size.** A finite set of non-zero vectors that is
closed under the reflections in all roots `e_i ± e_j` (for example, any orbit of the Weyl group
of `E₈`, which contains these reflections) is closed under negation and has even size. -/
/-- No Weyl-invariant set of non-zero vectors in `ℝ⁸` has 21 elements. -/
/-! ## 3. Permutahedron and braids -/

/-- Adjacent transpositions `swap a b`, `swap b c` multiply to a 3-cycle: the hexagonal 2-faces
of the permutahedron, i.e. the braid relation. -/

/-- Disjoint transpositions multiply to an element of order 2: the square 2-faces of the
permutahedron, i.e. the commutation relation. -/

/-- Faces of dimension `k` of the permutahedron `Perm_n` are the ordered set partitions of
`n` letters into `n - k` blocks, i.e. the surjections `Fin n → Fin (n - k)`. -/

/-- Face numbers `f₀, f₁, …` of `Perm_3` (hexagon), `Perm_4` (truncated octahedron) and
`Perm_5`. -/
/-- Euler–Poincaré for `Perm_n`, `n = 3, 4, 5` (the polytope itself counted in top degree). -/

/-- The 2-faces of `Perm_n` are `(n-2) · n!/6` hexagons (one per coset of `⟨sᵢ, sᵢ₊₁⟩`) plus
`C(n-2, 2) · n!/4` squares (one per coset of `⟨sᵢ, sⱼ⟩`, `|i - j| ≥ 2`), for `n = 3, 4, 5`. -/
/-- Every vertex of `Perm_n` lies on `n - 1` edges (one per adjacent transposition). -/
/-! ## 4. The `j`-function coefficient `196884` -/
/-- Truncated product of power series given by coefficient lists. -/
/-- Coefficients of `E₄ = 1 + 240 ∑ σ₃(n) qⁿ` through `q²`. -/
/-- Coefficients of `∏_{m ≥ 1} (1 - qᵐ)²⁴ = Δ / q` through `q²`. -/

/-- **`E₄³ = Δ · (q⁻¹ + 744 + 196884 q + …)` through order `q²`.** Dividing by `q`, this says
`E₄³ ≡ (Δ/q)·(1 + 744 q + 196884 q²)` modulo `q³`; so the coefficients `744` and `196884` of the
`j`-function are determined by the `E₈` theta series `E₄`. -/
/-- Coefficients of `∏_{m ≥ 1} (1 - qᵐ)⁸ = η⁸ / q^{1/3}` through `q²`. -/

/-- **The character of the `E₈` lattice vertex algebra starts `1 + 248 q + 4124 q²`.**
`[1, 8, 44]` is the inverse of `η⁸/q^{1/3}` modulo `q³`, and `E₄ · [1, 8, 44] = [1, 248, 4124]`.
The weight-one coefficient `248 = 240 + 8` is the dimension of the Lie algebra `E₈` (240 roots
plus an 8-dimensional Cartan subalgebra). The number `196884` does not occur here: it is a
coefficient of `E₄³/Δ`, i.e. of the 24-dimensional lattice `E₈³` (`j_coeffs_from_E4`). -/
/-! ## 5. One-loop cosmohedron numbers -/

/-- For a 3-polytope with 108 vertices and 62 facets, Euler's relation `V - E + F = 2` holds
exactly when there are 168 edges. -/

/-- A simple 3-polytope has `2E = 3V`; here `2 · 168 > 3 · 108`, so the one-loop
cosmohedron at three points is not simple (some vertex lies on at least four edges). -/

# Ternary strands: three Hopf fibres, the full twist, and 3-colourings

**Status: documentation note, not a theorem of the core corpus** (Lake library `QBXNotes`).
The corrections matter (a Hopf fibre is not a ternary strand; the `(3, q)` orbits are different
objects, see the core file `QBX.Formal.Connections.HopfStrands`), but the subject of this note is
Hebrew-letter numerology, so it lives outside `QBX.Formal`.

`QBX.Formal.Connections.HopfStrands` shows that a *single* Hopf fibre is a 1-strand closed braid.
Ternary structure appears in two other places, both checked here on the QBX braid group
`BraidGroup 3`.

**Three Hopf fibres.**  Any `n` distinct Hopf fibres form the torus link `T(n, n)`; for
`n = 3` this is the closure of the 3-strand torus braid `(σ₁σ₂)³ = Δ²`, the full twist.
(The identification of `n` Hopf fibres with `T(n, n)` is the standard picture of the Hopf
fibration — fibres over a circle of latitude in `S²` are `(1, 1)` curves on one torus — and is
cited, not re-proved.)  Proved:

* `threeFibres_pure`, `threeFibres_components`: the closure has three components;
* `crossMatrix_threeFibres`, `linkingSpectrum_threeFibres`: every pair of components links
  exactly once — the braid-side shadow of "any two Hopf fibres have linking number 1";
* `fullTwist_eq`, `fullTwist_central`: `(σ₁σ₂)³ = (σ₁σ₂σ₁)²` and it commutes with every braid.

**Ternary labels (Fox 3-colourings).**  Labelling strands by `ℤ/3` with the rule
"under-strand out = 2·over − under-strand in" gives an action `foxHom` of `B₃` on `(ℤ/3)³`
(`foxGen_rels` checks the braid relation).  The number of 3-colourings of the closure of `g`
is the number of labellings fixed by `g` (`colourings g`); the closure is *tricolourable* when
this exceeds the 3 constant colourings.  Proved:

* `fox_period`: `(σ₁σ₂)⁶` acts trivially;
* `colourings_torus`: `T(3, q)` has 27, 9 or 3 colourings according as `6 ∣ q`, `q` even but
  `6 ∤ q`, or `q` odd; hence `tricolourable_torus_iff`: `T(3, q)` is tricolourable iff `q` is
  even;
* `colourings_tenen`: Tenen's `(3, 10)` knot has 9 colourings, so it **is** tricolourable (the
  Meru JSON's claim checks out); `colourings_threeFibres`: three Hopf fibres (`T(3, 3)`) are
  **not** tricolourable.
-/
/-! ### Three Hopf fibres = the full twist on three strands -/
/-- The closure of `(σ₁σ₂)³`, i.e. `T(3, 3)`: three Hopf fibres. -/
/-- The full twist is a pure braid: each Hopf fibre closes up on itself. -/
/-- The closure has three components. -/
/-- Every pair of distinct strands of the full twist crosses twice (signed). -/

/-- **Any two of the three fibres link exactly once**: the linking spectrum of the closure is six
copies of `1` (one per ordered pair of distinct components). -/
/-- `(σ₁σ₂)³ = (σ₁σ₂σ₁)²`: the torus braid of three fibres is the square of Garside's `Δ`. -/
/-- **The full twist is central** in `B₃`. -/
/-! ### Fox 3-colourings: ternary labels on strands -/
/-- Labellings of three strand ends by `ℤ/3`. -/

/-- The labelling after the crossing `σᵢ`: the over-strand label moves left, the under-strand
label `a` becomes `2b − a` where `b` is the over-strand label. -/
/-- The inverse crossing. -/
/-- The crossing `σᵢ` as a permutation of labellings. -/
/-- The colouring moves satisfy the braid relation. -/
/-- The action of `B₃` on ternary labellings. -/
/-- Number of Fox 3-colourings of the closure of `g`: labellings fixed by `g`. -/
/-- The closure of `g` is tricolourable: it has a non-constant 3-colouring. -/
/-- `(σ₁σ₂)⁶` acts trivially on ternary labellings. -/
/-- **Colourings of `T(3, q)`**: 27 if `6 ∣ q`, 9 if `q` is even and `6 ∤ q`, 3 if `q` is odd. -/
/-- **`T(3, q)` is tricolourable iff `q` is even.** -/
/-- Tenen's `(3, 10)` torus knot has 9 Fox 3-colourings: it is tricolourable. -/
/-- Three Hopf fibres (`T(3, 3)`) have only the 3 constant colourings: not tricolourable. -/

/-!
# Can the top-quark coupling `0.993` be derived from the gauge constraints?

Audit of `sovereign/Sovereign/Physics/TopQuarkFixedPoint.lean`
(report: `docs/VOXEL_TOPQUARK_ZD32_2026-10-20.md`).

That module states the Pendleton–Ross ratio `R* = y_t² / g₃² = 2/9`, then separately sets
`y_t* = 0.993` by hand and checks `0.993 · 246.22 / √2 ∈ (171, 175)`. Everything below uses the
standard one-loop Standard-Model renormalisation-group equations (`t = log μ`, common factor
`1/(16π²)` dropped; `g'` is the hypercharge coupling in Standard-Model normalisation):

* `d(y_t²)/dt ∝ y_t² (9/2 y_t² − 8 g₃² − 9/4 g₂² − 17/12 g'²)`,
* `d(g₃²)/dt ∝ −7 g₃⁴`.

## Findings

1. **The gauge constraint, solved exactly.** The ratio `R = y_t²/g₃²` is stationary iff
   `y_t² = (2/9)(g₃² + 9/4 g₂² + 17/12 g'²)` (`ratio_stationary_iff`). Without the electroweak
   couplings this is the module's `R* = 2/9` (`ratio_stationary_iff_qcd`); the "`(9/2) R* = 8 − 7`"
   of its docstring is the same equation.
2. **It cannot give 173 GeV.** For any couplings in the physical range `g₃ ≤ 1.23`, `g₂ ≤ 0.66`,
   `g' ≤ 0.37`, the gauge-constrained coupling gives `m_t = y_t v/√2 < 140 GeV`
   (`mt_gauge_constrained_lt`), so **`0.993` is not derivable from this fixed point**, even with
   the electroweak corrections included.
3. **What ratio 173 GeV needs.** `m_t ≥ 171 GeV` with `g₃ ≤ 1.23` forces `R ≥ 0.63`
   (`ratio_needed_ge`), about `2.9 ×` the Pendleton–Ross value. The "`R_phys ≈ 1.05`" of the
   docstring together with `y_t = 0.993` would need `g₃ < 0.97` (`ratio_105_needs_small_g3`),
   far below the measured `g₃(m_Z) ≈ 1.22`.
4. **The flow of the ratio, solved exactly (QCD only).** With `α = g₃²` and `u = 1/R`, the
   one-loop system is solved by `α(t) = α₀/(1 + 7cα₀t)`,
   `u(t) = 9/2 + (u₀ − 9/2)(1 + 7cα₀t)^{1/7}` (`alphaFlow_hasDerivAt`, `uFlow_hasDerivAt`). So the
   deviation from the fixed point shrinks only like `(α₀/α)^{1/7}` (`uFlow_deviation`); while `α`
   grows by at most a factor 3 (roughly the whole range from the unification scale to `m_Z`) at
   least `85 %` of the initial deviation remains (`deviation_factor_ge`). The fixed point
   `R* = 2/9` is never reached at physical scales.
5. **The quasi-infrared fixed point overshoots.** Starting from an arbitrarily large Yukawa at the
   high scale (`u₀ = 0`) gives `R = 2 / (9 (1 − (α₀/α)^{1/7}))`, which is `≥ 1.48` whenever
   `α ≤ 3 α₀` (`qirfp_ratio_ge`). The observed top sits strictly between the two one-loop
   attractors: above `2/9`, below the QCD quasi-fixed point.

**Verdict.** At one loop the value `0.993` is an empirical input (essentially `√2 · m_t / v`),
not a consequence of the gauge constraints. To reconcile the module with `173 GeV` its structure
has to change: either state `y_t` as a measured input, or replace the fixed-point claim by the
condition `R(m_t) ≥ 0.63` (numerically `R ≈ 0.64 – 0.76` for `m_t ∈ [171, 175]`,
`g₃ ∈ [1.16, 1.23]`; see the report), or run the full two-loop flow with threshold
corrections from a stated high-scale boundary condition — which this repository does not
formalise.
-/
/-! ## 1. The gauge constraint -/

/-- One-loop `d(y_t²)/dt` (up to the positive factor `2/(16π²)`), in terms of squared couplings
`y = y_t²`, `a3 = g₃²`, `a2 = g₂²`, `a1 = g'²`. -/
/-- One-loop `d(g₃²)/dt` (same factor), `b₃ = −7`. -/
/-- Numerator of `d(y/a3)/dt` (quotient rule). -/
/-- **The ratio `y_t²/g₃²` is stationary iff `y_t² = (2/9)(g₃² + 9/4 g₂² + 17/12 g'²)`.** -/
/-- Without electroweak couplings this is the Pendleton–Ross value `R* = 2/9`. -/
/-! ## 2. The gauge-constrained coupling gives less than 140 GeV -/
/-- Higgs vacuum expectation value (GeV), as in the audited module. -/
/-- Tree-level top mass from the coupling: `m_t = y_t v / √2`. -/
/-- **For physical gauge couplings the gauge-constrained top mass is below 140 GeV.** -/
/-! ## 3. What 173 GeV requires -/
/-- **`m_t ≥ 171 GeV` with `g₃ ≤ 1.23` forces `R = y_t²/g₃² ≥ 0.63`.** -/
/-- **`y_t = 0.993` with `R = 1.05` (the docstring's `R_phys`) needs `g₃ < 0.97`.** -/
/-! ## 4. The exact one-loop flow of the ratio (QCD only) -/
/-- `dα/dt = −7 c α²` (one-loop running of `g₃²`, `b₃ = −7`). -/

/-- **`du/dt = −c α (9/2 − u)`**, i.e. `R = 1/u` obeys the one-loop equation
`dR/dt = c α R (9/2 R − 1)` with `α = g₃²`. -/
/-- **The deviation from the fixed point scales like `(α₀/α)^{1/7}`.** -/

/-- **While `α` grows by at most a factor 3, at least 85 % of the deviation survives**:
`(α₀/α)^{1/7} ≥ 0.85` for `α₀/α ≥ 1/3`. -/
/-! ## 5. The QCD quasi-infrared fixed point overshoots -/

/-- The quasi-infrared fixed point ratio: `u₀ = 0` (infinite Yukawa at the high scale), so
`R = 1 / ((9/2)(1 − ρ^{1/7}))` with `ρ = α₀/α`. -/

/-- **For `1/3 ≤ ρ < 1` the quasi-fixed-point ratio is at least `1.48`**, well above the
`≈ 0.64 – 0.76` needed for the observed top mass. -/

/-!
# Twin primes as the meeting point of several conjectures

**Status: documentation note** (Lake library `QBXNotes`).  Nothing here proves the twin prime
conjecture, which is open.  What *is* proved is the web of implications between the standard
conjectures and partial results around it, so that a "convergence" strategy can be stated
precisely: which hypotheses would each be enough, and which combinations of weaker statements
would close the gap.

## The objects

* `gapSpectrum` — the set of `h` such that `p` and `p + h` are both prime for infinitely many `p`.
  The twin prime conjecture is `2 ∈ gapSpectrum` (`tpc_iff_two_mem_gapSpectrum`); Polignac's
  conjecture is "every positive even number is in it".
* `BoundedGaps H` — infinitely many primes `p` have another prime in `(p, p + H]`.  Zhang (2013),
  Maynard (2015) and Polymath 8b proved `BoundedGaps 246`; those theorems are **not** in Mathlib and
  appear here only as hypotheses.
* `Admissible hs` — the shifts `hs` avoid some residue class modulo every prime.
* `PrimeTuplesConjecture`, `DicksonConjecture`, `SchinzelH` — the classical "all forms prime
  simultaneously" conjectures.
* `DHL k m` — the Dickson–Hardy–Littlewood statement used by Maynard and Tao: every admissible
  `k`-tuple has at least `m` primes among its translates infinitely often.  Maynard and Polymath
  proved `DHL 50 2` (again: not in Mathlib, hypothesis only).
* `HardyLittlewoodTwin C` — the twin prime counting function is asymptotic to `C x / log² x`.

## What is proved (no `sorry`)

**From above (strong conjectures, each implies TPC):**
`schinzel_implies_primeTuples`, `dickson_implies_primeTuples`, `primeTuples_implies_polignac`,
`polignac_implies_tpc`, `hardyLittlewood_implies_tpc` (for any constant `C > 0`).

**From below (the bounded-gap ladder):** `BoundedGaps` is monotone (`boundedGaps_mono`), fails for
`H ≤ 1` (`not_boundedGaps_one`), and its bottom rung *is* the conjecture:
`tpc_iff_boundedGaps_two`.  Every rung pins down a concrete even gap that occurs infinitely often
(`exists_even_gap_of_boundedGaps`); in particular `polymath_consequence` turns `BoundedGaps 246`
into "some even `h ≤ 246` lies in the gap spectrum".

**Tuples:** a non-admissible tuple is prime only finitely often
(`finite_of_not_admissible`, e.g. `prime_triplets_eq` : `p, p+2, p+4` prime only for `p = 3`), and
an admissible tuple that has two primes infinitely often produces a gap in the spectrum
(`gap_of_tuple`).  `DHL 2 2` is exactly Polignac's conjecture (`dhl_two_two_iff_polignac`), and
`DHL 3 2` already forces one of the gaps `2, 4, 6` (`dhl_three_two_gap`).

**The DHL ladder:** with kernel-checked admissible tuples, `DHL 50 2` (Maynard–Polymath)
gives `BoundedGaps 246` (`boundedGaps_246_of_dhl`, using the explicit 50-tuple `polymathTuple`
of diameter 246), `DHL 5 2` (Elliott–Halberstam) gives `BoundedGaps 12`, `DHL 3 2` (generalised
EH) gives `BoundedGaps 6`, and `DHL 2 2` is Polignac.  `admissible_of_small` reduces admissibility
to the primes `p ≤ |hs|`.

**Counting:** TPC holds iff `π₂` is unbounded (`tpc_iff_twinCount_unbounded`).

**Convergence:** `tpc_of_boundedGaps_of_exclusion` — a bounded-gap theorem with bound `H`,
together with the exclusion of every even gap `4 ≤ h ≤ H` from the spectrum, gives the twin prime
conjecture.  This is the precise shape of a "squeeze" argument; the second ingredient is open for
every `H ≥ 4`.  `convergence_web` collects every arrow into one statement.
-/
/-! ## The gap spectrum -/
/-- The primes `p` such that `p + h` is also prime. -/
/-- The gaps `h` that occur infinitely often between (not necessarily consecutive) primes. -/
/-- Polignac's conjecture: every positive even number is a prime gap infinitely often. -/
/-- **The twin prime conjecture is `2 ∈ gapSpectrum`.** -/
/-- `0` is in the spectrum (Euclid). -/
/-- Odd gaps occur at most once (one of `p`, `p + h` is even), so the spectrum is even. -/
/-! ## The bounded-gap ladder -/
/-- `BoundedGaps H`: infinitely many primes `p` have another prime in `(p, p + H]`. -/
/-- A gap `h ≥ 1` in the spectrum gives the rung `BoundedGaps h`. -/
/-- The ladder has no rung below `2`: only `p = 2` has a prime at distance `1`. -/
/-- **The bottom rung of the ladder is the twin prime conjecture.** -/

/-- **Pigeonhole:** a rung `BoundedGaps H` pins down one specific gap `1 ≤ h ≤ H` that occurs
infinitely often. -/
/-- The gap found by the pigeonhole is even, so it is at least `2`. -/

/-- **Polymath 8b, as a hypothesis.**  The bounded-gap theorem with `H = 246` (proved by
Maynard and Polymath, not formalised in Mathlib) yields an explicit even gap `≤ 246` that occurs
infinitely often. -/

/-- **Convergence from below.**  A bounded-gap theorem with bound `H`, together with the
exclusion of every gap `4 ≤ h ≤ H` from the spectrum, forces the twin prime conjecture. -/
/-! ## Admissible tuples -/
/-- A finite set of shifts is admissible if, modulo every prime, it misses some residue class. -/
/-- The `n` for which every translate `n + h`, `h ∈ hs`, is prime. -/

/-- **A non-admissible tuple is prime only finitely often**: some prime divides one of the
translates of every `n`, so that translate must equal the prime. -/

/-- `p, p + 2, p + 4` are all prime only for `p = 3` (the tuple `{0, 2, 4}` covers every residue
modulo `3`). -/
/-- `{0, h}` is admissible exactly when `h` is even. -/
/-- `{0, 2, 6}` is admissible. -/
/-! ## The classical conjectures from above -/

/-- The prime `k`-tuples conjecture (qualitative Hardy–Littlewood): every admissible tuple is
simultaneously prime infinitely often. -/
/-- Dickson's conjecture for linear forms `a n + b` (`a ≥ 1`) with no fixed prime divisor. -/

/-- Schinzel's Hypothesis H: finitely many irreducible integer polynomials with positive leading
coefficients whose product has no fixed prime divisor take prime values (in absolute value)
simultaneously infinitely often. -/
/-! ## Dickson–Hardy–Littlewood `DHL(k, m)` (Maynard–Tao) -/
/-- `DHL k m`: every admissible `k`-tuple has at least `m` prime translates infinitely often. -/

/-- **Pigeonhole on pairs:** if a tuple has two prime translates infinitely often, then some
difference of two of its shifts lies in the gap spectrum. -/
/-- `DHL k 2` applied to an admissible tuple of diameter `≤ H` gives the rung `BoundedGaps H`. -/
/-- **`DHL 2 2` is exactly Polignac's conjecture.** -/
/-- `DHL 3 2` (applied to `{0, 2, 6}`) forces one of the gaps `2, 4, 6` into the spectrum. -/
/-! ## Hardy–Littlewood asymptotics -/
/-- The twin prime counting function `π₂(x) = #{p ≤ x : p, p + 2 prime}`. -/

/-- The Hardy–Littlewood twin prime asymptotic `π₂(x) ~ C x / log² x` (conjecturally with
`C = 2 C₂ ≈ 1.3203`, `C₂` the twin prime constant). -/
/-- **Any positive Hardy–Littlewood constant implies the twin prime conjecture.** -/
/-- The twin prime conjecture is exactly the unboundedness of `π₂`. -/

/-! ## The DHL ladder with explicit admissible tuples

Maynard's sieve proves `DHL k 2` for large `k`; the bound `H` then comes from the narrowest
admissible `k`-tuple.  The known (cited, **not** formalised) inputs are:

| input                         | `DHL k 2` for | narrowest tuple used here    | rung              |
|-------------------------------|---------------|------------------------------|-------------------|
| Maynard–Polymath (theorem)    | `k = 50`      | `polymathTuple`, diameter 246 | `BoundedGaps 246` |
| Elliott–Halberstam (conj.)    | `k = 5`       | `{0, 2, 6, 8, 12}`           | `BoundedGaps 12`  |
| generalised EH (conj.)        | `k = 3`       | `{0, 2, 6}`                  | `BoundedGaps 6`   |
| Polignac = `DHL 2 2` (conj.)  | `k = 2`       | `{0, 2}`                     | `BoundedGaps 2` = TPC |

The sieve-theoretic *parity barrier* (Selberg; cited) is why the method stops at `k = 3`: the
last rung needs an input of a different kind.  Each row below is a proved implication
"`DHL k 2` ⇒ rung"; the admissibility of each tuple is checked by the Lean kernel.
-/

/-- **Only small primes matter for admissibility:** a prime `p > |hs|` can never be covered,
because `hs` meets at most `|hs| < p` residue classes. -/

/-- An admissible 50-tuple of diameter 246 (found by a residue-class sieve search; its
admissibility is checked below by the kernel). -/
/-- **Rung 246** from `DHL 50 2` (the Maynard–Polymath theorem, taken as a hypothesis). -/
/-- **Rung 12** from `DHL 5 2` (Maynard's consequence of Elliott–Halberstam). -/
/-- **Rung 6** from `DHL 3 2` (Polymath's consequence of generalised Elliott–Halberstam). -/
/-! ## The whole web in one statement -/

/-!
# Twin primes have density zero, and the tuple ladder is optimal

**Status: documentation note** (Lake library `QBXNotes`).  The twin prime conjecture is open and is
not proved here.  This file adds two *unconditional* results to the "convergence" picture of
`QBX.Notes.TwinPrimeConvergence`.

## 1. Twin primes have natural density zero (`twin_density_zero`)

Let `twinCountBelow N` be the number of primes `p < N` with `p + 2` prime.  Then
`twinCountBelow N / N → 0`.

The proof is the sieve of Eratosthenes–Legendre for the pair `(n, n + 2)`:

* for a finite set `S` of odd primes with product `M`, the residues `n mod M` for which no
  `p ∈ S` divides `n (n + 2)` number exactly `∏ (p - 2)` (`card_sifted`, by the Chinese remainder
  theorem, `card_filter_range_mul_coprime`, and the count `p - 2` for one prime,
  `card_avoid_two_residues`);
* every twin prime `p > M` survives the sieve, so
  `twinCountBelow N ≤ M + 1 + (N / M + 1) ∏ (p - 2)` (`twinCountBelow_le`);
* because `∑ 1/p` diverges (Mathlib: `Nat.Primes.not_summable_one_div`), the density
  `∏ (1 - 2/p) ≤ exp (-2 ∑ 1/p)` can be made as small as we like (`exists_sieve_small`).

This is much weaker than Brun's theorem (`π₂(x) ≪ x / log² x · (log log x)²`, so that
`∑ 1/p` over twin primes converges), which is not formalised here.  It is the first unconditional
"from above" statement in this development: whatever the truth of the conjecture, the twin primes
form a set of density zero.

## 2. The tuple ladder is optimal for `k = 3, 4, 5`

`boundedGaps_of_dhl` turns `DHL k 2` plus an admissible `k`-tuple of width `H` into
`BoundedGaps H`.  The rungs used in `TwinPrimeConvergence` (`H = 6` for `k = 3`, `H = 12` for
`k = 5`) and the new rung `H = 8` for `k = 4` (`boundedGaps_8_of_dhl`) are the best this method can
give: every admissible `k`-tuple fits in no window shorter than `6, 8, 12`
(`no_admissible_triple_width_lt_six`, `no_admissible_quadruple_width_lt_eight`,
`no_admissible_quintuple_width_lt_twelve`).  The finite checks are done by the kernel over all
`k`-subsets of the window, after a translation argument (`not_admissible_of_window`).
-/
/-! ## Counting periodic sets -/
/-- A set of period `M` meets `[0, kM)` exactly `k` times as often as `[0, M)`. -/
/-- A set of period `M` meets `[0, N)` at most `(N / M + 1)` times as often as `[0, M)`. -/
/-! ## The twin sieve -/
/-- The number of twin primes below `N`: primes `p < N` with `p + 2` also prime. -/

/-- **Chinese remainder count:** for coprime `q, M`, conditions periodic modulo `q` and modulo
`M` are independent on `[0, qM)`. -/
/-- For `q ≥ 3`, exactly `q - 2` residues `n mod q` have `q ∤ n` and `q ∤ n + 2`. -/
/-- `n` survives the twin sieve by the primes in `S`: no `p ∈ S` divides `n` or `n + 2`. -/
/-- Divisibility of `n + c` by a divisor `p` of `M` only depends on `n mod M`. -/
/-- Surviving the sieve only depends on `n` modulo any common multiple of the sieving primes. -/

/-- **The twin sieve count:** modulo `M = ∏_{p ∈ S} p` (odd primes), exactly `∏ (p - 2)`
residues survive. -/
/-! ## Density zero -/

/-- **Mertens-type smallness:** `∏ (1 - 2/p)` over a suitable finite set of odd primes is below
any `ε > 0`, since `∑ 1/p` diverges. -/
/-- **Sieve upper bound** for the twin prime count, for any finite set `S` of odd primes. -/
/-- **Twin primes have natural density zero:** `#{p < N : p, p + 2 prime} / N → 0`. -/
/-! ## Optimality of the tuple ladder -/
/-- A prime `p` all of whose residues are hit by the tuple witnesses non-admissibility. -/
/-- Admissibility is invariant under translation (the direction needed below). -/

/-- If no `k`-subset of `[0, w)` is admissible, then no `k`-tuple inside any window
`[m, m + w)` is admissible. -/

/-- A decidable certificate for `not_admissible_of_window`: every `k`-subset of `[0, w)` is
covered by some prime `p ≤ k`. -/
/-- No admissible triple fits in a window of length `6` (so `{0, 2, 6}` is optimal). -/
/-- No admissible quadruple fits in a window of length `8` (so `{0, 2, 6, 8}` is optimal). -/

/-- No admissible quintuple fits in a window of length `12` (so `{0, 2, 6, 8, 12}` is
optimal). -/
/-- The prime-quadruplet pattern `{0, 2, 6, 8}` is admissible. -/
/-- **Rung 8** from `DHL 4 2`, using the admissible quadruple `{0, 2, 6, 8}` (prime quadruplets). -/

/-- **The tuple ladder is optimal for `k = 3, 4, 5`.**  For each `k` the width `6, 8, 12` is
attained by an admissible tuple, and no admissible `k`-tuple fits in a shorter window.  So the
rungs `BoundedGaps 6`, `BoundedGaps 8`, `BoundedGaps 12` are the best that `DHL k 2` can give
through `boundedGaps_of_dhl`. -/

/-!
# Twin primes and the four quadratic "generators" of non-twin centres

**Status: documentation note, not a theorem of the core corpus** (Lake library `QBXNotes`).
The reformulation below is exact, and it does not touch the conjecture: it is kept as a precise
record of what "generators for twin primes" amounts to, not as progress.

Every twin-prime pair other than `(3, 5)` has the form `(6k - 1, 6k + 1)`.  Call `k` a
*twin centre* when both numbers are prime.  The composites among `6k ± 1` are products of two
numbers `≡ ±1 (mod 6)`, and multiplying out gives four quadratic *generator families*

* `k = 6ab + a + b`  (`6k + 1 = (6a + 1)(6b + 1)`),
* `k = 6ab - a - b`  (`6k + 1 = (6a - 1)(6b - 1)`),
* `k = 6ab + a - b`  (`6k - 1 = (6a - 1)(6b + 1)`),
* `k = 6ab - a + b`  (`6k - 1 = (6a + 1)(6b - 1)`),

with `a, b ≥ 1`.  The main results:

* `QBX.Notes.TwinPrime.isTwinCentre_iff`: for `k ≥ 1`, `k` is a twin centre iff `k` is produced
  by none of the four generator families;
* `QBX.Notes.TwinPrime.twinPrimeConjecture_iff`: the twin prime conjecture (infinitely many
  `p` with `p` and `p + 2` prime) holds iff infinitely many `k ≥ 1` escape all four generators.

This is an exact *reformulation*, not progress on the conjecture: it moves the problem into a
statement about the complement of the union of four quadratic value sets, which is still open.
It is the precise content of "using generators to attack twin primes" that can be checked; see
`QBX/docs/design/BRAID_BIOLOGY_STEIN_TWIN.md` §5.
-/
/-- `k` is a twin centre: `6k - 1` and `6k + 1` are both prime. -/

/-- `k` is produced by one of the four quadratic generator families (computed in `ℤ`, so that
`6ab - a - b` is never truncated). -/
/-- The twin prime conjecture. -/
/-- A number `n ≥ 2` coprime to `6` is `6a ± 1` with `a ≥ 1`. -/
/-- A composite `m ≥ 2` splits as `p * q` with `2 ≤ p` and `2 ≤ q`. -/
/-- Generated ⇒ not a twin centre (one of `6k ± 1` factors non-trivially). -/
/-- Not a twin centre ⇒ generated (for `k ≥ 1`). -/
-- 6k - 1 composite
-- 6k + 1 composite
/-- **Generator characterisation of twin centres.** -/
/-- Every twin pair with `p ≥ 5` is centred on a multiple of `6`. -/
/-- The lower twin primes `≥ 5` are exactly the numbers `6k - 1` with `k ≥ 1` a twin centre. -/
/-- **Twin prime conjecture ⇔ infinitely many `k` escape the four generators.** -/
/-! ### Small checks -/

/-!
# The repaired voxel pipeline: guarded standardisation and non-collapsing lattice projection

Companion of the refactored `voxel_nesting.py` and `lattice_quantizers.py`
(report: `docs/VOXEL_TOPQUARK_ZD32_2026-10-20.md`).

`QBX.Notes.PipelineClaims.standardize_const` showed that the old `build_word_vectors` sent every
word to the zero vector. The repaired pipeline relies on two facts, proved here in exact arithmetic.

1. **Guarded standardisation keeps the signal.** For a non-constant vector the z-score
   `(x - mean x) / (std x + eps)` (with `eps ≥ 0`) is non-zero (`standardize_ne_zero`), has mean
   `0` (`mean_standardize`) and standard deviation `std x / (std x + eps)`
   (`std_standardize`); with `eps = 0` that is exactly `1` (`std_standardize_zero`). The guarded
   version used in the script (`standardizeSafe`, which only centres when `std x = 0`) is non-zero
   for every non-constant input (`standardizeSafe_ne_zero`).
2. **Robust scaling prevents collapse to the zero lattice point.** If every point lies within
   `ρ` of the lattice `L` (covering radius `ρ`) and `0` is a nearest lattice point to `y`, then
   `‖y‖ ≤ ρ` (`norm_le_of_zero_nearest`). Hence once a vector is scaled to norm `> ρ`, none of its
   nearest lattice points is `0` (`nearest_ne_zero_of_norm_gt`). This is what
   `scale_for_lattice` does, with `ρ = 1` for `E₈` and `ρ = √2` for the Leech lattice
   (`4` in Conway's integer coordinates).
-/
/-- Guarded standardisation as in the repaired script: centre only, if the vector is constant. -/
/-- A vector is constant iff it equals its mean everywhere. -/
/-- A non-constant vector has positive standard deviation. -/
/-- **The z-score of a non-constant vector is not the zero vector** (for any `eps ≥ 0`). -/
/-- **The guarded standardisation never kills a non-constant vector.** -/
/-- The z-score has mean `0`. -/

/-- **The z-score has standard deviation `std x / (std x + eps)`** (so variance is kept, up to
the `eps` regulariser). -/
/-- With `eps = 0`, a non-constant vector is standardised to **unit** standard deviation. -/
/-! ## Robust scaling against collapse to the zero lattice point -/

/-- If every point is within `ρ` of `L` and `0` is a nearest point of `L` to `y`, then
`‖y‖ ≤ ρ`. -/

/-- **A vector of norm larger than the covering radius has no nearest lattice point equal to
`0`.** -/

/-!
# Nesting zero divisors

Report: `docs/ZERO_DIVISOR_USAGE_AUDIT_2026-10-20.md` (section "What happens if we nest them?").

Three precise readings of "nesting" a zero divisor, each checked here over `ℝ`.

1. **Nesting the algebra** (Cayley–Dickson doubling `CD ℝ n ⊂ CD ℝ (n+1)`, `a ↦ (a, 0)`).
   The inclusion is multiplicative (`cdMul_embed`), so a zero-divisor pair at one level stays a
   zero-divisor pair at every higher level (`isZDPair_embed`, `isZDPair_embed_iter`). Since the
   sedenions (level 4) contain the pair `e₁ + e₁₀`, `e₅ + e₁₄`, **every** level `m ≥ 4` has zero
   divisors (`zeroDivisors_every_level`). Nesting never removes zero divisors; it only adds more.
2. **Nesting a zero divisor in itself** (`x ↦ x · x`). Every Cayley–Dickson algebra satisfies
   `x x = t(x) x - N(x)`. For a pure imaginary `x` (trace `0`) this is the real scalar `-N(x)`,
   which is non-zero when `x ≠ 0` (`cdMul_self_of_trace_zero`, `cdMul_self_ne_zero_of_trace_zero`).
   So a pure imaginary zero divisor never annihilates itself: squaring it gives a non-zero real
   number, which is invertible. Example: `(e₁ + e₁₀)² = -2` (`sq_e1_add_e10`).
3. **Nesting the annihilation** (zero divisor times zero divisor). The product of two zero divisors
   need not be a zero divisor: `(e₁ + e₁₀)(e₁ + e₁₀) = -2` is not one (`zd_mul_zd_not_zd`).
-/
/-- `a, b` is a zero-divisor pair at level `n`: both non-zero, with product zero. -/
/-- The inclusion of level `n` into level `n + 1` as the first half, `a ↦ (a, 0)`. -/
/-- **The Cayley–Dickson inclusion is multiplicative**: `(a, 0)(b, 0) = (a b, 0)`. -/
/-- **A zero-divisor pair survives one doubling.** -/
/-- **A zero-divisor pair survives any number of doublings.** -/
/-- The sedenion pair `e₁ + e₁₀`, `e₅ + e₁₄`. -/
/-- **Every Cayley–Dickson level from the sedenions on has zero divisors.** -/
/-- `cdScalar r n = 0` only for `r = 0`. -/

/-- **Squaring a pure imaginary element gives a real number**: if `t(x) = 0` then
`x x = -N(x) · 1`. -/
/-- **A non-zero pure imaginary element never annihilates itself** (at any level). -/

/-- **A product of zero divisors need not be a zero divisor**: `e₁ + e₁₀` is a zero divisor, but
its square `-2` is not. -/

/-!
# The extended binary Golay code, a `[24, 4, 8]` doubly-even subcode, and its
# direct sum over the seven lines of the Fano plane

* `golay24` — the extended binary Golay code `G₂₄`, a `[24, 12, 8]` code with weights in
  `{0, 8, 12, 16, 24}`, given by the generator matrix `[I₁₂ | B]`.
* `golaySub` — a 4-dimensional subcode of `G₂₄`: it is a doubly-even self-orthogonal
  `[24, 4, 8]` code whose support is all 24 coordinates.
* `fanoLine` — the seven lines `{i, i+1, i+3}` of the Fano plane `PG(2, 2)` on `ZMod 7`.
* `fanoCode` — the direct sum, over the seven Fano lines, of copies of `golaySub`: a
  doubly-even self-orthogonal `[168, 28, 8]` code on qubits `Fin 7 × Fin 24`.

Linear independence of the generator rows is proved from the identity block.  The weight
enumeration over all 4096 codewords (`golayWord_weights`) is proved without enumerating them
(doubly-even rows, `B² = I` and the all-ones word); the small finite checks use
`decide +kernel`, and the file uses no `native_decide`.
-/
/-- Hamming weight of a binary vector. -/
/-! ## The extended Golay code -/
/-- The quadratic-residue pattern mod 11 used to build the Golay generator matrix. -/
/-- The `12 × 12` matrix `B` of the generator matrix `[I₁₂ | B]` of the extended Golay code. -/
/-- The `i`-th row of the generator matrix `[I₁₂ | B]` of the extended Golay code. -/
/-- The codeword of `G₂₄` with message `c`. -/
/-- The **extended binary Golay code** `G₂₄ ⊆ F₂²⁴`. -/

/-- The first 12 coordinates of a codeword are its message (the generator matrix is
`[I₁₂ | B]`). -/
/-- `G₂₄` has dimension 12. -/
/-- `G₂₄` is self-orthogonal (in fact self-dual). -/

/-! ### The weight enumeration, by the doubly-even / `B² = I` argument

The weights of `G₂₄` are proved without enumerating its 4096 codewords:
* every codeword has weight divisible by 4 (the rows have weight 8 or 12 and are pairwise
  orthogonal, and `wt (v + w) = wt v + wt w - 2 wt (v * w)`);
* `wt (golayWord c) = wt c + wt (c B)`, and `B² = I`, so the message `c B` has a codeword of
  the same weight with the two halves swapped; the 78 messages of weight at most 2 give
  codewords of weight at least 8, so every nonzero codeword has weight at least 8;
* the all-ones word is a codeword, so a codeword of weight 20 would give one of weight 4. -/
/-- The check half `c B` of the codeword with message `c`. -/
/-- `0/1` indicator of a nonzero bit. -/
/-- Every codeword of `G₂₄` has weight divisible by 4 (proved without the enumeration). -/
/-- `B² = I`: taking the check half twice gives the message back. -/
/-- A message of weight 1 or 2 gives a codeword of weight at least 8. -/
/-- Every nonzero codeword has weight at least 8 (proved without the enumeration). -/
/-- The weights of all 4096 codewords, by the argument above (no enumeration). -/
/-- Every nonzero codeword of `G₂₄` has weight 8, 12, 16 or 24. -/
/-- `G₂₄` has minimum distance (at least) 8. -/
/-- `G₂₄` is doubly even: all weights are divisible by 4. -/
/-! ## A doubly-even `[24, 4, 8]` subcode -/
/-- The message vector with bits given by the binary expansion of `m`. -/

/-- Generators of the subcode: two disjoint octads, the all-ones word and a fourth octad
(messages `2`, `121`, `4095`, `9`). -/
/-- The `[24, 4, 8]` doubly-even subcode of `G₂₄` used on each Fano line. -/
/-- The subcode is contained in the Golay code. -/
/-- The subcode has dimension 4. -/
/-- The subcode has minimum distance 8 (lower bound). -/
/-- The minimum distance 8 is attained. -/
/-- The subcode is doubly even. -/
/-- The subcode is self-orthogonal. -/
/-- The subcode contains the all-ones word, so its support is every coordinate. -/
/-! ## The Fano plane -/
/-- The seven lines `{i, i+1, i+3}` (indices mod 7) of the Fano plane. -/
/-- Every Fano line has three points. -/
/-- Any two distinct points of the Fano plane lie on exactly one common line. -/
/-- Any two distinct Fano lines meet in exactly one point. -/
/-! ## The direct sum over the Fano lines -/
/-- The qubits of the Golay–Fano code: 24 positions on each of the seven Fano lines. -/
/-- The restriction of a word on `FanoQubit` to the block of Fano line `ℓ`. -/
/-- The generator `subGen k` placed on the block of Fano line `ℓ`. -/

/-- The **Golay–Fano code**: the direct sum, over the seven Fano lines, of copies of the
`[24, 4, 8]` doubly-even Golay subcode. -/

/-- The Golay–Fano code is exactly the direct sum: a word lies in it iff each of its seven
blocks lies in the Golay subcode. -/
/-- The Golay–Fano code has dimension `7 × 4 = 28`. -/
/-- The Golay–Fano code has length 168. -/
/-- The Golay–Fano code has minimum distance (at least) 8. -/
/-- The minimum distance 8 of the Golay–Fano code is attained. -/
/-- The Golay–Fano code is doubly even. -/
/-- The Golay–Fano code is self-orthogonal. -/
/-- Every qubit is in the support of the Golay–Fano code. -/
