/-!
# What the Golay–Fano code does *not* do

This file checks two claims made about the Golay–Fano code (`QEC.fanoCode`, the direct sum
over the seven Fano lines of `[24, 4, 8]` doubly-even Golay subcodes).

1. **"The commutation relations of the code generate the 28-dimensional `so(8)`."**  This
   is false.  The stabilizers `X^a Z^b` (`a, b` in the code) of the CSS code built from the
   self-orthogonal Golay–Fano code pairwise commute, so the Lie algebra they generate under
   the matrix commutator is abelian (`stabLie_isLieAbelian`), whereas `so(8, ℂ)` is not
   abelian (`so8_not_isLieAbelian`).  Hence there is no surjective Lie algebra map, and in
   particular no isomorphism, from the stabilizer Lie algebra onto `so(8)`
   (`stabLie_not_surjects_so8`, `stabLie_not_equiv_so8`).

2. **"The code admits transversal Clifford + T gates."**  Clifford + T is a universal gate
   set, and the Eastin–Knill theorem rules out a universal transversal gate set on any code
   that detects single-qubit errors.  The infinitesimal core of that theorem is proved
   here for the Golay–Fano code: every single-qubit operator is sandwiched by the code
   projector to a scalar (`golayFano_detects_single_qubit`), so every *transversal*
   generator `∑_q h_q` (a sum of single-qubit operators) acts on the code space as a scalar
   (`golayFano_transversal_generator_trivial`).  Thus no continuous family of transversal
   gates can act non-trivially on the encoded qubits.  The full Eastin–Knill theorem (which
   also needs Lie group theory to conclude that the transversal logical group is finite) is
   not formalized, and the universality claim is **not** proved: it is false.
-/
/-! ## Lie algebras generated by commuting elements -/

/-- If the elements of `s` pairwise commute, so do all elements of the Lie subalgebra
generated by `s`. -/
/-! ## The stabilizer Lie algebra of the Golay–Fano code is abelian -/

/-- The Lie algebra (under the matrix commutator `⁅A, B⁆ = AB - BA`) generated by the
stabilizers `X^a Z^b`, `a, b ∈ fanoCode`, of the Golay–Fano CSS code. -/
/-- All commutators of the Golay–Fano stabilizers vanish. -/
/-- The Lie algebra generated by the Golay–Fano stabilizers is abelian. -/
/-- The matrix `E₀₁ - E₁₀ ∈ so(8)`. -/
/-- The matrix `E₁₂ - E₂₁ ∈ so(8)`. -/
/-- `so(8, ℂ)` is not abelian. -/

/-- **The `so(8)` claim is false.**  No Lie algebra homomorphism from the Lie algebra
generated by the Golay–Fano stabilizers onto `so(8, ℂ)` is surjective. -/
/-- In particular the stabilizer Lie algebra is not isomorphic to `so(8, ℂ)`. -/
/-! ## Single-qubit operators and the infinitesimal Eastin–Knill obstruction -/
/-- The single-qubit Pauli matrix `X^a Z^b` on `ℂ²` (basis indexed by `ZMod 2`). -/
/-- The four single-qubit Pauli matrices span all `2 × 2` complex matrices. -/
/-- The operator `m` acting on qubit `q` (and as the identity on all other qubits). -/

/-- **Single-qubit error detection for CSS codes.**  If `C` is self-orthogonal and every
qubit lies in the support of `C`, then for every operator `m` acting on a single qubit `q`,
the code projector `P` satisfies `P (m)_q P = c P` for some scalar `c` (the Knill–Laflamme
condition for single-qubit errors). -/

/-- **Transversal generators act trivially on CSS codes that detect single-qubit errors.**
For any choice of single-qubit operators `h q`, the transversal generator `∑_q (h q)_q`
is sandwiched by the code projector to a scalar multiple of the projector. -/

/-- If a transversal generator `H = ∑_q (h q)_q` preserves the code space (`H P = P H`),
then it acts on the code space as a scalar: `H P = c P`. -/

/-- An entry of the CSS projector: if `y` is orthogonal to `C` and `a ∈ C`, then the
`(y + a, y)` entry of the code projector is nonzero. -/
/-! ## The Golay–Fano code -/
/-- The code projector of the Golay–Fano CSS code is a nonzero projector. -/
/-- The Golay–Fano CSS code detects every single-qubit error. -/

/-- **Infinitesimal Eastin–Knill for the Golay–Fano code.**  Every transversal generator
acts on the code space as a scalar, so no continuous family of transversal gates acts
non-trivially on the encoded qubits. -/
/-! ## Transversal `T` is not a logical gate of the Golay–Fano code -/
/-- The eighth root of unity `ω = e^{iπ/4}`, the nontrivial eigenvalue of the `T` gate. -/
/-- The transversal `T` gate `T^{⊗n} = ⊗_q diag(1, ω)`: `|x⟩ ↦ ω^{wt x} |x⟩`. -/
/-- A weight-two word on Fano line `0`, orthogonal to the Golay–Fano code. -/

/-- **The transversal `T` gate does not preserve the Golay–Fano code space**:
`T^{⊗168}` does not commute with the code projector. -/

/-!
# Pauli operators on `n` qubits and CSS stabilizer codes

Basic infrastructure for the quantum-error-correction part of the project
(see `QEC_GOLAY_FANO_NOTES.md`).

Qubits are indexed by a finite type `Q`.  The computational basis of `(ℂ²)^{⊗Q}` is indexed
by bit strings `x : Q → ZMod 2`, and operators are matrices indexed by bit strings.
For `a b : Q → ZMod 2` the Pauli operator `X^a Z^b` is `pauli a b`.
-/
/-- The sign character `ZMod 2 → ℂ`, `u ↦ (-1)^u`. -/
/-- The binary dot product `a · b = ∑_q a_q b_q ∈ ZMod 2`. -/
/-- Operators on `n = |Q|` qubits: complex matrices indexed by computational basis strings. -/
/-- The bit-flip operator `X^a : |y⟩ ↦ |y + a⟩`. -/
/-- The phase-flip operator `Z^b : |y⟩ ↦ (-1)^{b·y} |y⟩`. -/
/-- The Pauli operator `X^a Z^b`. -/
/-- Multiplication rule `X^a Z^b · X^c Z^d = (-1)^{b·c} X^{a+c} Z^{b+d}`. -/
/-- The symplectic form on `F₂^{2n}`; two Pauli operators commute iff it vanishes. -/

/-- Commutation rule of Pauli operators:
`X^a Z^b · X^c Z^d = (-1)^{⟨(a,b),(c,d)⟩} X^c Z^d · X^a Z^b`. -/

/-- **Knill–Laflamme for detected errors.**  If `P` is absorbed by a stabilizer `S`
(`P S = S P = P`) and the error `E` anticommutes with `S`, then `P E P = 0`. -/
/-! ## CSS codes from self-orthogonal binary codes -/
/-- A binary linear code `C ⊆ F₂^Q` is self-orthogonal if `a · b = 0` for all `a, b ∈ C`. -/
/-- The stabilizer generators of the CSS code `CSS(C, C)`: all `X^a Z^b` with `a, b ∈ C`. -/
/-- The finite set of elements of a binary code. -/

/-- The code-space projector of `CSS(C, C)`: the average `|C|^{-2} ∑_{a,b ∈ C} X^a Z^b` of the
stabilizer group. -/
/-- The CSS code projector is idempotent. -/
/-- The CSS code projector is nonzero (the code space is nontrivial). -/

/-!
# The Steane code, its transversal Clifford group, and its embedding into `H_F`

* `steaneCode`: the doubly-even `[7, 3, 4]` simplex code `C` (the dual of the Hamming code).
  `CSS(C, C)` is the Steane `[[7, 1, 3]]` code.
* `steane_selfOrthogonal`, `steane_doublyEven`, `steane_fullSupport`, `steane_distance`
  (every nontrivial logical operator `v ∈ C^⊥ \ C` has weight `≥ 3`).
* The full transversal Clifford group is logical (`steane_transversal_clifford`):
  `H^{⊗7}`, `S^{⊗7}`, and `CNOT^{⊗7}` between two blocks; while `T^{⊗7}` is not
  (`steane_transT_not_logical`).
* `embedOp`: an isometric embedding of the operators on a qubit register into the operators on a
  bigger finite Hilbert space, multiplicative, additive and injective.
* `ACHilbert k N = Fin k × H_F`: the Hilbert space `ℓ²(X) ⊗ H_F` of the almost-commutative
  spectral triple over a discrete space `X` with `k` points and internal space the finite
  Standard-Model space `H_F` of `NCGStandardModel.lean` (with `N` generations).
  `steaneAC` embeds the Steane register into `ℓ²(X) ⊗ H_F` for two points and three generations,
  and all code-space statements transfer (`steaneAC_*`).
-/
/-! ## The Steane code -/

/-- Generators of the `[7, 3, 4]` simplex code: the rows of the parity-check matrix of the
Hamming `[7, 4, 3]` code. -/

/-- The classical code underlying the Steane code: `CSS(steaneCode, steaneCode)` is the
Steane `[[7, 1, 3]]` code. -/
/-- Orthogonality to the Steane code can be tested on the three generators. -/
/-- The Steane code is self-orthogonal. -/
/-- The Steane code is doubly even: every codeword has weight divisible by `4`. -/
/-- Every qubit lies in the support of the Steane code. -/

/-- **Distance of the Steane code.**  Every vector orthogonal to `C` but not in `C` (the
support of a nontrivial logical operator) has weight at least `3`. -/
/-! ## Transversal gates of the Steane code -/
/-- The Steane code detects every single-qubit error (Knill–Laflamme condition). -/

/-- **The transversal Clifford group of the Steane code.**  `H^{⊗7}` and `S^{⊗7}` preserve
the code space of one block, and `CNOT^{⊗7}` preserves the code space of two blocks. -/

/-- **Transversal `T` is not a logical gate of the Steane code**, as required by the
Eastin–Knill theorem (the Steane code has the full transversal Clifford group, which together
with `T` would be universal). -/
/-! ## Embedding a qubit register into a larger finite Hilbert space -/
/-- The isometry `V : ℂ^α → ℂ^β`, `|x⟩ ↦ |e x⟩`, induced by an injection `e : α ↪ β`. -/
/-- `V` is an isometry: `V† V = 1`. -/
/-- The embedding `M ↦ V M V†` of operators on `ℂ^α` into operators on `ℂ^β`. -/
/-- The embedding can be undone: `V† (V M V†) V = M`; in particular it is injective. -/
/-- Commutation relations transfer through the embedding (in both directions). -/
/-! ## The almost-commutative Hilbert space `ℓ²(X) ⊗ H_F` -/

/-- The Hilbert space (index set) of the almost-commutative spectral triple
`C(X) ⊗ A_F` over a discrete space `X` with `k` points: `ℓ²(X) ⊗ H_F`, where `H_F` is the
finite Standard-Model Hilbert space `NCG.HF N` with `N` generations. -/
/-- A qubit register with `n` qubits fits into `ℓ²(X) ⊗ H_F` as soon as `2^n ≤ k · 32 N`. -/

/-- A fixed embedding of the seven Steane qubits (`2^7 = 128` basis states) into
`ℓ²(X) ⊗ H_F` for a two-point space `X` and the three-generation `H_F` (`2 · 96 = 192`
states). -/
/-- The Steane code projector, embedded into `ℓ²(X) ⊗ H_F`. -/
/-- The embedded Steane code space is a nonzero projector on `ℓ²(X) ⊗ H_F`. -/

/-- **Transversal Clifford gates on `ℓ²(X) ⊗ H_F`.**  The embedded `H^{⊗7}` and `S^{⊗7}`
commute with the embedded code projector, while the embedded `T^{⊗7}` does not. -/

/-- **Knill–Laflamme on `ℓ²(X) ⊗ H_F`**: the embedded Steane code detects every embedded
single-qubit error. -/

comments.text:
/-!
# Decoding, the threshold bound, and concatenated codes

Error model: independent bit flips (`X` errors; by the `X ↔ Z` symmetry of `CSS(C, C)`
the same holds verbatim for `Z` errors), each qubit flipped with probability `p`.

* `errProb p e = ∏_q (p if e_q = 1 else 1 - p)`, `sum_errProb` (it is a probability
  distribution) and `prob_weight_gt_le`: `P(wt e > t) ≤ C(n, t+1) p^{t+1}` (union bound).
* `syndrome C e = (b · e)_{b ∈ C}`: the outcomes of measuring the `Z`-type stabilizers
  `Z^b`, `b ∈ C`, on the error `X^e`.  `mwDecode`: minimum-weight syndrome decoding.
* `mwDecode_corrects`: if every nontrivial logical operator has weight `> 2t`, the decoder
  corrects every error of weight `≤ t` (up to a stabilizer).
* `failProb_le`: the logical failure probability is at most `C(n, t+1) p^{t+1}`.
* `concatFail`: logical failure rate of the `L`-fold concatenated code (each level-`L` block is
  a qubit of level `L + 1`, failing independently with the level-`L` rate).
* `threshold_recursion` / `concat_threshold`: below threshold `p_th` (with
  `C(n, t+1) p_th^t ≤ 1`) the failure rate is at most `p_th (p / p_th)^{(t+1)^L}`.
* `steane_concat_threshold`: for the concatenated Steane code, `p_L ≤ (21 p)^{2^L} / 21`.
* `golayFano_no_single_error_correction`: in contrast, the Golay–Fano code of
  `QECGolay.lean` has a weight-two logical operator, so no syndrome decoder corrects all
  single-qubit errors.
-/
/-! ## The independent bit-flip channel -/

/-- Probability of the error pattern `e` when each qubit is flipped independently with
probability `p`. -/
/-- Sum of `errProb` over all patterns with prescribed values on each qubit. -/
/-- `errProb p` is a probability distribution. -/
/-- The probability that all qubits of `T` are flipped is `p^{|T|}`. -/
/-- **Union bound**: the probability of more than `t` flips is at most `C(n, t+1) p^{t+1}`. -/
/-! ## Syndrome decoding -/

/-- The syndrome of the error `X^e`: the outcomes `(-1)^{b·e}` of the stabilizers `Z^b`,
`b ∈ C`, recorded as `b · e ∈ ZMod 2`. -/

/-- **Minimum-weight decoding**: from the syndrome `s`, return an error of minimal weight
with syndrome `s`. -/

/-- **Minimum-weight decoding corrects `t` errors** when every nontrivial logical operator
(a vector orthogonal to `C` but outside `C`) has weight `> 2t`: the correction `X^d` returns
the state to the code space, i.e. `d + e ∈ C` is a stabilizer. -/

/-- Logical failure probability of minimum-weight decoding: the probability that the
correction does not return the error to the stabilizer group. -/
/-- **One level of coding**: logical failure probability `≤ C(n, t+1) p^{t+1}`. -/
/-! ## Concatenation and the threshold -/

/-- **Threshold recursion.**  If `f (L+1) ≤ A f(L)^m` with `A p_th^{m-1} ≤ 1` and
`0 ≤ f 0 ≤ p`, then `f L ≤ p_th (p / p_th)^{m^L}` for all `L`. -/

/-- Logical failure rate of the `L`-fold concatenated code: level `0` is the physical rate
`p`; at level `L + 1` each of the `n` qubits is a level-`L` block, failing independently
with the level-`L` rate, and the outer code is decoded by minimum-weight decoding. -/

/-- **Threshold theorem for concatenated codes.**  Suppose every nontrivial logical operator
has weight `> 2t`, and `p_th > 0` satisfies `C(n, t+1) p_th^t ≤ 1`.  Then the logical failure
rate of the `L`-fold concatenated code obeys `p_L ≤ p_th (p / p_th)^{(t+1)^L}`; in particular
it decays doubly exponentially in `L` whenever `p < p_th`. -/

/-- **Exponential threshold bound.**  Under the hypotheses of `concat_threshold` with
`t ≥ 1` and `p ≤ p_th`, `p_L ≤ p_th (p / p_th)^{2^L}`. -/
/-! ## The concatenated Steane code -/

/-- **Concatenated Steane code.**  The Steane code corrects one error (`t = 1`), `C(7, 2) = 21`,
and the threshold is `p_th = 1/21`: for every physical error rate `0 ≤ p ≤ 1`, the level-`L`
logical failure rate satisfies `p_L ≤ (21 p)^{2^L} / 21`. -/
/-- One level of the Steane code: logical failure probability `≤ 21 p²`. -/
/-! ## The Golay–Fano code cannot correct single-qubit errors -/

/-- The Golay–Fano code of `QECGolay.lean` has a nontrivial logical operator of weight `2`
(so its quantum distance is at most `2`, although the classical code has distance `8`). -/

/-- **No syndrome decoder for the Golay–Fano code corrects all single-qubit errors**: for
every decoder `dec` (any function of the syndrome), some weight-one error is not corrected. -/

comments.text: /-! ## Entries of the code projector -/
/-- Translation invariance of sums over a linear code (general coefficients). -/

/-- Entry formula for the projector of `CSS(C, C)`:
`P x y = |C|⁻² [x - y ∈ C] ∑_{b ∈ C} (-1)^{b·y}`. -/
/-- The support of the code projector: `P x y ≠ 0` forces `x - y ∈ C` and `y ⊥ C`. -/
/-! ## Logical Pauli operators -/

/-- **Logical Pauli operators.**  If `c, d` are orthogonal to `C`, the Pauli operator
`X^c Z^d` commutes with the projector of `CSS(C, C)`, i.e. it is a logical operator. -/
/-! ## Transversal Hadamard -/
/-- The unnormalised transversal Hadamard kernel `x, y ↦ (-1)^{x·y}`. -/
/-- The transversal Hadamard gate `H^{⊗n}`, `H = (1/√2) [[1, 1], [1, -1]]`. -/
/-- **Transversal Hadamard is logical** for every `CSS(C, C)` with `C` self-orthogonal. -/
/-! ## Transversal diagonal phase gates: `S` and `T` -/
/-- The transversal diagonal phase gate `diag(1, ω)^{⊗n}`: `|x⟩ ↦ ω^{wt x} |x⟩`. -/
/-- The transversal phase gate `S^{⊗n}`, `S = diag(1, i)`. -/
/-- The transversal `T` gate of `QECNoGo.lean` is the diagonal phase gate with `ω = e^{iπ/4}`. -/
/-- Weight of a sum: `wt (y + a) + 2 |y ∧ a| = wt y + wt a`. -/
/-- The overlap `|y ∧ a|` reduces mod 2 to the dot product `a · y`. -/

/-- A diagonal phase gate is logical as soon as `ω^{wt (y + a)} = ω^{wt y}` whenever
`a ∈ C` and `y ⊥ C`. -/

/-- **Transversal `S` is logical** for every `CSS(C, C)` with `C` doubly even (all weights
divisible by `4`; such a code is automatically self-orthogonal, which is not needed here). -/

/-- **Obstruction to transversal phase gates.**  If some `a ∈ C` and `y ⊥ C` satisfy
`ω^{wt (y + a)} ≠ ω^{wt y}`, then `diag(1, ω)^{⊗n}` does not preserve the code space. -/
/-! ## Transversal CNOT between two code blocks -/
/-- Two code blocks: the register `Q ⊕ Q` carrying the code `C ⊕ C`. -/
/-- The classical `CNOT` map on two blocks: `(u, v) ↦ (u, u + v)`. -/
/-- The transpose of `cnotMap` with respect to the dot product: `(u, v) ↦ (u + v, v)`. -/
/-- The transversal `CNOT` gate between two blocks: `|u, v⟩ ↦ |u, u + v⟩`. -/
/-- `cnotMapT` is the transpose of `cnotMap`: `b · L y = Lᵀ b · y`. -/
/-- **Transversal CNOT is logical** for two blocks of any `CSS(C, C)`. -/

comments.text:
/-!
# Triality, `G₂` and transversal `T` gates: a no-go

The request asked to prove that the triality automorphism of `Spin(8)` together with `G₂`
holonomy gives an exact transversal implementation of the non-Clifford `T` gate, "bypassing"
the Eastin–Knill theorem. That statement is **false**, and this file proves the precise
reasons:

* `triality_not_inner`: infinitesimal triality `θ₁ : so(8) → so(8)` (from `G2Triality.lean`)
  cannot be implemented by conjugation with *any* invertible `8 × 8` matrix. In particular no
  gate on the octonionic register `𝕆 ≅ ℂ⁸ ≅ (ℂ²)^{⊗3}` implements triality, transversal or
  not. The witness is `A = L_{e₁} − R_{e₁}`: it kills `1 ∈ 𝕆`, while
  `θ₁ A = L_{e₁} + 2 R_{e₁}` is invertible (`(L + 2R)(L − 2R) = 3`).
* `triality_trivial_on_g2`: on the `G₂`-holonomy algebra `𝔤₂`, triality is the identity, so it
  contributes no new generators there.
* `triality_T_gate_no_go`: for the Steane code (which has the full transversal Clifford group),
  transversal `T` is not logical, and every transversal generator acts on the code space as a
  scalar (the infinitesimal Eastin–Knill statement).
-/
/-- The imaginary unit `e₁ ∈ 𝕆`. -/

/-- The integer identity `(L − 2R)(L + 2R) = 3` for `L = L_{e₁}`,
`R = R_{e₁}`. -/
/-- `(L_{e₁} − 2R_{e₁})(L_{e₁} + 2R_{e₁}) = 3` over any field of characteristic zero. -/

/-- **Triality is not implemented by any gate.**  There is no invertible matrix `U` with
`U A = θ₁(A) U` for all `A ∈ so(8)`; i.e. infinitesimal triality is not conjugation by any
element of `GL(8)` (a fortiori not by a unitary gate on `𝕆 ≅ (ℂ²)^{⊗3}`). -/
/-- On the `G₂`-holonomy algebra `𝔤₂`, both triality maps are the identity. -/

/-- **No-go for "transversal `T` from triality and `G₂` holonomy".**
1. Triality is not implemented by conjugation with any invertible matrix on `𝕆 ≅ ℂ⁸`.
2. Triality acts as the identity on the `G₂`-holonomy algebra `𝔤₂`.
3. For the Steane code, whose transversal Clifford gates `H^{⊗7}`, `S^{⊗7}` are logical,
   transversal `T^{⊗7}` is not a logical gate.
4. (Infinitesimal Eastin–Knill.) Every transversal generator `∑_q (h_q)_q` is compressed by the
   Steane code projector to a scalar multiple of the projector. -/

/-!
# The equitable twin quotient of a graph

This file provides `Sovereign.Graph.SectorTwinQuotient`: the quotient of a simple graph by the
*twin* relation (two vertices are twins when they have the same open neighbourhood).

Main results:

* `Sovereign.Graph.twinQuotientGraph` — the quotient graph on twin classes; it is well defined
  because adjacency only depends on the twin classes of the endpoints.
* `Sovereign.Graph.not_adj_of_twin` — twins are never adjacent, so the quotient has no loops.
* `Sovereign.Graph.twin_partition_equitable` — the twin partition is **equitable**: a vertex `u`
  has either no neighbours or all of its neighbours in a given twin class, so the number of
  neighbours of `u` in a class `C` is `|C|` if `[u] ~ C` and `0` otherwise.
* `Sovereign.Graph.equitableQuotientMatrix_eq_smul` — if every twin class has `k` elements, the
  equitable quotient matrix is `k • B_χ`, where `B_χ` is the `0/1` adjacency matrix of the
  quotient graph. For the sedenion annihilation graph `k = 4`, which is where the Dirac operator
  `D = 4 B_χ` comes from.
* `Sovereign.Graph.adjMatrix_mulVec_lift` / `Sovereign.Graph.hasEigenvector_lift` — eigenvectors
  of the equitable quotient matrix lift to eigenvectors of the adjacency matrix of the original
  graph, so the quotient spectrum is part of the spectrum of the full graph.
-/

/-- The **twin relation** of a graph: `u` and `v` are twins when they have the same open
neighbourhood `N(u) = N(v)`. -/
/-- **The twin quotient** `V / twin` of a graph: its points are the twin classes. -/
/-- The quotient map `V → V / twin`. -/
/-- Twins have the same neighbours. -/

/-- **Twins are never adjacent** (in a simple graph): if `u ~ v` and `N(u) = N(v)` then
`v ∈ N(v)`, which is impossible. -/

/-- **The twin quotient graph** on `V / twin`: two twin classes are adjacent when some (equivalently
every) pair of representatives is adjacent. -/
/-- The twin quotient of a finite graph is finite. -/
/-- Decidable equality on the twin quotient (chosen classically). -/
/-- The twin class `C ⊆ V` of a point `c ∈ V / twin`, as a finset. -/

/-- **The twin partition is equitable.** For every vertex `u` and twin class `C`, the number of
neighbours of `u` inside `C` is `|C|` if `[u]` is adjacent to `C` in the quotient graph and `0`
otherwise. In particular it depends only on the class of `u`. -/

/-- **The equitable quotient matrix** `B` of the twin partition:
`B C C' = #{w ∈ C' | u ~ w}` for any representative `u ∈ C`. -/

/-- **The quotient adjacency matrix** `B_χ` of the twin quotient: the `0/1` adjacency matrix of
`twinQuotientGraph G`. -/

/-- If every twin class has exactly `k` elements, the equitable quotient matrix equals
`k • B_χ`. -/

/-- **Lifting along the equitable quotient.** For a function `x` on `V / twin`,
`A (x ∘ π) = (B x) ∘ π`, where `A` is the adjacency matrix of `G`, `B` the equitable quotient
matrix and `π : V → V / twin` the quotient map. -/

/-- **The quotient spectrum lies in the spectrum of the full graph.** If `x ≠ 0` is an
eigenvector of the equitable quotient matrix with eigenvalue `μ`, then `x ∘ π` is a nonzero
eigenvector of the adjacency matrix of `G` with the same eigenvalue. -/

/-- Componentwise subtraction on `CD R n`; this is the difference appearing in the
associator `[x, y, z] = (x ⋆ y) ⋆ z - x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)` of source document §2.3. -/

declarations.signature_heuristic:

  | 0, x, y => (x - y : R)
  | n + 1, x, y => (cdSub R n x.1 y.1, cdSub R n x.2 y.2)

right-hand side `2 e₇` of the obstruction of source document §2.3. -/

declarations.name: cdSmul
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def cdSmul (R : Type u) [Mul R] : ∀ n, R → CD R n → CD R n
  | 0, r, x => (r * x : R)
  | n + 1, r, x => (cdSmul R n r x.1, cdSmul R n r x.2)

/-- Cayley–Dickson conjugation: `conj (a, b) = (conj a, -b)` (source document §2.3, part of
the Cayley–Dickson construction of `𝕊`). -/

declarations.name: cdConj
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def cdConj (R : Type u) [Neg R] : ∀ n, CD R n → CD R n
  | 0, x => x
  | n + 1, x => (cdConj R n x.1, cdNeg R n x.2)

/-- **Cayley–Dickson multiplication** `⋆` of source document §2.3:
`(a, b) ⋆ (c, d) = (a c - d̄ b, d a + b c̄)`. At level `4` over `ℝ` this is the sedenion
product, which is non-associative. -/

declarations.name: cdMul
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def cdMul (R : Type u) [Add R] [Sub R] [Neg R] [Mul R] : ∀ n, CD R n → CD R n → CD R n
  | 0, x, y => (x * y : R)
  | n + 1, x, y =>
      (cdSub R n (cdMul R n x.1 y.1) (cdMul R n (cdConj R n y.2) x.2),
       cdAdd R n (cdMul R n y.2 x.1) (cdMul R n x.2 (cdConj R n y.1)))

/-- The Euclidean inner product `⟨·, ·⟩` on `CD R n`, i.e. the sum of the products of the
`2ⁿ` coordinates with respect to the canonical orthonormal basis. It is the pairing used in
the definition of the phase `ω(x, y, z) = ⟨(x ⋆ y) ⋆ z, x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)⟩` of source document
§2.3. -/

declarations.name: cdInner
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def cdInner (R : Type u) [Add R] [Mul R] : ∀ n, CD R n → CD R n → R
  | 0, x, y => (x * y : R)
  | n + 1, x, y => cdInner R n x.1 y.1 + cdInner R n x.2 y.2

/-- **The canonical orthonormal basis** `{e₀, e₁, …, e_{2ⁿ-1}}` of `CD R n`
(source document §2.3): the index `k` is read in binary, `e_k = (e_k, 0)` for `k < 2ⁿ` and
`e_k = (0, e_{k - 2ⁿ})` otherwise. -/

declarations.name: cdBasis
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def cdBasis (R : Type u) [Zero R] [One R] : ∀ n, ℕ → CD R n
  | 0, 0 => (1 : R)
  | 0, _ + 1 => (0 : R)
  | n + 1, k =>
      if k < 2 ^ n then (cdBasis R n k, cdZero R n) else (cdZero R n, cdBasis R n (k - 2 ^ n))

/-- **The 16-dimensional Cayley–Dickson sedenion algebra `𝕊`** of source document §2.3,

/-!
# The Cayley–Dickson sedenion algebra and its basis associator obstruction

This file formalizes Section 2.3 of the source document
`THEORY_OF_LIE2GROUP_SEELEY_DEWITT.md` ("Concrete Sedenion Basis Associator Obstruction").

The document works in "16-dimensional Cayley-Dickson Sedenion algebra `𝕊`" with canonical
orthonormal basis `{e₀, …, e₁₅}`, defines the associator `[x, y, z] = (x ⋆ y) ⋆ z -
x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)`, and asserts

* `[e₁, e₂, e₄] = (e₁ ⋆ e₂) ⋆ e₄ - e₁ ⋆ (e₂ ⋆ e₄) = e₃ ⋆ e₄ - e₁ ⋆ e₆ = e₇ - (-e₇) = 2 e₇`;
* that the "normalized phase obstruction" `ω(x, y, z) = ⟨(x ⋆ y) ⋆ z, x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)⟩`
  satisfies the Mac Lane pentagon identity `δω = 0`.

Everything is built from scratch here: the Cayley–Dickson doubling tower `CD R n`
(so `CD ℝ 0 = ℝ`, `CD ℝ 1 ≃ ℂ`, `CD ℝ 2 ≃ ℍ`, `CD ℝ 3 ≃ 𝕆`, `CD ℝ 4 = 𝕊`), its
multiplication `(a, b) ⋆ (c, d) = (a c - d̄ b, d a + b c̄)`, conjugation, the canonical
basis, the Euclidean inner product, and the associator.

The first assertion above is proved verbatim (`sedenion_associator_e1_e2_e4`), together
with each intermediate step of the document's computation.

The second assertion is **false** as literally stated, i.e. read additively, and this is also
proved here
(`sedenion_omega_not_pentagon_cocycle`, with the explicit counterexamples
`sedenion_delta_omega_e1_e2_e4_e8` and `sedenion_delta_omega_e0`): the quantity `δω` of
§2.3 evaluates to `-3` on `(e₁, e₂, e₄, e₈)` and to `1` on `(e₀, e₀, e₀, e₀)`. The reason
is structural: `ω` as defined there is multiplicative-phase valued (`ω = 1` on any
associative quadruple), and the alternating sum of the five terms of `δω` therefore equals
`1`, not `0`, already in the associative case.

The intended, multiplicative reading of the same assertion of §2.3 is **true**, and it is
proved in `RequestProject/SedenionCocycle.lean`
(`SovereignEngine.CayleyDickson.sedenion_omega_multiplicative_pentagon`): the alternating
*product* of the same five terms equals `1` on the canonical basis, because `ω` is the
multiplicative coboundary of the sign 2-cochain of the basis group `(ℤ/2)⁴`.
-/

/-- **The Cayley–Dickson doubling tower** over a base ring `R`: `CD R 0 = R` and
`CD R (n+1) = CD R n × CD R n`. For `R = ℝ` the levels are the reals, the complex numbers,
the quaternions, the octonions and — at level `4`, with `2^4 = 16` real dimensions — the
sedenion algebra `𝕊` of source document §2.3. -/
/-- The zero element of the Cayley–Dickson level `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- The unit `e₀` of the Cayley–Dickson level `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- Componentwise addition on the Cayley–Dickson level `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- Componentwise negation on the Cayley–Dickson level `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/

/-- Componentwise subtraction on `CD R n`; this is the difference appearing in the
associator `[x, y, z] = (x ⋆ y) ⋆ z - x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)` of source document §2.3. -/

/-- Scalar multiplication by an element of the base ring on `CD R n`; used to express the
right-hand side `2 e₇` of the obstruction of source document §2.3. -/

/-- Cayley–Dickson conjugation: `conj (a, b) = (conj a, -b)` (source document §2.3, part of
the Cayley–Dickson construction of `𝕊`). -/

/-- **Cayley–Dickson multiplication** `⋆` of source document §2.3:
`(a, b) ⋆ (c, d) = (a c - d̄ b, d a + b c̄)`. At level `4` over `ℝ` this is the sedenion
product, which is non-associative. -/

/-- The Euclidean inner product `⟨·, ·⟩` on `CD R n`, i.e. the sum of the products of the
`2ⁿ` coordinates with respect to the canonical orthonormal basis. It is the pairing used in
the definition of the phase `ω(x, y, z) = ⟨(x ⋆ y) ⋆ z, x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)⟩` of source document
§2.3. -/

/-- **The canonical orthonormal basis** `{e₀, e₁, …, e_{2ⁿ-1}}` of `CD R n`
(source document §2.3): the index `k` is read in binary, `e_k = (e_k, 0)` for `k < 2ⁿ` and
`e_k = (0, e_{k - 2ⁿ})` otherwise. -/

/-- **The 16-dimensional Cayley–Dickson sedenion algebra `𝕊`** of source document §2.3,
realised as level `4` of the Cayley–Dickson tower over `ℝ`. -/
/-- The sedenion product `x ⋆ y` of source document §2.3. -/

/-- The canonical orthonormal basis vector `e k` of the sedenions
(source document §2.3, `{e₀, e₁, …, e₁₅}`). -/

/-- The sedenion `2 • x`, used for the right-hand side `2 e₇` of the basis obstruction of
source document §2.3. -/

/-- **The sedenion associator** `[x, y, z] = (x ⋆ y) ⋆ z - x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)` of source
document §2.3. -/

/-- **The normalized phase obstruction** `ω(x, y, z) = ⟨(x ⋆ y) ⋆ z, x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)⟩` of
source document §2.3. -/

/-- **The pentagon coboundary of the phase obstruction** of source document §2.3:
`δω(x, y, z, w) = ω(y, z, w) - ω(x ⋆ y, z, w) + ω(x, y ⋆ z, w) - ω(x, y, z ⋆ w)
+ ω(x, y, z)`. -/
/-- `e₁ ⋆ e₂ = e₃`: the first step of the computation of source document §2.3. -/
/-- `e₃ ⋆ e₄ = e₇`: the second step of the computation of source document §2.3. -/
/-- `e₂ ⋆ e₄ = e₆`: the third step of the computation of source document §2.3. -/
/-- `e₁ ⋆ e₆ = -e₇`: the fourth step of the computation of source document §2.3. -/

/-- **The sedenion basis associator obstruction** of source document §2.3:
`[e₁, e₂, e₄] = (e₁ ⋆ e₂) ⋆ e₄ - e₁ ⋆ (e₂ ⋆ e₄) = e₇ - (-e₇) = 2 e₇`. -/

/-- **Non-triviality of the sedenion basis associator obstruction**
(source document §2.3, "associativity fails non-trivially"): `[e₁, e₂, e₄] = 2 e₇ ≠ 0`.
This replaces the document's §3 `theorem sedenion_basis_obstruction_verified`, which merely
restated a `Float` field of a structure and carried no mathematical content. -/

/-- The sedenion algebra of source document §2.3 is **not associative**: the triple
`(e₁, e₂, e₄)` violates associativity. -/

/-- The value of the phase obstruction of source document §2.3 on the obstructed triple:
`ω(e₁, e₂, e₄) = -1`, reflecting `(e₁ ⋆ e₂) ⋆ e₄ = e₇` and `e₁ ⋆ (e₂ ⋆ e₄) = -e₇`. -/

/-- On an associative quadruple the phase of source document §2.3 is `1`, hence its
pentagon coboundary is `δω(e₀, e₀, e₀, e₀) = 1 ≠ 0`. -/

/-- A second, genuinely non-associative counterexample to the pentagon identity claimed for
`ω` in source document §2.3: `δω(e₁, e₂, e₄, e₈) = -3`. -/

/-- **Refutation of the pentagon claim of source document §2.3.** The document asserts that
the phase `ω(x, y, z) = ⟨(x ⋆ y) ⋆ z, x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)⟩` satisfies the Mac Lane pentagon identity
`δω(x, y, z, w) = 0`. This is false: `δω` takes the value `1` at `(e₀, e₀, e₀, e₀)` (and
`-3` at `(e₁, e₂, e₄, e₈)`). For the corrected, multiplicative form of the claim — which is
true — see `SovereignEngine.CayleyDickson.sedenion_omega_multiplicative_pentagon` in
`RequestProject/SedenionCocycle.lean`. -/

declarations.name: sbasis
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def sbasis (R : Type u) [Zero R] : ∀ n, R → ℕ → CD R n
  | 0, s, 0 => s
  | 0, _, _ + 1 => (0 : R)
  | n + 1, s, k =>
      if k < 2 ^ n then (sbasis R n s k, cdZero R n)
      else (cdZero R n, sbasis R n s (k - 2 ^ n))

/-- **The sign 2-cochain** `σ` of the canonical basis of `CD R n` (source document §2.3):
the basis vectors multiply by `e_i ⋆ e_j = σ(i, j) e_{i ⊕ j}`, and `σ(i, j) = ±1`.
It is read off from the Cayley–Dickson product `(a, b) ⋆ (c, d) = (ac - d̄b, da + bc̄)`. -/

declarations.name: cdSign
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def cdSign : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → ℤ
  | 0, _, _ => 1
  | n + 1, i, j =>
      if i < 2 ^ n then
        (if j < 2 ^ n then cdSign n i j else cdSign n (j - 2 ^ n) i)
      else
        (if j < 2 ^ n then (if j = 0 then cdSign n (i - 2 ^ n) j else -cdSign n (i - 2 ^ n) j)
         else -(if j - 2 ^ n = 0 then cdSign n (j - 2 ^ n) (i - 2 ^ n)
                else -cdSign n (j - 2 ^ n) (i - 2 ^ n)))

/-! ### Elementary identities in the Cayley–Dickson tower -/

section Basic

variable [CommRing R]

/-- Negation fixes the zero element of `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
@[simp] theorem cdNeg_zero (n : ℕ) : cdNeg R n (cdZero R n) = cdZero R n

declarations.name: cdMul_zero_and_zero_mul
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem cdMul_zero_and_zero_mul (n : ℕ) :
    (∀ x : CD R n, cdMul R n x (cdZero R n) = cdZero R n) ∧
      (∀ x : CD R n, cdMul R n (cdZero R n) x = cdZero R n)

declarations.name: cdConj_sbasis
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem cdConj_sbasis (n : ℕ) (s : R) (k : ℕ) :
    cdConj R n (sbasis R n s k) = sbasis R n (if k = 0 then s else -s) k

declarations.name: sbasis_one
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem sbasis_one (n : ℕ) (k : ℕ) [One R] : sbasis R n (1 : R) k = cdBasis R n k

declarations.name: sub_two_pow_lt
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem sub_two_pow_lt {n k : ℕ} (hk : k < 2 ^ (n + 1)) (hkn : ¬ k < 2 ^ n) :
    k - 2 ^ n < 2 ^ n

declarations.name: cdInner_sbasis_self
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem cdInner_sbasis_self (n : ℕ) (s t : R) (k : ℕ) (hk : k < 2 ^ n) :
    cdInner R n (sbasis R n s k) (sbasis R n t k) = s * t

declarations.name: two_pow_xor_eq_add
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem two_pow_xor_eq_add {n x : ℕ} (hx : x < 2 ^ n) : 2 ^ n ^^^ x = 2 ^ n + x

declarations.name: xor_two_pow_add
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem xor_two_pow_add {n i j : ℕ} (hi : i < 2 ^ n) (hj : j < 2 ^ n) :
    i ^^^ (2 ^ n + j) = 2 ^ n + (i ^^^ j)

declarations.name: two_pow_add_sub
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem two_pow_add_sub {n k : ℕ} (hkn : ¬ k < 2 ^ n) : 2 ^ n + (k - 2 ^ n) = k

declarations.name: cdMul_sbasis
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem cdMul_sbasis [CommRing R] :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (s t : R) (i j : ℕ), i < 2 ^ n → j < 2 ^ n →
      cdMul R n (sbasis R n s i) (sbasis R n t j)
        = sbasis R n (s * t * ((cdSign n i j : ℤ) : R)) (i ^^^ j)
  | 0, s, t, i, j, hi, hj => by
      have hi0 : i = 0

declarations.name: cdSign_mul_self
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem cdSign_mul_self : ∀ (n i j : ℕ), cdSign n i j * cdSign n i j = 1
  | 0, _, _ => by simp [cdSign]
  | n + 1, i, j => by
      simp only [cdSign]
      split_ifs <;>
        simp [cdSign_mul_self n]

/-- The sign 2-cochain of source document §2.3 takes only the values `1` and `-1`. -/

declarations.name: cdSign_eq_one_or_neg_one
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem cdSign_eq_one_or_neg_one (n i j : ℕ) : cdSign n i j = 1 ∨ cdSign n i j = -1

declarations.name: cdInner_assoc_sbasis
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem cdInner_assoc_sbasis [CommRing R] (n : ℕ) (s t u : R) (i j k : ℕ)
    (hi : i < 2 ^ n) (hj : j < 2 ^ n) (hk : k < 2 ^ n) :
    cdInner R n (cdMul R n (cdMul R n (sbasis R n s i) (sbasis R n t j)) (sbasis R n u k))
        (cdMul R n (sbasis R n s i) (cdMul R n (sbasis R n t j) (sbasis R n u k)))
      = (s * t * u) * (s * t * u) *
          ((cdSign n i j * cdSign n (i ^^^ j) k * cdSign n j k * cdSign n i (j ^^^ k) : ℤ) : R)

declarations.name: signCoboundary
declarations.signature_heuristic: def signCoboundary (σ : ℕ → ℕ → ℤ) (i j k : ℕ) : ℤ

declarations.name: signCoboundary_pentagon
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem signCoboundary_pentagon (σ : ℕ → ℕ → ℤ) (hσ : ∀ a b, σ a b * σ a b = 1)
    (i j k l : ℕ) :
    signCoboundary σ j k l * signCoboundary σ (i ^^^ j) k l * signCoboundary σ i (j ^^^ k) l *
        signCoboundary σ i j (k ^^^ l) * signCoboundary σ i j k = 1

declarations.name: e_eq_sbasis
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem e_eq_sbasis (k : ℕ) : e k = sbasis ℝ 4 (1 : ℝ) k

declarations.name: sedMul_sbasis
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem sedMul_sbasis (s t : ℝ) (i j : ℕ) (hi : i < 16) (hj : j < 16) :
    sbasis ℝ 4 s i ⋆ sbasis ℝ 4 t j
      = sbasis ℝ 4 (s * t * ((cdSign 4 i j : ℤ) : ℝ)) (i ^^^ j)

declarations.name: omegaPhase_sbasis
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem omegaPhase_sbasis (s t u : ℝ) (i j k : ℕ) (hi : i < 16) (hj : j < 16) (hk : k < 16) :
    omegaPhase (sbasis ℝ 4 s i) (sbasis ℝ 4 t j) (sbasis ℝ 4 u k)
      = (s * t * u) * (s * t * u) * ((signCoboundary (cdSign 4) i j k : ℤ) : ℝ)

declarations.name: sedenion_omega_basis_eq_coboundary
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem sedenion_omega_basis_eq_coboundary (i j k : ℕ) (hi : i < 16) (hj : j < 16)
    (hk : k < 16) :
    omegaPhase (e i) (e j) (e k) = ((signCoboundary (cdSign 4) i j k : ℤ) : ℝ)

declarations.name: sedenion_omega_basis_sq
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem sedenion_omega_basis_sq (i j k : ℕ) (hi : i < 16) (hj : j < 16) (hk : k < 16) :
    omegaPhase (e i) (e j) (e k) * omegaPhase (e i) (e j) (e k) = 1

declarations.name: deltaOmegaMul
declarations.signature_heuristic: def deltaOmegaMul (x y z w : Sedenion) : ℝ

declarations.name: sedenion_omega_multiplicative_pentagon
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem sedenion_omega_multiplicative_pentagon (i j k l : ℕ) (hi : i < 16) (hj : j < 16)
    (hk : k < 16) (hl : l < 16) :
    deltaOmegaMul (e i) (e j) (e k) (e l) = 1

/-!
# The sedenion associator phase is a genuine 3-cocycle (multiplicative form)

This file completes the formalization of Section 2.3 of the source document
`THEORY_OF_LIE2GROUP_SEELEY_DEWITT.md` ("Concrete Sedenion Basis Associator Obstruction").

The document asserts that the *normalized phase* obstruction

`ω(x, y, z) = ⟨(x ⋆ y) ⋆ z, x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)⟩`

"satisfies the Mac Lane pentagon identity"

`δω(x, y, z, w) = ω(y, z, w) - ω(x ⋆ y, z, w) + ω(x, y ⋆ z, w) - ω(x, y, z ⋆ w) + ω(x, y, z)
= 0`.

`Sedenion.lean` shows that this *additive* reading is false
(`sedenion_omega_not_pentagon_cocycle`). The reason is purely notational: `ω` is a **phase**,
taking the values `±1` on the canonical basis, so it is a `2`-cochain with values in the
*multiplicative* group `{±1}` and the alternating sum of the five terms must be read as an
alternating **product**. This file proves that under this (intended) reading the assertion of
§2.3 is correct, on the canonical basis `{e₀, …, e₁₅}` of the sedenions and, more generally,
at every level of the Cayley–Dickson tower:

`ω(e_j, e_k, e_l) · ω(e_i ⋆ e_j, e_k, e_l) · ω(e_i, e_j ⋆ e_k, e_l) · ω(e_i, e_j, e_k ⋆ e_l)
  · ω(e_i, e_j, e_k) = 1`

(`sedenion_omega_multiplicative_pentagon`), the inverses in the alternating product being
harmless because every factor is its own inverse (`sedenion_omega_basis_sq`).

The mechanism behind the identity is also formalized, and it is the exact analogue for the
basis group of the cohomological statement of §2.2. Products of canonical basis vectors are
signed basis vectors,

`e_i ⋆ e_j = σ(i, j) · e_{i ⊕ j}`,     `σ(i, j) ∈ {±1}`,

where `⊕` is the bitwise `xor`, so that the index set `{0, …, 2ⁿ - 1}` is the elementary
abelian group `(ℤ/2)ⁿ` (`cdMul_sbasis`). The sign `σ` is a `2`-cochain on that group with
values in `{±1}`, and the phase is exactly its multiplicative coboundary,

`ω(e_i, e_j, e_k) = σ(i, j) · σ(i ⊕ j, k) · σ(j, k) · σ(i, j ⊕ k) = (δ₂σ)(i, j, k)`

(`sedenion_omega_basis_eq_coboundary`). Hence `ω` is a 3-cocycle whose class is trivial,
`[ω] = 0`, exactly as `δ₃ ∘ δ₂ = 0` in §2.2 (`coboundary3_coboundary2` of
`CrossedModule.lean`). This is the correct statement of the claim of §2.3: the sedenion
associator phase does satisfy the Mac Lane pentagon identity, and it does so because it is a
coboundary — the genuine non-triviality of §2.3 is the *associator* `[e₁, e₂, e₄] = 2e₇ ≠ 0`,
not the phase.
-/
/-! ### Signed basis vectors and the sign 2-cochain -/

/-- **Signed basis vector** `s · e_k` of the Cayley–Dickson level `CD R n`
(source document §2.3, canonical orthonormal basis `{e₀, …, e₁₅}` scaled by `s`).
Products of basis vectors of `CD R n` are signed basis vectors, which is why this is the
convenient class of elements to compute with. -/

/-- **The sign 2-cochain** `σ` of the canonical basis of `CD R n` (source document §2.3):
the basis vectors multiply by `e_i ⋆ e_j = σ(i, j) e_{i ⊕ j}`, and `σ(i, j) = ±1`.
It is read off from the Cayley–Dickson product `(a, b) ⋆ (c, d) = (ac - d̄b, da + bc̄)`. -/
/-! ### Elementary identities in the Cayley–Dickson tower -/
/-- Negation fixes the zero element of `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- Conjugation fixes the zero element of `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- `x + 0 = x` in `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- `0 + x = x` in `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- `x - 0 = x` in `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- `0 - x = -x` in `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- `x ⋆ 0 = 0` and `0 ⋆ x = 0` in `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- `x ⋆ 0 = 0` in `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- `0 ⋆ x = 0` in `CD R n` (source document §2.3). -/
/-- Negation of a signed basis vector negates its coefficient (source document §2.3). -/

/-- Conjugation of a signed basis vector: `conj (s e_k) = s e_k` for `k = 0` and
`conj (s e_k) = -s e_k` otherwise (source document §2.3). -/

/-- The signed basis vector with coefficient `1` is the canonical basis vector `e_k` of
source document §2.3. -/
/-- The Euclidean inner product of `0` with itself vanishes (source document §2.3). -/

/-- If `k < 2 ^ (n + 1)` fails to be `< 2 ^ n`, then `k - 2 ^ n < 2 ^ n`: the index
bookkeeping of the Cayley–Dickson doubling of source document §2.3. -/

/-- The Euclidean inner product of two signed basis vectors with the same index is the
product of the coefficients (source document §2.3, orthonormality of `{e₀, …, e₁₅}`). -/
/-! ### The index group `(ℤ/2)ⁿ` -/

/-- Adding `2 ^ n` to an index `< 2 ^ n` is the same as `xor`-ing with it: the index
bookkeeping of the Cayley–Dickson doubling of source document §2.3, which exhibits the index
set `{0, …, 2ⁿ - 1}` as the elementary abelian group `(ℤ/2)ⁿ` under `xor`. -/
/-- `xor` with an index in the upper half of `{0, …, 2ⁿ⁺¹ - 1}` (source document §2.3). -/

/-- An index of the upper half of `{0, …, 2ⁿ⁺¹ - 1}` is recovered from its lower part
(source document §2.3). -/
/-! ### Products of basis vectors are signed basis vectors -/

/-- **The multiplication rule of the canonical basis** of the Cayley–Dickson algebra
`CD R n` (source document §2.3): `(s e_i) ⋆ (t e_j) = s t σ(i, j) e_{i ⊕ j}`, where `⊕` is the
bitwise `xor` and `σ = cdSign` is the sign 2-cochain. In particular products of canonical
basis vectors of the sedenions are, up to sign, again canonical basis vectors, and the index
set `{0, …, 15}` carries the group structure of `(ℤ/2)⁴`. -/
-- both indices in the lower half
-- `i` lower, `j` upper
-- `i` upper, `j` lower
-- both indices in the upper half
/-! ### The sign 2-cochain takes the values `±1` -/

/-- **The sign 2-cochain of source document §2.3 is a phase**: `σ(i, j) ∈ {1, -1}`, i.e.
`σ(i, j)² = 1`. This is what makes the alternating *product* the right reading of the Mac
Lane pentagon identity for the phase `ω` of §2.3. -/
/-- The sign 2-cochain of source document §2.3 takes only the values `1` and `-1`. -/
/-! ### The phase of a triple of signed basis vectors -/

/-- **The phase `ω` of source document §2.3 on signed basis vectors**:
`⟨((s e_i) ⋆ (t e_j)) ⋆ (u e_k), (s e_i) ⋆ ((t e_j) ⋆ (u e_k))⟩
  = (s t u)² σ(i, j) σ(i ⊕ j, k) σ(j, k) σ(i, j ⊕ k)`.

The right-hand side is exactly the *multiplicative coboundary* `δ₂σ` of the sign 2-cochain
`σ` on the index group `(ℤ/2)ⁿ`, which is the reason for the pentagon identity below. -/
/-! ### The multiplicative coboundary of the sign 2-cochain -/

/-- **The multiplicative 2-coboundary of a sign 2-cochain** `σ` on the index group `(ℤ/2)ⁿ`:
`(δ₂σ)(i, j, k) = σ(i, j) σ(i ⊕ j, k) σ(j, k)⁻¹ σ(i, j ⊕ k)⁻¹`, the inverses being written as
plain factors because `σ` takes the values `±1`. This is the multiplicative analogue, for
the basis group of the sedenions of source document §2.3, of the operator `δ₂` of §2.2. -/

/-- **The Mac Lane pentagon identity for a multiplicative 2-coboundary** on the index group
`(ℤ/2)ⁿ`: this is `δ₃ ∘ δ₂ = 1`, the multiplicative form of the identity
`coboundary3_coboundary2` of source document §2.2, and it is the mechanism behind the
pentagon identity claimed for the sedenion phase in §2.3. -/
/-! ### The sedenion phase `ω` of §2.3 and its pentagon identity -/

/-- The canonical basis vector `e_k` of source document §2.3 is the signed basis vector with
coefficient `1`. -/

/-- **The multiplication rule of the sedenion basis** (source document §2.3):
`(s e_i) ⋆ (t e_j) = s t σ(i, j) e_{i ⊕ j}` for `i, j < 16`. -/

/-- **The sedenion phase of source document §2.3 on signed basis vectors**:
`ω(s e_i, t e_j, u e_k) = (s t u)² (δ₂σ)(i, j, k)`. -/

/-- **The sedenion phase of §2.3 is the multiplicative coboundary of the basis sign**:
`ω(e_i, e_j, e_k) = σ(i, j) σ(i ⊕ j, k) σ(j, k) σ(i, j ⊕ k) = (δ₂σ)(i, j, k)`.
In the language of §2.2 this says that the phase `ω` of §2.3 is a 2-coboundary, hence a
3-cocycle of trivial class. -/

/-- **The sedenion phase of §2.3 is a phase**: on the canonical basis it takes the values
`±1`, so that each factor of the pentagon identity is its own inverse. -/

/-- **The pentagon coboundary of the phase obstruction, read multiplicatively**
(source document §2.3): `δω(x, y, z, w) = ω(y, z, w) ω(x ⋆ y, z, w)⁻¹ ω(x, y ⋆ z, w)
ω(x, y, z ⋆ w)⁻¹ ω(x, y, z)`. Because `ω` takes the values `±1` on the canonical basis
(`sedenion_omega_basis_sq`), the inverted factors may be written as plain factors. -/

/-- **The Mac Lane pentagon identity for the sedenion phase of source document §2.3.**

The document claims that the normalized phase `ω(x, y, z) = ⟨(x ⋆ y) ⋆ z, x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)⟩`
satisfies the pentagon identity. Read additively the claim is false
(`sedenion_omega_not_pentagon_cocycle` in `Sedenion.lean`), simply because `ω` is a *phase*:
it takes the values `±1`, and the neutral element of the group in which it takes its values
is `1`, not `0`. Read multiplicatively — which is the reading the word "phase" and the
normalization `ω = 1` on associative triples call for — the claim of §2.3 is **correct** on
the canonical basis `{e₀, …, e₁₅}`:

`δω(e_i, e_j, e_k, e_l) = 1`.

The proof exhibits `ω` as the multiplicative coboundary `δ₂σ` of the sign 2-cochain `σ` of
the basis group `(ℤ/2)⁴` and then applies `δ₃ ∘ δ₂ = 1`, exactly as in §2.2. -/

declarations.name: SeeleyDeWittInvariants
declarations.signature_heuristic:

/-!
# Higher Seeley–DeWitt gravitational heat-kernel expansions

This file formalizes Section 2.4 of the source document
`THEORY_OF_LIE2GROUP_SEELEY_DEWITT.md` ("Higher Seeley-DeWitt Gravitational Expansions").

The document considers a compact `d`-dimensional Riemannian manifold `(M, g)` with a
Laplace/Dirac type operator `𝒟² = -(∇^μ ∇_μ + E)` and the small-`t` asymptotics
`Tr(e^{-t𝒟²}) ∼ (4πt)^{-d/2} ∑_k a_{2k} t^k`, and it lists the coefficients
`a₀`, `a₂`, `a₄`, `a₆` in terms of curvature invariants.

Two things are formalized here.

1. **The coefficients.** The invariants that occur in the formulas of §2.4 — the volume,
   `∫ R`, `∫ E`, `∫ R²`, `∫ R_{μν}R^{μν}`, `∫ R_{μνρσ}R^{μνρσ}`, `∫ RE`, `∫ E²`,
   `∫ F_{μν}F^{μν}`, and the three cubic invariants displayed in `a₆` — are packaged in a
   structure `SeeleyDeWittInvariants`, and `a₀`, `a₂`, `a₄`, `a₆` are defined by exactly the
   linear combinations printed in the document.  (The document writes `a₆` with a trailing
   `+ …`; only the three displayed cubic terms are formalized, as recorded in the docstring
   of `a6`.)

2. **The asymptotic expansion itself.** `HeatTraceAsymptotics d a Tr` is the statement
   `Tr(t) ∼ (4πt)^{-d/2} ∑_{k} a_k t^k` as `t → 0⁺`, in the standard sense that for every
   `N` the remainder after `N` terms is `o(t^N · (4πt)^{-d/2})`. Two genuine theorems are
   proved about it: the leading-order limit (`heatTrace_tendsto_a0`) and uniqueness of the
   whole coefficient sequence (`heatTrace_coeff_unique`), which is what makes it legitimate
   to speak of *the* Seeley–DeWitt coefficients `a_{2k}` of §2.4.
-/
/-- `∫_M d^d x √g R_{μνρσ}R^{μνρσ}`. -/
/-- `∫_M d^d x √g R_{μνρσ}R^{μνρσ} R`. -/
/-- `∫_M d^d x √g R_{μν}R^{μν} R`. -/

/-- **`a₀`, the volume term** of source document §2.4:
`a₀ = ∫_M d^d x √g = Vol(M)`. -/

/-- **`a₂`, the Einstein–Hilbert scalar term** of source document §2.4:
`a₂ = (1/6) ∫_M d^d x √g (R + 6E)`. -/

/-- **`a₄`, the quadratic gravitational / Yang–Mills term** of source document §2.4:
`a₄ = (1/360) ∫_M d^d x √g (5R² - 2R_{μν}R^{μν} + 2R_{μνρσ}R^{μνρσ} + 60RE + 180E²
+ 30F_{μν}F^{μν})`. -/

/-- **`a₆`, the cubic gravitational / Euler density term** of source document §2.4:
`a₆ = (1/5040) ∫_M d^d x √g (R_{μνρσ}R^{μνρσ}R - R_{μν}R^{μν}R + R³ + …)`.
The document truncates the cubic invariant with "`+ …`"; only the three displayed terms are
formalized. -/

/-- The Seeley–DeWitt coefficient sequence `k ↦ a_{2k}` of source document §2.4, assembled
from `a₀`, `a₂`, `a₄`, `a₆`. Odd-index coefficients `a_{2k+1}` vanish on a closed manifold
and the terms beyond `a₆` are not specified in the document, so the sequence is set to `0`
from index `4` on. -/

/-- On flat space with vanishing endomorphism and gauge curvature, all curvature integrals
vanish and only the volume term of source document §2.4 survives:
`a₂ = a₄ = a₆ = 0` and `a₀ = Vol(M)`. -/
/-- **The heat-kernel prefactor** `(4πt)^{-d/2}` of source document §2.4. -/
/-- The prefactor `(4πt)^{-d/2}` of source document §2.4 is strictly positive for `t > 0`. -/

/-- **The Seeley–DeWitt asymptotic heat-kernel expansion** of source document §2.4:
`Tr(e^{-t𝒟²}) ∼ (4πt)^{-d/2} ∑_{k=0}^∞ a_{2k} t^k` as `t → 0⁺`.

Formally, for every truncation order `N` the remainder of the expansion is
`o(t^N (4πt)^{-d/2})` as `t → 0⁺`; this is the standard meaning of the asymptotic
expansion symbol `∼` used in the document. -/

/-- Near `0⁺` the variable `t` is positive and `< 1`; a convenience filter fact used in the
asymptotic arguments about the expansion of source document §2.4. -/

/-- Auxiliary fact: if `c • g` is `o(g)` for `g t = t ^ N * (4πt)^{-d/2}` near `0⁺`, then
`c = 0`. Used for uniqueness of the Seeley–DeWitt coefficients of source document §2.4. -/

/-- **Leading order of the Seeley–DeWitt expansion** of source document §2.4: if
`Tr(e^{-t𝒟²}) ∼ (4πt)^{-d/2} ∑ a_{2k} t^k`, then `(4πt)^{d/2} Tr(e^{-t𝒟²}) → a₀`
as `t → 0⁺`; i.e. the volume coefficient `a₀ = Vol(M)` governs the leading small-`t`
behaviour of the heat trace. -/

/-- **Uniqueness of the Seeley–DeWitt coefficients** of source document §2.4: a heat trace
admits at most one asymptotic expansion `Tr(e^{-t𝒟²}) ∼ (4πt)^{-d/2} ∑ a_{2k} t^k`, so the
coefficients `a₀, a₂, a₄, a₆, …` are well defined invariants of the operator. -/

/-!
# The Legendre density of a finite sieve

Let `S` be a finite set of primes and `M = ∏_{p ∈ S} p`.  The set of integers killed by the
sieve is periodic mod `M`, and in one period the survivors are exactly the residues coprime to
`M`, of which there are `φ(M) = ∏_{p ∈ S} (p - 1)`.  Hence

* `card_survivors_range` : `#{n < M * k : ∀ p ∈ S, ¬ p ∣ n} = k * ∏_{p ∈ S} (p - 1)`,
* `card_sieved_range`    : `#{n < M * k : ∃ p ∈ S, p ∣ n} = k * (M - ∏ (p - 1))`,
* `density_sieved`       : the density of the sieved set is `1 - ∏_{p ∈ S} (1 - 1/p)`.

For `S = {2, 3}` this reads `1 - (1/2)(2/3) = 2/3`: crossing out the multiples of the first two
primes already removes exactly four of every six integers (`two_three`).
-/
/-- The modulus of the sieve: the product of the sieving primes. -/
/-- `n` is killed by the sieve if one of the sieving primes divides it. -/

/-- **A periodic predicate is counted blockwise.**  If membership depends only on the residue
mod `m`, then the count over `range (m * k)` is `k` times the count over one period. -/
/-- Each sieving prime divides the modulus. -/
/-- The sieve is periodic modulo `M = ∏ p`. -/
/-- Surviving the sieve is the same as being coprime to the modulus. -/
/-- In one period there are exactly `φ(M)` survivors. -/
/-- The modulus is positive. -/
/-- `φ(M) = ∏ (p - 1)` for a product of distinct primes. -/

/-- **The survivors of a finite sieve, counted exactly.**  Among the first `M * k` naturals,
exactly `k * ∏ (p - 1)` avoid all the primes of `S`. -/

/-- **The sieved set, counted exactly.**  Among the first `M * k` naturals, exactly
`k * (M - ∏ (p - 1))` are divisible by some prime of `S`. -/

/-- **Legendre density.**  The proportion of the first `M * k` naturals removed by sieving with
the primes of `S` is exactly `1 - ∏_{p ∈ S} (1 - 1/p)`. -/

/-- **Specialisation to `S = {2, 3}`.**  The modulus is `6` and the sieved count over
`range (6 * k)` is `4 * k`: the first two primes already remove two thirds of the integers. -/

/-!
# What survives the sieve by `2` and `3`

`RequestProject.Sieve.Legendre` counts the survivors of a sieve by a finite set of primes; for
`S = {2, 3}` exactly two residues out of every six survive (`Sieve.two_three`).  This file
records what those two surviving classes are, and connects them to the digital-root trinity:

* `prime_mod_six` : every prime `p > 3` lies in one of the two surviving classes `±1 mod 6`;
* `prime_digitalRoot` : consequently the decimal digital root of such a prime avoids the
  trinity `{3, 6, 9}`, i.e. it is one of `1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8`.

Note that `6 = 2 · 3` is the modulus of the sieve while `9 = 3 ^ 2` is the modulus governing
digital roots: the "3, 6, 9" of `RequestProject.DigitalRoot.Decimal` is the same arithmetic seen
through the primes `2` and `3`.
-/
/-- **Every prime past `3` hides in the two surviving classes** `1` and `5` mod `6`. -/

/-- **Bridge to the digital-root trinity.**  Since a prime `p > 3` is not divisible by `3`, its
digital root avoids `3, 6, 9`: it is one of `1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8`. -/

/-!
# Certificates of harmonic invariance for spectral lines with `ΔE / E < 10⁻⁶`

A resonance (acoustic) or a spectral line (optical) is observed twice: a reference
realisation with energy `E` and an observed realisation with energy `E'`.  We say the line
is *stable* when its relative energy deviation satisfies `|E' - E| / E < 10⁻⁶`.

* `EnergyCertificate E E'` bundles the checked consequences of the bound at the level of
  energies: `E, E' > 0`, `|E' - E| < 10⁻⁶ E`, the ratio `E'/E ∈ (1 - 10⁻⁶, 1 + 10⁻⁶)` and the
  amplitude ratio `√(E'/E)` within `10⁻⁶` of `1`.  `EnergyCertificate.of_relDev` produces it.
* `HarmonicCertificate x y` (for sampled signals `x, y : ZMod N → ℂ`) states that the bound
  holds both in the time domain and in the DFT domain, and that it is invariant under the
  full harmonic symmetry group (all cyclic time translations and all frequency
  modulations), together with the invariance of the magnitude spectra under translations.
* `certify`: **every** pair of sampled signals with `ΔE / E < 10⁻⁶` has a
  `HarmonicCertificate`.
* `certify_spectral_line`: the same for a line measured directly in the frequency domain.
* `certify_physical`: for continuous band-limited physical signals whose physical energies
  `T⁻¹∫|x|²` satisfy `ΔE / E < 10⁻⁶`, sampling above the Nyquist rate yields a
  `HarmonicCertificate` for the samples and an `EnergyCertificate` for the discrete
  spectrum certificates.
* `certify_wavelet`: the Haar wavelet energies at every depth inherit the certificate.
* `a440_certificate`: a worked example (a 440 Hz tone whose amplitude drifts by `10⁻⁷`).
-/
/-- The tolerance `10⁻⁶`. -/
/-- Relative energy deviation `ΔE / E = |E' - E| / E`. -/
/-- The certified consequences of `ΔE / E < 10⁻⁶` at the level of energies. -/
/-- A relative deviation below `10⁻⁶` generates an energy certificate. -/
/-- Relative deviation is unchanged by a common positive rescaling of both energies. -/
/-- The normalized spectral energy `N⁻¹ ∑ₖ ‖X k‖²` of a sampled signal. -/
/-- A certificate of harmonic invariance for a reference line `x` and observed line `y`. -/
/-- the energy bound in the time domain -/
/-- the energy bound in the frequency (DFT) domain -/
/-- the bound is invariant under every time translation and frequency modulation -/
/-- the magnitude spectra are invariant under time translation -/

/-- **Certificate generation**: any reference/observed pair of sampled lines with
`ΔE / E < 10⁻⁶` automatically carries a certificate of harmonic invariance. -/

/-- An optical (or acoustic) spectral line measured directly in the frequency domain as
DFT spectra `X`, `Y`: a relative spectral-energy deviation below `10⁻⁶` certifies the
corresponding time-domain signals. -/

/-- **Physical certificate**: for continuous band-limited physical signals (reference `x`
and observed `y`) whose physical energies `T⁻¹∫₀ᵀ|·|²` satisfy `ΔE / E < 10⁻⁶`, sampling
at `N` points above the Nyquist rate generates a certificate of harmonic invariance for
the samples, and the discrete spectrum certificates satisfy the same energy bound. -/
/-- The Haar wavelet energies at every decomposition depth inherit the certificate. -/
/-! ## Worked example: a 440 Hz resonance -/

/-- A 440 Hz resonance whose amplitude drifts from `1` to `1 + 10⁻⁷` has
`ΔE / E ≈ 2·10⁻⁷ < 10⁻⁶`, and hence a certificate of harmonic invariance for its
4-point samples. -/

/-!
# The discrete Fourier transform and Parseval's identity

We work with discrete signals indexed by `ZMod N` (`N` samples, cyclically indexed).

* `dft x k = ∑ₙ x n · e^{-2πi n k / N}` is the discrete Fourier transform, and
  `idft` is its inverse (`idft_dft`, `dft_idft`).  The operator agrees with Mathlib's
  `ZMod.dft` (`dft_eq_zmod_dft`).
* `parseval_dft`: `∑ₖ ‖X k‖² = N · ∑ₙ ‖x n‖²` (Parseval / Plancherel).
* `translate` (time shift) and `modulate` (frequency shift) are the harmonic
  symmetries; the magnitude spectrum is invariant under time shifts
  (`norm_dft_translate`) and the energy is invariant under both
  (`energy_translate`, `energy_modulate`).
-/
/-- The primitive `N`-th root-of-unity character `n ↦ e^{2πi n / N}` on `ZMod N`. -/
/-- Orthogonality of the discrete harmonics. -/
/-- The discrete Fourier transform `X k = ∑ₙ x n · e^{-2πi n k / N}`. -/
/-- The inverse discrete Fourier transform `x n = N⁻¹ ∑ₖ X k · e^{2πi n k / N}`. -/
/-- Our `dft` is Mathlib's `ZMod.dft`. -/
/-- Discrete energy of a sampled signal, `∑ₙ ‖x n‖²`. -/
/-- **Parseval's identity** for the DFT: `∑ₖ ‖X k‖² = N · ∑ₙ ‖x n‖²`. -/

/-- Parseval in normalized form: the spectral energy `N⁻¹ ∑ ‖X k‖²` equals the
signal energy. -/
/-- Cyclic time translation by `j` samples. -/
/-- Modulation (frequency shift by `l` bins). -/
/-- Shift theorem: translating in time multiplies the spectrum by a phase. -/
/-- Modulation theorem: modulating in time shifts the spectrum. -/
/-- The magnitude spectrum is invariant under time translation. -/

/-!
# From continuous physical signals to discrete spectrum certificates

A continuous, periodic, band-limited physical signal (an audio pressure wave or a
mechanical vibration) of period `T` is modelled as a trigonometric polynomial
`x(t) = ∑_{m ∈ S} c_m e^{2πi m t / T}` with a finite set `S ⊆ ℤ` of harmonics
(`PhysSignal`).  Real-valued signals are the special case `c_{-m} = conj c_m`.

* `PhysSignal.energy` is the physical mean-square energy
  `T⁻¹ ∫₀ᵀ |x(t)|² dt`; `energy_eq_sum_sq` computes it as `∑ |c_m|²`.
* `PhysSignal.sample x N` samples `x` at the `N` instants `t_n = n T / N`, and
  `PhysSignal.spectrum x N = N⁻¹ · DFT(samples)` is the discrete spectrum certificate.
* `spectrum_eq_alias_sum`: the discrete spectrum at bin `k` is the sum of all
  coefficients `c_m` with `m ≡ k (mod N)` (aliasing formula).
* `NyquistOK x N`: distinct harmonics fall into distinct bins; this holds as soon as
  all harmonics lie in a window of `N` consecutive integers (`nyquistOK_of_subset_Ico`).
* **Parseval** (`parseval_physical`): under the Nyquist condition,
  `∑ₖ |spectrum k|² = T⁻¹ ∫₀ᵀ |x(t)|² dt`, i.e. the discrete spectral `L²` norm equals
  the physical energy; also the sample energy matches (`sample_energy_eq_energy`).
-/
/-- A band-limited periodic physical signal `x(t) = ∑_{m ∈ S} c_m e^{2πi m t / T}`. -/
/-- the period -/
/-- the (finite) set of harmonics present -/
/-- the complex amplitudes of the harmonics -/
/-- The value of the signal at time `t`. -/
/-- Physical mean-square energy over one period, `T⁻¹ ∫₀ᵀ |x(t)|² dt`. -/
/-- Uniform sampling at `t_n = n T / N`. -/
/-- The discrete spectrum certificate: the normalized DFT of the samples. -/
/-- Anti-aliasing (Nyquist) condition: distinct harmonics land in distinct DFT bins. -/
/-- Orthogonality of the continuous harmonics on one period. -/
/-- Expansion of `|x(t)|²` into harmonics. -/
/-- The physical energy equals the sum of the squared harmonic amplitudes. -/
/-- The samples are discrete harmonics. -/
/-- DFT of the samples: each harmonic contributes `N · c_m` to the bin `m mod N`. -/

/-- **Aliasing formula**: the discrete spectrum at bin `k` collects all harmonics
`m ≡ k (mod N)`. -/

/-- If all harmonics lie in a window of `N` consecutive integers (e.g. `|m| < N/2`), the
Nyquist condition holds. -/

/-- **Parseval's energy identity** for a sampled physical signal: under the Nyquist
condition, the discrete spectral `L²` norm of the spectrum certificate equals the
physical mean-square energy `T⁻¹ ∫₀ᵀ |x(t)|² dt`. -/
/-- The time average of the squared samples equals the physical energy. -/
/-- Unnormalized Parseval: `∑ₖ |DFT(samples)ₖ|² = N² · (physical energy)`. -/

declarations.name: DiscreteCertificate
declarations.signature_heuristic:
structure DiscreteCertificate (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] : Prop where
  /-- Lipschitz continuity: consecutive samples differ by at most `L · T / N` -/
  lipschitz_step : ∀ n : ℕ,
    ‖F.signal.eval (F.time N (n + 1)) - F.signal.eval (F.time N n)‖ ≤
      F.signal.lipConst * (F.signal.T / N)
  /-- bounded variation: the discrete total variation over a period is at most `L · T` -/
  bounded_variation : ∑ n ∈ range N,
    ‖F.signal.eval (F.time N (n + 1)) - F.signal.eval (F.time N n)‖ ≤
      F.signal.lipConst * F.signal.T
  /-- harmonic conservation: sample energy and spectral energy equal the physical energy -/
  harmonic_conservation :
    energy (F.signal.sample N) = N * F.signal.energy ∧
      ∑ k : ZMod N, ‖F.signal.spectrum N k‖ ^ 2 = F.signal.energy
  /-- the `H¹` bound -/
  sobolev : F.signal.sobolevSq ≤ (1 + (2 * π * F.B / F.signal.T) ^ 2) * F.signal.energy

/-!
# Continuous sensor stream ingestion with certified 3σ events

This file extends the `Spectral` development (`PhysSignal`, sampling, Parseval) to an
ingestion pipeline for physical sensor feeds.

* **Trajectories.** A `SensorFeed` (accelerometer, microphone or photodiode) carries a
  band-limited periodic trajectory `x(t) = ∑_{|m| ≤ B} c_m e^{2πi m t/T}`.
  `PhysSignal.derivSig` is its exact derivative (`hasDerivAt_eval`), `sobolevSq` is the squared
  `H¹` norm `‖x‖² + ‖x'‖²` (mean square over a period), `sobolevSq_eq_sum` computes it,
  `SensorFeed.memH1` records `H¹` membership and `SensorFeed.derivEnergy_le` /
  `SensorFeed.sobolevSq_le` are the Bernstein bounds `‖x'‖² ≤ (2πB/T)² ‖x‖²`.
* **Regularity.** `PhysSignal.norm_eval_sub_le` / `lipschitzWith_eval`: Lipschitz continuity
  with the explicit constant `lipConst = ∑ |c_m| 2π|m|/T`; `boundedVariationOn_eval`:
  bounded variation on every compact interval.
* **Discrete certificate generator.** `SensorFeed.DiscreteCertificate F N` bundles, for the
  samples `x(nT/N)`: the Lipschitz step bound, the discrete total-variation bound `≤ L·T`,
  harmonic (energy) conservation (sample energy `= N·E`, spectral energy `= E`) and the `H¹`
  bound.  `SensorFeed.generate` produces it for every `N ≥ 2B + 1`.
* **3σ events.** `mean`, `variance`, `stdDev` of a baseline window and
  `Exceeds3Sigma l r : 3σ < |r - μ|`.  `chebyshev_three_sigma`: at most `1/9` of any baseline
  are themselves 3σ outliers.  `compile_event`: any reading of a feed exceeding 3σ yields an
  `EventCertificate` (the 3σ fact, its persistence on an explicit time window around the event,
  and the discrete certificate).  Certificates are propositions, hence unique
  (`EventCertificate.unique`).
* **Kernel-checked compilation of ADC readings.** `check3Sigma` decides 3σ events on integer
  ADC counts; `check3Sigma_iff` proves it sound and complete, and the command
  `certify_event name from baseline reading r` elaborates to a new declaration
  `theorem name : Exceeds3Sigma baseline r` proved by `decide`.
-/
/-! ## Derivative, Sobolev energy, Lipschitz constant of a band-limited signal -/
/-- The derivative signal: harmonic `m` is multiplied by `2πi m / T`. -/

/-- The squared Sobolev `H¹` norm over one period: `‖x‖²_{L²} + ‖x'‖²_{L²}`
(both mean-square over one period). -/
/-- The Lipschitz constant `L = ∑_m |c_m| · 2π|m| / T`. -/
/-- **Lipschitz continuity** of every band-limited trajectory. -/
/-- **Bounded variation** on every compact interval. -/
/-! ## Sensor feeds -/
/-- The three physical sensor modalities. -/
/-- A continuous sensor feed: a band-limited trajectory with harmonics in `[-B, B]`. -/
/-- the bandwidth (highest harmonic index) -/
/-- The physical reading at time `t` (the real part of the trajectory). -/
/-- The `n`-th sampling instant `t_n = n T / N`. -/
/-- **Bernstein inequality**: the derivative energy is at most `(2πB/T)²` times the energy. -/
/-- The `H¹` norm of a band-limited trajectory is controlled by its energy. -/

/-- `H¹` membership: the trajectory is differentiable with the explicit derivative, and both
the trajectory and its derivative are square integrable over a period. -/
/-! ## The discrete certificate generator -/
/-- The discrete certificate attached to sampling the feed at `N` points per period. -/
/-- Lipschitz continuity: consecutive samples differ by at most `L · T / N` -/
/-- bounded variation: the discrete total variation over a period is at most `L · T` -/
/-- harmonic conservation: sample energy and spectral energy equal the physical energy -/
/-- the `H¹` bound -/
/-- **Certificate generator**: every feed sampled at `N ≥ 2B + 1` points gets a certificate. -/
/-! ## 3σ statistics -/
/-- Empirical mean of a list of readings. -/

/-- the event persists on the whole window `L |t - t₀| < |r - μ| - 3σ` -/

/-! ## Integer ADC readings: a decision procedure -/
/-- Decision procedure for 3σ events on integer ADC counts. -/

/-!
# The discrete Haar wavelet transform and its energy conservation

A discrete signal is a finite list of real samples.

* `Haar.step` is one level of Haar analysis: consecutive pairs `(a, b)` are sent to the
  approximation coefficient `(a + b)/√2` and the detail coefficient `(a - b)/√2`
  (a trailing unpaired sample is kept as an approximation coefficient).
* `Haar.synth` is one level of synthesis; `synth_step` is perfect reconstruction.
* `Haar.dwt J` is the `J`-level (Mallat pyramid) Haar transform, with inverse
  `Haar.idwt` (`idwt_dwt`).
* `energy_step`, `energy_dwt`: the transforms are orthogonal, i.e. they preserve the
  energy `∑ xᵢ²` (Parseval's identity for the Haar wavelet basis).
* `sampleList f Δ n` samples a continuous signal `f : ℝ → ℝ` at `t = iΔ`;
  `energy_dwt_sample` states that the wavelet energy of the sampled signal equals
  the Riemann-sum energy `Δ ∑ f(iΔ)²` of the physical signal.
-/
/-- The energy `∑ xᵢ²` of a list of samples. -/
/-- One level of the Haar analysis: returns (approximation, detail) coefficients. -/
/-- One level of Haar synthesis (the inverse of `step`). -/
/-- Perfect reconstruction for one level. -/
/-- Energy conservation for one level of the Haar transform. -/

/-- The `J`-level Haar discrete wavelet transform: returns the coarsest approximation
and the list of detail bands (finest first). -/
/-- The inverse Haar wavelet transform. -/
/-- Perfect reconstruction for the multi-level transform. -/
/-- The wavelet-domain energy: approximation energy plus all detail-band energies. -/

/-- **Parseval's identity for the Haar wavelet transform**: the wavelet-domain energy
equals the energy of the signal. -/
/-- Sampling a continuous signal `f` at the `n` instants `t = iΔ`, `i < n`. -/

/-- The wavelet energy of a sampled physical signal (with sampling step `Δ`) equals
the Riemann-sum energy `Δ ∑ f(iΔ)²` of that signal. -/

/-!

continuous physical signal sampling, harmonic invariance certificates,
and continuous sensor stream ingestion into real-time verified Lean theorems.

/-!
# Seeley–DeWitt densities of an almost-commutative Dirac operator

Let `M` be a compact Riemannian spin `4`-manifold and `F = (A_F, H_F, D_F)` a finite
spectral triple with `dim H_F = N`.  The fluctuated Dirac operator of the product
`M × F` is `D_A = D_M ⊗ 1 + γ₅ ⊗ Φ`, where `D_M = -iγ^a ∇_a` contains the gauge
connection (curvature `F_ab`, anti-Hermitian) and `Φ` (Hermitian) contains the Higgs field.
By the generalized Lichnerowicz formula, `D_A² = -(∇^a∇_a + E)` with

`E = -(R/4) ⊗ 1 + ½ γ^aγ^b ⊗ F_ab + i γ^aγ₅ ⊗ D_aΦ - 1 ⊗ Φ²`,
`Ω_ab = ¼ R_abcd γ^cγ^d ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ F_ab`.

This file computes, pointwise and exactly, the traces entering the Seeley–DeWitt
coefficients (`tr` = trace over spinors ⊗ `H_F`):

* `trace_E`       : `tr E = -N R - 4 tr Φ²`;
* `trace_E_sq`    : `tr E² = N R²/4 + 2R tr Φ² + 4 tr Φ⁴ - 2 ∑ tr F_ab F_ab + 4 ∑ tr (D_aΦ)²`;
* `trace_Omega_sq`: `∑ tr Ω_abΩ_ab = -(N/2) R_abcd R_abcd + 4 ∑ tr F_ab F_ab`;

and assembles them into the Gilkey densities `a₀(x), a₂(x), a₄(x)`
(`a0Density_eq`, `a2Density_eq`, `a4Density_eq`).
-/

/-- **Pointwise data of an almost-commutative geometry `M⁴ × F`** at a point of `M`, in an
orthonormal frame: the Riemann tensor `R_abcd` (antisymmetric in each pair), the gauge
curvature `F_ab ∈ M_N(ℂ)` (antisymmetric in `a, b`, anti-Hermitian), the Higgs endomorphism
`Φ` (Hermitian) and its covariant derivatives `D_aΦ` (Hermitian). -/
/-- Riemann tensor in an orthonormal frame. -/
/-- Gauge field strength `F_ab`. -/
/-- The Higgs field (fluctuated finite Dirac operator). -/
/-- Covariant derivatives `D_aΦ`. -/
/-- Scalar curvature `R = ∑_{a,b} R_abab`. -/
/-- Ricci tensor `Ric_bd = ∑_a R_abad`. -/
/-- `Ric_{bd} Ric^{bd}`. -/
/-- `R_{abcd} R^{abcd}`. -/

/-- The endomorphism `E` of the generalized Lichnerowicz formula `D_A² = -(∇² + E)`:
`E = 1 ⊗ (-(R/4) - Φ²) + ∑_{a,b} γ^aγ^b ⊗ ½F_ab + ∑_a γ^aγ₅ ⊗ i D_aΦ`. -/

/-- The curvature `Ω_ab = ¼ R_abcd γ^cγ^d ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ F_ab` of the connection on
spinors ⊗ `H_F`. -/
/-- `∑_{a,b} tr F_ab F_ab` (non-positive, since `F_ab` is anti-Hermitian). -/

/-- Trace of the square of a bivector-valued endomorphism `∑ γ^aγ^b ⊗ G_ab` with `G`
antisymmetric: `-8 ∑ tr G_ab G_ab`. -/
/-! ## Real invariants and positivity -/
/-- `tr Φ²` (real part; it is real since `Φ` is Hermitian). -/
/-- `tr Φ⁴` (real part). -/
/-- `∑ tr F_ab F_ab` (real part; `≤ 0`). -/
/-- `∑ tr (D_aΦ)²` (real part). -/
/-- The Yang–Mills density is non-negative: `-∑ tr F_ab F_ab = ∑ ‖F_ab‖²_HS ≥ 0`. -/
/-! ## The Seeley–DeWitt densities -/

/-- The pointwise Seeley–DeWitt invariants of `D_A²` at the point `P`, i.e. the integrands
of the invariants of `SeeleyDeWittInvariants` with the fibre traces included
(`tr 1 = 4N` on spinors ⊗ `H_F`): `vol ↦ tr 1`, `R ↦ R tr 1`, `E ↦ tr E`,
`R² ↦ R² tr 1`, …, `RE ↦ R tr E`, `E² ↦ tr E²`, `F_{μν}F^{μν} ↦ ∑ tr Ω_ab Ω_ab`. -/
/-- **`a₀` density**: `a₀(x) = tr 1 = 4N`. -/

/-- **`a₂` density** of the almost-commutative geometry:
`a₂(x) = (1/6) tr(R + 6E) = -(N/3) R - 4 tr Φ²`. -/

/-- **`a₄` density** of the almost-commutative geometry:
`a₄(x) = (N/360)(5R² - 8 Ric² - 7 Riem²) + (1/3) R tr Φ² + 2 tr Φ⁴ + 2 ∑ tr (D_aΦ)²
- (2/3) ∑ tr F_ab F_ab`. -/

/-!
# Euclidean Dirac matrices in dimension four and their trace identities

This file provides the spinor-side algebra needed to compute the Seeley–DeWitt coefficients
of an almost-commutative Dirac operator `D_A = D_M ⊗ 1 + γ₅ ⊗ Φ` on `M⁴ × F`.

We use the chiral representation of the Euclidean Clifford algebra `Cl(ℝ⁴)`:
`γ^j = [[0, -iσ_j], [iσ_j, 0]]` (`j = 1, 2, 3`), `γ^4 = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]` and
`γ₅ = γ^1γ^2γ^3γ^4`.  All identities are first checked by exact computation over the
Gaussian integers `ℤ[i]` (entries are `0, ±1, ±i`) and then transported to `ℂ` along the
ring homomorphism `ℤ[i] → ℂ`.

Main results (frame indices `a, b, c, d ∈ Fin 4`):
* `gamma_mul_gamma_add` : `γ^a γ^b + γ^b γ^a = 2 δ^{ab}`;
* `gamma_conjTranspose`, `gamma5_conjTranspose`, `gamma5_mul_self`,
  `gamma5_anticomm` : hermiticity, `γ₅² = 1`, `γ₅ γ^a = -γ^a γ₅`;
* `trace_gamma2`, `trace_gamma4`, `trace_gamma_gamma5`, `trace_gamma3_gamma5`,
  `trace_gamma_gamma5_gamma_gamma5` : the trace identities
  `tr(γ^aγ^b) = 4δ^{ab}`,
  `tr(γ^aγ^bγ^cγ^d) = 4(δ^{ab}δ^{cd} - δ^{ac}δ^{bd} + δ^{ad}δ^{bc})`,
  `tr(γ^aγ₅) = 0`, `tr(γ^aγ^bγ^cγ₅) = 0`, `tr(γ^aγ₅γ^bγ₅) = -4δ^{ab}`.
-/
/-- The Gaussian integer `i`. -/

/-- Euclidean chiral Dirac matrices with Gaussian-integer entries (frame index `0,…,3`
standing for `γ^1, …, γ^4`). -/
/-- Complex conjugation on `ℤ[i]`, used to express hermiticity before transport. -/
/-! ## Transport to `ℂ` -/
/-- The ring homomorphism `M₄(ℤ[i]) → M₄(ℂ)`. -/
/-- The Euclidean Dirac matrices `γ^a ∈ M₄(ℂ)`. -/
/-- The chirality matrix `γ₅ = γ^1γ^2γ^3γ^4 ∈ M₄(ℂ)`. -/

/-- The four-gamma trace contracted against an antisymmetric matrix-valued tensor:
`∑ tr(γ^aγ^bγ^cγ^d) tr(G_ab G_cd) = -8 ∑ tr(G_ab G_ab)`. -/

/-!
# The asymptotic expansion of the spectral action `Tr f(D/Λ)`

This file proves the analytic half of the spectral action principle: if the heat trace of
`D²` has the Seeley–DeWitt small-time expansion
`Tr e^{-tD²} ∼ (4πt)^{-2} ∑_k a_{2k} t^k` (dimension `4`), then the spectral action
`Tr f(D/Λ)` of an even Laplace-type cutoff `f(x) = χ(x²)`, `χ(u) = ∫ e^{-su} dμ(s)`, has
the large-`Λ` expansion

`Tr f(D/Λ) ∼ (4π)^{-2} ∑_k m_{k-2} a_{2k} Λ^{4-2k}`,  `m_j = ∫ s^j dμ(s)`,

to every order.  The first three coefficients are the familiar
`f₄ Λ⁴ a₀ + f₂ Λ² a₂ + f₀ a₄` with `f₀ = χ(0)`, `f₂ = m_{-1} = ∫₀^∞ χ`,
`f₄ = m_{-2} = ∫₀^∞ u χ(u) du`.

The Dirac operator is modelled by its (countable) spectrum with multiplicity, and the
spectral action is the genuine trace `∑_n f(λ_n/Λ)`.  No assumption is made beyond
the heat-trace expansion itself and finiteness of the moments of `μ`.

**Remark on the earlier definition.** `SovereignEngine.SeeleyDeWitt.HeatTraceAsymptotics`
(from a previous formalization in this project) demands that the remainder after `N`
terms be `o(t^N (4πt)^{-d/2})`; this is off by one and forces every coefficient to vanish
(`heatTraceAsymptotics_forces_zero` below).  The corrected notion, used throughout, is
`HeatTraceExpansion`: the remainder after `N` terms is `O(t^N (4πt)^{-d/2})`.
-/
/-! ## Heat-trace expansions -/

/-- **Seeley–DeWitt heat-trace expansion** (corrected form).
`HeatTraceExpansion d a K` says `K(t) ∼ (4πt)^{-d/2} ∑_k a_k t^k` as `t → 0⁺`: for every
`N`, the remainder after the terms `k < N` is `O(t^N (4πt)^{-d/2})`. -/

/-- The earlier definition `HeatTraceAsymptotics` (remainder `o(t^N ⋯)` after `N` terms)
forces all coefficients to vanish, so it cannot describe a heat trace with `a₀ = Vol ≠ 0`.
This is why the corrected `HeatTraceExpansion` is used in this file. -/

/-- The truncated Seeley–DeWitt model `(4πt)^{-2} ∑_{k<N} a_k t^k`, written with integer
powers: `(16π²)⁻¹ ∑_{k<N} a_k t^{k-2}`. -/

/-- **Global remainder bound.** If `K ≥ 0` is non-increasing on `(0,∞)` and has the
Seeley–DeWitt expansion, then for every `N ≥ 2` the remainder after `N` terms is bounded by
`C t^{N-2}` for *all* `t > 0` (not only near `0`). -/
-- near zero: the `O`-estimate
-- away from zero: monotonicity and crude bounds
/-! ## Laplace-type cutoff functions -/

/-- **A Laplace-type cutoff.** A finite positive measure `μ` on `(0, ∞)` all of whose
moments `∫ s^j dμ`, `j ∈ ℤ`, are finite.  It defines the cutoff
`χ(u) = ∫ e^{-su} dμ(s)` and the even test function `f(x) = χ(x²)` of the spectral action.
(Example: `μ = δ₁` gives the heat-kernel cutoff `f(x) = e^{-x²}`, see `diracCutoff`.) -/
/-- The Laplace measure. -/
/-- `μ` is carried by `(0, ∞)`. -/
/-- All moments are finite. -/
/-- The cutoff profile `χ(u) = ∫ e^{-su} dμ(s)`. -/
/-- The even test function `f(x) = χ(x²)` of the spectral action `Tr f(D/Λ)`. -/
/-- The moments `m_j = ∫ s^j dμ(s)`, `j ∈ ℤ`.  `m_{-2} = f₄`, `m_{-1} = f₂`, `m_0 = f₀`. -/
/-- `μ`-almost every `s` is positive. -/
/-- All moments are positive: `m_j > 0` whenever `μ ≠ 0`. -/
/-- `u ↦ u^q e^{-su}` is integrable on `(0, ∞)` for `s > 0`. -/
/-! ## Discrete spectra, heat trace and spectral action -/

/-- **The spectrum of a Dirac operator** `D` with discrete spectrum: a countable family of
real eigenvalues `λ_i` (repeated with multiplicity) such that `Tr e^{-tD²}` converges for
every `t > 0`. -/
/-- The eigenvalues of `D`, with multiplicity. -/
/-- The heat trace `K(t) = Tr e^{-tD²} = ∑ e^{-tλ_i²}`. -/
/-- **The spectral action** `Tr f(D/Λ) = ∑_i f(λ_i/Λ)`. -/
/-! ## Integrals against the Laplace measure -/
/-- The rescaled heat trace `s ↦ Tr e^{-(s/Λ²) D²}` is `μ`-integrable. -/
/-- **Tonelli step.** `Tr f(D/Λ) = ∫ Tr e^{-(s/Λ²)D²} dμ(s)`. -/

/-- **The spectral action expansion, quantitative form.** If the heat trace of `D²` has
the Seeley–DeWitt expansion with coefficients `a_k` (in dimension `4`), then for every
`N ≥ 2` there is `C` with
`|Tr f(D/Λ) - ∑_{k<N} (4π)^{-2} m_{k-2} a_k Λ^{4-2k}| ≤ C Λ^{4-2N}` for all `Λ > 0`. -/
/-- The `k`-th term `(4π)^{-2} m_{k-2} a_k Λ^{4-2k}` of the spectral action expansion. -/

/-- **The full asymptotic expansion of the spectral action.** If `Tr e^{-tD²}` has the
Seeley–DeWitt expansion `∼ (4πt)^{-2} ∑ a_k t^k`, then for every order `N`

`Tr f(D/Λ) = ∑_{k<N} (4π)^{-2} m_{k-2} a_k Λ^{4-2k} + O(Λ^{4-2N})`  as `Λ → ∞`. -/

/-- **The first three terms of the spectral action.**
`Tr f(D/Λ) = (4π)^{-2} (f₄ a₀ Λ⁴ + f₂ a₂ Λ² + f₀ a₄) + O(Λ⁻²)` with
`f₄ = m_{-2}`, `f₂ = m_{-1}`, `f₀ = m_0 = χ(0)`; here `a 0, a 1, a 2` are the Seeley–DeWitt
coefficients usually called `a₀, a₂, a₄`. -/
/-! ## Non-vacuity: explicit cutoff and spectrum -/
/-- The heat-kernel cutoff `μ = δ₁`, i.e. `χ(u) = e^{-u}` and `f(x) = e^{-x²}`. -/
/-- A single zero mode: `D = 0` on a one-dimensional space. -/

/-- Sanity check of the notion of heat-trace expansion: the heat trace `K ≡ 1` of a
single zero mode has the expansion with `a₂ = 16π²` (the coefficient of `t⁰`) and all
other coefficients zero. -/
