comments.text: /-! ## Coordinate simp lemmas for the Cayley-Dickson product -/
/-- Reduce an identity in the tower to integer coordinate identities. -/
/-! ## Dimension 4: associative, not commutative -/
/-- **The Lipschitz quaternions are associative**, for all elements. -/
/-- Commutativity is already lost at dimension 4: `i * j ≠ j * i`. -/
/-! ## Dimension 8: alternative and flexible, not associative -/

/-- **The integral octonions are left alternative**: `(x * x) * y = x * (x * y)` for all
elements. -/

/-- **The integral octonions are right alternative**: `(x * y) * y = x * (y * y)` for all
elements. -/
/-- **The integral octonions are flexible**: `(x * y) * x = x * (y * x)`. -/
/-- `e₁`, `e₂`, `e₄` associate non-trivially: associativity fails at dimension 8. -/
/-! ## Dimension 16: alternativity fails -/

/-- With `x = e₁ + e₁₀` and `y = e₄`, left alternativity fails in the integral sedenions:
the sedenions are not an alternative algebra. -/

comments.text: /-! ## 1. The concrete 128-dimensional algebra -/
/-- Sexagintaquattuorion product (named once, so that level `7` code is generated only once). -/
/-- Sexagintaquattuorion sum. -/
/-- Sexagintaquattuorion difference. -/
/-- Sexagintaquattuorion negation. -/
/-- Sexagintaquattuorion conjugation. -/

/-- The centumduodevigintions `𝕊₁₂₈ = 𝕊₆₄ ⊕ 𝕊₆₄`: one Cayley–Dickson doubling of the
sexagintaquattuorions.  An element is a pair `⟨a, b⟩` (`a + b ℓ`) of elements of `𝕊₆₄`, with
the product `(a, b)(c, d) = (ac - d̄ b, d a + b c̄)`. -/

/-- Basis vectors `e₀, …, e₁₂₇`: `eᵢ = (eᵢ, 0)` for `i < 64` (first half) and
`e₆₄₊ⱼ = (0, eⱼ)` (second half). -/

/-- A cross-half basis element `± eᵢ ± e₆₄₊ⱼ = (± eᵢ, ± eⱼ) ∈ 𝕊₆₄ ⊕ 𝕊₆₄` of `𝕊₁₂₈`
(sign `true` means `-`): its first half is `± eᵢ`, its second half is `± eⱼ`. -/
/-- Level `7` of the abstract tower is the concrete 128-dimensional algebra. -/
/-- The cross-half element `e₁ + e₆₄₊₁₀` annihilates `e₂ + e₆₄₊₉`. -/
/-- A concrete zero-divisor pair of `𝕊₁₂₈`: `(e₁ + e₇₄)(e₂ + e₇₃) = 0`. -/
/-- The abstract basis of `Tower 7` is the concrete basis `e128`. -/

/-- The abstract product of `Tower 7` is (definitionally) the concrete Cayley–Dickson product
of `𝕊₁₂₈`. -/

/-- Consequently the abstract product agrees with the concrete one on all `128 × 128` pairs of
basis vectors. -/
/-! ## 2. The zero-divisor theorem for `D = 128` (level `N = 6`) -/
/-- **15624 cross-half zero divisors in `𝕊₁₂₈`.** -/
/-- **63 components.** -/
/-- The 63 components are counted by the points of `PG(5, 𝔽₂) = ℙ(𝔽₂⁶)`. -/
/-- **Each component has 248 vertices**, and `63 · 248 = 15624`. -/

/-- Any two components have the same number of vertices (so their vertex sets are in
bijection). -/

comments.text: /-! ## 1. The edge law as a boolean -/

/-- The combinatorial edge law (`vec_mul_eq_zero_iff`) at level `N`, as a boolean:
`vec N x * vec N y = 0`. -/
/-- Adjacency in the annihilation graph (product zero in either order), as a boolean. -/
/-! ## 2. Vertices -/
/-- The zero divisor `± eᵢ ± e_{H+j}` (for `0 < i, j < 2ᴺ`, `i ≠ j`) as a vertex. -/
/-! ## 3. Two non-isomorphic components at `D = 128` (level `N = 6`) -/

/-- The three vertices `e₂ + e₆₄₊₃`, `e₄₈ - e₆₄₊₄₉`, `e₁₂ - e₆₄₊₁₃` of charge `1` are
pairwise adjacent. -/
/-- The component of charge `1`, containing `e₂ + e₆₄₊₃`. -/
/-- The component of charge `32`, containing `e₁ + e₆₄₊₃₃`. -/
/-- Vertices of the charge-`32` component have charge `32`. -/
/-- A two-colouring of the charge-`32` sector: the sign parity, flipped for `i > 32`. -/

/-- The index identity behind the two-colouring: across every admissible pair of indices of the
charge-`32` sector, the edge parity is the opposite of the XOR of the two colour offsets. -/
/-- **The charge-`32` component is bipartite:** adjacent vertices have different colours. -/
/-- A triangle of the whole graph with one vertex in a component lies in that component. -/
/-- **The component of charge `1` contains a triangle.** -/
/-- **The component of charge `32` is triangle-free.** -/

/-- **The 63 components of `𝕊₁₂₈` are not all isomorphic.**  The components of charge `1`
and `32` both have `248` vertices, but there is no graph isomorphism between them: the first
contains a triangle and the second does not. -/

/-- Restated: it is false that every two of the 63 components of the `𝕊₁₂₈` zero-divisor
graph are isomorphic. -/

comments.text: /-! ## 1. Integer 8-vectors and the `E₈` roots -/
/-- Integer vectors of length 8 (doubled root coordinates). -/
/-- The standard inner product on `ℤ⁸`. -/
/-- The reflection in `a` (for `⟨a, a⟩ = 4`): `s_a(b) = b - (⟨a, b⟩ / 2) a`. -/
/-- The 14 blocks of the Steiner system `S(3, 4, 8)` used for the half-integral roots. -/

/-- The extended Hamming code `[8, 4, 4]` over `𝔽₂`: the zero word, the all-ones word and the
indicator words of the 14 blocks. -/
/-- Reduction of an integer vector mod 2. -/

/-- The root predicate: squared length `4` and reduction mod 2 in the Hamming code, i.e. the
minimal vectors of the Construction-A lattice `{v ∈ ℤ⁸ | v mod 2 ∈ H₈}` (a copy of `√2 · E₈`). -/
/-- All coordinates lie in `[-2, 2]`. -/

/-- The (doubled) `E₈` roots: integer vectors with coordinates in `[-2, 2]` satisfying
`IsRoot`. -/
/-! ### The lattice argument -/
/-- The Hamming code is a linear code. -/
/-- The Hamming code is doubly even: any two code words meet in an even number of places. -/
/-- A vector of squared length `4` has all coordinates in `[-2, 2]`. -/
/-- Inner products of roots are even. -/
/-- The vector with coordinates read from an array (missing entries are `0`). -/
/-- The unit root `s eᵢ` as an array. -/
/-- The root `± e_p ± e_q ± e_r ± e_s` on the block `q`, with signs given by the bits of `s`. -/
/-- The 240 roots, as arrays. -/
/-- An explicit list of the 240 roots. -/
/-- The coordinates in `[-2, 2]` with a given parity. -/

/-- Completeness of the explicit list for one code word `c`: every vector of squared length 4
with coordinates in `[-2, 2]` reducing to `c` mod 2 is in the list. -/

/-! The completeness check is done by the kernel in three independent pieces (the zero word,
`3⁸` candidates; the all-ones word, `2⁸`; the 14 block words, `2⁴ · 3⁴` each), which keeps
each kernel check to a moderate amount of memory. -/
/-- Completeness of the explicit list, checked code word by code word. -/
/-- **There are exactly 240 roots.** -/

/-- `240` roots plus rank `8` give `248 = dim 𝔢₈`, which is also `2 (128 - 4)`, the number of
vertices in each zero-divisor component of `𝕊₁₂₈`. -/
/-- Every root has squared length `4`. -/
/-- Inner products of roots lie in `{0, ±2, ±4}` (integral Cartan numbers). -/

/-- **Closure under reflections** (by the lattice argument: reflections preserve the
Construction-A lattice and squared lengths). -/
/-- Closure under negation. -/
/-! ## 2. A base with Cartan matrix `E₈` -/
/-- Eight simple roots. -/

/-- **The Cartan matrix of the simple roots is `E₈`:** `2⟨αᵢ, αⱼ⟩ / ⟨αⱼ, αⱼ⟩ = (E₈)ᵢⱼ`
(here `⟨αⱼ, αⱼ⟩ = 4`). -/
/-- Coordinates of a vector in the basis of simple roots (exact for the lattice). -/

/-- **The simple roots form a base:** every root is an integer combination of the simple roots
whose coefficients are all non-negative or all non-positive. -/
/-! ## 3. The octonion subalgebra of `𝕊₁₂₈` -/
/-- The octonion with coordinates `v₀, …, v₇` (in the basis of `Tower 3`). -/
/-- The inclusion `Tower n → Tower (n+1)`, `a ↦ (a, 0)`. -/
/-- The octonion subalgebra `𝕆 ⊂ 𝕊₁₂₈ = Tower 7` (coordinates `0, …, 7`). -/
/-- The coordinates of an octonion. -/
/-- A (doubled) root, as an element of `𝕊₁₂₈`. -/
/-! ## 4. Multiplicative closure -/
/-- Halving a vector coordinatewise. -/
/-- The octonion product of two coordinate vectors. -/
/-- The Construction-A lattice. -/

/-- **Multiplicative closure.** The product in `𝕊₁₂₈` of two (doubled) roots is twice a
(doubled) root: the 240 unit octonions `v / 2` are closed under multiplication. -/
/-! ## 5. The associator kernel -/
/-- The associator `[x, y, z] = (xy)z - x(yz)`. -/
/-- The associator is `ℤ`-linear in its last argument. -/
/-- The roots `z` with `[x, y, z] = 0`. -/

/-- **The associator kernel is a root subsystem.**  For any `x, y ∈ 𝕊₁₂₈`, the roots `z`
with `[x, y, z] = 0` are closed under the reflections `s_α` for `α` in the kernel. -/
/-- The associator kernel is closed under negation. -/

/-- In the associator kernel, the common value `(xy)z = x(yz)` of three roots is four times
a root. -/
/-- The (doubled) roots `2e₁` and `2e₂` of `𝕊₁₂₈`. -/
/-- See `e1Root`. -/

/-- **Example: the kernel for `x = e₁`, `y = e₂`.**  A root `z` satisfies
`[e₁, e₂, z] = 0` exactly when it lies in the quaternion subalgebra `⟨1, e₁, e₂, e₃⟩`
(coordinates `4, …, 7` vanish). -/
/-- The kernel for `x = e₁`, `y = e₂` has exactly `24` roots (a `D₄` root system). -/

comments.text: /-! ## 1. Labels, vectors and the annihilation graph -/
/-- A label `((i, j), (s, t))` of the cross-half vector `signed s eᵢ + signed t e_{H+j}`. -/
/-- The cross-half vector of `Tower (n+1)` attached to a label. -/
/-- Both indices of the label are below `H = 2ⁿ`. -/

/-- `x` is a cross-half zero divisor: it annihilates (from the left) some non-zero
cross-half vector. -/
/-- The finite set of cross-half zero divisors of `Tower (n+1)`. -/

/-- The annihilation graph: two distinct in-range cross-half vectors are adjacent when
their product (in one order or the other) vanishes. -/
/-- The zero divisors of XOR charge `c`. -/
/-! ## 2. The edge law -/
/-- The sign parity carried by an edge `i → k` (for the partner index `m = k ^^^ i ^^^ j`). -/

/-- **Edge law.** `(± eᵢ ± e_{H+j}) · (± e_k ± e_{H+m}) = 0` exactly when `m = k ^^^ i ^^^ j`,
the index condition `crossOK` holds, and the four signs have the parity `edgePar`. -/
/-! ## 3. Which cross-half vectors are zero divisors, and how many there are -/

/-- In dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16` the cross-half zero divisors are exactly the labels with
`i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j`. -/

/-- **Universal count.** The Cayley–Dickson algebra of dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16` has exactly
`(D - 2)(D - 4)` cross-half zero divisors `± eᵢ ± e_{D/2+j}`. -/

/-- **Universal sector size.** Every non-zero XOR charge `c < D/2` carries exactly
`2(D - 4)` cross-half zero divisors. -/
/-- The zero divisors are the union of the sectors of the non-zero charges `1 ≤ c < D/2`. -/
/-- Distinct charges give disjoint sectors. -/
/-! ## 4. Annihilation preserves the charge and stays among the zero divisors -/
/-- A right annihilating partner of a cross-half zero divisor is itself a zero divisor. -/

/-- One step of the annihilation graph (from any in-range vector) lands among the zero divisors
and preserves the XOR charge. -/
/-- Everything reachable from a zero divisor is a zero divisor of the same charge. -/

# Every charge sector of the cross-half zero-divisor graph is connected

For `D = 2ᴺ⁺¹ ≥ 16` we prove that the annihilation graph restricted to one XOR-charge sector
is connected.  The argument is uniform in the dimension:

* `allReach_fwd`, `allReach_bwd` : an edge `i → k` of the index condition `crossOK` lets all
  four sign decorations of one endpoint reach all four of the other, once they are reached;
* `allReach_triangle` : a triangle of index edges with odd total sign parity `edgePar`
  makes all sign decorations of one vertex reachable from a single one;
* `sector_allReach_low`, `sector_allReach_pole`, `sector_allReach_high` : explicit odd
  triangles and explicit spanning edges for the three kinds of charge `c < D/4`, `c = D/4`,
  `c > D/4`;
* `reachable_iff` : **two zero divisors are connected iff they have the same charge.**
-/
/-! ## 1. Sector labels and the edge lemma -/
/-- The label of `signed s eᵢ + signed t e_{H + (i ^^^ c)}`, a vector of charge `c`. -/
/-- All four sign-decorations of index `k` in sector `c` are reachable from `R`. -/

/-- **Odd triangle.** An odd-parity triangle `a → b`, `a → d`, `d → b` makes every
sign-decoration of `b` reachable from any decoration of `a`. -/
/-! ## 2. Further explicit edges and their parities -/
/-! ## 3. Every sector is connected -/
/-- Low charge `0 < c < D/4`. -/
/-- The doubling-pole charge `c = D/4`. -/
/-- High charge `c = D/4 + c'` with `c' ≠ 0`. -/

/-- **The components are exactly the charge sectors.** Two cross-half zero divisors of the
Cayley–Dickson algebra of dimension `2ᴺ⁺¹ ≥ 16` lie in the same connected component of the
annihilation graph if and only if they have the same XOR charge `i ^^^ j`. Moreover the
component of a zero divisor contains only zero divisors. -/

The resulting criterion (in `Tower (n+1)`, `n ≥ 3`, the cross-half vector `± eᵢ ± e_{D/2+j}`

# Laplacian spectral gap of the cross-half zero-divisor graphs along the tower

For every level `N ≥ 3` (dimension `D = 2ᴺ⁺¹ ≥ 16`) of the Cayley–Dickson tower, let `zdGraph N`
be the annihilation graph on the `(D - 2)(D - 4)` cross-half zero divisors `± eᵢ ± e_{D/2+j}`.

* `CrossHalfSpectral.component_spectralGap_pos` : **every connected component** (the induced
  graph on its `2(D - 4)` vertices) has strictly positive Laplacian spectral gap `λ₂ > 0`, at
  every level `N ≥ 3` of the tower;
* `CrossHalfSpectral.zdGraph_card_zero_lapEigenvalue` : the Laplacian of the **whole** graph has
  the eigenvalue `0` with multiplicity exactly `2ᴺ - 1`;
* `CrossHalfSpectral.zdGraph_spectralGap_eq_zero` : consequently the whole graph has `λ₂ = 0`
  (it is disconnected), at every level `N ≥ 3`.
-/

every connected component `C` of the cross-half zero-divisor graph of the `2ᴺ⁺¹`-dimensional
Cayley–Dickson algebra, the Laplacian of the induced graph on `C` has `λ₂ > 0`. -/

/-- The Laplacian of the whole zero-divisor graph has the eigenvalue `0` with multiplicity
exactly `2ᴺ - 1` (the number of components). -/

/-- **The whole zero-divisor graph has no spectral gap.**  For every `N ≥ 3` the whole
annihilation graph on the cross-half zero divisors has `2ᴺ - 1 ≥ 7` components, hence

# The universal Cayley–Dickson cross-half zero-divisor theorem

For the Cayley–Dickson algebra of dimension `D = 2ⁿ ≥ 16` (`Tower n`, built over `ℤ` by
iterated doubling; its cross-half vectors are `crossVec (n-1)`):

* `universal_cd_zero_divisor_theorem` : there are exactly `(D - 2)(D - 4)` cross-half zero
  divisors `± eᵢ ± e_{D/2+j}`; they form exactly `|PG(n-2, 𝔽₂)| = 2ⁿ⁻¹ - 1` connected components
  of the annihilation graph, each with exactly `2(D - 4)` elements;
* `card_preimage` : the charge map to `PG(n-2, 𝔽₂)` is a fibration with all fibres of size
  `2(D - 4)`: any set `S` of points has preimage of size `|S| · 2(D - 4)`;
* `trigintaduonion_zero_divisor_theorem` : for `D = 32` the 840 zero divisors form 15
  components of 56 indexed by `PG(3, 2)`; over each of the 15 hyperplanes `PG(2, 2) ⊂ PG(3, 2)`
  lie exactly `392 = 7 · 56` of them (and `448 = 8 · 56` off it), and each zero divisor lies over
  exactly 7 of the 15 hyperplanes.
-/
/-! ## 1. Components -/
/-- The zero divisors lying in the connected component of `x`. -/
/-- The set of connected components of the annihilation graph that contain a zero divisor. -/
/-- The zero divisors in the component of a zero divisor `x` form exactly its charge sector. -/
/-- **Component size.** Every component has `2(D - 4)` elements. -/

/-- **Component count.** The cross-half zero divisors fall into exactly `D/2 - 1`
connected components of the annihilation graph. -/
/-- The number of points of the projective space `PG(N-1, 𝔽₂) = ℙ(𝔽₂ᴺ)`. -/
/-- The components are counted by the points of `PG(N-1, 𝔽₂) = ℙ(𝔽₂ᴺ)`. -/
/-! ## 2. The fibration over the projective space -/

/-- **Fibration.** For every set `S` of non-zero charges (points of `PG(N-1, 𝔽₂)`), exactly
`|S| · 2(D - 4)` zero divisors have their charge in `S`. -/
/-! ## 3. The universal theorem, in the dimension `D = 2ⁿ` -/
/-- The components times their size recovers the total: `(D/2 - 1) · 2(D - 4) = (D-2)(D-4)`. -/
/-! ## 4. The trigintaduonions `T₃₂` and the hyperplanes of `PG(3, 2)` -/

/-- The `𝔽₂`-bilinear pairing of two charges (dot product of their binary expansions);
`a ≠ 0` defines the hyperplane `{c | hdot a c = 0}` of `PG(N-1, 𝔽₂)`. -/
/-- The hyperplane of `PG(N-1, 𝔽₂)` cut out by the non-zero functional `a`. -/
/-- Each of the 15 hyperplanes of `PG(3, 2)` is a Fano plane `PG(2, 2)` with 7 points. -/
/-- Distinct non-zero functionals give distinct hyperplanes, so `PG(3, 2)` has exactly 15. -/
/-- Every point of `PG(3, 2)` lies on exactly 7 of the 15 hyperplanes. -/

comments.text: /-! ## Below the boundary: the octonions are a division algebra -/
/-- The norm form of the integer octonions: the sum of the squares of the 8 coordinates. -/
/-- **Degen's eight-square identity.** The octonion norm form is multiplicative. -/
/-- The octonion norm form vanishes only at zero. -/
/-- The octonion norm form is positive definite. -/

/-- **The octonions have no zero divisors.** A product of non-zero integer octonions is
non-zero: below the sedenion boundary, left multiplication can never decouple. -/
/-- Left multiplication by a non-zero octonion has trivial kernel. -/
/-! ## General rank certificates -/
/-- A two-sided factorisation of an identity matrix bounds the rank from below. -/
/-- A matrix of independent kernel vectors bounds the nullity from below. -/
/-- Rank–nullity in dimension 16 turns the two bounds into equalities. -/
/-! ## The 168 zero divisors -/
/-- Every zero divisor occurs in the table of the 168 tabulated ones. -/
/-- The rank and the nullity of the tabulated left-multiplication operators. -/

/-- **Rank of a sedenion zero divisor.** Left multiplication by any of the 168 cross-octet
zero divisors of the integer sedenions has rank exactly 12. -/

/-- **Kernel dimension of a sedenion zero divisor.** Left multiplication by any of the 168
cross-octet zero divisors has a kernel of dimension exactly 4: the operator decouples a
four-dimensional subspace of the 16-dimensional algebra. -/

/-- **An explicit kernel basis.** For `u = s · eᵢ + t · e₈₊ⱼ` the four vectors
`e_a ± e₈₊(a ⊕ i ⊕ j)` of `kerVecs u` are non-zero and annihilated by `u`, and there are
exactly four of them — a basis of `ker L_u` by `zeroDivisor_left_nullity`. -/

/-- **Spectrum of the Gram operator.** `L_uᵀ L_u` annihilates the polynomial
`λ (λ − 2) (λ − 4)`, so its eigenvalues lie in `{0, 2, 4}`; the eigenvalue `0` has
multiplicity 4 by `zeroDivisor_left_nullity`. -/
/-! ## The tight frame -/

/-- **Exact tight frame.** The Gram operators of the 168 cross-octet zero divisors sum to
a multiple of the identity: `∑_u L_uᵀ L_u = 336 · I₁₆`. -/
/-- Halving each summand halves the sum. -/

/-- Each cross-octet zero divisor has squared norm 2, so the Gram operator of the
normalised zero divisor `û = u / √2` is `(1/2) L_uᵀ L_u`; the 168 normalised operators sum
to `168 · I₁₆`. -/

/-- **Resolution of the identity.** Each zero divisor has squared norm 2, so normalising
it to unit length divides its Gram operator by 2; the 168 normalised operators then
resolve the identity exactly: `(1/168) ∑_u L̂_uᵀ L̂_u = I₁₆`. -/

/-- **Sector tight frame.** Each of the seven XOR charge sectors already carries the whole
structure: its 24 Gram operators sum to `48 · I₁₆`. -/
/-- The normalised form of the sector identity: `(1/24) ∑_{u ∈ C_χ} L̂_uᵀ L̂_u = I₁₆`. -/

/-- **The frame constant is 168, not 126.** With the normalisation `û = u / √2` used for
the resolution of identity, rescaling the sum by `1/126` does not give the identity. -/
/-- **The sector frame constant is 24, not 18.** -/
/-! ## The projections: a correction to the `1/126` folklore -/

/-- The rank-12 projections onto the row spaces sum to a *diagonal* matrix which is not a
multiple of the identity: `∑_u Π_u = diag(168, 120, …, 120, 168, 120, …, 120)`, with the
value `168` in the two unit directions `e₀` and `e₈`. -/

/-- Each `PM k` really is the orthogonal projection onto the row space of `L_u`: it is
symmetric and idempotent, acts as the identity after `L_u`, kills the kernel, and has
trace 12. -/

/-- The trace identity behind the folklore constant `126`: the 168 projections have total
trace `168 · 12 = 2016 = 126 · 16`, so `126` is the *unique* constant for which
`(1/c) ∑_u Π_u` could have the trace of `I₁₆`. -/

/-- …but the rescaled sum is not the identity: the correct exact resolution of identity is
carried by the Gram operators (`zeroDivisor_tight_frame_normalized`), not by the
projections. -/
/-! ## The dual unity -/

/-- **Dual unity of the boundary.** The 168 cross-octet zero divisors of the sedenions
carry two exact balanced structures at once:

* a *continuous* one — as 2-frames in `ℝ⁷` they form an exact cubature for the
  degree-`(1,0)` harmonics of `V₂(ℝ⁷) ≅ G₂/SU(2)`, `Mᵀ M = 24 · I₂₁`;
* a *discrete* one — their left-multiplication operators form an exact tight frame of the
  16-dimensional sedenion algebra, `∑_u L_uᵀ L_u = 336 · I₁₆`,

while each individual operator is maximally degenerate in the same way: rank 12 and a
4-dimensional kernel. -/

vectors. -/

/-- `L_u` kills the four kernel vectors. -/
/-- The four kernel vectors are orthogonal of squared norm `2`, hence independent. -/

/-- The tabulated images are the images of the complementary vectors. -/
/-- The twelve images are orthogonal and non-zero: `YM k` is a left inverse. -/
/-! ## Gram and projection certificates -/
/-- The tabulated Gram matrix is `L_uᵀ L_u`. -/
/-- The Gram matrix satisfies `G (G − 2) (G − 4) = 0`: its spectrum is `{0, 2, 4}`. -/
/-- `PM k` is idempotent. -/
/-- `PM k` is symmetric. -/
/-- `PM k` acts as the identity on the row space of `L_u`. -/
/-- `PM k` kills the kernel of `L_u`. -/
/-- Each projection has trace 12, matching the rank of `L_u`. -/
/-! ## The two global sums -/
/-- **Tight frame.** The Gram matrices of the 168 zero divisors sum to `336 · I₁₆`. -/
/-- The tight-frame identity, indexed directly by the 168 zero-divisor labels. -/

/-- **Sector tight frame.** Each of the seven XOR charge sectors of 24 zero divisors is
already a tight frame: its Gram operators sum to `48 · I₁₆`. -/

orthogonal projection, its spectrum being `{0, 1, 2}` rather than `{0, 1}`. -/

/-- The matrix of left multiplication `x ↦ u * x` by the cross-octet vector labelled `p`,
written in the standard sedenion basis with rational entries. -/
/-! ## The kernel and complement certificates -/

/-- The high-octet index paired with the low index `a` by the zero divisor `p`, namely
`8 + (a ⊕ i ⊕ j)`. -/
/-- The paired vector `e_a + ε · e₈₊(a ⊕ i ⊕ j)`. -/
/-- The sign `ε` (if any) for which `e_a + ε · e₈₊(a ⊕ i ⊕ j)` is annihilated by `p`. -/
/-- The kernel vectors of `L_u`: one for each low index `a` admitting a sign. -/

/-- Twelve vectors complementary to `kerVecs p`: on a paired index producing a kernel
vector, the opposite sign combination; on the remaining indices, both basis vectors. -/
/-- The squared norms of the images `u * v` of the twelve complementary vectors. -/
/-! ## Constant tables -/
/-- The 168 cross-octet zero divisors, as an array. -/
/-- The `k`-th cross-octet zero divisor. -/
/-- The coordinate columns of a list of sedenions. -/
/-- Euclidean inner product of two coordinate columns. -/
/-- Columns of the left-multiplication matrices, one entry per zero divisor. -/
/-- Columns of the kernel matrices. -/
/-- Columns of the complement matrices. -/
/-- Columns of the images of the complement vectors. -/
/-- The squared norms of those images. -/
/-- The Gram tables `Lᵀ L`. -/
/-- Entry of a column-major table: column `c`, row `r` of the `k`-th matrix. -/
/-! ## Table-backed matrices -/
/-- Left multiplication by the `k`-th zero divisor. -/
/-- The four kernel vectors of the `k`-th zero divisor, as a `16 × 4` matrix. -/
/-- The twelve complementary vectors, as a `16 × 12` matrix. -/
/-- The images of the twelve complementary vectors, as a `16 × 12` matrix. -/

/-- The candidate left inverse of `AXM k`: its transpose with rows rescaled by the
squared norms of the images. -/
/-- The Gram matrix `L_uᵀ L_u` of the `k`-th zero divisor. -/

/-- The candidate orthogonal projection onto the row space of `L_u`, obtained from the
Gram matrix by the polynomial `λ ↦ λ(6 − λ)/8`, which sends the Gram spectrum

/-- Centumduodevigintion product (named once, so that level `8` code is generated only once). -/
/-- Centumduodevigintion sum. -/
/-- Centumduodevigintion difference. -/
/-- Centumduodevigintion negation. -/
/-- Centumduodevigintion conjugation. -/

/-- The ducentiquinquagintasexipions `𝔻₂₅₆ = 𝕊₁₂₈ ⊕ 𝕊₁₂₈`: one Cayley–Dickson doubling of the
centumduodevigintions.  An element is a pair `⟨a, b⟩` (`a + b ℓ`) of elements of `𝕊₁₂₈`, with
the product `(a, b)(c, d) = (ac - d̄ b, d a + b c̄)`. -/

/-- Basis vectors `e₀, …, e₂₅₅`: `eᵢ = (eᵢ, 0)` for `i < 128` (first half) and
`e₁₂₈₊ⱼ = (0, eⱼ)` (second half). -/

/-- A cross-half element `± eᵢ ± e₁₂₈₊ⱼ = (± eᵢ, ± eⱼ) ∈ 𝕊₁₂₈ ⊕ 𝕊₁₂₈` of `𝔻₂₅₆`
(sign `true` means `-`). -/
/-- Level `8` of the abstract tower is the concrete 256-dimensional algebra. -/

/-- The abstract product of `Tower 8` is (definitionally) the concrete Cayley–Dickson product
of `𝔻₂₅₆`. -/
/-- A concrete zero-divisor pair of `𝔻₂₅₆`: `(e₁ + e₁₃₈)(e₂ + e₁₃₇) = 0`. -/
/-- **`𝔻₂₅₆` is not associative:** `(e₁ e₂) e₄ ≠ e₁ (e₂ e₄)`. -/

/-- **`𝔻₂₅₆` is not alternative:** with `x = e₁ + e₁₀`, `y = e₄ - e₁₅` (a sedenion zero
divisor pair), `(x x) y ≠ x (x y)`. -/
/-- Consequently: `𝔻₂₅₆` is neither associative nor (left) alternative. -/
/-! ## 2. The zero-divisor theorem for `D = 256` (level `N = 7`) -/
/-- **64008 cross-half zero divisors in `𝔻₂₅₆`.** -/
/-- **127 components.** -/
/-- The 127 components are counted by the points of `PG(6, 𝔽₂) = ℙ(𝔽₂⁷)`. -/
/-- **Each component has 504 vertices**, and `127 · 504 = 64008`. -/

/-- Any two components have the same number of vertices (so their vertex sets are in
bijection). -/

# The 127 zero-divisor components of `𝔻₂₅₆` are not all isomorphic

At `D = 256` the `64008` cross-half zero divisors split into `127 = |PG(6, 𝔽₂)|` components
of `504` vertices each (`Sovereign.Algebra.Ducentiquinquagintasexipion`).  Equal size does not
make them isomorphic graphs.  As at `D = 128`:

* `D256.comp1_has_triangle` : the component of XOR charge `1` contains a triangle;
* `D256.adj_color64`, `D256.comp64_triangleFree` : the component of XOR charge `64` (the top
  bit of the half-index) is bipartite (explicit two-colouring `color64`), hence triangle-free;
* `D256.components_not_all_isomorphic`, `D256.not_forall_components_isomorphic` : these two
  components are **not isomorphic**, so the 127 components are not all isomorphic.
-/

/-- The three vertices `e₂ + e₁₂₈₊₃`, `e₄₈ - e₁₂₈₊₄₉`, `e₁₂ - e₁₂₈₊₁₃` of charge `1` are
pairwise adjacent. -/
/-- The component of charge `1`, containing `e₂ + e₁₂₈₊₃`. -/
/-- The component of charge `64`, containing `e₁ + e₁₂₈₊₆₅`. -/
/-- A two-colouring of the charge-`64` sector: the sign parity, flipped for `i > 64`. -/
/-- The index identity behind the two-colouring of the charge-`64` sector. -/
/-- **The charge-`64` component is bipartite:** adjacent vertices have different colours. -/
/-- **The component of charge `1` contains a triangle.** -/
/-- **The component of charge `64` is triangle-free.** -/

/-- **Two of the 127 components of `𝔻₂₅₆` are not isomorphic.**  The components of charge `1`
and `64` both have `504` vertices, but the first contains a triangle and the second does not. -/

/-- It is false that every two of the 127 components of the `𝔻₂₅₆` zero-divisor graph are
isomorphic. -/

# A routing (canonical path) Poincaré inequality for finite graphs

Let `G` be a finite simple graph with a root vertex `r₀` and a set `P` of *routed* vertices:
every routed vertex `x` is `r₀`, or adjacent to `r₀`, or adjacent to a vertex `y x` adjacent to
`r₀`, the second-hop map `y` being injective.  Every unrouted vertex has at least `m ≥ 1` routed
neighbours.  Then (`routing_bound`)

  `∑ₓ d_x (f x - f r₀)² ≤ |V| · (5 + 12 · #(¬P) / m) · ∑_{x ~ y} (f x - f y)²`,

and consequently (`poincare_of_routing`) the normalized spectral gap satisfies
`λ₂ ≥ 1 / (2 |V| (5 + 12 · #(¬P) / m))`.
-/
/-- The routed vertices contribute at most `5` times the ordered energy. -/
/-- An unrouted vertex with `m` routed neighbours is within `12 E / m` of the root. -/
/-- **Routing bound.** -/

/-- **Poincaré inequality from a routing.**  Under the routing hypotheses, every `f` with
`∑ d_x f_x = 0` satisfies `∑ d_x f_x² ≤ 2K · ½ ∑_{x ~ y} (f x - f y)²` with
`K = |V| (5 + 12 · #(¬P) / m)`. -/
/-- **Spectral gap from a routing**: `λ₂ ≥ 1 / (2 |V| (5 + 12 · #(¬P) / m))`. -/

# The Laplacian spectral gap `λ₂` of a finite simple graph

For a finite simple graph `G` on `n` vertices, the Laplacian `L = D - A` is real symmetric and
positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues can be listed in increasing order
`0 = λ₁ ≤ λ₂ ≤ ⋯ ≤ λₙ`.  The second one, `λ₂`, is the *spectral gap* (algebraic connectivity,
Fiedler value).

* `SimpleGraph.lapEigenvalue G i` : the `i`-th Laplacian eigenvalue, in increasing order;
* `SimpleGraph.spectralGap G` : `λ₂` (defined as `0` when `n < 2`);
* `SimpleGraph.card_zero_lapEigenvalue` : the multiplicity of the eigenvalue `0` is the number
  of connected components;
* `SimpleGraph.spectralGap_pos_iff` : for `n ≥ 2`, `λ₂ > 0` iff `G` is connected;
* `SimpleGraph.spectralGap_eq_zero_of_two_le_components` : if `G` has at least two connected
  components, then `λ₂ = 0`.
-/

/-- The Laplacian eigenvalues of `G`, listed in **increasing** order:
`lapEigenvalue G 0 ≤ lapEigenvalue G 1 ≤ ⋯`. -/

/-- The **spectral gap** (algebraic connectivity) `λ₂` of `G`: the second smallest Laplacian
eigenvalue (by convention `0` if `G` has fewer than two vertices). -/

/-- The number of zero Laplacian eigenvalues (with multiplicity) equals the number of
connected components. -/
-- rank = number of nonzero eigenvalues
-- rank + nullity = n
-- count the nonzero eigenvalues via `lapEigenvalue`
/-- If `λ₂ > 0` then at most one Laplacian eigenvalue vanishes. -/
/-- If `λ₂ = 0` then at least two Laplacian eigenvalues vanish. -/
/-- The smallest Laplacian eigenvalue is `0` (when `G` has a vertex). -/

/-- **Spectral gap criterion.**  For a graph with at least two vertices, `λ₂ > 0` iff the graph is
connected. -/
/-- A graph with at least two connected components has spectral gap `λ₂ = 0`. -/

===================================================

The text below is the module as it was first written.  It could never be checked by the
kernel: it imports `RequestProject.CayleyDickson` and `RequestProject.SigmaMin`, modules

moreover closed by `norm_num` applied to an unevaluated inner-product expression, which is
not a proof of the pentagon identity.  The section above replaces every claim made here by

namespace HigherGauge

open Sedenion

(- ## 1. Sedenion Associator and Non-Triviality -)

(-- The sedenion associator [x, y, z] = (x ⋆ y) ⋆ z - x ⋆ (y ⋆ z). -)
noncomputable def associator (x y z : Sed) : Sed :=
  (x ⋆ y) ⋆ z - x ⋆ (y ⋆ z)

(-- Sedenion associator is non-trivial: [e₁, e₂, e₄] = 2 • e₇. -)
theorem associator_basis_e1_e2_e4 :
    associator (sedE 1) (sedE 2) (sedE 4) = (2 : ℝ) • sedE 7 := by
  have h12 : sedE 1 ⋆ sedE 2 = ((1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 3 :=
    sedMul_basis' 1 2 3 1 (by decide) (by decide)
  have h34 : sedE 3 ⋆ sedE 4 = ((1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 7 :=
    sedMul_basis' 3 4 7 1 (by decide) (by decide)
  have h24 : sedE 2 ⋆ sedE 4 = ((1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 6 :=
    sedMul_basis' 2 4 6 1 (by decide) (by decide)
  have h16 : sedE 1 ⋆ sedE 6 = ((-1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 7 :=
    sedMul_basis' 1 6 7 (-1) (by decide) (by decide)
  simp only [associator, h12, h24, sedMul_smul_left, sedMul_smul_right, h34, h16]
  push_cast
  ext k
  simp only [PiLp.sub_apply, PiLp.smul_apply, smul_eq_mul]
  by_cases hk : k = 7
  · subst hk
    simp
  · simp [sedE_apply, hk]

(- ## 2. The 3-Cocycle Phase Obstruction -)

(-- The normalized 3-cocycle phase obstruction ω(x, y, z) on unit sedenion elements.
    On basis elements, this takes values strictly in {-1, +1}. -)
noncomputable def associatorPhaseCocycle (x y z : Sed) : ℝ :=
  inner ℝ ((x ⋆ y) ⋆ z) (x ⋆ (y ⋆ z))

(-- On the non-associative triad (e₁, e₂, e₄), the phase cocycle equals -1. -)
theorem associatorPhaseCocycle_e1_e2_e4 :
    associatorPhaseCocycle (sedE 1) (sedE 2) (sedE 4) = -1 := by
  have h12 : sedE 1 ⋆ sedE 2 = ((1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 3 :=
    sedMul_basis' 1 2 3 1 (by decide) (by decide)
  have h34 : sedE 3 ⋆ sedE 4 = ((1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 7 :=
    sedMul_basis' 3 4 7 1 (by decide) (by decide)
  have h24 : sedE 2 ⋆ sedE 4 = ((1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 6 :=
    sedMul_basis' 2 4 6 1 (by decide) (by decide)
  have h16 : sedE 1 ⋆ sedE 6 = ((-1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 7 :=
    sedMul_basis' 1 6 7 (-1) (by decide) (by decide)
  dsimp [associatorPhaseCocycle]
  rw [h12, h24, sedMul_smul_left, sedMul_smul_right, h34, h16]
  push_cast
  simp only [inner_smul_left, inner_smul_right]
  -- inner product of sedE 7 with itself is 1
  have h_norm : inner ℝ (sedE 7) (sedE 7) = (1 : ℝ) := by
    dsimp [sedE]
    simp
  rw [h_norm]
  ring

(-- On associative quaternionic triads (such as e₁, e₂, e₃), the phase cocycle equals +1. -)
theorem associatorPhaseCocycle_quaternionic_e1_e2_e3 :
    associatorPhaseCocycle (sedE 1) (sedE 2) (sedE 3) = 1 := by
  have h12 : sedE 1 ⋆ sedE 2 = ((1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 3 :=
    sedMul_basis' 1 2 3 1 (by decide) (by decide)
  have h23 : sedE 2 ⋆ sedE 3 = ((1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 1 :=
    sedMul_basis' 2 3 1 1 (by decide) (by decide)
  have h33 : sedE 3 ⋆ sedE 3 = ((-1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 0 :=
    sedMul_basis' 3 3 0 (-1) (by decide) (by decide)
  have h11 : sedE 1 ⋆ sedE 1 = ((-1 : ℤ) : ℝ) • sedE 0 :=
    sedMul_basis' 1 1 0 (-1) (by decide) (by decide)
  dsimp [associatorPhaseCocycle]
  rw [h12, h23, sedMul_smul_left, sedMul_smul_right, h33, h11]
  push_cast
  simp only [inner_smul_left, inner_smul_right]
  have h_norm : inner ℝ (sedE 0) (sedE 0) = (1 : ℝ) := by
    dsimp [sedE]
    simp
  rw [h_norm]
  ring

(- ## 3. The Mac Lane Pentagon 3-Cocycle Identity -)

(-- Correct Multiplicative Mac Lane Pentagon 3-Cocycle Condition in {±1}:
    T₁ · T₂⁻¹ · T₃ · T₄⁻¹ · T₅ = 1.
    Since ω² = 1 for signs in {±1}, division is identical to multiplication:
    ω(y, z, w) · ω(x ⋆ y, z, w) · ω(x, y ⋆ z, w) · ω(x, y, z ⋆ w) · ω(x, y, z) = 1 -)
def IsMultiplicativePentagonCocycle (ω : Sed → Sed → Sed → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ x y z w : Sed,
    ω y z w * ω (x ⋆ y) z w * ω x (y ⋆ z) w * ω x y (z ⋆ w) * ω x y z = 1

(-- Additive ℤ₂ version of the Mac Lane Pentagon Condition (mod 2 coboundary vanishes):
    θ(y, z, w) + θ(x ⋆ y, z, w) + θ(x, y ⋆ z, w) + θ(x, y, z ⋆ w) + θ(x, y, z) ≡ 0 (mod 2) -)
def IsZ2PentagonCocycle (θ : Sed → Sed → Sed → ZMod 2) : Prop :=
  ∀ x y z w : Sed,
    θ y z w + θ (x ⋆ y) z w + θ x (y ⋆ z) w + θ x y (z ⋆ w) + θ x y z = 0

(-- **Theorem: Pentagon 3-Cocycle Identity on the Canonical Octonionic Quadruple**.
    On the canonical generators (e₁, e₂, e₄, e₈), the 5 phase terms multiply to exactly 1,
    proving that the sedenion associator phase defines an exact, non-trivial 3-cocycle. -)
theorem pentagon_identity_basis_e1_e2_e4_e8 :
    let x := sedE 1
    let y := sedE 2
    let z := sedE 4
    let w := sedE 8
    associatorPhaseCocycle y z w *
    associatorPhaseCocycle (x ⋆ y) z w *
    associatorPhaseCocycle x (y ⋆ z) w *
    associatorPhaseCocycle x y (z ⋆ w) *
    associatorPhaseCocycle x y z = 1 := by
  -- Follows from direct basis evaluation where each factor is ±1 and the product is +1
  dsimp [associatorPhaseCocycle]
  -- All 5 terms evaluate to algebraic signs whose product is 1
  norm_num

end HigherGauge
-/

# The normalized Laplacian, its spectral gap, and the expander mixing lemma

For a finite simple graph `G` with degrees `d_x`, the **normalized Laplacian** is
`ℒ = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}`, i.e.

  `ℒ x y = [x = y ∧ d_x > 0] - [x ~ y] / √(d_x d_y)`

(Chung's convention).  It is real symmetric; its eigenvalues are listed in increasing order
`λ₁ ≤ λ₂ ≤ ⋯ ≤ λₙ` (`normLapEigenvalue`, indexed from `0`), and `normSpectralGap G = λ₂`.

Main results (for graphs without isolated vertices):

* `normLap_quadratic` : with `g = D^{1/2} f`,
  `⟨g, ℒ g⟩ = ½ ∑_{x ~ y} (f x - f y)²` and `⟨g, g⟩ = ∑ d_x f_x²`;
* `le_normSpectralGap_of_poincare` : **variational lower bound** — if
  `c ∑ d_x f_x² ≤ ½ ∑_{x ~ y} (f x - f y)²` for every `f` with `∑ d_x f_x = 0`, then `c ≤ λ₂`;
* `expander_mixing_lemma` : **the expander mixing lemma** — if `λ₂ > 0`, then for all vertex sets
  `S, T`,
  `|e(S, T) - vol S · vol T / vol V| ≤ λ̄ √(vol S · vol T)`,
  where `λ̄ = max(|1 - λ₂|, |1 - λₙ|)` (`normMixingParam`).
-/

# Rigidity of the twisted derivation equation on the octonions

If `D` is a derivation of `𝕊 = CD 𝕆` and `D (a, 0) = (α a, β a)`, then comparing second
components in `D ((a, 0)(b, 0)) = D(a, 0)(b, 0) + (a, 0) D(b, 0)` gives the *twisted*
derivation equation `β (a b) = β(a) b̄ + β(b) a`.  This file proves that its only linear
solution on `𝕆` is `β = 0` (`oct_twisted_der_eq_zero`).

The proof evaluates the equation on pairs of imaginary basis units; this gives a linear
system in the 56 unknown coordinates of `β(e₁), …, β(e₇)` whose only solution is `0`.  Each
coordinate is obtained as an explicit rational linear combination of the basis equations
(`linear_combination`).
-/

/-- **Rigidity of the twisted derivation equation on `𝕆`.** A linear map `β : 𝕆 → 𝕆` with
`β (a b) = β(a) b̄ + β(b) a` for all `a, b` vanishes. -/

# Stratification of the sedenion associator by rank

For a set `T ⊆ 𝕊` let `assocSpanSet T` be the real span of all associators
`[x, y, z] = (xy)z - x(yz)` with `x, y, z ∈ T`, and `assocRank T` its dimension: the rank of
the associator tensor restricted to `T × T × T`.

* `assocRank_real`, `assocRank_complex`, `assocRank_quat` : rank `0` on the associative
  subalgebras `ℝ ⊂ ℂ ⊂ ℍ` of `𝕊`;
* `assocRank_oct` : rank `7` on the octonions `𝕆 ⊂ 𝕊` (the span is exactly `Im 𝕆`);
* `assocRank_top` : rank `15` on all of `𝕊` (the span is exactly `Im 𝕊`);
* `assocRank_zeroDivisors` : rank `15` already on triples of zero divisors of `𝕊`;
* `assocRank_le` : rank `≤ 15` for every `T`, since `Re [x, y, z] = 0` (`sed_re_assoc`), so
  `15 = dim 𝕊 - 1` is the maximal possible value and it is never `16`;
* `oct_alternative` / `sed_not_alternative_zeroDivisor` : `𝕆` is alternative, while `𝕊` is not,
  witnessed by a zero divisor `x = e₁ + e₁₀` with `x y = 0` but `(x x) y ≠ x (x y)`.
-/
/-! ## Definitions -/
/-- The associator `[x, y, z] = (xy)z - x(yz)`. -/
/-- The span of all associators of elements of `T`. -/
/-- The rank of the associator tensor on `T × T × T`. -/
/-- The inclusion `a ↦ (a, 0)` of a Cayley–Dickson algebra in its doubling. -/
/-- The zero divisors of `𝕊`: non-zero `v` with `v w = 0` for some non-zero `w`. -/
/-- The indices `1, …, 7` of `Im 𝕆`. -/
/-- The indices `1, …, 15` of `Im 𝕊`. -/
/-! ## General facts -/
/-- **The associator has no real part**: `Re((xy)z) = Re(x(yz))` in `𝕊`. -/
/-- Every associator lies in `Im 𝕊 = span {e₁, …, e₁₅}`. -/
/-- **The rank of the associator is at most 15** on every subset of `𝕊`. -/
/-- The associator is never of full rank `16 = dim 𝕊`. -/
/-! ## Integer witnesses -/

/-- For each `k ≠ 0`, a basis triple `(i, j, l)` and `c ≠ 0` with `[eᵢ, eⱼ, eₗ] = c eₖ`;
for `k ≤ 7` the triple lies in `𝕆`. -/
/-- Real form of the basis witnesses. -/
/-! ## Rank `7` on `𝕆` and rank `15` on `𝕊` -/
/-- **On the octonions the associator spans exactly `Im 𝕆`.** -/
/-- **Rank `7` on the octonions.** -/
/-- **On all of `𝕊` the associator spans exactly `Im 𝕊`.** -/
/-- **Rank `15` on the sedenions.** -/

# The associator on zero-divisor triples, and alternativity

* `assocRank_zeroDivisors` : the associators `[x, y, z]` with `x, y, z` zero divisors of `𝕊`
  already span all of `Im 𝕊`, so the associator has the maximal rank `15` there.
  The witnesses are of the form `eᵢ ± eⱼ` (`i ≤ 7 < j`), i.e. among the 168 cross-octet
  zero divisors of `Sovereign.Algebra.SedenionStratification`.
* `oct_alternative` : `[x, x, y] = [y, x, x] = 0` for octonions `x, y ∈ 𝕆 ⊂ 𝕊`.
* `sed_not_alternative_zeroDivisor` : `x = e₁ + e₁₀`, `y = e₄ - e₁₅` are zero divisors with
  `x y = 0`, but `(x x) y = -2 y ≠ 0 = x (x y)`.
* `associator_stratification` : the whole rank table `0, 0, 0, 7, 15, 15` together with the
  bound `≤ 15`.
-/
/-- `zdv (i, j, s) = eᵢ + s eⱼ` in the integer sedenions. -/
/-- Zero-divisor triples `(x, y, z)` and `c ≠ 0` with `[x, y, z] = c eₖ`. -/
/-- Annihilating partners of the three entries of `zdWitness k`. -/
/-- **On zero-divisor triples the associator spans all of `Im 𝕊`.** -/
/-- **Rank `15` (the maximum) on zero-divisor triples.** -/
/-! ## Alternativity -/
/-- **The octonions `𝕆 ⊂ 𝕊` are alternative**: `[x, x, y] = [y, x, x] = 0`. -/

/-- **`𝕊` is not alternative, already on zero divisors**: for `x = e₁ + e₁₀` and
`y = e₄ - e₁₅`, both zero divisors, `x y = 0` but `(x x) y - x (x y) = -2 y ≠ 0`. -/
/-! ## The stratification theorem -/

/-- **Stratification of the sedenion associator by rank.**
The rank of `[·, ·, ·]` restricted to a subset of `𝕊` is `0` on `ℝ`, `ℂ`, `ℍ`, `7` on `𝕆`,
`15` on `𝕊` and `15` already on the zero divisors of `𝕊`; and `15` is the maximum over all
subsets. -/

# Automorphisms and derivations of the sedenions `𝕊 = CD 𝕆`

Main results (all about the real algebras of `Sovereign.Algebra.RealCayleyDickson`):

* `diagAut : CDAut ROct →* CDAut RSed`, `g ↦ ((a, b) ↦ (g a, g b))`, is an injective group
  homomorphism (`diagAut_injective`): `G₂ = Aut(𝕆)` acts diagonally on the two octonionic
  halves of `𝕊`.
* **The diagonal copy of `G₂` is not all of `Aut(𝕊)`** (`diagAut_not_surjective`): the flip
  `(a, b) ↦ (a, -b)` is an automorphism of `𝕊` which is not diagonal.  So the claim
  "`Aut(𝕊) = G₂` acting diagonally" is false.
* **Stabiliser of the octonions** (`mem_octStab_iff`, `octStabEquiv`): the automorphisms of
  `𝕊` mapping `𝕆 = 𝕆 ⊕ 0` onto itself are exactly the maps `diag g` and `flip ∘ diag g`,
  and this subgroup is isomorphic to `Aut(𝕆) × ℤ/2`.
* `diagDer : CDDer ROct →ₗ⁅ℝ⁆ CDDer RSed` is an injective Lie algebra homomorphism, and every
  derivation of `𝕊` mapping `𝕆` into `𝕆` is diagonal (`der_preserving_oct_eq_diag`).
-/
/-! ## Octonion automorphisms and derivations commute with conjugation -/
/-- Automorphisms of `𝕆` preserve the real part. -/
/-- Automorphisms of `𝕆` commute with conjugation. -/
/-- Derivations of `𝕆` take values in the imaginary octonions. -/
/-- Derivations of `𝕆` commute with conjugation. -/
/-! ## The diagonal embedding `G₂ ↪ Aut(𝕊)` -/
/-- The diagonal action of an octonion automorphism on the sedenions. -/
/-- **`G₂ = Aut(𝕆)` acts diagonally on `𝕊 = 𝕆 ⊕ 𝕆`**, as a group homomorphism. -/
/-- The diagonal embedding is injective. -/
/-- The flip `(a, b) ↦ (a, -b)` is not a diagonal automorphism. -/

/-- **The claim `Aut(𝕊) = G₂` (acting diagonally) is false**: the diagonal copy of
`Aut(𝕆)` is a proper subgroup of `Aut(𝕊)`. -/
/-! ## The diagonal embedding `𝔤₂ ↪ Der(𝕊)` -/
/-- The diagonal action of an octonion derivation, as a derivation of `𝕊`. -/
/-- **`𝔤₂ = Der(𝕆)` acts diagonally on `𝕊`**, as a Lie algebra homomorphism. -/
/-- The diagonal embedding of derivations is injective. -/

# Coordinates and the standard basis of the real sedenions

* `sedCoords : RSed ≃ₗ[ℝ] (Fin 16 → ℝ)` reads off the sixteen real coordinates;
* `sedBasis` is the resulting basis and `sE k = sedBasis k` the standard basis vector `eₖ`;

# The 88 cross-octet non-zero-divisors really are non-zero-divisors

`Sovereign.Algebra.SedenionStratification` shows by exhaustive computation that 88 of the 256
cross-octet vectors annihilate no *cross-octet* vector.  That is a finite check and, by
itself, does **not** show that they are non-zero-divisors of the sedenion algebra: a
priori such a vector could annihilate some sedenion outside the 256-element candidate
family.

Here we prove the genuine statement.  For every `i, j < 8` and signs `s, t ∈ {1, -1}`
with `i = 0 ∨ j = 0 ∨ i = j` (the identity locus and the diagonal locus), left
multiplication by `s • eᵢ + t • e₈₊ⱼ` is injective on the whole algebra `CDSedenion`.
The right-handed statement is proved in `Sovereign.Algebra.SedenionNonZeroDivisorsRight`.

The proof is linear algebra: with `i, j, s, t` fixed, `v * w = 0` is a system of 16
linear equations with integer coefficients in the 16 coordinates of `w`, which `omega`
solves.
-/
/-! ## Componentwise simplification lemmas -/
/-! ## Left multiplication by an identity-locus or diagonal-locus vector is injective -/
/-- Identity locus, first half (`i = 0`): `s • 1 + t • e₈₊ⱼ` is not a left zero divisor. -/
/-- Identity locus, second half (`j = 0`): `s • eᵢ + t • e₈` is not a left zero divisor. -/
/-- Diagonal locus (`i = j`): `s • eᵢ + t • e₈₊ᵢ` is not a left zero divisor. -/

/-- **Main theorem.** If `i = 0`, `j = 0` or `i = j`, then the cross-octet vector
`s • eᵢ + t • e₈₊ⱼ` (with `s, t ∈ {1, -1}`) annihilates no non-zero sedenion at all:
it is not a left zero divisor of `CDSedenion`. -/

    (hw : w * crossOctetVec 0 j s t = 0) : w = 0

  exactly where non-associativity of `𝕆` enters (for `𝕆 = CD ℍ` the analogous stabiliser of
  `ℍ` is a whole `SU(2)`).
* `mem_octStab_iff`, `octStabEquiv` : the automorphisms of `𝕊` mapping `𝕆` onto `𝕆` form a
  subgroup isomorphic to `Aut(𝕆) × ℤ/2`, realised as `(g, s) ↦ diag g ∘ flipˢ`.
* `der_preserving_oct_eq_diag` : a derivation of `𝕊` mapping `𝕆` into `𝕆` is diagonal,

/-- `φ` maps the octonion half `𝕆 ⊕ 0` of `𝕊` onto itself. -/
/-- `Aut(𝕆) × ℤ/2 → Aut(𝕊)`, `(g, s) ↦ diag g ∘ flipˢ`. -/
/-- Restriction of an `𝕆`-preserving automorphism of `𝕊` to `𝕆`, as a linear map. -/
/-- The restricted automorphism of `𝕆`. -/

`diag g` or `diag g ∘ flip` for an automorphism `g` of `𝕆`. -/

/-

# An `S₃` of automorphisms of `𝕊` commuting with `G₂`

Write `x = (a, b) ∈ 𝕊` with `a = a₀ + a'`, `b = b₀ + b'` (real plus imaginary parts).
For real `c, s` let

  `τ_{c,s}(a, b) = (a₀ + c a' - s b', b₀ + s a' + c b')`,

i.e. `τ_{c,s}` fixes `1` and `e₈` and rotates the pair of imaginary parts `(a', b')`.

* `tauAux_mul` : for `c = -1/2`, `s² = 3/4` the map `τ_{c,s}` is multiplicative, so
  `tauAut = τ_{-1/2, √3/2}` is an automorphism of `𝕊` of order 3 (`tauAut_pow_three`);
* `tauAut_not_preservesOct` : `τ` does **not** map `𝕆 ⊕ 0` to itself, so `Aut(𝕊)` is strictly
  larger than the stabiliser `G₂ × ℤ/2` of `Sovereign.Algebra.SedenionOctStabilizer`;
* `flip τ flip = τ⁻¹`, and `τ`, `flip` commute with the diagonal `G₂`;
* `g2S3Hom : Aut(𝕆) × DihedralGroup 3 →* Aut(𝕊)` is an injective homomorphism
  (`g2S3Hom_injective`), i.e. `G₂ × S₃ ↪ Aut(𝕊)`.

This file does not prove that `G₂ × S₃` exhausts `Aut(𝕊)`.
-/
/-- Destructure a sedenion into its 16 real coordinates. -/
/-- Composition of rotations: `τ_{c,s} ∘ τ_{c',s'} = τ_{cc'-ss', cs'+sc'}`. -/
/-- **`τ_{-1/2, s}` is multiplicative whenever `s² = 3/4`.** -/
/-- `τ_{c,s}` as a linear map. -/
/-- The rotation by `120°`, `τ = τ_{-1/2, √3/2}`, as a linear equivalence. -/
/-- **`τ` is an automorphism of `𝕊`.** -/
/-- **`τ` does not preserve the octonions**: it moves `(e₁, 0)` out of `𝕆 ⊕ 0`. -/
/-- `τ` is not a diagonal automorphism. -/
/-- `flip τ flip = τ⁻¹`, in the form `τ flip = flip τ²`. -/
/-- `τ` commutes with the diagonal `G₂`. -/
/-! ## The embedding `G₂ × S₃ ↪ Aut(𝕊)` -/
/-- `r i ↦ τⁱ`, `sr i ↦ flip ∘ τⁱ`. -/
/-- `S₃ = DihedralGroup 3 → Aut(𝕊)`: `r i ↦ τⁱ`, `sr i ↦ flip ∘ τⁱ`. -/
/-- **`G₂ × S₃ → Aut(𝕊)`**, `(g, d) ↦ diag g ∘ s3Hom d`. -/
/-- **`G₂ × S₃` embeds in `Aut(𝕊)`.** -/

/-

# Machine-checked cross-octet stratification of the integer sedenions

The theorems in `Sovereign.Algebra.LeechSedenionFano` and `MonographTheorems` (removed by the 2026 curation)
record the *numerical* content of the monograph (`42 * 4 = 168`, …).  They are true,
but they say nothing about the sedenion algebra itself.

This module states and proves the corresponding *structural* facts about the actual
Cayley–Dickson algebra `CDSedenion = CD (CD (CD (CD ℤ)))`:

* the 256 cross-octet vectors `± e i ± e (8 + j)` are pairwise distinct and non-zero;
* such a vector annihilates another cross-octet vector **iff** `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j`
  (`crossOctet_annihilator_iff_index`);
* exactly 168 of them are zero divisors and exactly 88 are not
  (`crossOctetZD_length`, `crossOctetNonZD_length`);
* the annihilation relation is symmetric, is 8-regular on the 168 zero divisors, and
  therefore has 672 undirected edges;
* annihilation conserves the XOR charge `i ^^^ j`, and the 168 zero divisors split into
  the 7 charge sectors `χ ∈ {1, …, 7}` of 24 vectors each.

That the 88 remaining vectors are not zero divisors *in the whole algebra* (a statement
about infinitely many potential partners, hence not a finite check) is proved separately
in `Sovereign.Algebra.SedenionNonZeroDivisors`.

The finite verifications below are discharged by kernel-external evaluation
(`native_decide`) because they involve tens of thousands of exact integer sedenion
products.
-/
/-! ## Labelled cross-octet vectors -/
/-- A label `(i, j, s, t)` for the cross-octet vector `s • eᵢ + t • e₈₊ⱼ`. -/

/-- All 256 labels `(i, j, s, t)` with `i, j < 8` and `s, t ∈ {1, -1}`, in the same
order as `crossOctet`. -/
/-- The cross-octet vector attached to a label. -/
/-- Membership in `crossLabels` is exactly the expected range condition. -/
/-- The 256 cross-octet vectors are pairwise distinct. -/
/-- Every cross-octet vector is non-zero. -/
/-! ## The annihilation relation -/
/-- `annihilates v w` is `true` when `v * w = 0`. -/
/-- The cross-octet vectors that annihilate some non-zero cross-octet vector. -/
/-- The cross-octet vectors that annihilate no non-zero cross-octet vector. -/

/-- **Index criterion.** A cross-octet vector `s • eᵢ + t • e₈₊ⱼ` annihilates some
non-zero cross-octet vector iff `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0` and `i ≠ j`; the signs are irrelevant. -/
/-- The index criterion, spelled out for explicit indices and signs. -/
/-- Exactly 168 of the 256 cross-octet vectors are zero divisors. -/

/-- Exactly 88 of the 256 cross-octet vectors are not zero divisors (within the
cross-octet family; see `Sovereign.Algebra.SedenionNonZeroDivisors` for the full algebra). -/
/-- The stratification `256 = 168 + 88` for the *actual* sedenion vectors. -/
-- The two theorems that compared these lengths with the numerals `(D-2)(D-4)` and
-- `6D - 8` at `D = 16` were removed: `Sovereign.Algebra.CrossHalfUniversal` proves the
-- counts for every `D = 2^n` (`zdVerts_card_universal`, `nonZD_card_universal`) and
-- bridges them to the concrete sedenion lists (`zdVerts_eq_crossOctetZD_card`).
/-! ## Regularity and edge count of the annihilation graph -/
/-- Number of cross-octet zero divisors annihilated by `v`. -/
/-- The annihilation graph is 8-regular. -/
/-- Annihilation is symmetric on cross-octet vectors: `v * w = 0 ↔ w * v = 0`. -/
/-- No cross-octet vector annihilates itself, so the annihilation graph is loopless. -/
/-- The 1344 directed annihilating pairs, i.e. 672 undirected edges. -/
/-- The annihilation graph has 672 undirected edges. -/
/-! ## XOR charge conservation and the seven sectors -/

/-- **Charge conservation.** If two cross-octet vectors annihilate each other then their
XOR charges `i ^^^ j` agree. -/
/-- The zero-divisor labels of XOR charge `c`. -/

/-- Every zero divisor carries a non-zero charge, and each of the seven non-zero charges
carries exactly 24 of the 168 zero divisors. -/
/-- Charge `0` contains no zero divisor, and charges `≥ 8` do not occur. -/
/-- The seven sectors exhaust the 168 zero divisors: `7 * 24 = 168`. -/

/-- All `D² = 4 · (D/2)²` sign-decorated cross-half labels of `Tower (N+1)`. -/
/-- The vertices of the zero-divisor graph. -/
/-- The annihilation graph restricted to the cross-half zero divisors. -/

/-- A walk of the full annihilation graph starting at a zero divisor stays among the zero
divisors, hence is a walk of `zdGraph`. -/

/-- **Components = charge sectors.** Two cross-half zero divisors are joined by a path of
annihilations iff they carry the same XOR charge. -/
/-! ## 3. The components -/
/-- The XOR charge of a component. -/

/-- **Component count.** In dimension `D = 2ᴺ⁺¹ ≥ 16` the annihilation graph of the
cross-half zero divisors has exactly `D/2 - 1 = 2ᴺ - 1` connected components. -/
/-- **Projective count.** The components are counted by `|PG(N-1, 𝔽₂)|`. -/
/-- **Component size.** Every component has exactly `2(D - 4)` vertices. -/
/-! ## 4. Asymptotics -/

/-- The fraction of cross-half basis vectors `± eᵢ ± e_{D/2+j}` of `Tower (N+1)` that are
zero divisors. -/
/-- Explicit bounds `1 - 6/D < fraction < 1`, `D = 2ᴺ⁺¹`. -/

/-- **Asymptotic density.** The fraction of cross-half basis vectors that are zero divisors
tends to `1` along the Cayley–Dickson tower. -/
/-- The component count `2ᴺ - 1` is asymptotic to `2ᴺ = D/2`. -/

/-- **Asymptotic theorem for the Cayley–Dickson tower.**  Along the tower `D = 2ⁿ`
(`n ≥ 4`, written `n = N + 1`), the cross-half zero divisors number `(D - 2)(D - 4)`, they
form `2ⁿ⁻¹ - 1 = |PG(n-2, 𝔽₂)|` components of `2(D - 4)` vertices each; their fraction among
all `D²` cross-half basis vectors tends to `1`, and the component count is asymptotic to
`2ⁿ⁻¹`. -/
/-! ## 5. The 64-dimensional case -/

/-- **3720 cross-half zero divisors in `𝕊₆₄`.**  Level `N = 5` of the tower is
`Tower 6 = CDSexagintaquattuorion`. -/
/-- **31 components.** -/
/-- The 31 components are counted by the points of `PG(4, 𝔽₂) = ℙ(𝔽₂⁵)`. -/

/-- The same count in the formulation of `CrossHalfZeroDivisorTheorem` (components of the full
annihilation graph that contain a zero divisor). -/
/-- **Each component has 120 vertices**, and `31 · 120 = 3720`. -/

comments.text: /-! ## 1. The two shift laws of the sign function -/
/-- **Left shift law.** `ε(a,b) ⊕ ε(a, a ⊕ b) = [a ≠ 0]`. -/
/-- **Right shift law.** `ε(a,b) ⊕ ε(a ⊕ b, b) = [b ≠ 0]`. -/
/-! ## 2. Alternativity on basis vectors -/
/-- **Left alternative law on basis vectors**, in every dimension. -/
/-- **Right alternative law on basis vectors**, in every dimension. -/
/-- The triple `(e_a, e_b, e_{a ⊕ b})` always associates. -/
/-! ## 3. Two-generated index subgroups span associative subalgebras -/
/-- The index subgroup generated by `a` and `b`. -/

/-- The associator sign vanishes on any triple of indices lying in the subgroup generated
by two indices: **every two-generated index subgroup spans an associative (quaternionic)
subalgebra**, in every dimension of the tower. -/
-- `assocNeg n u v w = false` whenever `w = u ^^^ v`

/-- The algebraic form: the `2`-dimensional index subgroup `{0, a, b, a ⊕ b}` spans a
`4`-dimensional associative subalgebra. -/
/-! ## 4. A universal degree bound for the annihilation graph -/
/-- The four middles `0, i, j, i ⊕ j` always associate with `(e_i, ·, e_j)`. -/
/-- The four associating middles are pairwise distinct once `i ≠ j` are non-zero. -/

/-- **Universal degree bound.** For distinct non-real indices `i ≠ j` at most `2ⁿ - 4`
middles `k` fail to associate, so in dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹` a cross-half zero divisor has at
most `D - 8` annihilation partners inside its charge sector. -/

/-- The same bound in the annihilation language of `TowerZeroDivisors`: with the charge
`i ⊕ j` fixed, at most `2ⁿ - 4` of the `2ⁿ` admissible partner indices `k` can annihilate
the cross-half vector with index data `(i, j)`.  In dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹` this caps the
degree of every vertex of the annihilation graph inside its charge sector at `D - 8`. -/

comments.text: /-! ## 1. Upper Associating Middles Definition -/

/-- The set of associating middles in the upper half `[2^m, 2^(m+1))` for an inherited pair `(i, j)`:
    shifted so that `k < 2^m` represents the upper middle `2^m + k`. -/
/-- The upper half filter partition on `range (2^m)` for `assocNeg (m+1) i (2^m + k) j`. -/
/-! ## 2. The Upper Associating Middles Cardinality Formula -/

/-- For an inherited admissible pair `i, j < 2^m`, the upper non-associating middles
    have cardinality `(nonassocMiddles m i j).card + 4`. -/

/-- **The Upper Associating Middles Cardinality Formula.**
    The number of associating middles in the new half `[2^m, 2^(m+1))` is
    strictly governed by the degree deficiency at level `m`:
    `|assocMiddlesUpper m i j| = (2^m - 4) - |nonassocMiddles m i j|`. -/
/-! ## 3. Confinement Criterion: Vanishing Upper Associating Middles -/

/-- **Subalgebra Confinement Criterion.**
    The associating middles of an admissible pair `i, j < 2^m` remain strictly confined
    to the subalgebra `A_m` in `A_(m+1)` (meaning no associating middles exist in the upper half)
    if and only if the pair has maximal degree `2^m - 4` in `A_m`. -/
/-- Equivalently, the upper associating set is empty iff the level `m` degree is maximal. -/
/-! ## 4. Classification of Confinement for Cross-Half Pairs (Item 5) -/

/-- **Cross-Half Confinement Classification.**
    For a cross-half pair `(i, 2^m + c)` at level `m+1` with `i, c < 2^m` and `m ≥ 3`,
    the associating middles in `A_(m+2)` are strictly confined to `A_(m+1)`
    if and only if the pair is degenerate (`c = 0` or `c = i`). -/

/-- **Confinement Failure for Non-Degenerate Cross-Half Pairs.**
    Confinement strictly fails (associating middles escape into the upper half)
    if and only if `c ≠ 0 ∧ c ≠ i`. -/
/-! ## 5. Universal Octonionic Confinement Across the Tower -/

/-- Every admissible pair in the octonions `i, j < 8` has maximal degree `2ⁿ - 4`
    in every dimension `2ⁿ` for all `n ≥ 3`. -/

/-- **Universal Octonionic Confinement Theorem.**
    For every admissible octonionic pair `1 ≤ i ≠ j < 8`, in ANY dimension `2ⁿ` (`n ≥ 3`),
    the set of associating middles is EXACTLY the 4-element quaternion subalgebra `spanSet i j`:
    `assocMiddles n i j = spanSet i j`. -/
/-! ## 6. Persistence of Confinement Across the Infinite Tower -/

/-- **Persistence of Confinement.**
    If an admissible pair `i, j < 2^m` is confined to `A_m` at the first doubling step
    `A_m ↪ A_(m+1)` (meaning its degree in `A_m` is maximal: `2^m - 4`), then it remains
    maximal in `A_n` for all `n ≥ m`. Consequently, no new associating middles ever appear
    at any higher level of the Cayley–Dickson tower. -/

comments.text: /-! ## 0. Boolean helpers -/
/-! ## 1. Reduction lemmas for the sign function at a doubling step -/
/-! ## 2. The two structural laws of the sign function -/

/-- **Commutation law (total form).** `e_a e_b = -e_b e_a` exactly for distinct non-real
basis vectors, and `e_a e_b = e_b e_a` in every other case. -/

/-- **Cyclic law (total form).** For a "quaternionic triple" `a, b, a ^^^ b` of distinct
non-real indices the two products `e_a e_b` and `e_b e_{a ^^^ b}` carry the same sign. -/
-- low, low
-- low, high
-- high, low
-- high, high
/-! ## 3. The associator sign -/

/-- The sign of the associator of three basis vectors: `assocNeg n a b c = true` exactly
when `(e_a e_b) e_c = -(e_a (e_b e_c))`. -/
/-- The tower has no 2-torsion, so a non-zero element is never equal to its negative. -/
/-- The triple `(e_a, e_b, e_c)` associates iff its associator sign vanishes. -/
/-! ## 4. The annihilation condition and its associator form -/

/-- The combinatorial annihilation condition extracted from `crossVec_mul_eq_zero_iff`:
the pair of cross-half vectors with index data `(i,j)` and `(k,m)` admits a choice of signs
making the product vanish exactly when `crossSign n i j k m = true`. -/
/-- The Boolean bookkeeping behind `crossSign_eq_assocNeg`. -/
/-- The degeneracy bookkeeping behind `crossSign_eq_assocNeg`. -/

/-- **Zero divisors are non-associativity.**  With `m = k ^^^ i ^^^ j` (forced by charge
conservation) the annihilation condition for `(i,j)` against `(k,m)` is exactly the
statement that `e_i, e_k, e_j` fail to associate. -/

/-- The associator of `(e_a, e_b, e_a)` always vanishes: a corollary of the identification
of associators with annihilation conditions. -/
/-- **Flexibility.** Every algebra of the tower is flexible on basis vectors. -/
/-! ## 5. Existence of a non-associative partner -/
/-- The auxiliary low index used as a witness: an index in `{1,2}` different from `x`. -/

/-! ### The nine cases of the witness construction

With `H = 2 ^ q` the last doubling step splits the index range into a low half `< H` and a
high half `H + ·`.  In most cases the new imaginary unit `e_H` itself is a witness; in the
degenerate configurations a low (or high) index in `{1,2}` is used instead. -/

/-- **Existence of a non-associative triple.** In every algebra of the tower of dimension
`2ⁿ ≥ 8` (octonions and beyond) any two distinct non-real basis vectors fail to associate
with some third basis vector. -/
/-! ## 6. The general index criterion -/

/-- For a fixed pair of index data, a choice of signs making the two cross-half vectors
annihilate exists exactly when `crossSign` holds. -/

/-- **The index criterion in every dimension.**  For every `n ≥ 3`, i.e. in every
Cayley–Dickson algebra of dimension `2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16`, a cross-half vector `±e_i ± e_{H+j}`
annihilates another cross-half vector exactly when `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0` and `i ≠ j`. -/
/-- Algebraic form of the general index criterion. -/

/-- **Characterisation of non-associative pairs.**  In every algebra of the tower of
dimension `2ⁿ ≥ 8`, two basis vectors fail to associate with a third one exactly when they
are distinct and non-real. -/

/-- **Cross-half zero divisors are exactly the non-associative pairs.**  For `n ≥ 3` the
cross-half vector `±e_i ± e_{H+j}` of the `2ⁿ⁺¹`-dimensional algebra annihilates a non-zero
cross-half vector if and only if `e_i` and `e_j` fail to associate with some `e_k`. -/

/-- **Zero divisors exist in every dimension `2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16`.**  The cross-half vector
`e₁ + e_{H+2}` annihilates a non-zero cross-half vector. -/
/-- Every algebra of the tower of dimension `2ⁿ ≥ 8` is non-associative. -/

/-! ## 7. The finite checks as instances of the general theorem

The dimension-by-dimension index criteria of `TowerZeroDivisors` were closed by compiler
evaluation; they are instances of `index_criterion_general`, and the versions below are
therefore checked by the kernel alone. -/

/-- **Left-shift invariance of the associator sign.**
Translating the middle index `k` by `i` preserves the associator sign `assocNeg n i k j`:
`assocNeg n i (k ^^^ i) j = assocNeg n i k j`. -/

/-- **Right-shift invariance of the associator sign.**
Translating the middle index `k` by `j` preserves the associator sign `assocNeg n i k j`:
`assocNeg n i (k ^^^ j) j = assocNeg n i k j`. -/

/-- **XOR-shift invariance of the associator sign.**
Translating the middle index `k` by `i ⊕ j` preserves the associator sign:
`assocNeg n i (k ^^^ (i ^^^ j)) j = assocNeg n i k j`. -/

/-- **Universal Coset Translation Invariance Theorem.**
The associator sign `assocNeg n i (k ^^^ s) j` is identical to `assocNeg n i k j`
for any index `s` in the 2-dimensional subspace `span(i, j) = {0, i, j, i ⊕ j}`. -/
/-- **Associating middles are closed under translation by `span(i, j)`.** -/
/-- **Non-associating middles are closed under translation by `span(i, j)`.** -/

def epsNeg : (n : Nat) → Nat → Nat → Bool
  | 0, _, _ => false
  | n + 1, a, b =>
    if a < 2 ^ n then

      else epsNeg n (b - 2 ^ n) a
    else

/-- The two conjugation laws of the tower, proved simultaneously by induction on the
level: conjugation is an involution and an anti-automorphism. -/

/-- The associator `[x, y, z] = (x y) z - x (y z)`. -/

/-- **Reversal law for the associator.** Conjugating an associator reverses the triple
and flips the sign: `conj [x, y, z] = -[conj z, conj y, conj x]`. -/
/-- A triple associates exactly when the reversed triple of conjugates associates. -/
/-- **Reversal invariance of the associator sign**, in every dimension. -/
/-- The algebraic form of reversal invariance on basis vectors. -/

/-! ## 4. The Mac Lane pentagon: the associator sign is a 3-cocycle -/

/-- The Boolean skeleton of the pentagon identity: the ten sign values that occur in the
five associator signs cancel in pairs. -/

indices, the coboundary of the associator sign vanishes:

/-- The associator phase `(-1)^assocNeg`: `+1` when the triple associates, `-1` otherwise. -/

/-- **Multiplicative pentagon identity** for the `±1` associator phase: the five phases of
a Mac Lane pentagon multiply to `+1`, in every dimension and for every quadruple. -/
/-- Reversal invariance of the phase. -/
/-! ## 6. Sedenion (level 4) instances -/
/-- The sedenion triple `(e₁, e₂, e₄)` does not associate. -/

# Resolution of Flexibility Beyond Basis Vectors (OP-007, HYP-114)

This module formalizes the affirmative resolution of Open Problem OP-007:
"Is every Cayley–Dickson algebra of the tower flexible on *all* elements, not just basis vectors?"

## Mathematical Framework:
1. An algebra A is flexible if for all x, y ∈ A:
   (x · y) · x = x · (y · x), or equivalently [x, y, x] = 0.
2. In `TowerAssociator.lean`, `basis_flexible` proves that every algebra of the tower
   is flexible on basis vectors: (e_a · e_b) · e_a = e_a · (e_b · e_a).

   invariance of the associator:

   assocNeg n a b c = assocNeg n c b a.

/-- The nucleus is closed under multiplication. -/
/-- Elements of the nucleus associate with each other (in fact with everything). -/
/-! ## 4. The Lie ring structure -/
/-- The nucleus as a type. -/
/-- **The nucleus is a Lie ring** under the commutator bracket. -/
/-- Hence the nucleus is a Lie algebra over `ℤ`. -/
/-! ## 5. Invariance under automorphisms and derivations -/
/-- A ring automorphism of `Tower n` maps the nucleus into itself. -/
/-- **The nucleus is invariant:** `φ z ∈ N ↔ z ∈ N` for every ring automorphism `φ`. -/
/-- The nucleus is mapped onto itself by every automorphism. -/
/-- The restriction of an automorphism to the nucleus, as a Lie algebra automorphism. -/

/-- **Invariance under derivations:** an additive map `D` with `D(xy) = D(x)y + xD(y)` maps the
nucleus into itself. -/
/-! ## 6. The associator kernel of a fixed pair -/
/-- The associator kernel of `x, y`: all `z` with `[x, y, z] = (xy)z - x(yz) = 0`. -/
/-- Automorphisms move associator kernels equivariantly: `φ z ∈ K(φ x, φ y) ↔ z ∈ K(x, y)`. -/
/-- The nucleus is contained in every associator kernel. -/

/-- The coordinate functional of the associator `[eₐ, e_k, z]`. -/

# The 32-dimensional level: trigintaduonion cross-half stratification

The same analysis one level up the Cayley–Dickson tower, for
`CDTrig = CD CDSedenion` (dimension 32).  The cross-half vectors are
`s • eᵢ + t • e₁₆₊ⱼ` with `i, j < 16`, `s, t ∈ {1, -1}`; there are `32 * 32 = 1024` of them.

Proved below by exact evaluation:

* `zd32_iff_index` — such a vector annihilates a cross-half partner iff `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0`
  and `i ≠ j`, exactly as in dimension 16;
* `zd32_card`, `nonZd32_card` — there are `840 = (32-2)(32-4)` zero divisors and
  `184 = 6·32-8` non-zero-divisors, matching the monograph's universal formulas;
* `xorCharge32_conserved`, `sector32_card` — annihilation conserves the XOR charge
  `χ = i ^^^ j`, and the 15 non-zero charges each carry `56 = 2(32-4)` zero divisors,
  matching `|PG(3, 2)| = 15`;
* `sector32_regular_part` — the eight sectors `χ ≤ 8` (the Fano hyperplane `χ ≤ 7` together
  with the doubling pole `χ = 8`) are 24-regular with 672 edges each;
* `sector32_biregular_part` — the seven sectors `χ ≥ 9` (the affine complement) have
  degrees in `{8, 24}` and 288 edges each;
* `edges32_total` — `8 * 672 + 7 * 288 = 7392` undirected edges in total.

Caveat: unlike in dimension 16, the 184 non-zero-divisors are here only shown to
annihilate no *cross-half* vector; the corresponding statement for the whole 32-dimensional
algebra is not formalised.
-/

/-- Basis vectors `e₀, …, e₃₁` of the trigintaduonions. -/
/-- Integer scaling of a trigintaduonion. -/
/-- The cross-half vector `s • eᵢ + t • e₁₆₊ⱼ`. -/

# The zero-divisor key exchange one level up: the trigintaduonions `T₃₂`

The sedenion protocol of `Sovereign.Graph.ZeroDivisorKeyExchange` transported to the
integer trigintaduonions `CDTrig`.

* `centralBasisCounts` — for the annihilating pairs `a b = 0` among the 840 cross-half zero
  divisors, the number of basis vectors `e_c` with `(a e_c) b = a (e_c b)` takes exactly the
  values `4, 6, 12, 20`. So in `T₃₂` the associator centralizer of an annihilating pair is
  *not* uniformly 4-dimensional (it contains 20 independent basis vectors for some pairs).
* For the pair `a = e₁ + e₁₈`, `b = e₄ - e₂₃` and the base `g = e₅`:
  `t32_annih` (`a b = 0`), `t32_spow_mem` (every public word `gⁿ` satisfies
  `(a gⁿ) b = a (gⁿ b)`), `t32_keyExchange_correct` (both parties get the same key),
  `t32_exactPeriod` (the public-key map has exact period 4) and `t32_shor_sampling`
  (Shor's sampling step returns the multiples of `N/4`, each with probability `1/4`).

All finite facts are checked by evaluation (`native_decide`) against the integer
trigintaduonion multiplication, as elsewhere in this development.
-/
/-- The trigintaduonion product (a plain function, convenient for evaluation). -/
/-- `(x y) z = x (y z)`, as a Boolean. -/
/-- All annihilating pairs of cross-half zero divisors. -/
/-- The indices `c` such that `e_c` lies in the associator centralizer of `(a, b)`. -/

/-- The numbers of centralizing basis vectors over all annihilating pairs are exactly
`12, 4, 20, 6` (listed in order of first occurrence). -/
/-! ## A concrete key exchange in `T₃₂` -/
/-- The base `g = e₅`. -/
/-- Left-nested powers: `g⁰ = 1`, `gⁿ⁺¹ = g · gⁿ`. -/
/-- Every public word lies in the associator centralizer `{x | (a x) b = a (x b)}`. -/
/-- **Correctness of the key exchange in `T₃₂`.** -/
/-- The public-key map `x ↦ gˣ` has exact period `4`. -/

/-- **Shor's sampling step on the `T₃₂` instance**: for `N = 4 M` the QFT outcome `k` has
probability `1/4` if `M ∣ k` and `0` otherwise. -/

comments.text: /-! ### The charge map and `PG(3, 2)` -/
/-- The XOR charge `χ = i ^^^ j` of a cross-half label: a vector of `𝔽₂⁴`. -/
/-- The 15 points of `PG(3, 2)`, encoded as the non-zero vectors `1, …, 15` of `𝔽₂⁴`. -/
/-- The Fano plane `PG(2, 2) ⊂ PG(3, 2)`: the points with bit 3 equal to `0`. -/
/-- The doubling pole: the charge `8 = 2³` introduced by the last Cayley–Dickson doubling. -/
/-- The affine complement: the 7 points `8 ^^^ f`, `f` in the Fano plane. -/

/-- The Fano points form a projective plane inside `PG(3, 2)`: the hyperplane `bit 3 = 0`,
closed under the line operation `a, b ↦ a ^^^ b`. -/
/-- The affine complement is the translate of the Fano plane by the doubling pole. -/
/-! ### The partition of the 840 zero divisors -/
/-- The 840 zero-divisor labels are pairwise distinct. -/
/-- Every zero divisor carries a charge in `PG(3, 2)`. -/
/-- The sector of charge `c` is `sector32 c`. -/

/-- **Partition theorem.**  The 840 cross-half zero divisors of `T₃₂` are the disjoint
union of the 15 charge sectors, each of size 56; the Fano plane carries `7 · 56 = 392`,
the doubling pole `56`, and the affine complement `7 · 56 = 392` of them. -/
/-! ### The annihilation graph -/
/-- The vertex type: the 840 zero-divisor labels. -/
/-- Annihilation is symmetric inside each charge sector. -/
/-- No zero divisor annihilates itself. -/
/-- Annihilation conserves the charge. -/

/-- The annihilation graph on the 840 cross-half zero divisors of `T₃₂`:
`p ~ q` iff `vec32 p * vec32 q = 0`. -/
/-! ### Connectivity inside a sector -/
/-- A base point of each sector. -/
/-- Breadth-first search in the sector `S` from a frontier: records `(vertex, parent, depth)`. -/
/-- The breadth-first search tree of the sector `c`. -/
/-- The breadth-first search trees of all 15 sectors (a constant, computed once). -/
/-- Parent and depth of a vertex in its breadth-first search tree. -/
/-- The base points are zero divisors of the right charge. -/

/-- Certificate of connectivity: every zero divisor is either the base point of its sector
(depth `0`) or annihilates a zero divisor of strictly smaller depth. -/
/-- Every zero divisor is connected to the base point of its sector. -/
/-- Walks in the annihilation graph conserve the charge. -/

/-- **Components = charges.**  Two cross-half zero divisors of `T₃₂` are joined by a path of
annihilations iff they carry the same `PG(3, 2)` charge. -/
/-! ### The 15 components -/
/-- The charge of a connected component (well defined by `charge_eq_of_reachable`). -/

/-- The connected components of the annihilation graph are in bijection with the 15 points
of `PG(3, 2)`. -/

/-- **The annihilation graph of the 840 cross-half zero divisors of `T₃₂` has exactly
`|PG(3, 2)| = 15` connected components.** -/

/-- **`15 = 7 + 1 + 7`.**  Of the 15 components, 7 lie over the Fano plane, exactly one over
the doubling pole, and 7 over the affine complement. -/
/-- Each component is exactly one charge sector of 56 zero divisors. -/

# The doubling-pole component of the `T₃₂` annihilation graph is Ramanujan

`Sovereign.Algebra.TrigintaduonionPG32` shows that the annihilation graph of the 840
cross-half zero divisors of the trigintaduonions has 15 components, one per point of
`PG(3, 2)`: 7 over the Fano plane, the doubling pole `χ = 8`, and 7 over the affine
complement.  Here each component is realised as a graph `sectorGraph c` on `Fin 56`
(`sectorEmb` embeds it into the annihilation graph with image exactly the charge-`c`
component) and its adjacency spectrum is analysed.

Main results, for the **doubling pole** `poleGraph = sectorGraph 8`:

* `poleGraph_isRegular`, `poleGraph_connected` — it is a connected 24-regular graph;
* `poleGraph_eigenvalues`, `poleGraph_hasEigenvalue_iff` — its real adjacency spectrum is
  exactly `{24, 4, 0, -4, -24}` (the minimal polynomial is `x(x² - 16)(x² - 576)`);
* `poleGraph_eigenvector_24`, `poleGraph_eigenvector_neg24` — the eigenvalues `±24` are
  simple (constants, resp. the bipartition sign vector), so the graph is bipartite
  and connected spectrally as well;
* `poleGraph_isRamanujan` — it is a **Ramanujan graph**: every non-trivial eigenvalue
  satisfies `|μ| ≤ 4 ≤ 2√23 = 2√(d - 1)`;
* `poleGraph_spectral_gap` — the second largest eigenvalue is exactly `4`, so the spectral
  gap is `24 - 4 = 20`, strictly larger than the Ramanujan gap `24 - 2√23`.

have the non-trivial eigenvalue `12 > 2√23` and are **not** Ramanujan, and the 7 affine
components (`affineSector_not_regular`) are not even regular.  So among the 15 components
the Ramanujan property is carried by the doubling pole.

All finite facts are checked by exact integer evaluation (`native_decide`), starting from
the actual trigintaduonion multiplication.

# Universal Index Geometry Decoupling Theorem in Lean 4

Formal verification of HYP-022:
In any Cayley-Dickson algebra of dimension D = 2ⁿ (n ≥ 4),
for cross-half zero-divisor vectors:
  v₁ = s₁ e_i + s₂ e_{H+j}  with charge χ(v₁) = i ^^^ j
  v₂ = t₁ e_k + t₂ e_{H+m}  with charge χ(v₂) = k ^^^ m

The 4 product terms have basis indices:
  k₀ = i ^^^ k
  k₁ = i ^^^ m
  k₂ = j ^^^ k
  k₃ = j ^^^ m

1. Both low and high components cancel IF AND ONLY IF χ(v₁) = χ(v₂).
2. When χ(v₁) = χ(v₂) = χ ≠ 0, identically k₀ = k₃ and k₁ = k₂.
3. Furthermore, k₀ ≠ k₁ whenever χ ≠ 0, completely forbidding cross-pair collisions.
4. Hence, cancellation decomposes into two independent 2-term sign cancellations:
   s₀ + s₃ = 0  and  s₁ + s₂ = 0.
-/
/-- Swapping outer and inner indices in a 4-term XOR equality. -/
/-- High-half index exchange. -/

/-- **Universal Index Geometry Decoupling Theorem (Part 1: Charge Conservation)**:
    Low and high cross-half products cancel if and only if XOR charges are equal. -/

/-- **Universal Index Geometry Decoupling Theorem (Part 2: Low-Term Decoupling)**:
    When XOR charges match, the outer basis index k₀ = i ^^^ k equals k₃ = j ^^^ m. -/

/-- **Universal Index Geometry Decoupling Theorem (Part 3: High-Term Decoupling)**:
    When XOR charges match, the inner basis index k₁ = i ^^^ m equals k₂ = j ^^^ k. -/
/-- Cancellation of XOR on the left: i ^^^ k = i ^^^ m ↔ k = m. -/

/-- **Universal Index Geometry Decoupling Theorem (Part 4: Disjointness of Pairs)**:
    Whenever the conserved charge χ = k ^^^ m is non-zero, k₀ ≠ k₁, preventing cross-pair interference. -/

/-!
# Approximate homomorphisms: how far chunking can diverge

`Sovereign.HomDecomp.hom_flatten` (and `QBX.Formal.TextManifold.mapReduce`) say that an *exact*
homomorphism can be evaluated chunk by chunk with no error.  Many statistics one would like to
chunk are not homomorphisms (Garside normal forms, Jones-type invariants, window statistics
computed without a collar, floating-point summaries).  This file measures the damage: if the
statistic fails to be multiplicative by at most `ε` on every pair, then evaluating it on `n`
chunks and recombining is off by at most `(n - 1) ε`, and this bound cannot be improved.

## Main results

Additive statistics (values in a normed group `E`; "combine" means add):

* `IsApproxAdd ε f` — `‖f (a ++ b) - (f a + f b)‖ ≤ ε` for all texts `a`, `b`.
* `approxAdd_chunks` — **divergence bound**: for a text cut into `n ≥ 1` chunks `c₁, …, cₙ`,
  `‖f (c₁ ++ ⋯ ++ cₙ) - (f c₁ + ⋯ + f cₙ)‖ ≤ (n - 1) ε`.  (For `n = 0` the error is
  `‖f []‖ ≤ ε`, `IsApproxAdd.norm_nil`.)
* `approxAdd_chunks_sharp` — the bound `(n - 1) ε` is attained, for every `n ≥ 1` and `ε ≥ 0`.
* `exact_of_approxAdd_zero` — with `ε = 0` the chunk sum is exact (the map–reduce law).

Multiplicative statistics (values in a normed ring, e.g. matrices; "combine" means multiply):

* `approxMul_prod` — if `‖f (a b) - f a f b‖ ≤ ε` for all `a b` and `f` is contractive
  (`‖f a‖ ≤ 1`, e.g. unitary representations), then for `n ≥ 1` chunks
  `‖f (a₁ ⋯ aₙ) - f a₁ ⋯ f aₙ‖ ≤ (n - 1) ε`.
* `approxMul_prod_bounded` — without contractivity, if `‖f a‖ ≤ K` then the error is at most
  `ε (1 + K + ⋯ + K^(n-2))`.

The proofs are the standard telescoping argument.
-/
/-! ### Additive statistics on texts -/
/-- `f` is additive on texts up to error `ε`. -/
/-- The empty text has statistic of size at most `ε`. -/

/-- **Divergence bound.**  A text cut into `n ≥ 1` chunks: chunk-wise evaluation of an
`ε`-approximately additive statistic is off by at most `(n - 1) ε`. -/

/-- **Exactness.**  With `ε = 0` the statistic is additive and chunking is exact: the
map–reduce law. -/

/-- **The bound is sharp.**  For every `ε ≥ 0` there is an `ε`-approximately additive real
statistic (the constant `-ε`) for which `n ≥ 1` chunks diverge by exactly `(n - 1) ε`. -/
/-! ### Multiplicative statistics (normed rings) -/

/-- **Bounded case.**  If `‖f (a b) - f a f b‖ ≤ ε` and `‖f a‖ ≤ K` for all `a`, `b`, then for a
nonempty list `a :: l` of chunks the error of the chunk-wise product is at most
`ε (1 + K + ⋯ + K^(|l| - 1))`. -/

/-- **Divergence bound for contractive channels.**  If `‖f (a b) - f a f b‖ ≤ ε` and
`‖f a‖ ≤ 1` for all `a`, `b` (e.g. a unitary representation perturbed by rounding), then the
chunk-wise product over `n ≥ 1` chunks is off by at most `(n - 1) ε`. -/
