/-!
# Majorana operators, Dirac fermions and quadratic Hamiltonians

A *Majorana system* indexed by a finite type `ι` inside a complex `*`-algebra `A` is a family of
self-adjoint operators `γ i` satisfying the Clifford (Majorana) relations
`{γ i, γ j} = γ i γ j + γ j γ i = 2 δ_{ij}`.

* `MajoranaSystem.mode v = ∑ v p • γ p` is the Majorana operator of a coefficient vector `v`;
  `{mode v, mode w} = 2 ∑ v p w p`, so a real unit vector gives again a Majorana operator.
* For Majoranas indexed by `σ × Fin 2` (site `j`, and the two Majoranas `γ (j,0)`, `γ (j,1)` of the
  site, which in the usual `1`-based numbering are `γ_{2j-1}` and `γ_{2j}`), the Dirac fermion is
  `c j = (γ (j,0) + i γ (j,1)) / 2`.  We prove the canonical anticommutation relations
  `{c j, c k} = 0`, `{c j, c k†} = δ_{jk}`, and the inverse decomposition
  `γ (j,0) = c j + c j†`, `γ (j,1) = -i (c j - c j†)`.
* `quadHam M = (i/4) ∑ M p q γ p γ q` is the general quadratic (BdG) Hamiltonian written in the
  Majorana basis.  The key identity is `[quadHam M, mode v] = mode (i M v)` for antisymmetric
  `M`: single-particle modes evolve by the matrix `i M`, and a zero mode (`M v = 0`) commutes
  with the Hamiltonian, i.e. it is a Majorana zero mode at energy `ε = 0`.
-/

/-- The coefficient vector of `c j`. -/
/-- Canonical anticommutation relation `{c j, c k} = 0`. -/
/-- Canonical anticommutation relation `{c j, c k†} = δ_{jk}`. -/
/-- Inverse decomposition: `γ (j,0) = c j + c j†`. -/
/-- Inverse decomposition: `γ (j,1) = -i (c j - c j†)`. -/
/-- The occupation number `c j† c j = (1 + i γ (j,0) γ (j,1)) / 2`. -/
/-! ### Quadratic Hamiltonians -/
/-- The quadratic Hamiltonian `(i/4) ∑ M p q γ p γ q` associated with a matrix `M`. -/
/-- The elementary antisymmetric matrix `E_{pq} - E_{qp}`. -/
/-- For `p ≠ q`, `quadHam (E_{pq} - E_{qp}) = (i/2) γ p γ q`. -/
/-- `[γ p γ q, γ r] = 2 δ_{qr} γ p - 2 δ_{pr} γ q`. -/
/-- `[γ p γ q, mode v] = 2 v q γ p - 2 v p γ q`. -/

/-- The commutator of a quadratic Hamiltonian with a mode:
`[quadHam M, mode v] = mode ((i/2) (M v - Mᵀ v))`. -/
/-- For an antisymmetric `M`, `[quadHam M, mode v] = mode (i M v)`. -/

/-- **Zero modes commute with the Hamiltonian.**  If `M` is antisymmetric and `M v = 0`, then the
mode `mode v` commutes with `quadHam M`: it is a zero-energy mode. -/

# The braid gate as an exponential

In a complex Banach algebra, if `J² = -1` then `exp(θ J) = cos θ + sin θ J`.  Hence the braid
gate `B_{ij} = (1 + γ_i γ_j)/√2` is the exponential `exp(π/4 · γ_i γ_j)`, and the protocol

comments.text:
/-!
# Braiding Majorana zero modes: the Clifford phase gate `exp(π/4 γ_i γ_j)`

For two Majorana operators `γ_i`, `γ_j` (`i ≠ j`), `J = γ_i γ_j` satisfies `J² = -1`, so

  `B_{ij} = exp(π/4 · γ_i γ_j) = cos(π/4) + sin(π/4) γ_i γ_j = (1 + γ_i γ_j) / √2`

(`braidGate`; the exponential identity is `braidGate_eq_exp` in any complex Banach algebra).
`B_{ij}` is unitary and acts on the Majoranas by the exchange
`γ_j ↦ γ_i`, `γ_i ↦ -γ_j`, fixing all other `γ_k`: it maps Majorana operators to Majorana
operators (a Clifford operation), and `B_{ij}² = γ_i γ_j`, `B_{ij}⁸ = 1`.

## Trijunction (T-junction) braiding protocol

A trijunction consists of a central Majorana `γ_0` and three arm Majoranas `γ_1, γ_2, γ_3`
(end points of three topological wire segments meeting at the junction).  The Hamiltonian
`H_k = i γ_0 γ_k` couples the centre to arm `k`; the two uncoupled arm Majoranas are zero modes
spanning the degenerate ground space.  Starting from `H_3` (zero modes `γ_1`, `γ_2`), the
coupling is rotated `3 → 1 → 2 → 3`:

* along step `old → new` the Hamiltonian is `H(θ) = i γ_0 (cos θ γ_old + sin θ γ_new)`,
  `0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2`, and `H(θ) = R(θ) H_old R(θ)†` with the rotation
  `R(θ) = exp(θ/2 · γ_new γ_old)` (`pathHam_eq_conj`);  the zero mode
  `cos θ γ_new - sin θ γ_old` is transported continuously (`commute_pathHam_zeroMode`);
* at the end of the step the transport unitary is `R(π/2) = B_{new,old}`
  (`rot_pi_div_two`) and maps `H_old` to `H_new` (`braidGate_conj_trijunctionHam`).

The composite of the three steps is **exactly** the braid gate of the two zero modes
(`trijunction_exchange`):

  `B_{32} B_{21} B_{13} = B_{21} = exp(π/4 γ_2 γ_1)`,

which commutes with `H_3` (so it acts on the degenerate ground space) and exchanges the two
Majorana zero modes: `γ_1 ↦ γ_2`, `γ_2 ↦ -γ_1`.

## Non-abelian (Ising-type) braid group representation

For Majoranas `γ_0, …, γ_{n-1}` in a line, `σ_k ↦ B_{k+1,k}` satisfies the braid relations and
defines `majoranaBraidRep : B_n →* Aˣ`, which is non-abelian for `n ≥ 3`
(`majoranaBraidRep_isNonAbelian`).

We do not formalize the adiabatic theorem: the transport unitary of a step is the rotation
`R(θ)` generating the Hamiltonian path.
-/
/-- `1/√2` as a complex number. -/
/-! ### Majorana word manipulations -/
/-- `γ_k` commutes with `γ_i γ_j` when `k ∉ {i, j}`. -/
/-- Bilinears on disjoint pairs commute. -/
/-- If `x` and `v` both anticommute with `w`, then `x v` commutes with `w`. -/
/-! ### The braid gate -/
/-- The braid gate `B_{ij} = (1 + γ_i γ_j) / √2 = exp(π/4 γ_i γ_j)`. -/
/-- The braid gate is unitary. -/
/-- `B_{ij} ∈ unitary A`. -/
/-- The braid gate sends `γ_j ↦ γ_i`. -/
/-- The braid gate sends `γ_i ↦ -γ_j`. -/
/-- The braid gate fixes `γ_k` for `k ∉ {i, j}`. -/
/-- Conjugation by an element `u` with `u⋆ u = 1` is multiplicative. -/
/-- `B_{ij}² = γ_i γ_j`: the square of the braid is a Majorana parity operator. -/
/-! ### The rotation generating one step of the protocol -/
/-- The rotation `R(θ) = exp(θ/2 · γ_a γ_b) = cos(θ/2) + sin(θ/2) γ_a γ_b`. -/
/-- At `θ = π/2` the rotation is the braid gate. -/
/-- `R(θ) γ_b R(θ)† = cos θ γ_b + sin θ γ_a`. -/
/-- `R(θ)` fixes `γ_k` for `k ∉ {a, b}`. -/
/-! ### The trijunction -/
/-- The trijunction Hamiltonian `H_k = i γ_0 γ_k` coupling the centre `γ_0` to arm `k`. -/

/-- The Hamiltonian along a step of the protocol, rotating the coupling from arm `old` to arm
`new`: `H(θ) = i γ_0 (cos θ γ_old + sin θ γ_new)`. -/

/-- **Each protocol step is generated by the rotation `R(θ)`:**
`H(θ) = R(θ) H_old R(θ)†` with `R(θ) = exp(θ/2 γ_new γ_old)`. -/
/-- Along the step, `cos θ γ_new - sin θ γ_old` is a zero mode of `H(θ)`. -/
/-- **End of a step:** the transport unitary `B_{new,old} = R(π/2)` maps `H_old` to `H_new`. -/
/-- The three transport unitaries of the protocol `3 → 1 → 2 → 3`. -/
/-- Second step `1 → 2`. -/
/-- Third step `2 → 3`. -/

/-- **The trijunction exchange.**  The composite of the three transport unitaries is exactly
the braid gate `B_{21} = (1 + γ_2 γ_1)/√2 = exp(π/4 γ_2 γ_1)` of the two Majorana zero modes. -/
/-- The exchange commutes with `H_3`: it acts on the degenerate ground space of `H_3`. -/

/-- **Trijunction braiding protocol** (summary).  Starting from `H_3`, the three steps map
`H_3 ↦ H_1 ↦ H_2 ↦ H_3`, their composite is exactly `exp(π/4 γ_2 γ_1) = B_{21}`, which is
unitary, commutes with `H_3`, and exchanges the two zero modes: `γ_1 ↦ γ_2`, `γ_2 ↦ -γ_1`,
while fixing `γ_0`, `γ_3`. -/
/-! ### Non-abelian braid statistics -/

/-- Quaternion-type braid identity: if `a² = b² = -1` and `ab = -ba` then
`(1+a)(1+b)(1+a) = (1+b)(1+a)(1+b)`. -/
/-- The braid relation `B_{ji} B_{kj} B_{ji} = B_{kj} B_{ji} B_{kj}` for distinct `i, j, k`. -/
/-- Braid gates on disjoint pairs commute. -/
/-- The braid gate as a unit. -/

/-- **The Majorana braid group representation** `B_n →* Aˣ`, `σ_k ↦ B_{k+1,k}`, exchanging
neighbouring Majorana zero modes `γ_k`, `γ_{k+1}`. -/

/-- **Non-abelian statistics.**  For `n ≥ 3` Majorana zero modes (in a non-trivial algebra) the
braid representation is non-abelian: exchanging modes `(0,1)` and `(1,2)` do not commute. -/

# The Majorana edge-mode profile of the Kitaev chain

For the Kitaev chain with hopping `t`, pairing `Δ` and chemical potential `μ`, a Majorana zero
mode built from the `γ_{2j-1}` Majoranas, `Γ = ∑_{j ≥ 1} α_j γ_{2j-1}`, commutes with the
Hamiltonian of the semi-infinite (open) chain exactly when the amplitudes solve the
zero-mode equation

  `(t + Δ) α_{k+2} + μ α_{k+1} + (t - Δ) α_k = 0`,  with the open-boundary condition `α_0 = 0`.

`edgeProfile t Δ μ` is the solution normalized by `α_1 = 1`.  Its characteristic polynomial is
`(t + Δ) x² + μ x + (t - Δ)`.  We show that in the topological phase `|μ| < 2t` (with `t, Δ > 0`)
both roots lie strictly inside the unit disk, and deduce that the profile is exponentially
localized at the edge (`edgeProfile_isExpLocalized`).
-/

/-- The edge-mode amplitudes: `α 0 = 0`, `α 1 = 1`,
`α (k+2) = -(μ α (k+1) + (t - Δ) α k) / (t + Δ)`. -/
/-- The edge profile solves the zero-mode (transfer) equation of the Kitaev chain. -/

/-- **Roots in the unit disk.**  If `t, Δ > 0` and `|μ| < 2t`, every complex root of
`(t + Δ) x² + μ x + (t - Δ)` has modulus `< 1`. -/

/-- The complete homogeneous sums `h (j+1) = x₁ h j + x₂ ^ j`, `h 0 = 0`, i.e.
`h j = ∑_{k < j} x₁ ^ k x₂ ^ (j-1-k)`. -/
/-- The edge profile equals the complete homogeneous sum of the two characteristic roots. -/

/-- **Exponential localization of the Majorana edge mode.**  In the topological phase
`|μ| < 2t` (with `t, Δ > 0`) the edge profile decays exponentially. -/
-- a root of the characteristic polynomial
-- polynomial times geometric decay

/-!
# Majorana braiding on the degenerate ground space of a trijunction

We realize the trijunction explicitly on the Fock space `ℂ² ⊗ ℂ²` of two fermion modes
(Jordan–Wigner): the central Majorana and arm `3` form the first mode, `γ_0 = X ⊗ 1`,
`γ_3 = Y ⊗ 1`, and the two zero modes `γ_1 = Z ⊗ X`, `γ_2 = Z ⊗ Y` form the second mode.

* The trijunction Hamiltonian is `H_3 = i γ_0 γ_3 = -(Z ⊗ 1)`; it squares to `1`, so its
  spectrum is `{±1}`, and its ground space (energy `-1`) is
  `{v | v (1, ·) = 0} ≅ ℂ²`: it is **two-fold degenerate** (`finrank_groundSpace`).  The encoded
  qubit is the fermion parity of the pair of Majorana zero modes `γ_1, γ_2`.
* The braid `B_{21} = exp(π/4 γ_2 γ_1)` produced by the trijunction protocol equals
  `e^{-iπ/4} (1 ⊗ S)` with the phase gate `S = diag(1, i)` (`braidGate_eq_phaseGate`).  It
  preserves the ground space and acts on it as the Clifford phase gate `e^{-iπ/4} S`
  (`braid_acts_on_groundSpace`).  `S` is Clifford: `S X S† = Y`, `S Z S† = Z`.
-/

/-- Labels of the trijunction Majoranas in the two-mode Jordan–Wigner system:
`γ_0 ↦ X ⊗ 1`, `γ_1 ↦ Z ⊗ X`, `γ_2 ↦ Z ⊗ Y`, `γ_3 ↦ Y ⊗ 1`. -/
/-- The trijunction Majorana system on `ℂ² ⊗ ℂ²`. -/
/-- The trijunction Hamiltonian `H_3 = i γ_0 γ_3 = -(Z ⊗ 1)`. -/
/-- The spectrum of `H_3` is contained in `{1, -1}`. -/
/-- The ground space of the trijunction: the eigenspace of `H_3` at the ground energy `-1`. -/
/-- The ground space is identified with `ℂ²` (the state of the second mode). -/
/-- **The ground space is two-fold degenerate.** -/
/-- The Clifford phase gate `S = diag(1, i)`. -/
/-- `S` is a Clifford gate: `S X S† = Y`. -/
/-- `S` is a Clifford gate: `S Z S† = Z`. -/
/-- **The braid is the phase gate:** `B_{21} = exp(π/4 γ_2 γ_1) = e^{-iπ/4} (1 ⊗ S)`. -/
/-- The braid preserves the ground space (it commutes with `H_3`). -/

/-- **Braiding two Majorana zero modes implements the Clifford phase gate on the degenerate
ground space:** in the identification `groundSpace ≅ ℂ²`, the braid
`B_{21} = exp(π/4 γ_2 γ_1)` acts as `e^{-iπ/4} S`. -/

/-!
# The Jordan–Wigner representation: Majorana systems exist on the fermionic Fock space

The Fock space of `n` spinless fermion modes has basis `Fin n → Fin 2` (occupation numbers),
so operators are `2ⁿ × 2ⁿ` complex matrices.  The Jordan–Wigner construction realizes `2n`
Majorana operators on it:

  `γ_{(0,0)} = X ⊗ 1`, `γ_{(0,1)} = Y ⊗ 1`, `γ_{(j+1,s)} = Z ⊗ γ_{(j,s)}`

(Pauli matrices `X, Y, Z`; `Z` is the Jordan–Wigner string).  This gives a Majorana system
`jordanWigner n` indexed by `Fin n × Fin 2` for every chain length `n`, so all results about the
Kitaev chain apply to a genuine (non-trivial) Fock-space representation.

* `MajoranaSystem.extend`: from a Majorana system on `ι` acting on `ℂ^m`, the system on
  `Fin 2 ⊕ ι` acting on `ℂ² ⊗ ℂ^m` given by `X ⊗ 1`, `Y ⊗ 1`, `Z ⊗ γ_i`.
* `MajoranaSystem.map`: transport along a `⋆`-algebra homomorphism.
-/
/-! ### Pauli matrices -/
/-- The Pauli matrix `X`. -/
/-- The Pauli matrix `Y`. -/
/-- The Pauli matrix `Z`. -/
/-- The single-mode Majorana system `γ_0 = X`, `γ_1 = Y` on `ℂ²`. -/
/-! ### Transport along `⋆`-homomorphisms -/
/-- Transport of a Majorana system along a `⋆`-algebra homomorphism. -/
/-! ### Adding one fermion mode -/
/-- Adding one fermion mode: `γ (inl 0) = X ⊗ 1`, `γ (inl 1) = Y ⊗ 1`, `γ (inr i) = Z ⊗ γ i`. -/
/-- Reindexing of square matrices as a `⋆`-algebra homomorphism. -/
/-- The site/Majorana relabelling `(0, s) ↦ inl s`, `(j + 1, s) ↦ inr (j, s)`. -/
/-- **The Jordan–Wigner Majorana system** on the Fock space `(ℂ²)^{⊗ n}` of `n` fermion modes. -/
/-- The Fock space of `n` modes has dimension `2ⁿ`. -/

/-!
# The Kitaev p-wave chain and its Majorana edge modes

Spinless fermions `c_j` on an open chain of `N = n + 1` sites with nearest-neighbour hopping `t`,
`p`-wave superconducting pairing `Δ` and chemical potential `μ`:

  `H = -μ ∑_j (c_j† c_j - 1/2) + ∑_j [ -t (c_j† c_{j+1} + c_{j+1}† c_j)
                                       + Δ (c_j c_{j+1} + c_{j+1}† c_j†) ]`.

The fermions are decomposed into Majoranas `c_j = (γ (j,0) + i γ (j,1)) / 2`
(`γ_{2j-1}`, `γ_{2j}` in `1`-based numbering), see `Sovereign.Quantum.Majorana.Algebra`.

* `kitaevHam_eq`: the Majorana form
  `H = (i/2) ∑_j [ -μ γ_{j,0} γ_{j,1} + (Δ - t) γ_{j,0} γ_{j+1,1} + (Δ + t) γ_{j,1} γ_{j+1,0} ]`,
  and `kitaevHam_eq_quadHam`: `H = (i/4) ∑ M_{pq} γ_p γ_q` for an explicit real antisymmetric
  matrix `M = kitaevMatrix t Δ μ`.  The single-particle (BdG) Hamiltonian `h = i M` is Hermitian
  and particle–hole symmetric, and `[H, ∑ v_p γ_p] = ∑ (h v)_p γ_p`; in particular a zero mode of
  `h` gives an operator commuting with `H` (a zero-energy mode).
* `leftEdgeMode`, `rightEdgeMode`: the Majorana operators
  `Γ_L = ∑_j α_{j+1} γ_{j,0}` and `Γ_R = ∑_j α_{N-j} γ_{j,1}` built from the edge profile `α`.
  They are self-adjoint, anticommute with each other (they are *unpaired*: `Γ_L` only involves
  the `γ_{·,0}` Majoranas and `Γ_R` only the `γ_{·,1}` ones), and
  `[H, Γ_L] = -i (t + Δ) α_{N+1} γ_{N-1,1}`, `[H, Γ_R] = i (t + Δ) α_{N+1} γ_{0,0}`.
  The only obstruction to an exact zero mode is the amplitude `α_{N+1}` beyond the far edge.
* `kitaev_majorana_edge_modes`: in the topological phase `|μ| < 2t` (`t, Δ > 0`), the edge
  profile is exponentially localized, so `Γ_L` and `Γ_R` are exponentially localized at the two
  ends, and the residual commutators are exponentially small in the chain length: the edge
  modes are at energy `ε = 0` up to an exponentially small splitting.  For the semi-infinite
  chain the zero-mode equation holds exactly (`edgeProfile_rec`).
* `kitaev_sweet_spot`: at `μ = 0`, `Δ = t` the end Majoranas `γ_{0,0}` and `γ_{N-1,1}` commute
  exactly with `H` for every chain length.
-/

/-! ### The Kitaev Hamiltonian -/

/-- The Kitaev chain Hamiltonian on `N = n + 1` sites (open boundary conditions), with hopping
`t`, pairing `Δ` and chemical potential `μ`. -/
/-- **Majorana form of the Kitaev chain.** -/
/-- The real antisymmetric Majorana matrix `M` of the Kitaev chain: `H = (i/4) ∑ M_{pq} γ_p γ_q`. -/
/-- The Kitaev Majorana matrix is antisymmetric. -/
/-- The Kitaev Majorana matrix is real. -/
/-- The single-particle Bogoliubov–de Gennes Hamiltonian `h = i M` of the Kitaev chain. -/
/-- The Kitaev Hamiltonian is the quadratic Hamiltonian of its Majorana matrix. -/
/-- Single-particle dynamics: `[H, ∑ v_p γ_p] = ∑ (h v)_p γ_p` with `h = i M` the BdG matrix. -/

    (edgeProfile t Δ μ 0 = 0 ∧ edgeProfile t Δ μ 1 = 1 ∧
      (∀ k, (t + Δ) * edgeProfile t Δ μ (k + 2) + μ * edgeProfile t Δ μ (k + 1) +
        (t - Δ) * edgeProfile t Δ μ k = 0) ∧
      IsExpLocalized (edgeProfile t Δ μ)) ∧
    ∃ C ξ : ℝ, 0 < ξ ∧ ∀ (n : ℕ) (S : MajoranaSystem (Fin (n + 1) × Fin 2) A),
      star (S.leftEdgeMode t Δ μ) = S.leftEdgeMode t Δ μ ∧
      star (S.rightEdgeMode t Δ μ) = S.rightEdgeMode t Δ μ ∧
      S.leftEdgeMode t Δ μ * S.rightEdgeMode t Δ μ +
        S.rightEdgeMode t Δ μ * S.leftEdgeMode t Δ μ = 0 ∧
      ⁅S.kitaevHam t Δ μ, S.leftEdgeMode t Δ μ⁆ =
        (-(I * edgeSplitting t Δ μ n)) • S.γ (Fin.last n, 1) ∧
      ⁅S.kitaevHam t Δ μ, S.rightEdgeMode t Δ μ⁆ = (I * edgeSplitting t Δ μ n) • S.γ (0, 0) ∧
      |edgeSplitting t Δ μ n| ≤ C * Real.exp (-(n : ℝ) / ξ)

/-!
# Unpaired Majorana edge modes of the open Kitaev chain

See the module documentation of `Sovereign.Quantum.Majorana.KitaevChain` for the overview.
-/
/-- Coefficients of the left edge mode `Γ_L = ∑_j α_{j+1} γ_{j,0}`. -/
/-- Coefficients of the right edge mode `Γ_R = ∑_j α_{N-j} γ_{j,1}` (`N = n + 1`). -/
/-- The energy splitting `(t + Δ) α_{N+1}` of the edge modes of the `N = n + 1` site chain. -/
/-- The left Majorana edge mode `Γ_L = ∑_j α_{j+1} γ_{j,0}`. -/
/-- The right Majorana edge mode `Γ_R = ∑_j α_{N-j} γ_{j,1}`. -/

/-- **Commutator of the Hamiltonian with the left edge mode.**
`[H, Γ_L] = -i (t + Δ) α_{N+1} γ_{N-1,1}`. -/

/-- **Commutator of the Hamiltonian with the right edge mode.**
`[H, Γ_R] = i (t + Δ) α_{N+1} γ_{0,0}`. -/
/-! ### Properties of the edge modes -/
/-- The two edge modes are independent (unpaired) Majoranas: `{Γ_L, Γ_R} = 0`. -/
/-- `Γ_L² = ∑_j α_{j+1}²`: after normalization `Γ_L` is a Majorana operator. -/
/-- In the topological phase the edge splitting is exponentially small in the chain length. -/

/-- **Majorana edge modes of the open Kitaev chain in the topological phase.**
If `t, Δ > 0` and `|μ| < 2t`:

1. (*semi-infinite chain*) the edge profile `α` is an exact solution of the zero-mode equation
   with the open-boundary condition `α_0 = 0`, normalized by `α_1 = 1`, and it is exponentially
   localized at the edge;
2. (*finite open chain of `N = n + 1` sites*) the left and right edge modes
   `Γ_L = ∑ α_{j+1} γ_{j,0}` and `Γ_R = ∑ α_{N-j} γ_{j,1}` are unpaired self-adjoint Majorana
   operators (`{Γ_L, Γ_R} = 0`), whose commutators with the Hamiltonian are
   `[H, Γ_L] = -i ε_n γ_{N-1,1}` and `[H, Γ_R] = i ε_n γ_{0,0}` with an energy splitting `ε_n`
   that is exponentially small in the length: `|ε_n| ≤ C exp(-n / ξ)`. -/
/-! ### The sweet spot `μ = 0`, `Δ = t` -/

/-- **Kitaev's sweet spot.**  At `μ = 0`, `Δ = t > 0` the end Majoranas `γ_{0,0}` (i.e. `γ_1`)
and `γ_{N-1,1}` (i.e. `γ_{2N}`) commute exactly with the Hamiltonian: exact zero modes for
every chain length. -/

/-!
# Kitaev chains, Majorana zero modes and their braiding: main results

This file collects the headline statements.

* `kitaev_majorana_edge_modes` (in `KitaevEdgeModes`): in the topological phase `|μ| < 2t`
  the open Kitaev chain hosts unpaired, exponentially localized Majorana edge modes at energy
  `ε = 0` (exactly for the semi-infinite chain, up to an exponentially small splitting for a
  chain of finite length).  `leftEdgeMode_ne_zero` shows these edge modes are non-zero
  operators in any non-trivial representation, e.g. the Jordan–Wigner Fock representation
  `jordanWigner`.
* `trijunction_braiding` (in `Braiding`): the trijunction protocol composes to the braid
  `B_{21} = exp(π/4 γ_2 γ_1)`.
* `majorana_braiding_clifford_phase_gate`: in the explicit two-mode Fock representation of the
  trijunction, the protocol unitary is the matrix exponential `exp(π/4 γ_2 γ_1)`, the ground
  space of the trijunction Hamiltonian is two-fold degenerate, and the braid acts on it as the
  Clifford phase gate `e^{-iπ/4} S`, `S = diag(1, i)`.
* `majoranaBraidRep_isNonAbelian` (in `Braiding`): the braid group representation generated by
  exchanges of Majorana zero modes is non-abelian.
-/
/-- The left edge mode is a non-zero operator: `Γ_L² = ∑ α_{j+1}² ≥ α_1² = 1`. -/

/-- The Kitaev chain in the Jordan–Wigner Fock representation: in the topological phase, the
left edge mode of the `N = n + 1` site chain is a non-zero operator on the `2^N`-dimensional
Fock space whose commutator with the Hamiltonian is exponentially small in `N`. -/

/-!
# Sovereign.Quantum.Majorana Root Index

Kitaev chains, Majorana zero modes, and non-abelian trijunction braiding:
- Algebra: Majorana canonical anticommutation relations and Clifford algebras
- EdgeProfile: Exponentially localized Majorana edge mode wavefunctions
- KitaevChain: Open Kitaev wire Hamiltonian and quadratic Majorana form
- KitaevEdgeModes: Zero-energy Majorana bound states and topological phase diagram
- Braiding: Trijunction transport cycle and non-abelian braid representations
- BraidExp: Matrix exponential representation of the braid generator B = exp((pi/4) gamma_i gamma_j)
- JordanWigner: Fock space representation of Majorana systems via Jordan-Wigner transformation
- GroundSpace: Topological ground state degeneracy and Clifford S phase gate action
- Main: Summary theorems and non-vanishing certificates
-/

/-!
# Braiding Majorana zero modes generates the two-qubit Clifford group

On the two qubits encoded in six Majorana zero modes (`Hexon`), the elementary exchanges
`B_{k+1,k}` of neighbouring Majoranas act by the Pauli rotations
`g_0 = R(-Z₁)`, `g_1 = R(X₁)`, `g_2 = R(-Z₁X₂)`, `g_3 = R(Z₂)`, `g_4 = R(X₂)`,
`R(P) = exp(-iπ/4 P) = (1 - iP)/√2`.

We prove (`braid_generates_clifford`) that the subgroup of `U(4)` generated by these five
logical braids and the global phases **equals** the Clifford group
`⟨H₁, H₂, S₁, S₂, CNOT⟩ · U(1)`:

* `⊇`: `S = e^{iπ/4} R(Z)`, `H = S R(X) S`, and
  `CNOT = e^{iπ/4} R(Z₁) R(X₂) R(-Z₁X₂)`, so the Hadamard and phase gates on both qubits and the
  CNOT gate are all obtained by braiding (up to a global phase);
* `⊆`: every logical braid is Clifford: `R(Z₁) = e^{-iπ/4} S₁`, `R(X₁) = H₁ R(Z₁) H₁`,
  `R(Z₁Z₂) = CNOT R(Z₂) CNOT`, `R(Z₁X₂) = H₂ R(Z₁Z₂) H₂`, and so on.

In particular braiding generates the full single-qubit Clifford group `⟨H, S⟩` on each encoded
qubit, and the entangling CNOT.
-/
/-! ### The Clifford gates -/
/-- The unnormalized Hadamard matrix `√2 H`. -/
/-- Projector on `|0⟩`. -/
/-- Projector on `|1⟩`. -/
/-- `H` on the first qubit. -/
/-- `H` on the second qubit. -/
/-- `S` on the first qubit. -/
/-- `S` on the second qubit. -/
/-- The controlled-NOT gate (control: qubit 1, target: qubit 2). -/
/-- The unnormalized rotation `√2 R(P) = 1 - iP`. -/
/-! ### Explicit `4 × 4` identities -/
/-- Close an identity between complex numbers built from `I` and rationals. -/
/-- Entrywise verification of an identity between explicit two-qubit matrices. -/
/-! ### Pauli operators and Pauli rotations -/
/-- A Hermitian involution (a Pauli operator up to sign). -/
/-! ### The unitary group `U(4)` and its Clifford subgroup -/
/-- The unitary group of the two encoded qubits. -/
/-- A Pauli rotation as an element of `U(4)`. -/
/-- A global phase as an element of `U(4)`. -/
/-- The global phases `U(1) ⊆ U(4)`. -/

/-- **The two-qubit Clifford group**, generated by `H` and `S` on each qubit, `CNOT`, and the
global phases. -/
/-! ### The logical braid group -/
/-- The logical action of the elementary braid `σ_k` as an element of `U(4)`. -/
/-- The group generated by the logical actions of all braids (and global phases). -/
/-! ### Relations between Pauli rotations and Clifford gates -/
/-- `e^{-iπ/4} = (1 - i)/√2` has modulus one. -/
/-- The phase `e^{-iπ/4}` in `U(4)`. -/
/-! ### Main theorem -/
/-- **Braiding produces the phase gate on qubit 1** (up to a global phase). -/
/-- **Braiding produces the phase gate on qubit 2** (up to a global phase). -/
/-- **Braiding produces the Hadamard gate on qubit 1.** -/
/-- **Braiding produces the Hadamard gate on qubit 2.** -/
/-- **Braiding produces the entangling CNOT gate** (up to a global phase). -/
/-- **Every elementary braid acts on the encoded qubits by a Clifford gate.** -/

/-- **Braiding generates the full Clifford group on the encoded Majorana qubits.**  The group
generated by the logical actions of the elementary Majorana exchanges (together with global
phases) is exactly the two-qubit Clifford group `⟨H₁, H₂, S₁, S₂, CNOT⟩ · U(1)`. -/

/-!
# Majorana stabilizer codes with plaquette parity checks, and fault-tolerant error correction

A *Majorana code* on the Majorana modes `M` is given by a family of plaquettes `plaq p ⊆ M`
(`p : P`); the stabilizer of plaquette `p` is the parity operator `γ_{plaq p} = ∏_{a ∈ plaq p} γ_a`.
We require every plaquette to contain an even number of Majoranas (so the stabilizers are bosonic,
i.e. preserve fermion parity) and any two plaquettes to overlap in an even number of Majoranas
(so the stabilizers commute, `stab_commute`).

Errors are Majorana strings `γ_{supp e}`, `e : M → 𝔽₂`.  Every physical local error is of this
form: a phase error on an island is `i γ_a γ_b`, a bit flip transfers a fermion between islands
and is again a bilinear `i γ_a γ_b`, and quasiparticle poisoning is a single `γ_a`.

* The binary picture is the `CSSComplex` of `Sovereign.Quantum.ToroidalLatticeSurgery` with
  checks = generators = plaquettes (a *self-dual* sector): the syndrome of `e` is
  `σ_p(e) = |plaq p ∩ supp e| mod 2`, which is exactly the sign picked up when commuting the error
  through the stabilizer (`stab_mul_errorOp`).  Logical operators are syndrome-free strings which
  are not products of plaquettes; `distance` is the minimal weight of a logical string.
* `residual_isStabilizer`: if `2t < d` then for every error `e` and every correction `c` of weight
  `≤ t` with the same syndrome, `c + e` is a product of plaquettes.
* `recovery`: **fault tolerance on the operator level.**  In any representation of the Majorana
  operators, on the joint eigenspace (the ground space of `H = -∑_p ε̄_p γ_{plaq p}`) the error
  followed by the correction acts as a global phase: every encoded (ground) state is restored and
  the ground space with its full degeneracy is mapped onto itself.
-/
/-- A Majorana stabilizer code given by plaquette parity checks. -/
/-- The Majorana modes in each plaquette. -/
/-- Plaquette stabilizers are products of an even number of Majoranas. -/
/-- Any two plaquettes share an even number of Majoranas. -/
/-- The binary (self-dual CSS) description of a Majorana code. -/
/-- The syndrome of a Majorana string: `σ_p(e) = ∑_{a ∈ plaq p} e_a`. -/
/-- Products of plaquette stabilizers. -/
/-- Logical strings: syndrome-free, but not a product of plaquettes. -/
/-- The number of independent logical Majorana strings, `dim H₁`. -/
/-- The code distance: the minimal weight of a logical string. -/

/-- **Decoding succeeds below half the distance:** if `2t` is smaller than the weight of every
logical string, then an error and a correction of weight `≤ t` with the same syndrome differ by a
product of plaquette stabilizers. -/

/-- **Error detection below the distance:** a syndrome-free error lighter than every logical
string is a product of plaquette stabilizers. -/
/-- The minimum-weight decoder: a lightest string with the given syndrome. -/
/-- **The minimum-weight decoder corrects every error of weight `t` with `2t < d`.** -/
/-! ### Operator level: plaquette stabilizers, syndromes and recovery -/
/-- The plaquette parity stabilizer `γ_{plaq p}`. -/
/-- **The plaquette stabilizers commute.** -/
/-- **The syndrome is the commutation sign of an error with the stabilizers.** -/

/-- The joint eigenspace of the plaquette stabilizers with eigenvalues `ε`, i.e. the degenerate
ground space of the plaquette Hamiltonian `H = -∑_p ε̄_p γ_{plaq p}` in the sector `ε`. -/

/-- **Syndrome extraction:** an error `γ_{supp e}` maps the ground space of sector `ε` into the
sector `ε_p (-1)^{σ_p(e)}`, so measuring the plaquette parities reveals the syndrome. -/
/-- A product of plaquette stabilizers acts on the ground space as a phase. -/

/-- **Fault-tolerant recovery.**  Let `2t` be smaller than the weight of every logical string
(e.g. `2t < d`).  If an error string `e` of weight `≤ t` occurs and a correction string `c` of
weight `≤ t` with the same syndrome is applied, then on the whole ground space the net operation
is a global phase `λ` with `|λ| = 1`: every encoded state is recovered, and the degenerate
ground space is mapped onto itself. -/

/-- **Minimum-weight decoding is fault tolerant up to half the code distance.** For every error
string `e` of weight `t` with `2t < d`, measuring the syndrome and applying the minimum-weight
correction restores every ground state up to a global phase. -/

/-!
# Encoded Majorana qubits: two qubits in six Majorana zero modes

Two logical qubits are encoded in six Majorana zero modes `γ_0, …, γ_5` (e.g. the six
twist/end modes brought together at the trijunctions of the network) in the sector of fixed
total fermion parity `Γ = (-i)³ γ_0 γ_1 γ_2 γ_3 γ_4 γ_5 = +1`: the Fock space of three fermion
modes is `8`-dimensional and its even-parity sector is `4 = 2²`-dimensional.

**Construction.**
* `pauliTriple`: the three Pauli matrices form a Majorana system (`Cl₃`) on `ℂ²`; by
  `MajoranaSystem.extend` we get five Majoranas `X⊗1, Y⊗1, Z⊗X, Z⊗Y, Z⊗Z` on `ℂ² ⊗ ℂ²`.
* `MajoranaSystem.double`: from Majoranas `μ_i` on `ℂ^m` we get Majoranas on `ℂ^m ⊕ ℂ^m`:
  `γ_i = [[0, μ_i], [μ_i, 0]]` and one more, `γ_∗ = [[0, -i], [i, 0]]`.  Every bilinear
  `γ_a γ_b` is block diagonal, so it preserves the *code space* `ℂ^m ⊕ 0`.
* `hexon`: the resulting six Majoranas on `ℂ⁴ ⊕ ℂ⁴`, ordered as
  `γ_0 = Y₁`, `γ_1 = X₁`, `γ_2 = γ_∗`, `γ_3 = Z₁X₂`, `γ_4 = Z₁Y₂`, `γ_5 = Z₁Z₂`.
* `hexon_parity`: the total parity is `Γ = diag(1, -1)`, so the code space `ℂ⁴ ⊕ 0` is exactly
  the even-parity sector.

**Braids on the code space** (`hexon_braid_acts`): the elementary exchange
`B_{k+1,k} = (1 + γ_{k+1} γ_k)/√2 = exp(π/4 γ_{k+1} γ_k)` (the image of the braid generator
`σ_k` under `majoranaBraidRep`) preserves the code space and acts there as `logicalGen k`, where
(with `R(P) = (1 - iP)/√2 = exp(-iπ/4 P)`)

  `g_0 = R(-Z₁)`, `g_1 = R(X₁)`, `g_2 = R(-Z₁X₂)`, `g_3 = R(Z₂)`, `g_4 = R(X₂)`.
-/

/-- Five Majoranas on two qubits: `X⊗1, Y⊗1, Z⊗X, Z⊗Y, Z⊗Z`. -/
/-! ### Doubling: adding one Majorana and a parity qubit -/
/-- Upper-right block of the doubled Majoranas. -/
/-- Lower-left block of the doubled Majoranas. -/
/-- **Doubling.** The Majoranas `[[0, μ_i], [μ_i, 0]]` together with `[[0, -i], [i, 0]]`. -/
/-- The logical action (on the code space) of the braid `B_{op}`. -/
/-- The embedding of `ℂ^m` as the code space `ℂ^m ⊕ 0`. -/
/-- The code space `ℂ^m ⊕ 0`. -/
/-! ### The hexon: six Majoranas encoding two qubits -/
/-- Qubit index type: two qubits. -/
/-- **Six Majorana zero modes** on the `8`-dimensional Fock space `ℂ⁴ ⊕ ℂ⁴` of three fermions. -/

/-!
# Majorana surface codes on trijunction networks: main results

* `trijunction_protocol_realizes_braid`: in any Majorana system, the three-step trijunction
  transport protocol (a coupler `γ_o`, the two modes `γ_a`, `γ_b` to be exchanged and an
  auxiliary zero mode `γ_e`) composes to the elementary braid `B_{ba} = exp(π/4 γ_b γ_a)`.
* `hexon_braid_group_acts`: every braid of the six Majorana zero modes encoding two qubits
  preserves the encoded space (the even-parity sector) and acts there by an element of the
  logical braid group, which is the Clifford group (`braidLogicalGroup_eq_cliffordGroup`).
* `majorana_braiding_clifford`: summary of the gate-synthesis results.
* `trijunction_network_fault_tolerance`: summary of the error-correction results for the
  trijunction network on a genus-`g` surface.
-/
/-! ### Braids realized by the trijunction protocol -/

/-- **The trijunction transport protocol realizes the braid in any Majorana system.**  With a
coupler `o`, the two zero modes `a`, `b` and an auxiliary zero mode `e` (all distinct), the
three transport steps `a → e`, `b → a`, `e → b` compose to `B_{ba} = (1 + γ_b γ_a)/√2`. -/
/-! ### Every braid acts on the encoded qubits by a Clifford gate -/
/-- `x` preserves the encoded space and acts on it by the matrix `g`. -/
/-- Braids whose action on the code space lies in the logical braid group. -/

/-- **Every braid of the six Majorana zero modes acts on the encoded two-qubit space by a
Clifford gate:** it preserves the even-parity sector and acts there by an element of
`braidLogicalGroup = cliffordGroup`. -/
/-- A phase error on the island `e`: the string `i γ_{(e,1)} γ_{(e,2)}` (the island's `Z`). -/
/-- A bit-flip error on the island `e`: the string `i γ_{(e,0)} γ_{(e,1)}` (the island's `X`). -/
/-- The error string of phase flips on the islands `Zs` and bit flips on the islands `Xs`. -/

/-- A pattern of `|Zs|` local phase errors and `|Xs|` local bit flips has weight at most
`2 (|Zs| + |Xs|)`. -/

/-- **Fault tolerance of the trijunction network.**  Let `S` be a cellulated closed surface of
genus `g` and consider the Majorana surface code of its trijunction network, realized by any
Majorana system `Maj` acting on a space `W`.
1. The code has `2g` logical qubits (`4g` independent logical Majorana strings; in the
   stabilizer formalism a `2^{2g}`-fold degenerate ground space), a topological invariant.
2. The plaquette parity stabilizers commute.
3. For any pattern of `m` local phase and bit-flip errors on the islands with `4m < d`
   (`d` the code distance), measuring the plaquette parities and applying the minimum-weight
   correction restores every ground state up to a global phase `|λ| = 1`; in particular the
   degenerate ground space is mapped onto itself and no encoded information is lost.
4. More generally every Majorana error string of weight `t` with `2t < d` is corrected. -/

/-!
# Trijunction networks of Kitaev chains: the Majorana surface code of a cellulated surface

Let `S : SurfaceCode V E F` be a cellulated closed surface of genus `g` (from
`Sovereign.Quantum.ToroidalLatticeSurgery`).  We place a superconducting island on every edge
`e`.  The island is made of Kitaev chain segments whose four Majorana end (zero) modes are
`γ_{(e,0)}, γ_{(e,1)}, γ_{(e,2)}, γ_{(e,3)}`.  At every vertex the wires of the incident edges
meet in a junction (a *trijunction* for a trivalent cellulation, `IsTrijunctionNetwork`, e.g.
the honeycomb lattice); the Majoranas `(e,0), (e,1)` of the incident islands are coupled there.
Around each face the Majoranas `(e,1), (e,2)` of the boundary islands are coupled.

The plaquette parity stabilizers of the resulting *Majorana surface code*
(`SurfaceCode.majoranaNetwork`) are

* the **vertex (junction) parities** `∏_{e ∋ v} γ_{(e,0)} γ_{(e,1)}`,
* the **face (plaquette) parities** `∏_{e ∈ ∂f} γ_{(e,1)} γ_{(e,2)}`,
* the **island parities** `γ_{(e,0)} γ_{(e,1)} γ_{(e,2)} γ_{(e,3)}` (fixed by the charging energy).

All plaquettes are even and overlap evenly, so this is a Majorana stabilizer code.

**Topological degeneracy** (`numLogical_majoranaNetwork`): the network encodes `4g` independent
logical Majorana strings (`dim H₁ = 4g` over `𝔽₂`), i.e. `2g` logical qubits
(`numLogicalQubits_majoranaNetwork`).  In the standard stabilizer formalism this corresponds to a
`2^{2g}`-fold degenerate ground space in each stabilizer sector (the dimension count of the
Hilbert space itself is not formalized here).  The count only depends on the topology of the
surface (its genus), not on the size of the network.
-/
/-- The junction parity at vertex `v`: the Majoranas `(e,0), (e,1)` of all incident islands. -/
/-- The face parity of `f`: the Majoranas `(e,1), (e,2)` of the islands on `∂f`. -/
/-- The island parity of the island on edge `e`. -/
/-- All plaquettes of the network, indexed by `V ⊕ F ⊕ E`. -/
/-- The network is built from trijunctions: every vertex joins exactly three islands. -/
/-- At a trijunction, the junction parity involves six Majoranas. -/
/-- **The Majorana surface code of the trijunction network** on the surface `S`. -/
/-- The kernel of the network's boundary map is spanned by the vertex and face kernels. -/

/-- **Topological degeneracy of the trijunction network:** the Majorana surface code on a
closed surface of genus `g` has `4g` independent logical Majorana strings. -/
/-- The number of logical qubits: two logical Majorana strings (`X̄`, `Z̄`) per qubit. -/
/-- **The trijunction network on a genus-`g` surface encodes `2g` logical qubits.** -/
/-- On the torus the trijunction network encodes two logical qubits. -/

/-!
# Majorana strings (monomials in the Majorana operators)

Every local error and every stabilizer of a Majorana surface code is a *Majorana string*, a
product of Majorana operators.  For a word `l : List ι` we write `S.word l = γ_{l₀} ⋯ γ_{lₖ}`
and for a set of modes `s : Finset ι` we write `S.mono s` for the product over `s` (in an
arbitrary but fixed order).

* `γ_mul_word`, `word_mul_word`: the sign rule `W_l W_m = (-1)^{|l||m| + #(l ∩ m)} W_m W_l`.
* `mono_mul_mono`: `γ_s γ_t = (-1)^{|s||t| + |s ∩ t|} γ_t γ_s`.
* `word_signEq_mono`: up to a sign, a word only depends on the parities of the multiplicities
  of its letters, `W_l = ± γ_{supp (count l mod 2)}`.  This is the dictionary between Majorana
  strings and vectors over `𝔽₂` used for error correction.
-/
/-- Equality up to sign. -/
/-- The Majorana string of a word: `γ_{l₀} γ_{l₁} ⋯ γ_{lₖ}`. -/
/-- Moving a Majorana through a string: `γ_i W_l = (-1)^{|l| + #_i l} W_l γ_i`. -/
/-- The sign rule for Majorana strings. -/
/-- Permuting a string only changes its sign. -/
/-- The Majorana string over a set of modes (product in a fixed order). -/
/-- Multiplying a string by a Majorana: `γ_i γ_s = ± γ_{s ∆ {i}}`. -/
/-- The sign rule for strings over sets: `γ_s γ_t = (-1)^{|s||t| + |s ∩ t|} γ_t γ_s`. -/
/-- Even strings commute exactly when they overlap evenly. -/
/-- The `𝔽₂`-vector of letter multiplicities of a word. -/
/-- **A Majorana string is determined, up to sign, by the parities of its letters.** -/
/-- Products of two strings: `γ_{supp u} γ_{supp v} = ± γ_{supp (u + v)}`. -/

# The sampling step of Shor's period-finding algorithm

Shor's algorithm finds the period `r` of a function `f : ℕ → X` as follows. Prepare
`N^{-1/2} ∑_{x < N} |x⟩|f x⟩`, measure the second register (obtaining some value `f x₀`),
which leaves the first register in the uniform superposition over the fibre
`S = {x < N | f x = f x₀}`, apply the quantum Fourier transform `|x⟩ ↦ N^{-1/2} ∑_k ω^{xk} |k⟩`
with `ω = e^{2πi/N}`, and measure. By the Born rule the outcome `k` has probability

  `P(k) = |∑_{x ∈ S} ω^{xk}|² / (|S| · N)`.

This file proves, for any `f` with exact period `r` and `N = r M`:

* `fibre_card` : `|S| = M`;
* `outcomeProb_eq` : `P(k) = 1/r` if `M ∣ k` and `P(k) = 0` otherwise;
* `outcomeProb_pos_iff` : for `k < N` the possible outcomes are exactly `k = c M`, `c < r`
  (so `k / N = c / r`, from which `r` is read off by continued fractions);
* `outcomeProb_sum` : these probabilities sum to `1`.

The only property of `f` that is used is exact periodicity (`ExactPeriod`); no
commutativity or associativity of whatever structure produced `f` enters.
-/
/-- `f` has exact period `r`: `f (x + r) = f x`, and `f` is injective on `[0, r)`. -/
/-- The fibre `S = {x < N | f x = f x₀}` left after measuring the output register. -/
/-- The (unnormalised) Fourier amplitude `∑_{x ∈ S} ω^{xk}` of outcome `k`. -/
/-- Born-rule probability of outcome `k` after the QFT on the post-measurement state. -/

/-- **Shor sampling.** For `f` of exact period `r` and `N = r M`, after measuring any output
value the QFT outcome `k` has probability `1/r` if `M ∣ k` and `0` otherwise. -/
/-- The possible outcomes `k < N` are exactly the multiples `k = c M` with `c < r`. -/
/-- The outcome probabilities over `k < N` sum to `1`. -/

/-

Released under Apache 2.0 license as described in the file LICENSE.

# The quantum Hamming (sphere-packing) bound for non-degenerate stabilizer codes

A stabilizer code `C` on `n` qubits with `k` logical qubits is a *non-degenerate*
`[[n, k, d]]` code when every nonzero element of its centralizer — logical operators *and*
stabilizers — acts on at least `d` qubits (`StabilizerCode.HasPureDistance d`).  For such a code
(`quantum_hamming_bound`)

  `∑_{j = 0}^{⌊(d-1)/2⌋} 3ʲ · (n choose j) ≤ 2^(n - k)`.

Proof.
1. **Counting Paulis** (`card_pwt_le`): there are exactly `∑_{j ≤ t} 3ʲ (n choose j)` Paulis of
   weight `≤ t` (choose the support, then one of `X, Y, Z` on each qubit of it).  This is a special
   case of the count of words of Hamming weight `≤ t` over an alphabet of size `q`
   (`card_hammingNorm_le`), applied to the alphabet `𝔽₂ × 𝔽₂` of single-qubit Paulis.
2. **Syndromes**: the syndrome of an error is its class modulo the centralizer; the syndrome
   space `Pauli n ⧸ centralizer` has dimension `dim S = n - k`, hence `2^(n-k)` elements.
3. **Non-degeneracy**: two distinct errors of weight `≤ t` with `2t < d` differ by a nonzero
   Pauli of weight `< d`, which is not in the centralizer, so their syndromes differ.

The five-qubit code is perfect: it meets the bound with equality, `1 + 3·5 = 2⁴`
(`fiveQubit_perfect`).
-/
/-! ## Counting words of bounded Hamming weight -/
/-- The number of words with a prescribed support `s` is `(q - 1)^|s|`. -/
/-- The number of words of Hamming weight exactly `j` is `(n choose j) (q - 1)^j`. -/

/-- **Volume of a Hamming ball**: the number of words of Hamming weight at most `t` over an
alphabet of size `q` is `∑_{j ≤ t} (n choose j) (q - 1)^j`. -/
/-! ## Counting Paulis of bounded weight -/
/-- A Pauli as a word over the four-letter alphabet `𝔽₂ × 𝔽₂` of single-qubit Paulis. -/
/-- **Number of Paulis of weight at most `t`**: `∑_{j ≤ t} 3ʲ (n choose j)`. -/
/-! ## The syndrome space -/
/-- The syndrome space `Pauli n ⧸ centralizer` has `2^(n - k)` elements. -/

/-- **Non-degenerate codes separate low-weight errors by syndrome.**  If every nonzero
centralizer element has weight `≥ d` and `2t < d`, then distinct errors of weight `≤ t` have
distinct syndromes. -/

/-- **Quantum Hamming bound for non-degenerate stabilizer codes.**  If `C` is a non-degenerate
`[[n, k, d]]` stabilizer code (every nonzero element of the centralizer, stabilizers included,
has weight at least `d`), then

  `∑_{j = 0}^{⌊(d-1)/2⌋} 3ʲ (n choose j) ≤ 2^(n - k)`. -/

/-- The five-qubit `[[5, 1, 3]]` code is **perfect**: it is non-degenerate and meets the quantum
Hamming bound with equality, `1 + 3 · 5 = 2⁴`. -/
/-- The bound rules out a non-degenerate `[[4, 1, 3]]` code: `1 + 3 · 4 = 13 > 2³`. -/

# The quantum Singleton bound for stabilizer codes

For a stabilizer code on `n` qubits with `k ≥ 1` logical qubits and distance `d`,
`k + 2(d - 1) ≤ n` (`quantum_singleton`).  The proof here is purely linear-algebraic over
`𝔽₂`, in the symplectic model of `Sovereign/Quantum/SymplecticStabilizer.lean`:

1. **Support and restriction.**  `restrict A` keeps the tensor factors in a region `A` and
   replaces the others by the identity.  Paulis with disjoint supports commute
   (`symp_eq_zero_of_disjoint`).
2. **Correctable regions.**  A region `A` is *correctable* if every element of the
   centralizer supported in `A` is a stabilizer.  Any region with fewer than `d` qubits is
   correctable (`correctable_of_card_lt`).
3. **Cleaning lemma** (`cleaning`): if `A` is correctable, every logical operator is
   equivalent, modulo the stabilizer, to one acting trivially on `A`.  Proof: the orthogonal
   complement of `restrict A (S) + (Paulis supported off A)` is exactly the set of stabilizers
   supported in `A`, and a logical operator is orthogonal to those.
4. **Counting** (`logicalQubits_add_card_le`): if `A`, `B` are disjoint correctable regions,
   then `k + |A| + |B| ≤ n`.  The logical operators supported off `A` surject onto the
   `2k`-dimensional logical space and, after restriction to the remaining region `C`,
   inject modulo the stabilizer (because `B` is correctable), so `2k ≤ 2|C|`.
-/
/-! ## Restriction to a region -/
/-- Keep the tensor factors in `A`; act as the identity elsewhere. -/
/-- `a` acts trivially outside `A` iff `restrict Aᶜ a = 0`. -/
/-- **Disjoint supports commute.** -/
/-- For `q` supported in `A`, only the part of `s` inside `A` matters for commutation. -/
/-- A Pauli supported in `A` has weight at most `|A|`. -/
/-- A Pauli orthogonal to every Pauli supported off `A` is supported in `A`. -/
/-! ## Correctable regions -/

/-- `A` is correctable for `C`: every centralizer element supported in `A` is a
stabilizer (no logical operator fits inside `A`). -/

/-- **Small regions are correctable**: a region of fewer than `d` qubits is correctable for
a code of distance `d`. -/

/-- **Cleaning lemma.**  If `A` is correctable, every element of the centralizer can be
multiplied by a stabilizer so that it acts trivially on `A`. -/
/-! ## Counting -/
/-- The coordinates of a Pauli on a region `C`. -/

/-- **Counting lemma.**  If `A` and `B` are disjoint correctable regions, then
`k + |A| + |B| ≤ n`. -/
-- (1) `NB + S = N` by cleaning.
-- (2) Restricting `NB` to the remaining region `Cr`.

/-- **Quantum Singleton bound.**  A stabilizer code on `n` qubits with at least one logical
qubit and distance `d` satisfies `k + 2(d - 1) ≤ n`. -/
/-- The five-qubit code saturates the quantum Singleton bound: `1 + 2·(3 - 1) = 5`. -/

/-- The quantum Singleton bound rules out, e.g., a five-qubit code with one logical qubit and
distance `4`. -/

This module formalizes the indifferentiability of the `RamanujanSponge` construction
from an ideal random oracle up to O(2^{c/2}) queries in the ideal permutation model:

1. Sponge State Conservation & Bit Widths:
   - State width b = r + c (rate r, capacity c).
   - Canonical 256-bit configuration: r = 64 bits (8 bytes), c = 192 bits (24 bytes).
   - Classical collision security level: s = c / 2 = 96 bits.
   - Balanced configuration: r = 128 bits, c = 128 bits, s = 64 bits.
   - High-capacity configuration: r = 32 bits, c = 224 bits, s = 112 bits.

2. Indifferentiability Advantage Bound in the Ideal Permutation Model:
   - For a sponge construction with capacity c bits in the ideal permutation model,
     there exists a simulator S such that any distinguisher D making Q total queries
     (to sponge and permutation or random oracle and simulator) has advantage:
       Adv(D) ≤ Q² / 2^c
   - Inner-state (capacity) collision probability: P(coll) ≤ Q(Q - 1) / (2 * 2^c) ≤ Q² / 2^{c+1}.

3. Negligible Advantage for Sub-Capacity Queries:
   - For Q ≤ 2^{(c - k) / 2}, the advantage satisfies Adv(D) ≤ 2^{-k}.
   - In particular, for any Q < 2^{c/2}, Adv(D) < 1.0.

4. Query Complexity Lower Bound for Advantage Ω(1):

       Q ≥ √(ε * 2^c) = √ε * 2^{c/2} queries.
   - In particular, for constant advantage ε = 1/2, Q ≥ 2^{(c - 1) / 2}.

5. Refutation of OP-055 Falsification Criterion:
   - OP-055 falsification: "A distinguishing adversary with advantage Ω(1) using fewer than 2^{c/2} queries."
   - We prove that any adversary with advantage Adv ≥ 1/2 strictly requires Q ≥ 2^{(c - 1) / 2} = Ω(2^{c/2}),

comments.text: /-! ## Pauli weight -/
/-- The qubits on which a Pauli acts nontrivially. -/
/-- The weight of a Pauli: the number of qubits on which it acts nontrivially. -/
/-- **Subadditivity** of the Pauli weight (product of Paulis). -/
/-- An `X`-type Pauli `(x, 0)` has the Hamming weight of `x`. -/
/-- A `Z`-type Pauli `(0, z)` has the Hamming weight of `z`. -/
/-! ## Distance -/

/-- `C` has distance at least `d`: every logical operator — a Pauli commuting with all
stabilizers but not itself a stabilizer — acts on at least `d` qubits. -/

/-- `C` has *pure* distance at least `d`: every nonzero element of the centralizer (logical
operators *and* stabilizers) acts on at least `d` qubits. -/

/-- **Error detection.**  `C` has distance `≥ d` exactly when every error of weight `< d`
either anticommutes with some stabilizer (so it is detected by measuring the checks) or is
itself a stabilizer (so it acts trivially on the code space). -/

/-- **Error correction.**  If `2t < d`, any two errors of weight `≤ t` that produce the same
syndrome (the same commutation pattern with every stabilizer) differ by a stabilizer, so one
recovery operation corrects both. -/

/-- Membership in the centralizer of a code given by checks only has to be tested on the
checks themselves. -/

/-- An element of the centralizer that anticommutes with another element of the centralizer
is a genuine logical operator: it is not a stabilizer. -/
/-! ## CSS codes: quantum distance from classical distance -/

/-- The centralizer of a CSS code: `(x, z)` commutes with all checks iff `x ∈ ker HZ` and
`z ∈ ker HX`. -/

/-- **CSS distance bound.**  If every nonzero vector of `ker HZ` and every nonzero vector of
`ker HX` has Hamming weight `≥ d`, then every nonzero element of the centralizer of the CSS
code has Pauli weight `≥ d`.  In particular the quantum code has distance `≥ d`. -/
/-- The stabilizer group of a CSS code is the product of the row spaces of `HX` and `HZ`. -/
/-- Dimension of a product of subspaces. -/
/-- **CSS dimension formula**: `dim S = rank HX + rank HZ`. -/
/-- **CSS logical qubits**: `k = n - rank HX - rank HZ`. -/
/-! ## The five-qubit code has distance 3 -/

/-- Every Pauli on five qubits commuting with the four checks of the five-qubit code and
acting on at most two qubits is the identity (finite check over all `4⁵` Paulis). -/
/-- **The five-qubit code has (pure) distance at least 3.** -/

/-- A weight-three logical operator of the five-qubit code: `I Y Y I X`, i.e. the logical
`X̄ = XXXXX` multiplied by the check `XZZXI`. -/
/-- The logical `Z̄ = ZZZZZ`. -/

/-- **The five-qubit code is a `[[5, 1, 3]]` code**: one logical qubit, distance at least 3,
and a logical operator of weight exactly 3 (so the distance is exactly 3). -/
/-! ## The `[[4, 2, 2]]` code has distance 2 -/

/-- Every nonzero Pauli on four qubits commuting with `XXXX` and `ZZZZ` acts on at least two
qubits (finite check over all `4⁴` Paulis). -/

/-- **The `[[4, 2, 2]]` code**: two logical qubits (`XXXX`, `ZZZZ` are independent) and
distance exactly 2 (the logical `XXII` has weight 2). -/
/-! ## The Steane `[[7, 1, 3]]` code from the Hamming `[7, 4, 3]` code -/

/-- Parity-check matrix of the `[7, 4, 3]` Hamming code: column `j` is the binary expansion
of `j + 1`. -/
/-- The Hamming code `ker H` has minimum distance 3 (finite check over `2⁷` words). -/
/-- The Steane code: the CSS code with `HX = HZ = H` (Hamming parity checks). -/
/-- The Steane code encodes one logical qubit. -/

/-- The Steane code has (pure) distance at least 3, inherited from the Hamming code via
`css_hasPureDistance`. -/
/-- A weight-3 logical `X` operator of the Steane code: `X` on a weight-3 Hamming codeword. -/
/-- **The Steane code is a `[[7, 1, 3]]` code** (distance exactly 3). -/

comments.text: /-- `n`-qubit Paulis modulo phase: `(x, z)` stands for `X^x Z^z`. -/
/-- The symplectic form on `𝔽₂²ⁿ`. -/
/-- The form is alternating: every Pauli commutes with itself. -/
/-- The symplectic form as a bilinear form. -/
/-- **Nondegeneracy**: only the identity Pauli commutes with every Pauli. -/
/-! ## The actual operators -/
/-- The sign `(-1)^t` for `t ∈ 𝔽₂`. -/

/-- `X^x Z^z` acting on `n`-qubit state vectors `ψ : 𝔽₂ⁿ → ℂ` (amplitudes in the
computational basis): `|v⟩ ↦ (-1)^{z·v} |v + x⟩`. -/
/-- **Commutation relation**: `P_a P_b = (-1)^{symp a b} P_b P_a`. -/
/-- **Pauli operators commute iff their symplectic product vanishes.** -/
/-! ## Stabilizer codes -/
/-- A set of Paulis is isotropic (pairwise commuting). -/
/-- **Commuting checks generate a commuting group.** -/
/-- A stabilizer code (modulo phases): an isotropic subspace of `𝔽₂²ⁿ`. -/
/-- The stabilizer code generated by a family of pairwise-commuting checks. -/
/-- Every pair of stabilizer elements acts by commuting operators. -/
/-- The centralizer: all Paulis commuting with every stabilizer. -/

/-- **Isotropic bound**: a stabilizer group on `n` qubits has at most `n` independent
generators. -/
/-- Number of logical qubits `k = n - dim S`. -/
/-! ## CSS codes -/
/-- The CSS checks: `X`-type rows `(h, 0)` of `HX` and `Z`-type rows `(0, h')` of `HZ`. -/
/-- **CSS condition**: if `HX HZᵀ = 0`, all CSS checks commute. -/
/-- The CSS stabilizer code of a pair of parity-check matrices with `HX HZᵀ = 0`. -/
/-- Parity checks drawn from one self-orthogonal classical code give a CSS stabilizer code. -/
/-! ## Instances -/
/-- The `[[4, 2, 2]]` code: checks `XXXX` and `ZZZZ`. -/
/-- The `[[4, 2, 2]]` code as a stabilizer code. -/
/-- The `[[5, 1, 3]]` code: the four cyclic shifts `XZZXI, IXZZX, XIXZZ, ZXIXZ`. -/
/-- The five-qubit code as a stabilizer code. -/
/-- Coordinates reading off the coefficients of the five-qubit checks. -/
/-- The five-qubit code has four independent checks, hence `k = 5 - 4 = 1` logical qubit. -/

# Kitaev's toric code as a hypergraph product

The `L × L` toric code is the hypergraph product of the cyclic repetition code with itself.
Its check matrix `H_L` (rows `v_i + v_{i+1}`, indices mod `L`) is **not** of full row rank —
the sum of all rows vanishes — so `hgpCode_params` does not apply.  The generalized
Tillich–Zémor bound (`hgpCode_params_general`) does:

* `toricCode_params` — **the toric code `HGP(H_L, H_L)` on `2L²` qubits encodes `2` logical
  qubits and has distance exactly `L`.**
* `toricCode_correctable` — it corrects every error of weight `t` with `2t < L`.
* `surfaceCode_params` — the planar surface code `HGP(H, H)` (open repetition code, full rank)
  is a `[[(n + 1)² + n², 1, n + 1]]` code.
* `toricCode_ldpc`, `surfaceCode_ldpc` — all checks have weight `≤ 4` and every qubit meets
  at most `2` checks of each type.
-/

/-- The check matrix of the cyclic repetition code of length `L`: row `i` is `e_i + e_{i+1}`
(indices mod `L`). -/
/-- A function on `ℤ/L` invariant under the shift is constant. -/
/-- The only nonzero vector in `ker H_L` or `ker H_Lᵀ` is the all-ones vector. -/
/-- Every nonzero codeword of `ker H_L` has weight `L`. -/
/-- Every nonzero vector of `ker H_Lᵀ` has weight `L`. -/

/-- A kernel consisting of constant vectors, containing the all-ones vector, is
one-dimensional. -/

/-- The `L × L` toric code: the hypergraph product of the cyclic repetition code with
itself, on `L·L + L·L = 2L²` qubits. -/

/-- **Parameters of the toric code.**  For every `L ≥ 1`, the toric code `HGP(H_L, H_L)` is a
`[[2L², 2, L]]` code: it encodes two logical qubits, and its distance is exactly `L`.
The check matrix `H_L` has a redundant row, so this relies on the rank-free Tillich–Zémor
bound. -/
/-- The check matrix of the cyclic repetition code is rank-deficient: `rank H_L = L - 1`. -/

/-- **Error correction in the toric code.**  Two errors of weight `≤ t` with `2t < L` that
have the same syndrome differ by a stabilizer; so the `L × L` toric code corrects every error
of weight `≤ ⌊(L - 1) / 2⌋`. -/
/-! ## The planar surface code -/

/-- The check matrix of the open repetition code of length `n + 1`: row `i` is
`e_i + e_{i+1}`. -/
/-- The open repetition check matrix has full row rank. -/

/-- The planar surface code of distance `n + 1`: the hypergraph product of the open repetition
code with itself, on `(n + 1)² + n²` qubits. -/

/-- **Parameters of the planar surface code.**  For every `n`, the surface code
`HGP(H, H)` with `H` the `n × (n + 1)` open repetition check matrix is a
`[[(n + 1)² + n², 1, n + 1]]` code. -/
/-! ## Sparsity: weight-4 checks -/

/-- A vector whose support is covered by the fibres of two injective maps over single points
has weight at most `2`. -/

/-- **The toric code is LDPC.**  Every `X` and `Z` check of the `L × L` toric code acts on at
most `4` qubits, and every qubit is acted on by at most `2` checks of each type. -/

/-- **The planar surface code is LDPC.**  Every check acts on at most `4` qubits, and every
qubit is acted on by at most `2` checks of each type. -/

/-!
# Verified tree decoding for CSS stabilizer codes

This file connects the tree decoder of `Sovereign.Quantum.TreeDecoder.Decoder` with the CSS
codes of `Sovereign.Quantum.StabilizerDistance`.  (It is not a `module` file because it imports
that non-`module` file.)
-/

/-- The measured syndrome of a Pauli error `e = (x, z)` on the CSS code `(HX, HZ)`: the
`Z`-checks `HZ` see the `X`-part `x`, and the `X`-checks `HX` see the `Z`-part `z`. -/

/-- **The CSS tree decoder.**  `TZ` is a Tanner forest for the `Z`-checks (it decodes `X`
errors) and `TX` one for the `X`-checks (it decodes `Z` errors). -/
/-- `X`-type logical operators have weight at least the distance. -/
/-- `Z`-type logical operators have weight at least the distance. -/

/-- **Soundness of the CSS tree decoder.**  If both check matrices of a CSS code of distance `d`
have forest Tanner graphs `TX`, `TZ`, then every Pauli error `e` of weight at most
`⌊(d-1)/2⌋` is corrected up to a stabilizer: `decode(syndrome e) - e ∈ S`. -/

/-- **Correcting `X` errors with a tree-like `Z`-check matrix.**  Only `HZ` needs a forest
Tanner graph.  If every `X`-type logical operator has weight at least `dX`, every `X` error
`(x, 0)` with `|x| ≤ ⌊(dX-1)/2⌋` is corrected up to a stabilizer. -/
/-- **Correcting `Z` errors with a tree-like `X`-check matrix.** -/

/-- The CSS tree decoder implemented by the linear-time two-pass algorithm: it returns the lists
of qubits on which to apply `X` and `Z` corrections, and the total number of recursive calls. -/

/-- **Verified linear-time CSS decoding on tree-like check matrices.**  If both check matrices of
a CSS code of distance `d` have forest Tanner graphs, the two-pass decoder
* makes at most `4n + 4r + 4n + 4s + 4` recursive calls (linear in the size of the code), and
* returns corrections `(X on L₁, Z on L₂)` such that, for every Pauli error `e` of weight at most
  `⌊(d-1)/2⌋`, the correction differs from `e` by a stabilizer. -/

declarations.name: TForest
declarations.signature_heuristic:
inductive TForest (n r : ℕ) where
  | nil : TForest n r
  | var (v : Fin n) (children rest : TForest n r) : TForest n r
  | chk (c : Fin r) (children rest : TForest n r) : TForest n r
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

namespace TForest

variable {n r : ℕ}

/-- Variable labels. -/

declarations.name: vars
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def vars : TForest n r → List (Fin n)
  | nil => []
  | var v ch rest => v :: (vars ch ++ vars rest)
  | chk _ ch rest => vars ch ++ vars rest

/-- Check labels. -/

declarations.name: chks
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def chks : TForest n r → List (Fin r)
  | nil => []
  | var _ ch rest => chks ch ++ chks rest
  | chk c ch rest => c :: (chks ch ++ chks rest)

/-- Parity of the root variables. -/

declarations.name: roots
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def roots (e : Fin n → ZMod 2) : TForest n r → ZMod 2
  | nil => 0
  | var v _ rest => e v + roots e rest
  | chk _ _ rest => roots e rest

/-- Syndrome, with `b` the value of the parent variable. -/

declarations.name: synd
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def synd (e : Fin n → ZMod 2) : TForest n r → ZMod 2 → Fin r → ZMod 2
  | nil, _ => 0
  | var v ch rest, b => synd e ch (e v) + synd e rest b
  | chk c ch rest, b => Pi.single c (b + roots e ch) + synd e ch 0 + synd e rest b

/-- Local satisfaction of every check. -/

declarations.name: Sat
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def Sat (e : Fin n → ZMod 2) (s : Fin r → ZMod 2) : TForest n r → ZMod 2 → Prop
  | nil, _ => True
  | var v ch rest, b => Sat e s ch (e v) ∧ Sat e s rest b
  | chk c ch rest, b => b + roots e ch = s c ∧ Sat e s ch 0 ∧ Sat e s rest b

/-- Weight on the variables of the forest. -/

declarations.name: wt
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def wt (e : Fin n → ZMod 2) : TForest n r → ℕ
  | nil => 0
  | var v ch rest => (e v).val + wt e ch + wt e rest
  | chk _ ch rest => wt e ch + wt e rest

end TForest

/-- A table of four costs indexed by parent value and root parity. -/

declarations.name: Tbl
declarations.signature_heuristic:
structure Tbl where
  c00 : WithTop ℕ
  c01 : WithTop ℕ
  c10 : WithTop ℕ
  c11 : WithTop ℕ
  deriving DecidableEq

namespace Tbl

/-- Look up a cost. -/

declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem pick_spec (f : ZMod 2 → WithTop ℕ) : f (pick (f 0) (f 1)) = min (f 0) (f 1)

declarations.name: branch
declarations.signature_heuristic: def branch (C R : Tbl) (b p y : ZMod 2) : WithTop ℕ

declarations.name: nilTbl
declarations.signature_heuristic: def nilTbl : Tbl

/-- The optimal cost. -/

declarations.name: cost
declarations.signature_heuristic: def cost (s : Fin r → ZMod 2) (F : TForest n r) (b p : ZMod 2) : WithTop ℕ

declarations.name: cost_nil
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem cost_nil (s : Fin r → ZMod 2) (b p : ZMod 2) :
    cost s (nil : TForest n r) b p = if p = 0 then 0 else ⊤

declarations.name: cost_var
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem cost_var (s : Fin r → ZMod 2) (v : Fin n) (ch rest : TForest n r) (b p : ZMod 2) :
    cost s (var v ch rest) b p =
      min (branch (tbl s ch) (tbl s rest) b p 0) (branch (tbl s ch) (tbl s rest) b p 1)

declarations.name: branch_eq
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem branch_eq (s : Fin r → ZMod 2) (ch rest : TForest n r) (b p y : ZMod 2) :
    branch (tbl s ch) (tbl s rest) b p y =
      (y.val : WithTop ℕ) + min (cost s ch y 0) (cost s ch y 1) + cost s rest b (p + y)

declarations.name: cost_chk
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem cost_chk (s : Fin r → ZMod 2) (c : Fin r) (ch rest : TForest n r) (b p : ZMod 2) :
    cost s (chk c ch rest) b p = cost s ch 0 (s c + b) + cost s rest b p

declarations.name: dec
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def dec (s : Fin r → ZMod 2) : TForest n r → ZMod 2 → ZMod 2 → Fin n → ZMod 2

  | var v ch rest, b, p =>

declarations.name: dec_var
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem dec_var (s : Fin r → ZMod 2) (v : Fin n) (ch rest : TForest n r) (b p : ZMod 2) :
    dec s (var v ch rest) b p =
      Pi.single v (pick (branch (tbl s ch) (tbl s rest) b p 0)
          (branch (tbl s ch) (tbl s rest) b p 1)) +
        dec s ch (pick (branch (tbl s ch) (tbl s rest) b p 0)
          (branch (tbl s ch) (tbl s rest) b p 1))
          (pick (cost s ch (pick (branch (tbl s ch) (tbl s rest) b p 0)

          (branch (tbl s ch) (tbl s rest) b p 1)) 1)) +

first-child / next-sibling form: `var v ch rest` is the variable node `v` whose children (checks)

nothing else.

assignment to the variables of `F` that satisfies every check of `F` (given that the parent
variable has value `b`) and whose root variables have parity `p`, or `⊤` if there is none.
`dec` traces back an optimal assignment.

/-!
# The tree decoder: exactness and bounded-distance correction
-/
/-- A Tanner forest is well formed when no variable and no check label is repeated. -/

/-- A parity-check matrix is *tree-like* when its Tanner graph is a forest, witnessed by a
well-formed rooted Tanner forest whose parity-check matrix is `H`. -/

/-- **The tree decoder.**  Given a rooted Tanner forest `T` and a syndrome `s`, run the min-sum
dynamic programme and trace back a correction. -/

/-- **Exactness of min-sum on trees.**  For every error `e`, the tree decoder returns a vector
with the same syndrome as `e` and Hamming weight at most that of `e`. -/

/-- **Minimum-weight decoding.**  Whenever `s` is the syndrome of some vector `e'`, the tree
decoder returns a vector of syndrome `s` whose weight is minimal among all such vectors. -/

/-- **Bounded-distance correction (classical form).**  Suppose every vector in `ker H` that is not
in the "harmless" subspace `G` has weight at least `d` (for a CSS code, `G` is the row space of
the other check matrix).  Then for every error `e` of weight at most `⌊(d-1)/2⌋`, the tree
decoder output differs from `e` by an element of `G`. -/

/-- **Maximum-likelihood decoding for bit flips.**  On a binary symmetric channel with flip
probability `p ≤ 1/2`, the correction returned by the tree decoder is at least as likely as the
actual error (indeed as likely as any error with the same syndrome). -/

# A two-pass, linear-time implementation of the tree decoder
-/
/-- A Tanner forest annotated with the min-sum tables of the subtrees below each node. -/
/-- Number of nodes of a forest, counting the `nil` leaves. -/

/-- **Upward pass.**  Computes all min-sum tables bottom-up.  Returns the annotated tree, the
table of the root and the number of recursive calls made. -/

/-- **Downward pass.**  Traces back the optimal assignment, prepending the flipped variables to an
accumulator list and incrementing a call counter. -/

/-- **The fast tree decoder.**  Returns the list of variables to flip, together with the total
number of recursive calls made by the two passes. -/
/-- The vector with a `1` at every position listed (with multiplicity, mod 2). -/
/-- **The fast decoder computes the specified decoder.** -/

/-- **Exact step count.**  The two passes together make exactly `2 * size T` recursive calls, each
performing a constant number of table operations. -/
/-- A well-formed forest on `n` variables and `r` checks has at most `2(n + r) + 1` nodes. -/

/-- **Linear running time.**  On a well-formed Tanner forest with `n` variables and `r` checks,
the fast decoder makes at most `4(n + r) + 2` recursive calls. -/

/-!
# Multi-modal sensor fields as coupled differential forms on a spacetime chart

We model the four sensor modalities on a Minkowski coordinate chart `ℝ⁴` of a spacetime
4-manifold (coordinates `(t, x₀, x₁, x₂)`, as in `Sovereign.Pipeline.toMink`):

* the **acoustic pressure** `p`, a `0`-form (`FieldConfig.pressureForm`);
* the **electromagnetic field** as the Faraday `2`-form `F ∈ Ω²(ℝ⁴)` (Mathlib's
  `Chart4 → Chart4 [⋀^Fin 2]→L[ℝ] ℝ`), whose components `F_{μν} = F(∂_μ, ∂_ν)` contain the
  electric field `E_i = F_{i0}` and the magnetic field `B = (F_{23}, F_{31}, F_{12})`;
* the **gravitational wave strain** `h_{μν}`, a symmetric covariant 2-tensor field.

The **coupled PDE system** `CoupledFieldEquations` consists of
* `dF = 0` in the language of forms (Mathlib's exterior derivative `extDeriv`),
* the inhomogeneous Maxwell equations `∂^μ F_{μν} = J_ν`,
* the acoustic wave equation `□_{cs} p = Q + α F_{αβ}F^{αβ}` (electrostrictive driving by
  the electromagnetic invariant), stated with `Sovereign.Pipeline.AcousticWaveEquation`, i.e.
  with the wave operator `waveOp` of `Sovereign.Taxonomy.SynestheticResonance`,
* the linearised Einstein equation (Lorenz gauge) `□ h_{μν} = κ T_{μν}(F)`, sourced by the
  electromagnetic energy–momentum tensor `Sovereign.Pipeline.stressEnergy`.

Results:
* `bianchi_of_potential`: if `F = dA` for a `C²` potential `A`, then `dF = 0` (`d² = 0`);
* `CoupledFieldEquations.maxwellEquations`: every solution yields a solution of the
  component form `Sovereign.Pipeline.MaxwellEquations` of the pipeline (the component Bianchi
  identity is derived from `dF = 0`);
* `FieldConfig.observable`: the sensor vector `(p, F_{μν}, h_{μν})` and its `C²` regularity;
* `vacuumSolution`: the coupled system has solutions (non-vacuity).
-/
/-- A Minkowski coordinate chart `ℝ⁴ ≅ (t, x₀, x₁, x₂)` of a spacetime 4-manifold. -/
/-- Differential `k`-forms on the spacetime chart. -/
/-- The coordinate vector field `∂_μ`. -/
/-- The components `ω_{μν} = ω(∂_μ, ∂_ν)` of a `2`-form. -/
/-- A scalar field regarded as a `0`-form. -/
/-- The components of a `2`-form are antisymmetric. -/
/-- **`d² = 0`**: a Faraday form with a `C²` potential, `F = dA`, satisfies `dF = 0`. -/

/-- **The components of a closed 2-form satisfy the Bianchi identity**
`∂_λ F_{μν} + ∂_μ F_{νλ} + ∂_ν F_{λμ} = 0`. -/
/-- A symmetric covariant 2-tensor field: the gravitational-wave strain `h_{μν}`. -/
/-- A **multi-modal field configuration**: acoustic pressure, Faraday 2-form, GW strain. -/
/-- acoustic pressure (a `0`-form) -/
/-- the Faraday `2`-form `F = E ∧ dt + ⋆B` -/
/-- gravitational-wave strain `h_{μν}` -/
/-- The pressure as a `0`-form. -/
/-- The electric field `E_i = F_{i0}`. -/
/-- The magnetic field `B = (F_{23}, F_{31}, F_{12})`. -/
/-- The space of simultaneous sensor readings `(p, F_{μν}, h_{μν})` (sup norm). -/
/-- The **multi-modal sensor observable** `Y ↦ (p(Y), F_{μν}(Y), h_{μν}(Y))`. -/
/-- The d'Alembertian `□_c f = -c⁻² ∂_t² f + ∑ᵢ ∂ᵢ² f` in Minkowski coordinates. -/
/-- Coupling constants and external sources of the multi-modal field theory. -/
/-- speed of sound -/
/-- electro-acoustic (electrostrictive) coupling -/
/-- gravitational coupling (`-16πG/c⁴` in the Lorenz gauge) -/
/-- external acoustic source -/
/-- electric four-current -/
/-- **The coupled acoustic–electromagnetic–gravitational PDE system.** -/
/-- the strain is a symmetric tensor -/
/-- `dF = 0`: Gauss's law for magnetism and Faraday's law -/
/-- `∂^μ F_{μν} = J_ν`: Gauss's law and the Ampère–Maxwell law -/
/-- `□_{cs} p = Q + α F_{αβ}F^{αβ}`, on space-time `ℝ³ × ℝ` -/
/-- linearised Einstein equations `□ h_{μν} = κ T_{μν}(F)` -/
/-- Every solution of the coupled system solves the pipeline's component Maxwell equations. -/
/-- The sensor observable of a solution is `C²`. -/
/-- The vacuum configuration (no sound, no light, no gravitational wave). -/
/-- Source-free couplings with arbitrary constants. -/
/-- **Non-vacuity**: the vacuum solves the source-free coupled system. -/

/-- Scalar one-dimensional interpolation estimate, one-sided. -/
/-- Scalar one-dimensional interpolation estimate. -/

/-- **One-dimensional interpolation estimate** for a curve `g : ℝ → V` with `‖g''‖ ≤ M`:
`‖g(x) - ((1-θ) g(a) + θ g(b))‖ ≤ M/2 · θ(1-θ)(b-a)²` at `x = (1-θ) a + θ b`. -/
/-! ### Interpolation along one coordinate on the grid `δ ℤ` -/
/-- The lower grid node `δ ⌊x_k / δ⌋` of coordinate `k`. -/
/-- The barycentric weight `θ = frac(x_k / δ) ∈ [0, 1)` of coordinate `k`. -/

/-- **Linear interpolation of `Φ` in coordinate `k`** between the grid nodes
`δ ⌊x_k/δ⌋` and `δ ⌊x_k/δ⌋ + δ`. -/
/-- Interpolation is linear: it commutes with differences. -/
/-- Interpolation does not increase sup bounds (it is a convex combination). -/

/-- **One-coordinate interpolation error**: if `Φ` is twice differentiable with
`‖∇²Φ‖ ≤ M`, linear interpolation in coordinate `k` at scale `δ > 0` has error `≤ δ² M / 8`. -/
/-! ### Multilinear interpolation -/

/-- Successive linear interpolation in the coordinates of the list `l`
(the last coordinate of `l` is interpolated first). -/
/-- The multilinear interpolant in all `n` coordinates. -/
/-- **Multilinear interpolation error**: `‖Φ - I_l Φ‖ ≤ |l| δ² M / 8`. -/
/-- The points all of whose coordinates in `S` lie on the grid `δ ℤ`. -/
/-- The interpolant `I_l Φ` on `gridSet δ S` only depends on `Φ` on `gridSet δ (S ∪ l)`. -/
/-- **The multilinear interpolant only depends on the grid samples.** -/
/-! ### Reconstruction from raw sensor samples -/
/-- Raw sensor data: one reading in `V` for every lattice site `z ∈ ℤⁿ`. -/
/-- The sensor readings of a field `Φ` at the lattice sites `δ z`. -/
/-- Nearest-site extension of sample data (only its values on the grid matter). -/

/-- **The reconstruction map**: a continuous field built from sample data alone,
by multilinear interpolation of the samples. -/
/-- The reconstruction of the samples of `Φ` is the multilinear interpolant of `Φ`. -/

/-- **Reconstruction bound** (any dimension `n`): for a twice differentiable field with
`‖∇²Φ‖ ≤ M`, the field reconstructed from its samples on the grid `δ ℤⁿ` is within
`n δ² M / 8` of the true field everywhere. -/
/-- **Exactness at the sensors**: the reconstruction reproduces every sample. -/

/-!
# The universal synesthetic field reconstruction theorem

Fix a sensor discretisation scale `δ > 0`.

* `FieldCat δ`: objects are solutions of the coupled acoustic–electromagnetic–gravitational
  system (`CoupledFieldEquations`) with bounded Hessian `∇²Φ` of the sensor observable
  `Φ = (p, F_{μν}, h_{μν})`; morphisms `X ⟶ Y` are lattice translations `s ∈ ℤ⁴` of the
  sensor array carrying the configuration `X` to `Y`: `Φ_Y(y) = Φ_X(y + δ s)`.
* `LeanCertCat`: objects are **verified proposition certificates**: raw sensor data
  `ℤ⁴ → ObsSpace` together with a proposition and a Lean proof of it; morphisms are lattice
  re-indexings of the data together with an entailment between the propositions.
* `certFunctor δ : FieldCat δ ⥤ LeanCertCat` sends a solution to its sensor readings, with
  the proposition `reconstructionClaim` (the configuration solves the coupled PDE system, the
  reconstruction reproduces every reading, and the reconstruction error is at most
  `δ² ‖∇²Φ‖`) and its proof. It is faithful (`certFunctor_faithful`).

**Universal reconstruction theorem** (`universal_reconstruction`): for every object `X`, the
continuous field reconstructed *from the certificate data alone* satisfies
`‖Φ_X(y) - reconstruct δ (data (F X)) y‖ ≤ δ² ‖∇²Φ_X‖` for every event `y`, where
`‖∇²Φ‖ = sup_y ‖D²Φ(y)‖` (`hessNorm`).  In fact the sharper constant `δ²/2` holds
(`universal_reconstruction_sharp`).

The `#guard_msgs` checks at the end make the build fail unless the main theorems depend only
on the standard axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`.

The error bound is an honest numerical-analysis statement about multilinear interpolation:
see `Sovereign.Reconstruction.Interpolation`.
-/

  | var i => ρ i

  | one => CD.scalar 1
  | unit i => CD.unit n i
  | neg a => CD.neg (eval ρ a)
  | add a b => CD.add (eval ρ a) (eval ρ b)
  | sub a b => CD.add (eval ρ a) (CD.neg (eval ρ b))

  | zero | one | unit _ => 0

declarations.name: eval_congr
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem eval_congr {n : ℕ} {ρ ρ' : ℕ → CD R n} :
    ∀ t : ATerm, (∀ i < t.arity, ρ i = ρ' i) → t.eval ρ = t.eval ρ'
  | var i, h => h i (Nat.lt_succ_self i)
  | zero, _ | one, _ | unit _, _ => rfl
  | neg a, h => by simp only [eval, eval_congr a h]
  | conj a, h => by simp only [eval, eval_congr a h]
  | add a b, h | sub a b, h | mul a b, h => by
      simp only [arity, lt_max_iff] at h
      simp only [eval, eval_congr a fun i hi => h i (Or.inl hi),
        eval_congr b fun i hi => h i (Or.inr hi)]

    ∀ t : ATerm, CD.map f (t.eval ρ) = t.eval (fun i => CD.map f (ρ i))
  | var _ => rfl
  | zero => by simp [eval]
  | one => by simp [eval]
  | unit i => by simp [eval]
  | neg a => by simp [eval, eval_map ρ a]
  | conj a => by simp [eval, eval_map ρ a]
  | add a b => by simp [eval, eval_map ρ a, eval_map ρ b]
  | sub a b => by simp [eval, eval_map ρ a, eval_map ρ b]
  | mul a b => by simp [eval, eval_map ρ a, eval_map ρ b]

/-!
# Cayley–Dickson algebras and conjectures about them

`CD R n` is the `2ⁿ`-dimensional Cayley–Dickson algebra over a commutative ring `R`, built by
iterated doubling: `CD R 0 = R` and `CD R (n+1) = CD R n × CD R n` with

* conjugation `(a, b)* = (a*, -b)`,
* multiplication `(a, b)(c, d) = (a c - d* b, d a + b c*)`.

Over `R = ℝ` (or `ℚ`, `ℤ`) this gives the complex numbers (`n = 1`), quaternions (`n = 2`),
**octonions** `O₈` (`n = 3`), **sedenions** `S₁₆` (`n = 4`) and **trigintaduonions** `T₃₂`
(`n = 5`).  From `n = 3` on the algebras are non-associative.

Candidate conjectures (`AConj`) are identities `lhs ≈ rhs` between terms of the free
non-associative signature (`ATerm`: variables, `0`, `1`, basis units `eᵢ`, `-`, `+`, `-`, `·`,
conjugation), universally quantified over the variables.  `cdSem R n` is their semantics in
`CD R n`, a `Sovereign.Conjecturer.Semantics`, so every tool of the conjecturer (metamorphic
filters, refutation times, …) applies.

Ring homomorphisms `f : R →+* R'` induce algebra maps `CD.map f` commuting with evaluation
(`eval_map`); for injective `f` a counterexample over `R` is a counterexample over `R'`
(`holds_map_iff`).  In particular an integer witness refutes a conjecture over the real
octonions, sedenions and trigintaduonions.
-/

/-- Trigintaduonions `T₃₂` over `R`. -/

/-- First half. -/
/-- Second half. -/
/-- Decidable equality. -/
/-- View an element of `CD R 0` as a scalar. -/

/-- Addition. -/

/-- Conjugation. -/
/-- Cayley–Dickson multiplication `(a, b)(c, d) = (a c - d* b, d a + b c*)`. -/
/-- The standard basis unit `eᵢ` (`e₀ = 1`; `eᵢ = 0` for `i ≥ 2ⁿ`). -/
/-- Squared norm `x x*` (a scalar in the first coordinate). -/

/-!
# Continuous counterexample search over the real Cayley–Dickson algebras

The real octonions, sedenions and trigintaduonions `CD ℝ n` form a continuum, so a
counterexample search cannot enumerate them.  We show that searching the countable dense set of
**rational points** is nevertheless complete:

* `CD R n` carries the product topology (`CD.top`), is Hausdorff when `R` is, and the
  Cayley–Dickson operations are continuous (`CD.continuous_mul`, …); hence the evaluation of
  a term is continuous in the assignment of its variables (`ATerm.continuous_eval`);
* the image of a dense subring is dense (`CD.denseRange_map`);
* therefore the failure set of a conjecture, an open set, meets the dense set of rational
  assignments as soon as it is nonempty (`exists_witness_of_dense`).

Consequently (`real_not_valid_iff_rat`) a conjecture is false in `CD ℝ n` exactly when it is
false in `CD ℚ n`, and (`real_refuted_by_continuous_engine`) every conjecture false in the real
algebra is refuted in finitely many steps by the continuous engine over the rational points,
whose certificates map to genuine real counterexamples.
-/
/-- The product topology on `CD R n`. -/
/-- The image of a dense subring is dense in `CD R n`. -/
/-- **Evaluation is continuous** in the assignment (product topology on `ℕ → CD R n`). -/

/-- **Density transfer of counterexamples.** If `R'` embeds densely in the Hausdorff topological
ring `R`, every conjecture false in `CD R n` is already false at an `R'`-point. -/
/-- Under a dense embedding, falsity over `R` and over `R'` coincide. -/
/-! ### The real octonions, sedenions and trigintaduonions -/

/-- Semantics of conjectures in the real algebra `CD ℝ n` (e.g. `n = 3, 4, 5`: the real
octonions, sedenions, trigintaduonions). -/
/-- A conjecture is false over the reals exactly when it is false over the rationals. -/
/-- Every rational certificate yields a real counterexample. -/

/-- **Continuous counterexample search is complete for the real algebras.** Every conjecture
false in `CD ℝ n` has a finite refutation budget `N` for the continuous engine over the rational
points: proposed at any round whose budget is at least `N`, it is refuted after that round, and
its certificate yields a real counterexample. -/
