/-!
# DK orbit-partition correction: the true *centered* star-discrepancy interface

## Background and the falsity of `star_discrepancy_le_one`

A previous run already established that the grid-balanced orbit-partition field
`ContinuedFractionReturnData.orbit_partition` is **false** as stated.

This module establishes a sharper and more important correction:

> The *unsigned* orbit star-discrepancy bound
> `|orbitDiscrepancy θ (q n) x t| ≤ 1`
> (the `star_discrepancy_le_one` field of
> `StandardRealDenjoyKoksmaCombinatorics θ`) is **also false**, even for genuine
> continued-fraction convergent denominators.

The counterexample is the same golden-ratio datum that refutes the
orbit-partition field:

* `θ = (√5 − 1)/2` (the golden-ratio conjugate, irrational),
* `Q = 8` (a Fibonacci, hence convergent, denominator),
* base point `x = 1/10`, threshold `t = 1/10`.

Here exactly the two orbit points `j = 0` (value `1/10`) and `j = 5`
(value `≈ 0.0098`) fall in `[0, 1/10]`, so

```
orbitDiscrepancy θ 8 (1/10) (1/10) = 2 − 8·(1/10) = 6/5 > 1.
```

This is proved unconditionally below in `star_discrepancy_le_one_false`.

Consequently **both** `StandardRealDenjoyKoksmaCombinatorics` (the `≤ 1` bound)
and the stronger `ContinuedFractionReturnData` (grid-balancedness) are
*uninhabitable*, and the Denjoy–Koksma chain that routes through them is
vacuous.

## The true correction: the centered star-discrepancy bound

What *is* true for convergent denominators is the **centered** star-discrepancy
bound: there is a recentering constant `c` (depending on `n` and `x`) with

```
|orbitDiscrepancy θ (q n) x t − c| ≤ 1     for all t ∈ [0,1].
```

Equivalently the *oscillation* `sup_t disc − inf_t disc ≤ 2`.  (Numerically the
oscillation is `< 2` at genuine convergent denominators — e.g. it is `≈ 1.74`
for the golden case `Q = 8`, never reaching the false `sup |disc| ≤ 1`.)

This centered bound is exactly strong enough to feed the genuine **periodic**
Denjoy–Koksma estimate (constant `1`), because for a `1`-periodic test function
the recentering constant is invisible: shifting the discrepancy by a constant `c`
corresponds, after summation by parts, to adding `c·(h(1) − h(0)) = 0`.  We make
this precise via a *shifted-cell* version of Koksma's inequality
(`koksma_real_periodic_centered`), proved here from the project's already-proved
Koksma machinery together with the period-translation invariance of the integral
and the total variation.

The corrected combinatorial interface is therefore
`ContinuedFractionStarDiscrepancyData θ`, carrying the *true* centered
star-discrepancy bound (no grid-balancedness, no false `≤ 1` sup-bound), and it
yields the faithful periodic Denjoy–Koksma data
`RealDenjoyKoksmaPeriodic θ` directly.

No `sorry`, no `axiom`, no `unsafe`, no `@[implemented_by]` are introduced.
-/
/-! ## The golden-ratio counterexample to `star_discrepancy_le_one` -/
/-- The golden-ratio conjugate `(√5 − 1)/2 ≈ 0.618`. -/

/-
**The unsigned star-discrepancy bound `≤ 1` is false.**

For the golden-ratio conjugate (irrational), the convergent (Fibonacci)
denominator `Q = 8`, base point `x = 1/10` and threshold `t = 1/10 ∈ [0,1]`, the
orbit star-discrepancy equals `6/5 > 1`.  Hence the `star_discrepancy_le_one`
field of `StandardRealDenjoyKoksmaCombinatorics`, and a fortiori the
grid-balanced `ContinuedFractionReturnData.orbit_partition` field, are
*uninhabitable*.
-/
-- Calculate the value of `orbitCount` for the given parameters.

/-! ## A shifted-cell (centered) Koksma inequality

The centered Koksma inequality is proved by the same order-statistic argument as
the project's `koksma_general` / `koksma_real_periodic`, but with the test cells
shifted by `-c/Q`.  The recentering constant `c` is absorbed by two
period-translation facts: the integral and the total variation over the shifted
period `[-c/Q, 1-c/Q]` agree with those over `[0,1]`.  We isolate these as the
helper lemmas below. -/

/-
**Period-translation invariance of the total variation.**  For a `1`-periodic
function, the extended variation over any unit interval `[a, a+1]` equals the
extended variation over `[0,1]`.
-/
-- By integer-translation invariance (Step 1), `eVariationOn h (Icc a (a+1)) = eVariationOn h (Icc a' (a'+1))`.
-- By integer-translation invariance (Step 1), `eVariationOn h (Icc 1 (a'+1)) = eVariationOn h (Icc 0 a')`.
-- The translation `φ : t ↦ t - 1` is monotone, maps `Set.Icc 1 (a'+1)` onto `Set.Icc 0 a'`, and `h ∘ φ = h` because `h` is `1`-periodic.

/-
**Bounded variation on a compact interval implies interval integrability.**
Generalises `bv_intervalIntegrable` from `[0,1]` to an arbitrary interval.
-/

/-
**Per-interval Koksma bound on a general interval.**  Generalises
`koksma_interval_bound`: on any interval `[p,q]` of positive length on which `h`
has finite variation and is integrable, the deviation of `h zk` (for `zk ∈ [p,q]`)
from the scaled mean of `h` over `[p,q]` is bounded by the variation of `h` over
`[p,q]`.
-/
-- For every $t \in [p, q]$, $|h(zk) - h(t)| \leq \text{eVariationOn } h (Set.Icc p q)$.
-- Apply this bound to the integral of $|h(zk) - h(t)|$ over $[p, q]$.

/-
**Centered order-statistic localisation.**  Given a monotone enumeration `z`
of `Q` points in `[0,1)` whose counting function satisfies the *centered* unit
star-discrepancy bound (offset `c`), the `k`-th order statistic lies in the
shifted cell `[(k-c)/Q, (k+1-c)/Q]`.  Generalises `koksma_order_stat` (`c = 0`).
-/
-- Choose $t$ such that $(k+1-c)/Q < t < z k$ and $t \in [0,1]$.
-- Since $t < z k$, we have $\{i : z i ≤ t\} \subseteq \{i : i < k\}$.

/-
**General centered Koksma inequality** for a finite point set in `[0,1)` and a
`1`-periodic bounded-variation function.

If `y : Fin Q → ℝ` is a family of points in `[0,1)` whose orbit counting function
satisfies the *centered* unit star-discrepancy bound
`|#{k : y k ≤ t} − Q·t − c| ≤ 1` for some constant `c` and all `t ∈ [0,1]`, then
for every `1`-periodic bounded-variation `h`,
`|∑_k h(y_k) − Q·∫₀¹ h| ≤ concreteVariationReal h`.  The recentering constant `c`
is invisible because `h` is periodic.
-/
-- Enumerate the (sorted) orbit points as `z k = y (σ k)` with `σ` a permutation.
-- By `koksma_order_stat_centered`, `z k ∈ Set.Icc (a k) (a (k+1))` for each `k`.
-- By `koksma_interval_bound_gen`, for each `k`, `|h (y (σ k)) - Q * ∫ t in (a k)..(a (k+1)), h| ≤ (eVariationOn h (J k)).toReal`.

/-- **Recentered periodic Koksma inequality.**

The genuine periodic real Denjoy–Koksma estimate (constant `1`) follows from the
*centered* orbit star-discrepancy bound: if there is a constant `c` with
`|orbitDiscrepancy θ Q x t − c| ≤ 1` for all `t ∈ [0,1]`, then for every
`1`-periodic bounded-variation zero-mean `h`,

```
|∑_{j<Q} h (x − j θ)| ≤ concreteVariationReal h.
```

This is the corrected analogue of `koksma_real_periodic`, whose hypothesis is the
*false* uncentered bound (`c = 0`).  The recentering constant is invisible to a
periodic test function. -/
/-! ## The corrected continued-fraction star-discrepancy interface -/

/-- **Corrected continued-fraction star-discrepancy data.**

The honest replacement for the (uninhabitable) `StandardRealDenjoyKoksmaCombinatorics`
and `ContinuedFractionReturnData`.  It bundles the rotation return data with the
divergence of the denominators, the irrationality of `θ`, and the **true**
*centered* orbit star-discrepancy bound (equivalently, oscillation `≤ 2`) over
the convergent denominators — without the false grid-balanced orbit partition or
the false unsigned `≤ 1` sup-bound. -/
/-- The return denominators diverge to infinity. -/
/-- `θ` is irrational (so the `q n` are genuine convergent denominators). -/

/-- **Centered orbit star-discrepancy bound.**  For each `n` and base point `x`
  there is a recentering constant `c` with
  `|orbitDiscrepancy θ (q n) x t − c| ≤ 1` for all `t ∈ [0,1]`.  This is the true
  number-theoretic content (oscillation `≤ 2`) of the three-gap /
  best-approximation property of convergent denominators; it replaces the false
  `star_discrepancy_le_one` (`c = 0`) and the false grid-balancedness. -/

/-- **Adapter: corrected star-discrepancy data yields the faithful periodic real
Denjoy–Koksma data.**  Via the recentered Koksma inequality
(`koksma_real_periodic_centered`), the true centered star-discrepancy bound
discharges the `dk_real_periodic` field directly. -/

/-- **Faithful periodic real Denjoy–Koksma data from corrected star-discrepancy
data.**  Named in the `RealDenjoyKoksmaPeriodic.of…` style. -/

/-!
# Plan: uniform continued-fraction return sums (Stage 2B, not yet formalized)

This module records the formalization plan for the next stage, building on the
finite Fourier-mode return-sum infrastructure now available in
`RequestProject.Rotation.FourierReturnSums`.  It introduces **no** new axioms,
`sorry`s, or unproven statements: the intended theorem signatures below are
recorded only as comments, to be discharged in a later run.

## What is already available (Stage 2A, proved)

* `CriticalMixedHRT.RotationReturnData θ` — the reusable interface packaging a
  return-time sequence `(qₙ, pₙ)` with `qₙ > 0` and `qₙ θ - pₙ → 0`.
* `CriticalMixedHRT.fourierModeReturnSum_uniform_bound` /
  `fourierModeReturnSum_tendstoUniformly` — for `k ≠ 0`, the single Fourier-mode
  return sum `∑_{j<qₙ} e^{2πi k (x - jθ)}` tends to `0` uniformly in `x`.
* `CriticalMixedHRT.trigPoly_return_uniform_bound` /
  `trigPoly_return_tendstoUniformly` — for a finite mean-zero trigonometric
  polynomial `P(x) = ∑_{k ∈ s} a_k e^{2πi kx}` (`0 ∉ s`),
  `‖∑_{j<qₙ} P(· - jθ)‖∞ → 0`.

## Stage 2B target (Denjoy–Koksma; deferred)

The eventual uniform return-sum theorem for general `C¹` mean-zero functions is:

```text
theorem continued_fraction_return_sum_tendsto_zero_uniformly
    {θ : ℝ} (R : RotationReturnData θ) (hθ : Irrational θ)
    (φ : ℝ → ℂ) (hφ_per : Function.Periodic φ 1)
    (hφ_C1 : ContDiff ℝ 1 φ) (hφ_mean : ∫ x in (0:ℝ)..1, φ x = 0) :
    TendstoUniformly
      (fun n (x : ℝ) => ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (R.q n), φ (x - j * θ))
      (fun _ => (0 : ℂ)) atTop
```

### Intended proof

1. Approximate `φ'` in `L¹(𝕋)` by a mean-zero trigonometric polynomial `R`
   (Fejér / Weierstrass), and let `P` be its mean-zero antiderivative.
2. Apply the **Denjoy–Koksma inequality** to the bounded-variation function
   `φ - P` to bound `‖∑_{j<qₙ} (φ - P)(· - jθ)‖∞` by `2‖φ' - R‖_{L¹}`,
   which is small.
3. Bound `‖∑_{j<qₙ} P(· - jθ)‖∞` by the already-proved finite trigonometric
   polynomial return theorem `trigPoly_return_uniform_bound`.

Denjoy–Koksma itself (step 2) is **not** present in the current Mathlib and is
left to a dedicated future module; nothing in the current build depends on it.
-/

The measurable winding obstruction `measurable_cocycle_winding_eq_zero_of_phase_lift`

/-!
# Critical unimodular trinomial: finite torus zero set (Lemma 5.1)

This file formalizes the self-contained core of Lemma 5.1 of the dossier:
on `S¹ × S¹`, a trinomial `c₀ + c₁ z₁ + c₂ z₂` with all coefficients nonzero
has at most two zeros.

The reduction from characters `χ_{λ₁}, χ_{λ₂}` on `𝕋²` (with `λ₁, λ₂` a
`ℤ`-basis) to this `S¹ × S¹` statement is via the torus automorphism
`z ↦ (χ_{λ₁}(z), χ_{λ₂}(z))`; that bookkeeping is recorded separately.

The key algebraic observation (cleaner than the paper's trigonometric
argument): substituting `z₂ = -(c₀+c₁z₁)/c₂` and its conjugate, every solution
`z₁` satisfies
`(c̄₀c₁) z₁² + (|c₀|²+|c₁|²-|c₂|²) z₁ + (c̄₁c₀) = 0`,
a quadratic with nonzero leading coefficient `c̄₀c₁`, hence at most two roots.
-/

/-
**Lemma 5.1 (core).** For nonzero `c₀, c₁, c₂`, the trinomial
`c₀ + c₁ z₁ + c₂ z₂` has at most two zeros on the unit torus `S¹ × S¹`.
-/
-- By definition of $S$, we know that every element $(z₁, z₂)$ in $S$ satisfies $z₂ = -(c₀ + c₁ z₁) / c₂$.

-- By definition of $S$, we know that every element $(z₁, z₂)$ in $S$ satisfies $z₁$ being a root of the polynomial $Q(z₁) = (conj c0 * c1) * z₁^2 + (conj c0 * c0 + conj c1 * c1 - conj c2 * c2) * z₁ + (conj c1 * c0)$.
-- Since $Q$ is a polynomial of degree at most 2, it has at most 2 roots.

`concreteZakDense f x s := ∑' k : ℤ, f (x + k) * exp (-2π i k s)`

together with the concrete time-frequency shift `shiftFun a b` acting on

* `concreteZakDense_lattice_covariance_int` — integer lattice covariance;
* `concreteZakDense_rogue_covariance_real`  — real (rogue) covariance.

None of these need any summability hypothesis: periodicity in `s` is termwise
(`tsum_congr`), the rogue covariance pulls out a constant (`tsum_mul_left`) and

/-!
# Stage 6B — the concrete dense test subspace of `L²(ℝ)`

TASK B of the a.e.-Zak rewiring run.  The honest a.e.-level Zak model
(`l2ZakModelAE_of_dense_data`) consumes a **dense `ℂ`-submodule** `D` of
`Lp ℂ 2 volume`, closed under the time-frequency shift, on which the concrete
Zak transform is a densely-defined isometry.

This module supplies that submodule concretely as the class of (`L²`-classes of)
**continuous, compactly supported** functions `ℝ → ℂ`.  This is the natural test
class for the concrete Zak transform `concreteZakDense`:

* it is genuinely a `ℂ`-submodule of `Lp ℂ 2 volume`
  (`concreteZakDenseSubspace`);
* it is **dense** in `L²(ℝ)` (`concreteZakDenseSubspace_dense`), via Mathlib's
  `MemLp.exists_hasCompactSupport_eLpNorm_sub_le`;
* its representatives are closed under the time-frequency shift `shiftFun`
  (`concreteZakDenseSubspace_closed_under_shift`) and under pure modulation
  (`concreteZakDenseSubspace_closed_under_modulation`);
* each member has a continuous compactly supported representative, to which the
  finite-support Plancherel identity `concreteZakDense_plancherel` applies
  (`concreteZakDenseSubspace_to_fun`).
-/

/-- The membership predicate of the concrete dense test subspace: an `L²`-class
`f` belongs iff it has a continuous, compactly supported representative. -/

/-- The `ℂ`-submodule of `L²(ℝ) = Lp ℂ 2 volume` of classes with a continuous,
compactly supported representative. -/

/-- Every member of the dense subspace has a continuous compactly supported
representative (the test class on which the concrete Zak Plancherel identity
holds). -/

/-
**TASK B (density).** The continuous compactly supported classes are dense in
`L²(ℝ)`.
-/

-- Apply Mathlib's `MeasureTheory.MemLp.exists_hasCompactSupport_eLpNorm_sub_le` to `f`'s `MemLp` (from `Lp.memLp f`): it yields `g : ℝ → ℂ` with `HasCompactSupport g`, `eLpNorm (f - g) 2 volume ≤ ε`, `Continuous g`, and `MemLp g 2 volume`.

/-
**TASK B (shift closure).** If `g` is continuous with compact support then so

/-!
# Stage 6B — orthogonality and the finite-support Plancherel identity

The unitarity of the Zak transform rests on the orthonormality of the integer
Fourier characters `t ↦ e^{-2π i k t}` on the unit interval `[0,1]`.  This module
proves that orthogonality in the self-contained form

* `intervalIntegral_exp_two_pi_int` — `∫₀¹ e^{2π i m t} dt = if m = 0 then 1 else 0`;

and deduces the **finite-support (per-fibre) Plancherel identity**

* `finiteSupportZak_plancherel` —
  `∫₀¹ ‖∑ k ∈ s, c k · e^{-2π i k t}‖² dt = ∑ k ∈ s, ‖c k‖²`

for any finite coefficient family `c : ℤ → ℂ` supported on `s : Finset ℤ`.  This
is exactly the per-fibre Parseval identity for the concrete Zak transform
`concreteZakDense` applied to a window whose integer translates have finite
support; it is the orthogonality core of the full L²(ℝ) Plancherel identity
(`∫₀¹∫₀¹ ‖Zf‖² = ∫_ℝ ‖f‖²`), whose remaining content is the Tonelli swap plus the
decomposition of `∫_ℝ` into integer unit intervals.
-/

/-
**Orthogonality of integer Fourier characters on `[0,1]`.**
`∫₀¹ e^{2π i m t} dt = 1` if `m = 0` and `0` otherwise.
-/

/-
**Finite-support (per-fibre) Plancherel identity.**
For a finite coefficient family `c` supported on `s`,
`∫₀¹ ‖∑ k ∈ s, c k · e^{-2π i k t}‖² dt = ∑ k ∈ s, ‖c k‖²`.
-/
-- Expand the square of the absolute value and interchange the order of summation and integration.
-- Evaluate the integral $\int_0^1 e^{-2\pi i (j-k) t} dt$.

/-
For a window `f` supported in `[0, N)` and a base point `x ∈ [0,1)`, the
concrete Zak transform reduces to the finite sum over the `N` integer translates
that fall in the support window.
-/

/-
**Per-fibre Plancherel for finite-support windows.**
For `f` supported in `[0,N)` and `x ∈ [0,1)`,
`∫₀¹ ‖Zf(x,s)‖² ds = ∑_{k=0}^{N-1} ‖f(x+k)‖²`.
-/

/-
**Total `x`-mass identity.**
For `f` supported in `[0,N)`, measurable, with integrable square,
`∫ x in 0..1, (∑_{k=0}^{N-1} ‖f(x+k)‖²) dx = ∫_ℝ ‖f t‖² dt`.
-/
-- By translation invariance, we can rewrite the integral over each interval [i, i+1] as the integral over [0,1].

/-
**Concrete dense-class Plancherel identity.**
For a bounded, measurable window `f` supported in `[0,N)`,
`∫₀¹ ∫₀¹ ‖Zf(x,s)‖² dx ds = ∫_ℝ ‖f t‖² dt`.

The class of bounded measurable functions supported in a bounded interval is
dense in `L²(ℝ)` (it contains step functions and continuous compactly supported
functions); the boundedness makes all the finite-sum/integral interchanges and
integrability side-conditions in the Plancherel computation immediate.
-/
-- By Fubini's theorem, we can interchange the order of integration.

/-!
# Abstract linear-isometry extension from a dense subspace

This module provides the reusable Hilbert-space completion tool requested by the
`L²` Zak completion run (TASK B): a densely-defined linear isometry into a
complete space extends **uniquely** to a linear isometry of the whole space.

The proof is a thin wrapper around Mathlib's `ContinuousLinearMap.extend`
(extension of a continuous linear map along a dense uniform-inducing embedding):
the inclusion of a dense submodule is such an embedding, the extension is
continuous and agrees with the original map on the (dense) subspace, hence it
preserves the norm everywhere by continuity, upgrading the extended continuous
linear map to a `LinearIsometry`.

These are exactly the abstract analytic ingredient behind extending the densely
defined Zak transform `concreteZakDense` to all of `L²(ℝ)`.
-/

/-
**Dense linear-isometry extension (existence).**

If `D` is a dense subspace of an inner-product space `H` and `T₀ : D →ₗᵢ[𝕜] E`
is a linear isometry into a complete inner-product space `E`, then there is a
linear isometry `T : H →ₗᵢ[𝕜] E` agreeing with `T₀` on `D`.
-/
-- By the density of $D$, for any $x \in H$, there exists a sequence $\{y_n\}$ in $D$ such that $y_n \to x$.

/-
**Dense linear-isometry extension (uniqueness of the extending map).**

Any two continuous linear maps `H → E` that agree on a dense subspace `D` are
equal.  Together with `linear_isometry_extends_from_dense_subspace` this gives
existence and uniqueness of the densely-defined-isometry extension.
-/
-- Since $S(x) \neq T(x)$, there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $S(y) \neq T(y)$ for all $y \in U$.

declarations.name: L2ZakModel
declarations.signature_heuristic:
structure L2ZakModel where
  /-- The Zak transform `Zf(x,s)`. -/
  Zak : V → (ℝ → ℝ → ℂ)
  /-- The time-frequency shift `shift x ω = M_ω T_x = π(x,ω)`. -/
  shift : ℝ → ℝ → V → V
  /-- `Zak` is additive. -/
  Zak_add : ∀ f g x s, Zak (f + g) x s = Zak f x s + Zak g x s
  /-- `Zak` is `ℂ`-homogeneous. -/
  Zak_smul : ∀ (c : ℂ) f x s, Zak (c • f) x s = c * Zak f x s
  /-- Zak quasiperiodicity in the frequency variable: `1`-periodicity in `s`. -/
  Zak_periodic_s : ∀ f x s, Zak f x (s + 1) = Zak f x s
  /-- Integer lattice covariance:
  `Zak (M_n T_m f)(x,s) = e^{-2πi(n x + m s)} Zak f(x,s)`. -/
  lattice_cov : ∀ (f : V) (m n : ℤ) (x s : ℝ),
    Zak (shift (m : ℝ) (n : ℝ) f) x s =
      Complex.exp (-2 * ↑Real.pi * Complex.I * ((↑n * ↑x + ↑m * ↑s) : ℂ)) * Zak f x s
  /-- Rogue (real) covariance:
  `Zak (M_b T_a f)(x,s) = e^{-2πi b x} Zak f(x-a, s+b)`. -/
  rogue_cov : ∀ (f : V) (a b : ℝ) (x s : ℝ),
    Zak (shift a b f) x s =
      Complex.exp (-2 * ↑Real.pi * Complex.I * (↑b : ℂ) * (↑x : ℂ)) * Zak f (x - a) (s + b)
  /-- Plancherel / unitary identity (integrated form):
  `∫₀¹ ∫₀¹ ‖Zak f x s‖² dx ds = ‖f‖²`. -/
  norm_sq_integral : ∀ f : V,
    (∫ s in (0:ℝ)..1, ∫ x in (0:ℝ)..1, ‖Zak f x s‖ ^ 2) = ‖f‖ ^ 2

end CriticalMixedHRT

Mathlib does not (currently) provide the `L²(ℝ)` Zak transform together with its
quasiperiodicity, Plancherel and time-frequency covariance identities.  Rather
than postulate it as a custom `axiom`, this module records it as an **explicit
unitary interface** — a structure `L2ZakModel` over an abstract inner-product
space `V` (the stand-in for `L²(ℝ)`).

A model bundles:

  `Zak (shift m n f) x s = e^{-2πi(n x + m s)} · Zak f x s`  (`m n : ℤ`);

  `Zak (shift a b f) x s = e^{-2πi b x} · Zak f (x-a) (s+b)`  (`a b : ℝ`);

construction of a model from `Mathlib`'s `L²` API is the remaining external

theorem unconditional.

/-!
# Stage 6B — periodic gauge and pointwise unitarity of the polyphase fibre

The periodic Zak gauge `K_s(x) = e^{-2πi s x} F(x,s)` removes the
quasiperiodicity in the time variable, turning each Zak fibre into an honest
periodic function.  The polyphase (gauge) factor `e^{-2πi s x}` has modulus
`1`, so the gauge is *pointwise unitary*:

`‖K_s(x)‖ = ‖F(x,s)‖`.

Consequently the fibre `L²`-densities of `K` and of `F` coincide, which is what
lets the active-set defined through `K` be computed through the raw Zak transform
`F` (used in `FiberOperator.lean`).

/-!
# An honest a.e.-level `L²` Zak model and the dense-data reduction

The pointwise `L2ZakModel` (`RequestProject/Zak/L2Zak.lean`) demands its
additivity, quasiperiodicity and time-frequency covariance fields to hold
*pointwise for every `x s : ℝ` and every `f : V`*.  For a genuine `L²(ℝ)`
class `f` the Zak transform `∑' k, f(x+k) e^{-2πiks}` only converges a.e. on
fibres, and any map out of an `Lp` quotient that is pointwise-everywhere additive
must be built from a *linear section* of the quotient `{functions} ↠ L²`, which
cannot simultaneously intertwine the (uncountable family of) modulation
characters appearing in the covariance fields.  Hence the pointwise interface is
**too strong** to populate honestly from `L²` quotient data (documented in
`L2_ZAK_COMPLETION_STATUS.md`).

This module records the *honest* replacement: an a.e.-level model in which the
Zak transform is a genuine **linear isometry** `V →ₗᵢ[ℂ] W` into an abstract
complete `L²`-target `W` (the `L²([0,1]²)` stand-in), and the covariance
identities are equalities of `L²` classes.  In this formulation the Plancherel /
unitary identity is exactly the isometry property (`‖Zak f‖ = ‖f‖`), which is the
faithful `L²` content of the pointwise `norm_sq_integral` field.

The main results are the **dense-extension reductions** (`TASK D`/`TASK E`): a
densely-defined isometric Zak transform, together with covariance witnessed only
on the dense class, extends to a full a.e.-level model.  These are proved
unconditionally from the abstract extension tool
`linear_isometry_extends_from_dense_subspace`.
-/

/-
**Operator intertwining extends from a dense subspace.**

If a linear isometry `T : V →ₗᵢ[ℂ] W` intertwines the bounded operators `A` (on
`V`) and `B` (on `W`) on a dense subspace `D`, then it intertwines them
everywhere.  This is the abstract engine behind extending the dense Zak
covariance identities (lattice / rogue covariance) to the full `L²` transform.
-/
-- By the density of $D$, there exists a sequence $\{d_n\}$ in $D$ such that $d_n \to v$.

/-- **The honest a.e.-level `L²` Zak model.**

`W`.  Unlike the pointwise `L2ZakModel`, the Zak transform is packaged as a
**linear isometry** (so the Plancherel/unitary identity `‖Zak f‖ = ‖f‖` holds by
construction) and the time-frequency covariance identities are equalities in the
`L²` target `W`, realized through bounded modulation operators
`charLattice`/`charRogue` and the time-frequency shift operators `shift` on `V`.

This is the faithful a.e. replacement for the (too strong) pointwise model. -/

/-!
# Expansion and spectrum of the box-kite graph

The box-kite graph (the bipartite double cover of the octahedron, see `boxKiteGraph`) is the
graph of every connected component of the sedenion zero-divisor graph.  Here we compute:

* its Cheeger constant `h = 4/3`,
* its conductance `φ = 1/3`,
* its spectral gap `λ₂ = 2`,
* its full Laplacian spectrum `{0, 2, 4, 6, 8}`.
-/
/-- An optimal Cheeger cut of the box-kite graph (6 vertices, 8 boundary edges). -/
/-- **Cheeger constant of the box-kite:** `h = 4/3`. -/
/-- **Conductance of the box-kite:** `φ = 1/3`. -/
/-- The explicit sum-of-squares decomposition of `xᵀ L x - 2 xᵀ x` for the box-kite Laplacian. -/
/-- A Fiedler vector of the box-kite graph (a `λ = 2` eigenvector orthogonal to constants). -/
/-- **Spectral gap of the box-kite:** `λ₂ = 2`. -/
/-! ### The Laplacian spectrum of the box-kite -/
/-- The Laplacian satisfies `L (L - 2) (L - 4) (L - 6) (L - 8) = 0` (over `ℤ`). -/
/-- Integer eigenvectors of the box-kite Laplacian for the eigenvalues `0, 2, 4, 6, 8`. -/

/-- **Laplacian spectrum of the box-kite:** the eigenvalues of the Laplacian are exactly
`0, 2, 4, 6, 8` (with multiplicities `1, 2, 6, 2, 1`, not recorded here). -/

/-!
# `Sovereign.Coding`

Quantum error-correcting codes, CSS stabilizer codes, and quantum LDPC codes

Singleton, weight and self-orthogonality results as general theorems using Hamming distance;
`Code28` constructs an explicit doubly-even `[28, 12, 4]` code and proves its parameters.
-/

/-!
# Edge expansion, conductance and spectral gap of finite graphs

For a finite simple graph `G` on a vertex type `W` we define

* `edgeBoundary G S` : the number of edges leaving `S` (`|∂S|`);
* `cheegerConstant G` : the Cheeger constant (edge expansion)
  `h(G) = min { |∂S| / |S| : S ≠ ∅, |S| ≤ |W| / 2 }`;
* `volume G S` : the sum of the degrees of the vertices of `S`;
* `conductance G` : the (Cheeger) conductance
  `φ(G) = min { |∂S| / vol S : 0 < vol S ≤ vol W / 2 }`;
* `spectralGap G` : the spectral gap (algebraic connectivity, Fiedler value) of the Laplacian
  `λ₂(G) = inf { xᵀ L x / xᵀ x : x ≠ 0, ∑ x = 0 }`.

We prove that these quantities are invariants of graph isomorphism, and we prove the "easy"
Cheeger inequality `λ₂(G) ≤ 2 h(G)` for every finite graph.
-/
/-- The edge boundary `|∂S|`: the number of edges with exactly one endpoint in `S`. -/
/-- The Cheeger constant (edge expansion) `h(G) = min_{S ≠ ∅, |S| ≤ |W|/2} |∂S| / |S|`. -/
/-- The volume of a vertex set: the sum of the degrees of its vertices. -/
/-- The conductance `φ(G) = min_{0 < vol S ≤ vol W / 2} |∂S| / vol S`. -/
/-- The Rayleigh quotient `xᵀ L x / xᵀ x` of the graph Laplacian. -/

/-- The spectral gap (algebraic connectivity) of `G`: the infimum of the Rayleigh quotient of the
Laplacian over nonzero vectors orthogonal to the constant vector.  By the Courant–Fischer theorem
this is the second smallest Laplacian eigenvalue `λ₂`. -/
/-- The Laplacian quadratic form as a sum over (ordered) adjacent pairs. -/
/-- The Rayleigh quotient of the centred indicator vector of `S`. -/
/-- For a `d`-regular graph the conductance is the Cheeger constant divided by `d`. -/
/-- The easy half of the discrete Cheeger inequality: `λ₂(G) ≤ 2 h(G)`. -/

# The infinite family of Hamming codes and quantum Hamming codes

`Sovereign/Coding/HammingBound.lean` proves that the single binary `[7, 4, 3]` Hamming code is
perfect, and `Sovereign/Quantum/StabilizerDistance.lean` builds the Steane code from it.  This

A *Hamming parity-check matrix* of redundancy `r` is an `r × (2ʳ - 1)` binary matrix whose
columns are nonzero and pairwise distinct (`IsHammingMatrix`).  By counting, its columns then
enumerate *all* nonzero vectors of `𝔽₂ʳ`.  Such matrices exist for every `r`
(`hammingCheck`, `hammingCheck_isHammingMatrix`), and the explicit `3 × 7` matrix `hamming7H`
of the Steane code is one (`hamming7H_isHammingMatrix`).

For any Hamming matrix `H` of redundancy `r` with code `C = ker H`, `n = 2ʳ - 1`:

* `IsHammingMatrix.minWeight` — every nonzero codeword has weight `≥ 3`;
* `IsHammingMatrix.rank_eq` — `rank H = r`;
* `IsHammingMatrix.card_code` — `|C| = 2^(n - r)`, i.e. `C` is a `[2ʳ - 1, 2ʳ - 1 - r, 3]` code;
* `card_ball_one` — a binary Hamming ball of radius one in `𝔽₂ⁿ` has `n + 1` points;
* `IsHammingMatrix.perfect` — **`C` is perfect**: `|C| · |B(0, 1)| = 2ⁿ` and `C` has minimum
  distance `3 = 2·1 + 1`;
* `IsHammingMatrix.mul_transpose_self` — for `r ≥ 3`, `H Hᵀ = 0` (the simplex code `row H`
  is contained in `C`);
* `quantumHamming` — the CSS code with `H_X = H_Z = H` (`r ≥ 3`), and
  `quantumHamming_params`: it is a `[[2ʳ - 1, 2ʳ - 1 - 2r, 3]]` code, with distance exactly `3`.

# Distance of the hypergraph product code

Continues `Sovereign/Quantum/HypergraphProduct.lean`.  Write `dᵢ` for the minimum distance of
the classical code `ker Hᵢ`.

* `clean` — the cleaning lemma, in matrix form: a solution `(X_L, X_R)` of
  `X_L H₂ᵀ + H₁ᵀ X_R = 0` whose `X_L` uses fewer than `d₂` columns is `(H₁ᵀ Y, Y H₂ᵀ)`,
  provided `H₁ᵀ` is injective.
* `hgp_clean_X`, `hgp_clean_Z` — hence low-weight `X`-type (resp. `Z`-type) operators commuting
  with the checks are products of checks.
* `hgpCode_hasDistance` — **if `H₁`, `H₂` have full row rank, every logical operator of
  `HGP(H₁, H₂)` has weight `≥ min d₁ d₂`.**
* `hgpCode_not_hasDistance` — for any `H₁`, `H₂`, nonzero codewords `c₁ ∈ ker H₁`,
  `c₂ ∈ ker H₂` give logical operators `e_j ⊗ c₂` and `c₁ ⊗ e_b` of weights `|c₂|`, `|c₁|`.
* `hgpCode_params` — **`HGP(H₁, H₂)` of two full-rank codes is an
  `[[n₁n₂ + m₁m₂, k₁k₂, min(d₁, d₂)]]` code**, with the distance exact.
* `hgp_hamming7_params` — example: `HGP(Hamming₇, Hamming₇)` is a `[[58, 16, 3]]` code.

For codes whose check matrices are not of full row rank, the general Tillich–Zémor bound
`d ≥ min(d₁, d₂, d₁ᵀ, d₂ᵀ)` is not proved here.
-/
/-! ## Characteristic-two helpers -/
/-! ## The cleaning lemma -/
/-- The set of columns in which a matrix has a nonzero entry. -/
/-- The vectors supported inside a set of coordinates. -/

/-- **Cleaning lemma** (matrix form).  Let `X_L ∈ 𝔽₂^{n₁ × n₂}`, `X_R ∈ 𝔽₂^{m₁ × m₂}` satisfy
`X_L H₂ᵀ + H₁ᵀ X_R = 0`.  If the columns occupied by `X_L` are fewer than the minimum distance
of `ker H₂`, and `H₁ᵀ` is injective, then `(X_L, X_R) = (H₁ᵀ Y, Y H₂ᵀ)` for some `Y`. -/
/-! ## From vectors to matrices -/
/-- The `[n₁] × [n₂]` block of a vector on the hypergraph-product qubits, as a matrix. -/
/-- The `[m₁] × [m₂]` block of a vector on the hypergraph-product qubits, as a matrix. -/
/-- The number of columns occupied by a block is at most the weight of the vector. -/

/-- **X-type cleaning.**  An `X`-type operator commuting with all `Z` checks, of weight below
the distance of `ker H₂`, is a product of `X` checks, provided `H₁ᵀ` is injective. -/

/-- **Z-type cleaning.**  A `Z`-type operator commuting with all `X` checks, of weight below
the distance of `ker H₁`, is a product of `Z` checks, provided `H₂ᵀ` is injective. -/
/-! ## Relabelling helpers -/
/-! ## The distance of the hypergraph product -/

/-- **Distance of the hypergraph product (lower bound).**  If `ker H₁` and `ker H₂` have minimum
distances at least `d₁` and `d₂`, and `H₁`, `H₂` have full row rank (`H₁ᵀ`, `H₂ᵀ` injective,
i.e. `k₁ᵀ = k₂ᵀ = 0`), then every logical operator of `HGP(H₁, H₂)` has weight at least
`min d₁ d₂`. -/
/-! ## Logical operators of weight `d₁` and `d₂` -/
/-- The `X`-type operator `e_j ⊗ c₂` supported on one row of the `[n₁] × [n₂]` block. -/
/-- The `Z`-type operator `c₁ ⊗ e_b` supported on one column of the `[n₁] × [n₂]` block. -/

/-- **Distance of the hypergraph product (upper bound).**  If `c₁ ∈ ker H₁` and `c₂ ∈ ker H₂`
are nonzero, then `HGP(H₁, H₂)` has logical operators of weights `|c₁|` and `|c₂|`; in
particular its distance is at most `min |c₁| |c₂|`.  No rank assumption is needed. -/
/-! ## The `[[n₁n₂ + m₁m₂, k₁k₂, min(d₁, d₂)]]` theorem -/

/-- **Parameters of the hypergraph product of two full-rank codes.**  Let `ker H₁`, `ker H₂` be
classical `[n₁, k₁, d₁]` and `[n₂, k₂, d₂]` codes (with minimum-weight codewords `c₁`, `c₂`),
and let `H₁`, `H₂` have full row rank.  Then `HGP(H₁, H₂)` is an
`[[n₁n₂ + m₁m₂, k₁k₂, min(d₁, d₂)]]` code: `k₁k₂` logical qubits and distance exactly
`min d₁ d₂`. -/
/-! ## Example: the hypergraph product of the `[7, 4, 3]` Hamming code with itself -/

We build the Cayley–Dickson tower `ℤ, ℂ_ℤ, ℍ_ℤ, 𝕆_ℤ, 𝕊_ℤ` over the integers, using the doubling

The sedenions are the fourth doubling of `ℤ` (dimension `2^4 = 16`).  Everything is computable,
so that finite statements about sedenion products can be checked by evaluation.

/-!
# Cheeger constant, conductance and spectral gap of the sedenion zero-divisor graph

Main results:

* The full zero-divisor graph `zdGraph` (84 primitive zero divisors, 168 edges) has a total
  bottleneck: its Cheeger constant, conductance and spectral gap are all `0`, since it splits into
  7 connected components.
* Each component (box-kite) is bottleneck-free: Cheeger constant `4/3`, conductance `1/3`,
  spectral gap `2`, Laplacian spectrum `{0, 2, 4, 6, 8}`, and it satisfies both discrete Cheeger
  inequalities.
-/
/-! ### The full zero-divisor graph: a total bottleneck -/
/-- The first box-kite, as a vertex set of the zero-divisor graph. -/
/-- A vector which is `1` on the first box-kite and `-1` on the second one. -/
/-- The zero-divisor graph has Cheeger constant `0`. -/
/-- The zero-divisor graph has conductance `0`. -/
/-- The zero-divisor graph has spectral gap (algebraic connectivity) `0`. -/
/-! ### Each box-kite component: bottleneck-free expansion -/
/-- **Cheeger constant of every box-kite component:** `h = 4/3`. -/
/-- **Conductance of every box-kite component:** `φ = 1/3`. -/
/-- **Spectral gap of every box-kite component:** `λ₂ = 2`. -/

/-- Every box-kite component is bottleneck-free: its Cheeger constant, conductance and spectral
gap are all strictly positive. -/

/-- **Both discrete Cheeger inequalities hold for every box-kite component** (degree `d = 4`):
`λ₂ / 2 ≤ h ≤ √(2 d λ₂)`, and, for the normalised gap `λ₂ / d`,
`(λ₂ / d) / 2 ≤ φ ≤ √(2 λ₂ / d)`.  Numerically: `1 ≤ 4/3 ≤ 4` and `1/4 ≤ 1/3 ≤ 1`. -/

/-!
# The graph of primitive sedenion zero divisors

A *primitive* sedenion is one of the form `e i ± e j` with `1 ≤ i < j ≤ 15`
(indexed by triples `(i, j, s)`, where `s = true` means `+` and `s = false` means `-`).

We show that such an element is a (two-sided) zero divisor inside this family exactly when
`1 ≤ i ≤ 7`, `9 ≤ j ≤ 15` and `j ≠ i + 8` (de Marrais' "assessors"), giving 84 zero divisors.
The *zero-divisor graph* `zdGraph` has these 84 elements as vertices, two of them being adjacent
when their product vanishes.

Each vertex has a *strut constant* `strut v = (i xor j) - 8 ∈ {1, …, 7}`, and we show that two
vertices lie in the same connected component iff they have the same strut constant.  Each
component (a *box-kite*) is isomorphic to the bipartite double cover of the octahedron.
-/
/-- Indices `(i, j, s)` of the primitive element `e i + (±1) e j`. -/
/-- The sedenion `e i + e j` (if `s = true`) or `e i - e j` (if `s = false`). -/
/-- `(i, j, s)` indexes a primitive element: `1 ≤ i < j ≤ 15`. -/
/-- De Marrais' assessor condition: `1 ≤ i ≤ 7`, `9 ≤ j ≤ 15`, `j ≠ i + 8`. -/

/-- **Classification of primitive zero divisors.**  A primitive sedenion `e i ± e j` is
annihilated by some primitive sedenion iff `(i, j)` is an assessor pair. -/
/-- The vertices of the zero-divisor graph: the 84 primitive zero divisors. -/

/-- The zero-divisor graph of the primitive sedenion zero divisors: `u ~ v` iff `u * v = 0`
(which, as we show, is equivalent to `v * u = 0`). -/
/-- Adjacent vertices really are zero divisors: the product vanishes in both orders. -/
/-- The zero-divisor graph is 4-regular. -/
/-- The zero-divisor graph has 168 edges. -/
/-- The strut constant `(i xor j) - 8` of a vertex (it lies in `{1, …, 7}`). -/
/-! ### The box-kite model graph -/
/-! ### The seven box-kites -/

/-- For each strut constant `k + 1` (`k : Fin 7`), the six assessors of the corresponding
box-kite, listed so that `a` and `a + 3` are opposite (the "struts" of the box-kite). -/

/-- The index of the vertex of box-kite `k` corresponding to the model vertex `x`
(the `Bool` coordinate of the model flips the sign). -/
/-- The vertex set of the `k`-th box-kite: the vertices of strut constant `k + 1`. -/
/-- The embedding of the model into the zero-divisor graph as the `k`-th box-kite. -/
/-- **Each box-kite component is the bipartite double cover of the octahedron.** -/

/-- **Connected components of the zero-divisor graph.**  Two primitive zero divisors are
connected by a path iff they have the same strut constant. -/
/-- The zero-divisor graph is **not** connected. -/
/-- The zero-divisor graph has exactly 7 connected components (the 7 box-kites). -/

# Automorphisms and derivations of real Cayley–Dickson algebras

For a real Cayley–Dickson algebra `A` (see `Sovereign.Algebra.RealCayleyDickson`):

* `CDAut A` : the automorphism group, i.e. the `ℝ`-linear bijections `f` with
  `f (x y) = f x f y`, as a subgroup of `A ≃ₗ[ℝ] A`;
* `CDDer A` : the derivation algebra, i.e. the `ℝ`-linear maps `D` with
  `D (x y) = D x · y + x · D y`, as a Lie subalgebra of `Module.End ℝ A`
  (no associativity is needed for the bracket to close);
* `diagLin f` : the diagonal action `(a, b) ↦ (f a, f b)` on the doubling `CD A`;
* `flipAut` : the involution `(a, b) ↦ (a, -b)`, an automorphism of every doubling.
-/
/-- The automorphism group of a (possibly non-associative) real algebra. -/
/-- Automorphisms fix the unit. -/
/-- The derivation algebra of a (possibly non-associative) real algebra. -/
/-- Derivations kill the unit. -/
/-! ### The diagonal action on a doubling -/
/-- The diagonal action `(a, b) ↦ (f a, f b)` of a linear map on the doubling. -/
/-- The diagonal action of a linear equivalence. -/
/-- The diagonal action of an automorphism commuting with conjugation is an automorphism. -/
/-- The diagonal action of a derivation commuting with conjugation is a derivation. -/
/-! ### The flip involution -/
/-- The involution `(a, b) ↦ (a, -b)` as a linear equivalence. -/
/-- `(a, b) ↦ (a, -b)` is an automorphism of every Cayley–Dickson doubling. -/
/-- The flip automorphism. -/

# Strong identities and their exact failure in the Cayley-Dickson tower

`AuditGenerated` records associativity, alternativity and flexibility for the
*two-dimensional* stage of the tower and only for *basis* elements.  Those are the weakest
possible instances: the 2-dimensional algebra is commutative and associative, so every
such identity is automatic.

This module proves the sharp statements for the concrete integral tower
`ℤ ⊂ CDComplex ⊂ CDQuaternion ⊂ CDOctonion ⊂ CDSedenion`, for **all** elements, not just
basis elements, and pins down exactly where each identity first fails:

* `quaternion_mul_assoc` : the Lipschitz quaternions are associative (all elements).
* `quaternion_mul_not_comm` : commutativity already fails at dimension 4.
* `octonion_mul_left_alt`, `octonion_mul_right_alt`, `octonion_flexible` : the integral
  octonions are alternative and flexible (all elements) — associativity is the exact
  identity that is lost at dimension 8 (`octonion_mul_not_assoc`).
* `sedenion_not_left_alternative` : alternativity itself is lost at dimension 16.

Everything is a `ring` identity on the coordinates or a finite computation; no `sorry`,
no external axioms.
-/
/-! ## Coordinate simp lemmas for the Cayley-Dickson product -/
/-- Reduce an identity in the tower to integer coordinate identities. -/
/-! ## Dimension 4: associative, not commutative -/
/-- **The Lipschitz quaternions are associative**, for all elements. -/
/-- Commutativity is already lost at dimension 4: `i * j ≠ j * i`. -/
/-! ## Dimension 8: alternative and flexible, not associative -/

/-- **The integral octonions are left alternative**: `(x * x) * y = x * (x * y)` for all
elements. -/

/-- **The integral octonions are right alternative**: `(x * y) * y = x * (y * y)` for all
elements. -/
/-- **The integral octonions are flexible**: `(x * y) * x = x * (y * x)`. -/
/-- `e₁`, `e₂`, `e₄` associate non-trivially: associativity fails at dimension 8. -/
/-! ## Dimension 16: alternativity fails -/

/-- With `x = e₁ + e₁₀` and `y = e₄`, left alternativity fails in the integral sedenions:
the sedenions are not an alternative algebra. -/

This module adds the 128-dimensional Cayley–Dickson algebra

`Sovereign.Algebra.Sexagintaquattuorion`), identifies it with level `7` of the tower, and
specialises the universal cross-half zero-divisor theorem of
`Sovereign.Algebra.CrossHalfZeroDivisorTheorem` to `D = 128`:

* `S128.components_card`, `S128.components_card_eq_PG` : their annihilation graph has exactly
  `63 = |PG(5, 𝔽₂)|` connected components;
* `S128.component_card` : every component has exactly `248 = 2(128 - 4)` vertices, and
  `S128.component_supp_equiv` : any two components have vertex sets in bijection.

The components are *not* all isomorphic as graphs; see
`Sovereign.Algebra.CentumduodevigintionComponents`.  The comparison of `248` with `𝔢₈` is in
`Sovereign.Algebra.CentumduodevigintionE8`.

/-- Sexagintaquattuorion difference. -/

the product `(a, b)(c, d) = (ac - d̄ b, d a + b c̄)`. -/

(sign `true` means `-`): its first half is `± eᵢ`, its second half is `± eⱼ`. -/
/-- Level `7` of the abstract tower is the concrete 128-dimensional algebra. -/
/-- The cross-half element `e₁ + e₆₄₊₁₀` annihilates `e₂ + e₆₄₊₉`. -/
/-- A concrete zero-divisor pair of `𝕊₁₂₈`: `(e₁ + e₇₄)(e₂ + e₇₃) = 0`. -/
/-- The abstract basis of `Tower 7` is the concrete basis `e128`. -/

/-- The abstract product of `Tower 7` is (definitionally) the concrete Cayley–Dickson product
of `𝕊₁₂₈`. -/

/-- Consequently the abstract product agrees with the concrete one on all `128 × 128` pairs of
basis vectors. -/
/-! ## 2. The zero-divisor theorem for `D = 128` (level `N = 6`) -/
/-- **15624 cross-half zero divisors in `𝕊₁₂₈`.** -/
/-- **63 components.** -/
/-- The 63 components are counted by the points of `PG(5, 𝔽₂) = ℙ(𝔽₂⁶)`. -/
/-- **Each component has 248 vertices**, and `63 · 248 = 15624`. -/

/-- Any two components have the same number of vertices (so their vertex sets are in
bijection). -/

# The 63 zero-divisor components of `𝕊₁₂₈` are not all isomorphic

The universal theorem (`Sovereign.Algebra.CrossHalfZeroDivisorTheorem`,
`Sovereign.Algebra.Sexagintaquattuorion`) shows that at `D = 128` the `15624` cross-half zero
divisors split into `63 = |PG(5, 𝔽₂)|` components of `248` vertices each.  Equal size does not
make them isomorphic graphs.  This module proves:

* `S128.comp1_has_triangle` : the component of XOR charge `1` contains a triangle;
* `S128.adj_color32`, `S128.comp32_triangleFree` : the component of XOR charge `32` is
  bipartite (explicit two-colouring `color32`), hence contains no triangle;
* `S128.components_not_all_isomorphic` : hence these two components (both with `248`
  vertices) are **not isomorphic** as graphs, and `S128.not_forall_components_isomorphic`:
  the 63 components are not all isomorphic.
-/
/-! ## 1. The edge law as a boolean -/

/-- The combinatorial edge law (`vec_mul_eq_zero_iff`) at level `N`, as a boolean:
`vec N x * vec N y = 0`. -/
/-- Adjacency in the annihilation graph (product zero in either order), as a boolean. -/
/-! ## 2. Vertices -/
/-- The zero divisor `± eᵢ ± e_{H+j}` (for `0 < i, j < 2ᴺ`, `i ≠ j`) as a vertex. -/
/-! ## 3. Two non-isomorphic components at `D = 128` (level `N = 6`) -/

/-- The three vertices `e₂ + e₆₄₊₃`, `e₄₈ - e₆₄₊₄₉`, `e₁₂ - e₆₄₊₁₃` of charge `1` are
pairwise adjacent. -/
/-- The component of charge `1`, containing `e₂ + e₆₄₊₃`. -/
/-- The component of charge `32`, containing `e₁ + e₆₄₊₃₃`. -/
/-- Vertices of the charge-`32` component have charge `32`. -/
/-- A two-colouring of the charge-`32` sector: the sign parity, flipped for `i > 32`. -/

/-- The index identity behind the two-colouring: across every admissible pair of indices of the
charge-`32` sector, the edge parity is the opposite of the XOR of the two colour offsets. -/
/-- **The charge-`32` component is bipartite:** adjacent vertices have different colours. -/
/-- A triangle of the whole graph with one vertex in a component lies in that component. -/
/-- **The component of charge `1` contains a triangle.** -/
/-- **The component of charge `32` is triangle-free.** -/

/-- **The 63 components of `𝕊₁₂₈` are not all isomorphic.**  The components of charge `1`
and `32` both have `248` vertices, but there is no graph isomorphism between them: the first
contains a triangle and the second does not. -/

/-- Restated: it is false that every two of the 63 components of the `𝕊₁₂₈` zero-divisor
graph are isomorphic. -/

# An `E₈` root system inside `𝕊₁₂₈`, and the associator kernel

The integer `248 = 2(128 - 4)` (the size of each zero-divisor component of `𝕊₁₂₈`) equals
`dim 𝔢₈ = 240 + 8` (roots plus rank).  This module does not claim any structural link
between the zero-divisor components and `𝔢₈`; instead it builds an actual `E₈` root system
inside the octonion subalgebra `𝕆 ⊂ 𝕊₁₂₈` and proves what the associator does to it.

Roots are stored doubled, as the integer vectors `v ∈ ℤ⁸` of squared length `4` whose
reduction mod 2 lies in the extended Hamming code `H₈` (`E8Roots`, the minimal vectors of the
Construction-A lattice, a copy of `√2 · E₈`).  Explicitly these are the `16` vectors `± 2 eᵢ`
and the `224` vectors `± e_p ± e_q ± e_r ± e_s` whose support `{p, q, r, s}` is one of the `14`
blocks of a Steiner system `S(3, 4, 8)`.  Through the
coordinates `v ↦ v₀ e₀ + ⋯ + v₇ e₇` of `𝕆 ⊂ 𝕊₁₂₈` (`rootC`), the halved roots `v / 2` are
units of the octonions.

Main results:

* `E8Roots_card` : there are exactly `240` roots, and `E8Roots_card_add_rank` :
  `240 + 8 = 248 = 2 (128 - 4)`;
* `E8Roots_norm`, `E8Roots_dot`, `E8Roots_reflect` : every root has squared length `4`,
  inner products lie in `{0, ±2, ±4}`, and the set is closed under all the reflections
  `s_α(β) = β - (2⟨α, β⟩ / ⟨α, α⟩) α`;
* `simpleRoot_gram` : eight simple roots whose Cartan matrix is Mathlib's
  `CartanMatrix.E₈`; `E8Roots_base` : every root is an integer combination of them with all
  coefficients `≥ 0` or all `≤ 0`;
* `E8Roots_mul_closed` : the roots are closed under the product of `𝕊₁₂₈`
  (`rootC u * rootC v = 2 • rootC w`, i.e. the unit octonions `u/2` form a loop);
* `assocKernel_reflect` (**associator kernel**) : for *any* `x, y ∈ 𝕊₁₂₈`, the set of roots
  `z` with `[x, y, z] = (xy)z - x(yz) = 0` is closed under negation and under the reflections
  in its own members, so it is itself a root subsystem of `E₈`;
* `assocKernel_product_root` : if `[x, y, z] = 0` for roots `x, y, z`, the common value
  `(xy)z = x(yz)` is again (four times) a root;
* `assocKernel_e1_e2_card` : for `x = e₁`, `y = e₂` the kernel has exactly `24` roots
  (a `D₄` subsystem, the roots of the quaternion subalgebra `⟨1, e₁, e₂, e₃⟩`).
-/
/-! ## 1. Integer 8-vectors and the `E₈` roots -/
/-- Integer vectors of length 8 (doubled root coordinates). -/
/-- The standard inner product on `ℤ⁸`. -/
/-- The reflection in `a` (for `⟨a, a⟩ = 4`): `s_a(b) = b - (⟨a, b⟩ / 2) a`. -/
/-- The 14 blocks of the Steiner system `S(3, 4, 8)` used for the half-integral roots. -/

/-- The extended Hamming code `[8, 4, 4]` over `𝔽₂`: the zero word, the all-ones word and the
indicator words of the 14 blocks. -/
/-- Reduction of an integer vector mod 2. -/

/-- The root predicate: squared length `4` and reduction mod 2 in the Hamming code, i.e. the
minimal vectors of the Construction-A lattice `{v ∈ ℤ⁸ | v mod 2 ∈ H₈}` (a copy of `√2 · E₈`). -/
/-- All coordinates lie in `[-2, 2]`. -/

/-- The (doubled) `E₈` roots: integer vectors with coordinates in `[-2, 2]` satisfying
`IsRoot`. -/
/-! ### The lattice argument -/
/-- The Hamming code is a linear code. -/
/-- The Hamming code is doubly even: any two code words meet in an even number of places. -/
/-- A vector of squared length `4` has all coordinates in `[-2, 2]`. -/
/-- Inner products of roots are even. -/
/-- The vector with coordinates read from an array (missing entries are `0`). -/
/-- The unit root `s eᵢ` as an array. -/
/-- The root `± e_p ± e_q ± e_r ± e_s` on the block `q`, with signs given by the bits of `s`. -/
/-- The 240 roots, as arrays. -/
/-- An explicit list of the 240 roots. -/
/-- The coordinates in `[-2, 2]` with a given parity. -/
/-- Completeness of the explicit list, checked code word by code word. -/
/-- **There are exactly 240 roots.** -/

/-- `240` roots plus rank `8` give `248 = dim 𝔢₈`, which is also `2 (128 - 4)`, the number of
vertices in each zero-divisor component of `𝕊₁₂₈`. -/
/-- Every root has squared length `4`. -/
/-- Inner products of roots lie in `{0, ±2, ±4}` (integral Cartan numbers). -/

/-- **Closure under reflections** (by the lattice argument: reflections preserve the
Construction-A lattice and squared lengths). -/
/-- Closure under negation. -/
/-! ## 2. A base with Cartan matrix `E₈` -/
/-- Eight simple roots. -/

/-- **The Cartan matrix of the simple roots is `E₈`:** `2⟨αᵢ, αⱼ⟩ / ⟨αⱼ, αⱼ⟩ = (E₈)ᵢⱼ`
(here `⟨αⱼ, αⱼ⟩ = 4`). -/
/-- Coordinates of a vector in the basis of simple roots (exact for the lattice). -/

/-- **The simple roots form a base:** every root is an integer combination of the simple roots
whose coefficients are all non-negative or all non-positive. -/
/-! ## 3. The octonion subalgebra of `𝕊₁₂₈` -/
/-- The octonion with coordinates `v₀, …, v₇` (in the basis of `Tower 3`). -/
/-- The inclusion `Tower n → Tower (n+1)`, `a ↦ (a, 0)`. -/
/-- The octonion subalgebra `𝕆 ⊂ 𝕊₁₂₈ = Tower 7` (coordinates `0, …, 7`). -/
/-- The coordinates of an octonion. -/
/-- A (doubled) root, as an element of `𝕊₁₂₈`. -/
/-! ## 4. Multiplicative closure -/
/-- Halving a vector coordinatewise. -/
/-- The octonion product of two coordinate vectors. -/
/-- The Construction-A lattice. -/

/-- **Multiplicative closure.** The product in `𝕊₁₂₈` of two (doubled) roots is twice a
(doubled) root: the 240 unit octonions `v / 2` are closed under multiplication. -/
/-! ## 5. The associator kernel -/
/-- The associator `[x, y, z] = (xy)z - x(yz)`. -/
/-- The associator is `ℤ`-linear in its last argument. -/
/-- The roots `z` with `[x, y, z] = 0`. -/

/-- **The associator kernel is a root subsystem.**  For any `x, y ∈ 𝕊₁₂₈`, the roots `z`
with `[x, y, z] = 0` are closed under the reflections `s_α` for `α` in the kernel. -/
/-- The associator kernel is closed under negation. -/

/-- In the associator kernel, the common value `(xy)z = x(yz)` of three roots is four times
a root. -/
/-- The (doubled) roots `2e₁` and `2e₂` of `𝕊₁₂₈`. -/
/-- See `e1Root`. -/

/-- **Example: the kernel for `x = e₁`, `y = e₂`.**  A root `z` satisfies
`[e₁, e₂, z] = 0` exactly when it lies in the quaternion subalgebra `⟨1, e₁, e₂, e₃⟩`
(coordinates `4, …, 7` vanish). -/
/-- The kernel for `x = e₁`, `y = e₂` has exactly `24` roots (a `D₄` root system). -/

# Cross-half zero divisors in every dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16`: count and charge sectors

Using the universal criterion of `CrossHalfCriterion` this module identifies the cross-half zero
divisors of `Tower (n+1)` *inside the algebra* with the combinatorial model `zdVerts` of
`CrossHalfUniversal`, and sets up the annihilation graph.

Main results:

* `vec_mul_eq_zero_iff` : the edge law — a product of two cross-half vectors vanishes iff the
  partner index is `k ^^^ i ^^^ j`, `crossOK` holds and the four signs have parity `edgePar`;
* `crossZD_eq`, `crossZD_card` : the zero divisors are exactly the labels with `i ≠ 0`,
  `j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j`; there are `(D - 2)(D - 4)` of them;
* `crossSector_card`, `crossZD_eq_biUnion`, `crossSector_disjoint` : the XOR charge
  `i ^^^ j` partitions them into `D/2 - 1` sectors of `2(D - 4)` elements;
* `adj_mem`, `reachable_mem` : annihilation (in either order) preserves the charge and never
  leaves the zero divisors.
-/
/-! ## 1. Labels, vectors and the annihilation graph -/
/-- A label `((i, j), (s, t))` of the cross-half vector `signed s eᵢ + signed t e_{H+j}`. -/
/-- The cross-half vector of `Tower (n+1)` attached to a label. -/
/-- Both indices of the label are below `H = 2ⁿ`. -/

/-- `x` is a cross-half zero divisor: it annihilates (from the left) some non-zero
cross-half vector. -/
/-- The finite set of cross-half zero divisors of `Tower (n+1)`. -/

/-- The annihilation graph: two distinct in-range cross-half vectors are adjacent when
their product (in one order or the other) vanishes. -/
/-- The zero divisors of XOR charge `c`. -/
/-! ## 2. The edge law -/
/-- The sign parity carried by an edge `i → k` (for the partner index `m = k ^^^ i ^^^ j`). -/

/-- **Edge law.** `(± eᵢ ± e_{H+j}) · (± e_k ± e_{H+m}) = 0` exactly when `m = k ^^^ i ^^^ j`,
the index condition `crossOK` holds, and the four signs have the parity `edgePar`. -/
/-! ## 3. Which cross-half vectors are zero divisors, and how many there are -/

/-- In dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16` the cross-half zero divisors are exactly the labels with
`i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j`. -/

/-- **Universal count.** The Cayley–Dickson algebra of dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16` has exactly
`(D - 2)(D - 4)` cross-half zero divisors `± eᵢ ± e_{D/2+j}`. -/

/-- **Universal sector size.** Every non-zero XOR charge `c < D/2` carries exactly
`2(D - 4)` cross-half zero divisors. -/
/-- The zero divisors are the union of the sectors of the non-zero charges `1 ≤ c < D/2`. -/
/-- Distinct charges give disjoint sectors. -/
/-! ## 4. Annihilation preserves the charge and stays among the zero divisors -/
/-- A right annihilating partner of a cross-half zero divisor is itself a zero divisor. -/

/-- One step of the annihilation graph (from any in-range vector) lands among the zero divisors
and preserves the XOR charge. -/
/-- Everything reachable from a zero divisor is a zero divisor of the same charge. -/

theorem eps_ll {n a b : Nat} (ha : a < 2 ^ n) (hb : b < 2 ^ n) :
    epsNeg (n + 1) a b = epsNeg n a b

declarations.name: eps_lh

# The universal cross-half zero-divisor criterion

`TowerZeroDivisors` reduces annihilation of cross-half vectors `± eᵢ ± e_{H+j}` of the
Cayley–Dickson algebra `Tower (n+1)` (dimension `D = 2H = 2ⁿ⁺¹`) to sign conditions on the
structure sign `epsNeg`, and checks the resulting index criterion by evaluation for
`D = 16, 32, 64, 128`.  This module proves the criterion **for every `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16`**.

Main results:

* `epsNeg_xor_laws` : the quaternionic sign laws `eₚ(eₚ e_q) = -e_q` and
  `(eₚ e_q) e_q = -eₚ` (for `p ≠ 0`, resp. `q ≠ 0`) at the level of signs, in every dimension;
* `hasCrossPartner_iff` : a cross-half vector has a cross-half annihilator iff some index `k`
  satisfies the sign-free condition `crossOK` (the partner is then `± e_k ± e_{H + k ^^^ i ^^^ j}`);
* `crossOK_valid` : `crossOK` forces `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j` (necessity, all dimensions);
* `exists_crossOK` : conversely, for `n ≥ 3` every such `(i, j)` has a partner index, given by
  an explicit case analysis on the top bit, with the sedenion case as base (sufficiency);
* `crossVec_zeroDivisor_iff` : **the universal criterion** — for `D ≥ 16`, `± eᵢ ± e_{D/2+j}`
  annihilates a non-zero cross-half vector iff `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0` and `i ≠ j`.
-/
/-! ## 1. The structure sign one level up -/
/-! ## 2. The left and right quaternionic sign laws -/
/-- `eₚ (eₚ e_q) = -e_q` and `(eₚ e_q) e_q = -eₚ` at the level of signs. -/
/-! ## 3. Reduction of the annihilation problem to an index condition -/

/-- The sign-free index condition: the cross-half vector `± eᵢ ± e_{H+j}` of `Tower (n+1)`
is annihilated by a cross-half vector `± e_k ± e_{H+m}` (for suitable signs) exactly when
`m = k ^^^ i ^^^ j` and this condition holds. -/
/-! ## 4. Necessity -/
/-! ## 5. Sufficiency -/
/-- An index different from `0` and from `a`, of size at most `2`. -/
/-- The sedenion base case, checked by evaluation. -/
/-! ## 6. The universal zero-divisor criterion in the algebra -/

/-- **Universal cross-half zero-divisor criterion.** In the Cayley–Dickson algebra
`Tower (n+1)` of dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16`, the cross-half vector `± eᵢ ± e_{D/2+j}`
(`i, j < D/2`) annihilates a non-zero cross-half vector if and only if `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0` and
`i ≠ j`. -/

# Hub indices of the cross-half zero-divisor components

At level `N = n + 1` (dimension `D = 2ᴺ⁺¹`, half-dimension `H = 2ᴺ`), the component of XOR
charge `c` of the cross-half zero-divisor graph has vertices `± eᵢ ± e_{H + (i ^^^ c)}`.  This
module exhibits, for every charge `c`, a **hub index** `h = hubIdx n c`:

* `c < 2ⁿ`  : `h = 2ⁿ`;
* `c = 2ⁿ`  : `h = 1`;
* `c > 2ⁿ`  : `h = c - 2ⁿ`,

and proves, for every other index `i` of the component (`i ∉ {0, c, h, h ^^^ c}`), the four facts
(`hub_facts`):

1. `crossOK N i (i ^^^ c) h` — every block is annihilated by a vertex of the hub block `h`;
2. `crossOK N i (i ^^^ c) (h ^^^ c)` — and by a vertex of the partner hub block `h ^^^ c`;
3. `crossOK N i (i ^^^ c) (i ^^^ h)` — block `i` is annihilated by block `i ^^^ h`;
4. the triangle `i, i ^^^ h, h` is *frustrated*: the three edge parities have odd sum.

These are the combinatorial input of the spectral-gap estimate in `CrossHalfPoincare`.
All proofs are symbolic (valid in every dimension), via the recursive structure sign `epsNeg`.
-/
/-- All structure signs among `a, b, a ^^^ b` are determined by `epsNeg n a b`. -/
/-- Proves an identity between `^^^`-expressions bitwise. -/
/-- The four hub facts, in a uniform shape. -/
/-! ## The six cases -/
/-- Charge `c < 2ⁿ`, `i` low. -/
/-- Charge `c < 2ⁿ`, `i = 2ⁿ + a` high. -/
/-- Charge `c = 2ⁿ + b` (`0 < b`), `i = a` low. -/
/-- Charge `c = 2ⁿ + b` (`0 < b`), `i = 2ⁿ + a` high. -/
/-- Charge `c = 2ⁿ`, hub `1`, `i = a` low. -/
/-- Charge `c = 2ⁿ`, hub `1`, `i = 2ⁿ + a` high. -/
/-- The hub index of the component of charge `c` at level `n + 1`. -/

/-- **The hub facts, uniformly.**  For every charge `0 < c < 2ⁿ⁺¹` and every index `i` of the
component of charge `c` other than the two hub indices `h = hubIdx n c` and `h ^^^ c`:
the block `i` is annihilated by the hub blocks `h` and `h ^^^ c` and by the block `i ^^^ h`, and
the triangle `(i, i ^^^ h, h)` has odd parity. -/

# A uniform normalized spectral gap for every cross-half zero-divisor component

For every level `N ≥ 7` (dimension `D = 2ᴺ⁺¹ ≥ 256`) and every connected component `C` of the
cross-half zero-divisor graph `zdGraph N`, the induced graph on `C` (with `2(D - 4)` vertices)
satisfies

* `component_degree_pos` : no isolated vertices;
* `component_normSpectralGap_ge` : `λ₂(ℒ) ≥ 1 / (24 (D - 4))`;
* `component_normSpectralGap_ge_cos` : `λ₂(ℒ) ≥ 2 (1 - cos (π / (D - 4)))`;
* `component_expander_mixing` : the expander mixing lemma
  `|e(S, T) - vol S · vol T / vol C| ≤ λ̄ √(vol S · vol T)`.

The proof is a routing argument (`SimpleGraph.normSpectralGap_ge_of_routing`) built on the hub
facts of `CrossHalfHub`: the root is the vertex `+e_h + e_{H + (h ^^^ c)}` of the hub block `h`;
every other block `i` reaches the hub block directly, or through its partner block `i ^^^ h`
(the frustrated triangle); the eight hub vertices each have `D/2 - 4` non-hub neighbours.

# Universal cross-half zero-divisor combinatorics for every Cayley–Dickson dimension

The modules `SedenionStratification` (`D = 16`), `Trigintaduonion` (`D = 32`) and
`HigherTower` (`D = 128, 256`) record the cross-half zero-divisor invariants
*dimension by dimension*: the first two by exact evaluation in the algebra, the last one
as hand-checked arithmetic identities about the specific numerals `15624`, `248`, …

This module proves the corresponding statements **once and for all**, for every
Cayley–Dickson dimension `D = 2ⁿ` simultaneously, from the index criterion

  `s • eᵢ + t • e_{H+j}` (with `H = D/2`) is a cross-half zero divisor
  ⟺ `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j`,

which is *kernel-verified in the actual algebra* for `D = 16`
(`crossOctet_annihilator_iff_index`) and `D = 32` (`zd32_iff_index`).

Main results (all for arbitrary `k`, with `H = 2ᵏ` and `D = 2H = 2ᵏ⁺¹`):

* `zdIdx_card` : there are `(H-1)(H-2)` cross-half zero-divisor index pairs, hence
  `zdVerts_card_universal` : `(D-2)(D-4)` signed cross-half zero divisors;
* `nonZD_card_universal` : the remaining cross-half vectors number exactly `6D - 8`;
* `sector_card` : every non-zero XOR charge `χ ∈ 𝔽₂^{n-1} ∖ {0}` carries exactly
  `H - 2` index pairs, i.e. `2(D-4)` signed zero divisors (`sector_verts_card_universal`);
* `charge_count_mul_sector_card` : the `D/2 - 1` non-zero charges times the common
  sector size recovers the total, and `zdIdx_card_eq_sum` proves that the sectors really
  do partition the zero-divisor set;
* `zd_triangular_universal` : `(D-2)(D-4) = 8 · T_{(D-4)/2}` — the eightfold-triangular
  law, for every `D = 2ⁿ` at once;
* `transpose_involutive`, `transpose_ne_self`, `sector_card_even` : the transposition
  `τ : (i,j) ↦ (j,i)` is a fixed-point-free, charge-preserving involution of every sector.

The last section derives the previously hand-written numerical invariants for
`D = 16, 32, 64, 128, 256` as instances of the universal theorems, and links the general
count back to the kernel-verified sedenion and trigintaduonion computations.
-/
/-! ## 1. The cross-half index model -/

/-- All index pairs `(i, j)` of cross-half vectors `s • eᵢ + t • e_{H+j}` in the
Cayley–Dickson algebra of dimension `D = 2H`. -/
/-- The index pairs satisfying the zero-divisor criterion `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j`. -/
/-- The XOR charge `χ = i ^^^ j` of an index pair. -/
/-- The zero-divisor index pairs of XOR charge `c`. -/

/-- A signed cross-half zero divisor: an index pair together with the two signs
`s, t ∈ {1, -1}` (encoded as booleans). -/
/-- The signed cross-half zero divisors of XOR charge `c`. -/
/-! ## 2. Elementary XOR lemmas -/
/-! ## 3. Membership characterisations -/
/-! ## 4. The universal zero-divisor count `(D-2)(D-4)` -/
/-- There are exactly `(H-1)(H-2)` cross-half zero-divisor index pairs in dimension `D = 2H`. -/

/-- **Universal zero-divisor count.** In the Cayley–Dickson algebra of dimension
`D = 2ᵏ⁺¹` there are exactly `(D - 2)(D - 4)` signed cross-half zero divisors. -/

/-- **Universal non-zero-divisor count.** The remaining cross-half vectors — those with
`i = 0`, `j = 0` or `i = j` — number exactly `6D - 8`. -/

/-- The total number of cross-half vectors is `D² = 4H²`, and it splits as
`(D-2)(D-4) + (6D-8)`. -/
/-! ## 5. XOR charge sectors -/
/-- Every sector of non-zero charge `c < H = 2ᵏ` is the graph of `i ↦ i ^^^ c`. -/

/-- **Universal sector size.** For every non-zero charge `χ < H = 2ᵏ` there are exactly
`H - 2` zero-divisor index pairs of charge `χ`. -/
/-- Signed form of the sector size: `2(D-4)` signed zero divisors per non-zero charge. -/
/-- The zero divisors are the disjoint union of their charge sectors. -/

/-- **Universal component count × component size = total.** There are `D/2 - 1` non-zero
XOR charges, each carrying `H - 2` index pairs, and together they exhaust the
`(H-1)(H-2)` cross-half zero-divisor index pairs. -/
/-! ## 6. The eightfold-triangular law -/
/-- Triangular numbers. -/

/-- **Universal eightfold-triangular law.** `(D-2)(D-4) = 8 · T_{(D-4)/2}` for every
Cayley–Dickson dimension `D = 2ᵏ⁺¹`, `k ≥ 1`. -/
/-! ## 7. The transposition involution -/
/-- The transposition `τ : (i, j) ↦ (j, i)`. -/

/-- Every charge sector has even cardinality — as it must, since `τ` is a fixed-point-free
involution of it (`transpose_mem_sector`, `transpose_involutive`, `transpose_ne_self`). -/
/-! ## 8. Instances: the classical dimensions, derived from the universal theorems -/
/-- `D = 16` (sedenions): `168 = (16-2)(16-4)` signed cross-half zero divisors. -/
/-- The seven Fano sectors of the sedenions have `24 = 2(16-4)` signed zero divisors each. -/
/-- The fifteen `PG(3,2)` sectors of the trigintaduonions have `56 = 2(32-4)` each. -/
/-- The sixty-three `PG(5,2)` sectors of the `D = 128` algebra have `248 = 2(128-4)` each. -/
/-! ## 9. Agreement with the kernel-verified algebra computations -/

/-- The universal count reproduces the sedenion computation in the actual algebra:
`crossOctetZD` (the 168 cross-octet zero divisors of `CDSedenion`, obtained by exact
evaluation of sedenion products) has exactly `(zdVerts 8).card` elements. -/

/-- The universal count reproduces the trigintaduonion computation: `zd32` (the cross-half
zero divisors of `CD CDSedenion`, obtained by exact evaluation) has `(zdVerts 16).card`
elements. -/

/-- Sectorwise agreement in dimension 32: the universal sector size `2(32-4) = 56` equals the
size of every non-zero charge sector computed inside the algebra. -/
/-! ## 10. The charge index set is the point set of `PG(n-2, 𝔽₂)` -/
/-- The binary expansion of a charge as a vector of `𝔽₂^k`. -/

/-- The charge map turns XOR into addition in `𝔽₂^k`: charges form an elementary abelian
2-group, exactly the vector space underlying `PG(k-1, 𝔽₂)`. -/

/-- **Universal projective indexing of the components.** The non-zero XOR charges of the
cross-half zero divisors of the dimension-`2ᵏ⁺¹` Cayley–Dickson algebra correspond
bijectively, via binary expansion, to the non-zero vectors of `𝔽₂^k` — the points of
`PG(k-1, 𝔽₂)`. -/

/-- The number of charge sectors equals the number of points of `PG(k-1, 𝔽₂)`,
i.e. `D/2 - 1`. -/

# Cayley–Dickson Doubling Functor (Settles OP-036)
  **Epistemic Classification:** [A] Category Theory & Functorial Doubling

This module formally certifies the Cayley–Dickson Doubling Functor 𝓕_CD,
its natural sub-algebra embeddings, and the functorial preservation of zero
divisors across the doubling tower.

Key Theorems Formally Certified:
1. Doubling Functor Object and Morphism Action:
   - For an algebra A with involution (*), 𝓕_CD(A) = A × A.
   - Multiplication: (a, b) * (c, d) = (a*c - d**b, d*a + b*c*).
2. Canonical Sub-algebra Embedding ι:
   - ι(a) = (a, 0).
   - ι is an algebra homomorphism: ι(a * b) = ι(a) * ι(b).
3. Zero Divisor Preservation under ι:
   - If a * b = 0, then ι(a) * ι(b) = 0.
4. Upper Conjugate Embedding ι*:
   - ι*(a) = (0, a).
   - For imaginary orthogonal zero divisors (a* = -a, b a = 0),
     ι*(a) * ι*(b) = 0 in the doubled algebra.
5. Cross-Half Multiplication Factorization:
   - (a, 0) * (0, d) = (0, d * a).
   - Vanishes if and only if d * a = 0.

/-- Doubled algebra pair (a, b) over a ring R. -/
/-- Canonical lower embedding ι: R → CDPair R. -/
/-- Upper conjugate embedding ι*: R → CDPair R. -/
/-! ## 2. Multiplication Laws -/
/-- Canonical multiplication of lower embeddings: (a, 0) * (b, 0) = (a * b, 0). -/
/-- Lower embedding preserves zero divisors: a * b = 0 → ι(a) * ι(b) = (0, 0). -/
/-! ## 3. Cross-Half Factorization -/

/-- Cross-half multiplication: (a, 0) * (0, d) = (0, d * a).
    In the CD multiplication (a, b)*(c, d) = (ac - d* b, da + b c*),
    setting b = 0 and c = 0 yields (0, da). -/

# The invariant boundary of the Cayley–Dickson tower

The Cayley–Dickson tower `ℝ → ℂ → ℍ → 𝕆 → 𝕊` loses a structural property at every step,
and at the last step recorded here — from the octonions to the sedenions — it loses the
division property: non-trivial zero divisors appear.  This module makes the two sides of
that boundary precise for the integer models used throughout the project.

**Below the boundary (octonions).**  `octNormSq_mul` is the eight-square identity: the
norm form of `CDOctonion` is multiplicative.  Consequently `octonion_no_zero_divisors`
holds: a product of non-zero integer octonions is non-zero, so left multiplication by a
non-zero octonion has trivial kernel.

**At the boundary (sedenions).**  For each of the 168 cross-octet zero divisors
`u = s · eᵢ + t · e₈₊ⱼ` (`i, j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j`) the left-multiplication operator
`L_u : 𝕊 → 𝕊` is a genuine projection-like map:

* `zeroDivisor_left_rank`     : `rank L_u = 12`;
* `zeroDivisor_left_nullity`  : `dim ker L_u = 4`, with an explicit basis
  `e_a ± e₈₊(a ⊕ i ⊕ j)` (`zeroDivisor_kernel_basis`);
* `zeroDivisor_gram_spectrum` : `L_uᵀ L_u` has spectrum contained in `{0, 2, 4}`, with
  `0` of multiplicity 4;
* `zeroDivisor_tight_frame`   : `∑_u L_uᵀ L_u = 336 · I₁₆`, i.e. after normalising each
  zero divisor to unit length the 168 operators form an exact tight frame,
  `(1/168) ∑_u L̂_uᵀ L̂_u = I₁₆` (`zeroDivisor_tight_frame_normalized`).

**The discrete/continuous duality.**  The same 168 points form an exact cubature for the
degree-`(1,0)` harmonics of the Stiefel manifold `V₂(ℝ⁷) ≅ G₂/SU(2)` — the identity
`Mᵀ M = 24 · I₂₁` of `Sovereign.Geometry.StiefelCubature` — so the discrete failure locus of
division is a balanced sample of the continuous `G₂` geometry.  `dual_unity` records the
two identities together.

**Corrections to the `126` folklore (HYP-207).**  Two statements that circulate in the
project notes are refuted here.

* The Gram operator of a unit zero divisor is *not* a rank-12 orthogonal projection: its
  eigenvalues lie in `{0, 1, 2}`, the eigenvalue `0` having multiplicity 4, and the
  operator is not idempotent (`unit_gram_not_idempotent`, `zeroDivisor_gram_spectrum`).
* Consequently the frame constants are `168` globally and `24` per XOR charge sector, not
  `126` and `18`: `(1/168) ∑_u L̂_uᵀ L̂_u = I₁₆` and `(1/24) ∑_{u ∈ C_χ} L̂_uᵀ L̂_u = I₁₆`
  hold exactly, while `(1/126) ∑_u L̂_uᵀ L̂_u ≠ I₁₆` (`unit_frame_constant_ne_126`) and
  `(1/18) ∑_{u ∈ C_χ} L̂_uᵀ L̂_u ≠ I₁₆` (`unit_sector_frame_constant_ne_18`).

The constant `126` is the one forced by the *trace* of the genuine rank-12 projections
`Π_u`, since `168 · 12 = 126 · 16` (`projection_trace_identity`), which is why it looks
right on average.  But the projections themselves do not resolve the identity either: they
sum to a diagonal matrix with two distinct diagonal values,
`∑_u Π_u = diag(168, 120, …, 120, 168, 120, …, 120)` (`zeroDivisor_projection_sum`), so
`(1/126) ∑_u Π_u ≠ I₁₆` (`projection_resolution_false`).  The exact resolution of identity
is carried by the Gram operators, not by the projections.
-/
/-! ## Below the boundary: the octonions are a division algebra -/
/-- The norm form of the integer octonions: the sum of the squares of the 8 coordinates. -/
/-- **Degen's eight-square identity.** The octonion norm form is multiplicative. -/
/-- The octonion norm form vanishes only at zero. -/
/-- The octonion norm form is positive definite. -/

/-- **The octonions have no zero divisors.** A product of non-zero integer octonions is
non-zero: below the sedenion boundary, left multiplication can never decouple. -/
/-- Left multiplication by a non-zero octonion has trivial kernel. -/
/-! ## General rank certificates -/
/-- A two-sided factorisation of an identity matrix bounds the rank from below. -/
/-- A matrix of independent kernel vectors bounds the nullity from below. -/
/-- Rank–nullity in dimension 16 turns the two bounds into equalities. -/
/-! ## The 168 zero divisors -/
/-- Every zero divisor occurs in the table of the 168 tabulated ones. -/
/-- The rank and the nullity of the tabulated left-multiplication operators. -/

/-- **Rank of a sedenion zero divisor.** Left multiplication by any of the 168 cross-octet
zero divisors of the integer sedenions has rank exactly 12. -/

/-- **Kernel dimension of a sedenion zero divisor.** Left multiplication by any of the 168
cross-octet zero divisors has a kernel of dimension exactly 4: the operator decouples a
four-dimensional subspace of the 16-dimensional algebra. -/

/-- **An explicit kernel basis.** For `u = s · eᵢ + t · e₈₊ⱼ` the four vectors
`e_a ± e₈₊(a ⊕ i ⊕ j)` of `kerVecs u` are non-zero and annihilated by `u`, and there are
exactly four of them — a basis of `ker L_u` by `zeroDivisor_left_nullity`. -/

/-- **Spectrum of the Gram operator.** `L_uᵀ L_u` annihilates the polynomial
`λ (λ − 2) (λ − 4)`, so its eigenvalues lie in `{0, 2, 4}`; the eigenvalue `0` has
multiplicity 4 by `zeroDivisor_left_nullity`. -/
/-! ## The tight frame -/

/-- **Exact tight frame.** The Gram operators of the 168 cross-octet zero divisors sum to
a multiple of the identity: `∑_u L_uᵀ L_u = 336 · I₁₆`. -/
/-- Halving each summand halves the sum. -/

/-- Each cross-octet zero divisor has squared norm 2, so the Gram operator of the
normalised zero divisor `û = u / √2` is `(1/2) L_uᵀ L_u`; the 168 normalised operators sum
to `168 · I₁₆`. -/

/-- **Resolution of the identity.** Each zero divisor has squared norm 2, so normalising
it to unit length divides its Gram operator by 2; the 168 normalised operators then
resolve the identity exactly: `(1/168) ∑_u L̂_uᵀ L̂_u = I₁₆`. -/

/-- **Sector tight frame.** Each of the seven XOR charge sectors already carries the whole
structure: its 24 Gram operators sum to `48 · I₁₆`. -/
/-- The normalised form of the sector identity: `(1/24) ∑_{u ∈ C_χ} L̂_uᵀ L̂_u = I₁₆`. -/

/-- **The frame constant is 168, not 126.** With the normalisation `û = u / √2` used for
the resolution of identity, rescaling the sum by `1/126` does not give the identity. -/
/-- **The sector frame constant is 24, not 18.** -/

/-- **The Gram operator of a unit zero divisor is not a projection.** Its spectrum is
contained in `{0, 1, 2}`, not in `{0, 1}`: the rank-12 orthogonal projection
onto the row space is a different operator, obtained from the Gram operator by the
polynomial `λ ↦ λ(3 − λ)/2`. -/
/-! ## The projections: a correction to the `1/126` folklore -/

/-- The rank-12 projections onto the row spaces sum to a *diagonal* matrix which is not a
multiple of the identity: `∑_u Π_u = diag(168, 120, …, 120, 168, 120, …, 120)`, with the
value `168` in the two unit directions `e₀` and `e₈`. -/

/-- Each `PM k` really is the orthogonal projection onto the row space of `L_u`: it is
symmetric and idempotent, acts as the identity after `L_u`, kills the kernel, and has
trace 12. -/

/-- The trace identity behind the folklore constant `126`: the 168 projections have total
trace `168 · 12 = 2016 = 126 · 16`, so `126` is the *unique* constant for which
`(1/c) ∑_u Π_u` could have the trace of `I₁₆`. -/

/-- …but the rescaled sum is not the identity: the correct exact resolution of identity is
carried by the Gram operators (`zeroDivisor_tight_frame_normalized`), not by the
projections. -/
/-! ## The dual unity -/

/-- **Dual unity of the boundary.** The 168 cross-octet zero divisors of the sedenions
carry two exact balanced structures at once:

* a *continuous* one — as 2-frames in `ℝ⁷` they form an exact cubature for the
  degree-`(1,0)` harmonics of `V₂(ℝ⁷) ≅ G₂/SU(2)`, `Mᵀ M = 24 · I₂₁`;
* a *discrete* one — their left-multiplication operators form an exact tight frame of the
  16-dimensional sedenion algebra, `∑_u L_uᵀ L_u = 336 · I₁₆`,

while each individual operator is maximally degenerate in the same way: rank 12 and a
4-dimensional kernel. -/

# Finite certificates for the zero-divisor boundary of the sedenions

Every statement of this module is a finite verification about the 168 cross-octet zero
divisors `u = s · eᵢ + t · e₈₊ⱼ` (`i, j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j`) of the integer sedenions, discharged
by kernel-external evaluation.  Their linear-algebraic consequences — the exact rank and
kernel dimension of every `L_u`, and the tight-frame identity — are proved in
`Sovereign.Algebra.DualUnityBoundary`.
-/
/-! ## Indexing -/
/-- There are 168 cross-octet zero divisors. -/
/-- The tabulated matrices agree with the left-multiplication matrices. -/
/-! ## Kernel certificates -/
/-- The four vectors `kerVecs u` are genuinely annihilated by `u`. -/

/-- Every zero divisor admits exactly four such kernel vectors and twelve complementary
vectors. -/
/-- The kernel vectors are non-zero. -/
/-- `L_u` kills the four kernel vectors. -/
/-- The four kernel vectors are orthogonal of squared norm `2`, hence independent. -/
/-! ## Rank certificates -/
/-- The tabulated images are the images of the complementary vectors. -/
/-- The twelve images are orthogonal and non-zero: `YM k` is a left inverse. -/
/-! ## Gram and projection certificates -/
/-- The tabulated Gram matrix is `L_uᵀ L_u`. -/
/-- The Gram matrix satisfies `G (G − 2) (G − 4) = 0`: its spectrum is `{0, 2, 4}`. -/
/-- `PM k` is idempotent. -/
/-- `PM k` is symmetric. -/
/-- `PM k` acts as the identity on the row space of `L_u`. -/
/-- `PM k` kills the kernel of `L_u`. -/
/-- Each projection has trace 12, matching the rank of `L_u`. -/
/-! ## The two global sums -/
/-- **Tight frame.** The Gram matrices of the 168 zero divisors sum to `336 · I₁₆`. -/
/-- The tight-frame identity, indexed directly by the 168 zero-divisor labels. -/

/-- **Sector tight frame.** Each of the seven XOR charge sectors of 24 zero divisors is
already a tight frame: its Gram operators sum to `48 · I₁₆`. -/
/-- The canonical zero divisor `e₁ + e₁₀` is one of the 168. -/

/-- The Gram operator of a *unit* zero divisor is not idempotent: `L̂_uᵀ L̂_u` is not an
orthogonal projection, its spectrum being `{0, 1, 2}` rather than `{0, 1}`. -/

/-- The projections do **not** sum to a multiple of the identity: their sum is the diagonal
matrix with entries `168` in the two unit directions `e₀, e₈` and `120` elsewhere. -/

# Rational-matrix model of sedenion left multiplication (definitions)

For a cross-octet zero divisor `u = s · eᵢ + t · e₈₊ⱼ` of the integer sedenions this module

* `compWeights u` — the squared norms of the images of those twelve vectors, which turn

that the kernel-external evaluations in `Sovereign.Algebra.DualUnityBoundaryCerts` compute the
sedenion products once rather than once per matrix entry.

For the principal S¹-bundle S³ → S² (Hopf fibration), the equatorial transition function
g_{NS}: S¹ → U(1) has winding number w = 1.
The first Chern number c₁ equals the winding number w of the clutching function:

and admits no global continuous section over S².

Global Section Obstruction Theorem:
A principal U(1)-bundle over S² with first Chern class c₁ admits a global continuous section
if and only if c₁ = 0 (the bundle is trivial).
For the Hopf fibration with c₁ = 1, the existence of a global section is obstructed.

Bulk Poincaré Ball Contractibility and Gauge Triviality Theorem:
For the 3-dimensional open unit ball 𝔹³ (Poincaré bulk), the second integer cohomology vanishes:
H²(𝔹³; ℤ) = 0.
Consequently, any U(1)-bundle over 𝔹³ has vanishing Chern class c₁(𝔹³) = 0,
meaning the bundle over the bulk is topologically trivial (𝔹³ × S¹).
Therefore, the fiber phase over the interior bulk is a free gauge choice,
while the boundary ∂𝔹³ = S² carries the non-trivial Chern class c₁(S²) = 1.

# The associator 3-cocycle obstruction of a Lie 2-group model

This module formalizes the "higher gauge" reading of Cayley-Dickson non-associativity:
the associator of basis vectors defines a `±1`-valued phase `ω(a,b,c)`, and the
Mac Lane pentagon condition for that phase is exactly the 3-cocycle condition of the
associated Lie 2-group / monoidal-category model.

Everything is stated for the integer Cayley-Dickson tower `Tower n` of `TowerBasis`
(dimension `2ⁿ`), whose basis product law and associator sign are already kernel-checked
there and in `TowerAssociator`, and is proved for **every** level `n`, not only for the
sedenions:

* `pentagon_cocycle_assocPhase` : the multiplicative pentagon condition holds for the
  associator phase, for every quadruple of indices in every dimension;
* `pentagon_cocycle_assocClass` : the same statement for the `ZMod 2`-valued class;
* `assocClass_is_coboundary` : the obstruction class is the coboundary of the 2-cochain
  given by the Cayley-Dickson sign function, hence trivial in `H³((ℤ/2)ⁿ ; ℤ/2)`;
* `sedenion_*` : the level-4 instances (`D = 16`), including the non-associating triple
  `(e₁, e₂, e₄)` with associator `2 e₇` and phase `-1`, the associating quaternionic
  triple `(e₁, e₂, e₃)` with phase `+1`, and the pentagon on `(e₁, e₂, e₄, e₈)`.

The original source of this module, which could not be compiled, is preserved verbatim in
a comment at the end of the file together with an explanation.

/-- **The associator phase is a Mac Lane 3-cocycle**, in every dimension `2ⁿ`. -/
