# The degree census of the annihilation graph in every dimension

`TowerDegreeQuantization` determines the *set* of degrees of the annihilation graph of the
Cayley–Dickson tower (every degree is `≡ 4 mod 8` and every such value in `[4, 2ⁿ - 4]`
occurs) and `TowerDegreeFormula` computes the degree of an individual pair.  What was still
missing is the *distribution*: how many admissible pairs realise each degree.  Only the two
extreme multiplicities were known in general (`maxDegreePairs_card`, `minDegreePairs_card`),
together with complete censuses in the fixed dimensions `32` and `64`
(`nonassocMiddles_dim32_spectrum`, `dim64_degree_counts`).

This module computes the whole distribution in every dimension.

* `degreeCount n v` — the number of ordered admissible pairs `(i, j)` of indices below `2ⁿ`
  whose outer pair has exactly `v` non-associating middles.

* `degreeCount_succ_low` and `degreeCount_succ_high` — the two **doubling laws of the
  census**.  A doubling step sends the multiplicity of `v` to the multiplicity of `2v + 4`
  (the "low" family, `≡ 12 mod 16`) and of `2ⁿ⁺¹ - (2v + 4)` (the "high" family,
  `≡ 4 mod 16`), in both cases multiplied by two, and adds `6 (2ⁿ - 1)` degenerate pairs on
  top of the maximal degree.

* `censusT` and `degreeCount_eq_censusT` — the resulting `O(n)` evaluation of an arbitrary
  multiplicity: writing the degree as `8t + 4`, `degreeCount (q + 3) (8t + 4) = censusT q t`,
  where `censusT` descends on the binary expansion of `t`, halving it and reflecting it at
  every step where the low bit vanishes.

* `degreeCount_ge` — every degree occurring in dimension `2ⁿ` (`n ≥ 3`) is realised by at
  least `21 · 2ⁿ⁻²` ordered pairs, and `degreeCount_plateau` — the degrees in the middle
  band `8t + 4` with `2ⁿ⁻⁵ ≤ t ≤ 2ⁿ⁻³ - 1 - 2ⁿ⁻⁵` attain that minimum exactly.  So the
  degree distribution has a flat plateau of width `2ⁿ⁻³ - 2ⁿ⁻⁴` in the middle.

* `degreeCount_le_max` — the maximal degree `2ⁿ - 4` is the most frequent degree: no other
  degree is realised by more pairs.

* `census_dim128`, `census_dim256` — the explicit censuses in dimensions `128` and `256`,
  read off from the recursion rather than from an enumeration of pairs.
-/
/-! ## 1. The multiplicity function -/

/-- `degreeCount n v` is the number of ordered admissible pairs `(i, j)` with `i, j < 2ⁿ`
whose outer pair `(e_i, ·, e_j)` has exactly `v` non-associating middles. -/

/-- The indicator of an ordered admissible pair of degree `v`, written through the
recursion `towerDegree`. -/
/-! ## 2. Quantization and bounds, read through the recursion -/
/-! ## 3. Splitting a doubling step into its four blocks -/

/-! ## 4. Arithmetic separation of the two degree families

At a doubling step a degree is either of the form `2v + 4` (congruent to `12` modulo `16`)
or of the form `2ⁿ⁺¹ - (2v + 4)` (congruent to `4` modulo `16`).  The two families never
meet, which is what makes the census split cleanly. -/
/-- A complemented degree is never a doubled degree. -/
/-- A doubled degree is never a complemented degree. -/
/-- The degree indicator is symmetric in the outer pair. -/
/-! ## 5. The four blocks for a doubled degree `2v + 4` -/
/-! ## 6. The four blocks for a complemented degree `2ⁿ⁺¹ - (2v + 4)` -/
/-! ## 7. The two doubling laws of the census -/

/-- **Doubling law, low family.**  In dimension `2ᵐ⁺¹` the degree `2v + 4` is realised by
twice as many pairs as the degree `v` in dimension `2ᵐ`, plus the `6 (2ᵐ - 1)` degenerate
cross-half pairs when `2v + 4` is the maximal degree. -/

/-- **Doubling law, complemented family.**  The degree `2ᵐ⁺¹ - (2v + 4)` in dimension
`2ᵐ⁺¹` is realised by exactly twice as many pairs as the degree `v` in dimension `2ᵐ`. -/
/-! ## 8. Degenerate values of the census -/

/-- The octonionic base of the census: in dimension `8` all `42` admissible pairs have
four non-associating middles. -/
/-! ## 9. The census function and its closed evaluation -/

/-- `censusT q t` evaluates the multiplicity of the degree `8t + 4` in dimension `2^(q+3)`.
The descent halves `t` when its low bit is set and reflects it at `2^q - 1` when the low
bit vanishes; the extra term `6 (2^(q+3) - 1)` appears exactly at the maximal degree. -/

/-- **The census formula.**  In dimension `2^(q+3)` the degree `8t + 4` is realised by
exactly `censusT q t` ordered admissible pairs. -/
/-! ## 10. Structure of the distribution -/

/-- Every degree that occurs in dimension `2^(q+3)` is realised by at least `21 · 2^(q+1)`
ordered pairs. -/
/-- The maximal degree is the most frequent one. -/

/-- **The plateau.**  All degrees in the middle band attain the minimal multiplicity
`21 · 2^(r+3)`. -/
/-! ## 11. The census read back in terms of dimensions -/

/-- **Minimal multiplicity.**  In dimension `2ⁿ` (`n ≥ 3`) every degree that occurs is
realised by at least `21 · 2ⁿ⁻²` ordered admissible pairs. -/

/-- **The maximal degree is the most frequent.**  No degree is realised by more ordered
pairs than the maximal degree `2ⁿ - 4`. -/

/-- **The plateau, in terms of dimensions.**  In dimension `2ⁿ` with `n ≥ 5`, every degree
`8t + 4` whose index lies in the middle band `2ⁿ⁻⁵ ≤ t ≤ 2ⁿ⁻³ - 1 - 2ⁿ⁻⁵` is realised by
exactly `21 · 2ⁿ⁻²` ordered pairs — the minimum.  So the degree distribution is flat over a
band of `2ⁿ⁻³ - 2ⁿ⁻⁴` consecutive degrees. -/
/-! ## 12. Completeness of the census -/

/-- **The census is complete.**  The multiplicities of the `2^q` possible degrees add up to
the number `(2^(q+3) - 1)(2^(q+3) - 2)` of ordered admissible pairs. -/

/-- The census is complete, in terms of dimensions: in dimension `2ⁿ` the multiplicities of
the degrees `8t + 4`, `t < 2ⁿ⁻³`, add up to the number of ordered admissible pairs. -/

# Exact Closed-Form Distribution Formula for the Annihilation Graph Degree Census

`TowerDegreeCensus` computes the multiplicity of the degree `8t + 4` in dimension `2^(q+3)`
via the descent recursion `censusT q t`.
This module formalizes the exact non-recursive **Closed-Form Census Formula** `censusClosedForm q t`
that computes the multiplicity in O(1) from the binary prefix of `t` (HYP-221):

* `censusPlateau q = 21 · 2^(q+1)`: the flat minimal plateau multiplicity covering the middle 75% band.
* `censusWingExcess q k = 24 · ((k - 1) · 2^q - (2^(q-2) - 2^(q-1-k)))`:
  the exact dyadic excess for an interior degree whose binary expansion has k = max(lz(t), lo(t)) >= 2.
* `censusClosedForm q t`: unified closed-form formula matching `censusT q t` across all `q ≥ 2`
  and all `t < 2^q` (`censusT_eq_censusClosedForm`), hence an `O(1)` evaluation of the whole
  degree census of the annihilation graph in every dimension
  (`degreeCount_eq_censusClosedForm`).

The closed form reads the multiplicity off the *prefix depth* `prefixDepth q t`, the larger of
the number of leading zeros and the number of leading ones of the `q`-bit word `t`: away from
the two extreme degrees the multiplicity is `censusInteriorVal q (prefixDepth q t)`, and the
two extreme degrees carry the boundary values `censusZeroVal q` and `censusMaxVal q`.  In
particular the multiplicity depends on `t` only through its prefix depth, so the census is a
symmetric staircase: a flat plateau of multiplicity `21 · 2^(q+1)` on the middle half, and
`24 · 2^q`-sized steps towards each end.
-/
/-! ## 1. Plateau and Wing Excess Definitions -/
/-- Minimal plateau multiplicity in dimension `2^(q+3)`: `21 * 2^(q+1)`. -/

/-- The exact dyadic excess over the plateau for a degree with prefix depth `k ≥ 2` (`k < q`):
  `24 * ((k - 1) * 2^q - (2^(q-2) - 2^(q-1-k)))`. -/
/-- Total interior multiplicity for prefix depth `k ≥ 2`: plateau + wing excess. -/

/-- Boundary multiplicity at `t = 0` (minimal non-zero degree 4):
  `censusInteriorVal q (q - 1) + 24 * 2^q - 12`. -/

/-- Boundary multiplicity at `t = 2^q - 1` (maximal degree `2^(q+3) - 4`):
  `censusInteriorVal q (q - 1) + 24 * 2^(q+1) - 18`. -/
/-! ## 2. Verification of Explicit Dimensions -/
/-- Dimension 128 (q = 4): exact multiplicities [1740, 1368, 1008, 672 (plateau), 1008, 1368, 2118]. -/
/-! ## 3. Master Census Closed-Form Theorem -/

/-- **Master Closed-Form Census Theorem (HYP-221)**:
  Every multiplicity level across the infinite Cayley-Dickson tower is exactly determined
  by the closed algebraic form `(censusPlateau, censusInteriorVal, censusZeroVal, censusMaxVal)`. -/

/-! ## 4. Bit-length arithmetic

`Nat.size t` is the number of binary digits of `t`; the three lemmas below are the doubling
laws of `Nat.size` used to track the leading bits of `t` along the census recursion. -/
/-! ## 5. The prefix depth of a degree index -/
/-- The number of leading zero bits of `t` read as a `q`-bit word. -/

/-- The **prefix depth** of `t < 2 ^ q`: the larger of the number of leading zeros and the
number of leading ones of the `q`-bit word `t`.  The census multiplicity of the degree
`8t + 4` depends on `t` only through this number. -/
/-- The prefix depth is invariant under complementation of the `q`-bit word. -/

/-- Appending a one to the binary word leaves the prefix depth unchanged, as long as the
result is not the all-ones word. -/
/-- Appending a zero to a nonzero binary word leaves the prefix depth unchanged. -/

/-- An interior word has prefix depth at most `q - 1`: only `0` and `2 ^ q - 1` are
constant words. -/
/-! ## 6. The doubling laws of the closed form -/
/-- The subtraction-free normal form of the wing excess, for `1 ≤ k ≤ q - 1`. -/

/-- **Interior doubling law.**  An interior multiplicity doubles from one dimension to the
next at a fixed prefix depth. -/

/-- **Top-level law.**  The deepest interior multiplicity of dimension `2^(q+4)` is twice the
minimal-degree multiplicity of dimension `2^(q+3)`. -/

/-- **Minimal-degree law.**  The minimal-degree multiplicity of dimension `2^(q+4)` is twice
the maximal-degree multiplicity of dimension `2^(q+3)`. -/

/-- **Maximal-degree law.**  The maximal-degree multiplicity doubles and picks up the
`6 (2^(q+3) - 1)` degenerate pairs created by the doubling step. -/
/-! ## 7. The closed form -/

/-- The **closed-form census**: the multiplicity of the degree `8t + 4` in dimension
`2^(q+3)`, read off the prefix depth of the `q`-bit word `t` without unwinding any
recursion. -/

/-- **The closed-form census formula.**  For every `q ≥ 2` and every `t < 2 ^ q` the descent
recursion `censusT` agrees with the closed form `censusClosedForm`. -/

/-- **The degree census in closed form.**  In dimension `2^(q+3)` (`q ≥ 2`) the number of
ordered admissible index pairs whose outer pair has exactly `8t + 4` non-associating middles
is `censusClosedForm q t`, an `O(1)` expression in the prefix depth of `t`. -/
/-- The census is a symmetric staircase: complementary degrees have equal multiplicities. -/

# The level structure of the degree census: how many degrees carry each multiplicity

`TowerDegreeCensusClosedForm` evaluates the multiplicity of an individual degree of the
annihilation graph in closed form: in dimension `2^(q+3)` the degree `8t + 4` is realised by
`censusClosedForm q t` ordered admissible pairs, a value depending on `t` only through its
prefix depth.  This module counts the degrees at each multiplicity, which turns the closed
form into the complete degree multiset of the graph in every dimension.

* `prefixDepth_ge_iff` — the prefix depth of a `q`-bit word is at least `k` exactly when the
  word lies in the bottom or the top block of size `2^(q-k)`; hence
  `card_prefixDepth_eq`: exactly `2^(q-k)` of the `2^q` words have prefix depth `k`,
  for `1 ≤ k ≤ q - 1`.
* `censusInteriorVal_strictMonoOn` — the interior multiplicities are strictly increasing in
  the prefix depth, and `censusInteriorVal_lt_censusZeroVal`,
  `censusZeroVal_lt_censusMaxVal` place the two boundary multiplicities above all of them.
  So the `q + 1` values `censusInteriorVal q 1, …, censusInteriorVal q (q-1)`,
  `censusZeroVal q`, `censusMaxVal q` are pairwise distinct.
* `degreeCount_level_card` — **the multiplicity census**: for `1 ≤ k ≤ q - 1` exactly
  `2^(q-k)` degrees of the dimension-`2^(q+3)` graph are realised by
  `censusInteriorVal q k` ordered pairs; the minimal degree `4` and the maximal degree
  `2^(q+3) - 4` are the only two degrees outside this list.
* `tower_degree_census_multiset` — the resulting complete description of the degree multiset,
  together with the count `2^q` of degrees it accounts for.
-/

/-- A `q`-bit word has at least `k` leading zeros exactly when it is below `2^(q-k)`. -/

/-- A `q`-bit word has prefix depth at least `k` exactly when it lies in the bottom or in the
top block of size `2^(q-k)`. -/
/-- Every word has prefix depth at least one: the leading bit is either a zero or a one. -/

/-- **The prefix-depth census.**  Exactly `2^(q-k)` of the `2^q` words of length `q` have
prefix depth `k`, for every `1 ≤ k ≤ q - 1`. -/
/-! ## 2. The interior multiplicities are strictly increasing -/
/-! ## 3. A dyadic sum -/
/-! ## 4. The multiplicity census of the annihilation graph -/

/-- Away from the two extreme degrees the multiplicity is the interior value at the prefix
depth of the degree index. -/

/-- **The multiplicity census.**  In dimension `2^(q+3)` exactly `2^(q-k)` of the `2^q`
degrees are realised by `censusInteriorVal q k` ordered admissible pairs, for every
`1 ≤ k ≤ q - 1`. -/

/-- **The degree multiset of the annihilation graph in every dimension.**  In dimension
`2^(q+3)` (`q ≥ 2`) the minimal degree `4` is realised by `censusZeroVal q` ordered

/-

# A non-recursive closed form for the degree of an arbitrary pair

`TowerDegreeFormula` gives the exact degree of an admissible outer pair `(i, j)` as an
`O(n)`-time *recursion* `towerDegree n i j` on the binary expansions of the two indices,
and `TowerDegreeQuantization` determines the set of attained values.  What neither gives is
a closed expression: a formula that reads the answer off the bit pattern of `(i, j)` without
unwinding the recursion.

This module supplies one.

* `stopLevel n i j` — the highest level at which the truncated pair
  `(i mod 2^ℓ, j mod 2^ℓ)` becomes degenerate: one of the two indices is the new imaginary
  unit `2^(ℓ-1)`, or the two indices are diagonal.  Below that level the descent is frozen
  at the extremal value, above it the descent alternates.
* `altSum d L n` — the alternating dyadic sum carried by the set bits of `d = i ⊕ j` in the
  window `[L, n)`: bit `l` contributes `± 8 · 2^(n-1-l)`, the sign being the parity of the
  number of set bits above `l`, and the leading term `± 2^(n-1)` carries the parity of the
  whole window.  `altSum_succ` is the doubling law that drives everything: adding a bit
  either doubles the sum or reflects it in `4`.
* `degreeClosed n i j = 2^(n-1) - 4 + altSum (i ⊕ j) (stopLevel n i j) n`, and
  `nonassocMiddles_card_eq_degreeClosed` — **the closed formula**: for every `n ≥ 3` and
  every admissible pair, the number of non-associating middles equals `degreeClosed n i j`.
  `towerDegree_eq_degreeClosed` is the same statement for the recursion.

Two consequences are recorded in the last section.  Because the degree of a single pair is
now a bounded computation, the complete degree census of the 64-dimensional annihilation
graph (`dim64_degree_counts`) and the exact list of its regular charge sectors
(`dim64_regular_sectors`, `dim64_regular_sector_iff`) are finite checks; the latter confirms
in dimension 64 the criterion `is_regular_sector_criterion` — regular iff `chi < 8` or `chi`
is a power of two — which had only been observed in dimensions 16 and 32.
-/

/-! ## 1. Reading the degree recursion one doubling step at a time

The following unfoldings of `towerDegree` are the four doubling laws in the form needed
below; `towerDegree_comm` records that the degree does not depend on the order of the outer
pair. -/
/-- The degree of an admissible pair is symmetric in the two outer indices. -/
/-! ## 2. The closed form -/

/-- The level at which the degree descent degenerates.  Going down from level `n`, the
descent stops at the first level `ℓ` at which the truncated pair
`(i mod 2^ℓ, j mod 2^ℓ)` has one of the three extremal shapes: one of the two indices is
the new unit `2^(ℓ-1)`, or the two indices are diagonal (they differ exactly by
`2^(ℓ-1)`).  If no such level exists the descent runs all the way down to the octonionic
base level `3`. -/
/-- The number of set bits of `d` in the window `[l, n)`. -/
/-- The alternating dyadic sum carried by the set bits of `d` in the window `[L, n)`. -/

/-- **The closed form of the degree.**  Above the stop level the degree is a single
alternating dyadic sum over the set bits of `d = i ⊕ j`: each set bit at position `l`
contributes `± 8 · 2^(n-1-l)`, the sign being the parity of the number of set bits strictly
above `l`, and the leading term `± 2^(n-1)` carries the parity of the whole window. -/
/-! ### Elementary properties of the window statistics -/

/-- **The doubling law for the alternating sum.**  Extending the window by one bit either
doubles the sum (bit clear) or reflects it (bit set). -/
-- the leading exponent
-- the tail terms
/-- The alternating sum only depends on the bits inside its window. -/
/-! ### Bit bookkeeping for one doubling step -/
/-! ### The degenerate branches -/
/-- Every degenerate shape is extremal for the recursion. -/
/-! ### The inductive step for the closed form -/
/-- The degree recursion and the closed form agree. -/
-- non-degenerate: the descent continues one more level
-- both indices inherited
-- `j` from the new half
-- `i` from the new half

/-- **Closed formula for the degree of an arbitrary pair.**  For every `n ≥ 3` and all
distinct non-real indices `i, j < 2ⁿ`, the number of middles that fail to associate with the
outer pair `(e_i, ·, e_j)` is given by the non-recursive expression `degreeClosed n i j`. -/

/-! ## 3. The regular charge sectors, in every dimension

A charge sector is *regular* when every pair carrying that charge attains the maximal
degree.  Dimensions 16 and 32 suggested the criterion "`chi < 8` or `chi` is a power of
two"; the maximality criterion of `TowerDegreeFormula` proves it in every dimension. -/

/-- A charge sector is *regular* when all its admissible pairs attain the maximal degree
`2ⁿ - 4`. -/

/-- **Classification of the regular charge sectors, in every dimension.**  For a non-zero
charge `chi < 2ⁿ`, the sector of charge `chi` is regular — every admissible pair with
`i ⊕ j = chi` attains the maximal degree `2ⁿ - 4` — if and only if `chi < 8` or `chi` is a
power of two. -/

/-! ## 4. Consequences: the degree census in dimension 64

Evaluating the degree of a single pair is a bounded computation, so global statistics of the
annihilation graph become finite checks. -/

/-- **The exact degree census in dimension 64.**  Among the `930` admissible index pairs of
the 32-dimensional base algebra, exactly `252` pairs have `4` non-associating middles
(degree `8` in the cross-half annihilation graph), `168` have `12` (degree `24`), `168`
have `20` (degree `40`) and `342` have `28` (degree `56`).  This is the complete degree
distribution of the 64-dimensional annihilation graph; the two extreme multiplicities agree
with `minDegreePairs_card_dim32` and `maxDegreePairs_card_dim32`. -/

/-- **The regular charge sectors in dimension 64.**  A charge sector of the 64-dimensional
annihilation graph is regular (all its pairs have the maximal degree `56`) exactly for the
charges `1, …, 8` and `16`. -/

/-- **The regularity criterion in dimension 64**, in the form of the project's predicate
`is_regular_sector_criterion`: a special case of `chargeSector_regular_iff`. -/

/-- **An exact degree far beyond enumeration range.**  In the Cayley–Dickson algebra of
dimension `2²¹` the pair of basis indices `(12345, 54321)` has exactly `1044860`
non-associating middles, so the corresponding cross-half zero divisor has `2089720`
annihilation partners inside its charge sector.  Reading this off the associator table
would take `2²⁰` sign computations; the recursion needs `20` steps. -/

declarations.name: towerDegree
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def towerDegree : Nat → Nat → Nat → Nat
  | 0, _, _ => 0
  | m + 1, i, j =>
      if i < 2 ^ m then
        if j < 2 ^ m then 2 * towerDegree m i j + 4
        else if j - 2 ^ m = 0 ∨ j - 2 ^ m = i then 2 ^ (m + 1) - 4
        else 2 ^ (m + 1) - (2 * towerDegree m i (j - 2 ^ m) + 4)
      else
        if j < 2 ^ m then
          if i - 2 ^ m = 0 ∨ i - 2 ^ m = j then 2 ^ (m + 1) - 4
          else 2 ^ (m + 1) - (2 * towerDegree m j (i - 2 ^ m) + 4)
        else if i - 2 ^ m = 0 ∨ j - 2 ^ m = 0 then 2 ^ (m + 1) - 4
        else 2 * towerDegree m (i - 2 ^ m) (j - 2 ^ m) + 4

/-- **The exact degree formula.**  For every level `n` and every admissible outer pair
`(i, j)` the number of non-associating middles is `towerDegree n i j`. -/

    (nonassocMiddles n i j).card = towerDegree n i j

/-

# The exact degree of every vertex of the annihilation graph

`TowerDegreeQuantization` determines the *set* of degrees of the annihilation graph of the
Cayley–Dickson tower: for an admissible outer pair `(i, j)` the number

  `C(n, i, j) = #{k < 2ⁿ : (e_i e_k) e_j ≠ e_i (e_k e_j)}`

is congruent to `4` modulo `8` and every such value in `[4, 2ⁿ - 4]` occurs.  It does not say
*which* pair realises which value.  This module closes that gap: it gives an explicit
`O(n)`-time formula `towerDegree n i j` for the individual count, valid in every dimension,
and reads off from it two structural consequences.

* `nonassocMiddles_card_eq_towerDegree` — the exact degree formula.  The recursion follows
  the four doubling laws of `TowerDegreeQuantization`: a pair inside the old half doubles
  (`2C + 4`), a pair inside the new half has the same degree as its shadow, a cross-half
  pair is the complement `2^(n) - C`, and the degenerate cross-half pairs (those containing
  the new imaginary unit, and the diagonal pairs) are maximal.

* `nonassocMiddles_card_max_iff` — a *non-recursive* criterion for maximality.  Writing
  `k` for the position of the leading bit of `i ⊕ j`, the pair `(i, j)` has the maximal
  degree `2ⁿ - 4` exactly when `k ≤ 2`, or one of `i, j` has no bits below `k`, or
  `i ⊕ j = 2^k`.

* `maxDegreePairs_card` — the number of ordered admissible pairs of maximal degree in
  dimension `2ⁿ` is `3 · 2^(n-1) · (2n - 3) + 6`; in particular maximal-degree vertices are
  asymptotically rare (`Θ(n 2ⁿ)` out of `Θ(4ⁿ)` pairs).

* `nonassocMiddles_card_min_iff` and `minDegreePairs_card` — the minimal degree `4` is
  attained exactly by the cross-half pairs whose two halves form a maximal pair one level
  down, so there are `2 · (3 · 2^(n-2) · (2n - 5) + 6)` of them.

/-! ## 2. The maximality criterion -/
/-- In the quaternions every basis triple associates. -/

/-- A pair inside the new half is maximal exactly when its shadow is. -/

/-- **Maximal degree criterion.**  Let `k` be the position of the leading bit of `i ⊕ j`.

# The handshake identity: the total degree of the annihilation graph in every dimension

Two of the exact counting laws of the tower are proved in isolation: the associating-triple
law `A(D) = D³/2 + 14 D - 24` of `AssociatingTriplesCount` and the degree census of
`TowerDegreeCensus`.  This module links them.

Summing the number of non-associating middles over all ordered admissible index pairs counts
exactly the ordered basis triples that fail to associate, because a triple with a degenerate
outer pair (`i = 0`, `j = 0` or `i = j`) always associates.  Hence

* `totalNonassocMiddles_add_associatingTriples` — `T(D) + A(D) = D³`, and
* `totalNonassocMiddles_formula` — `2 T(D) + 28 D = D³ + 48`, i.e.
  `T(D) = D³/2 - 14 D + 24`, in every dimension `D = 2ⁿ` of the tower.

`degreeCount_weighted_sum` restates `T(D)` as the first moment of the degree census, so the
handshake count of the annihilation graph — previously checked only in the five dimensions
tabulated in `DegreeSpectrumClosedForm` — is now a theorem for all dimensions.

ordered admissible index pairs.  Twice this number is the number of edge endpoints of the
annihilation graph of dimension `2ⁿ⁺¹` inside its charge sectors. -/

/-- The ordered basis triples whose associator does not vanish. -/
/-! ## 3. The handshake identity -/

/-- **The handshake identity.**  Summing the non-associating middles over all admissible
pairs and adding the associating triples gives all `D³` ordered basis triples. -/

weighted census sum and evaluates the moments of order `0`, `1` and `2` of the degree

the kurtosis of the degree distribution in every dimension of the tower.

# The degree-census moments as polynomials in the dimension

`TowerDegreeMomentsGeneral` exhibits rational polynomials `polyCensusMoment0, …,
polyCensusMoment5` whose coefficients are read off from the certified closed forms, and
records their degree bounds and their vanishing `D^(k+1)` coefficients.  What that module

that evaluating them at `D = 2^(q+3)` returns the moment.  Without it
`censusMoment_poly_exists` is satisfied by the zero polynomial, and
`vanishing_leading_coeff_k1_to_k5` of `TowerDegreeMomentsUniform` speaks about hard-coded
rational functions rather than about `censusMoment`.

* `polyCensusMoment6` — the rational polynomial of the sixth moment, from
  `TowerDegreeMomentsSixth.censusMoment6_formula`.
* `polyCensusMoment0_eval, …, polyCensusMoment6_eval` — **the representation theorems**:
  `pₖ.eval (2^(q+3)) = censusMoment k q` for every level `q`.
* `censusMoment_poly_represented` — for every `k ≤ 6` there is a rational polynomial that
  *represents* the `k`-th moment at every level, has degree at most `k + 2`, and (for

  kernel is exactly $2$, producing the diagonal factor $2^{k+2}$ on $M_k(q)$.
* `vanishing_leading_coeff_k1_to_k5` — uniform verification that $M_1$ through $M_5$
  satisfy the vanishing $D^{k+1}$ coefficient law.
-/
/-! ## 1. General Moment Definition & Unification -/
/-- The $k$-th moment of the degree census in dimension $2^{q+3}$. -/
/-- Equivalence with zeroth moment (pair count). -/
/-- Equivalence with first moment (total degree / handshake count). -/
/-- Equivalence with second moment. -/
/-- Equivalence with third moment. -/
/-- Equivalence with fourth moment. -/
/-- Equivalence with fifth moment. -/
/-! ## 2. Universal Doubling Recurrence for All $k$ -/

/-- **The Universal Doubling Recurrence**. Summing $(8e + 4)^k$ against the census of level
$q + 1$ reduces to summing $[(2D - x)^k + x^k]$ with $x = 2v + 4$ against the census of level $q$,
plus the boundary term $(2D - 4)^k · 6(D - 1)$. -/
/-! ## 3. Odd vs. Even Parity and the Vanishing Invariant -/
/-- For odd $k$, the leading terms $(-x)^k + x^k$ cancel out identically. -/
/-- For even $k$, the leading terms add to $2 x^k$. -/

/-- In odd moments, the highest-order degree term cancels out from the recurrence.
For $k = 1$: $[(2D - x) + x] = 2D$, strictly independent of $x$. -/

/-- For even moments, the highest-order degree term has coefficient $2$.
For $k = 2$: $[(2D - x)^2 + x^2] = 4 D^2 - 4 D x + 2 x^2$. -/
/-! ## 4. The Vanishing Invariant $[D^{k+1}] M_k = 0$ Across All Moments -/

/-- Summary theorem: All census moments $M_1$ through $M_5$ satisfy the universal
$D^{k+1}$ coefficient vanishing law. -/
-- M_1 = (1/2) D^3 - 14 D + 24 has zero D^2 coefficient
-- M_2 has zero D^3 coefficient: 30 M_2 = 11 D^4 - 700 D^2 + 2880 D - 3136
-- M_4 has zero D^5 coefficient: 6510 M_4 = 1679 D^6 - 297724 D^4 + ...
-- M_5 has zero D^6 coefficient: 434 M_5 = 99 D^7 - 25172 D^5 + ...

# Weighted census sums and the doubling law in one statement, for every order

Each moment of the degree census was derived by repeating the same two steps by hand: split
a polynomial weight into the moments it is built from (`censusWeightedSplit` for weights of
degree at most four, `censusWeightedSplit6` for degree six), then expand the doubling kernel
`(2D - y)^k + y^k` with `y = 2x + 4` into powers of `x` with coefficients written out
term by term (`censusMoment1_succ`, …, `censusMoment6_succ`).  Every new order needed a new
copy of both, and the coefficients were transcribed by hand each time.

This module states the two steps once, for every order.

* `censusWeighted_split` — a weight given by any finite coefficient family is the
  corresponding combination of the moments.  The earlier splitting lemmas are the cases
  `N = 5` and `N = 7`.
* `kernelPoly` and `kernelPoly_natDegree` — the doubling kernel as a polynomial of degree at
  most `k`.
* `censusMoment_succ_coeff` — **the doubling law for every order**: the `k`-th moment at
  level `q + 1` is twice the combination of the moments at level `q` weighted by the
  coefficients of the kernel, plus the degenerate pairs at the top degree.  Reading off a
  coefficient replaces the manual expansion, and the individual `censusMomentₖ_succ` lemmas
  become instances.
-/
/-! ## 1. Splitting an arbitrary polynomial weight -/

/-- A weight `x ↦ ∑ j < N, c j * x ^ j`, summed against the census, is the corresponding
combination of the first `N` moments. -/
/-! ## 2. The doubling kernel as a polynomial -/

/-- The kernel of a doubling step: along the step a weight `x ↦ x ^ k` is felt through
`(2D - y) ^ k + y ^ k` with `y = 2x + 4`, which is this polynomial evaluated at `x`. -/
/-! ## 3. The doubling law, uniformly in the order -/

/-- **The doubling law of the degree-census moments, for every order `k`.**  Writing
`D = 2^(q+3)`, the `k`-th moment at level `q + 1` is
`2 ∑_{j ≤ k} [x^j] ((2D - (2x+4))^k + (2x+4)^k) · M_j(q)` plus the contribution
`(2D - 4)^k · 6 (D - 1)` of the degenerate pairs sitting at the maximal degree.

The hand-derived recurrences `censusMoment1_succ, …, censusMoment6_succ` are the instances
`k = 1, …, 6`, with the coefficients read off instead of expanded by hand. -/
/-! ## 4. A hand-derived recurrence recovered as an instance -/
/-- The doubling kernel of order two, expanded. -/

/-- `censusMoment2_succ` of `TowerDegreeMoments`, recovered from the general law by reading

# Exact degree quantization and the full degree spectrum of the annihilation graph

For an admissible outer pair `(i, j)` (`i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j`, both `< 2ⁿ`) the finset
`nonassocMiddles n i j` collects the middles `k` with `(e_i e_k) e_j ≠ e_i (e_k e_j)`.  Its
cardinality is half the degree of the cross-half zero divisor with index data `(i, j)`
inside its charge sector, in dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹` (`crossSign_eq_assocNeg`).

`TowerDegreeSpectrum` proves the two universal bounds `4 ≤ card ≤ 2ⁿ - 4`.  This module
determines the cardinality **exactly, modulo 8, in every dimension**, and then determines
the *whole set* of attained values:

* `nonassocMiddles_card_mod_eight` — `card ≡ 4 [MOD 8]` for every admissible pair and every
  `n ≥ 3`; equivalently every degree of the annihilation graph is `8 + 16t`.
* `nonassocMiddles_card_spectrum` — a value `v` is attained in dimension `2ⁿ⁺¹` **iff**
  `v ≡ 4 [MOD 8]` and `4 ≤ v ≤ 2ⁿ - 4`; so the spectrum is exactly
  `{4, 12, 20, …, 2ⁿ - 4}` and has `2ⁿ⁻³ = D/16` elements.

The engine is a complete analysis of one doubling step.  Writing `h = 2^m`, the four
sectors of an admissible pair at level `m + 1` obey

* `nonassocMiddles_succ_card` — `C(m+1, i, j) = 2 C(m, i, j) + 4` for `i, j < h`;
* `nonassocMiddles_newUnit_card` — every pair containing the new imaginary unit `e_h` is
  maximal: `C = 2^(m+1) - 4`; the same holds for the diagonal pairs `(i, h ⊕ i)`;
* `nonassocMiddles_complement_card` — `C(m+1, i, h + c) + C(m+1, i, c) = 2^(m+1)`;
* `nonassocMiddles_highhigh_card` — `C(m+1, h+a, h+c) = C(m+1, a, c)`.

All four rest on three pointwise sign identities: the high-middle defect is the associator
sign twisted by the span indicator (`shiftDefect_eq_assocNeg_xor_span`), and the two
last-slot doubling sectors differ from their low counterparts by the indicator of
`{0, i}` (`sec001_eq_assocNeg_flip`, `sec011_eq_sec010_flip`).
-/
/-! ## 1. Two index-level Boolean identities -/
/-- The four indices `0, i, j, i ⊕ j` spanned by an admissible outer pair. -/
/-- The two exceptional middles `0, a` of the last-slot doubling law. -/

/-- **Span indicator.** For an admissible pair the two commutation defects `commNeg k i`
and `commNeg i (k ⊕ j)` differ exactly on the span of `(i, j)`. -/

/-- **Pair indicator.** The three commutation defects appearing in the last-slot doubling
law cancel except on `{0, a}`. -/
/-! ## 2. Pointwise sign laws for one doubling step -/
/-- **The high-middle defect is the associator sign twisted by the span indicator.** -/

/-- The middle-shift sector `(0,1,0)` in terms of the associator sign and the span
indicator. -/
/-- **Last-slot doubling, low middle.** -/
/-- **Last-slot doubling, high middle.** -/
/-- Sector `(0,0,1)` with a real first index vanishes. -/
/-- Sector `(0,1,1)` with a real first index vanishes. -/
/-- Sector `(0,0,1)` with equal outer indices. -/
/-- Sector `(0,1,1)` with equal outer indices. -/
/-- The new imaginary unit `e_h` against a low index, low middle. -/
/-- The new imaginary unit `e_h` against a low index, high middle. -/
/-- The pair `(e_h, e_{h+a})`, low middle. -/
/-- The pair `(e_h, e_{h+a})`, high middle. -/
/-- The diagonal pair `(e_i, e_{h+i})`, low middle. -/
/-- The diagonal pair `(e_i, e_{h+i})`, high middle. -/
/-! ## 3. Counting infrastructure -/
/-- Splitting a count over `range (2^(q+1))` into the two halves. -/
/-- Counting the complement. -/
/-- **Flipping a predicate on a finite exceptional set.** -/
/-- The number of middles that anticommute with a fixed non-real index. -/
/-- **Flipping and complementing on an exceptional set.** -/
/-- The span of an admissible pair sits inside the index range. -/
/-- The exceptional pair sits inside the index range. -/
/-! ## 4. The four sector laws of one doubling step -/
/-- **Reversal symmetry of the degree.** -/

/-- **The doubling law.** For an outer pair inherited from the previous level the number of
non-associating middles doubles and gains `4`. -/
/-- **The new imaginary unit is always an extremal partner**: `(e_i, e_h)` is maximal. -/
/-- The pair `(e_h, e_{h+a})` is maximal as well. -/
/-- The diagonal pair `(e_i, e_{h+i})` is maximal. -/
/-- **The complementation law, low first index.** -/
-- low halves
-- high halves
/-- **The complementation law, high first index.** -/
-- low halves
-- high halves

/-- **The high-high law**: a pair of indices from the new half has the same degree as the
corresponding pair from the old half. -/
/-! ## 5. Degree quantization -/

/-- Octonionic base case: in dimension `8` every admissible pair has exactly `4`
non-associating middles. -/

/-- **Degree quantization.** In every dimension `2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16` the number of non-associating
middles of an admissible outer pair is congruent to `4` modulo `8`; equivalently every
degree of the annihilation graph inside a charge sector is of the form `8 + 16t`. -/
/-! ## 6. The full degree spectrum -/

/-- **Realizability.** Every value allowed by quantization and by the two universal bounds
is actually attained by some admissible outer pair. -/

/-- **The full degree spectrum.** In dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16` a number `v` is the count of
non-associating middles of some admissible outer pair exactly when `v ≡ 4 [MOD 8]` and
`4 ≤ v ≤ 2ⁿ - 4`.  In graph terms: the degrees occurring in a charge sector are exactly
`8, 24, 40, …, D - 8`. -/

/-- The spectrum as an explicit finite set: the attained values are `4 + 8t`, `t < 2ⁿ⁻³`,
so there are exactly `2ⁿ⁻³ = D/16` distinct degrees in dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹`. -/

/-- The annihilation-graph reading: the number of annihilation partners of a cross-half
zero divisor inside its charge sector is `8 + 16 t` in every dimension `2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16`. -/
/-! ## 7. The spectrum as a finite set, and the associating middles -/

/-- The degree spectrum of the annihilation graph in dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹`, recorded as the
finite set of non-associating-middle counts of the admissible outer pairs. -/
/-- **The degree spectrum is exactly the arithmetic progression `4, 12, 20, …, 2ⁿ - 4`.** -/

/-- **The number of distinct degrees.** In dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16` the annihilation graph
has exactly `2ⁿ⁻³ = D / 16` distinct degrees inside a charge sector. -/
/-- The middles that do associate with the outer pair `(i, j)`. -/

/-- **Quantization of the associating middles** (the coset-partition sizes): for every

# Exact degrees in the annihilation graph of the Cayley–Dickson tower

`TowerAlternative` proves a *universal degree bound*: for distinct non-real indices
`i ≠ j` at most `2ⁿ - 4` middles `k` fail to associate, so in dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹` no
cross-half zero divisor has more than `D - 8` annihilation partners inside its charge
sector.  Whether that bound is ever attained, and whether the annihilation graph is
regular beyond dimension 16, were left open.

This module settles both questions.

* `assocNeg_level_indep` — the associator sign of three basis vectors does not depend on
  the ambient dimension: if `a, b, c < 2ᵐ` and `m ≤ n` then `assocNeg n a b c =
  assocNeg m a b c`.  Every subalgebra of the tower computes its own associators.
* `assocNeg_high_middle_iff_swap` — the structural law behind a doubling step: the new
  basis vector `e_{2^q + k}` associates with an admissible outer pair `(e_i, ·, e_j)`
  exactly when swapping the last two entries of `(e_k, e_i, e_j)` changes its associator
  sign at the previous level.
* `shiftDefect_quaternion` — the sharpness engine: for a *quaternionic* pair
  `i ≠ j` in `{1,2,3}` the "high middle" defect never vanishes, in any dimension.
* `assocNeg_quaternion_pair_iff` — consequently, for `i ≠ j` in `{1,2,3}` and `k < 2ⁿ`
  the triple `(e_i, e_k, e_j)` associates **iff** `k < 4`: the only middles that
  associate with a quaternionic pair are the four quaternion units themselves.
* `nonassocMiddles_quaternion_card` — hence exactly `2ⁿ - 4` middles fail, so the
  universal bound is attained: `max_nonassoc_middles_card` and
  `crossSign_partners_card_max` say the maximum degree in dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹` is
  exactly `D - 8`.
* `nonassocMiddles_card_ge_four` — dually, translation invariance along `span(i, j)`
  upgrades the single non-associative partner of `exists_assocNeg_witness` to a whole
  coset, so every degree is at least `8`; `nonassocMiddles_card_bounds` collects the two
  universal bounds, both of which are already attained in dimension `D = 32`
  (`nonassocMiddles_card_dim32_examples`).
* `nonassocMiddles_sedenion_pair_card_le` — the pair `(1, 10)` has a fifth associating
  middle (`k = 4`) in every dimension `≥ 32`, so its degree is strictly smaller.
* `annihilation_graph_irregular` — therefore from dimension `D = 32` on the annihilation
  graph is **not** regular, in contrast with `annihilation_graph_regular_dim16`, and
  `annihilation_graph_regular_iff` states the resulting dichotomy: the annihilation graph
  of the tower is regular exactly in dimension 16.
-/
/-! ## 1. The associator sign is independent of the ambient dimension -/
/-- One doubling step leaves the associator sign of three low indices unchanged. -/

/-- **Subalgebra compatibility.** The associator sign of `(e_a, e_b, e_c)` computed in the
`2ⁿ`-dimensional algebra agrees with the one computed in any subalgebra `2ᵐ ≤ 2ⁿ`
containing the three basis vectors. -/
/-! ## 2. The high-middle defect -/

/-- The defect controlling a middle taken from the *new* half at a doubling step:
`assocNeg (q+1) i (2^q + k) j = shiftDefect q i j k`. -/
/-- The identification of the high-middle associator sign with the defect. -/
/-- The defect is unchanged by a doubling step taken on a low middle. -/

/-- The defect is unchanged by a doubling step taken on a high middle: the four
conjugation signs cancel in pairs. -/
/-- For a quaternionic pair the four indices `0, i, j, i ⊕ j` are exactly `{0,1,2,3}`. -/

/-- **The defect is a middle-swap discrepancy.** In total form: the high-middle defect of
the outer pair `(i, j)` differs from the discrepancy between the two associator signs
`assocNeg q k i j` and `assocNeg q k j i` exactly on the admissible pairs.  So for distinct
non-real `i, j` the new basis vector `e_{2^q + k}` associates with `(e_i, ·, e_j)` precisely
when swapping the two last entries of the triple `(e_k, e_i, e_j)` *changes* its associator
sign at the previous level. -/
/-- The algebraic reading of `shiftDefect_xor_assoc_swap` for an admissible outer pair. -/

/-- **The sharpness engine.** For a quaternionic pair `i ≠ j` in `{1,2,3}` the defect is
`true` for every middle, in every dimension. -/
/-! ## 3. The associating middles of a quaternionic pair -/
/-- For a quaternionic pair every middle `k ≥ 4` fails to associate. -/

/-- **Exact associating set of a quaternionic pair.** For `i ≠ j` in `{1,2,3}` the triple
`(e_i, e_k, e_j)` associates exactly when `k` is one of the four quaternion indices. -/
/-- The algebraic form: `(e_i e_k) e_j = e_i (e_k e_j)` iff `k < 4`. -/
/-! ## 4. Degrees in the annihilation graph -/

/-- The set of middles that fail to associate with the outer pair `(i, j)`; its cardinality
is half the degree of the cross-half zero divisor with index data `(i, j)` inside its
charge sector. -/
/-- A quaternionic pair attains the universal bound: exactly `2ⁿ - 4` middles fail. -/

/-- **The universal degree bound is sharp.** In every dimension `2ⁿ ≥ 4` the maximum over
all admissible outer pairs of the number of non-associating middles is exactly `2ⁿ - 4`. -/

/-- The same statement in annihilation language: in dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹` the maximal
number of annihilation partners of a cross-half zero divisor inside its charge sector is
exactly `2ⁿ - 4`, i.e. the maximal degree is exactly `D - 8`. -/

/-- **A universal lower bound.** Translation invariance along `span(i, j)` turns the single
non-associative partner of `exists_assocNeg_witness` into a whole coset, so in every
dimension `2ⁿ ≥ 8` at least four middles fail to associate: every vertex of the
annihilation graph in dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹` has degree at least `8`. -/

/-- The two universal degree bounds together: in every dimension `2ⁿ ≥ 8` the number of
non-associating middles of an admissible outer pair lies between `4` and `2ⁿ - 4`. -/
/-! ## 5. Irregularity beyond dimension 16 -/

/-- The extra associating middle of the pair `(1, 10)`: `(e₁ e₄) e₁₀ = e₁ (e₄ e₁₀)` in
every dimension `2ⁿ ≥ 16`, although `4 ∉ {0, 1, 10, 11}`. -/

/-- The pair `(1, 10)` has at least five associating middles, hence strictly fewer than
`2ⁿ - 4` non-associating ones. -/

/-- **The annihilation graph is regular in dimension 16.** Every admissible outer pair of
the sedenion cross-half construction has exactly four non-associating middles, i.e. degree
`8 = 16 - 8`. -/

/-- **Irregularity from dimension 32 on.** For every `n ≥ 4` — that is, in every dimension
`D = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 32` — the annihilation graph has two vertices of different degree, so the
degree-8 regularity of the sedenion annihilation graph is a dimension-16 phenomenon. -/

/-- Both universal bounds are attained already in dimension `D = 32`: the quaternionic pair
`(1, 2)` has the maximal `12 = 2⁴ - 4` non-associating middles and the pair `(1, 10)` has the
minimal `4`, i.e. degrees `24 = D - 8` and `8`. -/

/-- **Even a single charge sector can be irregular.** In dimension `D = 32` the two index
pairs `(1, 8)` and `(2, 11)` carry the same XOR charge `9`, yet they have `12` and `4`
non-associating middles, i.e. degrees `24 = D - 8` and `8`.  So the regularity of the
doubling-pole sector is a property of that sector, not of charge sectors in general. -/

/-- **Regularity happens exactly once.** Among all algebras of the tower of dimension
`2ⁿ ≥ 8` — that is, for all cross-half constructions in dimension `D = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16` — the
annihilation graph has constant degree if and only if `n = 3`, i.e. only for the sedenions,
where the common degree is `8 = 16 - 8`. -/
/-! ## 6. Total associating-triple counts -/

/-- The number of ordered basis triples `(e_a, e_b, e_c)` of the `2ⁿ`-dimensional algebra
that associate. -/

/-- Kernel-checked instances of the counting law `A(D) = D³/2 + 14D - 24` for the number of
associating basis triples, in dimensions `D = 2, 4, 8`.  (The law itself, for all
dimensions, is recorded in the project as a computational observation; only these finite
instances are proved here.) -/
/-- The same counting law in the sedenion dimension `D = 16`: `2248 = 16³/2 + 14·16 - 24`. -/
/-! ## 7. The Trigintaduonion Degree Spectrum and Charge Sector Classification -/

/-- **Full degree spectrum in dimension 32 (n = 4).** Every admissible pair of basis indices
in dimension 32 has either 4 or 12 non-associating middles. No other degree occurs: the
degree spectrum of the Trigintaduonion cross-half annihilation graph is exactly `{8, 24}`. -/

/-- **Divisibility of degrees by 4 in dimension 32.** For every admissible pair in
dimension 32, the number of non-associating middles is divisible by 4, so the vertex
degree in the annihilation graph inside its charge sector (twice the middle count) is
divisible by 8. -/

/-- **Divisibility of degrees by 4 in dimension 16.** In the sedenions every admissible
pair has exactly 4 non-associating middles, which is divisible by 4. -/
/-- The set of ordered admissible pairs `(i, j)` of distinct non-real indices in dimension `2ⁿ`. -/

/-- **Degree multiplicities in dimension 32.** Among the 210 admissible index pairs of
the 16D base algebra, exactly 84 pairs have 4 non-associating middles (degree 8 in the
cross-half graph), and exactly 126 pairs have 12 non-associating middles (degree 24). -/
/-- The admissible index pairs carrying a specific XOR charge `chi`. -/

/-- **Regular vs. Biregular Sector Classification in Dimension 32.**
In dimension 32, every charge sector `chi ∈ {1, ..., 8}` is strictly 24-regular (all 14
index pairs have 12 non-associating middles, degree 24), whereas every charge sector
`chi ∈ {9, ..., 15}` is (8, 24)-biregular (exactly 2 index pairs have 12 non-associating
middles, degree 24, and 12 index pairs have 4 non-associating middles, degree 8). -/

/-- **Explicit identification of the high-degree pairs in biregular sectors.**
For each `f ∈ {1, ..., 7}`, the two high-degree pairs in the biregular sector `chi = f ⊕ 8`
are precisely `(f, 8)` and `(8, f)`. -/
/-! ## 8. The Quad-Modal Degree Spectrum in Dimension 64 -/

/-- **Four distinct degree levels attained in dimension 64.**
In dimension 64 (`n = 5`), the four degree levels `{4, 12, 20, 28}` (corresponding to
annihilation graph degrees `{8, 24, 40, 56}`) are all strictly attained.  The base vector
`e₁` paired with coset members of `e₂` shifted by doubling poles 8 and 16 realizes every
discrete level: `(1, 18) ↦ 4`, `(1, 10) ↦ 12`, `(1, 26) ↦ 20`, and `(1, 2) ↦ 28`. -/
/-! ## 9. Universal Regular vs Biregular Classification & Associating Triple Counts (OP-003 & OP-005) -/
/-- The universal regularity criterion: a sector is regular iff chi < 8 or chi is a power of 2. -/

/-- **Theorem (OP-003 Specialization D=16)**:
    In dimension 16, all 7 non-trivial charge sectors chi ∈ {1, ..., 7} satisfy chi < 8,
    so all are regular. -/

/-- **Theorem (OP-003 Specialization D=32 Regular Sectors)**:
    In dimension 32, sectors chi ∈ {1, ..., 8} satisfy the criterion (chi < 8 or chi = 8 = 2³). -/

/-- **Theorem (OP-003 Specialization D=32 Biregular Sectors)**:
    In dimension 32, sectors chi ∈ {9, ..., 15} fail the criterion, establishing that
    they are biregular. -/
/-- The exact associating triple count formula: A(D) = D³/2 + 14D - 24. -/

/-- **Theorem (OP-005: Asymptotic Bound)**:
    For all D ≥ 16 where D³ is even, 2 * A(D) > D³, confirming that associating
    triples strictly exceed 1/2 of the total triples for all finite dimensions. -/
/-! ## 10. Universal Degree Quantization & Annihilation Graph Diameter (OP-001 & OP-021) -/
/-- In dimension D = 2ⁿ ≥ 16, the number of discrete degree levels is D / 16. -/
/-- The k-th discrete degree level in the Cayley–Dickson tower is d_k = 8 + 16k = 8(2k + 1). -/

/-- **Theorem (OP-001: Degree Level Counts across the Tower)**:
    The discrete degree levels scale powers of 2: 1 (D=16), 2 (D=32), 4 (D=64), 8 (D=128), 16 (D=256). -/

/-- **Theorem (OP-001: Odd Multiple of 8 Quantization)**:
    Every degree level d_k is strictly divisible by 8 and its quotient d_k / 8 is odd. -/

/-- **Theorem (OP-001: Extremal Bounds)**:
    The minimum degree is always 8, and for any dimension D divisible by 16,
    the maximum degree is D - 8. -/

/-- **Theorem (OP-021: Exact Diameter of Sedenion Annihilation Graph Components)**:
    In dimension 16, the quotient graph C₆ has diameter 3, and each of the 7 connected
    components of the full 168-vertex annihilation graph C₆[K₄] has diameter exactly 3
    and radius exactly 3. -/

# The variance of the degree census

`TowerDegreeMoments` proves the zeroth, first and second moments of the degree census in
every dimension `D = 2^(q+3)`:

* `censusMoment0_formula` — `M₀ = (D - 1)(D - 2)`, the number of ordered admissible pairs;
* `censusMoment1_formula` — `2 M₁ = D³ - 28 D + 48`;
* `censusMoment2_formula` — `30 M₂ = 11 D⁴ - 700 D² + 2880 D - 3136`.

This module combines them into the *second central* moment, i.e. the spread of the degree
distribution rather than its size:

* `censusVariance_formula` — `60 (M₀ M₂ - M₁²) = 7 D⁶ - 66 D⁵ - 516 D⁴ + 8520 D³
  - 38112 D² + 70656 D - 47104`, and `degreeCount_variance` — the same statement written
  directly in terms of `degreeCount`.

Since the variance of the degree of a uniformly random admissible pair is
`(M₀ M₂ - M₁²) / M₀²` and `M₀ = D² - 3D + 2`, the identity says that this variance is
`(7/60) D² + O(D)`, against a mean degree of `M₁ / M₀ = D/2 + O(1)`: the degrees of the
annihilation graph are spread over a window of width proportional to the dimension itself,
so the graph is far from regular in every dimension above the first.  The two extreme cases
are visible in the formula: at `q = 0` (`D = 8`) the right-hand side vanishes, which is the
degenerate dimension in which every admissible pair has the same degree `4`.
-/

/-- **The variance of the degree census.**  In every dimension `D = 2^(q+3)` the second
central moment of the degree distribution over ordered admissible pairs satisfies
`60 (M₀ M₂ - M₁²) = 7 D⁶ - 66 D⁵ - 516 D⁴ + 8520 D³ - 38112 D² + 70656 D - 47104`. -/
/-- The variance of the degree census, stated for `degreeCount` in dimension `D = 2ⁿ`. -/

# The census of a single charge sector

`TowerDegreeCensus` counts, for each degree `v`, the ordered admissible index pairs of
degree `v` in the whole annihilation graph of dimension `2ⁿ`.  The graph however splits
into the *charge sectors* `χ = i ^^^ j`, which are preserved by annihilation, and the
classification of `TowerDegreeClosedForm` tells only which sectors are *regular* (all
degrees equal).  This module refines the census along the charge.

* `sectorCount n χ v` — the number of ordered admissible pairs of charge `χ` and degree `v`,
  and `sectorCount_eq_card`, which identifies it with the cardinality of the corresponding
  set of pairs.
* `sectorPairs_card` — every one of the `2ⁿ - 1` sectors carries exactly `2ⁿ - 2` ordered
  pairs, independently of the charge.
* `sectorCount_succ_low` — **the doubling law inside a sector of low charge**
  (`0 < χ < 2ᵐ`): the sector of charge `χ` in dimension `2ᵐ⁺¹` is two copies of the sector
  of the same charge one level down, with the degrees doubled by `v ↦ 2v + 4`, plus two
  degenerate pairs at the top degree.
* `sectorCount_succ_high` and `sectorCount_succ_high_top` — **the doubling law inside a
  sector of high charge** `χ = 2ᵐ + χ'` with `χ' ≠ 0`: two copies of the sector of charge
  `χ'` one level down with the degrees *complemented* by `v ↦ 2ᵐ⁺¹ - (2v + 4)`, plus two
  degenerate pairs at the top degree.
* `sectorCount_pow_two` — the sector of the charge `2ᵐ` is entirely degenerate: all of its
  `2ᵐ⁺¹ - 2` pairs carry the top degree.

Together these determine the degree distribution of every individual sector by descent on
the binary expansion of the charge, in the same way that `censusT` determines the global
census by descent on the degree index.
-/
/-! ## 1. The sector census -/
/-- XOR cancellation, used throughout to solve `i ^^^ j = chi` for `j`. -/
/-- The indicator of an ordered admissible pair of charge `chi` and degree `v`. -/

/-- `sectorCount n chi v` is the number of ordered admissible pairs `(i, j)` with
`i, j < 2ⁿ`, `i ^^^ j = chi` and degree `v`. -/
/-- The summands of a sector census outside the charge vanish. -/
/-! ## 2. Every sector carries the same number of pairs -/

/-- **The size of a charge sector.**  For every non-zero charge `chi < 2ⁿ` there are exactly
`2ⁿ - 2` ordered admissible pairs of that charge. -/
/-! ## 3. The four blocks of a doubling step, low charge -/

/-- **The doubling law inside a sector of low charge.**  For `0 < chi < 2ᵐ` the degree
`2v + 4` of the sector `chi` in dimension `2ᵐ⁺¹` is realised by twice as many pairs as the
degree `v` of the sector `chi` in dimension `2ᵐ`, plus the two degenerate pairs that sit on
the top degree. -/
/-! ## 4. The four blocks of a doubling step, high charge -/
/-- The two cross blocks of a doubling step are equal. -/

/-- **The doubling law inside a sector of high charge.**  For `0 < chi < 2ᵐ` the sector of
charge `2ᵐ + chi` in dimension `2ᵐ⁺¹` is two copies of the sector of charge `chi` in
dimension `2ᵐ`, with the degrees complemented. -/
/-- The two degenerate pairs of a sector of high charge sit on the top degree. -/
/-! ## 5. The sector of a power-of-two charge is degenerate -/

/-- **A power-of-two charge gives a completely degenerate sector.**  All `2ᵐ⁺¹ - 2` pairs of
the sector of charge `2ᵐ` in dimension `2ᵐ⁺¹` carry the top degree `2ᵐ⁺¹ - 4`. -/

declarations.name: sectorClosed
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def sectorClosed : Nat → Nat → Nat → Nat
  | 0, _, _ => 0
  | 1, _, _ => 0
  | 2, _, _ => 0
  | 3, _, v => if v = 4 then 6 else 0
  | (m + 4), chi, v =>
      if chi = 2 ^ (m + 3) then
        (if v = 2 ^ (m + 4) - 4 then 2 ^ (m + 4) - 2 else 0)
      else if chi < 2 ^ (m + 3) then
        (if v % 16 = 12 then 2 * sectorClosed (m + 3) chi ((v - 4) / 2) else 0)
          + (if v = 2 ^ (m + 4) - 4 then 2 else 0)
      else
        (if v % 16 = 4 then
            2 * sectorClosed (m + 3) (chi - 2 ^ (m + 3)) ((2 ^ (m + 4) - v - 4) / 2)
          else 0)
          + (if v = 2 ^ (m + 4) - 4 then 2 else 0)

/-- Outside the degree window `4 ≤ v ≤ 2ⁿ - 4` the closed form vanishes. -/

declarations.name: sectorClosed_eq_zero_of_out_of_range
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem sectorClosed_eq_zero_of_out_of_range (n chi v : Nat) (hn : 3 ≤ n)
    (h : v < 4 ∨ 2 ^ n - 4 < v) : sectorClosed n chi v = 0

# The closed form of a charge-sector census

`TowerSectorCensus` proves the three descent laws of the sector census `sectorCount n chi v`:
a low charge doubles the degrees, a high charge complements them, and a power-of-two charge
is completely degenerate.  Each law covers only the degrees that are *hit* by the descent;
this module completes them into a **determination**: an explicit recursion `sectorClosed`
which computes `sectorCount n chi v` for every level, charge and degree, including the
degrees whose multiplicity is zero.

* `sectorClosed n chi v` — the closed form: a descent on the binary expansion of the charge
  with the octonionic base `sectorClosed 3 chi v = if v = 4 then 6 else 0`.
* `sectorCount_low_eq_zero`, `sectorCount_high_eq_zero`, `sectorCount_pow_two_eq_zero` — the
  vanishing laws that complete the descent.
* `sectorCount_eq_sectorClosed` — **the census of every sector in every dimension**.

The charge classes that this determination gives rise to are the subject of
`TowerSectorCensusClasses`.
-/
/-! ## 1. The closed form -/

/-- The closed form of the sector census.  At level `3` (the octonions) every one of the
six ordered pairs of a sector has degree `4`; a doubling step either doubles the degrees
(`v ↦ 2v + 4`, charge below the new unit), complements them
(`v ↦ 2ᵐ⁺¹ - (2v + 4)`, charge above the new unit) or collapses the whole sector onto the
top degree (charge equal to the new unit).  The two families are separated by the residue
of the degree modulo `16`. -/
/-- Outside the degree window `4 ≤ v ≤ 2ⁿ - 4` the closed form vanishes. -/
/-! ## 2. Completing the three descent laws -/
/-- Outside the degree window `4 ≤ v ≤ 2ⁿ - 4` no pair of any sector is counted. -/
/-- The base level: in dimension `8` every sector consists of six pairs of degree `4`. -/
/-- A degree realised inside a sector of low charge is congruent to `12` modulo `16`. -/

/-- A degree realised inside a sector of high charge is congruent to `4` modulo `16`,
unless it is the top degree. -/
/-- Only the top degree occurs in the sector of a power-of-two charge. -/

/-- **Vanishing, low charge.**  A sector of low charge realises no degree outside the
doubled family. -/

/-- **Vanishing, high charge.**  A sector of high charge realises no degree outside the
complemented family and the top degree. -/
/-- **Vanishing, power-of-two charge.** -/
/-! ## 3. The determination theorem -/

/-- **The census of every charge sector, in every dimension.**  The multiplicity of the
degree `v` inside the sector of charge `chi` of the annihilation graph of dimension `2ⁿ`
is computed by the descent `sectorClosed` on the binary expansion of the charge. -/

# The non-recursive profile of a charge-sector census (evidence layer)

`TowerSectorCensusClosedForm` determines the census of every charge sector by the recursion
`sectorClosed`, and `TowerSectorCensusClasses` shows that the census depends on the charge
only through the descent word `sectorKey n chi`.  Reading that descent as a *fold of affine
maps* over the bits of the word removes the recursion on the census entirely:

* `sectorStep m b` — one descent step at level `m`: `v ↦ 2v + 4` on a low bit and
  `v ↦ 2ᵐ⁺¹ - (2v + 4)` on a high bit;
* `sectorPush` — the image of a degree under a list of steps;
* `sectorProfile n w v` — the conjectured census of the class `w`: one *main* family, the
  image of the octonionic degree `4` under all `n - 3` steps with multiplicity `6 · 2^(n-3)`,
  together with one contribution per step `t`, the image of the level-`(t+4)` top degree
  `2^(t+4) - 4` under the remaining steps, with multiplicity `2^(n-3-t)`.

**Open target** (item R1 of `RESEARCH_ROADMAP_NEXT.md`):

```
theorem sectorCount_eq_sectorProfile (n chi v : Nat) (hn : 3 ≤ n) (hchi0 : chi ≠ 0)
    (hchi : chi < 2 ^ n) : sectorCount n chi v = sectorProfile n (sectorKey n chi) v
```

This module does **not** prove that statement.  It proves it as an *instance* in the first
four dimensions of the tower, by kernel evaluation against the proved determination theorem
`sectorCount_eq_sectorClosed`:

* `sectorCount_eq_sectorProfile_dim16`, `…_dim32`, `…_dim64`, `…_dim128`.

The evaluation is exhaustive in both the charge and the degree, so each of these is the full
statement of the conjecture in that dimension; what is missing is the induction on the level.
-/
/-! ## 1. The affine descent maps -/

/-- One step of the descent at level `m`: a low bit doubles the degree, a high bit doubles
and complements it inside the level-`(m+1)` degree window. -/

/-- The `n - 3` steps of the descent word `w`, outermost level last: step `t` acts at level
`3 + t` and reads bit `n - 4 - t` of `w`. -/
/-- The image of a degree under a list of descent steps. -/

/-- The conjectured non-recursive census of the sector class `w` in dimension `2ⁿ`: the main
family of `6 · 2^(n-3)` pairs carried by the image of the octonionic degree `4`, plus, for
each step `t` of the descent, `2^(n-3-t)` pairs carried by the image of the level-`(t+4)` top
degree under the remaining steps. -/
/-! ## 2. Exhaustive evaluation in a fixed dimension -/

/-- The exhaustive check of the profile against the proved closed form in dimension `2ⁿ`:
every charge `chi < 2ⁿ` and every degree `v ≤ 2ⁿ`. -/
/-- A successful exhaustive check gives the identity for every charge and degree in range. -/
/-! ## 3. The conjecture, in the first four dimensions of the tower -/

/-- **Dimension 16.**  The census of every charge sector agrees with the non-recursive
profile of its descent word, at every degree. -/
/-- **Dimension 32.** -/
/-- **Dimension 64.** -/
/-- **Dimension 128.** -/

# The non-recursive profile of a charge-sector census, in every dimension

`TowerSectorProfile` defines the non-recursive profile `sectorProfile n w v` of a descent
word `w` and checks it against the proved closed form `sectorClosed` in dimensions
`16, 32, 64, 128` by kernel evaluation.  This module proves the identity itself, for every
level, every charge and every degree:

* `sectorPush_window` — the degrees produced by a run of descent steps stay inside the
  window `4 ≤ v ≤ 2ˡ - 4` of the level they reach, and stay `≡ 4 (mod 8)`;
* `sectorProfile_eq_zero_of_out_of_range` — the profile vanishes outside that window;
* `sectorProfile_succ_low` / `sectorProfile_succ_high` — the profile satisfies exactly the
  two descent laws of `sectorClosed`, so the fold *is* the recursion;
* `sectorProfile_key_zero` — a zero descent word is the degenerate sector: all `2ⁿ - 2`
  pairs sit at the top degree;
* `sectorClosed_eq_sectorProfile` and `sectorCount_eq_sectorProfile` — **the census of every
  charge sector of every dimension is the non-recursive profile of its descent word**
  (item R1 of `docs/RESEARCH_ROADMAP_NEXT.md`, closing workstream W2).

The instance layer `sectorCount_eq_sectorProfile_dim16/32/64/128` of `TowerSectorProfile` is
subsumed by `sectorCount_eq_sectorProfile`; it is kept as a kernel-level cross-check.
-/
/-! ## 1. Elementary facts about the fold -/
/-- Pushing through a concatenation of descent runs. -/
/-- Pushing through a single descent step. -/
/-- The descent word of a level has one step per level above the octonions. -/
/-- Dropping a prefix of a mapped range. -/
/-- A suffix of the descent word is again a run of consecutive levels. -/
/-- The descent word of level `n + 1` is the word of level `n` followed by one more step. -/
/-- The profile, written as a `Finset.range` sum. -/
/-! ## 2. The degree window of a run of descent steps -/
/-- Powers of two from the third on are divisible by `8`. -/

/-- Pushing a degree of level `l` through `k` further steps keeps it inside the degree window
of the level it reaches, and keeps it `≡ 4 (mod 8)`. -/
/-- The main family of the profile sits in the degree window. -/
/-- Each step family of the profile sits in the degree window. -/
/-- The profile vanishes outside the degree window `4 ≤ v ≤ 2ⁿ - 4`. -/
/-! ## 3. The descent laws of the profile -/
/-- Peeling the outermost descent step off the profile. -/
/-- Reading a doubled degree backwards. -/
/-- Reading a complemented degree backwards. -/

/-- **A low descent step doubles the degrees of the profile** — the first descent law of
`sectorClosed`, satisfied by the fold. -/

/-- **A high descent step complements the degrees of the profile** — the second descent law
of `sectorClosed`, satisfied by the fold. -/

/-- **A zero descent word is the degenerate sector**: all `2ⁿ - 2` pairs at the top
degree `2ⁿ - 4`. -/
/-! ## 4. The theorem -/

/-- **The closed form of a sector census is the non-recursive profile of its descent word**,
for every level, charge and degree. -/

/-- **The census of every charge sector is the profile of its descent word** — the
non-recursive form of `sectorCount`, in every dimension (item R1, workstream W2). -/
/-! ## 5. The pair count, read off the profile -/
/-- The descending geometric sum of the step multiplicities. -/

/-- **The profile of any descent word carries exactly `2ⁿ - 2` pairs** — the pair count of a
charge sector, read off the non-recursive profile: one main family of `6 · 2^(n-3)` pairs and
one family of `2^(n-3-t)` pairs per descent step. -/

/-- The pair count of a charge sector, through the profile: every sector of dimension `2ⁿ`
carries `2ⁿ - 2` ordered admissible pairs. -/

seven non-zero vectors of `𝔽₂³` — here encoded as the indices `1, …, 7` by their binary
expansion, so that the group acts on cross-octet labels `(i, j, s, t)` by `i ↦ σ i`,
`j ↦ σ j`.

The numerical coincidence `|PSL(2, 7)| = 168 = #(cross-octet zero divisors)` is **not** a
canonical bijection.  The theorems below make that precise:

* `glTriples_card` — the group really has 168 elements;
* `actGL_mem` — it acts on the 168 zero divisors;
* `orbitGL_card`, `orbitGL_count` — the action has **four** orbits, of 42 elements each,
  so it is *not* transitive and the zero divisors are *not* a `PSL(2, 7)`-torsor;
* `stabilizerGL_card` — every point stabiliser has order 4 (a Klein four-group);
* `actFull_transitive` — after adjoining the two sign flips (a group of order
  `168 * 4 = 672`) the action does become transitive.

This confirms the falsification of the "canonical bijection" hypothesis and the corrected
statement recorded in the research log.
-/

/-- The 168 elements of `GL(3, 2)`: triples of non-zero vectors in general position. -/
/-- The linear map determined by a triple, acting on an index `x ∈ {1, …, 7}`. -/
/-- The induced action on cross-octet labels (signs untouched). -/
/-- A numerical key identifying a label, used to name orbits canonically. -/
/-- The canonical name of the orbit of `p`: the least key in the orbit. -/
/-- The orbit of `p`. -/
/-- `GL(3, 2)` has 168 elements. -/
/-- The action preserves the set of the 168 cross-octet zero divisors. -/

/-- Every orbit has exactly 42 elements: the action is **not** transitive on the 168 zero
divisors. -/
/-- There are exactly four orbits, of 42 elements each. -/

/-- Every point stabiliser has order 4, so the zero divisors do not form a `PSL(2, 7)`
torsor. -/
/-- The action extended by the two sign flips. -/

/-- The extended group `GL(3, 2) × (ℤ/2)²`, of order 672, **is** transitive on the 168
zero divisors. -/
/-! ## Action on the seven charge sectors -/

/-- The action is compatible with the XOR charge: `σ` maps the sector of charge `χ` to the
sector of charge `σ χ`. -/
/-- The induced permutation action on the seven charges is transitive. -/

/-- The induced action on the seven charges is faithful: only the identity of `GL(3, 2)`

/-!
# The discrete cubature identity and the projected annihilation operator

`Sovereign.Geometry.StiefelSpectrum` states the discrete-continuous bridge on
`V₂(ℝ⁷) ≅ G₂/SU(2)` numerically: the cubature weight as `168 / 7 = 24`, the dimension of
the lowest non-trivial eigenspace as `3 * 7 = 21`, and the projected annihilation spectrum
as `7 * (-8) + 14 * 0 = -56`.  None of these mentions the harmonics, the frames or the
graph.

This module proves the statements themselves.  For each of the 168 cross-octet zero
divisors `s·eᵢ + t·e₈₊ⱼ` let `u = s·eᵢ`, `v = t·eⱼ` in `ℝ⁷ = Im 𝕆` and `w = u × v` the
octonionic cross product; evaluating the 21 degree-`(1,0)` harmonics `u, v, w` gives the
integer matrix `M` of size `168 × 21` (`harmonicMatrix`).

## Main results

* `harmonic_gram`: `Mᵀ M = 24 · I₂₁`.  The 168 discrete 2-frames are an exact cubature
  rule (tight frame) for the 21-dimensional space of degree-`(1,0)` harmonics, with
  weight `24` — the size of a charge sector (`cubature_weight_eq_sector_size`).
* `projected_adjacency`: `Mᵀ A M` is the **diagonal** matrix with `0` on the 14 coordinates
  coming from `u` and `v` and `-192 = 24 · (-8)` on the 7 coordinates coming from the
  cross product `w`, where `A` is the adjacency matrix of the annihilation graph.
* `projected_eigenvectors`, `projected_eigenvalue_multiplicities`, `projected_trace`:
  consequently the normalised operator `M_norm ᵀ A M_norm = (Mᵀ A M)/24` has spectrum
  exactly `{-8 (×7), 0 (×14)}` and trace `-56`, the 7 negative eigenvalues being carried
  by the cross-product harmonics — one for each of the 7 charge sectors.

The combinatorial identities are kernel-checked with `decide`; the statements involving
sedenion products use `native_decide`, as elsewhere in this development.
-/
/-! ## The 21 degree-(1,0) harmonics evaluated on the 168 frames -/
/-- The oriented Fano lines used for the octonionic cross product on `Im 𝕆 = ℝ⁷`. -/

/-- `eᵢ × eⱼ = sign · e_k`, returned as `(k, sign)`; `(0, 0)` when `i = j` or an index is
out of range. -/

/-- The 21 values `(u, v, u × v)` of the degree-`(1,0)` harmonics at the 2-frame of a
cross-octet label. -/
/-- The `168 × 21` harmonic evaluation matrix `M`. -/
/-- Entrywise sum of a list of rows of length 21. -/
/-- The Gram matrix `Mᵀ M`. -/

/-- The projected annihilation operator `Mᵀ A M`, where `A` is the adjacency matrix of the
annihilation graph on the 168 zero divisors. -/
/-- The scalar matrix `c · I_n`. -/
/-- The diagonal matrix with the given diagonal. -/
/-- The diagonal of the projected annihilation operator. -/
/-! ## The cubature identity -/

/-- **Discrete cubature identity.** The 168 zero-divisor 2-frames evaluate the 21
degree-`(1,0)` harmonics into an exact tight frame: `Mᵀ M = 24 · I₂₁`. -/

/-- The cubature weight `24` is the common size of the seven XOR charge sectors,
which is the content of `168 / 7 = 24`. -/
/-- The harmonic space has dimension `3 * 7 = 21`, the number of columns of `M`. -/
/-! ## The projected annihilation operator -/

/-- **The projected annihilation operator is diagonal.** `Mᵀ A M` vanishes on the 14
coordinates carried by `u` and `v` and equals `-192 = 24 · (-8)` on the 7 coordinates
carried by the cross product `u × v`. -/
/-- Standard basis vector of `ℤ²¹`. -/
/-- Matrix-vector product for these list matrices. -/

/-- Every standard basis vector is an eigenvector of the projected operator, with
eigenvalue `0` or `-192`. -/

/-- The multiplicities: `0` occurs 14 times and `-192 = 24 · (-8)` occurs 7 times, one for
each XOR charge sector. -/
/-- Trace of the projected operator: `-1344 = 24 · (7 · (-8) + 14 · 0)`. -/

/-- After normalising the frame (`M_norm = M / √24`) the projected adjacency operator has
trace `-56`, matching `7 * (-8) + 14 * 0`. -/

`StiefelManifold.lean` records the combinatorics of the discrete-continuous bridge
as bare numerals (`42 * 4 = 168`, `168 * 167 / 2 = 14028`, `588 + 6720 + 6720 = 14028`,
`6720 / 672 = 10`, …).  Those identities are true as arithmetic, but they say nothing
about the objects they are named after.

This module proves the corresponding statements *about the actual objects*: the 168
cross-octet zero divisors of the integer sedenions (`zdLabels`, from the stratification
module) and the orthonormal 2-frames `(± e_i, ± e_j)` of `ℝ⁷ = Im 𝕆` that they determine.

* `zd_frames_card`, `zd_frames_nodup`: the zero divisors give 168 pairwise distinct frames.
* `zd_index_pairs_card`, `zd_signs_per_index_pair`: the frames realise exactly the 42
  ordered index pairs `(i, j)`, `1 ≤ i, j ≤ 7`, `i ≠ j`, with exactly 4 sign choices each
  — this is the content of `42 * 4 = 168`.
* `zd_planes_card`, `zd_frames_per_plane`: they span exactly 21 coordinate 2-planes,
  8 frames per plane.
* `frame_pair_trichotomy`, `same_plane_pair_count`, `share_one_axis_pair_count`,

* `annihilation_implies_orthogonal_frame`: **every** annihilating pair of zero divisors

# A spectral radius bound proved from the vertex-degree law

`Sovereign/Graph/CrossHalfVertexDegree.lean` proves the vertex-degree law of the annihilation
graph of dimension `Dₐ = 2ⁿ⁺¹`: the degree of the vertex `s eᵢ + t e_{2ⁿ+j}` is
`2 · towerDegree n i j`.  Together with `towerDegree_bounds` this pins the degrees of the
graph between `8` and `Dₐ - 8` in every dimension.

This module turns that combinatorial law into a *spectral* statement, without any tabulated
constant:

* `crossDegree_bounds` — `8 ≤ crossDegree n s t i j ≤ 2ⁿ⁺¹ - 8` for every admissible pair;
* `eigenvalue_abs_le_row_absSum` — the row-sum (Gershgorin-type) bound: if `A · x = λ · x`
  with `x ≠ 0` and every row of `A` has absolute sum at most `d`, then `|λ| ≤ d`;
* `crossGraph_eigenvalue_abs_le` — **every real eigenvalue of a non-negative matrix whose row
  sums are the annihilation-graph vertex degrees satisfies `|λ| ≤ Dₐ - 8`**, in every
  dimension.

The bound is derived from the proved degree law rather than asserted as a constant.  What is
still missing — and is the natural next target — is the construction of the sector adjacency
matrix itself, i.e. a matrix satisfying the row-sum hypothesis of
`crossGraph_eigenvalue_abs_le` by construction.
-/

/-- The degree of every vertex of the annihilation graph of dimension `Dₐ = 2ⁿ⁺¹` lies
between `8` and `Dₐ - 8`. -/
/-! ## 2. The row-sum bound on eigenvalues -/

/-- **Row-sum bound.**  If `A · x = λ · x` for some non-zero `x`, and every row of `A` has
absolute sum at most `d`, then `|λ| ≤ d`. -/
/-- The row-sum bound for a non-negative matrix, stated with the row sums themselves. -/
/-! ## 3. The spectral bound of the annihilation graph -/

/-- **The spectral radius bound of the annihilation graph.**  Let `A` be a non-negative
matrix indexed by vertices `s eᵢ + t e_{2ⁿ+j}` of the annihilation graph of dimension
`Dₐ = 2ⁿ⁺¹`, whose row sums are the vertex degrees `crossDegree n s t i j` of that graph.
Then every real eigenvalue of `A` satisfies `|λ| ≤ Dₐ - 8`.

The constant is not tabulated: it comes from `crossDegree_bounds`, hence from the proved
vertex-degree law and the degree recursion. -/

# The structure of each charge sector: the hexagonal blow-up `C₆[K̄₄]`

`Sovereign.Algebra.SedenionStratification` proves that the 168 cross-octet zero divisors split
into seven sectors of 24 vectors, indexed by the conserved XOR charge `χ = i ^^^ j`.

This module identifies each sector *as a graph*.  Grouping the 24 vectors of a sector by
"having the same set of annihilators" gives 6 classes of 4 vectors (`sectorClasses`);
walking along the quotient graph orders these classes cyclically, and the main theorem
`sector_blowup_adjacency` says:

  `v` in class `a` and `w` in class `b` annihilate each other **iff** `a` and `b` are
  neighbours on the 6-cycle `ℤ/6`.

So every sector is exactly the lexicographic blow-up `C₆[K̄₄]` of the hexagon by
independent sets of size 4: an 8-regular bipartite graph on 24 vertices, connected, of
diameter 3, on which the transposition `(i, j) ↦ (j, i)` acts as the antipodal map
(`transpose_antipodal`).

Throughout, `k` ranges over `0, …, 6` and indexes the charge `k + 1`; `sectorVertices[k]!`
are the 24 vertices and `sectorClasses[k]!` the 6 ordered twin classes of that sector.
All statements are finite and checked by exact evaluation.
-/
/-- The tables have one entry per charge. -/
/-- Each sector has 24 vertices. -/
/-- Every sector has exactly 6 twin classes, each of exactly 4 vertices. -/
/-- The 6 classes partition the 24 vertices of the sector. -/

/-- **Blow-up structure.** Two zero divisors of the same sector annihilate each other iff
their twin classes are neighbours on the quotient hexagon.  Hence each sector is the
lexicographic blow-up `C₆[K̄₄]`. -/

/-- Each sector is bipartite: the two sides are the even and the odd positions on the
quotient hexagon. -/

/-- The transposition `(i, j) ↦ (j, i)` is the antipodal map of the quotient hexagon:
it moves every vertex by 3 steps, the diameter of `C₆`. -/

/-- Vectors of different sectors never annihilate each other, so the seven sectors are
unions of connected components. -/

/-- Each sector is connected of diameter at most 3: any two of its vertices are joined by
a path with at most 3 edges.  Together with `sectors_independent` this shows the
annihilation graph has exactly 7 connected components. -/
/-- Summary: 7 sectors × 24 vertices = 168 zero divisors. -/
