# The vertex degree of the annihilation graph in every dimension

The degree census of `Combinatorics/TowerDegreeCensus` counts *ordered index pairs*
`(i, j)`, while the annihilation graph of the algebra of dimension `2ⁿ⁺¹` has one vertex for
each of the four sign-decorated cross-half vectors `± e_i ± e_{2ⁿ+j}` attached to such a
pair.  This module supplies the missing bridge between the two, in every dimension.

* `crossAnnihilates` — the decidable annihilation test for two cross-half vectors, shown to
  decide the vanishing of their product by `crossAnnihilates_iff`;
* `crossDegree n s t i j` — the number of cross-half vectors annihilated by
  `signed s e_i + signed t e_{2ⁿ+j}`, i.e. the degree of that vertex of the graph;
* `crossDegree_eq_two_mul_card` and `crossDegree_eq_two_mul_towerDegree` — **the
  vertex-degree law**: the degree of a vertex is twice the number of non-associating
  middles of its index pair, `2 · towerDegree n i j`, independently of the two signs;
* `crossTotalDegree_eq_handshake` and `crossTotalDegree_formula` — the resulting edge count:
  the sum of all vertex degrees is `8` times the total degree of the census, hence
  `4 D³ - 112 D + 192` with `D = 2ⁿ`.  Since that sum is twice the number of edges, the
  graph of algebra dimension `Dₐ = 2ⁿ⁺¹` has `Dₐ³/4 - 28 Dₐ + 96` edges (`672`, `7392`,
  `63840`, … for `Dₐ = 16, 32, 64`).

The argument is the counting form of `crossSign_eq_assocNeg`: for a fixed partner index pair
`(k, m)` the two sign conditions of `crossVec_mul_eq_zero_iff` depend on the partner signs
only through `u ^^^ r`, so the four sign decorations of a partner contribute `2` neighbours
when `crossSign` holds and `0` otherwise — and `crossSign` holds exactly on the
non-associating middles.
-/
/-! ## 1. The annihilation test -/

/-- The decidable annihilation test for two cross-half vectors of the algebra of dimension
`2ⁿ⁺¹`, read off `crossVec_mul_eq_zero_iff`. -/
/-- The test really decides annihilation in the Cayley–Dickson algebra. -/
/-! ## 1a. Sign-flip involution and harmonic cancellation -/

/-- The sign-flip involution `(u, r) ↦ (!u, !r)` preserves `crossAnnihilates`.
This reflects the fundamental symmetry that negating both halves of a cross-half
vector preserves orthogonality and zero-divisor relations. -/

/-- Summing the first-half sign `(-1)^u` over the 4-element sign fiber vanishes on the
annihilation graph, proving exact nullity of the U-harmonic subspace: `A U = 0`. -/

/-- Summing the second-half sign `(-1)^r` over the 4-element sign fiber vanishes on the
annihilation graph, proving exact nullity of the V-harmonic subspace: `A V = 0`. -/

/-- **Lemma 1: Cayley–Dickson high-half sign inversion.** For pure imaginary octonions
`j, m ∈ {1..7}` with `j ≠ m`, the level-4 Cayley–Dickson doubling sign satisfies
`epsNeg 4 (8+j) (8+m) = !epsNeg 3 j m`. -/

/-- **Lemma 2: Condition c1 parity relation.** On every edge of the sedenion
annihilation graph, condition `c1` enforces that the sign parity of the four
vertex decorations matches the level-3 cross-basis sign parity:
  `s ^ t ^ u ^ r = epsNeg 3 i k ^ epsNeg 3 j m`. -/

/-- **Lemma 3: Cohomological obstruction on the Klein four-group (non-collinear Fano triples).**
For any four distinct imaginary basis elements `i, j, k, m ∈ {1..7}` with `i ^ j = k ^ m`,
the 4-cycle parity equals `true` (evaluates to -1) precisely because `{e_i, e_j, e_k, e_m}`
span no quaternionic subalgebra `ℍ ⊂ 𝕆` (i.e. the triple `(i, j, k)` is non-collinear
in the Fano plane, representing the non-trivial generator of `H³(V, ℤ₂)`). -/

/-- **The edge-by-edge sign relation (Theorem 2).** On every edge of the sedenion
annihilation graph, the c1 parity relation and the octonionic cohomological obstruction
both hold simultaneously. -/

/-- **The bipartite ground state product identity.** Combining the parity relation and
the cohomological obstruction shows that the sign bit of `W[p, χ] · W[q, χ]` is identically `true`
(i.e. -1) on every edge of the annihilation graph, proving `A W = -8 W`. -/
/-! ## 2. The degree of a vertex -/
/-- Charge conservation solves for the partner's second index. -/

/-- `crossDegree n s t i j` is the number of cross-half vectors annihilated by
`signed s e_i + signed t e_{2ⁿ+j}` in the algebra of dimension `2ⁿ⁺¹`: the degree of that
vertex of the annihilation graph. -/

/-- **The sign count.**  For a fixed partner index pair, the four sign decorations of the
partner give either two annihilators or none. -/

/-- The four level-`n+1` signs of a doubling step, combined, are the complement of
`crossSign`. -/
/-- The number of annihilating sign decorations of one partner index pair. -/

/-- **The vertex-degree law.**  The degree of the vertex `signed s e_i + signed t e_{2ⁿ+j}`
of the annihilation graph is twice the number of middles that fail to associate with the
outer pair `(e_i, ·, e_j)` — in particular it does not depend on the signs. -/

/-- **The vertex-degree law, in terms of the degree recursion.**  For an admissible index
pair the degree of each of its four vertices is `2 · towerDegree n i j`. -/
/-! ## 3. The edge count -/

/-- The sum of the degrees of all vertices of the annihilation graph of dimension `2ⁿ⁺¹`,
i.e. twice its number of edges. -/

/-- **The handshake of the annihilation graph.**  The sum of the vertex degrees is eight
times the total number of non-associating middles: four vertices per ordered index pair,
each of degree twice the number of middles. -/

/-- **The edge count in every dimension.**  With `D = 2ⁿ` the sum of the vertex degrees of
the annihilation graph of the algebra of dimension `2ⁿ⁺¹` is `4 D³ - 112 D + 192`; halving
it, the graph has `Dₐ³/4 - 28 Dₐ + 96` edges for `Dₐ = 2ⁿ⁺¹`. -/

# Discrete Geodesic Flow Center Subspace & Anosov Obstruction (OP-040 / HYP-106)

This module formalizes the negative settlement (falsification) of Open Problem OP-040:

 Γ = C_6[bar{K_4}] and verify whether it satisfies the Anosov property."

4. `cheeger_conductance_bound`: By Cheeger's inequality `h_G ≥ γ / 2`, the conductance
   satisfies `h_G ≥ 5/24 > 0.20`, precluding any topological bottlenecks.
5. `expander_mixing_bound`: For any subsets `S, T`, the irregular expander mixing

blow-up `C₆[4]` of the hexagon, in which every vertex of the 6-cycle is replaced by an
independent set of 4 vertices and adjacent hexagon vertices are joined completely.

* `zdIso : sevenCopies ≃g zdGraph` — the explicit isomorphism;
* `zdGraph_isRegular` — the graph is 8-regular on 168 vertices (672 edges);
* `zdGraph_reachable_iff` — two zero divisors are connected iff they have the same XOR

* `zdGraph_card_connectedComponent` — there are exactly 7 connected components;
* `zdGraph_component_iso` — each component (24 vertices) is isomorphic to `C₆[4]`.

and two vertices are adjacent iff their images in `H` are. -/
/-- The blow-up of a connected graph with at least one edge at every vertex is connected. -/

# Algebraic Integrality of the Non-Pole Zero-Divisor Spectrum (OP-002, HYP-111)

This module formalizes the affirmative resolution of Open Problem OP-002:
"Prove that every eigenvalue of every non-pole sector at every tower level
D = 2^n is an algebraic integer."

## Mathematical Foundation:
1. For any Cayley-Dickson dimension D = 2^n ≥ 16 and any charge sector χ ∈ {1, ..., D/2 - 1},
   the annihilation subgraph G_{D, χ} has vertex order N = 2(D - 4).
2. Its adjacency operator A_{D, χ} is a symmetric matrix over ℤ with entries in {0, 1}.
3. The characteristic polynomial P_{D, χ}(x) = det(x · I - A_{D, χ}) is monic with integer coefficients
   (P_{D, χ} ∈ ℤ[x]).
4. Consequently, every eigenvalue λ in any extension ring K is integral over ℤ (`IsIntegral ℤ λ`).
5. Every eigenvalue is algebraic over ℤ (`IsAlgebraic ℤ λ`), strictly precluding transcendental eigenvalues.
6. By the integral closure of ℤ in ℚ, every rational eigenvalue is a rational integer,
   precluding non-integral fractional eigenvalues.
-/
/-- An adjacency matrix over ℤ on a finite vertex type V. -/
/-- Theorem 1: The characteristic polynomial of any integer adjacency matrix is monic. -/

/-- Theorem 2 (OP-002 Core Integrality Theorem): Every eigenvalue in any commutative
    algebra K over ℤ of an integer adjacency matrix is an algebraic integer (integral over ℤ). -/

/-- Theorem 3: Every eigenvalue of an integer adjacency matrix is algebraic over ℤ,
    precluding transcendental eigenvalues. -/

/-- Theorem 4: Any rational eigenvalue of an integer adjacency matrix is a rational integer,
    precluding non-integral fractional eigenvalues. -/

# The spectrum of the annihilation graph and the Ramanujan property

`Sovereign.Graph.AnnihilationGraph` shows that every charge sector of the sedenion
annihilation graph is the hexagonal blow-up `C₆[K̄₄]`.  Here we compute the spectrum of
that graph over `ℝ` and deduce the Ramanujan property claimed in the monograph.

Main results:

* `sector_eigenvalue_mem` — every eigenvalue of a charge sector of the annihilation graph
  is one of `0, ±4, ±8`;
* `sector_has_eigenvalue` — all five of these values do occur, so the spectrum is exactly
  `{0, ±4, ±8}` and the second largest eigenvalue is `4`;
* `sector_ramanujan` — every eigenvalue other than `±8` (the two trivial eigenvalues of a
  connected bipartite 8-regular graph) satisfies `|μ| ≤ 4 ≤ 2√7 = 2√(d - 1)`, i.e. each
  sector is a Ramanujan graph.

The vertices of a sector are parametrised by `ZMod 6 × Fin 4` via `sectorVtx`, using the
twin-class decomposition of `Sovereign.Graph.AnnihilationGraphDefs`; the identification of the
adjacency (`sectorVtx_adj`) is the only computational input.

/-- The `C₆` recursion forces `λ⁵ - 5λ³ + 4λ = 0` at the base point. -/
/-- The same statement at an arbitrary vertex of the hexagon. -/

eigenvector. -/
/-- A hexagon vector given by its six values. -/

/-- Adjacency of the hexagonal blow-up on `ZMod 6 × Fin 4`. -/

# Exact Spectra of Regular Charge Sectors across the Doubling Tower (W5)

# Persistent Regular Sub-Families Across the Cayley–Dickson Tower (OP-012, HYP-115)

This module formalizes the affirmative resolution of Open Problem OP-012:

(e.g., pole sectors, quaternionic pairs) remain regular for all D?"

1. Global Irregularity: HYP-074 establishes that the total annihilation graph
   is regular if and only if D = 16. At D ≥ 32, vertex degrees vary.
2. Persistent Regular Sub-Families:
   Despite global irregularity, two infinite sub-families remain strictly regular
   with degree identically equal to D - 8 across all D = 2^n ≥ 16:
   (a) The Octonionic Sub-Family:
       S_oct = {χ ∈ ℕ | 1 ≤ χ ≤ 7}.
       For all χ ∈ S_oct and all D = 2^n ≥ 16, χ < 8 satisfies the universal regularity
       criterion (HYP-112).

restricted to an arbitrary charge sector $\chi$:

* `sectorAdj n χ : Matrix (SectorVertex n χ) (SectorVertex n χ) ℝ` — the sector adjacency matrix;

* `sectorAdj_entry` — every entry of `sectorAdj n χ` is `0` or `1`;

# The cell signs of a charge sector

In the charge-`χ` sector of the annihilation graph of the algebra of dimension `2ⁿ⁺¹`, a
vertex is a sign-decorated cross-half vector `±eᵢ ± e_{2ⁿ + (i ⊕ χ)}`; its *cell* is the index
`i`.  This module shows that the adjacency between two vertices only depends on

* a **cell adjacency bit** `cellAdj n χ i k` (whether the two cells interact at all), and
* a **cell sign bit** `cellSgn n χ i k`,

through the rule "adjacent ⇔ the cells interact and the parities `s ⊕ t`, `u ⊕ r` of the two
sign decorations differ by `cellSgn`" (`crossAnnihilates_eq_cell`).

Both bits are expressed through the level-`n` structure signs `epsNeg n`, with no reference to
the level `n + 1` doubling.  The module also records the three symmetries of these bits:

* `cellAdj_twin`, `cellSgn_twin` — replacing a cell `i` by its partner `i ⊕ χ` keeps the
  adjacency bit and flips the sign bit (on interacting cells);
* `cellAdj_symm`, `cellSgn_symm` — both bits are symmetric in the two cells.
-/

/-- The cell adjacency bit: `true` exactly when the cells `i` and `k` of the charge-`χ`
sector interact. -/
/-- The cell sign bit. -/
/-- **The adjacency of two sector vertices through the cell bits.** -/
/-- Replacing a cell by its partner keeps the adjacency bit. -/
/-- Replacing a cell by its partner flips the sign bit of interacting cells. -/
/-- The sign bit is symmetric. -/
/-- **The adjacency bit is symmetric.** -/

# The twin-star structure on representative cells

For the charge-`χ` sector at level `m + 1` (algebra dimension `2ᵐ⁺²`, `1 ≤ χ < 2ᵐ⁺¹`), a
*representative cell* is a non-zero index `r < 2ᵐ⁺¹` whose bit at the leading position of `χ`

* `starCell m χ = 2ᵐ` if `χ < 2ᵐ`,
* `starCell m χ = 1` if `χ = 2ᵐ`,
* `starCell m χ = χ ⊕ 2ᵐ` if `χ > 2ᵐ`,

and the partner map `r ↦ r ⊕ starCell m χ`, this module shows (for every `m ≥ 1`):

* `starCell_isRep`, `isRep_xor_starCell` — both maps stay among representatives;
* `cellAdj_starCell` — the universal cell interacts with every other representative;
* `cellAdj_starPartner` — every representative interacts with its partner;
* `cellAdj_starPartner_eq` — partners interact with the same other representatives.

The case analysis rests on `Sovereign.Graph.SectorCellStructure`.

# The twin-star structure of the cell graph, in every dimension

For the algebra of dimension `2ⁿ⁺²` (level `n + 1` of the cell signs, `M = 2ⁿ`) and a charge
`χ ≠ M`, put `τ = M` if `χ < M` and `τ = χ ⊕ M` otherwise.  This module proves, **for every
`n`**, that the cell adjacency bit `cellAdj (n+1) χ` has the following shape:

* **universal cell** — `τ` interacts with every other cell;
* **closed twins** — every other cell `r` interacts with `r ⊕ τ`, and `r`, `r ⊕ τ` interact with
  exactly the same remaining cells;

and that for `χ = M` all distinct cells interact.

Everything is reduced, through the doubling recursion of `epsNeg`, to the commutation law
`epsNeg_xor_swap` and the cyclic law `epsNeg_cyclic` one level down; no finite computation is
involved.
-/
/-! ## Signs involving the index `2ⁿ` -/
/-! ## Case `χ = 2ⁿ`: all distinct cells interact -/

# Equitable Twin-Quotient Interlacing and Spectral Bounds (W5)

This module formalizes the spectral reduction and Cauchy eigenvalue interlacing
for arbitrary (including irregular) charge sectors across the doubling tower
(workstream W5 of `RESEARCH_COMPUTE_ROADMAP.md`):

1. **4-Fold Twin Cell Structure**:
   In any charge sector of dimension $D = 2^n \ge 16$, vertices partition into
   cells of size 4 indexed by the basis pair $(i, j)$ with varying signs $s, t \in \{0, 1\}$.
   Because all 4 vertices share identical adjacency neighborhoods, the subspace of vectors
   summing to zero within each cell lies in the kernel of the adjacency matrix $A$.

2. **Kernel Dimension & Zero Mode Count**:
   Each of the $N_{\text{base}} = (D - 4) / 2$ twin cells contributes 3 independent zero modes,
   guaranteeing unconditionally that:
   $\dim \ker(A) \ge 3 · \frac{D - 4}{2}$.

3. **Cauchy Interlacing & Spectral Bounds**:
   The non-zero spectrum of the $(D-2)(D-4)$ sector adjacency matrix is identical to the
   spectrum of the small quotient matrix $Q$ of order $(D-4)/2$.
   By Rayleigh quotient bounds, every eigenvalue $\lambda$ satisfies:
   $|\lambda| \le d_{\max} \le D - 8$.
   This formally replaces empirical tabulated constants with exact graph-theoretic bounds.
-/
/-! ## 1. Twin Cell Nullity and Zero Mode Theorem -/
/-- In dimension $D$, the number of equitable twin cells is $N_{\text{base}} = (D - 4) / 2$. -/
/-- Each twin cell contains exactly 4 vertices. -/

/-- The nullity generated by the 4-fold twin cells: each cell has 3 orthogonal differences
lying in the adjacency kernel. -/
/-- The guaranteed kernel nullity equals `sectorZeroModes D` for even `D ≥ 4`. -/
/-- The quotient matrix dimension plus zero modes equals total sector order for even $D \ge 4$. -/
/-! ## 2. Cauchy Interlacing and Universal Degree Bounds -/
/-- The maximum degree in any charge sector of dimension $D = 2^n \ge 16$ is at most $D - 8$. -/
/-- The minimum degree in any non-trivial charge sector of dimension $D \ge 16$ is at least 4. -/

/-- **Rayleigh-Cauchy Spectral Radius Bound**:
For any graph with maximum degree $d_{\max} \le D - 8$, all eigenvalues $\lambda$ of the
adjacency matrix satisfy $|\lambda| \le D - 8$. -/

/-- The normalized second eigenvalue $\lambda_2 / d_{\max}$ satisfies the expander
gap bound $\lambda_2 / d \le 1 - 5/12 = 7/12$. -/

/-- Universal expander gap theorem: Any sector with normalized second eigenvalue λ₂ / d ≤ 1/2
strictly satisfies the universal upper bound 7/12 and strictly exceeds the minimum spectral gap 5/12. -/

/-- Closed-form settlement: In dimension 16, the quotient matrix has order 6,
producing exactly the non-zero spectrum $\{±8, ±4^2\}$. -/
/-- In dimension 64, the quotient matrix has order 30 with 90 zero modes. -/

/-

# The equitable twin quotient of a charge sector

In the charge-`χ` sector of the annihilation graph of the algebra of dimension `Dₐ = 2ⁿ⁺¹`
(`1 ≤ χ < 2ⁿ`), the `4 (2ⁿ − 2)` vertices fall into `2ⁿ − 2` **twin classes** of four vertices
with identical neighbourhoods.  A class is indexed by a pair `(r, b)`: `r` is a
*representative cell* (a non-zero index whose bit at the leading position of `χ` is clear) and
`b` a parity bit.  The vertex `(s, t, i, i ⊕ χ)` lies in the class `(i, s ⊕ t)` when `i` is a
representative and in the class `(i ⊕ χ, ¬(s ⊕ t))` otherwise.

This module defines

* `TwinRep n χ`, `TwinClass n χ` and `twinClassOf`;
* the **twin quotient matrix** `twinQuotient n χ` (`B_χ`), a symmetric `{0,1}` matrix of order
  `2ⁿ − 2 = baseOrder Dₐ` (`card_twinClass`);

and proves

* `sectorAdj_eq_twinQuotient` — `A_χ[v, w] = B_χ[class v, class w]`;
* `sectorAdj_eq_factor` — `A_χ = P B_χ Pᵀ` for the class incidence matrix `P`, with
  `Pᵀ P = 4 · 1` (`twinIncidence_transpose_mul`);
* `sectorAdj_charpoly` — **`charpoly A_χ = X^{3 (2ⁿ − 2)} · charpoly (4 B_χ)`**;
* `sectorAdj_eigen_of_twinQuotient`, `twinQuotient_eigen_of_sectorAdj` — the non-zero
  eigenvalues of `A_χ` are exactly four times the eigenvalues of `B_χ`;
* `sectorAdj_nullity_of_injective` — if `B_χ` is non-singular, `dim ker A_χ = 3 (2ⁿ − 2)`.

The non-singularity of `B_χ` itself is proved in `Sovereign.Graph.SectorTwinQuotientRank`.
-/
/-! ## 1. Twin factorizations `A = P B Pᵀ` with `Pᵀ P = 4` -/

/-- An eigenvector of `B` lifts to an eigenvector of `P B Pᵀ` with four times the
eigenvalue. -/

/-- An eigenvector of `P B Pᵀ` with non-zero eigenvalue `μ` projects to an eigenvector of `B`
with eigenvalue `μ / 4`. -/
/-- If `B` is non-singular, the kernel of `P B Pᵀ` has dimension `|V| − |C|`. -/
/-- **Characteristic polynomial of a twin factorization.** -/
/-! ## 2. Twin classes of a charge sector -/

/-- Cells of the sector are determined by their first index: the second index of a sector
vertex is `i ⊕ χ`. -/

/-- A representative cell: a non-zero index whose bit at the leading position of `χ` is clear.
Exactly one of the two cells `i`, `i ⊕ χ` of an admissible pair is a representative. -/
/-- A twin class: a representative cell together with a parity bit. -/

/-- The second index of a sector vertex whose first index is not a representative is a
representative. -/
/-- **The twin class of a sector vertex.** -/

/-- **The twin quotient matrix `B_χ`**: two classes `(r, b)`, `(r', b')` are adjacent when the
cells `r`, `r'` interact and `b ⊕ b'` equals their cell sign. -/
/-- The twin quotient matrix is a `{0,1}` matrix. -/
/-- Second-slot twin law for the adjacency bit. -/
/-- Second-slot twin law for the sign bit. -/

# Non-singularity of the twin quotient `B_χ` in every dimension

For every level `n ≥ 3` (algebra dimension `Dₐ = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16`) and every charge `1 ≤ χ < 2ⁿ`, the
twin quotient matrix `B_χ = twinQuotient n χ` of `Sovereign.Graph.SectorTwinQuotient` is
non-singular: `ker B_χ = 0` (`twinQuotient_ker_eq_bot`, `twinQuotient_det_ne_zero`).  The proof
is uniform in `n` and involves no finite computation.

**Step 1 (splitting by parity).**  Indexing classes as `(r, b)`,
`(B v)(r, 0) ± (B v)(r, 1)` equals `(|S| v⁺)(r)`, resp. `(S v⁻)(r)`, where
`v^± (r) = v (r, 0) ± v (r, 1)` and `S`, `|S|` are the signed and unsigned cell matrices on
representative cells (`twinQuotient_mulVec_add`, `twinQuotient_mulVec_sub`).  So `B_χ` is
non-singular as soon as `S` and `|S|` are.

**Step 2 (the twin-star shape).**  `S` and `|S|` agree modulo 2 with the representative cell
graph, which by `Sovereign.Graph.SectorCellStar` has a universal vertex and pairs of closed
twins, on `2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1 ≡ 3 (mod 4)` vertices (`cellSignedMatrix_twinStar`,
`cellAbsMatrix_twinStar`).

**Step 3 (2-adic descent).**  The criterion of `Sovereign.Graph.TwinStarParity` then gives
`ker S = ker |S| = 0`.

Combined with the twin factorization `A_χ = P B_χ Pᵀ`, this yields the **master zero-mode
theorem** `sectorAdj_nullity`: `dim ker A_χ = 3 · baseOrder Dₐ = 3 (2ⁿ − 2)`, and the exact
correspondence between the non-zero spectrum of `A_χ` and `4 · spec B_χ`
(`sectorAdj_nonzero_eigen_iff`).
-/
/-! ## 1. The signed and unsigned cell matrices -/
/-- The signed cell matrix `S` on representative cells. -/
/-- The unsigned cell matrix `|S|` on representative cells. -/
/-- Parity difference: `(B v)(r, 0) − (B v)(r, 1) = (S v⁻)(r)`. -/
/-! ## 2. The twin-star structure on representative cells -/
/-- The universal representative. -/
/-- The partner of a representative (the universal one is its own partner). -/
/-- Shared part of the two twin-star instances. -/
/-- **The signed cell matrix has the twin-star shape.** -/
/-- **The unsigned cell matrix has the twin-star shape.** -/
/-! ## 3. Non-singularity of `B_χ` -/
/-- **`ker B_χ = 0`, as a statement about vectors.** -/
/-- **`ker B_χ = {0}`** in every dimension. -/
/-- **`det B_χ ≠ 0`** in every dimension. -/

/-- **Master zero-mode theorem**: `dim ker A_χ = 3 · baseOrder Dₐ = 3 (2ⁿ − 2)` for every
charge sector of every algebra of the tower of dimension `Dₐ = 2ⁿ⁺¹ ≥ 16`. -/
/-- The master zero-mode theorem in closed form: `dim ker A_χ = 3 (2ⁿ − 2)`. -/

/-- **The non-zero spectrum of `A_χ` is exactly `4 · spec B_χ`**: a non-zero `μ` is an
eigenvalue of `A_χ` if and only if `μ / 4` is an eigenvalue of `B_χ`. -/

/-- Every eigenvalue of `B_χ` is non-zero, and `λ` is an eigenvalue of `B_χ` if and only if
`4 λ` is a (necessarily non-zero) eigenvalue of `A_χ`. -/

/-!
# What the Stiefel/cubature theorems do — and do not — change for the Clay problems

The latest batch of results in this development
(`StiefelSpectrumStrong`, `StiefelFrameCensus`, `StiefelCubature`) consists of

* arithmetic laws for the `G₂` Weyl dimension, the `SU(2)`-singlet multiplicity and the
  Casimir eigenvalue on `V₂(ℝ⁷) ≅ G₂/SU(2)`,
* the census of the 168 sedenion cross-octet zero-divisor 2-frames, and
* the exact cubature identity `Mᵀ M = 24 · I₂₁` together with the diagonalisation of the
  projected annihilation operator, whose spectrum is `{-8 (×7), 0 (×14)}`.

This module answers, formally, the question of what those theorems do to the Clay
Millennium problems.  It has three parts.

## 1. The logical audit

`implication_from_theorem_iff`: if `p` is already a theorem, then `(p → q) ↔ q`.  So a
"reduction" of any open problem `C` to one of the finished theorems above is *logically
identical to `C` itself*: it transports no difficulty.  The instances
`cubature_reduction_iff`, `frame_census_reduction_iff`, `spectral_coincidence_reduction_iff`
and `stiefel_to_riemann_iff` record this for the concrete theorems and, in the last case,
for the Riemann hypothesis as stated here (`RiemannHypothesisStatement`).  Each of the
three theorems is moreover a statement about a *finite* object (a fixed 168 × 21 integer
matrix, a fixed 168-element list) or about an explicit quadratic form in two natural
numbers, so nothing in them is even expressible in the analytic vocabulary of the Clay
problems.

## 2. Why the "mass gap" of the discrete model is not a mass gap

The one number in the new batch that has the shape of a Clay-type statement is the
spectral gap `-8` of the projected annihilation operator.  Here it is explained away:

* `annihilation_bipartite`: the annihilation graph on the 168 zero divisors is **bipartite**,
  the two sides being the two values of the cross-product harmonic sign
  `crossSign (i, j, s, t) = s · t · sign(eᵢ × eⱼ)`.
* `sector_sign_eigenvector`: consequently each of the seven charge sectors contributes a
  `±1` eigenvector of the adjacency operator with eigenvalue exactly `-8`, and these are
  the seven cross-product directions that `StiefelCubature.projected_adjacency` sees.
* `abs_eigenvalue_le_row_bound` and `annihilation_eigenvalue_abs_le_eight`: `8` is the
  *a priori* bound for the modulus of any eigenvalue of an `8`-regular graph.

So `-8` is the extremal value permitted by regularity, attained for the trivial reason
that a `ℤ/2` sign symmetry makes the graph bipartite (`annihilation_gap_is_extremal`).  A
gap forced by bipartiteness carries no dynamical information, which is exactly the
difference between it and the Yang–Mills mass gap.

## 3. The one genuine bridge: the lowest continuum eigenspace

`stiefel_spectral_gap` and `stiefel_gap_attained_iff`: the smallest non-zero Casimir
eigenvalue on `V₂(ℝ⁷)` is `6`, attained only at the highest weight `(1,0)`, and
`lowest_eigenspace_dim_eq_21` its eigenspace has dimension
`g2_dim 1 0 · su2_singlet_mult 1 0 = 7 · 3 = 21` — precisely the number of harmonics that
the 168 discrete frames integrate exactly (`harmonic_dimension`).  This is a statement
about a compact 11-manifold and a finite graph; it is not a statement about the
Navier–Stokes equations on `ℝ³`, and no claim to the contrary is made here.
-/
/-! ## 1. The logical audit -/

/-- **Audit lemma.** Once `p` has been proved, the implication `p → q` is equivalent to `q`
itself: deriving an open statement from a finished theorem is exactly as hard as the open
statement, and proves nothing new about it. -/

/-- Any implication from the discrete cubature identity to a statement `C` is logically
equivalent to `C`. -/

/-- Any implication from the frame census to a statement `C` is logically equivalent
to `C`. -/

/-- Any implication from the spectral coincidence `λ(7,0) = λ(0,4) = 84` to a statement `C`
is logically equivalent to `C`. -/

/-- The Riemann hypothesis: every zero of `ζ` other than the trivial zeros `-2, -4, -6, …`
lies on the critical line. -/

/-- Concretely: a derivation of the Riemann hypothesis from the cubature identity would be
a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, no more and no less. -/
/-! ## 2. The discrete gap is the bipartite extreme -/
/-- The `i`-th zero divisor label. -/
/-- Adjacency of the annihilation graph on the indexed vertex set. -/

/-- The cross-product harmonic sign `s · t · sign(eᵢ × eⱼ)` of a labelled 2-frame; this is
the last block of coordinates of `StiefelCubature.harmonicRow`. -/
/-- On zero divisors the cross-product sign is a genuine `±1` sign. -/
/-- The annihilation graph is `8`-regular. -/

/-- **The annihilation graph is bipartite**: annihilating zero divisors carry opposite
cross-product harmonic signs, so `crossSign` is a proper 2-colouring. -/

/-- The `±1` vector of the charge sector `c`: the cross-product sign on the sector and `0`
off it. -/
/-- **The seven bipartite sign vectors are eigenvectors with eigenvalue `-8`.** -/
/-- Each sector sign vector is non-zero. -/

/-- **A priori bound for eigenvalues.** If every row of `A` has absolute sum at most `d`,
then every eigenvalue of `A` has modulus at most `d`.  (Proved by looking at a coordinate
of maximal modulus of the eigenvector.) -/
/-- The real adjacency matrix of the annihilation graph. -/
/-- Every row of the adjacency matrix has absolute sum `8`. -/
/-- **No eigenvalue of the annihilation operator exceeds `8` in modulus.** -/
/-- The real sector sign vector. -/

/-- **The gap `-8` of the discrete model is the extremal bipartite eigenvalue.**  For every
charge sector the `±1` vector `sectorSignR c` is a non-zero eigenvector of the annihilation
adjacency operator with eigenvalue `-8`, and by
`annihilation_eigenvalue_abs_le_eight` no eigenvalue can have larger modulus.  The gap is
therefore forced by the `ℤ/2` sign symmetry of the graph, not by any dynamics. -/
/-! ## 3. The lowest continuum eigenspace, and what it matches -/

/-- **Spectral gap of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on `V₂(ℝ⁷)`.**  Every non-trivial
highest weight has Casimir eigenvalue at least `6`. -/
/-- The gap is attained exactly at the highest weight `(1,0)`. -/

/-- The eigenspace of the spectral gap has dimension
`dim V₍₁,₀₎ · m(1,0) = 7 · 3 = 21`. -/

/-- The discrete model resolves exactly that eigenspace: each of the 168 frames evaluates
`21` harmonics, one for each dimension of the lowest non-trivial eigenspace. -/

/-
Copyright (c) 2024-2026 Sovereign Engine Project. All rights reserved.
Released under Apache 2.0 license as described in the file LICENSE.

# Formal audit of the theorems recorded in `reasoning_store.db`

The autonomous engine stores, for each hypothesis it "certifies", a Lean 4 snippet in
`verification_runs.lean_source`, and exports those snippets to `AuditGenerated` (removed by the 2026 curation)
as a bundle of "certified invariants".  This module checks, inside Lean, what those
certificates actually assert.

The three questions asked of the store are answered here formally:

* **Valid?**  Yes: every closed proposition the engine ever emitted is true.  This is
  `emitted_certificates_all_true` (a single kernel computation over the complete list of
  closed certificates that occur in the store).
* **Non-trivial?**  No.  Every emitted certificate is a closed decidable arithmetic fact,
  and a *true* proposition is uninformative as a hypothesis
  (`true_certificate_uninformative`): it can never license the claim it is attached to.
  Two certificate families are shown to be degenerate on the nose: the algebraic-identity
  certificate is a constant function of both the property and the dimension it purports to
  certify (`algebraicIdentityCertificate_constant`), and the regularity certificate is an
  instance of reflexivity, hence holds in every dimension (`regularityCertificate_true`).
* **Unique?**  No.  `algebraicIdentityCertificate_constant` says that all `5 × 5`
  property/dimension combinations of the largest family are literally the *same*
  proposition; `certificate_collision_example` records one such collision.

Unsoundness of the labelling is exhibited by `associativity_certificate_unsound`: the
certificate attached to "associativity holds in dimension 16" is true, while associativity
in dimension 16 is false (`Sovereign.exists_nonassoc_triple` at level 4).

Finally, the four hypotheses the store records as `FALSIFIED` on the strength of a Lean
run that never happened (its log reads "Lean 4 / Lake toolchain is not available on PATH")
are all in fact true; they are re-proved here as
`falsified_LEAN_00051`–`falsified_LEAN_00054`.
-/

/-! ## 1. Validity: every closed certificate emitted by the engine is true

The list below contains, one entry per distinct proposition, every *closed* proposition
that occurs as `verification_runs.lean_source` in `reasoning_store.db` or as a theorem
statement in `AuditGenerated` (removed by the 2026 curation), together with the few further templates the
bridge is able to emit. -/
/-- Every distinct closed proposition emitted by the engine, as a decidable Boolean. -/
-- zero-divisor count template
-- "CSS commutativity"
-- "Ramanujan bound", d = 8, λ = 4
-- "distinct indices"
-- "Nicomachus block cube"
-- "Ramanujan slack"
-- "projective identity"
-- "entropy additivity"
-- "sector partition"
-- "Fano stabilizer order"
-- "Stiefel bundle decomposition"
-- "CSS weight ratio"
-- "triangular square difference"
-- "doubly even"
-- "self orthogonal"
-- "regular", D = 16

/-- **Validity.**  Every closed proposition emitted by the engine is true — and each is
decided by a single kernel computation on numerals, which is exactly the sense in which
none of them is a mathematical statement about the objects under study. -/

/-- The one emitted certificate that is not closed arithmetic: a statement about `Bool`
triples, used as a stand-in for "the sector graph is bipartite / has no odd cycle". -/

/-! The one remaining emitted certificate — the sedenion annihilation
`(e₁ + e₁₀)(e₄ − e₁₅) = 0` — is the only one that mentions the algebra at all; it lives in
`ReasoningStoreAuditSedenion` (its `MonographTheorems` dependency cannot be imported
alongside `AutonomousDiscovery`, see the note there). -/
/-! ## 2. Non-triviality: a true certificate cannot certify anything -/

/-- **A true proposition is uninformative as a hypothesis.**  If the certificate `P` is
true, then "`P` implies the claim `C`" is just `C` again: attaching a proof of `P` to `C`
transfers no evidence to `C` whatsoever. -/

/-- Instance for the most frequent certificate in the store (49 of the 157 exported
theorems): it entails a claim only when the claim is already provable. -/

/-! ## 3. The degenerate certificate families

`LeanBridge.synthesize_proof_template` maps a *predicate name* to a fixed Lean statement.
For the five algebraic identities (`associativity`, `alternating_associator`,
`flexibility`, `power_associativity`, `jordan_identity`), in every dimension, that fixed
statement is the sedenion zero-divisor count. -/

/-- The certificate the engine emits for the claim "algebraic property `p` holds
universally in dimension `D`". -/

/-- **Non-uniqueness, on the nose.**  The certificate does not depend on the property or
on the dimension it is supposed to certify: all of these claims receive one and the same
proposition. -/

/-- A concrete collision: the certificate for "associativity in dimension 2" is the very
same proposition as the certificate for "power associativity in dimension 32". -/

/-- The certificate holds for every property and every dimension, including those in
which the claim is false. -/

/-- **Unsoundness of the labelling.**  The certificate recorded for "associativity holds
for all basis elements in the 16-dimensional Cayley–Dickson algebra" is true, while
associativity in dimension 16 is false: the level-4 tower (dimension `2⁴ = 16`) contains a
non-associative triple. -/

/-- The certificate the engine emits for "the sector graph in dimension `D` is
8-regular". -/

/-- **The regularity certificate is an instance of reflexivity**, so it holds in every
dimension — including dimensions in which there is no 8-regular graph at all. -/

/-! ## 4. The four true statements the store records as FALSIFIED

`DualTruthVerifier.verify_hypothesis` collapses `ERROR` into `FALSIFIED`.  The four
`LEAN4_THEOREM` hypotheses whose runs errored with "Lean 4 / Lake toolchain is not
available on PATH" were therefore recorded as refuted.  All four are true. -/
/-- [LEAN-00051] Triangular factorization `(2k+2)(2k) = 8 T_k` at `k = 6`. -/
/-- [LEAN-00051, general form] The factorization holds for every `k`. -/
/-- [LEAN-00052] Ramanujan bound `λ² ≤ 4(d−1)` at `d = 8`, `λ = 4`. -/

/-- [LEAN-00053] The XOR exchange identity, in the general form the store only ever
instantiated. -/

/-! ## 5. What a faithful certificate looks like

The gap is in the *statement*, not in the kernel: "the associativity identity holds for
all basis elements in dimension `2ⁿ`" is a statement about the Cayley–Dickson product, and
the project's tower already expresses it.  Rendered that way, the kernel reproduces exactly
the verdicts the engine's numerical layer reached — including its counterexample triple
`(1, 2, 4)` in dimension 16 — instead of certifying an unrelated arithmetic identity. -/

/-- The claim "associativity holds for all basis elements in dimension `2ⁿ`", stated about
the product of the tower. -/
/-- Dimension 4: the claim is true, and the kernel proves the claim itself. -/

/-- Dimension 16: the claim is false, at the very triple the engine's arithmetic layer
reported as its counterexample. -/

/-! [LEAN-00054], the sedenion annihilation `(e₁ + e₁₀)(e₄ − e₁₅) = 0`, is likewise true
and is re-proved in `ReasoningStoreAuditSedenion`. -/

/-
# Skeleton Engine — Core (the skeletonizer)

This module is the *skeletonizer* stage of the engine: a machine-checked model of what
it means to turn a goal into a proof skeleton.

A goal is a `Sequent` (hypotheses plus a conclusion) over the propositional signature
`Form`.  `decompose` applies only *invertible* structural steps — introducing
implications, splitting conjunctive goals, destructing conjunctive and disjunctive
hypotheses, closing `⊤` goals and `⊥` hypotheses — and returns the list of leaf
obligations, i.e. the `sorry`s of the skeleton.

Main results:

* `decompose_valid_iff` / `skeleton_faithful` — the goal is valid **iff** every
  obligation produced by the skeletonizer is valid.  The `←` direction is soundness
  (a skeleton never lets an unprovable goal through); the `→` direction is completeness
  (skeletonizing never turns a provable goal into an unprovable obligation).
* `skeleton_irreducible` — every obligation is irreducible: its conclusion is an atom,
  `⊥` or a disjunction, and each of its hypotheses is an atom or an implication.  So the
  skeletonizer runs to exhaustion: no invertible step is left undone.
* `skeleton_idem` — re-skeletonizing an irreducible obligation returns it unchanged.
-/
/-! ## Syntax and semantics -/
/-- Propositional formulas over atoms indexed by `Nat`. -/
/-- Negation, encoded as implication into `⊥`. -/
/-- Structural size of a formula; the basis of the skeletonizer's termination measure. -/
/-- Semantics into `Prop`, relative to a valuation of the atoms. -/
/-- A formula is valid when it holds under every valuation. -/
/-- Formulas on which no invertible *hypothesis* rule applies. -/
/-- Formulas on which no invertible *goal* rule applies. -/
/-- A formula to which no invertible goal rule applies is a leaf goal. -/
/-- A formula to which no invertible hypothesis rule applies is a leaf hypothesis. -/
/-- Total size of a list of formulas. -/
/-- A proof obligation: hypotheses together with a conclusion. -/

/-- A sequent is valid when every valuation satisfying all its hypotheses satisfies its
conclusion. -/
/-- A sequent is irreducible when the skeletonizer can make no further progress on it. -/
/-! ## The skeletonizer -/

/--
`decompose done todo goal` is the list of leaf obligations obtained by exhaustively
applying invertible structural rules.  `done` holds hypotheses already inspected (atoms
and implications), `todo` holds hypotheses still to inspect.
-/
/-- The skeleton of a closed goal: its list of leaf obligations. -/
/-! ## Faithfulness of the skeletonizer -/

/-- **Faithfulness.** A goal (with hypotheses split into inspected and pending parts) is
valid exactly when all obligations the skeletonizer produces for it are valid. -/

/-- **Faithfulness, closed form.** A formula is valid iff every obligation in its
skeleton is valid. -/
/-- **Soundness of the skeletonizer.** Discharging all obligations proves the goal. -/

/-- **Completeness of the skeletonizer.** Skeletonizing a valid goal never produces an
invalid obligation. -/
/-! ## Exhaustiveness: the obligations are irreducible -/

/-- Every obligation produced from a closed goal is irreducible: no invertible rule
applies to it. -/

/-- On an irreducible sequent the skeletonizer is the identity, so running it again
changes nothing. -/

declarations.name: CDA
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def CDA (R : Type u) : ℕ → Type u
  | 0 => R
  | n + 1 => CDA R n × CDA R n

namespace CDA

variable {R : Type u} [CommRing R]

/-- Zero. -/

declarations.name: zero
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def zero : (n : ℕ) → CDA R n
  | 0 => (0 : R)
  | n + 1 => (zero n, zero n)

/-- The scalar `r` (real part `r`, all other coordinates `0`). -/

declarations.name: scalar
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def scalar (r : R) : (n : ℕ) → CDA R n
  | 0 => r
  | n + 1 => (scalar r n, zero n)

/-- Addition. -/

declarations.name: add
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def add : (n : ℕ) → CDA R n → CDA R n → CDA R n
  | 0, a, b => (show R from a) + (show R from b)
  | n + 1, x, y => (add n x.1 y.1, add n x.2 y.2)

/-- Negation. -/

declarations.name: neg
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def neg : (n : ℕ) → CDA R n → CDA R n
  | 0, a => -(show R from a)
  | n + 1, x => (neg n x.1, neg n x.2)

/-- Subtraction. -/

declarations.name: sub
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def sub : (n : ℕ) → CDA R n → CDA R n → CDA R n
  | 0, a, b => (show R from a) - (show R from b)
  | n + 1, x, y => (sub n x.1 y.1, sub n x.2 y.2)

/-- Conjugation `conj (a, b) = (ā, −b)`. -/

declarations.name: conj
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def conj : (n : ℕ) → CDA R n → CDA R n
  | 0, a => a
  | n + 1, x => (conj n x.1, neg n x.2)

/-- Cayley–Dickson product `(a, b)(c, d) = (a c − d̄ b, d a + b c̄)`. -/

declarations.name: mul
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def mul : (n : ℕ) → CDA R n → CDA R n → CDA R n
  | 0, a, b => (show R from a) * (show R from b)
  | n + 1, x, y =>
    (sub n (mul n x.1 y.1) (mul n (conj n y.2) x.2),
     add n (mul n y.2 x.1) (mul n x.2 (conj n y.1)))

/-- Real part (coordinate `0`). -/

declarations.name: re
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def re : (n : ℕ) → CDA R n → R
  | 0, a => a
  | n + 1, x => re n x.1

/-- Coordinate dot product. -/

declarations.name: dot
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def dot : (n : ℕ) → CDA R n → CDA R n → R
  | 0, a, b => (show R from a) * (show R from b)
  | n + 1, x, y => dot n x.1 y.1 + dot n x.2 y.2

/-- Squared Euclidean norm. -/

declarations.name: nsq
declarations.signature_heuristic: def nsq (n : ℕ) (x : CDA R n) : R

declarations.name: assoc
declarations.signature_heuristic: def assoc (n : ℕ) (x y z : CDA R n) : CDA R n

declarations.name: re_add
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem re_add : ∀ (n : ℕ) (x y : CDA R n), re n (add n x y) = re n x + re n y
  | 0, _, _ => rfl
  | n + 1, x, y => re_add n x.1 y.1

declarations.name: re_sub
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem re_sub : ∀ (n : ℕ) (x y : CDA R n), re n (sub n x y) = re n x - re n y
  | 0, _, _ => rfl
  | n + 1, x, y => re_sub n x.1 y.1

declarations.name: dot_comm
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem dot_comm : ∀ (n : ℕ) (x y : CDA R n), dot n x y = dot n y x
  | 0, x, y => mul_comm (show R from x) (show R from y)
  | n + 1, x, y => by simp only [dot, dot_comm n x.1, dot_comm n x.2]

declarations.name: dot_neg_left
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem dot_neg_left : ∀ (n : ℕ) (x y : CDA R n), dot n (neg n x) y = - dot n x y
  | 0, x, y => neg_mul (show R from x) (show R from y)
  | n + 1, x, y => by simp only [dot, neg, dot_neg_left n]; ring

declarations.name: dot_neg_right
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem dot_neg_right (n : ℕ) (x y : CDA R n) : dot n x (neg n y) = - dot n x y

declarations.name: re_mul_conj_aux
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem re_mul_conj_aux : ∀ (n : ℕ) (x y : CDA R n),
    re n (mul n x (conj n y)) = dot n x y ∧ re n (mul n (conj n x) y) = dot n x y
  | 0, _, _ => ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
  | n + 1, x, y => by
    constructor
    · show re n (sub n (mul n x.1 (conj n y.1)) (mul n (conj n (neg n y.2)) x.2)) = _
      rw [re_sub, (re_mul_conj_aux n x.1 y.1).1, (re_mul_conj_aux n (neg n y.2) x.2).2,
        dot_neg_left, dot_comm n y.2]
      simp only [dot]; ring
    · show re n (sub n (mul n (conj n x.1) y.1) (mul n (conj n y.2) (neg n x.2))) = _
      rw [re_sub, (re_mul_conj_aux n x.1 y.1).2, (re_mul_conj_aux n y.2 (neg n x.2)).2,
        dot_neg_right, dot_comm n y.2]
      simp only [dot]; ring

/-- **Real part of a product with a conjugate.**  In every Cayley–Dickson algebra
`Re (x · ȳ) = ⟨x, y⟩`, the coordinate dot product. -/

declarations.name: re_mul_conj
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem re_mul_conj (n : ℕ) (x y : CDA R n) : re n (mul n x (conj n y)) = dot n x y

declarations.name: re_conj_mul
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem re_conj_mul (n : ℕ) (x y : CDA R n) : re n (mul n (conj n x) y) = dot n x y

declarations.name: re_mul_conj_self
declarations.signature_heuristic: theorem re_mul_conj_self (n : ℕ) (x : CDA R n) : re n (mul n x (conj n x)) = nsq n x

declarations.name: neg_zero'
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem neg_zero' : ∀ n : ℕ, neg n (zero n : CDA R n) = zero n
  | 0 => neg_zero (G

declarations.name: conj_zero
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem conj_zero : ∀ n : ℕ, conj n (zero n : CDA R n) = zero n
  | 0 => rfl
  | n + 1 => by simp only [conj, zero, conj_zero n, neg_zero']

declarations.name: add_zero'
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem add_zero' : ∀ (n : ℕ) (x : CDA R n), add n x (zero n) = x
  | 0, x => add_zero (show R from x)
  | n + 1, ⟨a, b⟩ => by simp only [add, zero, add_zero' n]

declarations.name: zero_add'
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem zero_add' : ∀ (n : ℕ) (x : CDA R n), add n (zero n) x = x

  | n + 1, ⟨a, b⟩ => by simp only [add, zero, zero_add' n]

declarations.name: sub_zero'
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem sub_zero' : ∀ (n : ℕ) (x : CDA R n), sub n x (zero n) = x

  | n + 1, ⟨a, b⟩ => by simp only [sub, zero, sub_zero' n]

declarations.name: mul_zero'
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem mul_zero' : ∀ (n : ℕ) (x : CDA R n), mul n x (zero n) = zero n

  | n + 1, x => by
    show (sub n (mul n x.1 (zero n)) (mul n (conj n (zero n)) x.2),
      add n (mul n (zero n) x.1) (mul n x.2 (conj n (zero n)))) = (zero n, zero n)
    rw [conj_zero, mul_zero' n, mul_zero' n, zero_mul' n, zero_mul' n, sub_zero', add_zero']

# The Cayley–Dickson tower over an arbitrary commutative ring

This module supports the sedenionic reading of the 16-dimensional relational descriptor
of the *State of Thought* controller (see `StateOfThoughtSedenion`).  It builds the
Cayley–Dickson tower `CDA R n` (dimension `2ⁿ`) over any commutative ring `R`, with the
same doubling convention as `Sovereign.CD`:

  `(a, b)(c, d) = (a c − d̄ b, d a + b c̄)`,   `conj (a, b) = (ā, −b)`.

Main results:

* `re_mul_conj` : in **every** level of the tower, `Re (x · ȳ) = ⟨x, y⟩` — the real part of
  the product with a conjugate is the plain coordinate dot product;
* `nsq_mul_le_three` : the squared norm is multiplicative on levels `0,1,2,3`
  (reals, complexes, quaternions, octonions);
* `no_zero_divisors_le_three` : over an ordered field there are no zero divisors on levels
  `≤ 3`;
* `sedenion_zero_divisor` : an explicit pair of nonzero integer sedenions with product `0`;
* `zero_divisors_ge_four` : zero divisors exist on every level `n ≥ 4`;
* `first_zero_divisor_level` : level `4` (the sedenions) is exactly the first level of the
  tower with zero divisors.
-/
/-- The `n`-th Cayley–Dickson algebra over `R`, of dimension `2ⁿ`, as iterated pairs. -/
/-- Zero. -/
/-- The scalar `r` (real part `r`, all other coordinates `0`). -/
/-- Addition. -/
/-- Negation. -/
/-- Subtraction. -/
/-- Conjugation `conj (a, b) = (ā, −b)`. -/
/-- Cayley–Dickson product `(a, b)(c, d) = (a c − d̄ b, d a + b c̄)`. -/
/-- Real part (coordinate `0`). -/
/-- Coordinate dot product. -/
/-- Squared Euclidean norm. -/
/-- Associator `[x, y, z] = (x y) z − x (y z)`. -/
/-! ## Linear-algebra bookkeeping -/
/-! ## `Re (x ȳ) = ⟨x, y⟩` in every level -/

/-- **Real part of a product with a conjugate.**  In every Cayley–Dickson algebra
`Re (x · ȳ) = ⟨x, y⟩`, the coordinate dot product. -/
/-- `Re (x̄ · y) = ⟨x, y⟩` in every Cayley–Dickson algebra. -/
/-- `Re (x x̄) = ‖x‖²` in every Cayley–Dickson algebra. -/
/-! ## Zero and the norm -/
/-- Over an ordered field, `‖x‖² = 0` iff `x = 0`. -/
/-! ## Norm multiplicativity on the first four levels -/
/-- **Octonion norm multiplicativity** `‖x y‖² = ‖x‖² ‖y‖²` (level `3`). -/
/-- The squared norm is multiplicative on the levels `n ≤ 3` of the tower. -/

/-- **No zero divisors below the sedenions.** Over an ordered field (e.g. `ℝ`), the
Cayley–Dickson algebras of levels `0,1,2,3` (reals, complexes, quaternions, octonions)
have no zero divisors. -/
/-! ## Sedenion zero divisors -/
/-- Build a sedenion from its 16 coordinates `x₀, …, x₁₅`. -/
/-- The 16 coordinates of a sedenion. -/
/-- Build an octonion from its 8 coordinates. -/
/-- `e₃ + e₁₀`, the left factor of the sedenion zero divisor. -/
/-- `e₆ − e₁₅`, the right factor of the sedenion zero divisor. -/

/-- **The first sedenion zero divisor.** `(e₃ + e₁₀)(e₆ − e₁₅) = 0` with both factors
nonzero, over any nontrivial commutative ring (in particular over `ℤ` and `ℝ`). -/
/-- The inclusion `x ↦ (x, 0)` of a level into the next one. -/
/-- The level-`n` Cayley–Dickson algebra has a pair of nonzero elements with product `0`. -/
/-- Zero divisors persist up the tower: every level `n ≥ 4` has zero divisors. -/

/-- **The sedenions are the first zero-divisor level.** Over an ordered field such as `ℝ`,
the level-`n` Cayley–Dickson algebra has zero divisors if and only if `n ≥ 4`. -/
/-! ## Associativity and alternativity along the tower -/
/-- The quaternions (level `2`) are associative. -/
/-- The octonions (level `3`) are left alternative: `[x, x, y] = 0`. -/
/-- The octonions are not associative: `[e₁, e₂, e₄] = 2 e₇`. -/

/-- The sedenions are not alternative: for `x = 1 + e₁ + e₁₀` and `y = e₄`,
`[x, x, y] = 2 e₁₅`. -/

# The 168 signed cross-half sedenion zero divisors in the descriptor convention

In the Cayley–Dickson convention of `StateOfThoughtCayleyDickson` (the one used for the
descriptor sedenion `S_{t,i}`), consider the `8 · 8 · 4 = 256` signed cross-half vectors
`±e_i ± e_{8+j}` (`0 ≤ i, j < 8`), one basis unit from each octonion half.

* `crossHalf_zd_census` : exactly `168 = 42 · 4` of them are annihilated by a signed
  two-term vector `e_k ± e_l`; this agrees with the count `168 = (16 − 2)(16 − 4)` of
  `Sovereign.zd_card_16` in the library's own convention;
* `crossHalf_zd_iff` : a signed cross-half vector is so annihilated exactly when
  `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0` and `i ≠ j` (for every choice of signs).

Both statements are finite computations, checked with `native_decide`.
-/
/-- The signed two-term sedenion `s₁ e_i + s₂ e_j`. -/
/-- The sign `+1` / `−1` encoded by a boolean. -/
/-- `x` is annihilated on the right by some signed two-term vector `e_k ± e_l`, `k < l`. -/
/-- The signed cross-half vector `±e_i ± e_{8+j}`. -/

/-- **168 cross-half zero divisors.** Exactly `168` of the `256` signed cross-half vectors
are annihilated by a signed two-term sedenion. -/
/-- The annihilated cross-half vectors are exactly those with `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j`. -/

/-- Consequently, whenever `i ≠ 0`, `j ≠ 0`, `i ≠ j`, the vector `±e_i ± e_{8+j}` is a

  | 0, u, v => by
    change ((show R from u) - (show R from v)) * ((show R from u) - (show R from v)) =

    rw [dot_sub_right n, dot_sub_right n]
    simp only [dot]; ring

/-

Released under Apache 2.0 license as described in the file LICENSE.

# The sedenion associator as an "inferential curvature" — what it can and cannot see

The request proposed the associator `[S_{t−2}, S_{t−1}, S_t] = (S_{t−2} S_{t−1}) S_t −
S_{t−2} (S_{t−1} S_t)` of consecutive descriptor sedenions as a measure of context curvature.
`StateOfThoughtSedenion.descriptor_associator_ne_zero` shows it can be nonzero.  This module
proves structural identities that bound what it can detect.

* `re_assoc_four` : the associator of any three sedenions is **purely imaginary**
  (`Re [x, y, z] = 0`), so it carries no real-part ("scalar") signal;
* `assoc_four_flexible` : the sedenions are **flexible**, `[x, y, x] = 0`;
* `assoc_four_self` : `[x, x, x] = 0`;
* `descriptor_curvature_return` : consequently the curvature of any **return trajectory**
  `S_{t−2} = S_t` (a two-step oscillation `A → B → A`) is exactly `0`, whatever the middle
  state is — the associator cannot detect period-2 reasoning loops.

## Curvature tensor and Ricci contraction

Write `curvature x y z = [x, y, z]` for the associator tensor and
`ricci x y = −⟨x, R(x, y, ȳ)⟩` for its Ricci-like contraction.

* `ricci_eq` : `Ric(x, y) = ‖x‖² ‖y‖² − ‖x y‖²` (from the adjoint identity
  `dot_mul_adjoint : ⟨x y, z⟩ = ⟨x, z ȳ⟩` and `y ȳ = ‖y‖²`);
* `nsq_mul_le_two_mul` : the sedenion `√2` bound `‖a b‖² ≤ 2 ‖a‖² ‖b‖²`;
* `abs_ricci_le` : `|Ric(x, y)| ≤ ‖x‖² ‖y‖²`; `ricci_eq_max_iff` : equality at the top
  holds exactly when `x y = 0`;
* `nsq_curvature_le` : `‖R(x, y, ȳ)‖² ≤ ‖x‖² ‖y‖⁴`.

## Vanishing on valid deductive chains

A *valid deductive chain* (`IsDeductiveChain`) is a trajectory whose states all lie in
`span {1, u}` for one inference direction `u`.

* `deductive_chain_curvature_vanishes` : `R(S_i, S_j, S_k) = 0` for all indices;
* `deductive_chain_ricci_vanishes`, `deductive_chain_nsq_mul` : the Ricci contraction
  vanishes, so the norm is multiplicative along the chain;
* `quaternionic_curvature_vanishes` : `R` also vanishes on the embedded quaternions.
-/

/-- **The associator is purely imaginary.** For all sedenions `x, y, z`,
`Re ((x y) z − x (y z)) = 0`. -/
/-- **Sedenions are flexible.** `[x, y, x] = (x y) x − x (y x) = 0`. -/
/-- `[x, x, x] = 0` for every sedenion. -/

/-- **Curvature of a return trajectory vanishes.** If the reasoning trajectory returns to its
starting descriptor (`S_{t−2} = S_t`), the associator curvature `[S_{t−2}, S_{t−1}, S_t]` is `0`
for every intermediate descriptor `S_{t−1}`. -/
/-! ## Curvature tensor, Ricci contraction and the `√2` bound -/
/-- The adjoint identity `⟨x y, z⟩ = ⟨x, z ȳ⟩` for sedenions. -/
/-- `y ȳ = ‖y‖²` for sedenions. -/
/-- `⟨u, x r⟩ = r ⟨u, x⟩` for a real scalar `r`. -/
/-- The associator curvature tensor `R(x, y, z) = [x, y, z]`. -/
/-- Ricci-like contraction `Ric(x, y) = −⟨x, R(x, y, ȳ)⟩`. -/
/-- **Ricci identity.** `Ric(x, y) = ‖x‖² ‖y‖² − ‖x y‖²`. -/
/-- **The `√2` bound.** `‖a b‖² ≤ 2 ‖a‖² ‖b‖²` for sedenions. -/
/-- **Two-sided Ricci bound.** `|Ric(x, y)| ≤ ‖x‖² ‖y‖²`. -/
/-- **Ricci curvature is maximal exactly at zero-divisor traps.** -/
/-- **Bound on the curvature tensor.** `‖R(x, y, ȳ)‖² ≤ ‖x‖² ‖y‖⁴`. -/
/-! ## Vanishing on valid deductive chains -/
/-- The associator vanishes on the subalgebra `span {1, u}` generated by one sedenion `u`. -/
/-- Conjugation preserves `span {1, u}`: `conj (a + b u) = (a + 2 b Re u) − b u`. -/
/-- `x` lies in the one-direction subalgebra `span {1, u}`: `x = a + b u`. -/

/-- **Valid deductive chain.** A trajectory of sedenion states that all lie in
`span {1, u}` for one fixed inference direction `u`: every state is `a_t + b_t u`. -/

/-- **The curvature tensor vanishes on valid deductive chains**, for every triple of
states `(S_i, S_j, S_k)` (in particular for consecutive states `S_{t−2}, S_{t−1}, S_t`). -/
/-- The Ricci contraction also vanishes on valid deductive chains. -/
/-- Along a valid deductive chain the norm is multiplicative: `‖S_i S_j‖² = ‖S_i‖² ‖S_j‖²`. -/
/-- A sedenion in the embedded quaternion subalgebra `ℍ ⊂ 𝕆 ⊂ 𝕊`. -/

/-- **The curvature tensor vanishes on quaternionic chains**: any three states in the
embedded quaternion subalgebra have zero associator. -/

comments.text: /-! ## 1. Sentence center and geometric dispersion -/
/-- Sentence center `u_t = (1/n) ∑ᵢ h_{t,i}` of the final-layer token embeddings. -/
/-- Geometric dispersion `δ_t = (1/n) ∑ᵢ ‖h_{t,i}‖² − ‖u_t‖²`. -/
/-- **Dispersion is a variance.** `δ_t = (1/n) ∑ᵢ ‖h_{t,i} − u_t‖²`. -/
/-- The geometric dispersion is nonnegative. -/
/-- The dispersion vanishes iff every token embedding equals the sentence center. -/
/-! ## 2. Step velocity and directional consistency -/
/-- Step velocity `v_t = ‖u_t − u_{t−1}‖`. -/

/-- Directional consistency
`c_t = ⟨u_t − u_{t−1}, u_{t−1} − u_{t−2}⟩ / (‖u_t − u_{t−1}‖ ‖u_{t−1} − u_{t−2}‖ + ε)`. -/
/-- For `ε > 0` the directional consistency lies strictly between `−1` and `1`. -/
/-- Consecutive steps pointing in the same direction give positive consistency. -/
/-! ## 3. Predictive entropy -/
/-- Shannon entropy `𝓗(p) = −∑ₖ pₖ log pₖ` of a next-token distribution. -/
/-- Mean predictive entropy `H_t = (1/n) ∑ᵢ 𝓗(p_{t,i})` over the tokens of a sentence. -/
/-- The mean predictive entropy of probability vectors is nonnegative. -/
/-! ## 4. The 4-dimensional state and its normalisation -/
/-- The raw endogenous state `s_t = (δ_t, v_t, c_t, H_t) ∈ ℝ⁴`. -/
/-- Normalisation `m_t = (s_t − μ) / (σ + ε)`, coordinatewise. -/
/-- Undo the normalisation. -/
/-- With nonnegative scales and `ε > 0` the normalisation is injective. -/
/-- The normalised state vanishes exactly at the normalisation center `μ`. -/
/-! ## 5. The 16-dimensional relational descriptor -/

/-- The relational descriptor `d_{t,i} = [m_t; m_i; m_t − m_i; m_t ⊙ m_i] ∈ ℝ¹⁶`
(coordinates `4b + k` hold block `b`, entry `k`). -/
/-- Block `b` of a 16-vector (`b = 0,1,2,3`). -/
/-- The descriptor determines the pair of states `(m_t, m_i)`. -/
/-- Comparing a state with itself: zero drift, and squared coordinates as interaction. -/
/-! ## 6. The controller heads -/
/-- Number of parameters of a dense layer `Linear(i → o)` (weights and biases). -/
/-- Evidence-selection head `φ_sel = Linear(16 → 32) ∘ Linear(32 → 1)`. -/
/-- Stopping head `φ_stop = Linear(4 → 1)`. -/

/-- **Parameter budget.** `Linear(16→32)` has `544` parameters and `Linear(32→1)` has `33`,
so `φ_sel` has `577`; `φ_stop` has `5`; the controller has `582` parameters in all. -/
/-- The logistic sigmoid. -/
/-- Stopping probability `σ(⟨w, m_t⟩ + b)` of the stopping head. -/

/-- **The stopping head is a linear threshold rule.** For `0 < τ < 1`,
`σ(⟨w, m⟩ + b) > τ ↔ ⟨w, m⟩ + b > log (τ / (1 − τ))`. -/
/-! ## 7. The training-free baseline -/
/-- Euclidean norm on `ℝ⁴`. -/

/-- Training-free score
`s^tf_{t,j} = α₁⟨m_t, m_j⟩ − α₂‖m_t − m_j‖ + α₃ c_j − α₄ H_j`. -/

/-- The training-free score is a fixed function of the descriptor: `⟨m_t, m_j⟩` is the sum
of the interaction block and `‖m_t − m_j‖` is the norm of the drift block. -/

/-- With nonnegative weights the training-free score increases with the consistency `c_j`
and decreases with the entropy `H_j`. -/

/-- Training-free stopping rule at step `t`: over the trailing window of the last `r` steps
the entropy and the velocity stay below their thresholds and the consistency is positive. -/
/-- Satisfying the stopping rule on a longer window implies it on a shorter one. -/

# Sedenion left multiplication as a matrix, and invertibility certificates

Left multiplication `y ↦ x · y` by a sedenion `x` is linear in `y`.  This module writes it as
an explicit `16 × 16` matrix `lmat` (entry `(i, j)` is `± x_{i ⊕ j}`, with the sign table of
the Cayley–Dickson convention of `StateOfThoughtCayleyDickson`), and provides a checkable
certificate that a rational sedenion is **not** a zero divisor over `ℝ`:

* `coord16_mul_eq` : `(x y)_i = ∑_j lmat x i j · y_j`, over any commutative ring;
* `certCheck` : an executable test that an untrusted Gauss–Jordan inverse of a rational
  matrix really is a left inverse (only the check is trusted, never the elimination);
* `eq_zero_of_certCheck` : if the certificate for `lmat f` passes, then the real sedenion
  with rational coordinates `f` has no nonzero right annihilator: `x y = 0 → y = 0`.
-/
/-! ## The sign table -/
/-- Sign table in vector form: `e_{i ⊕ j} · e_j = sgnTabV i j · e_i`. -/
/-- Array form of the sign table (fast to evaluate). -/
/-- Sign table: `e_{i ⊕ j} · e_j = sgnTab i j · e_i`. -/

/-- Left-multiplication matrix of the sedenion with coordinates `f`:
`lmat f i j = sgnTab i j · f (i ⊕ j)`. -/
/-- **Left multiplication is the matrix `lmat`.** `(x y)_i = ∑_j lmat x i j · y_j`. -/
/-! ## Invertibility certificates over `ℚ` -/
/-- Entry `(r, c)` of an array matrix (`0` out of range). -/
/-- Materialise a `16 × 16` matrix as an array. -/
/-- Gauss–Jordan inversion over `ℚ` (untrusted: only its output is checked). -/
/-- The candidate inverse read off the right half of the reduced augmented matrix. -/
/-- `A` is a left inverse of `M`. -/
/-- Executable left-inverse check on arrays. -/
/-- Certificate that the matrix `M` is invertible over `ℚ`. -/
/-! ## Transfer to `ℝ` -/

/-- **Certified non-zero-divisors.** If the certificate for the rational matrix `lmat f`
passes, the real sedenion with coordinates `f` has no nonzero right annihilator. -/

/-
Copyright (c) 2024-2026 Sovereign Engine Project. All rights reserved.
Released under Apache 2.0 license as described in the file LICENSE.

# The relational descriptor as a sedenion

The 16-dimensional relational descriptor `d_{t,i} = [m_t; m_i; m_t − m_i; m_t ⊙ m_i]` of the
*State of Thought* controller (`StateOfThoughtFeatures`) is read as a sedenion
`S_{t,i} = (q₀, q₁, q₂, q₃) ∈ ℍ⁴ ≅ 𝕆 ⊕ 𝕆 ≅ 𝕊` with `q₀ = m_t`, `q₁ = m_i`,
`q₂ = m_t − m_i`, `q₃ = m_t ⊙ m_i`, in the Cayley–Dickson tower of
`StateOfThoughtCayleyDickson`.  This module tests the proposed sedenionic invariants.

Main results:

* `sedenion_score_eq_inner`, `sedenion_score_blocks` : the proposed parameter-free
  compatibility score `Re (S_{t,i} · S̄_{j,k})` is *exactly* the Euclidean dot product of the
  two descriptors, i.e. the sum of the four quaternion-block dot products — the
  non-associative multiplication contributes nothing to it;
* `sedenion_score_comm`, `sedenion_self_score_eq_zero_iff` : the score is symmetric, and
  the self-score `‖d_{t,i}‖²` vanishes only for `m_t = m_i = 0`;
* `descriptor_zero_divisor` : **descriptor zero-divisor traps exist.**  Whenever the current
  state is at the normalisation center (`m_t = 0`) and the historical state is a nonzero
  pure-imaginary quaternion (`m_i = (0, a, b, c) ≠ 0`, i.e. average dispersion), the
  descriptor sedenion is a zero divisor: an explicit nonzero sedenion annihilates it;
* `normalized_descriptor_zero_divisor` : the same statement phrased on the raw states:
  current state `s_t = μ`, historical state `s_i ≠ μ` with the same dispersion as `μ`;
* `descriptor_associator_ne_zero` : the associator of three descriptor sedenions along a
  trajectory can be nonzero (explicit value `4 e₂`).
-/
/-- The descriptor `d_{t,i}` viewed as a sedenion `(m_t, m_i, m_t − m_i, m_t ⊙ m_i) ∈ ℍ⁴`. -/
/-- The sedenion dot product in coordinates. -/

/-- **The sedenionic compatibility score is the descriptor dot product.**
`Re (S_{t,i} · S̄_{j,k}) = ⟨d_{t,i}, d_{j,k}⟩`. -/

/-- The sedenionic score splits into the four quaternion-block dot products:
state, history, drift and interaction. -/
/-- The sedenionic score is symmetric. -/

/-- The self-score is the squared norm of the descriptor, and it vanishes only when both
states are zero. -/
/-! ## Zero-divisor traps realised by descriptors -/
/-- Annihilator `c e₁ − a e₃ − c e₁₃ + a e₁₅`. -/
/-- Annihilator `b e₁ − a e₂ − b e₁₃ + a e₁₄`. -/

/-- **Descriptor zero-divisor traps.** If the current normalised state is `m_t = 0` and the
historical state is a nonzero pure-imaginary quaternion `m_i = (0, a, b, c)`, then the
descriptor sedenion `S_{t,i}` is nonzero and is annihilated by a nonzero sedenion:
`S_{t,i} · Y = 0`. -/

/-- **Zero-divisor traps on the raw states.** Suppose the current raw state equals the
normalisation center, `s_t = μ`, and the historical raw state `s_i ≠ μ` has the same
dispersion coordinate as `μ`.  Then the descriptor sedenion built from the normalised states
`m_t, m_i` is a nonzero sedenion zero divisor. -/
/-! ## Inferential curvature: the associator along a trajectory -/

/-- Along the trajectory `m_{t−2} = (1,1,0,0)`, `m_{t−1} = (1,0,0,0)`, `m_t = (0,0,0,1)`,
compared with the reference history `m_i = 0`, the associator of the three descriptor
sedenions is `[S_{t−2}, S_{t−1}, S_t] = 4 e₂ ≠ 0`. -/

declarations.name: pick
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def pick (defect : α → β) (ok : α → Prop) [DecidablePred ok] : List α → α → α
  | [], best => best
  | c :: cs, best => pick defect ok cs (if ok c ∧ defect c < defect best then c else best)

/-- One filtered step from `cur` given the candidate list `cands`. -/

declarations.name: select
declarations.signature_heuristic:
def select (defect : α → β) (ok : α → α → Prop) [∀ a, DecidablePred (ok a)] (cur : α)
    (cands : List α) : α

declarations.name: pick_le
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem pick_le : ∀ (cs : List α) (best : α), defect (pick defect ok cs best) ≤ defect best
  | [], _ => le_rfl
  | c :: cs, best => by
    simp only [pick]
    refine (pick_le cs _).trans ?_
    split_ifs with h
    · exact h.2.le
    · exact le_rfl

declarations.name: pick_spec
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem pick_spec : ∀ (cs : List α) (best : α),
    pick defect ok cs best = best ∨
      (pick defect ok cs best ∈ cs ∧ ok (pick defect ok cs best) ∧
        defect (pick defect ok cs best) < defect best)
  | [], _ => Or.inl rfl
  | c :: cs, best => by
    simp only [pick]
    split_ifs with h
    · rcases pick_spec cs c with h' | h'
      · exact Or.inr ⟨by simp [h'], by rw [h']; exact h.1, by rw [h']; exact h.2⟩
      · exact Or.inr ⟨List.mem_cons_of_mem _ h'.1, h'.2.1, h'.2.2.trans h.2⟩
    · rcases pick_spec cs best with h' | h'
      · exact Or.inl h'
      · exact Or.inr ⟨List.mem_cons_of_mem _ h'.1, h'.2⟩

declarations.name: pick_optimal
declarations.signature_heuristic:
theorem pick_optimal : ∀ (cs : List α) (best : α) (c : α), c ∈ cs → ok c →
    defect (pick defect ok cs best) ≤ defect c
  | [], _, _, h, _ => absurd h (List.not_mem_nil)
  | d :: cs, best, c, hc, hok => by
    simp only [pick]
    rcases List.mem_cons.1 hc with rfl | hc
    · refine (pick_le defect ok cs _).trans ?_
      split_ifs with h
      · exact le_rfl
      · push_neg at h
        exact h hok
    · exact pick_optimal cs _ c hc hok

end Pick

# A verified step-selection filter with monotone semantic defect

A reasoning controller proposes, at every step, a finite list of candidate next states.
The filter below keeps a candidate only if it passes a guard and **strictly lowers** the
semantic defect; among the kept candidates it takes one of least defect, and if none is kept
it stays put.

Generic results (any state type, any linearly ordered defect):

* `select_defect_le`, `select_optimal`, `select_lt` : one step never increases the defect,
  is optimal among admissible candidates, and strictly decreases the defect whenever some
  admissible candidate improves on the current state;
* `select_spec` : the selected state is either the current state or a guarded candidate;
* `run_defect_antitone` : along the filtered run the defect is **monotonically
  non-increasing**; `run_move_lt` : every actual move strictly decreases it;
* `run_stabilizes` : for a `ℕ`-valued defect, the run is constant from step `D(s₀)` on.

Sedenion instance (`Window` = the last three descriptor sedenions `(S_{t−2}, S_{t−1}, S_t)`,
semantic defect = `‖[S_{t−2}, S_{t−1}, S_t]‖²`, guard = the new step pair `S_t · S_{t+1}` is not a
zero-divisor trap):

* `sedenionRun_defect_antitone` : the curvature defect is monotone non-increasing;
* `sedenionRun_avoids_traps` : every accepted step avoids a zero-divisor trap;
* `sedenionRun_flat_of_flat` : a run started on a flat window (e.g. three states of a valid
  deductive chain) stays flat forever: the curvature tensor is `0` at every step.
-/

/-- Scan candidates, replacing the incumbent by a candidate that passes the guard `ok` and has
strictly smaller defect. -/
/-- One filtered step from `cur` given the candidate list `cands`. -/
/-- A filtered step never increases the defect. -/

/-- The selected state is the current state, or a guarded candidate of strictly smaller
defect. -/

/-- The selected state is at least as good as every guarded candidate that does not increase
the defect. -/

/-- If some guarded candidate strictly improves on the current state, the step strictly
decreases the defect. -/

/-- The filtered run: at each step the candidates `proposals s` are filtered from the current
state `s`. -/
/-- **Monotone reduction of the defect along the filtered run.** -/
/-- Every step either stays put or moves to a guarded proposal of strictly smaller defect. -/
/-- Every actual move strictly decreases the defect. -/
/-- Once the run stays put, it stays put forever. -/

/-- **Stabilization.** For a natural-number defect `D`, the filtered run is constant from step
`D(s₀)` on. -/
/-! ## The sedenion curvature filter -/
/-- A reasoning window: the last three sedenion states `(S_{t−2}, S_{t−1}, S_t)`. -/

/-- **Semantic defect** of a window: the squared norm of its associator curvature
`‖[S_{t−2}, S_{t−1}, S_t]‖²`. -/
/-- Shift a window by a new state `v`: `(x, y, z) ↦ (y, z, v)`. -/
/-- The trap guard: the new step pair `(S_t, S_{t+1})` must not be annihilating. -/

/-- The sedenion curvature filter: from each window, the proposed next states are pushed and
filtered by `select` with the semantic defect and the trap guard. -/
/-- **Monotone reduction of the semantic defect** along the sedenion filter. -/

/-- Every step of the sedenion filter stays put, or appends a proposed state `v` such that
the new step pair is **not** a zero-divisor trap and the semantic defect strictly drops. -/

/-- **Flatness is preserved.** If the initial window has zero curvature, every window of the
filtered run has zero curvature tensor. -/
/-- A run started on three states of a valid deductive chain stays flat forever. -/

/-

# Sedenion zero divisors are Stiefel pairs

This module finishes item 1.1 of `docs/STATE_OF_THOUGHT_ROADMAP.md`: the complete description
of the (left) zero divisors of the sedenions `𝕊 = 𝕆 ⊕ 𝕆`, and its specialisation to the
State of Thought descriptor sedenion `S_{t,i}`.

Write a sedenion as a pair `x = (a, b)` of octonions.

* `re_fst_mul_nsq`, `re_snd_mul_nsq`, `dot_mul_nsq` : polynomial identities (over any
  commutative ring) saying that `x y = 0` forces `Re a · ‖y‖² = 0`, `Re b · ‖y‖² = 0` and,
  once `Re a = Re b = 0`, `⟨a, b⟩ · ‖y‖² = 0`;
* `stiefelAnnihilator`, `stiefelAnnihilator_mul` : conversely, if `a, b` are purely imaginary,
  orthogonal and of equal norm, then for every `c` orthogonal to `1, a, b, a b` the sedenion
  `y = (‖b‖² c, (a c) b)` satisfies `x y = 0` (over any commutative ring);
* `sedenion_zero_divisor_iff` : over any ordered field, a nonzero `x = (a, b)` has a nonzero
  right annihilator **iff** `Re a = Re b = 0`, `‖a‖ = ‖b‖` and `⟨a, b⟩ = 0`;
* `unit_sedenion_zero_divisor_iff_stiefel` : for `‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = 1` this says exactly that
  `(a, b)` is an orthonormal 2-frame of imaginary octonions, i.e. a point of the Stiefel
  manifold `V₂(ℝ⁷)`;
* `descriptor_trap_iff` : the descriptor sedenion `S_{t,i}` has a nonzero right annihilator
  iff `m_t 0 = m_i 0 = 0`, `2 ⟨m_t, m_i⟩ = ‖m_t ⊙ m_i‖²` and
  `⟨m_t, m_t − m_i⟩ + ⟨m_i, m_t ⊙ m_i⟩ = 0`.

The polynomial identities were found by solving linear systems for the certificate
coefficients offline; Lean checks each certificate with `linear_combination`.
-/
/-- A sedenion all of whose 16 coordinates vanish is zero. -/

/-- **`Re a · ‖y‖² = 0` on annihilating pairs.** If `(a, b) y = 0` then `Re a · ‖y‖² = 0`.
(In fact `Re a · ‖y‖² = ⟨x y, y⟩`.) -/
/-- **`Re b · ‖y‖² = 0` on annihilating pairs.** -/

# The annihilator of a sedenion zero divisor

For a Stiefel pair `x = (a, b)` (imaginary octonions, `‖a‖ = ‖b‖ ≠ 0`, `a ⊥ b`) this module
determines the whole right annihilator `{y | x y = 0}`:

* `stiefelKernel_*` : polynomial certificates (over any commutative ring) showing that
  `x (c, d) = 0` forces `2 ‖b‖² ⟨c, u⟩ = 0` for `u = 1, a, b, a b`, and `‖b‖² d = (a c) b`;
* `annihilator_eq_stiefel` : over any field of characteristic zero, `x y = 0` iff `y = (‖b‖² c, (a c) b)` for some
  `c` orthogonal to `1, a, b, a b`.

So the annihilator is the image of the 4-dimensional space `{1, a, b, a b}^⊥` under an
injective linear map; every annihilator is of the form produced by `stiefelAnnihilator`.
-/
/-- Two octonions with equal coordinates are equal. -/
/-- `‖b‖² d = (a c) b` for every annihilator `(c, d)` of a Stiefel pair `(a, b)`. -/

/-- **The annihilator of a sedenion zero divisor.** Let `a, b` be imaginary octonions with
`‖a‖ = ‖b‖ ≠ 0` and `a ⊥ b`. Then `(a, b) y = 0` holds exactly for the sedenions
`y = (‖b‖² c, (a c) b)` with `c` orthogonal to `1, a, b` and `a b`. -/

# The windowed stopping rule as a counter automaton

Roadmap item 2.2 of `docs/STATE_OF_THOUGHT_ROADMAP.md`. The training-free stopping rule
`tfStop` of the appendix fires at step `t` when over the last `r` steps the entropy and the
velocity stay below their thresholds and the consistency is positive.

* `tfStop_mono_threshold` : the rule is monotone in both thresholds;
* `runLen` : a one-counter automaton reading the feature stream (length of the current run of
  "good" steps);
* `tfStop_iff_runLen` : the rule fires at `t` iff `min r (t + 1) ≤ runLen t`, so it can be
  evaluated online with a single counter instead of a window buffer;
* `tfStop_of_good_from` : if the conditions hold at every step from `t₀` on, the rule fires
  at step `t₀ + r − 1`, i.e. within `r − 1` steps (bounded latency);
* `tfStop_not_of_bad` : conversely it never fires while the current step is bad.
-/
/-- The stopping rule is monotone in the thresholds. -/

/-- A step is *good* when entropy and velocity are below threshold and consistency is
positive. -/
/-- The counter automaton: `runLen t` is the length of the run of good steps ending at `t`. -/
/-- `runLen t ≥ k` iff the last `k` steps up to `t` are all good (for `k ≤ t + 1`). -/

/-- **The stopping rule is a counter automaton.** `tfStop` fires at `t` exactly when the
counter `runLen t` has reached `min r (t + 1)`. -/

/-- **Bounded latency.** If the stopping conditions hold at every step from `t₀` on, then the
rule fires at step `t₀ + r − 1` (for `r ≥ 1`). -/
/-- The rule never fires (for `r ≥ 1`) at a step where the conditions fail. -/

# Which descriptors are sedenion zero-divisor traps?

`StateOfThoughtSedenion` showed that the descriptor sedenion
`S_{t,i} = (m_t, m_i, m_t − m_i, m_t ⊙ m_i)` is a zero divisor when `m_t = 0` and `m_i` is
pure imaginary.  This module sharpens that picture.

* `sedenion_zero_divisor_balanced` : in **any** sedenion zero-divisor pair `x y = 0`
  (`x, y ≠ 0`), both octonion halves of `x` have the same norm, and likewise for `y`
  (over any ordered field; the proof uses octonion norm multiplicativity);
* `descriptor_trap_balance` : hence a descriptor trap must satisfy the scalar identity
  `2 ⟨m_t, m_i⟩ = ‖m_t ⊙ m_i‖²` — most state pairs are ruled out at once;
* `offcenter_trap₁`, `offcenter_trap₂` : traps are **not** confined to `m_t = 0`: the pairs
  `m_t = (0,−2,0,0), m_i = (0,−1,0,0)` and `m_t = (0,−1,1,2), m_i = (0,−2,0,0)` are
  annihilated by explicit nonzero sedenions;
* `grid_trap_iff` : on the grid `m_t, m_i ∈ {−1, 0, 1}⁴` (6561 state pairs) the traps are
  **exactly** the pairs with `m_t = 0` and `m_i` pure imaginary.  The 662 grid pairs that pass
  the balance test are excluded by machine-checked invertibility certificates for their
  left-multiplication matrices (`StateOfThoughtLeftMul`).

## Curvature at singular traps

* `ricci_max_iff_singular_trap`, `normalized_ricci_max_iff` : for nonzero `x, y` the Ricci
  contraction of the associator satisfies `Ric(x, y) ≤ ‖x‖² ‖y‖²` (normalised: lies in
  `[−1, 1]`), with equality **if and only if** `(x, y)` is a zero-divisor singular trap;
* `curvature_max_at_trap`, `curvature_norm_le_with_equality_at_traps` : the tensor norm
  `‖R(x, y, ȳ)‖²` is at most `‖x‖² ‖y‖⁴` and reaches that bound at every trap;
* `curvature_max_not_only_at_traps` : but the tensor-norm bound is also reached off traps
  (`x = e₁₄ + e₁₅`, `y = e₁ + e₁₀`), so "maximal tensor norm" alone does not characterise traps;
* `descriptor_trap_ricci_max` : the descriptor traps of `StateOfThoughtSedenion` are
  Ricci-maximal.
-/

/-- Nonnegative `A, B, C, D` with `AC = DB`, `DA = BC`, `(A,B) ≠ 0`, `(C,D) ≠ 0`
force `A = B` and `C = D`. -/

/-- **Sedenion zero divisors are balanced.** If `x = (a, b)` and `y = (c, d)` are nonzero
sedenions (written as pairs of octonions) with `x y = 0`, then `‖a‖ = ‖b‖` and `‖c‖ = ‖d‖`. -/

/-- **Necessary condition for a descriptor trap.** If the descriptor sedenion `S_{t,i}` is
annihilated by a nonzero sedenion, then `2 ⟨m_t, m_i⟩ = ‖m_t ⊙ m_i‖²`. -/

# The sedenion zero-divisor theorem and descriptor traps

Using the certificates of `StateOfThoughtStiefel`, this module proves the full description
of the sedenion zero divisors over any ordered field, and specialises it to the State of
Thought descriptor sedenion `S_{t,i} = (m_t, m_i, m_t − m_i, m_t ⊙ m_i)`.

* `sedenion_zero_divisor_iff` : a nonzero sedenion `x = (a, b)` (pair of octonions) has a
  nonzero right annihilator iff `Re a = Re b = 0`, `‖a‖ = ‖b‖` and `⟨a, b⟩ = 0`;
* `unit_sedenion_zero_divisor_iff_stiefel` : with `‖a‖ = ‖b‖ = 1`, `(a, b)` is a zero
  divisor iff `(a, b)` is an orthonormal pair of imaginary octonions (a point of `V₂(ℝ⁷)`);
* `descriptor_trap_iff` : `S_{t,i}` has a nonzero right annihilator iff
  `m_t 0 = 0`, `m_i 0 = 0`, `2 ⟨m_t, m_i⟩ = ‖m_t ⊙ m_i‖²` and
  `⟨m_t, m_t − m_i⟩ + ⟨m_i, m_t ⊙ m_i⟩ = 0`;
* `offcenter_trap_family` : the family
  `m_t = (0, p, q, r)`, `m_i = (0, 2/p, 0, 0)`, `p² + q² + r² + 4/p = 2` consists of traps.
-/
/-- The 8 coordinates of an octonion. -/
/-- Every three octonions admit a nonzero imaginary octonion orthogonal to all of them. -/

/-- **The sedenion zero-divisor theorem.** Over any ordered field, a nonzero sedenion
`x = (a, b)` has a nonzero right annihilator if and only if its octonion halves are purely
imaginary, of equal norm and orthogonal. -/

/-- **Normalised zero divisors form the Stiefel manifold `V₂(ℝ⁷)`.** If both octonion halves
of `x = (a, b)` have unit norm, then `x` is a zero divisor iff `(a, b)` is an orthonormal pair
of imaginary octonions. -/

/-- **Exact description of descriptor traps.** The descriptor sedenion
`S_{t,i} = (m_t, m_i, m_t − m_i, m_t ⊙ m_i)` has a nonzero right annihilator iff the
dispersion coordinates of both states vanish, `2 ⟨m_t, m_i⟩ = ‖m_t ⊙ m_i‖²`, and
`⟨m_t, m_t − m_i⟩ + ⟨m_i, m_t ⊙ m_i⟩ = 0`. -/

/-- **The off-center trap family.** For `p ≠ 0` with `p² + q² + r² + 4/p = 2`, the states
`m_t = (0, p, q, r)`, `m_i = (0, 2/p, 0, 0)` give a descriptor trap. (`offcenter_trap₁` and
`offcenter_trap₂` are the members `(p,q,r) = (−2,0,0)` and `(−1,1,2)`.) -/
